Defect-engineered topological qubits

Part I — Quantum mechanics from zero

Two chapters. One atom, then two. By the end you can predict a magnet experiment and say what is lost when you ignore half a pair.

Chapter 1 — A magnet that refuses to smear

A silver atom flies through a lopsided magnet and comes out in one of two places. That is already strange. A tiny compass needle in a crooked field should spray into a smear, not pick two spots and ignore the middle.

In 1922, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach saw the two spots. We need the smallest set of rules that predict the split, and then the second magnet, turned on its side.

No crystal yet. No computer. One atom, two answers, and the arithmetic that makes the second magnet surprising.

Two numbers that may cancel

Classically you would give each outcome a probability: a pair of nonnegative numbers that add to one. Quantum mechanics does something ruder. It first assigns each outcome a complex number, and turns those numbers into probabilities only at the last second.

A complex number looks like

\[ z = a + ib, \]

where \(a\) and \(b\) are ordinary real numbers and \(i^2 = -1\). Its partner is \(z^* = a - ib\). The useful real quantity hiding inside is

\[ |z|^2 = z^* z = a^2 + b^2. \]

That last thing cannot be negative. It is allowed to become a probability.

The complex number itself is not: it can be negative, or point somewhere in the plane, and two of them can add to zero before anyone squares anything. That last trick is interference.

It is why the second magnet will not behave like a polite coin.

Call the two amplitudes \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Stack them:

\[ |\psi\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{pmatrix}. \]

The funny brackets are a ket, pronounced “ket psi”: a column of numbers. The decoration is a name tag, so we can later tell a state from a measurement question.

Those two numbers are not free. The atom has to land somewhere, so

\[ |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1. \]

A state, in this chapter, is such a column, up to an overall complex factor of magnitude one. Quantum mechanics is peculiar. It still declines overdrafts.

Up, down, and both

Give the two spots names. “Along the magnet, up” and “along the magnet, down”:

\[ |z+\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad |z-\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Then the same atom is

\[ |\psi\rangle = \alpha |z+\rangle + \beta |z-\rangle. \]

This is a superposition in the \(z\) basis. It does not say a tiny classical arrow is secretly pointing both ways. It says: if you ask the \(z\) question, these are the two complex ingredients of the answer.

To ask a question you need the opposite of a ket. Flip the column over and conjugate every entry. That row is a bra:

\[ \langle\psi| = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^* & \beta^* \end{pmatrix}. \]

Feed a ket to a bra and you get one complex number, the inner product \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\). For our atom,

\[ \langle\psi|\psi\rangle = |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1. \]

The space of all such columns, with this way of multiplying them, is what physicists later call a Hilbert space. You do not need that name to finish the chapter. You need the habit: add the columns, scale them by complex numbers, and compare them with an inner product.

Why a second magnet forgets the first

Idealize each Stern–Gerlach magnet as a fork with two exits. Keep one exit, block the other. That prepares the corresponding state.

A magnet turned on its side asks a different question. Call those exits \(x+\) and \(x-\), and define

\[ |x+\rangle = \frac{|z+\rangle + |z-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad |x-\rangle = \frac{|z+\rangle - |z-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

The minus sign is doing real work. The two new states are orthogonal:

\[ \langle x+|x-\rangle = \frac12 \bigl(\langle z+| + \langle z-|\bigr) \bigl(|z+\rangle - |z-\rangle\bigr) = \frac12(1-1) = 0. \]

Step 1. Send a mess of atoms through a \(z\) magnet. Block \(z-\). Keep \(z+\). Every surviving atom is now

\[ |\psi_1\rangle = |z+\rangle. \]

A second \(z\) magnet would send all of them up again. Amplitude \(1\), probability \(1\).

Step 2. Turn the next magnet on its side and keep only \(x+\). The amplitude is

\[ \langle x+|z+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \bigl(\langle z+| + \langle z-|\bigr)|z+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

So

\[ P(x+\mid z+) = \Bigl|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigr|^2 = \frac12. \]

About half the atoms survive. Each survivor is no longer \(z+\). It is

\[ |\psi_2\rangle = |x+\rangle = \frac{|z+\rangle + |z-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

Hence “chance the filter lets you through” and “state of the atom that made it” are different objects. The survivor is freshly normalized.

Step 3. Ask \(z\) again.

\[ \langle z+|x+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad \langle z-|x+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \]

so

\[ P(z+\mid x+) = P(z-\mid x+) = \frac12. \]

The sideways magnet erased the certainty we paid for in step 1. It did not peek at a hidden \(x\) label while leaving the \(z\) label untouched. In this ideal model, asking one question prepares an answer to that question, which is generally a mixture of answers to a different question.

For 100 atoms already in \(z+\), you expect about 50 through the \(x+\) door and then about 25 in each final \(z\) bucket. Small runs wobble. The conditional probabilities are still one half and one half.

Phase you can ignore, phase you cannot

If you multiply the whole ket by \(e^{i\gamma}\), every probability stays put:

\[ \bigl|\langle a|e^{i\gamma}\psi\rangle\bigr|^2 = |e^{i\gamma}|^2 \,\bigl|\langle a|\psi\rangle\bigr|^2 = \bigl|\langle a|\psi\rangle\bigr|^2. \]

So \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(e^{i\gamma}|\psi\rangle\) are the same physical state. People call this a ray. Remember the fact: an overall twist is invisible.

A relative twist is not. The two states

\[ \frac{|z+\rangle + |z-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} = |x+\rangle, \qquad \frac{|z+\rangle - |z-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}} = |x-\rangle \]

give the same \(z\) odds and opposite \(x\) answers. Drop the distinction between overall and relative phase, and the second magnet becomes inexplicable.

From amplitude to count

Let \(\{|a_j\rangle\}\) be a complete list of mutually exclusive answers: each pair is orthogonal, and there is nowhere else to go. The Born rule says the probability of answer \(j\) is

\[ P(j) = \bigl|\langle a_j|\psi\rangle\bigr|^2. \]

Born wrote the probability reading of the wavefunction in 1926. The modern packaging uses a projector

\[ \Pi_j = |a_j\rangle\langle a_j|. \]

Then

\[ P(j) = \langle\psi|\Pi_j|\psi\rangle. \]

These projectors are idempotent, Hermitian, and they add up to the identity:

\[ \sum_j \Pi_j = I. \]

That last line is why the probabilities add to one. If you actually see a unique answer \(j\), the ideal leftover state is \(|a_j\rangle\), or more generally the normalized projection

\[ |\psi_j\rangle = \frac{\Pi_j|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{\langle\psi|\Pi_j|\psi\rangle}}. \]

If you ignore which answer occurred, a single ket is no longer enough. That is the next chapter’s problem.

Asking a question with a matrix

An operator is a linear machine that eats a ket and returns a ket:

\[ A\bigl(c_1|u\rangle + c_2|v\rangle\bigr) = c_1 A|u\rangle + c_2 A|v\rangle. \]

In a finite list of basis states it is just a matrix. Flip it and conjugate the entries and you have the adjoint \(A^\dagger\). If

\[ A = A^\dagger, \]

the matrix is Hermitian. Ideal measurable quantities are Hermitian. Their possible readings — the eigenvalues — are real, and answers that belong to different readings are orthogonal. An eigenstate obeys

\[ A|a_j\rangle = a_j |a_j\rangle. \]

For our two-state atom,

\[ \sigma_z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Both are Hermitian. Direct multiplication gives

\[ \sigma_z |z\pm\rangle = \pm |z\pm\rangle, \qquad \sigma_x |x\pm\rangle = \pm |x\pm\rangle. \]

These Pauli matrices are dimensionless. For an ideal spin-\(1/2\), the actual angular-momentum pieces are

\[ S_z = \frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_z, \qquad S_x = \frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_x, \]

so an \(S_z\) measurement returns \(+\hbar/2\) or \(-\hbar/2\), in joule-seconds. Our labels \(z+\) and \(z-\) are just those two eigenstates.

The two matrices do not commute:

\[ [\sigma_z,\sigma_x] \equiv \sigma_z\sigma_x - \sigma_x\sigma_z \ne 0. \]

That is the compact reason they cannot share a full set of answers. The three-magnet sequence was the same fact wearing a lab coat.

Drop commutativity and you may imagine a hidden pair of labels, one for \(z\) and one for \(x\). Keep it, and that picture is already false.

The expectation value of \(A\) in \(|\psi\rangle\) is

\[ \langle A\rangle_\psi = \langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle = \sum_j a_j P(j). \]

It is the average over many identically prepared runs. It need not be a possible single-shot reading.

For \(|x+\rangle\), a \(\sigma_z\) measurement returns \(+1\) and \(-1\) equally often, so the average is \(0\). Zero is not on the menu.

If \(q = \langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle\) and \(A = A^\dagger\), then \(q^* = q\). Hermitian averages are real because they have nowhere complex to hide.

What happens between questions

Between measurements, an isolated system evolves in a way that never stretches or shrinks inner products. That kind of evolution is a unitary matrix \(U\):

\[ U^\dagger U = U U^\dagger = I. \]

If \(|\psi'\rangle = U|\psi\rangle\), then

\[ \langle\psi'|\psi'\rangle = \langle\psi|U^\dagger U|\psi\rangle = \langle\psi|\psi\rangle. \]

The generator of that motion is the energy operator, the Hamiltonian \(H\). Schrödinger’s equation is

\[ i\hbar \frac{d}{dt}|\psi(t)\rangle = H|\psi(t)\rangle. \]

Time \(t\) is in seconds. \(\hbar\) is in joule-seconds. The units match because

\[ [\hbar\, d/dt] = (\mathrm{J\,s})(1/\mathrm{s}) = \mathrm{J} = [H]. \]

If \(H\) does not depend on time,

\[ |\psi(t)\rangle = U(t)\,|\psi(0)\rangle, \qquad U(t) = e^{-iHt/\hbar}. \]

The exponential is its power series. \(Ht/\hbar\) has no units, \(H\) is Hermitian, and \(U(t)\) is therefore unitary.

A concrete case:

\[ H = \frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\sigma_z, \]

with \(\omega\) an angular frequency in radians per second. Starting from \(|x+\rangle\),

\[ |\psi(t)\rangle = \frac{e^{-i\omega t/2}|z+\rangle + e^{+i\omega t/2}|z-\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

The \(z\) odds stay fifty-fifty. The relative phase crawls. Ask \(x\) and you see it:

\[ P(x+;t) = \bigl|\langle x+|\psi(t)\rangle\bigr|^2 = \cos^2\bigl(\omega t/2\bigr). \]

Hence evolution can be invisible in one question and obvious in another. Amplitudes keep the phase that a single list of probabilities throws away.

What the 1922 magnet actually was

The boxes in our diagrams are not free-floating matrices. Stern and Gerlach had a source, a beam of neutral silver atoms, a magnet whose field changed from place to place, two paths, and detectors with finite patience. In a semiclassical cartoon the force is

\[ \mathbf F \approx \boldsymbol\nabla(\boldsymbol\mu\cdot\mathbf B), \]

with magnetic moment in joules per tesla and field in tesla. The gradient supplies inverse metres, so the right-hand side is a newton. The atom’s internal answer becomes a dent in its flight path.

The 1922 paper predates the 1925 proposal of electron spin. The tidy classroom story is a later translation.

Ground-state silver can be represented by a two-dimensional angular-momentum subspace. The real atom, magnet, and hallway occupy a much larger space.

Calling the experiment “a spin-1/2 measurement” is an effective description, not a claim that the rest of the atom left the building.

The ideal analyzer also compresses several physical steps into one projection. The magnet first ties internal state to path by ordinary unitary motion of a bigger system.

A detector or a blocker then makes a record. Real devices add sloppy preparation, overlapping beams, crooked fields, loss, and noisy counters.

Those change the counts. They do not hold a committee meeting about the Born rule.

A two-component ket is a physical degree of freedom in an effective model. It is not yet a computer bit, a protected code, or a strange particle hiding in a crystal.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Squaring a complex amplitude instead of taking \(|c|^2 = c^*c\). Drop the conjugate and the probability can become negative, or worse, complex.

  • Treating the column \((\alpha,\beta)^T\) as a basis-free object. Superposition is always relative to a question.

  • Confusing an overall phase, which does nothing, with a relative phase, which does everything.

  • Reading an expectation value as a single-shot result. Averages are not outcomes.

  • Calling a selected measurement “just more unitary evolution of the atom.” Projection throws alternatives away. The atom-plus-magnet may have been unitary before you conditioned on a click.

  • Assuming Hermitian means unitary. One names observables. The other preserves inner products. A Pauli matrix happens to be both. Most operators are neither.

  • Simulating these matrices on a laptop and announcing that the laptop contains a silver atom. A simulation follows a description. It does not become the thing described.

  • Finding two levels and declaring a protected qubit. Two levels are a stage. Preparation, control, readout, and protection are later auditions.

Check yourself

What predicts a pure-state experiment?

A normalized ket, up to an overall phase. Questions and time evolution act on it.

How does an amplitude become a probability?

Take \(\langle a_j|\psi\rangle\) and square its magnitude: \(P(j) = |\langle a_j|\psi\rangle|^2\).

Show that (||^2 +

||^2 = 1) is forced by the \(z\) question.

Those two numbers are the probabilities of the two \(z\) answers, and the atom lands somewhere.

What fails if \(A\) is not Hermitian?

Eigenvalues need not be real, and answers belonging to different readings need not be orthogonal. That is why it cannot represent an ideal measurement.

How is unitary motion different from picking an exit?

Unitary motion keeps every inner product. Picking an exit projects and renormalizes.

After \(z+\), then \(x+\), then \(z\) again, what are the odds? What would go wrong if the second magnet merely “peeked” at \(x\)?

One half and one half. A peek that left \(z+\) intact would send every survivor back up; the data refuse that story.

You now have a state, a way to ask it a question, and a way to let it tick between questions. Next we join two atoms and discover that “the state of the pair” is not always “a state for this one and a state for that one.”

Sources

  • [R038] W. Gerlach and O. Stern, “Der experimentelle Nachweis der Richtungsquantelung im Magnetfeld,” Zeitschrift für Physik 9, 349–352 (1922). DOI: 10.1007/BF01326983.

  • [R039] B. Friedrich and D. Herschbach, “Stern and Gerlach: How a Bad Cigar Helped Reorient Atomic Physics,” Physics Today 56(12), 53–59 (2003). DOI: 10.1063/1.1650229.

  • [R040] P. A. M. Dirac, The Principles of Quantum Mechanics, 4th ed., Oxford University Press (1958; reissued 1981). ISBN: 978-0-19-852011-5.

  • [R041] E. Schrödinger, “Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem (Vierte Mitteilung),” Annalen der Physik 386, 109–139 (1926). DOI: 10.1002/andp.19263861802.

  • [R004] M. A. Nielsen and I. L. Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information: 10th Anniversary Edition, Cambridge University Press (2010). DOI: 10.1017/CBO9780511976667.

Chapter 2 — Two coins that refuse to factor

Flip two coins. Each lands heads or tails, so the pair has four possible faces: HH, HT, TH, TT.

A fair pair gives each face one chance in four. A loaded pair can load those four numbers however it likes, as long as they stay nonnegative and add to one.

Replace the coins with two silver atoms of the kind that split in a magnet. Each atom still has two answers.

The pair still has four labels. The surprise is not the labels.

The surprise is that the pair can own four complex numbers that refuse to split into “this atom’s two” and “that atom’s two.”

No crystal yet. Two atoms, four labels, and a list that will not factor.

Four labels for a pair

Call the two atoms \(A\) and \(B\). Give each the same two answers as in Chapter 1, written \(0\) and \(1\) instead of \(z+\) and \(z-\). The pair then has four joint answers:

\[ |00\rangle,\quad |01\rangle,\quad |10\rangle,\quad |11\rangle. \]

The first digit belongs to \(A\). The second belongs to \(B\). So \(|01\rangle\) means \(A\) answered 0 and \(B\) answered 1.

A state of the pair is four complex amplitudes, one per label, whose squared magnitudes add to one. Relative phases among those four numbers are real: they change later measurements, just as the minus sign between \(z+\) and \(z-\) changed the sideways magnet.

How do you write a state of \(A\) next to a state of \(B\)? If \(A\) is \(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\) and \(B\) sits in \(|0\rangle\), the pair is

\[ (\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)\otimes|0\rangle =\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|10\rangle. \]

The symbol \(\otimes\) is a tensor product: write this atom’s state next to that atom’s state, and multiply the amplitudes. We take this as the definition. The same symbol later joins operators, not just kets.

If \(A\) has \(d_A\) independent answers and \(B\) has \(d_B\), the pair has \(d_A d_B\) joint labels. Two two-answer atoms make four.

A three-answer system next to a four-answer system makes twelve. Dimensions multiply; they do not add.

An operator that acts only on \(A\) becomes \(M_A\otimes I_B\) on the pair, where \(M_A\) is the original operator and \(I_B\) leaves \(B\) unchanged. Do the thing here. Leave the partner alone.

Drop the product rule and you would count four labels as if they were four extra answers of a single atom. They are not. Each label is a pair of answers.

A pair you can factor

Some four-amplitude lists are just two two-amplitude lists written side by side. Take

\[ |0\rangle_A\otimes|0\rangle_B = |00\rangle. \]

Atom \(A\) is definitely 0. Atom \(B\) is definitely 0. Nothing about one depends on the other.

Or take both atoms in the sideways state from Chapter 1,

\[ |+\rangle = \frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

Then

\[ |+\rangle_A\otimes|+\rangle_B = \frac{|00\rangle+|01\rangle+|10\rangle+|11\rangle}{2}. \]

Every joint label has the same amplitude. Measure both atoms and each of the four faces appears one time in four. The two answers are independent: the probability of any pair is the product of the two single-atom probabilities.

A joint state that can be written this way — one ket for \(A\), one ket for \(B\), and the joining symbol between them — is a product state. Either two local kets multiply to the pair, or they do not.

Hence “the pair is in a product state” is a factorization claim, not a claim that the answers look uncorrelated in one particular basis. We will need that distinction in a moment.

A pair you cannot factor

Here is a different four-amplitude list:

\[ |\Phi^+\rangle_{AB} =\frac{|0\rangle_A|0\rangle_B+|1\rangle_A|1\rangle_B}{\sqrt{2}} =\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

People call this a Bell state. The two joint labels that appear are orthogonal, so the state is normalized:

\[ \langle\Phi^+|\Phi^+\rangle=\frac{1+1}{2}=1. \]

Measure both atoms in the \(\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}\) basis. The only outcomes are 00 and 11, each with probability \(1/2\). The answers match every time.

Could this be a product? Suppose

\[ |\Phi^+\rangle=(a|0\rangle+b|1\rangle)_A\otimes(c|0\rangle+d|1\rangle)_B. \]

Expand the right side. The four amplitudes are \(ac\), \(ad\), \(bc\), and \(bd\), sitting on \(|00\rangle\), \(|01\rangle\), \(|10\rangle\), and \(|11\rangle\). Matching the Bell pair requires

\[ ac=\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\qquad ad=0,\qquad bc=0,\qquad bd=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}. \]

The first equation makes \(a\) and \(c\) nonzero, so \(ad=0\) forces \(d=0\). Then \(bd\) cannot equal \(1/\sqrt2\). Hence no such \(a,b,c,d\) exist.

A pure joint state that refuses this factorization is entangled. That is a statement about the pair, not about a secret message traveling between the atoms. The list of four amplitudes simply does not split.

There is a faster test once you trust a little more algebra. Any pure pair can be rewritten

\[ |\Psi\rangle_{AB}=\sum_{k=1}^{r}s_k|u_k\rangle_A|v_k\rangle_B, \]

with nonnegative numbers \(s_k\) that obey \(\sum_k s_k^2=1\), and with two orthonormal lists of local states. This rewriting is the Schmidt decomposition.

The number \(r\) of nonzero \(s_k\) is the Schmidt rank. It equals 1 exactly when the state is a product.

For the Bell pair, \(r=2\) and \(s_1=s_2=1/\sqrt2\).

Drop the demand that the local lists be orthonormal and you can write many states as sums of products. That does not make them product states. The Schmidt rank is the test.

When a column is no longer enough

If you know the pair is exactly \(|\Phi^+\rangle\), a ket is enough. Often you do not.

Maybe someone flipped a fair coin and prepared either \(|00\rangle\) or \(|11\rangle\). Maybe you can see only atom \(A\).

A single column cannot carry “this or that.”

The replacement is a square table of complex numbers. For a ket \(|\psi\rangle\), the table is the outer product \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\). For the Bell pair,

\[ \rho_{AB}=|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+| =\frac12\left( |00\rangle\langle00|+|00\rangle\langle11| +|11\rangle\langle00|+|11\rangle\langle11| \right). \]

That table is a density operator, also called a density matrix once a basis has been chosen. The same object covers a definite ket, a coin-flip over kets, and — in the next section — the leftover state of one atom after you ignore its partner.

Any legal density operator \(\rho\) has three jobs:

  • it equals its own adjoint, \(\rho^\dagger=\rho\);

  • it never returns a negative number to a bra-ket sandwich, \(\langle\chi|\rho|\chi\rangle\ge0\) for every \(|\chi\rangle\);

  • its diagonal, added up, is one: \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\).

If a preparation produces the pure state \(|\psi_k\rangle\) with ordinary probability \(p_k\), the table is

\[ \rho=\sum_k p_k|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|. \]

Ask a yes-or-no question with projector \(P_m\). The probability of the yes labeled \(m\) is

\[ \Pr(m)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho P_m). \]

A density operator that came from a single ket satisfies \(\rho^2=\rho\), or equivalently \(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)=1\). It has rank 1. The Bell pair, looked at as a pair, is like that: \(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{AB}^2)=1\).

Hence a density operator is not a more mysterious state. It is the smallest table that still predicts every probability when a ket is no longer enough. Drop Hermiticity, positivity, or unit trace, and those probabilities can become negative, complex, or fail to add to one.

Throwing one atom away

Suppose only \(A\) is on the table. You still want every prediction that a measurement on \(A\) alone can make. The right local table is obtained by summing the partner’s answers out of the joint table:

\[ \rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B(\rho_{AB}) =\sum_{b=0}^{1}{}_B\langle b|\rho_{AB}|b\rangle_B. \]

That sum is a partial trace. It is not “destroy \(B\).” It is “write the statistics you would see if you never ask \(B\) a question.”

The useful identity, term by term, is

\[ \operatorname{Tr}_B\left(|a b\rangle\langle a' b'|\right) =\langle b'|b\rangle\,|a\rangle\langle a'| =\delta_{b'b}|a\rangle\langle a'|, \]

where \(\delta_{b'b}\) is 1 when \(b'=b\) and 0 otherwise. The Bell pair’s cross terms contain \(|0\rangle_B\langle1|\) or \(|1\rangle_B\langle0|\), so they vanish. What remains is

\[ \rho_A=\frac12\left(|0\rangle\langle0|+|1\rangle\langle1|\right) =\frac{I_A}{2}, \]

where \(I_A\) is the identity on \(A\) — the two-by-two table of ones on the diagonal and zeros off it.

The pair was pure. Either atom alone is as mixed as a two-answer system can be. Check:

\[ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho_A^2)=\operatorname{Tr}\left(\frac{I_A}{4}\right)=\frac12. \]

Hence globally pure does not imply locally pure. This mixedness is not “we forgot which local ket we prepared.” There is no local ket.

Operationally, every measurement you can do on \(A\) alone is predicted completely by \(\rho_A\). An operator that acts only on \(A\) becomes \(M_A\otimes I_B\) on the pair. Its average is

\[ \langle M_A\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\rho_{AB}(M_A\otimes I_B)\right]. \]

The reduced table \(\rho_A\) is the unique operator that reproduces every such average:

\[ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho_A M_A) =\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\rho_{AB}(M_A\otimes I_B)\right]. \]

For a product operator the partial trace is even simpler:

\[ \operatorname{Tr}_B(X_A\otimes Y_B)=X_A\operatorname{Tr}(Y_B). \]

Linearity extends the rule to every joint table.

Drop uniqueness and you could invent many local tables that agree on one measurement and disagree on another. The partial trace is the one that agrees on all of them.

A phase only the pair can see

Compare the Bell pair with a twisted cousin

\[ |\Phi_\theta\rangle=\frac{|00\rangle+e^{i\theta}|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \]

where \(\theta\) is a relative phase. The joint table contains the cross terms \(e^{-i\theta}|00\rangle\langle11|\) and \(e^{i\theta}|11\rangle\langle00|\). Both vanish under \(\operatorname{Tr}_B\), leaving \(\rho_A=I/2\) for every \(\theta\).

Hence joint measurements can see the phase, and no measurement on \(A\) alone can. The information did not leave the pair. It stopped being local.

If you assumed every relative phase of a pair must show up on one of the atoms, this family would be a counterexample.

Matching answers are not enough

Take this other table:

\[ \rho_{\mathrm{cc}}=\frac12|00\rangle\langle00|+\frac12|11\rangle\langle11|. \]

Measure both atoms in the \(0/1\) basis and the answers still match every time, just as they did for \(|\Phi^+\rangle\). But this table is an ordinary coin flip between two product states.

A mixed pair is separable if it can be written

\[ \rho_{AB}=\sum_k p_k\,\rho_A^{(k)}\otimes\rho_B^{(k)}, \qquad p_k\ge0,\quad \sum_kp_k=1. \]

The superscript \((k)\) labels a possible component, not an exponent. \(\rho_{\mathrm{cc}}\) is separable on sight. A mixed state with no such writing is entangled.

Hence one pattern of matching bars does not prove entanglement. The Bell pair and \(\rho_{\mathrm{cc}}\) agree on every \(0/1\) question and disagree as soon as you ask a sideways question.

Stricter tests exist. Bell inequalities ask whether correlations among several different questions can be explained by shared leftover randomness [R042]; [R043]; [R044]. [Theory] Some entangled mixed states do not violate a given Bell inequality, so “entangled” and “Bell-nonlocal” are not the same word [R044].

How mixed is mixed

The number \(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\) is the purity. It is dimensionless. In a system with \(d\) answers it runs from \(1/d\), for the maximally mixed table \(I/d\), up to 1, for a pure state.

For a mixed state in a finite list of answers,

\[ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)<1. \]

The decomposition of a mixed table into a story about which kets were prepared is not unique. For one two-answer atom,

\[ \frac{I}{2} =\frac12|0\rangle\langle0|+\frac12|1\rangle\langle1| =\frac12|+\rangle\langle+|+\frac12|-\rangle\langle-|, \]

where \(|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\). Hence the table, not a preferred bedtime story about the ensemble, contains the operational predictions.

Drop uniqueness and you may think you have learned which local states were prepared. You have not. You have learned \(\rho\).

The off-diagonal numbers

Start with one atom in

\[ |+\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \qquad \rho_+=|+\rangle\langle+|=\frac12 \begin{pmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The matrix is written in the ordered basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\). The diagonal entries are populations: chances of 0 and of 1.

The off-diagonal entries are coherences. They carry the relative-phase information that lets two paths interfere.

A noisy partner can steal those two numbers without changing the populations at all. That is the next calculation.

A knob that only shrinks the off-diagonal

Imagine a noisy process that leaves those populations alone and only shrinks the off-diagonal numbers. Give it a knob \(\lambda\) between 0 and 1: keep this fraction of each coherence. One model is

\[ \mathcal E_\lambda(\rho) :=K_0\rho K_0^\dagger+K_1\rho K_1^\dagger, \]

with

\[ K_0=\sqrt{\frac{1+\lambda}{2}}\,I, \qquad K_1=\sqrt{\frac{1-\lambda}{2}}\,Z, \qquad 0\le\lambda\le1. \]

Here \(I\) is the \(2\times2\) identity and

\[ Z=|0\rangle\langle0|-|1\rangle\langle1| =\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} \]

is the phase-flip operator from Chapter 1. These two pieces satisfy

\[ K_0^\dagger K_0+K_1^\dagger K_1=I, \]

so probabilities remain normalized. A map built this way — a few pieces \(K\), each sandwiching \(\rho\), adding up, and preserving the trace — is a quantum channel [R045].

Completely positive and trace-preserving are the adult names for “legal evolution when you do not watch everything.” You do not need those names to finish the chapter. You need the habit: sandwich, add, keep the trace.

This particular channel is dephasing. It attacks the phase and leaves the populations.

For a general input

\[ \rho=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c^*&b\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a+b=1, \]

where \(a\) and \(b\) are real populations and \(c\) is a complex coherence, direct multiplication gives

\[ \mathcal E_\lambda(\rho) =\begin{pmatrix}a&\lambda c\\\lambda c^*&b\end{pmatrix}. \]

Hence the populations are unchanged and the coherences shrink by \(\lambda\). Applied to \(|+\rangle\),

\[ \rho_+'=\frac12 \begin{pmatrix}1&\lambda\\\lambda&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Its purity is

\[ \operatorname{Tr}[(\rho_+')^2]=\frac{1+\lambda^2}{2}. \]

At \(\lambda=1\), the channel does nothing and the state is pure. At \(\lambda=0\), all coherence in this basis is gone and \(\rho_+'=I/2\). At an intermediate value, say \(\lambda=1/2\), the output is

\[ \rho_+'=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}[(\rho_+')^2]=\frac58. \]

This model is pure dephasing. Energy relaxation is a different channel: it moves population, usually by exchanging energy, instead of only shrinking the off-diagonal. Drop that distinction and a long-lived excited population will impersonate a phase that is still there.

Where the missing phase went

A microscopic picture explains where the missing coherence can go. Let the environment begin in \(|e\rangle\), and suppose joint unitary evolution produces

\[ |0\rangle|e\rangle\longmapsto |0\rangle|e_0\rangle, \qquad |1\rangle|e\rangle\longmapsto |1\rangle|e_1\rangle. \]

The initial \(|+\rangle|e\rangle\) becomes

\[ |\Psi\rangle_{SE}=\frac{|0\rangle|e_0\rangle+|1\rangle|e_1\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \]

where \(S\) labels the system and \(E\) the environment. Tracing out \(E\) yields

\[ \rho_S=\frac12 \begin{pmatrix} 1&\langle e_1|e_0\rangle\\ \langle e_0|e_1\rangle&1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The leftover coherence is the overlap of the two environment states. If \(|e_0\rangle\) and \(|e_1\rangle\) are identical, the environment learned nothing and the coherence remains. If they are orthogonal, the environment carries a perfectly distinguishable record and local coherence vanishes.

This process — uncontrolled interaction carrying phase information into degrees of freedom you do not monitor — is decoherence. The name is worth keeping because it is a process, not a third kind of state next to pure and mixed.

The reduced state often becomes mixed. Calling every mixed state “decohered” would be like calling every wet pavement “rained on.” Sometimes a sprinkler did it.

[Theory] Environment-induced entanglement and partial tracing are the standard open-system account of decoherence [R046]; [R047]. The total system-plus-environment state may remain pure and evolve unitarily throughout.

Hence decoherence is not a mandatory collapse postulate. In this description, system and environment can evolve unitarily while their entanglement suppresses local interference.

That account explains reduced-state dynamics. It does not, by itself, settle every interpretation of quantum measurement.

What the laboratory actually has

An ideal derivation hands us \(\rho\). A laboratory hands us detector clicks, voltages, fluorescence counts, and a preparation recipe.

Reconstructing a density operator requires measurements in several bases plus statistical inference, a procedure called quantum-state tomography. The result is an estimate conditioned on calibration and a model of the measurement apparatus.

A preparation described as “the same state repeated many times” is also an experimental assertion. Slow drift can make successive trials differ.

Leakage can make the assumed two-dimensional space incomplete. Selection rules and detector inefficiency can bias the apparent ensemble.

Density operators remain the right language, but the chosen space and noise model must earn their keep.

[Experiment] Bell tests with separated solid-state electron spins have observed correlations incompatible with a local-realist model while closing major detection and locality loopholes under the experiment’s stated assumptions [R048]. That is much stronger evidence than seeing matching 0/1 outcomes. It still does not mean every correlated density operator is entangled.

Experimental decoherence is inferred from loss of interference or decay of off-diagonal coherence, often summarized by fitted time constants. The single parameter \(\lambda\) above is a channel model, not a universal law of nature.

It may depend on elapsed time, pulse sequence, temperature, noise spectrum, and correlations with prior runs. Later chapters will introduce the distinct quantities \(T_1\), \(T_2\), and \(T_2^*\) rather than stuffing all unpleasantness into one Greek letter.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Treating “not a product” and “mixed” as synonyms. The Bell state is pure and entangled. The state \(I/2\) is mixed but, for one subsystem, has no pair left to be entangled with.

  • Reading matching answers as entanglement. The separable state \(\rho_{\mathrm{cc}}\) has perfect \(0/1\) correlation. Entanglement asks whether the full table has a separable writing, not whether one plot has matching bars.

  • Assuming a reduced mixture came from sloppy preparation. One half of a pure entangled state is mixed. Ignoring the partner is enough.

  • Calling every mixed state decohered. Intentionally flipping a fair coin to prepare \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\) produces \(I/2\) without any later environmental theft.

  • Treating decoherence as a mandatory collapse postulate. In the open-system description, system and environment can evolve unitarily while their entanglement suppresses local interference [R046]; [R047]. That account explains reduced-state dynamics. It does not, by itself, settle every interpretation of quantum measurement.

  • Confusing dephasing with relaxation. Pure dephasing preserves basis populations while shrinking off-diagonal terms. Relaxation transfers population, usually with energy exchange. Real channels can do both.

  • Treating an ensemble story as unique. Writing \(I/2\) as a 50–50 mixture of \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) does not prove those were the actual preparations. The same operator is a 50–50 mixture of \(|+\rangle\) and \(|-\rangle\).

  • Simulating a Bell pair on a laptop and announcing that the laptop now contains two entangled atoms. A simulation follows a description. It does not become the thing described.

Check yourself

What is the dimension of a pair whose parts have dimensions 3 and 4?

\(3\times4=12\). Tensor-product dimensions multiply.

Show that \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) is not a product state.

Matching the four amplitudes would require \(ac=1/\sqrt2\), \(ad=0\), \(bc=0\), and \(bd=1/\sqrt2\). The first forces \(a,c\neq0\), so \(d=0\), and then \(bd\) cannot be \(1/\sqrt2\).

What fails if you read matching \(0/1\) answers as entanglement?

The separable mixture \(\rho_{\mathrm{cc}}\) produces the same matching bars. Entanglement is the absence of a separable writing, not the presence of one correlated plot.

Why does tracing out half of \(|\Phi^+\rangle\) remove its cross terms?

Those terms contain orthogonal partner factors, and the partial trace contributes \(\langle1|0\rangle=0\).

Show that \(\mathcal E_{1/2}\) applied to \(|+\rangle\) has purity \(5/8\).

The output is \(\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}[(\rho_+')^2]=(1+(1/2)^2)/2=5/8\).

What fails if you call every mixed state decohered?

A coin-flip preparation of \(|0\rangle\) or \(|1\rangle\) already yields \(I/2\), with no later environmental record.

You now have a pair, a way to ignore half of it, and a way to watch a phase leak into something you are not watching.

Sources

  • [R042] A. Einstein, B. Podolsky, and N. Rosen, “Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?”, Physical Review 47, 777–780 (1935). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.47.777.

  • [R043] J. S. Bell, “On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen Paradox,” Physics Physique Fizika 1, 195–200 (1964). DOI: 10.1103/PhysicsPhysiqueFizika.1.195.

  • [R044] R. F. Werner, “Quantum states with Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlations admitting a hidden-variable model,” Physical Review A 40, 4277–4281 (1989). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.40.4277.

  • [R045] K. Kraus, “General state changes in quantum theory,” Annals of Physics 64, 311–335 (1971). DOI: 10.1016/0003-4916(71)90108-4.

  • [R046] W. H. Zurek, “Decoherence, einselection, and the quantum origins of the classical,” Reviews of Modern Physics 75, 715–775 (2003). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.75.715; arXiv: quant-ph/0105127.

  • [R047] M. Schlosshauer, “Decoherence, the measurement problem, and interpretations of quantum mechanics,” Reviews of Modern Physics 76, 1267–1305 (2005). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.76.1267; arXiv: quant-ph/0312059.

  • [R048] B. Hensen et al., “Loophole-free Bell inequality violation using electron spins separated by 1.3 kilometres,” Nature 526, 682–686 (2015). DOI: 10.1038/nature15759; arXiv: 1508.05949.

Part II — Qubits and quantum information

A two-level system is not yet a computer bit. These chapters add the lifecycle — set, flip, read — and the ways a bit forgets.

Chapter 3 — A needle you can set, flip, and read

A compass needle on the desk can be tapped north, flicked south, and glanced at. Three verbs. A computer bit is the same three verbs with uglier hardware.

A two-level quantum system is not a tiny compass. It has no secret classical arrow hiding inside. Even so, we will park it, tilt it, and read it — and then check which of those verbs the laboratory actually owns.

Two rungs on an energy ladder do not give you the verbs for free. The rungs may be too close to tell apart.

A tilt may knock the system onto a third rung. The detector may click for some other reason.

Prepare, twist, read

Keep the labels from Chapter 1. A spin-\(1/2\) particle sits in a magnetic field that picks out a \(z\)-axis.

The spin state with Pauli-\(Z\) eigenvalue \(+1\) is \(|0\rangle\). The state with eigenvalue \(-1\) is \(|1\rangle\).

Another laboratory may swap the stickers. That is a convention, not physics.

\[ |0\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad |1\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}. \]

We will do a phase-sensitive experiment in five steps: prepare \(|0\rangle\); turn by \(+\pi/2\) about the \(y\)-axis; let a phase \(\phi\) accumulate, which is a turn about \(z\); turn by \(-\pi/2\) about \(y\); measure in the \(\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}\) basis.

The turn about axis \(j\), where \(j\) is \(x\), \(y\), or \(z\), is the matrix

\[ R_j(\vartheta)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\vartheta\sigma_j}{2}\right). \]

Here \(i^2=-1\), \(\vartheta\) is an angle in radians, and \(\sigma_j\) is the matching Pauli matrix from Chapter 1. Those matrices \(R_j(\vartheta)\) are rotations. For the two axes we need,

\[ R_y(\vartheta)= \begin{pmatrix} \cos(\vartheta/2)&-\sin(\vartheta/2)\\ \sin(\vartheta/2)&\cos(\vartheta/2) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad R_z(\phi)= \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\phi/2}&0\\ 0&e^{i\phi/2} \end{pmatrix}. \]

The half-angles in the entries are not a typesetting accident. The first pulse gives

\[ R_y(\pi/2)|0\rangle =\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

The phase turn then gives

\[ R_z(\phi)R_y(\pi/2)|0\rangle =\frac{e^{-i\phi/2}|0\rangle+e^{i\phi/2}|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

A \(Z\)-basis measurement right here would return each result with probability \(1/2\). It would miss the relative phase entirely. The last pulse converts that phase into a population the magnet can see:

\[ |\psi_{\mathrm f}\rangle :=R_y(-\pi/2)R_z(\phi)R_y(\pi/2)|0\rangle =\cos(\phi/2)|0\rangle+i\sin(\phi/2)|1\rangle. \]

The Born rule therefore predicts

\[ P(0)=\cos^2(\phi/2), \qquad P(1)=\sin^2(\phi/2), \qquad P(0)+P(1)=1. \]

Hence the last pulse is an analyzer: it turns a relative twist into a count. For \(\phi=\pi/3\), the probabilities are \(P(0)=3/4\) and \(P(1)=1/4\).

In 100 independent repetitions, about 75 zeros and 25 ones are typical. Exactly 75 is not promised.

The standard deviation of the zero count is \(\sqrt{100\cdot(3/4)\cdot(1/4)}\approx 4.3\).

This little sequence is already an interferometer. The first pulse creates two amplitudes, the middle step changes their relative phase, and the final pulse recombines them.

Measurement reads the resulting interference. Drop the last rotation and the phase is still there; you just cannot see it with a \(Z\) magnet.

[Experiment] Resonant control producing coherent oscillations of a single electron spin, and single-shot conversion of a spin state into a detectable charge signal, have both been demonstrated in semiconductor quantum dots [R052]; [R053]. The algebra above is ideal. The cited experiments supply concrete physical control and readout.

Two leftover angles

Every pure state in this two-dimensional space can still be written

\[ |\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle, \]

with \(|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1\). A computational-basis measurement returns 0 with probability \(|\alpha|^2\) and 1 with probability \(|\beta|^2\).

A common overall phase does nothing: \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(e^{i\chi}|\psi\rangle\) are the same physical pure state for any real angle \(\chi\). A relative phase between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is an experiment, as the five-step run just showed.

Throw away the invisible overall phase and the leftover budget of \(|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1\). Two real numbers remain. Call them the polar angle \(\theta\), with \(0\leq\theta\leq\pi\), and the azimuthal angle \(\varphi\), with \(0\leq\varphi<2\pi\):

\[ |\psi(\theta,\varphi)\rangle =\cos(\theta/2)|0\rangle +e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)|1\rangle. \]

That is already a point on a sphere. We will now see the point as three ordinary averages.

Write the Pauli operators as

\[ X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. \]

These are the same matrices as \(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z\) from Chapter 1. The identity \(I\) leaves every state unchanged. For a state \(|\psi\rangle\), the expectation value of an operator \(A\) is \(\langle A\rangle=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle\). Stack the three Pauli averages into a vector

\[ \mathbf r=(\langle X\rangle,\langle Y\rangle,\langle Z\rangle). \]

Substitute the two-angle state and the trig collapses:

\[ \mathbf r= (\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\;\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\;\cos\theta). \]

Its length is one, because \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\). Hence every pure two-level state maps to the surface of a unit sphere.

North is \(|0\rangle\). South is \(|1\rangle\).

The \(+x\) point is \(|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\). The \(+y\) point is \((|0\rangle+i|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\).

That sphere is the Bloch sphere. A density operator \(\rho\) for any two-level state — pure or mixed — can be written

\[ \rho=\frac{1}{2}\left(I+\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\right), \]

where \(\boldsymbol\sigma=(X,Y,Z)\) and the dot means \(r_x X+r_y Y+r_z Z\). Pure states have \(|\mathbf r|=1\) and live on the surface.

Mixed states have \(|\mathbf r|<1\) and sit inside. The maximally mixed state \(I/2\) is the center.

Laboratory noise is not, in general, a pure-state arrow that merely wobbles. It is a point that shortens. Drop the length-one condition and you have already left the surface; the leftover object is still a legal two-level state.

For any unit vector \(\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)\), write \(\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma=n_x X+n_y Y+n_z Z\). The Pauli algebra gives \((\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2=I\). Split the exponential into even and odd powers:

\[ e^{-i\vartheta\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/2} =I\cos(\vartheta/2)-i(\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)\sin(\vartheta/2). \]

This unitary rotates the Bloch vector through angle \(\vartheta\) about \(\mathbf n\). The amplitudes contain \(\vartheta/2\) because a two-component state is a double cover of ordinary spatial rotations: a \(2\pi\) turn of the arrow is a minus sign on the ket, and only \(4\pi\) brings the ket back. The wrinkle is not negotiable.

A named turn

An intended operation on the two-level system is represented, ideally, by a unitary matrix \(U\), so that \(|\psi\rangle\mapsto U|\psi\rangle\). Up to a physically irrelevant overall phase, every such unitary is a rotation of the Bloch vector:

\[ U=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\vartheta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\right). \]

When that intended operation has a name on a circuit diagram, it is a gate. The symbol is a target transformation, not a recipe for the pulse that produces it.

The Pauli gates \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) correspond, up to global phase, to \(\pi\) rotations about their named axes. The Hadamard gate

\[ H=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} \]

maps \(|0\rangle\) to \(|+\rangle\) and converts between the \(Z\) and \(X\) measurement bases.

Hence drawing a box labeled \(H\) does not say how the laboratory produced \(H\). Different devices synthesize the same target with microwaves, optical fields, voltages, exchange couplings, frame updates, or combinations of them. The drawn box does not know which.

A pulse with a stopwatch

A control Hamiltonian connects the target gate to time. Suppose a resonant drive produces

\[ \widehat H_{\mathrm d} =\frac{\hbar\Omega}{2} \left(\cos\delta\,X+\sin\delta\,Y\right). \]

Here \(\widehat H_{\mathrm d}\) is energy, \(\hbar\) is Planck’s reduced constant in joule-seconds, \(\Omega\) is an angular frequency in radians per second, and \(\delta\) is the drive phase in radians. Applying the drive for duration \(t\), measured in seconds, gives

\[ U(t)=e^{-i\widehat H_{\mathrm d}t/\hbar} =\exp\!\left[-\frac{i\Omega t}{2} (\cos\delta\,X+\sin\delta\,Y)\right]. \]

The rotation angle is \(\vartheta=\Omega t\). The dimensional check is

\[ [\Omega t]=(\mathrm{s}^{-1})(\mathrm{s})=1, \]

as an exponent must be dimensionless. Choosing \(\delta=0\) produces an \(x\)-rotation. Choosing \(\delta=\pi/2\) produces a \(y\)-rotation.

That angular speed \(\Omega\) is the Rabi frequency. Fix \(\Omega\), pick \(t\), and you have picked the angle.

Hence a gate is an intended map, and a pulse is a timed Hamiltonian. Confuse the two and you will treat \(R_x(\pi/2)\) as if it were already a waveform.

[Experiment] Electrically or magnetically driven spin resonance implements this control logic in solid-state spins, although the microscopic coupling and calibration differ by platform [R051]; [R052]; [R054].

When two rungs become a bit

Preparing a specified start with known reliability is not “turning the apparatus on.” Waiting for relaxation toward a ground state is one method. Optical pumping, reservoir-assisted loading, measurement followed by a conditional pulse, and active reset are others.

An ideal computational-basis measurement has projectors

\[ M_0=|0\rangle\langle0|, \qquad M_1=|1\rangle\langle1|. \]

For a density operator \(\rho\), outcome \(m\) occurs with probability

\[ P(m)=\operatorname{Tr}(M_m\rho), \qquad m\in\{0,1\}. \]

The trace \(\operatorname{Tr}\) sums the diagonal elements of a matrix. Real instruments do not print \(m\).

They produce photons, currents, voltages, or charge-sensor traces. A classifier then maps that analog record to 0 or 1.

[Experiment] Energy-selective tunneling has been used to map a single electron’s spin state to a charge transition detectable by a nearby sensor [R053]. Optically interfaced solid-state defects use spin-dependent optical dynamics to initialize and infer spin states; the relevant mechanisms and limitations vary strongly among centers [R054].

The complete operational loop is therefore:

  • Choose \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\), their axis, and the conditions under which those two states stay isolated.

  • Prepare a known start and quantify whatever residual error remains.

  • Calibrate pulse amplitude, phase, frequency, and duration to implement target gates.

  • Allow the intended single-system, two-system, or sensing energy to act.

  • Rotate the desired measurement question onto the instrument’s readable basis.

  • Acquire a classical record and assign an outcome.

  • Reset and repeat, while checking that calibration has not drifted.

One result is a bit. Repeated results estimate quantum probabilities. The system does not print its wavefunction, which would admittedly be convenient.

A pair of levels plus this loop is a qubit. The name is worth keeping because it is an operational claim, not a compliment you pay to any doublet in a spectrum. DiVincenzo organized the claim into a widely used checklist: you must be able to tell the states apart, prepare one of them, do a useful set of coherent operations, and read the result — and, for computation, keep the errors low, limit escapes into other levels, recalibrate, and couple more than one of them [R050].

Drop isolation, or drop readout, and you still have two levels. You no longer have a qubit.

A bit written on several devices

Sometimes the two answers you care about are not two levels of one device. They are two patterns spread across several devices:

\[ |0_L\rangle=|\text{pattern A}\rangle, \qquad |1_L\rangle=|\text{pattern B}\rangle. \]

The patterns can be entangled states of many components. Quantum error-correcting codes choose the pair of patterns so that selected physical mistakes can be spotted or undone. That condition is a property of the code and the error set, not of the typography \(L\) [R055].

That pattern-pair is an encoded bit. Several devices can hold one encoded bit. One device is not automatically one encoded bit.

Hence counting hardware is not counting bits. A controllable, resettable, readable doublet is a candidate qubit.

A two-dimensional subspace written across several qubits is a candidate encoded bit. Programming ordinary qubits to reproduce the amplitudes of some other model is a calculation on the hardware you already have.

It does not change what the hardware is.

What sits around the pair

A spin in a real device is not a tiny isolated Pauli matrix. The device has orbital states, nearby spins, phonons, electromagnetic modes, control wiring or optics, and a detector. The two states we have been calling \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) are a selected pair inside that larger space.

For an ideal spin-\(1/2\) in a static field, one often writes

\[ \widehat H_0=-\frac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}Z, \]

where \(\omega_0\) is the angular transition frequency in radians per second. A resonant field drives transitions.

In an actual solid, spin–orbit coupling, hyperfine interactions, charge motion, strain, and higher-energy levels modify this cartoon. Later chapters will identify these terms for specific defects.

[Proposal] Electron spins confined in quantum dots were proposed as physical qubits with controlled exchange interactions [R051]. [Experiment] Subsequent experiments demonstrated ingredients including single-spin readout and coherent single-spin rotations [R052]; [R053]. A demonstration of an ingredient is evidence for that ingredient, not automatic evidence for a fault-tolerant processor.

The same caution applies to crystalline defects. [Experiment] Reviews of optically active solid-state spins document initialization, microwave or optical manipulation, and optical interfaces in several material platforms [R054].

Whether a particular defect qualifies as a useful qubit depends on charge state, temperature, magnetic field, collection efficiency, nearby noise, and the exact protocol. “The material contains spin” is the beginning of the device specification, not the end.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Finding two levels and declaring a bit. A transition can be too weak to drive, too broad to address, or indistinguishable from its neighbors. The system can also leak into a third state during control. A two-level approximation is justified only over specified energies, drives, temperatures, and times.

  • Treating the Bloch sphere as ordinary space. For a literal spin in a magnetic field, the axes can be related to physical spin components. For a superconducting circuit, a charge configuration, an orbital doublet, or a cluster encoding, the axes are abstract coordinates in a chosen basis. The drawn arrow is not necessarily pointing through the laboratory ceiling.

  • Reading one shot as an amplitude. One computational-basis measurement returns 0 or 1. Estimating \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), or a Bloch vector takes many identically prepared trials in several measurement bases. If preparation drifts between trials, the reconstructed state can be a fiction.

  • Confusing relative phase with population. The states \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) and \((|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) both produce 50–50 outcomes in the \(Z\) basis. They are nevertheless orthogonal. An analyzer rotation is needed to expose the difference. That was the whole point of the five-step run.

  • Confusing a gate with its control waveform. The equation \(R_x(\pi/2)\) names an ideal transformation. The laboratory implements a finite-duration pulse while unwanted energy terms continue to act. Pulse calibration, leakage, drift, and noise decide how closely the result matches the symbol.

  • Calling an encoded bit the same thing as one physical doublet. Several qubits can hold one encoded bit without anyone having invented a new kind of particle. A code can catch errors actively without the hardware supplying a quiet energy gap. The nouns do not do that work for you.

Check yourself

What extra claim turns two levels into a qubit?

That the selected pair supports a usable loop: prepare, control, read, reset, and stay isolated under stated conditions.

Show that a pure two-level state needs only two Bloch-sphere angles.

Normalization removes one real parameter from \(\alpha,\beta\), and an unobservable global phase removes another, leaving \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\).

Where is a mixed state on the Bloch sphere?

Inside it. Its density operator is \(\rho=(I+\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)/2\) with \(|\mathbf r|<1\); the center is maximally mixed.

Show that the five-step run yields \(P(0)=\cos^2(\phi/2)\).

The analyzer produces \(\cos(\phi/2)|0\rangle+i\sin(\phi/2)|1\rangle\). The Born rule then squares the first amplitude.

What fails if several devices hold two patterns labeled \(0_L\) and \(1_L\), and you count the devices as bits?

Those two patterns are one encoded bit. “Encoded” names a chosen two-dimensional subspace, not a head-count of hardware.

What fails if you treat one computational-basis shot as revealing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)?

The shot returns 0 or 1. The amplitudes are estimated from many repeated, identically prepared runs, usually in more than one basis.

You now have a two-level system you can set, flip, and read — when those verbs actually work. Next we attach times and error rates to every verb.

Sources

  • [R050] D. P. DiVincenzo, “The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation,” Fortschritte der Physik 48, 771–783 (2000). arXiv: quant-ph/0002077; DOI: 10.1002/1521-3978(200009)48:9/113.0.CO;2-E.

  • [R051] D. Loss and D. P. DiVincenzo, “Quantum Computation with Quantum Dots,” Physical Review A 57, 120–126 (1998). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.57.120.

  • [R052] F. H. L. Koppens, C. Buizert, K. J. Tielrooij, I. T. Vink, K. C. Nowack, T. Meunier, L. P. Kouwenhoven, and L. M. K. Vandersypen, “Driven Coherent Oscillations of a Single Electron Spin in a Quantum Dot,” Nature 442, 766–771 (2006). DOI: 10.1038/nature05065.

  • [R053] J. M. Elzerman, R. Hanson, L. H. Willems van Beveren, B. Witkamp, L. M. K. Vandersypen, and L. P. Kouwenhoven, “Single-Shot Read-Out of an Individual Electron Spin in a Quantum Dot,” Nature 430, 431–435 (2004). DOI: 10.1038/nature02693.

  • [R055] E. Knill and R. Laflamme, “Theory of Quantum Error-Correcting Codes,” Physical Review A 55, 900–911 (1997). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.55.900; arXiv: quant-ph/9604034.

Chapter 4 — A clock that forgets

You set a clock and walk away. When you come back, two different things may have gone wrong.

The hands may have stopped. Or the hands may still be moving, but every clock on the table now shows a different time, so you can no longer read the time you set.

A two-level quantum system fails in both ways, and they are not the same failure. The extra energy that marks “excited” can drain into the surroundings.

The relative twist between the two answers can smear, even while that energy is still sitting there. Those are different experiments.

They produce different numbers. Calling both of them “stability” is how a flattering lifetime impersonates a useful memory.

No crystal yet. No code. Just one two-level thing, a wait, and a question that used to have a clean answer.

Still up, or already down?

Prepare the upper of the two levels. Call it \(|1\rangle\). The lower level is \(|0\rangle\). Wait a time \(t\), measured in seconds. Ask: is it still up?

If you repeat the run many times, the fraction that answers “still up” is a population. It is a probability, between 0 and 1. At low enough temperature that the surroundings almost never kick the system back up, that leftover excited population drains, and it drains by the same factor in every equal interval of time.

That is an exponential. Write \(\rho_{11}\) for the excited population — the diagonal entry of the density operator from Chapter 2 that says how often you still find \(|1\rangle\).

The time constant of the fade is \(T_1\). It belongs to this one experiment: prepare excited, wait, measure population.

\[ \rho_{11}(t)=\rho_{11}(0)e^{-t/T_1}. \]

At finite temperature the population does not fall all the way to zero. It approaches a thermal leftover.

Then \(T_1\) is the time constant of the approach, not the time to emptiness. Bloch-equation treatments of solid-state qubits make this “along the energy axis” reading explicit [R058].

Hence a long \(T_1\) means the energy is still there. It does not mean you can still read a phase you wrote.

The twist that smears

You can also prepare an equal superposition, the state Chapter 1 called \(|x+\rangle\) and Chapter 3 put on the equator of the Bloch sphere:

\[ |+x\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

The useful number is no longer the excited population. It is the off-diagonal entry \(\rho_{01}\), a complex number that stores the relative twist between the two answers.

In the simplest model that does not remember its own past, that entry ticks at the transition frequency and fades. Write \(\omega\) for the angular transition frequency in radians per second.

The \(1/e\) time of the fade, under this model and this kind of wait, is \(T_2\). It is the decay constant of an off-diagonal entry, not a second copy of \(T_1\).

\[ \rho_{01}(t)=\rho_{01}(0)e^{-i\omega t}e^{-t/T_2}. \]

People call a no-memory process Markovian. The word is a warning label on the model, not a property of the atom.

Why does \(T_1\) show up inside \(T_2\)? Population is an amplitude squared.

If the excited population fades as \(e^{-t/T_1}\), the excited amplitude fades as \(e^{-t/(2T_1)}\). The coherence \(\rho_{01}\) carries one factor of that amplitude, so energy relaxation alone already multiplies \(\rho_{01}\) by \(e^{-t/(2T_1)}\).

Independent phase noise contributes a second factor, \(e^{-t/T_\phi}\). Here \(T_\phi\) is just the time constant of that phase-only piece. Multiplying the factors gives

\[ e^{-t/T_2}=e^{-t/(2T_1)}e^{-t/T_\phi}, \qquad \boxed{\frac{1}{T_2}=\frac{1}{2T_1}+\frac{1}{T_\phi}}. \]

Hence \(T_2\leq 2T_1\) in this model. Equality means no extra phase-only noise. It does not mean perfect pulses, perfect readout, or a good computer.

A long \(T_1\) is not a long \(T_2\). The energy can sit there while the twist is already gone.

Every clock a little wrong

Chapter 3 already walked a two-pulse dance with a fixed phase. Do it again, but let the leftover frequency mismatch wander.

In a frame that rotates with the control oscillator, the two levels pick up opposite phases if their energy difference does not quite match that oscillator. Write the leftover mismatch as an angular frequency \(\Delta\), in radians per second. The leftover energy is

\[ H=\frac{\hbar\Delta}{2}\sigma_z. \]

Here \(H\) is energy, \(\hbar\) is Planck’s reduced constant in joule-seconds, and \(\sigma_z\) has eigenvalue \(+1\) on \(|0\rangle\) and \(-1\) on \(|1\rangle\). A radian is dimensionless, so \(\Delta t\) is a dimensionless phase.

The pulse sequence, introduced in separated-field spectroscopy by Ramsey [R056], is

|0> -- pi/2 -- free evolution for t -- -pi/2 -- measure

Choose the first pulse so that

\[ |0\rangle\longrightarrow |+x\rangle =\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

Free evolution produces

\[ |\psi(t)\rangle =\frac{e^{-i\Delta t/2}|0\rangle+e^{+i\Delta t/2}|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

The second pulse converts the relative twist into a population. With this pulse convention, the ideal probability of measuring 0 is

\[ P_0^{\mathrm{Ramsey}}(t)=\frac{1+\cos(\Delta t)}{2}. \]

If \(\Delta\) is the same on every shot, that fringe never dies. It just oscillates.

Now make the mismatch a little different on each shot. Let the extra offset be a static random variable \(\delta\) with mean zero and Gaussian standard deviation \(\sigma\), measured in radians per second. Averaging the phase factor over shots gives

\[ \left\langle e^{i\delta t}\right\rangle =e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}. \]

The oscillating piece is now wearing a Gaussian envelope:

\[ P_0^{\mathrm{Ramsey}}(t) =\frac{1+e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}\cos(\Delta t)}{2}. \]

The time that makes the envelope read \(e^{-(t/T)^2}\) is \(T_2^*\). The asterisk is a warning that reversible, shot-to-shot frequency junk is included. It is not an instruction to multiply \(T_2\) by something.

\[ T_2^*=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sigma}, \qquad P_0^{\mathrm{Ramsey}}(t) =\frac{1+e^{-(t/T_2^*)^2}\cos(\Delta t)}{2}. \]

The dimensional check is immediate: \((\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}})^{-1}=\mathrm{s}\), because radians carry no physical dimension. Hence a short \(T_2^*\) can sit next to a long \(T_1\) without contradiction: the energy is still there, and the fringe is already washed out. People sometimes call the extra smear inhomogeneous broadening. The experiment is still “prepare, wait, read the fringe.”

A flip that rewinds the slow ones

A Hahn echo [R057] inserts a \(\pi\) pulse between two equal free-evolution intervals:

|0> -- pi/2 -- free tau -- pi -- free tau -- -pi/2 -- measure

Let the total free-evolution time be \(t=2\tau\). The \(\pi\) pulse reverses the sign with which a static mismatch accumulates phase. Write \(y(s)\) for a sign that equals \(+1\) before the pulse and \(-1\) after it. The unwanted phase is

\[ \phi_{\mathrm{echo}} =\delta\int_0^{2\tau}y(s)\,ds =\delta(\tau-\tau)=0. \]

An ideal echo therefore refocuses any mismatch that stays constant during that shot. It does not reverse energy relaxation, rapidly changing noise, or pulse error. Hahn’s pulse is a rewind button for one particular kind of phase history, not a small time machine.

For a concrete calculation, take \(\sigma/(2\pi)=100\ \mathrm{kHz}\). Then

\[ \sigma=2\pi\times10^5\ \mathrm{s^{-1}},\qquad T_2^*=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\pi\times10^5\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} =2.25\ \mu\mathrm{s}. \]

Suppose also that this hypothetical qubit has \(T_1=1.00\ \mathrm{ms}\) and a no-memory phase-only time \(T_\phi=100\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). The boxed relation from earlier gives \(T_2=95.2\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).

At \(t=10\ \mu\mathrm{s}\), the quasistatic Ramsey contrast is

\[ e^{-(10/2.25)^2}\approx2.7\times10^{-9}, \]

while an idealized echo limited only by the quoted exponential \(T_2\) retains

\[ e^{-10/95.2}\approx0.900 \]

of its transverse contrast. Meanwhile the excited population retains \(e^{-10/1000}\approx0.990\) of its initial excess. Hence one qubit, one time interval, three different answers. Nothing is inconsistent.

In many devices an echo time is longer than \(T_2^*\), because echo rejects a mismatch that looks constant on one shot. That is not a theorem. A noisy \(\pi\) pulse can make echo worse. A nonexponential envelope may be fitted as

\[ C(t)=C_0\exp[-(t/T)^n], \]

where \(C_0\) is dimensionless contrast, \(T\) is the reported time in seconds, and \(n\) is a dimensionless fit exponent. A useful coherence-time claim states the sequence, the observable, the envelope, the fit convention, the sample conditions, and the uncertainty.

The same noise, two sieves

Let \(\delta\omega(s)\) be a time-dependent angular-frequency wobble. The accumulated phase is

\[ \phi(t)=\int_0^t y(s)\delta\omega(s)\,ds. \]

Ramsey has \(y(s)=1\). Hahn echo has \(y(s)=+1\) for the first half and \(-1\) for the second.

A zero-frequency offset survives the Ramsey integral and cancels in echo. Noise that changes appreciably between the two halves does not cancel.

Additional pulses create other sieves. They change the measurement protocol, not the identity of the material. Filter-function theory is the bookkeeping that makes this sequence dependence explicit [R059].

Hence a longer echo time is not evidence that the material became quieter. It is evidence that this particular sieve rejected more of the noise.

How close is the leftover state?

“The experiment worked” is not a number. We want a score between 0 and 1 that says how much one quantum state still looks like another.

For states \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\), that score is the fidelity

\[ F(\rho,\sigma) =\left[\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{\sqrt{\rho}\,\sigma\sqrt{\rho}}\right]^2, \qquad 0\leq F\leq1. \]

This is the squared Uhlmann–Jozsa convention. Jozsa gives the mixed-state definition and its properties [R060]. Some authors call the unsquared square root “fidelity,” so a numerical report must say which one it is.

If the target is the pure state \(|\psi\rangle\), the formula collapses to a probability:

\[ F(|\psi\rangle,\rho)=\langle\psi|\rho|\psi\rangle. \]

That is the chance the leftover state still answers the \(\psi\) question. Hence a fidelity is always the fidelity of something. We have not yet said anything about a pulse, a readout box, or a code.

How close is the operation?

A gate is not a state. Let \(U\) be the target unitary and \(\mathcal{E}\) the operation the apparatus actually applies. For a \(d\)-dimensional computational space, the average gate fidelity is

\[ F_{\mathrm{avg}}(\mathcal{E},U) =\int d\psi\, \langle\psi|U^\dagger\mathcal{E}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)U|\psi\rangle, \]

where the integral is uniform over pure input states and \(d\psi\) is a normalized dimensionless measure. Nielsen derives practical formulas for this average [R061]. The score names both the object (a gate) and the average (every pure input, equally).

The complementary score \(r=1-F_{\mathrm{avg}}\) is the average gate infidelity. It is a probability-like dimensionless number. It is not a coherence time. It is not a worst-case error bound.

[Experiment] Randomized benchmarking estimates an average error parameter while reducing sensitivity to state-preparation and measurement errors under its modeling assumptions; interleaved benchmarking adds a target gate to estimate that gate’s contribution [R062]. It does not reveal the full noise channel. Coherent, correlated, time-dependent, or leakage errors can require additional diagnostics.

How often does the box guess right?

Readout ends in a classical decision. For binary single-shot readout, prepare \(|0\rangle\) many times and prepare \(|1\rangle\) many times, then average the two success rates:

\[ F_{\mathrm{RO}} =\frac{P(\widehat{0}\mid0)+P(\widehat{1}\mid1)}{2}. \]

Here \(P(\widehat{j}\mid j)\) is the conditional probability that the apparatus reports label \(j\) after \(j\) was prepared. This balanced assignment fidelity is one common readout-fidelity definition [R063]. Reporting the two conditional probabilities separately prevents their asymmetry from hiding inside a single average.

Hence the score includes whatever preparation errors the calibration has not independently removed. It is not Uhlmann state fidelity. It is not gate fidelity. It is a grade for a classical guess.

Population that left the room

A bit flip sends \(|0\rangle\) to \(|1\rangle\) and stays inside the two levels we agreed to use. Excitation to \(|2\rangle\) does not. Those are different mistakes.

Let \(P\) project onto the two-level subspace spanned by \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\), and let \(Q=I-P\) project onto every other level. For a state \(\rho\), the leakage is the population sitting outside that subspace:

\[ L(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(Q\rho)=1-\operatorname{Tr}(P\rho). \]

It is dimensionless and lies between 0 and 1. The name is a fence, not another error inside the room.

A channel can also be assigned leakage and seepage rates: leakage moves population from \(P\) to \(Q\), while seepage returns it [R064]. Postselecting away leaked shots may make the fidelity of the retained data look excellent while the unconditional operation is poor. The discarded fraction belongs beside the score.

Drop the fence and a high in-subspace number will impersonate a closed two-level system.

A message written on several atoms

Sometimes the thing you care about is not one physical two-level system. It is a message written across several of them, then protected by a declared protocol.

A logical lifetime is the decay time of a declared logical observable, or of a logical-state survival probability, under a declared noise model, control schedule, syndrome-extraction procedure, and decoder. Experimental surface-code work commonly reports the closely related logical error probability per correction cycle [R065]. The name is worth keeping because it belongs to that whole encoded experiment, not to any one physical clock.

It has units of seconds — or of cycles, if the cycle duration is supplied separately.

For a simple illustration, suppose each correction cycle lasts \(\tau_c\) seconds and independently causes an absorbing logical failure with probability \(p_L\). The survival probability after \(N\) cycles is

\[ S(N)=(1-p_L)^N =\exp\!\left[-\frac{N\tau_c}{T_L}\right], \]

which defines

\[ T_L=-\frac{\tau_c}{\ln(1-p_L)} \approx\frac{\tau_c}{p_L} \quad\text{when }p_L\ll1. \]

The approximation is dimensionally sound: seconds divided by a dimensionless probability gives seconds. A logical Pauli expectation under a symmetric Pauli channel follows a different factor, so the observable and the fit must be named. “Logical lifetime” without that metadata is unfinished arithmetic.

[Experiment] Surface-code experiments report logical error per correction cycle and compare code distances. Increasing distance improved the measured logical performance in the conditions of one 2023 experiment, but the per-cycle logical error remained finite [R065].

That is evidence of active error-correction scaling. It is not evidence that the superconducting hardware acquired an emergent topological phase.

A long \(T_L\) can arise from an ordinary repetition code, a decoherence-free encoding, active correction, passive energy barriers, or topological order. The mechanism must be stated separately. No single coherence time proves a phase.

What the laboratory actually has

The ideal equations hide preparation error, measurement error, pulse distortion, drift, several decay rates, and limited sampling. A laboratory therefore has protocols and fitted data, not little tags labeled \(T_2\) attached to atoms.

Claimed quantity | Minimal protocol | Direct observable | What it does not establish | |

\(T_1\) | prepare excited state; vary delay; measure population | population approach to equilibrium | phase coherence, gate accuracy, or fault tolerance | |

\(T_2^*\) | Ramsey/free induction | fringe contrast versus free time | irreversible dephasing alone | |

echo \(T_2\) | \(\pi/2-\tau-\pi-\tau\) sequence | refocused contrast versus \(2\tau\) | passive material protection or immunity to fast noise | |

gate fidelity | characterize a specified gate set and metric | tomography, randomized sequences, or another declared estimator | worst-case error, readout fidelity, or zero leakage | |

readout fidelity | prepare labels; construct assignment matrix | conditional classical outcome frequencies | premeasurement state fidelity |

leakage | resolve or infer levels outside the code space | population outside \(P\), preferably with return dynamics | an ordinary bit/phase error rate | |

logical lifetime | prepare encoded states; run full protocol; decode at varied duration | logical survival or observable decay | topological order or universal fault tolerance by itself | |

[Experiment] Ramsey and echo data are often analyzed with more than one envelope model, because different spectra produce Gaussian, exponential, stretched-exponential, or oscillatory decay [R058]; [R059]. Choosing the model after seeing the answer can move the quoted time. Residuals, confidence intervals, and the fit window are part of the result, although brochures rarely have room for them.

Comparisons also require matched conditions: temperature, magnetic field, qubit transition, sample, control power, pulse sequence, number of refocusing pulses, and whether the value comes from a single qubit or an ensemble. A many-pulse dynamical-decoupling time should not quietly enter a table column labeled “intrinsic \(T_2\).” The number may be correct. The noun is doing mischief.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Long \(T_1\), therefore a good memory. False. \(T_1\) constrains only energy relaxation. Slow frequency drift can make \(T_2^*\) short while \(T_1\) is long. In the no-memory relation, phase-only noise can dominate \(1/T_2\).

  • Echo increased the lifetime, therefore the state became passively protected. False. Echo is applied control. It cancels phase accumulated from sufficiently slow fluctuations. Remove the pulse and the Ramsey decay returns. Dynamical decoupling can be extremely useful without being a material energy barrier or topological protection.

  • A 99.9% number is a 99.9% number. False. State fidelity, average gate fidelity, postselected fidelity, readout assignment fidelity, and survival probability answer different questions. Even the same label can use squared or unsquared conventions. Write the object, the estimator, the subspace, the conditioning, and the averaging distribution.

  • High in-subspace gate fidelity means negligible leakage. False. A reported gate metric may condition on remaining in the computational space, or it may have weak sensitivity to rare excursions. Report \(F_{\mathrm{avg}}\) and leakage separately. Leakage can persist across cycles and create correlated downstream errors [R064].

  • A logical qubit outlived one physical qubit, therefore fault tolerance was achieved. Not necessarily. The physical comparison must be task-matched. Fault tolerance concerns controlled scaling of logical error as code resources increase below a threshold, including operations and measurements. A single favorable lifetime can be a milestone without proving scalable suppression. Conversely, an encoded qubit can be useful even when its protection is wholly non-topological.

  • One fitted time is a property of the material. Usually incomplete. Noise spectrum and pulse sieve jointly determine coherence decay. Sample preparation, nearby spins, charge motion, temperature, and control sequence matter. Report the protocol with the time.

  • Physical clocks characterize an encoded message, or a long encoded lifetime characterizes a phase. No. \(T_1\), \(T_2\), \(T_2^*\), physical-gate fidelity, physical readout fidelity, and physical leakage characterize a physical qubit and its controls. An encoded qubit has logical observables, logical gates, logical leakage, and a logical lifetime. A digital circuit that emulates a code may demonstrate logical behavior without an emergent many-body phase. Passive robustness of an emergent topological phase is an energy-operator property involving a gap, locality, system size, temperature, and perturbations. No single coherence time proves it.

Check yourself

Show that \(T_2\leq 2T_1\) in the no-memory model.

From \(1/T_2=1/(2T_1)+1/T_\phi\) and \(T_\phi>0\), the extra term is nonnegative, so \(T_2\leq 2T_1\). Equality requires \(1/T_\phi=0\).

What fails if a qubit has \(T_1=5\ \mathrm{ms}\) and Ramsey \(T_2^*=2\ \mu\mathrm{s}\), and you treat the long \(T_1\) as a good memory?

Population can relax slowly while quasistatic frequency noise rapidly washes out phase. Neither number establishes fault tolerance.

Ramsey fringes decay in \(3\ \mu\mathrm{s}\), while Hahn-echo contrast decays in \(80\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). What distinction is directly supported?

Much of the Ramsey decay is refocusable on the echo timescale, consistent with slow detuning noise. Echo does not prove passive protection, and the pulse sequence and envelope fits must accompany both numbers.

What fails if a gate’s retained shots have fidelity 0.999, but 0.02 of all shots occupy \(|2\rangle\), and you report only 0.999?

The escaped population is leakage \(L=0.02\). The high retained-shot fidelity does not erase it. Report both, plus the conditioning rule.

Is readout fidelity the same as the fidelity of the premeasurement quantum state?

No. Balanced readout fidelity averages two classical assignment probabilities. State fidelity compares density operators; preparation and measurement errors require separate calibration.

What fails if an encoded state survives for ten times the physical \(T_2^*\) and you call that topological order?

The gain could come from echo, a decoherence-free subspace, active correction, postselection, or another encoding. Demonstrating topological order requires independent many-body evidence; logical lifetime must name its observable and protocol.

You now have several times and several scores, and none of them is allowed to impersonate another. Next we ask how a crystal makes two levels you can attach those times to.
