Part III — Crystals and defects

A repeating crystal wants electrons to spread out. A missing tile can trap one anyway. Then a zoo of traps that are not interchangeable.

Chapter 5 — A crystal that looks the same after a slide

A crystal looks the same after a slide. Start at one atom, step a fixed length to the next identical atom, and the view repeats as far as you can see. A single extra electron can sit on any of those atoms.

Now change one atom, or leave its site empty. Almost nothing has changed — except right there.

That is the puzzle. In the perfect crystal the electron prefers to spread across every site.

At the altered site it can get stuck. We will write the smallest arithmetic that makes both facts true.

The same step, again and again

Pick a starting atom. Step a distance \(a\) to the next identical atom. Then take another step. Then another. The allowed landing spots are

\[ \ldots,\; -2a,\; -a,\; 0,\; a,\; 2a,\; \ldots \]

Nothing else is allowed if you want the crystal to look unchanged after the slide. That repeating set of landing spots is a lattice.

In one dimension it is the set \(a\mathbb{Z}\) for a fixed length \(a>0\). We take this as the definition.

In one dimension the step \(a\) is the lattice constant, measured in metres. Later crystals will have two or three independent steps. The idea does not change: a lattice is the list of slides that leave the pattern looking identical.

Hence two crystals may share a lattice and still disagree about the glue. The lattice names the legal slides, not the atoms themselves. Drop that distinction and you will treat every crystal with spacing \(a\) as the same object.

A leak to the next site

Give each lattice point one local orbital for the electron, written \(|n\rangle\). The label \(n\) is an integer: the electron is on site \(n\). The orbitals do not overlap,

\[ \langle m|n\rangle=\delta_{mn}, \]

where the Kronecker delta is 1 when the two labels match and 0 otherwise. Chapter 1 already taught that move. A bra meets a ket and returns a number.

The electron is not nailed to its site. It can leak onto a neighbor. The energy of that leak is the hopping \(t\), with \(t>0\), measured in joules or electronvolts.

Take \(N\) sites and identify site \(N\) with site \(0\). There is now no end of the chain to argue about.

Every site has two neighbors. The only processes we allow are “leave this site and appear on the next one,” and the reverse.

The energy operator that opens only those neighboring hops is

\[ H_0=-t\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(|n\rangle\langle n+1|+|n+1\rangle\langle n|\bigr), \]

with the indices wrapping around. The minus sign is a convention. It puts the lowest energy on the longest, gentlest wave.

Hence the electron is not an eigenstate of site number: \(H_0\) mixes neighbors. If \(t=0\), every site is an eigenstate and nothing propagates.

A model organized around local orbitals and nearest-neighbor leaks is often called tight binding. It is an approximation organized around that limit, not a rival law of nature [R067].

A range of allowed energies

Because every site is equivalent, try a state that advances by the same phase at every step:

\[ |k\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{ikna}|n\rangle. \]

The number \(k\) is a wavevector, measured in inverse metres, so the product \(ka\) has no units. It is a phase per step along the lattice. It is not a point on the two-level sphere from earlier chapters.

The chain closes on itself, so the phase after \(N\) steps must come back to one:

\[ e^{ikNa}=1. \]

That forces \(k=2\pi m/(Na)\) for integer \(m\). Act with the energy operator. Each hop contributes a neighboring phase factor, and you get

\[ H_0|k\rangle=-t\bigl(e^{ika}+e^{-ika}\bigr)|k\rangle=-2t\cos(ka)|k\rangle. \]

So the energy of this wave is

\[ E(k)=-2t\cos(ka). \]

As \(k\) runs through one complete set of distinct values, \(-\pi/a<k\leq\pi/a\), the cosine runs from \(-1\) to \(1\). The allowed energies therefore fill the interval \([-2t,2t]\).

That filled interval is one band. Its width is \(4t\), which has units of energy, as it must.

Hence translation symmetry does not pick a single energy. It picks a continuous range, labelled by \(k\).

The wave is spread out. Each site carries probability

\[ \bigl|1/\sqrt{N}\bigr|^2=1/N. \]

The electron is not jogging from site to site in a classical orbit. The stationary wavefunction simply has support on every site.

Double the chain and you halve the probability on each site. Drop translation symmetry and this labelling by \(k\) is no longer forced.

One site that is different

Now change the on-site energy of site \(0\) by an amount \(U\), also measured in energy:

\[ H=H_0+U|0\rangle\langle0|. \]

That local change is a defect. We take this as the definition: a departure from the ideal lattice, here the simplest possible, one number on one site.

For an infinite chain, look for a reflection-symmetric state whose amplitudes are

\[ \psi_n=\langle n|\psi\rangle=A\lambda^{|n|},\qquad |\lambda|<1. \]

The constant \(A\) will normalize the state. The inequality \(|\lambda|<1\) is the whole demand that the amplitude fall as you walk away.

Away from the defect the eigenvalue equation only sees the two neighboring hops. For \(n\geq 1\),

\[ E\,A\lambda^n=-t\bigl(A\lambda^{n-1}+A\lambda^{n+1}\bigr), \]

so

\[ E=-t\bigl(\lambda+\lambda^{-1}\bigr). \]

At site \(0\) the extra energy \(U\) is present, and the two neighbors are both \(A\lambda\):

\[ E=U-2t\lambda. \]

Set the two expressions for \(E\) equal:

\[ U=t\bigl(\lambda-\lambda^{-1}\bigr). \]

Multiply through by \(\lambda\) and you have a quadratic. Of the two roots, exactly one has magnitude below 1. Its magnitude and the corresponding bound-state energy are

\[ |\lambda|=\frac{\sqrt{U^2+4t^2}-|U|}{2t}, \qquad E_{\mathrm d}=\operatorname{sgn}(U)\sqrt{U^2+4t^2}. \]

The symbol \(E_{\mathrm d}\) is the defect-state energy. The sign function \(\operatorname{sgn}(U)\) is \(+1\) when \(U\) is positive and \(-1\) when \(U\) is negative.

Therefore \(|E_{\mathrm d}|>2t\): the defect state sits outside the clean chain’s band. For \(U<0\) it sits below the band and the amplitudes keep the same sign.

For \(U>0\) it sits above the band and the signs alternate.

Hence a single altered site, on an infinite chain, binds a normalizable state whose energy is forbidden to the traveling waves of \(H_0\).

The falling envelope can be written \(e^{-|n|a/\xi}\). That defines a localization length \(\xi\):

\[ \xi=-\frac{a}{\ln|\lambda|} =\frac{a}{\operatorname{arsinh}(|U|/2t)}. \]

Both \(a\) and \(\xi\) have units of length. The logarithm and the inverse hyperbolic sine eat dimensionless arguments. That check catches the common habit of stuffing an energy into a logarithm without dividing by another energy.

For a concrete choice, let \(U=-t\). Then

\[ E_{\mathrm d}=-\sqrt{5}\,t,\qquad |\lambda|=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}\approx0.618, \qquad \xi\approx2.08a. \]

Normalization gives

\[ |A|^2=\frac{1-|\lambda|^2}{1+|\lambda|^2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}. \]

About \(0.447\) of the probability sits on the defect site in this toy calculation. The rest forms exponentially decreasing tails.

The total probability is still exactly 1. [Theory] These numbers are consequences of the chosen one-dimensional energy recipe, not predictions for diamond, sapphire, or any other real host.

If \(U=0\), then \(|\lambda|=1\) and nothing decays. If you drop \(|\lambda|<1\) on the infinite chain, the candidate is not normalizable. On a finite ring the tail wraps; the state can still pile up near site \(0\), but it is not the infinite-chain bound state we just solved.

Why a forbidden energy cannot travel

A clean-chain energy satisfies \(E=-2t\cos(ka)\). For \(|E|\leq 2t\), a real \(k\) exists, and \(e^{ikna}\) has constant magnitude: it propagates. For \(|E|>2t\), no real \(k\) works.

Write \(k=i\kappa\) below the band, with inverse length \(\kappa>0\). Then

\[ e^{ikna}=e^{-\kappa na}. \]

The missing real wavevector becomes an exponential tail. Hence the defect has not erected an infinitely hard wall. It has placed the state where the host offers no traveling channel.

This bound state is localized, but it is not yet an in-gap state. The chain has only one band.

The extra level lives outside that band, not in a window between two bands. We will build the window in a moment.

Drop the mismatch \(|E|>2t\) and the same exponential ansatz is unnecessary: a real \(k\) already exists.

A plane wave times a repeating pattern

The chain was discrete. A real crystal is a continuous medium whose potential repeats:

\[ V(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=V(\mathbf r) \]

for every lattice translation \(\mathbf R\). Bloch’s theorem says an energy eigenfunction can then be written

\[ \psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r), \]

where \(\mathbf r\) is position, \(\mathbf k\) is the crystal wavevector, \(n\) labels which band you are in, and the leftover function repeats in every cell: \(u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)\) [R066]. The dot product \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r\) is dimensionless.

That object is a Bloch wave. The name is worth keeping because Felix Bloch wrote the crystal-wave theorem in 1929, and because the same last name already labels the two-level sphere from earlier chapters.

They are different objects. A Bloch wave is a plane-wave phase pattern multiplied by structure that repeats inside each cell.

The tight-binding wave \(|k\rangle\) above is the discrete version. Other useful cartoons start from nearly free electrons instead of from local orbitals. They are approximations organized around different limits, not rival laws of nature.

Hence periodicity of \(V\) does not force a plane wave by itself. It forces a plane wave times a cell-periodic leftover. Drop the periodicity of \(V\) and Bloch’s theorem does not apply.

You can add Bloch waves together to make a packet that sits near one cell. Those packets are sometimes called Wannier functions.

Whether you can choose them to fall off exponentially also carries extra information about the band; our elementary chain has no such obstruction [R068]. A defect-bound state is different again.

Translation symmetry is broken, and the envelope is pinned near a particular site.

A gap is a missing interval of energy

Our one-orbital chain has no internal window. It is one continuous band.

The smallest lattice that does have a window uses two unequal sites, \(A\) and \(B\), in each repeated block. Give them on-site energies \(+\Delta\) and \(-\Delta\), where \(\Delta\) is an energy, and connect nearest neighbors with the same hopping \(t\).

In the \((A,B)\) listing the energy operator at wavevector \(k\) is the two-by-two matrix

\[ H(k)= \begin{pmatrix} \Delta & -t(1+e^{-ika})\\ -t(1+e^{ika}) & -\Delta \end{pmatrix}. \]

Solving the two-by-two eigenvalue problem gives

\[ E_{\pm}(k)=\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2+4t^2\cos^2(ka/2)}. \]

The upper and lower bands never meet when \(\Delta\neq 0\). Their closest approach is at the edge of the \(k\) interval and has size

\[ E_{\mathrm g}=2|\Delta|. \]

That empty window is the gap. \(E_{\mathrm g}\) is an energy. It is an interval with no host traveling wave, not a hole in the crystal.

Hence two sites per repeat, with \(\Delta\neq 0\), split one band into two and leave a forbidden interval between them. If \(\Delta=0\), the two bands touch and \(E_{\mathrm g}=0\).

At zero temperature the lower band is the one electrons fill. People call it the valence band, with top edge \(E_{\mathrm v}\).

The next available band is the conduction band, with bottom edge \(E_{\mathrm c}\). Then \(E_{\mathrm g}=E_{\mathrm c}-E_{\mathrm v}>0\).

A state that cannot leave the altered site

Change one atom, remove it, or add a local orbital. In the atomic limit \(t=0\), a defect orbital whose on-site energy \(E_{\mathrm d}\) sits between \(-|\Delta|\) and \(+|\Delta|\) is perfectly local. Turn the hops back on and the state grows tails.

If the full eigenvalue remains between the two continua, the host still has no real traveling Bloch wave at that energy, so the tails die away. This is the gapped twin of the solved chain.

The decaying, normalizable wave that lives in the window is a localized in-gap state. Most of the probability sits near a bounded region, and the energy sits where the perfect host cannot carry a traveling wave.

An extended state is the opposite kind of object. It occupies a number of cells that grows with the sample.

Define the isolation margins

\[ \delta_{\mathrm v}=E_{\mathrm d}-E_{\mathrm v},\qquad \delta_{\mathrm c}=E_{\mathrm c}-E_{\mathrm d}. \]

Both must be positive for a one-electron level to lie in the gap. A wider \(E_{\mathrm g}\) permits, but does not require, larger margins.

Stronger coupling to the host can broaden or shift the level. A level inside a band becomes a resonance rather than a truly bound state.

Hence a gap is room, not tenancy. A weakly bound level near a band edge may stretch over many cells.

A level sitting farther from both edges often hugs the altered site more tightly. People say “shallow” and “deep” for those two habits.

Deep means energy within the gap, not physical depth below a surface.

That is the attraction of a wide-gap host: it supplies a large possible energy window in which a defect level may sit away from both continua. [Theory] A wide gap does not create a suitable defect, guarantee a spin, or make a qubit.

It merely makes energetic isolation more plausible. Candidate defects must still be judged by charge-state stability, wavefunctions, lattice relaxation, optical transitions, and coupling to noise [R069]; [R070]; [R071].

The nuclei also shake

The nuclei do not sit nailed at their equilibrium positions. For small displacements their collective normal modes are harmonic oscillators.

A quantum of one such normal mode is a phonon. It is a discrete packet of lattice vibration, the sound analogue of a photon.

A phonon mode is labelled by a wavevector \(\mathbf q\) and a branch \(\nu\). It has angular frequency \(\omega_{\mathbf q\nu}\) in radians per second, and energy

\[ E_{\mathrm{phonon}}=\hbar\omega_{\mathbf q\nu}\bigl(n_{\mathbf q\nu}+\tfrac12\bigr), \]

where \(n_{\mathbf q\nu}\) is a nonnegative integer and \(\hbar\) has units of joule-seconds.

Because electronic energies depend on nuclear positions, a defect electron couples to phonons. That coupling can create optical sidebands, shift energies, dephase a superposition, and enable nonradiative jumps by emitting several phonons.

[Theory] Quantitative nonradiative rates need potential-energy surfaces, vibrational modes, and electron-phonon matrix elements. A band diagram alone does not supply them [R072].

Hence a static lattice was a hypothesis, not a feature of the laboratory. Drop the dependence of electronic energy on nuclear positions and the electron does not couple to phonons.

Cooling reduces how many thermal phonons are already present. It does not freeze the nuclei into mathematical points.

What a real crystal adds

The tight-binding chain contains one electron, one orbital per site, static nuclei, nearest-neighbor hopping, and an adjustable scalar \(U\). A laboratory sample contains many electrons and nuclei, surfaces, strain, impurities, isotopes, electric fields, and finite temperature. The toy model teaches a mechanism, not a materials forecast.

A real calculation usually begins from nuclear species and positions and treats the electronic structure with an approximation such as density-functional theory, often in a periodically repeated supercell. Charged defects need careful electrostatic finite-size corrections.

Atomic coordinates must relax. Band-gap errors can put defect levels in the wrong place.

Reviews by Van de Walle and Neugebauer and by Freysoldt and collaborators explain why defect formation energies, charge corrections, chemical potentials, and transition levels require more care than reading a dot from a band sketch [R069]; [R070].

There are also several different “energies of a defect,” and swapping them causes trouble:

  • A single-particle orbital energy labels an orbital in an approximate independent-particle calculation.

  • A thermodynamic charge-transition level comes from total-energy differences between relaxed charge states. It tells where changing the electron chemical potential changes the stable charge.

  • A vertical optical transition happens faster than nuclei rearrange, so it connects states at approximately fixed nuclear geometry.

  • A zero-phonon optical transition connects vibrational ground levels. Phonon-assisted transitions make sidebands.

  • A spin excitation can occur within one electronic configuration and may be far lower in energy than an optical transition.

These quantities need not coincide. Kohn–Sham eigenvalues are useful ingredients, but most are not automatically measured quasiparticle addition or removal energies [R069]; [R070]. Correlation can also make a many-electron defect state qualitatively richer than “one electron in one orbital.”

[Experiment] Spectroscopy can reveal absorption or emission lines, phonon sidebands, ionization thresholds, and spin resonances. Those observations constrain a defect model, but assigning a microscopic structure generally combines experiment with electronic-structure calculations. [Theory] Systematic searches for solid-state spin defects therefore use several criteria at once: a suitable host, a stable charge state and spin, levels separated from host bands, controllable transitions, and tolerable coupling to the environment [R071].

A wide-gap material helps in three limited ways. First, it offers more energetic room for levels that are far from both band edges.

Second, visible or near-infrared transitions between defect states can occur without necessarily exciting carriers across the host gap. Third, thermal exchange with bands can be reduced when the relevant activation energy is large compared with \(k_{\mathrm B}T\), where \(k_{\mathrm B}\) is Boltzmann’s constant and \(T\) is absolute temperature.

None of that is automatic. The actual level positions, optical selection rules, and nonradiative pathways decide the outcome.

Ways to get this wrong

Suppose you draw a line in the gap and call it a localized state. A line on a schematic is a hypothesis.

Localization has to come from a wavefunction, an inverse participation measure, spatial charge or spin density, or experimentally supported modelling. A state near an edge may be very extended.

A computed state may also be an artifact of a finite supercell.

Suppose the host gap is wide and you conclude that every defect electron is trapped. A defect may introduce no gap state, a shallow state next to a band, or a resonance sitting inside a band.

It may prefer an unwanted charge state. The gap provides room, not tenancy.

Suppose you treat the toy chain as the electronic structure. Our \(t\), \(U\), and one basis orbital omit three-dimensional bonding, multiple orbitals, spin, Coulomb repulsion, screening, spin-orbit coupling, and nuclear relaxation.

Fitting a cartoon after seeing a result does not make it predictive. The value of the model is that it isolates the relation among propagation, forbidden energies, and exponential decay.

Suppose you find one in-gap orbital and declare a qubit. A qubit needs two controllable states, initialization, coherent gates, readout, and acceptable leakage and noise.

The orbital may be empty, doubly occupied, chemically unstable, optically dark, or strongly coupled to phonons. Chapter 3’s operational definition still applies.

Suppose “localized” is taken to mean isolated from everything. Spatial localization suppresses some overlaps, but the state still couples through electric fields, magnetic fields, strain, phonons, photons, nuclear spins, and exponentially small or dipolar interactions with other defects. Those couplings may be useful or harmful depending on what you are building.

Suppose a Bloch wave is a point on the Bloch sphere. A Bloch wave is a crystal wave labelled by \(\mathbf k\).

The Bloch sphere is a picture of a two-level atom. Do not lend them each other’s geometry.

A localized defect orbital is a microscopic electronic state. A spin on that defect becomes a physical qubit only after control and readout are demonstrated.

It is not an encoded qubit, an emergent quasiparticle, or topological order. Periodic boundary conditions in our calculation are a mathematical convenience, not a claim of protection.

Check yourself

Show that \(H_0|k\rangle=-2t\cos(ka)|k\rangle\).

Each hop multiplies by a neighboring phase \(e^{\pm ika}\). Adding them gives \(-t(e^{ika}+e^{-ika})=-2t\cos(ka)\).

What fails if the defect ansatz drops \(|\lambda|<1\)?

The amplitudes no longer decay, so the candidate is not a normalizable bound state on the infinite chain.

Show that \(|E_{\mathrm d}|>2t\) whenever \(U\neq 0\).

\(E_{\mathrm d}=\operatorname{sgn}(U)\sqrt{U^2+4t^2}\), and \(\sqrt{U^2+4t^2}>2t\) as soon as \(U\neq 0\).

What fails if \(\Delta=0\) in the two-site cell?

The two bands touch, \(E_{\mathrm g}=0\), and there is no internal window for an in-gap level.

What does a wide host gap guarantee?

Only a larger possible energy window. It does not guarantee a defect level, localization, a stable charge state, a spin, an optical transition, or a qubit.

Why can a band diagram be insufficient even when its level positions are correct?

It omits wavefunctions, occupations, many-electron multiplets, lattice relaxation, transition matrix elements, and environmental couplings.

You now have a lattice, a band of allowed energies, a forbidden window, a state that can sit in that window, and a name for the lattice’s vibrations. Next we look at the actual missing sites — substitutions, vacancies, and the mess they drag in.

Sources

  • [R066] F. Bloch, “Über die Quantenmechanik der Elektronen in Kristallgittern,” Zeitschrift für Physik 52, 555–600 (1929). DOI: 10.1007/BF01339455.

  • [R067] J. C. Slater and G. F. Koster, “Simplified LCAO Method for the Periodic Potential Problem,” Physical Review 94, 1498–1524 (1954). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.94.1498.

  • [R068] W. Kohn, “Analytic Properties of Bloch Waves and Wannier Functions,” Physical Review 115, 809–821 (1959). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.115.809.

  • [R069] C. G. Van de Walle and J. Neugebauer, “First-principles calculations for defects and impurities: Applications to III-nitrides,” Journal of Applied Physics 95, 3851–3879 (2004). DOI: 10.1063/1.1682673.

  • [R070] C. Freysoldt, B. Grabowski, T. Hickel, J. Neugebauer, G. Kresse, A. Janotti, and C. G. Van de Walle, “First-principles calculations for point defects in solids,” Reviews of Modern Physics 86, 253–305 (2014). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.86.253.

  • [R071] J. R. Weber, W. F. Koehl, J. B. Varley, A. Janotti, B. B. Buckley, C. G. Van de Walle, and D. D. Awschalom, “Quantum computing with defects,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107, 8513–8518 (2010). DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1003052107.

  • [R072] A. Alkauskas, Q. Yan, and C. G. Van de Walle, “First-principles theory of nonradiative carrier capture via multiphonon emission,” Physical Review B 90, 075202 (2014). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.90.075202.

Chapter 6 — An empty site is not a leftover spin

Replace one atom in a perfect crystal by a different element. Leave a neighboring site empty.

Those two accidents can sit next to each other and become one object. An extra atom wedged off the regular sites is a different object.

A whole line of the pattern that has slipped is ruder still.

None of those is automatically a leftover spin. None is automatically a qubit. We will sort the damage by geometry, then sit with one famous pair — a nitrogen atom next to a missing carbon — until charge, spin, strain, and nearby nuclei have names of their own.

Six kinds of damage

A perfect crystal repeats a block of atoms. Anything that breaks that repetition is a structural defect. The word names the geometry. It does not name a color, a spin, or a computer bit.

Sort the damage first by how much space it occupies.

Kind | What happened | What the electrons often notice | What not to assume | |

Wrong atom on a lattice site | A host atom is replaced by a different element | A different valence, size, electronegativity, and local potential | That it leaves an unpaired spin. It may just donate or accept charge. | |

Empty site | A lattice site has no atom | Neighboring leftover bonds may sit in the gap and the neighbors may lean in | That reconstruction has not paired every electron. Charge matters. | |

Extra atom stuffed in | An atom sits off the regular sites | Strong local squeeze and new bonds; the extra atom may wander | That there is only one geometry or one charge. | |

Two accidents bound together | Nearby defects lock into one structural unit | New symmetry and molecular-like combinations of the leftover bonds | That the pair is the sum of the two isolated level diagrams. | |

A slipped line | A one-dimensional line defect, marked by a Burgers vector — how far the lattice slipped | A messy core plus a long-range elastic field; sometimes a band of core states | That the whole line is one localized emitter. | |

A mis-stacked plane | The usual stacking of planes is interrupted | A local change of stacking, a shift of the bands, and an extended squeeze | That a sheet of electronic states is a point-like two-level system. | |

A substitution occupies a normal lattice site in place of a host atom. A vacancy is an empty site.

An interstitial occupies an extra non-lattice site. A bound pair is two of those close enough that you have to solve them together.

Slipped lines and mis-stacked planes are ruder: they alter a whole line or a whole plane.

Hence “how damaged is the crystal?” is the wrong first question. The useful question is what energies and shapes the combined host-plus-damage system actually has.

A pointlike accident can make a localized orbital in a wide gap. It can also make a shallow state that melts into a band, a closed shell with total spin zero, or a trap that dumps energy without shining.

Extended damage can trap carriers, squeeze nearby point centers, or just add noise. The table tells you where to begin, not where the calculation ends [R070]; [R073].

A frozen squeeze of the lattice is not a seventh species of defect. Neither is a vibration. Those two will come back as characters, not as extra rows.

An empty site is not a leftover spin

Take the empty site. Three or four neighboring atoms now have a bond that used to point at the missing atom and now points at nothing. It is tempting to say “there is a dangling electron, so there is a spin.”

The neighbors often lean in and remake the bonds. Electrons can also leave or arrive until the whole object is cheaper. What remains may be a closed shell with every spin paired.

The integer that decides this is the charge state: how many electrons the damaged region has, relative to the neutral atom count. The name is worth keeping because the same empty site with one extra electron and the same empty site with one electron missing are different objects. They can have different shapes, different colors, and different total spins.

Hence geometry does not fix spin. Before anyone draws a little arrow on the vacancy, ask how many electrons are actually there. Drop the charge label and you have mixed several distinct objects under one drawing.

Nitrogen next to a missing carbon

We need one object we can finish on paper. Replace one carbon atom in diamond by nitrogen and remove a neighboring carbon. That pair is famous because its leftover symmetry is visible, not because every vacancy-plus-impurity pair behaves this way.

The line from the nitrogen through the empty site picks a preferred axis, usually one of diamond’s \([111]\) directions. In the ideal unsqueezed structure the three leftover carbon neighbors are equivalent. You can rotate by \(120^\circ\) around the axis, or reflect through any of three mirrors, and the picture looks the same.

The list of those leftover rotations and reflections is the local point group. For this pair it is called \(C_{3v}\) [R074]; [R075].

Hence every later coupling that hopes to be allowed has to respect the same leftover symmetries, and every leftover symmetry we break will show up as a split line. Leftover symmetry does not compute the energy scale. If the three carbons stop being equivalent, \(C_{3v}\) is already gone, and degeneracies that the point group had protected need not survive.

Combinations the three carbons allow

Let \(|c_1\rangle\), \(|c_2\rangle\), and \(|c_3\rangle\) be the three carbon leftover-bond orbitals that face the empty site. The combinations that know about the threefold axis are

\[ |a_C\rangle=\frac{|c_1\rangle+|c_2\rangle+|c_3\rangle}{\sqrt 3}, \]

\[ |e_x\rangle=\frac{2|c_1\rangle-|c_2\rangle-|c_3\rangle}{\sqrt 6}, \qquad |e_y\rangle=\frac{|c_2\rangle-|c_3\rangle}{\sqrt 2}. \]

The first combination looks the same after a \(120^\circ\) turn. Call it \(a\).

The other two mix into each other under that turn, so they must share an energy as long as the three carbons stay equivalent. Call that pair \(e\).

The nitrogen leftover orbital also looks like an \(a\). It mixes with \(|a_C\rangle\) and produces two \(a_1\) combinations at different energies. The carbon \(e\) pair has no nitrogen partner of matching shape in this small basis, so it stays doubly degenerate while ideal \(C_{3v}\) holds.

That is the first bridge from a drawing to a level diagram:

N substitution + neighboring vacancy
|
v
C3v symmetry
|
+--------+--------+
| |
two a1 levels one e doublet

Hence leftover symmetry predicts which degeneracies are allowed and which mixings are forbidden. Real orbitals leak past four leftover bonds, and their energies need an electronic-structure calculation.

Symmetry does not supply the energy scale [R070]; [R075]. Drop the threefold axis and the \(e\) pair is no longer required to share an energy.

Count the leftover electrons

Geometry is not occupancy. The negatively charged version of this pair, written NV\(^{-}\), is described by six electrons in the configuration

\[ a_1(1)^2a_1(2)^2e^2. \]

The two filled \(a_1\) orbitals are closed shells. Two electrons remain in the \(e\) pair. Coulomb repulsion and exchange prefer those two to line up, giving a spin-triplet ground set with total electron spin \(S=1\), conventionally labeled \({}^{3}A_2\).

That conclusion is not hiding in the drawing of an empty lattice site. It follows from charge state, orbital order, and the interacting many-electron problem [R074]; [R075]. [Theory]

The set of many-electron states that share that spin and that leftover symmetry is a multiplet. It names a whole family of levels, not one leftover bond and not one chosen pair of levels.

Hence spin is not “the vacancy.” Spin is what the leftover electrons do once charge and orbital order are fixed. Change the charge, or invert two orbital energies, and a different multiplet can sit on the same atoms.

A splitting with the magnet off

For the ground triplet, a useful energy rule written in frequency units is

\[ \frac{H_{\mathrm{gs}}}{h} =D\!\left[S_z^2-\frac{S(S+1)}{3}\right] +E\left(S_x^2-S_y^2\right) +\frac{\mu_B}{h}\,\mathbf B\!\cdot\!\mathbf g\!\cdot\!\mathbf S. \]

Here \(H_{\mathrm{gs}}\) is energy and \(h\) is Planck’s constant, so each term on the right is a frequency. \(S_x\), \(S_y\), and \(S_z\) are dimensionless spin-1 operators.

\(D\) and \(E\) are zero-field-splitting frequencies in hertz. \(\mu_B\) is the Bohr magneton in joules per tesla, \(\mathbf B\) is magnetic field in tesla, and \(\mathbf g\) is the dimensionless electron \(g\)-tensor.

The first term separates \(m_s=0\) from \(m_s=\pm1\) even when no magnet is on. That gap is the zero-field splitting. It is a spin splitting, not the orbital splitting we will meet when neighbors stop being a sphere.

The second term appears when a sideways squeeze, or any other leftover-symmetry breaker, distinguishes \(x\) from \(y\). The third term is the magnet talking to the electron spin.

For NV\(^{-}\) near room temperature, the axial splitting is about \(D=2.87\ \mathrm{GHz}\) [R074]; [R076]. [Experiment] The units check: multiplying \(2.87\times10^9\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\) by \(h\) gives an energy.

The ideal \(C_{3v}\) model has \(E=0\). A real center commonly has a small sideways term.

Hence the magnet-off spectrum of this triplet is already split, and the size of that split is a measured frequency, not a drawing. Writing the rule does not mean “and therefore this is a qubit.” If \(D=0\) and \(E=0\), the three spin projections meet at one energy until a magnet pulls them apart.

Choosing two levels is still not a device

A magnetic field along the defect axis can pull \(m_s=+1\) away from \(m_s=-1\). You may then choose, for example, \(|0\rangle=|m_s=0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle=|m_s=-1\rangle\) as a two-level working space and drive it with a resonant microwave magnetic field.

NV\(^{-}\) also has a sharp optical line between the triplet ground and excited families near \(637\ \mathrm{nm}\), or about \(1.945\ \mathrm{eV}\) [R074]. [Experiment] A quick check uses \(hc\approx1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\):

\[ \frac{hc}{\lambda}\approx\frac{1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{637\ \mathrm{nm}} \approx1.95\ \mathrm{eV}. \]

Spin-dependent quiet pathways through intermediate singlet states let light pump the spin into a preferred level and make the fluorescence depend on which level you are on. Those pathways, plus charge-state preparation, microwave control, and photon collection, are what turn part of the spectrum into a laboratory qubit [R074]. [Experiment]

Name the layers so they cannot swap clothes. “Nitrogen next to a vacancy” is a structural pair.

“NV\(^{-}\)” adds a charge state. “\({}^{3}A_2\)” is a many-electron multiplet.

“The \(m_s=0,-1\) pair” is a chosen two-level subspace. “A qubit” means that subspace can be initialized, steered, read out, and kept isolated enough to finish the job.

Those are related sentences. They are not synonyms.

Hence two levels in a spectrum are a stage. Drop initialization, control, readout, or charge stability, and the stage is still not a device.

How expensive is the damage?

Suppose you want to know whether the crystal would rather host this accident. Compare the energy of a box of atoms that includes the damage with the energy of a perfect box.

Then pay or refund the atoms you added or removed, and pay or refund the electrons. The leftover is the formation energy.

For defect \(D\) in charge state \(q\),

\[ E_f(D^q)=E_{\mathrm{tot}}(D^q)-E_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathrm{bulk}) -\sum_i n_i\mu_i+q(E_F+E_{\mathrm{VBM}})+E_{\mathrm{corr}}. \]

Every term is an energy, usually in electronvolts. \(E_{\mathrm{tot}}(D^q)\) and \(E_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathrm{bulk})\) are total energies of the damaged and perfect simulation cells.

\(n_i\) counts atoms of species \(i\) added to the cell, and \(\mu_i\) is that species’ chemical potential. \(E_F\) is the electron Fermi energy measured upward from the valence-band maximum; \(E_{\mathrm{VBM}}\) places that maximum in the total-energy reference.

\(E_{\mathrm{corr}}\) patches artifacts of a finite cell.

Sign conventions for \(n_i\) vary, so a paper’s convention has to be checked rather than admired from across the room [R070].

Hence formation energy predicts thermodynamic favorability under stated chemical and electronic conditions. It does not predict implantation yield, kinetic trapping, optical brightness, or coherence.

Charge-transition levels mark where different \(q\) values swap which one is cheaper. A compensating impurity, a surface, a gate, or a lamp can therefore take the same atomic geometry from spin-active to spinless.

Same geometry. Different occupancy. Different story. If you omit the \(q(E_F+E_{\mathrm{VBM}})\) term, you have compared two charge states as if the surrounding electron reservoir were free.

Neighbors that are not a sphere

A free atom does not know which way is up. Neighbors pick directions.

The five \(d\)-shaped clouds that shared one energy on an isolated atom split into a pair and a trio once the neighbors sit at the corners of a tetrahedron or an octahedron. Which set lies lower depends on the geometry and the bonding.

That non-spherical electrostatic and covalent environment is the crystal field. Write \(H_{\mathrm{CF}}\) for its contribution.

Its eigenstates are orbital combinations labeled by leftover-symmetry names such as \(A\), \(E\), or \(T\). A further low-symmetry dent can split an \(E\) or \(T\) family again.

Hence crystal-field splitting is an orbital energy splitting. It is not the spin-triplet zero-field splitting \(D\), even though both can be present with the magnet off.

One rearranges clouds. The other rearranges spin levels of an already chosen multiplet.

If the neighbors were a perfect sphere, the five \(d\) clouds would still share one energy.

When orbit tugs on spin

An electron cloud that is circulating is a tiny magnet, and the electron’s own spin is another tiny magnet. They notice each other. In an isolated-family shorthand the coupling is

\[ H_{\mathrm{SO}}=\lambda\,\mathbf L\cdot\mathbf S, \]

where \(\mathbf L\) and \(\mathbf S\) are dimensionless orbital and spin angular-momentum operators and \(\lambda\) is an energy. A real defect often needs a tensor, or a version written in the leftover-symmetry language.

This is the spin–orbit term. It is a coupling, not a quality badge.

If the crystal field leaves an orbital degeneracy, spin–orbit can act at first order and strongly organize the levels. If the orbital ground state is a single nondegenerate cloud, orbital angular momentum is said to be quenched.

Spin–orbit still sneaks in by virtually mixing excited orbitals. It can make the \(g\)-factors direction-dependent, feed the zero-field splitting, and write spin-selective optical rules [R073]; [R075].

[Theory]

Hence the same term can help you address the spin with light and can make the spin a better antenna for lattice motion. Useful and noisy are allowed to be the same operator. If \(\lambda=0\), those first-order and virtual mixings are gone, and you have lost both the handle and the antenna.

Two unpaired electrons talking

Two or more unpaired electrons also interact as magnets. Projected into a total-spin multiplet, their dipolar and spin–orbit-mediated effects are often summarized by

\[ H_{\mathrm{SS}}=\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf D\cdot\mathbf S, \]

where \(\mathbf D\) is a zero-field-splitting tensor with energy units. In axial symmetry this reduces, up to an additive constant, to \(hD[S_z^2-S(S+1)/3]\). That is the same \(D\) we met on NV\(^{-}\).

Hence the magnet-off split of an integer-spin multiplet can come from the electrons talking to each other, not from an applied field. A half-integer spin has a leftover doublet at zero magnetic field when time-reversal is intact.

An integer spin is not guaranteed such a pair. Neither sentence is a promise of long memory.

A guaranteed doublet can still jiggle.

A magnet, and then the nuclei

An applied magnetic field adds the electron Zeeman term

\[ H_Z=\mu_B\,\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf S. \]

The leftover electron is still not alone. Some nearby nuclei have their own tiny magnets. They tug on the electron, and the electron tugs back.

If nucleus \(k\) has nuclear spin \(\mathbf I_k\), the coupling is

\[ H_{\mathrm{hf}}=\sum_k \mathbf S\cdot\mathbf A_k\cdot\mathbf I_k, \]

where \(\mathbf A_k\) is the hyperfine tensor for that nucleus, in energy units. It names a specific conversation: electron spin talking to nuclear spin.

The tensor has an approximately isotropic contact piece, sensitive to spin density at the nucleus, and an anisotropic dipolar piece. Nuclei with spin quantum number \(I_k\ge 1\) may also carry a quadrupole term \(\mathbf I_k\cdot\mathbf Q_k\cdot\mathbf I_k\), with \(\mathbf Q_k\) an energy tensor.

Hence the third character is the nucleus. Hyperfine coupling can resolve which nuclear configuration you have, store a state, or provide a conditional gate.

Uncontrolled host nuclei instead kick the electron transition around and chew up phase. The same term is a resource when the nucleus is known and controlled, and noise when it is neither [R073].

If every nearby nucleus has \(I=0\), this conversation is silent.

A squeeze that sits still

Let \(\mathbf u(\mathbf r)\) be the lattice displacement at position \(\mathbf r\), measured in metres. For small distortions the dimensionless strain tensor is

\[ \varepsilon_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial r_j} +\frac{\partial u_j}{\partial r_i}\right). \]

That frozen dent is the fourth character, strain. It is a deformation field, not a new defect species. A defect can make static strain, feel strain you apply from outside, and — in the next section — exchange energy with vibrations.

A projected defect family responds through leftover-symmetry-allowed operators \(O_\alpha\):

\[ H_\varepsilon=\sum_\alpha g_\alpha\varepsilon_\alpha O_\alpha. \]

Here \(\varepsilon_\alpha\) are symmetry-adapted combinations of strain components, \(O_\alpha\) are dimensionless orbital or spin operators, and the susceptibilities \(g_\alpha\) have energy units. Dimensionless strain times energy is energy, as it must be.

Axial strain may shift a transition without lifting a doublet. Transverse strain may lower leftover symmetry, split orbitals, or mix spin projections.

The allowed pattern follows from the point group. The coefficients need experiment or a microscopic calculation [R077].

[Theory]

Hence a static dent is already in the energy rule before anyone mentions a vibration. If \(\varepsilon=0\), this term is absent, and leftover degeneracies that strain would have split remain.

A squeeze that wiggles

Phonons, from Chapter 5, make strain time dependent. For normal mode \(k\), write angular frequency \(\omega_k\) in radians per second and let \(b_k^\dagger\) and \(b_k\) create and destroy one quantum of that vibration. Then

\[ H_{\mathrm{ph}}=\sum_k\hbar\omega_k\left(b_k^\dagger b_k+\frac12\right), \qquad H_{\mathrm{def-ph}}=\sum_{k,\alpha}\kappa_{k\alpha} (b_k+b_k^\dagger)O_\alpha, \]

where \(\kappa_{k\alpha}\) is a coupling energy. A phonon can drive a transition when its energy and leftover symmetry fit.

One-phonon emission or absorption, two-phonon Raman processes, and thermally activated hops through higher levels can relax the spin or scramble its phase. Which process wins depends on the defect spectrum, the phonon density of states, and the temperature [R078].

[Theory]

Cooling reduces how many thermal phonons are already in the lattice. It does not erase static strain, and it does not cancel every spontaneous emission.

Hence strain sits still and phonons wiggle. They use related leftover-symmetry channels and they are not the same object. Drop the operators \(b_k\) and you have kept a frozen dent while throwing away every dynamical jump the lattice can cause.

The whole energy rule

Add the pieces that this leftover family can feel:

\[ H_{\mathrm{system}}=H_{\mathrm{CF}}+H_{\mathrm{SO}}+H_{\mathrm{SS}}+H_Z +H_{\mathrm{hf}}+H_Q+H_\varepsilon+H_{\mathrm{ph}}+H_{\mathrm{def-ph}}. \]

That sum is the working Hamiltonian. It names the energy rule, not a certificate that the defect is a device.

Not every term survives in every family. Leftover symmetry may forbid a matrix element.

Projection may squash an orbital operator to zero. An isotope may have \(I=0\).

Conversely, a term left off a neat level diagram may own the laboratory linewidth.

Hence the recipe is now visible. Start with geometry and charge.

Solve the localized orbital problem. Build the many-electron states.

Only then project into a spin or orbital family and keep the terms that family can feel. If you start from a spin Hamiltonian and work backwards, you have assumed the projection that the earlier steps were supposed to earn.

Why leftover symmetry can force a zero

Suppose states \(|i\rangle\) and \(|f\rangle\) transform under leftover-symmetry patterns \(\Gamma_i\) and \(\Gamma_f\), while a perturbation \(O\) transforms as \(\Gamma_O\). The matrix element \(\langle f|O|i\rangle\) can be nonzero only if the product \(\Gamma_f^*\otimes\Gamma_O\otimes\Gamma_i\) contains the totally symmetric pattern — the one that looks the same under every leftover rotation and reflection.

That selection rule can kill a transition exactly in the ideal symmetry. If the product allows the transition, leftover symmetry says only “possibly nonzero.” It does not supply the wavefunction overlap, the coupling strength, or the lifetime. Strain can mix patterns and turn a forbidden matrix element into an allowed one.

Hence symmetry predicts zeros. It does not predict numbers. Drop the leftover symmetry — by strain, by a nearby defect, by a surface — and a former zero is no longer guaranteed.

What the laboratory actually has

A fabricated sample contains a distribution, not a single perfect defect.

[Experiment] Electron-paramagnetic resonance sees spin splittings and hyperfine structure. Photoluminescence locates optical transitions.

Optically detected magnetic resonance ties fluorescence to spin resonance. Stress and electric-field spectroscopy test leftover-symmetry assignments.

Agreement among these measurements and many-electron calculations supports a level model more strongly than any single colored line in a spectrum [R073]; [R074]; [R075].

The local environment varies from site to site. Isotopes change hyperfine coupling.

Residual impurities shift charge stability. Surfaces and interfaces bend the bands.

Implantation produces vacancies, extra atoms, and extended damage on top of the intended center. Annealing moves and recombines defects, sometimes building the pair you wanted and sometimes building an excellent quiet recombination center instead.

Slipped lines and mis-stacked planes add a spatially varying squeeze and may bring their own electronic states.

Ideal leftover symmetry is a reference point. Small perturbations split degenerate lines and rotate eigenstates.

That is not always bad: strain can tune two emitters into resonance, and hyperfine coupling can provide a nuclear memory. Reproducible engineering still requires measuring the perturbation and leaving it in the energy rule.

The NV example is unusually well characterized. It is not a generic promise about vacancy complexes.

Reviews of candidate spin defects emphasize a pile of simultaneous requirements: a stable charge state, suitable spin and optical transitions, controllable initialization and readout, long-enough coherence, and compatibility with fabrication and photonics [R073]. [Theory/Experiment synthesis] A material may satisfy three and fail the fourth with admirable consistency.

Ways to get this wrong

Suppose a vacancy leaves a dangling electron, and therefore a spin. Reconstruction and charge transfer may close the shell. Determine the charge state and the many-electron occupancy.

Suppose an in-gap level is a qubit. One level is not two controllable states. Even two levels need initialization, coherent control, readout, and tolerable leakage and noise.

Suppose a color center is a spin center. A color center absorbs or emits visible light. It can have total spin zero. Conversely, a spin-active center may have no useful optical cycle.

Suppose crystal-field splitting and zero-field splitting are the same. Crystal fields primarily split orbitals. Zero-field splitting separates spin sublevels and can come from electron spin–spin interaction and from spin–orbit-mediated effects.

Suppose static strain is a phonon. Static strain is a time-independent deformation in the model you wrote. Phonons are quantized dynamical modes. They couple through related leftover-symmetry channels and they leave different experimental fingerprints.

Suppose a slipped line is a large point defect. Its line core and long-range elastic field make it extended.

Likewise, a mis-stacked plane is planar. Their electronic states need not be spatially isolated two-level systems.

Suppose density-functional orbitals are the multiplet spectrum. A one-electron orbital diagram is useful input, but exchange, correlation, excited-state relaxation, and spin–orbit coupling determine many-electron states. Quantitative optical and spin assignments need an appropriate many-body treatment and experimental checks [R070]; [R075].

Suppose leftover point-group symmetry is the same protection as a many-body topological phase. Local leftover symmetry can forbid a matrix element until the symmetry is broken.

A many-body topological phase is a different object, with emergent excitations and global sectors. They solve different problems.

A vacancy, slipped line, or mis-stacked plane may be called a topological defect in the classical theory of ordered media because it carries a winding or a Burgers vector. That vocabulary does not hand you quantum topological order, anyons, or a protected logical qubit.

Arranging many structural defects on a lattice supplies microscopic degrees of freedom. Only a demonstrated many-body Hamiltonian and a phase analysis could establish an emergent topological phase.

Check yourself

Show that \(|a_C\rangle\) is unchanged by a cyclic permutation of the three carbon orbitals, while \(|e_x\rangle\) and \(|e_y\rangle\) mix.

Cycling \(c_1\to c_2\to c_3\to c_1\) leaves the equal-weight sum fixed and rotates the two \(e\) combinations into linear combinations of each other.

What fails if you assume an empty site leaves an unpaired spin?

Reconstruction and charge transfer can close the shell. Total spin follows occupancy, not geometry.

Show that a line at \(637\ \mathrm{nm}\) is about \(1.95\ \mathrm{eV}\).

\(hc/\lambda\approx 1240/637\approx 1.95\ \mathrm{eV}\).

What did \(C_{3v}\) leftover symmetry buy us for NV\(^{-}\)?

It organized the leftover-bond combinations into \(a_1\) singlets and an \(e\) doublet, constrained allowed mixing, and identified how a sideways squeeze can lift degeneracy. It did not supply numerical energies.

What fails if static strain is treated as a phonon?

Static strain is a time-independent deformation. Phonons are quantized dynamical modes. They use related leftover-symmetry channels and they are not the same object.

What extra facts turn a spin doublet into a qubit?

A demonstrated route to initialize it, drive coherent operations, read it out, hold its charge state, and suppress leakage and decoherence on the operation timescale.

You can now look at a damaged crystal and ask the questions in order: what geometry remains, which orbitals are stuck, how many electrons occupy them, what total spin follows, and which of crystal field, spin–orbit, spin–spin, hyperfine, strain, and phonons split or mix the levels. You also know why the answers still do not, by themselves, make a qubit. Next we take the same checklist into diamond and ask which famous centers actually survive it.

Part IV — Defect-spin platforms

Diamond, sapphire, silicon carbide, and a few cousins. The question is not who owns the prettiest isolated number. It is who can field an array.

Chapter 7 — A diamond that glows because something is missing

You shine a green laser into a diamond. A single point answers in red. The rest of the stone stays dark.

The carbon lattice is almost perfect. Almost.

One carbon is gone. Next to the hole sits a nitrogen that does not belong.

An extra electron lives on that pair, and that electron is what glows.

A jeweler would call the stone flawed. We treat the flaw as the object: first the red light, then the spin hiding inside it, then the cousins that glow at other colors.

A hole next to a nitrogen

Take one carbon out of diamond and put a nitrogen on a neighboring site. The pair is not a dye on the surface. It is a tiny object carved into the crystal: a preferred axis along the nitrogen–hole line, and no mirror that swaps the two ends.

Shine 532-nm green light on that pair. Red light comes back.

Most of the red is a smear. A thin slice of it is sharp, near 637 nm.

That sharp slice is the fingerprint of this particular missing-atom pair in this particular charge.

A defect that swallows one color and gives another back is a color center. We take this as the definition. The color is the laboratory signal. The center is one place in the crystal.

The useful member of this family is the negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center, written NV\(^-\). Its ground levels form a spin triplet.

It will run at room temperature. Its optical line still notices local electric fields, and only a small fraction of the glow sits in that sharp 637-nm slice.

Hence a color center is a spectroscopic object, not a qubit certificate. The rest of the chapter is the extra work that turns this particular one into a controllable spin.

The thin red line

Most of the red is useless if you want two defects to look like the same atom. Vibrations in the lattice steal energy on the way out and smear the color.

The leftover slice that leaves no vibration behind is the zero-phonon line. The name is worth keeping because the ordinary English suggests “no photon,” and that is exactly wrong: it is the photon that took none of the lattice with it. It is the only part of the glow that can match another center, if anything can.

For NV\(^-\) that line sits at 637 nm. If the extra electron leaves, you have NV\(^0\) instead, and the sharp line jumps to about 575 nm [R074].

Same hole, same nitrogen, different color. Already the glow is telling you the electron count.

A common room-temperature sequence looks like this:

532-nm light
|
v
3E excited triplet ---- red fluorescence ----> 3A2 ground triplet
| ^
+-- spin-selective leak into singlets -------------+
(stronger for m_s = ±1)

NV\(^-\) has a triplet ground manifold \(^3A_2\), an optically excited triplet \(^3E\), and intermediate singlet states [R074]. Green light lifts the electron into \(^3E\). From there it can fall straight back, or it can sneak through the singlets.

That sneak path is stronger when the spin projection along the NV axis is \(m_s = \pm 1\) than when it is \(m_s = 0\). Repeated green flashes therefore park more and more population in \(m_s = 0\). The early red flash is brighter for \(m_s = 0\) than for \(m_s = \pm 1\).

Hence one laser both prepares the spin and reads it, statistically. At room temperature a single ordinary flash usually does not tell you the state with certainty.

You repeat. Resonant light at low temperature, or a nearby nucleus used as a helper, can do much better.

Those are different experiments, with different conditions.

Drop the spin-selective leak and the same green light still makes the stone glow. It no longer parks the spin, and the brightness no longer reports \(m_s\).

The cycle is also not closed forever. Optical excitation can convert NV\(^-\) to NV\(^0\).

Charge-repump light puts the extra electron back, probabilistically. Charge conversion and spin relaxation can both make the desired red light disappear.

They are not the same failure.

How many electrons are sitting there

A structural label such as “NV” does not say how many electrons live on the defect. Change the count and you change the atom.

Chapter 6 already named that integer the charge state. The extra electron on NV\(^-\) is what gives the \(S = 1\) ground state used for most sensing and qubit work.

NV\(^0\) has a different electronic and optical structure; it is not the same triplet qubit. NV\(^+\) is generally optically dark in the usual experiments.

Nearby donors and acceptors, the surface, the optical power, and any electrodes all push which count is stable [R074].

Write NV\(^-\), not “the NV,” when you mean the qubit. The charge is part of the object.

The same warning is louder for the group-IV cousins below. SiV\(^-\), GeV\(^-\), SnV\(^-\), and the less mature PbV\(^-\) are the usual spin-and-photon labels.

Neutral SiV\(^0\) is a different \(S = 1\) center with a line near 946 nm. Neutral GeV and SnV have far less mature single-center qubit evidence.

Stabilizing the charge is a device requirement, not a typographical detail [R082].

A balanced cousin

Picture a second object in the same hard crystal. An impurity atom \(M\) — silicon, germanium, tin, or lead — sits between two missing carbons:

carbon lattice ... vacancy — M — vacancy ... carbon lattice
^ inversion center

The two holes balance. The middle of the pair is a point you can invert through and land on the same arrangement.

People write that approximate symmetry \(D_{3d}\). The NV, by contrast, has a preferred axis and no such center; that one is \(C_{3v}\).

Because the balanced defect looks the same after inversion, a uniform electric field does not, to first order, shove its optical line around. Different copies can sit closer in color. That is the point of the geometry.

The useful negative charge \(M\)V\(^-\) has an effective electronic spin \(S = 1/2\) inside orbitally degenerate ground and excited manifolds. Spin–orbit coupling splits those manifolds. Heavier impurities generally open a larger split, which quiets some phonon processes at a given cryogenic temperature — and also makes a direct microwave spin flip less convenient unless strain or field orientation mixes the states [R082].

Hence inversion symmetry is an optical-line property, not a promise that the spin is easy to turn. Drop the inversion and first-order electric-field shifts return. Keep it, and strain, higher-order Stark shifts, local charges, and fabrication damage still remain.

Microwaves that pick two of three

Now we need numbers for the NV\(^-\) ground spin, because a microwave pulse is how you turn the glow into a controlled two-level system.

Choose the NV axis as \(z\). Let \(S_x\), \(S_y\), and \(S_z\) be the dimensionless spin-1 matrices, with \(S_z|m_s\rangle = m_s|m_s\rangle\) and \(m_s \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\). Write energy as frequency by dividing by Planck’s constant \(h\). A useful ground-state model is

\[ \frac{H}{h}= D S_z^2 +\gamma_e\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf S +E(S_x^2-S_y^2) +\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf I -\gamma_n\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf I +P I_z^2. \]

Here \(D\) is the axial splitting already present at zero field, in hertz; \(\gamma_e\) is the electron gyromagnetic ratio, in hertz per tesla; \(\mathbf B\) is the magnetic field, in tesla; \(E\) is a transverse strain or electric-field splitting, in hertz; \(\mathbf I\) is the nitrogen nuclear-spin operator; \(\mathbf A\) is the hyperfine tensor, in hertz; \(\gamma_n\) is the nuclear gyromagnetic ratio, in hertz per tesla; and \(P\) is the quadrupole coefficient, present when the nucleus has \(I \ge 1\).

That axial number \(D\) is the zero-field splitting from Chapter 6. The 2.87 GHz you will hear in every NV talk is not a magnet. It is the crystal already splitting \(m_s = 0\) away from \(m_s = \pm 1\) before you turn anything on.

For the common \(^{14}\)NV\(^-\) center, \(I = 1\). For \(^{15}\)NV\(^-\), \(I = 1/2\), so there is no nuclear quadrupole term. The room-temperature axial splitting is approximately \(D = 2.87\) GHz, and \(\gamma_e \approx 28.0\) GHz/T [R074].

Ignore strain and hyperfine structure for one minute, and align the field with \(z\). Then

\[ \frac{E_{m_s}}{h}=D m_s^2+\gamma_e B_zm_s. \]

At \(B_z = 10\) mT \(= 0.010\) T, the Zeeman shift has units

\[ (28.0\ \mathrm{GHz/T})(0.010\ \mathrm T)=0.280\ \mathrm{GHz}. \]

The two microwave frequencies from \(|0\rangle\) are then

\[ f_{0\rightarrow +1}=3.150\ \mathrm{GHz},\qquad f_{0\rightarrow -1}=2.590\ \mathrm{GHz}. \]

Hence a resonant microwave pulse can select either line. Taking \(|0\rangle\) and \(|-1\rangle\) as the working pair leaves \(|+1\rangle\) as a leakage state. This is a qubit because preparation, rotation, and measurement exist — not merely because the spectrum contains two levels.

Drop the field alignment and the two lines mix through the \(E\) term. Drop the third level from the bookkeeping and you will mis-count every pulse that leaks into \(|+1\rangle\).

The nucleus next door

Most carbon in diamond is \(^{12}\)C, nuclear spin \(I = 0\). Natural diamond also contains about 1.1% \(^{13}\)C with \(I = 1/2\).

Enriching the crystal in \(^{12}\)C weakens that spin bath. A selected nearby \(^{13}\)C can instead be used as a long-lived memory [R074].

The impurity itself may add a nucleus:

nucleus | nuclear spin \(I\) | practical consequence | |

\(^{14}\)N / \(^{15}\)N | 1 / 1/2 | intrinsic NV hyperfine register; \(^{14}\)N also has quadrupole structure | |

\(^{29}\)Si | 1/2 | optional intrinsic SiV nuclear memory; spin-zero Si isotopes remove it | |

\(^{73}\)Ge | 9/2 | a larger intrinsic register, but a more crowded hyperfine spectrum | |

\(^{117}\)Sn, \(^{119}\)Sn | 1/2 | isotope-selectable SnV hyperfine degree of freedom | |

\(^{207}\)Pb | 1/2 | possible intrinsic PbV nuclear degree of freedom | |

The listed group-IV isotope spins and their spin-zero alternatives are summarized in the group-IV review [R082].

[Experiment] A nearby nuclear spin can extend storage and enable repetitive readout. It also creates extra spectral lines and calibration work. Calling every nucleus either “noise” or “memory” misses the choice: uncontrolled weak couplings form a bath; resolved, controllable couplings form a register.

Suppose the same \(^{13}\)C is both unresolved and uncontrolled. Then it is part of the bath, and isotopic purification helps.

Suppose it is resolved and driven. Then it is a register, and purifying it away throws the memory out with the noise.

Four cousins, four sets of conditions

Off-resonant green light, microwaves, and spin-dependent red fluorescence are the NV\(^-\) routine. Radio-frequency fields address \(^{14}\)N, \(^{15}\)N, or a resolved \(^{13}\)C.

Room temperature is ordinary. Low temperature is still useful when you need the optical line itself to be narrow enough to network.

The balanced cousins do not copy that routine.

SiV\(^-\). Resonant light can pump and read the spin through nearly cycling transitions.

Microwave or Raman control rotates it. The inversion-symmetric optical line is attractive when you want photons that look alike.

At roughly 4 K, though, phonons readily swap population between ground-state orbital branches separated by only tens of gigahertz, and the spin forgets. Cooling to about 100 mK suppressed that channel enough for \(T_2 = 13\) ms, \(T_1 > 1\) s, and 89% single-shot spin readout in one bulk-device experiment [R083].

Those three numbers belong together with “100 mK.”

GeV\(^-\). The optical zero-phonon line is near 602 nm and the ground orbital splitting is larger than SiV\(^-\)’s [R082].

Microwave control and optical readout have been demonstrated. [Experiment] A millikelvin experiment reported Ramsey \(T_2^* \approx 1.43\ \mu\)s, spin-echo coherence of roughly \(0.44\) ms, and more than 20 ms under CPMG dynamical decoupling [R084]. “More than 20 ms” is therefore not an unconditioned free-induction time.

SnV\(^-\). Its zero-phonon line is near 619 nm and its ground orbital splitting is about 0.85 THz, which reduces thermal orbital excitation at helium-like temperatures relative to SiV\(^-\) [R082].

Strain turns on magnetic transitions that would otherwise stay dark. [Experiment] In a cryogenic strained device with a superconducting microwave waveguide, Hahn echo reached about \(0.43\) ms and CPMG-64 extended \(T_2\) to \(10(1)\) ms; the reported single-pulse fidelity was about 99.1% [R085].

These are one-center, pulse-sequence-specific results — not array medians.

PbV\(^-\). Optical emitters assigned to a lead-vacancy split-vacancy family, and large spin–orbit splittings, have been reported [R082].

Coherent spin initialization, gates, readout, and pair coupling are not yet supported at the same maturity as NV\(^-\) through SnV\(^-\). A larger splitting may improve thermal isolation and can make microwave access worse.

[Proposal] PbV\(^-\) is a candidate to test, not a ready drop-in qubit.

Hence each cousin is a different bargain among optical contrast, phonon isolation, and microwave access. Quoting a \(T_2\) without its temperature and pulse sequence is quoting a different experiment.

A table that keeps its conditions

The rows below are published benchmarks, not typical constants. Different rows use different temperatures, fields, samples, pulse sequences, and definitions. The last column is deliberately severe.

center | useful electronic/optical facts | representative spin result and conditions | readout/control demonstrated | demonstrated coupling | evidence for a scalable interacting array | |

NV\(^-\) | \(S=1\); \(D\approx 2.87\) GHz; 637-nm ZPL; weak ZPL fraction | \(T_2 = 1.8\) ms in an isotopically engineered bulk sample at room temperature under Hahn echo [R079] | room-temperature optical preparation/fluorescence and microwave control; cryogenic resonant single-shot methods | two NV electron spins at about 25 nm were entangled at room temperature with dipolar coupling \(4.93(5)\) kHz [R080]; remote NV registers later supported a teleported CNOT [R081] | No. Pair and network-node demonstrations do not establish a uniform dense lattice | |

SiV\(^-\) | \(S=1/2\) Kramers branches; about 737-nm ZPL; strong ZPL emission and inversion symmetry [R082] | \(T_2 = 13\) ms and \(T_1 > 1\) s at about 100 mK in bulk diamond [R083] | resonant optical initialization/readout, Raman and microwave control; 89% single-shot readout in that experiment [R083] | two SiV optical emitters coupled through one nanocavity showed superradiant/subradiant collective modes [R086] | No. The cavity experiment was a selected emitter pair, not a fabricated spin lattice | |

GeV\(^-\) | \(S=1/2\); about 602-nm ZPL; larger orbital splitting than SiV\(^-\) [R082] | \(T_2^* \approx 1.43\ \mu\)s, echo \(\sim 0.44\) ms, CPMG \(> 20\) ms at millikelvin temperature [R084] | optical spin readout and coherent microwave control | local hyperfine coupling is usable; no multi-GeV spin entangling result is used as evidence here | No. Long coherence of one center says nothing about placement yield or coupling uniformity | |

SnV\(^-\) | \(S=1/2\); about 619-nm ZPL; ground orbital splitting \(\sim 0.85\) THz [R082] | echo \(\sim 0.43\) ms; CPMG-64 \(10(1)\) ms in a cryogenic strained, superconducting-waveguide device [R085] | optical preparation/readout and strain-enabled microwave control; about 99.1% single-pulse fidelity in that device [R085] | coupling to a nearby \(^{13}\)C was observed [R085]; photonic-interface work does not yet equal a two-SnV gate | No. Site-controlled creation exists, but a coherent interacting array has not been shown | |

PbV\(^-\) / SiV\(^0\) | PbV\(^-\): less mature group-IV optical center; SiV\(^0\): distinct neutral \(S=1\) center near 946 nm | no directly comparable benchmark adopted | partial optical/spin functionality, platform dependent [R082] | no array-level coupling evidence adopted | No; exploratory. Do not average these distinct charge states into the rows above | |

[Experiment] The 2026 NV network result implemented an unconditional teleported controlled-NOT between remote diamond registers, with \(^{13}\)C nuclei as data qubits and NV electrons providing local logic, readout, and photonic entanglement [R081]. That is a substantial systems result. It is also a modular, measurement-and-feed-forward interaction — not a static nearest-neighbor energy in a dense crystal array.

Likewise, the two-SiV nanocavity experiment observed coherent photon-mediated collective optical states [R086]. A shared photonic mode can couple selected emitters.

That is not a deterministic two-spin gate, a uniform coupling graph, or passive many-body order. The noun “interaction” needs its object and its operating protocol.

An NV electron spin is a physical qubit. Several electron and nuclear spins controlled as a register are a processor register only if an encoding is specified.

Two remote registers joined by heralded photons form a quantum network. None of those observations, by itself, is an emergent anyon, a topologically ordered medium, or a topologically protected logical qubit.

Three distances on a map

Color centers are made by putting the impurity in during chemical-vapor-deposition growth, by focused ion implantation followed by annealing, by creating vacancies near existing dopants, or by femtosecond-laser processing. Nanopillars, waveguides, and photonic-crystal cavities then improve collection or cavity coupling. Each step can add strain, surface charge noise, paramagnetic damage, or spectral diffusion [R082].

Three distances must not be collapsed into one.

  • Delivery resolution: where the beam or laser deposits energy.

  • Final defect distribution: broadened by ion straggle, vacancy migration, and complex formation.

  • Usable-qubit yield: sites in the correct charge state, orientation, optical line, and coherence class after processing.

[Experiment] A 2025 SnV\(^-\) study combined focused implantation with local laser annealing and in-situ fluorescence feedback. It reported sub-50-nm site positioning, doses down to a Poisson mean of one implanted ion per site, and site-selective creation of single SnV\(^-\) emitters [R087].

The same study treated high-yield activation as an outstanding scaling problem. Sub-50-nm site registration is not proof that every site contains exactly one mutually resonant, coherent SnV\(^-\) at a chosen three-dimensional coordinate.

CVD growth generally gives high crystal quality but statistical location. Implantation supplies masks and coordinates but causes damage and has conversion-yield and straggle penalties.

Laser feedback improves activation control and does not yet certify an interacting array. For an eventual defect Hamiltonian, fabrication must satisfy placement, orientation, charge, optical frequency, and coherence at once.

Multiplying five less-than-unity yields is a quick way to make a small number. No advanced topology is required for that calculation.

What still knocks the spin around

For NV\(^-\), important channels include the \(^{13}\)C nuclear bath, substitutional-nitrogen electron spins, surface spins for shallow centers, magnetic-field drift, temperature and strain shifts of \(D\), microwave amplitude error, optical spectral diffusion, and charge conversion [R074]. Isotopic purification removes much of one bath. It does not remove the surfaces or the control electronics.

For group-IV negative centers, inversion symmetry reduces first-order sensitivity of optical transitions to electric fields. It does not make the defect insensitive to strain, higher-order Stark shifts, local charges, or fabrication damage.

Their defining low-temperature problem is orbital-phonon scattering. Cooling, or opening a larger spin–orbit split, suppresses thermal occupation.

Strain used to enable control can also change selection rules and spectra [R082]; [R083]; [R084]; [R085].

Dense arrays add mechanisms that isolated-center optimization hides: implantation damage accumulates; optical lines crowd; microwave fields become nonuniform; dipolar neighbors become both resources and a spin bath; and surfaces sit closer in nanophotonic devices. [Speculation] A defect that wins in a pristine bulk sample may lose after the processing required to couple and address it. Only measurements on fabricated ensembles and arrays can settle that ordering.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Quoting the largest \(T_2\) without its pulse sequence. \(T_2^*\), Hahn echo, and CPMG values answer different noise questions. A many-body gate cannot automatically borrow a CPMG-protected memory time while applying incompatible interactions.

  • Treating wavelength as the whole optical interface. Zero-phonon fraction, linewidth, spectral diffusion, quantum efficiency, cavity cooperativity, collection loss, and charge stability all matter. A narrow line in bulk can broaden after nanofabrication.

  • Ignoring charge and isotope labels. NV\(^0 \ne\) NV\(^-\) and SiV\(^0 \ne\) SiV\(^-\). A \(^{73}\)GeV has a different hyperfine space from a spin-zero Ge isotope.

  • Projecting one center onto \(N\) centers. Single-center coherence does not measure the distribution of coherence, transition frequencies, charge stability, or coupling strengths over an array. Pair entanglement proves a pair protocol, not an extensible lattice.

  • Equating remote coupling with a material Hamiltonian. Heralded photons, cavity-mediated optical modes, direct magnetic dipoles, and hyperfine coupling are physically different resources. A teleported gate is real quantum coupling. It is not passive local exchange.

  • Calling a controlled register topological. The NV and group-IV results in this chapter demonstrate physical qubits, memories, and network primitives. No experiment cited here demonstrates emergent topological order in an array of diamond color centers.

Check yourself

Why must “NV” include a charge superscript in a qubit discussion?

Because the electron count determines the spin and optical level structure; NV\(^-\) is the standard \(S = 1\) qubit, while NV\(^0\) and NV\(^+\) are different systems.

Show that at \(B_z = 10\) mT the two microwave frequencies from \(|0\rangle\) are \(3.150\) GHz and \(2.590\) GHz.

The Zeeman piece is \((28.0\ \mathrm{GHz/T})(0.010\ \mathrm T) = 0.280\) GHz, so \(D \pm \gamma_e B_z\) gives \(2.87 + 0.28 = 3.15\) GHz and \(2.87 - 0.28 = 2.59\) GHz.

What fails if SiV\(^-\) is run at about 4 K rather than about 100 mK?

Phonons swap population between the nearby orbital branches, and the spin forgets. The cited \(T_2 = 13\) ms, \(T_1 > 1\) s, and 89% single-shot readout belong with the colder run.

What fails if a 10 ms CPMG result is treated as available gate time?

That number is coherence under a specified refocusing sequence. A many-body gate that is incompatible with those pulses cannot borrow the time.

What has direct two-NV dipolar entanglement established?

That a selected pair can be coherently coupled and entangled at room temperature. It has not established controlled yield or uniformity for a large array.

Show that sub-50-nm site registration is not yet a scalable interacting array.

Registration locates a delivery site. Occupancy, charge, resonance, coherence, and designed coupling are independent, and the cited SnV study treated high-yield activation as still open.

NV\(^-\) offers mature room-temperature spin control and a comparatively difficult optical interface. Inversion-symmetric group-IV negative centers offer stronger coherent optical emission and generally demand cryogenic, phonon-aware operation.

Charge state and isotope are part of the device specification. Direct dipolar, hyperfine, cavity-mediated, and remote photonic couplings have all been demonstrated in limited settings.

No cited single-center, pair, cavity, network, or site-placement result establishes a scalable interacting diamond array.
