Chapter 8 — A red stone that already has guests

A ruby is a hard, clear crystal that happens to be red. The red is not a dye. It is chromium sitting where aluminum should sit: a few guests in a house built of aluminum and oxygen.

Sapphire is the same house. Take the chromium out, or swap in a different guest, and the stone turns colorless, blue, yellow, or whatever the new impurity decides.

Jewelers grade the color. We are going to grade something else: whether those famous guests can do the job diamond already does with one nitrogen atom next to a missing carbon.

The first laser was a ruby. Early masers used ruby too.

Titanium in sapphire still powers the workhorse tunable laser in a thousand labs. So this crystal already hosts impurities the world has used for sixty years.

That is the puzzle. If the guests are this famous, why is diamond still the defect people initialize, rotate, and read one at a time?

The same house, two names

Picture a crate of oxygen ions packed almost as tightly as balls. Aluminum occupies two thirds of the leftover pockets.

That crystal is corundum. The name is worth keeping because gemstone words keep splitting one material into two reputations.

When some of those aluminum ions are replaced by chromium, people call the stone ruby. When they mean the same lattice as a window, a watch crystal, or a microwave box, they usually say sapphire.

The chemistry is convenient. Chromium and aluminum both like a \(+3\) charge, so chromium can sit on an aluminum site without dragging a compensating defect along.

Each chromium sits inside a slightly squashed cage of six oxygens. The cage is not decoration.

It sets which way the chromium’s three leftover electrons prefer to point, even before you turn on a magnet. Light can lift those electrons.

Microwaves can shuffle them among the lowest four shelves. That is why the same small red impurity made the first laser and still shows up on an electron-spin-resonance bench.

Hence ruby and sapphire are one lattice with different guests, not two platforms. A crystal full of identical cages is not a register of labelled qubits.

At the concentrations that make a ruby laser, a laser spot and a microwave resonator talk to a crowd. Thin the crowd enough that each ion is alone, and the signal disappears into the noise.

A superb microwave box is also not a many-body phase wearing a 1950s lab coat. We will keep those two compliments, and then ask the operational questions diamond already answers.

Four shelves on one ion

A chromium that has given up three electrons keeps three in its outer shell. Those three like to point the same way, so the leftover spin can take four values: \(m=-3/2,-1/2,+1/2,+3/2\).

Think of four shelves. A magnetic field can tilt them.

Even with the field off, the squashed cage already splits them into two pairs.

That leftover split, present with no magnet, is the zero-field splitting from Chapter 6. It is an energy you can measure in a microwave lab, not a metaphor for “the crystal does something.”

Spectroscopists write the same facts in their dialect. The ion is \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) with configuration \(3d^3\).

In the oxygen cage the three electrons occupy the lower-energy orbitals with parallel spins, giving an orbital-singlet ground term \({}^{4}A_2\) and total electron spin \(S=3/2\). The cage is slightly stretched along the crystal \(c\)-axis, and that stretch is what produces the split [R088].

Define dimensionless spin operators \(S_x,S_y,S_z\) whose \(S_z\) eigenvalues are those four \(m\) values. Let \(D\) be an energy, \(\mu_B\) the Bohr magneton in joules per tesla, \(B_i\) the magnetic-field components in tesla, and \(g_\parallel,g_\perp\) the dimensionless spin factors parallel and perpendicular to the \(c\)-axis. The useful ground-state Hamiltonian is

\[ H=g_\perp\mu_B(B_xS_x+B_yS_y)+g_\parallel\mu_B B_zS_z +D\left[S_z^2-\frac{S(S+1)}{3}\right]. \]

At zero field, \(S(S+1)/3=5/4\), so

\[ E_{\pm3/2}=D,\qquad E_{\pm1/2}=-D. \]

For ruby, \(D<0\). The \(|\pm3/2\rangle\) pair is therefore lower, and the separation is

\[ \nu_0=\frac{-2D}{h}\simeq 11.493\ \text{GHz}, \]

where \(h\) is Planck’s constant [R088]; [R089]. Time reversal keeps \(+m\) and \(-m\) glued together when the field is off. That pairing is why you still have two doublets, not four lonely lines.

A quick dimensional and thermal check:

\[ \frac{h\nu_0}{k_B} =\frac{(6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s})(11.493\times10^9\ \text{s}^{-1})} {1.381\times10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}} \approx0.552\ \text{K}. \]

Joule-seconds times inverse seconds gives joules. Division by joules per kelvin gives kelvin.

Hence passive polarization between these doublets wants temperatures comfortably below half a kelvin. A room-temperature ruby laser proves an optical cycle exists.

It does not prove the ground-state spin is sitting quietly in its lowest shelf.

For a field parallel to \(c\), the Hamiltonian stays diagonal:

\[ E_m=D\left(m^2-\frac54\right)+g_\parallel\mu_B B_zm. \]

Microwave magnetic-dipole transitions ordinarily change \(m\) by one. Tilt the field and the \(|m\rangle\) states mix, the allowed strengths change, and you can find field-insensitive “clock” points.

Clock transitions are promising for coherence. Promise is not a measured \(T_2\).

Drop time reversal and the zero-field doublets can split. Keep it, and you still have four levels, two pairs, and a leakage problem the moment you pretend the ion is a two-level atom.

Light sees volts, microwaves see microvolts

The same ion also eats red light. At cryogenic temperature two sharp lines sit near 693.6 nm and 692.2 nm, about 1.788 eV and 1.792 eV [R088].

Those photons jump from the four ground shelves to a higher pair. Spectroscopists tag the excited pair \({}^{2}E\).

You do not need the label to remember the numbers. You need it if you open the papers.

The jump is officially spin-forbidden. Lattice vibrations sneak it through anyway.

Resonant excitation can tell the ground-state branches apart, and fluorescence that rides a phonon can report their populations. That is ensemble optical initialization and ensemble detection of magnetic resonance.

It is not automatically a single-shot look at one chromium spin.

Why are the two gaps so different? The oxygen cage first reorganizes electron-volt-scale orbital terms.

A smaller stretch of the cage, plus the electrons’ own spin–orbit coupling, then leaves a gigahertz leftover inside the ground term. Optical photons bridge roughly \(1.8\ \text{eV}\).

Microwaves bridge tens of microelectron-volts.

Hence the optical line and the microwave line are not two pictures of one two-level atom. Treat them as one unexplained object and you hide the selection rules and the four-level leakage channels.

A box that barely leaks

Sapphire is transparent over a broad optical range, mechanically hard, chemically stable, and an exceptional microwave dielectric. Take a high-purity disk, launch a microwave that crawls around its rim, and the wave just keeps going.

How long it rings is the quality factor \(Q\): stored energy divided by energy lost per radian. A huge \(Q\) is a host-device asset, not a measured impurity-spin coherence time.

[Experiment] At about 100 mK, high-purity sapphire whispering-gallery resonators have shown microwave \(Q\) in the \(10^8\)–\(10^9\) range. One 11 GHz mode with \(Q=2\times10^9\) corresponds to a photon energy-decay timescale \(Q/(2\pi f)\approx29\ \text{ms}\) [R090].

The nuclear environment is less friendly than isotopically enriched diamond. Natural aluminum is essentially all \({}^{27}\text{Al}\), with nuclear spin \(I=5/2\), so every substitutional chromium is surrounded by a dense host nuclear-spin bath.

Natural \({}^{52}\text{Cr}\), the dominant chromium isotope, has \(I=0\), while \({}^{53}\text{Cr}\) carries \(I=3/2\) [R088]; [R090]. You can pick chromium isotopes and remove its own nucleus.

You cannot turn aluminum into a spin-zero isotope.

Hence hyperfine structure and spectral diffusion are structural issues, not merely dirty-growth issues. Drop the aluminum nuclear spin from the model and the crystal you wrote down is no longer corundum.

What they measured on ruby

A laser spot on a ruby is almost never one ion. It is a crowd that happens to sit under the same beam.

That crowd is an ensemble. A beautiful ensemble number is allowed to look like a single-spin number if you stop reading one sentence too soon.

[Experiment] Sewani and co-workers studied a 0.005% ruby crystal in a dilution refrigerator. Under 15 nW continuous resonant excitation they inferred a ruby temperature of \(143\pm7\ \text{mK}\), measured a maximum spin-lattice relaxation time \(T_1=3.67\pm0.35\ \text{s}\), and observed ODMR transitions [R088].

Their resonant confocal measurement sampled an area of roughly \(1\ \mu\text{m}^2\), not one ion. The paper presented coherence-time measurement as future work.

It did not report Ramsey fringes, Hahn-echo \(T_2\), single-qubit gates, single-shot readout, or two-ion entanglement.

That distinction prevents a common numerical accident: substituting \(T_1\) for \(T_2\). Seconds-long population relaxation at millikelvin temperature is encouraging. Phase memory may still die much sooner on the aluminum nuclei, chromium–chromium dipoles, field noise, and inhomogeneous strain.

[Experiment] A 2025 experiment placed a 0.05% ruby sample on a 5.5 GHz high-\(T_c\) superconducting resonator and measured ensemble spin–photon coupling from 30 mK to 16 K [R089].

At 65 mK, one transition reached collective coupling \(\bar\Omega/2\pi\approx21\ \text{MHz}\) with spin decay \(\gamma_s/2\pi\approx44\ \text{MHz}\), giving cooperativity about 15 but not the strict strong-coupling condition \(\bar\Omega>\gamma_s\) [R089]. The sample contained an estimated \(2.6\times10^{15}\) spins.

The authors inferred an average single-spin coupling of only about 0.41 Hz over all spins, or 1.25 Hz when counting the high-field-volume subset [R089].

This is valuable collective cavity physics. It is also a sharp negative result for individually selected neighbours.

The impressive 21 MHz is the \(\sqrt N\)-enhanced ensemble coupling, not one defect’s coupling. In that experiment spin damping was too fast for coherent photon re-emission.

Suppose you divide 21 MHz by one spin. Then you have invented a device that the same paper’s own model puts in the hertz range. The hypothesis that fails is “collective enhancement can be ignored.”

Other metal guests

Sapphire accepts many transition metals because they can occupy aluminum sites in several charge states. Different valence and charge-compensation histories produce very different objects.

Species in sapphire | Established behavior | What it is for us | |

\(\text{Cr}^{3+}\), \(S=3/2\) | Ruby R-line fluorescence, laser/maser gain, EPR/ODMR, seconds-scale \(T_1\) at mK, ensemble cavity coupling [R088]; [R089] | Best-characterized candidate, but the modern single-center coherent-control stack is absent | |

\(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), \(S=5/2\) | EPR and microwave transitions in nominally pure sapphire; useful or parasitic in frequency standards [R090] | Demonstrated ensemble spectroscopy, not optical single-spin initialization/readout | |

\(\text{V}^{2+}\), \(S=3/2\), \({}^{51}\text{V}\) with \(I=7/2\) | Eight-line hyperfine structure resolved by whispering-gallery ESR [R090] | Rich levels, but nuclear complexity and no demonstrated qubit lifecycle | |

\(\text{Ti}^{3+}\), \(3d^1\) | Broad vibronic gain underlying the tunable Ti:sapphire laser, approximately 650–1100 nm [R091] | Excellent classical gain medium; broad electron–phonon optical transitions are not evidence of a narrow spin–photon qubit interface | |

Co, Ni, Mn and other ions | Optical absorption/EPR reported under charge-state- and growth-dependent conditions | A spectroscopic line is a candidate identifier, not a scalable center | |

[Experiment] Farr and co-workers detected native \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\), and \(\text{V}^{2+}\) impurities at parts-per-billion to parts-per-million levels in high-purity sapphire near 115 mK using 8–19 GHz whispering-gallery spectroscopy [R090]. The sensitivity is double-edged. It proves that dilute spins couple to microwave modes, and that nominally “pure” sapphire already contains uncontrolled spin species.

Hence a catalog of guests is not a catalog of qubits. A line in a spectrum identifies a candidate. It does not initialize, rotate, or read one spin.

A hole where oxygen should be

Remove an \(\text{O}^{2-}\) ion and you leave an empty oxygen site \(V_O\). Charge-state language is easy to reverse, so define it with the leftover electrons, not the empty pocket.

A nominally neutral vacancy that traps two electrons is an \(F\) center. The literature uses it as a species, not as a vibe.

Take one electron away and the same pocket is an \(F^+\) center, \(V_O^+\) with one leftover electron. Vacancy aggregates are labelled \(F_2\), \(F_2^+\), and so on, though historical assignments can depend on how the sample was cooked.

[Experiment] Irradiated or reduced alpha-alumina shows an \(F\)-center absorption band near 6.1 eV and luminescence near 3.0 eV. The \(F^+\) center has absorption structure near 4.8 and 5.4 eV and emission near 3.8 eV [R092]; [R095].

The \(F\)-center emission lifetime was measured as \(36\pm4\ \text{ms}\), consistent with a spin-forbidden relaxed transition [R092]. [Theory] Modern hybrid-density-functional calculations reproduce the main absorption/emission assignments and distinguish internal vacancy transitions from transitions involving band edges [R093].

Agreement on optical energies does not establish a qubit.

The one-electron \(F^+\) center is paramagnetic and therefore visible to EPR in suitable samples. The two electrons of the neutral \(F\) center can form singlet and triplet configurations involved in its luminescence.

Yet, for the literature survey used here through 24 August 2026, no peer-reviewed report was located that demonstrates an isolated oxygen-vacancy center in bulk sapphire with all of the following: photon antibunching tied to that center, spin-selective optical initialization, coherent single-spin rotations, a measured single-center \(T_2\), and single-shot readout.

The positive literature establishes ensemble color-center spectroscopy and theory [R092]; [R093]; [R095]. The missing operational stack must be recorded as missing.

Oxygen vacancies can be created by irradiation, reducing growth, or annealing, and can aggregate or change charge under illumination. Those routes offer density control.

They also create displacement damage and heterogeneous local environments. Ultraviolet excitation around 5–6 eV is much less convenient for low-loss nanophotonics and biological or fiber interfaces than visible or near-infrared light.

Calling the vacancy “deep in a wide gap” is necessary physics, not a device plan.

Planting chromium where you want it

Bulk ruby growth gives a uniform average concentration and random atomic locations. A focused ion beam, or a masked implant, can put chromium at a chosen depth and a chosen patch of the surface.

[Experiment] Chromium implanted at 150 keV into sapphire, followed by a 1450 °C anneal, produced substitutional ruby-like R-line luminescence in a thin implanted layer [R094]. The demonstrated fluences were ensemble-scale, \(6\times10^{14}\) to \(4\times10^{15}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\), and the reported internal optical efficiency was about 50% under those processing conditions [R094].

This proves activation after implantation. The high anneal temperature, collision straggle, residual damage, charge-state control, and chromium diffusion all still complicate a nanometre-scale interaction graph.

No sapphire result located for this chapter combined deterministic single-ion registration, verified one-Cr optical/spin behavior, and a controllable two-Cr coupling. Diamond also suffers implantation straggle and surface noise, but it has crossed the single-defect verification threshold many times [R074].

Hence implantation of chromium is a materials result, not a placement proof. An R-line from a thin layer says the guests found aluminum sites. It does not say which sites, or that two chosen guests can talk.

Scoreboard against diamond

The fairest comparison uses demonstrated capability at stated conditions, not each platform’s best hypothetical feature.

Criterion | Sapphire/corundum evidence | Diamond reference point | For a chosen-neighbour register | |

Single-defect identification | Ruby and vacancy work reviewed here is predominantly ensemble spectroscopy; no intrinsic sapphire antibunching-plus-spin-control demonstration was located [R088]; [R092]; [R095] | Single NV centers support room-temperature confocal fluorescence, ODMR, initialization and coherent control; mature review in [R074] | Diamond decisively ahead | |

Coherence | Cr ruby: \(T_1=3.67\pm0.35\) s at mK; that study did not measure \(T_2\) [R088] | Single NV Hahn-echo \(T_2=1.8\) ms at room temperature in isotopically purified bulk diamond [R079] | Values are not directly comparable; sapphire’s needed single-spin \(T_2\) datum is absent | |

Optical interface | Narrow ruby R lines and ensemble resonant readout near 693 nm at cryogenic temperature [R088] | Single-NV spin–photon entanglement and remote-node building blocks have been demonstrated [R074] | Sapphire has spectroscopy, not a demonstrated single-spin network node | |

Microwave interface | Very high-\(Q\) sapphire resonators and collective coupling; 2025 ruby device had 21 MHz ensemble coupling versus 44 MHz spin decay [R089]; [R090] | Diamond spin ensembles and single NVs couple to microwave structures; single-defect control is routine [R074] | Sapphire excels as a resonator, not yet as an individually wired defect register | |

Placement | Random bulk doping; ensemble Cr implantation and activation after 1450 °C anneal [R094] | Implantation, delta doping, nanofabrication, and registration all demonstrated, with nonzero yield/straggle limitations [R074] | Neither is perfect; sapphire lacks the single-center end-to-end evidence | |

Density and selected interactions | Cr–Cr effects and collective \(\sqrt N\) enhancement exist, but chosen pairwise coherent gates were not located [R089] | Dipolar-coupled NV pairs and multi-spin registers have been coherently controlled [R074] | Ensemble interaction is not an addressable graph |

Temperature | Optical ruby operation is possible at room temperature, but the strongest quantum-spin characterization here used 65–186 mK [R088]; [R089] | NV spin initialization, control and readout operate at room temperature; high-quality optical networking usually uses cryogenics [R074] | Application-dependent, but sapphire does not show NV-like room-temperature qubit operation | |

Host spin bath | Unavoidable dense \({}^{27}\text{Al}\), \(I=5/2\) | \({}^{12}\text{C}\), \(I=0\), can be isotopically enriched [R074]; [R079] | Fundamental materials advantage to diamond | |

Claim | Status | Platform | Evidence | Reference | |

Optical population readout, ODMR and seconds-long \(T_1\) | Experimentally demonstrated | Cr:ruby ensemble, dilution refrigerator | Resonant PLE/ODMR and all-optical relaxation | [R088] | |

Coherent strong coupling of one Cr spin to one cavity photon | Not demonstrated | Cr:ruby | Inferred average single-spin coupling in hertz; collective mode failed \(\bar\Omega>\gamma_s\) | [R089] | |

Trace transition-metal spins couple to sapphire microwave modes | Experimentally demonstrated | Fe, Cr, V ensembles | Avoided crossings and ESR/hyperfine spectra | [R090] | |

Oxygen vacancies are optically active deep defects | Experimentally demonstrated and theoretically modeled | \(F\), \(F^+\) in alpha-alumina | Ensemble absorption/luminescence plus hybrid-DFT assignments | [R092]; [R093] |

Oxygen vacancy is an optically readable single spin qubit | No supporting demonstration located | Sapphire \(V_O\) | Required antibunching/control/readout sequence absent from located literature | [R092]; [R093] | |

Implanted chromium can be optically activated | Experimentally demonstrated, ensemble | Cr-implanted sapphire | R-line luminescence after high-temperature anneal | [R094] | |

Deterministic interacting array of sapphire defects | No supporting demonstration located | Any sapphire center | No selected pair gates, array calibration, or many-body Hamiltonian validation located | [R088]; [R089]; [R090]; [R091]; [R092]; [R093]; [R094] | |

Sapphire defects realize topological order | Speculation | Sapphire defect lattice | No microscopic implementation or phase diagnostic | — | |

A ruby ion is a physical spin. Two selected ions with a calibrated coherent interaction would be a coupled-qubit primitive.

A macroscopic spin ensemble collectively coupled to one cavity mode is a different degree of freedom. None of these is automatically an encoded qubit, an emergent anyon, or topological order.

The 2025 cavity anticrossing belongs with collective hybrid systems, not with topological materials.

Ways to get this wrong

Long \(T_1\) mistaken for long \(T_2\). Population can remain for seconds while phase coherence disappears rapidly. A credible array proposal needs Ramsey, echo, and driven-gate errors on the same defect, density, temperature, and geometry it proposes to use.

Collective coupling mistaken for local coupling. If \(N\) similar spins couple to one mode, the bright collective mode gains roughly \(\sqrt N\).

Dividing 21 MHz by one spin is not allowed. The measured ruby experiment’s own model put the average in the hertz range [R089].

Dark modes, inhomogeneous broadening, and the inability to address a chosen ion remain.

Color mistaken for spin readout. An absorption band says a defect has electronic transitions. Luminescence says some excitation returns radiatively. Single-photon antibunching, spin contrast, cycling stability, photon indistinguishability, and charge stability are separate tests.

A good host device mistaken for a good host defect. Sapphire’s huge microwave \(Q\) makes it an excellent resonator substrate.

It also makes unwanted parts-per-billion spins measurable [R090]. Score the resonator and the qubit separately.

Random density mistaken for fabrication. Raising chromium concentration shortens average separation.

It does not choose the interaction graph. It also introduces Cr pairs, energy transfer, dipolar broadening, and local strain.

A designed Hamiltonian wants calibrated signs, anisotropies, and connectivities, not merely “many spins nearby.”

A theoretical vacancy spectrum mistaken for a platform. First-principles agreement with optical bands validates defect assignment [R093]. It does not supply a fabrication yield, coherence distribution, readout fidelity, or two-qubit gate.

What we can honestly claim

[Experiment] Sapphire supports well-characterized paramagnetic dopants, narrow chromium optical lines, long low-temperature spin relaxation, exceptionally low-loss microwave modes, optical/microwave ensemble readout, radiation-induced vacancy color centers, and implanted chromium activation [R088]; [R089]; [R090]; [R091]; [R092]; [R093]; [R094]. These are substantial ingredients for masers, sensors, frequency standards, ensemble memories, and hybrid-resonator studies.

For the specific target of a dense, controllable interacting-defect architecture, the verdict as of 24 August 2026 is not competitive with diamond on demonstrated end-to-end qubit capability. The decisive absences are single-center spin-selective optical readout, modern single-center \(T_2\) and gate fidelities, deterministic verified placement, coherent gates between selected sapphire defects, and scalable nanophotonic integration around those defects. The unavoidable \({}^{27}\text{Al}\) nuclear bath is an additional materials disadvantage.

This is not proof of impossibility. [Proposal] A credible sapphire recovery program would first demonstrate one identified \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) or \(F^+\) center, measure \(T_2^*\), Hahn-echo \(T_2\), optical cycling and charge stability, then create and spectrally resolve a registered pair whose coherent coupling exceeds both linewidths.

Only after those milestones would an array-level Hamiltonian proposal become evidence-based. [Speculation] Jumping directly from ruby ensembles to Fibonacci-like order skips every hard arrow in the chain.

Check yourself

Why does \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) in ruby have four ground-state spin levels?

Its \(3d^3\) configuration gives \(S=3/2\), hence \(m=\pm3/2,\pm1/2\). The squashed cage splits them into two pairs that stay glued by time reversal.

Show that the 11.493 GHz zero-field splitting is only about half a kelvin.

\(h\nu_0/k_B=(6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s})(11.493\times10^9\ \text{s}^{-1})/(1.381\times10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1})\approx0.552\ \text{K}\). Strong passive polarization therefore wants sub-kelvin operation.

What fails if the 3.67 s \(T_1\) is treated as a coherence result?

\(T_1\) measures population relaxation. Phase noise can make \(T_2\) far shorter, and the cited millikelvin ruby study did not measure \(T_2\).

Show that the 21 MHz ruby cavity result cannot be a single-spin coupling.

About \(2.6\times10^{15}\) spins shared the mode. The paper’s own inference put the average per spin at 0.41 Hz, or 1.25 Hz in the high-field-volume subset. The 21 MHz is the \(\sqrt N\)-enhanced collective rate, and even that failed \(\bar\Omega>\gamma_s\).

What fails if an \(F^+\) center is called a qubit because it is paramagnetic and luminescent?

Isolation, coherent control, spin-dependent readout, stability, and measured error rates are still missing. Ensemble color is not that stack.

What is sapphire’s strongest clear advantage and its clearest defect-array weakness?

Its microwave dielectric loss can be extraordinarily low. Its single-defect qubit and selected-interaction evidence is presently sparse compared with diamond.

You now have a ruby ion with four ground shelves, an 11.5 GHz split, a seconds-long \(T_1\) that is not a \(T_2\), and a scoreboard that still favors diamond. Next we ask silicon carbide the same operational questions, and we will not award points for a band gap alone.

Chapter 9 — A factory crystal and its neighbors

A wafer of silicon carbide is not a gem. It is already sitting in electric-car inverters: hard, wide-gap, sold by the crate. Someone can knock two neighboring atoms out of that wafer — one silicon, one carbon — and the leftover electrons still have a spin we can talk to.

That missing pair is the industrial cousin of the diamond vacancy. The crystal around it is a factory product.

Wafers, ion beams, etches, electronics, and waveguides already exist for this material. We are going to see how far those tools take a spin, and then we are going to open the other drawers.

No winner. Each host is a toolbox.

Silicon carbide is the drawer with the most industrial tools. Hexagonal boron nitride is a sheet.

Rare-earth crystals are superb memories. Silicon is the other semiconductor.

Oxides are a catalog. Diamond remains the benchmark from two chapters ago.

The question is narrower than “which material has the longest memory.” It is: which drawer lets us place, distinguish, couple, tune, and measure many spins under one compatible set of conditions?

One good spin is not a row of them

A single defect can be excellent. It can start on cue, hold still, and be heard. That is one spin.

A row of them is a different job. You need the same kind of defect in chosen sites, a way to turn one without turning the next, a way to hear each one, and a process that does not ruin the neighbors.

A six-hour memory in the wrong geometry is still the wrong part. A neatly patterned grid of unidentified blinking lights is not a shortcut either.

Call the first scorecard single-defect quality: initialization, coherent control, coherence, and readout for one spin. Call the second an array: many spins that you can place, distinguish, couple, tune, and measure under one set of conditions.

The name is worth keeping because it is a different object. Ten beautiful isolated spins are not an array.

Write the two scorecards as labels, not yet as numbers:

  • \(Q_{\mathrm{single}}\) is the quality of initialization, coherent control, coherence, and readout for one defect;

  • \(Q_{\mathrm{array}}\) is placement yield, interaction reproducibility, addressability, routing, and compatibility with fabrication.

The engineering rule is a bottleneck:

\[ Q_{\mathrm{array}}\ \text{is limited by its weakest required operation.} \]

A long \(T_2\) cannot replace a missing two-spin interaction. Atomic placement cannot replace a missing readout. Multiplying record values from different samples, temperatures, and pulse sequences produces an imaginary device — usually a very photogenic one.

Drop the bottleneck and you may crown the host with the longest published memory. Keep it, and a six-hour nuclear coherence with no designed nearest neighbor is still not an array.

Two missing atoms

Silicon carbide’s leading defects are a neighboring missing silicon and carbon, commonly written \(V_{\mathrm{Si}}V_{\mathrm C}^0\), and a negatively charged missing silicon, \(V_{\mathrm{Si}}^-\).

The missing pair is a divacancy. The name just means two vacancies sitting next to each other.

The neutral one has electronic spin \(S=1\). The silicon vacancy commonly used in 4H-SiC has \(S=3/2\).

Silicon carbide does not come in one stacking. The same atoms can pile up in more than one repeating pattern.

The common wafer we will use is 4H-SiC. Different stackings and different lattice sites give different optical and spin spectra.

That variety is either a tuning toolbox or a catalog-management problem, depending on the day.

Hence “a spin in SiC” is not one object. Charge, stacking, and site all change the spectrum before anyone writes a control pulse.

Dial one spin

Take a single spin-1 divacancy in 4H-SiC. Use dimensionless spin operators \(S_x,S_y,S_z\), and write its ground-state energy as a frequency:

\[ \frac{H}{h} = D\!\left(S_z^2-\frac{S(S+1)}{3}\right) +E(S_x^2-S_y^2) +\gamma_e\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf S. \]

Here \(H\) is energy in joules, \(h\) is Planck’s constant in joule-seconds, \(D\) and \(E\) are axial and transverse zero-field-splitting frequencies in hertz, \(\mathbf B\) is the magnetic field in tesla, and \(\gamma_e=g\mu_B/h\) is the electron-spin gyromagnetic ratio in hertz per tesla. The electron \(g\)-factor is near 2, so \(\gamma_e\approx28\ \mathrm{GHz\,T^{-1}}\).

For a field \(B_z\) along the defect axis and \(E\) small compared with the other terms, the microwave frequencies from \(m_s=0\) to \(m_s=\pm1\) are approximately

\[ \nu_\pm=D\pm\gamma_e B_z. \]

A 2024 SiC-on-insulator experiment measured a PL6 center with \(D=1340.4\pm1.3\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and a field slope of \(2.82\pm0.02\ \mathrm{MHz\,G^{-1}}\), while coherently controlling the implanted single spin at room temperature [R099]. Take \(B_z=5.0\ \mathrm{mT}=50\ \mathrm G\). Then

\[ \gamma_e B_z =(2.82\ \mathrm{MHz\,G^{-1}})(50\ \mathrm G) =141\ \mathrm{MHz}, \]

so

\[ \nu_-\approx1.199\ \mathrm{GHz},\qquad \nu_+\approx1.481\ \mathrm{GHz}. \]

The units check: \(\mathrm{MHz/G}\times\mathrm G=\mathrm{MHz}\). An optical pulse initializes the spin, a microwave tone near one transition drives Rabi oscillations, and spin-dependent fluorescence or spin-to-charge conversion provides readout. [Experiment] Those operations have each been demonstrated for SiC divacancies, although not all record values occur in one room-temperature dense array [R096]; [R097]; [R098]; [R099].

Hence one implanted PL6 spin can be dialed. That is a \(Q_{\mathrm{single}}\) result. It does not yet say who sits next door.

Talk to one, miss the next

Now make the same spin an addressability test. Suppose — this is a design assumption, not a reported array result — that local strain or a magnetic-field gradient separates neighboring transitions by \(\Delta=20\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Drive one site with cyclic-frequency Rabi rate \(\Omega=2\ \mathrm{MHz}\). A resonant \(\pi\) pulse lasts

\[ t_\pi=\frac{1}{2\Omega}=250\ \mathrm{ns}. \]

The neighbor is not quite on resonance. The leading leftover population on the wrong site scales roughly as

\[ p_{\mathrm{xtalk}}\sim\left(\frac{\Omega}{\Delta}\right)^2=10^{-2}. \]

That leftover is crosstalk: you meant to turn one spin and you jiggled the next. The error is geometric, not moral.

Larger \(\Omega\) gives faster gates but more of it. Larger \(\Delta\) helps selection but demands reproducible gradients or tuning, and can make nominally identical couplings unequal.

Selective control is still not an interaction. A two-spin coupling rate \(J\) must also beat the relevant linewidth and decoherence. The next chapter will put numbers on that bargain rather than hiding it under the word “scalable.”

The implanted object above is a physical defect-spin qubit. An electron plus a nearby \(^{13}\mathrm C\) nuclear spin is a small quantum register. Patterning 64 sites changes the fabrication count, not the category.

Drop the detuning and the same pulse that turns one site turns both. Keep a huge detuning and you may no longer have a uniform \(J_{ij}\). Addressability and coupling pull in opposite directions.

Who is wired to whom

For many defects indexed by \(i\), a minimal many-spin energy is

\[ \frac{H_{\mathrm{array}}}{h} = \sum_i \frac{H_i}{h} + \sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j + \frac{H_{\mathrm{drive}}}{h}. \]

Here \(H_i\) is the single-defect Hamiltonian just defined, \(J_{ij}\) is a coupling frequency in hertz between sites \(i\) and \(j\), and \(H_{\mathrm{drive}}\) contains optical, microwave, electric, or strain control. The isotropic product \(\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j\) is only a placeholder. Magnetic dipolar coupling is anisotropic, exchange depends strongly on wavefunction overlap, and a cavity or a phonon has its own mode structure.

The list of who is coupled to whom, including the unwanted edges, is the interaction graph. Geometry is not the graph. Two spots on a photograph do not tell you \(J_{ij}\).

An array proposal must therefore specify five maps:

  • site map: intended position \(\rightarrow\) actual active defect and charge state;

  • spectrum map: actual defect \(\rightarrow\) optical and microwave transition frequencies;

  • control map: control line or beam \(\rightarrow\) addressed subset and crosstalk;

  • interaction map: geometry \(\rightarrow J_{ij}\), including unwanted edges;

  • measurement map: physical signal \(\rightarrow\) inferred local or collective observable.

Missing one map is not a small omission. It is usually where the device actually lives.

What the factory has actually shipped

[Experiment] Individual neutral divacancies in high-purity 4H-SiC have been optically isolated and coherently controlled; ensemble Hahn-echo coherence exceeded \(1\ \mathrm{ms}\) at low temperature [R096]. In isotopically purified 4H-SiC at \(5\ \mathrm K\), a single divacancy reached \(T_2=5.3\pm1.3\ \mathrm s\) using up to 16,384 dynamical-decoupling pulses, with end-to-end spin-to-charge readout fidelity \(80.8\pm0.6\%\) [R097]. The condition matters: “five-second coherence” is not a bare Hahn echo, not room temperature, and not an implanted dense array.

SiC also survives useful processing. [Experiment] Implanted \(V_{\mathrm{Si}}^-\) centers retained nearly lifetime-limited optical emission and high spin coherence in etched nanophotonic waveguides, with control of nearby nuclear spins [R098].

[Experiment] In 2024, selective carbon implantation through an \(8\times8\) mask of 100-nm-diameter holes created a designed PL6 array in SiC-on-insulator; the same study integrated an electron–nuclear register into a waveguide and reported ambient-condition entangled-state fidelities of 0.89 before and 0.88 after integration [R099]. This is unusually complete materials evidence.

[Experiment] The electronics path also advanced in 2025: room-temperature photoelectrical magnetic-resonance readout of a single \(V_{\mathrm{Si}}^-\) spin produced a signal-to-noise ratio 1.7–2 times that of optical detection in the same study [R104]. This is evidence for integrable charge collection, not yet parallel high-fidelity readout of a coupled array.

It is not yet the desired interacting electron-spin lattice. The mask pitch and activation statistics do not imply nanometer-accurate final coordinates.

One bright spot may contain zero, one, or several relevant defects. The 2024 entanglement was between one defect electron and a nearby nuclear spin, not between selected electron defects across the \(8\times8\) pattern [R099].

SiC leads the industrial drawer because several necessary technologies coexist, not because the interaction graph has been demonstrated.

Hence \(Q_{\mathrm{single}}\) for SiC is already serious, and pieces of \(Q_{\mathrm{array}}\) exist. The bottleneck is still the missing electron–electron edges.

A crystal one atom thick

A monolayer or few-layer sheet of hexagonal boron nitride puts every defect close to a surface, a gate, a resonator, and a neighbor. That is attractive if you want a flat interaction graph and easy photonics. It is also attractive if you are a noisy adsorbate.

[Experiment] Single carbon-related hBN defects showed room-temperature optically detected magnetic resonance: the fluorescence changed when a microwave tone hit the spin. In the reported material only 27 of more than 400 investigated isolated defects showed a measurable signal — about 5% — and saturated linewidths were about 35 MHz [R100]. The microscopic structures and spin multiplicities were not uniquely established.

This is a sharp example of promising single-site behavior with immature yield and identity control. A two-dimensional host shortens the route to an interface. It also shortens the route from every dirty molecule on the surface to the spin.

Drop the surface and you no longer have the sheet. Keep it, and chemical identity, uniformity, lifetime, and yield remain independent problems.

Ions that hide their electrons

Some crystals are doped with rare-earth ions such as Eu\(^{3+}\), Er\(^{3+}\), and Yb\(^{3+}\). Their partly filled \(4f\) shell sits inside closed outer shells, so the optical lines can be extremely narrow and the spin memories extremely long.

[Experiment] \(^{151}\mathrm{Eu}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y_2SiO_5}\) reached \(370\pm60\) minutes of hyperfine coherence at \(2\ \mathrm K\) with dynamical decoupling [R101]. [Experiment] A single \(^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^{3+}\) ion in a YVO\(_4\) nanophotonic cavity showed an optical linewidth below 1 MHz, spin coherence beyond 30 ms, and conditional single-shot readout above 95% [R102]. Those are superb node and memory credentials.

For a dense local energy, though, dilute dopants are commonly random in space, direct interactions are weak or inhomogeneous, and operation is generally cryogenic. Spectral multiplexing can identify many ions in one optical mode, but a frequency address book is not automatically a designed nearest-neighbor lattice.

Hence a long memory can raise \(Q_{\mathrm{single}}\) without touching \(Q_{\mathrm{array}}\). The bottleneck here is the interaction map, not the clock.

The other semiconductor

Silicon is the strongest counterargument to an optical-defect-only worldview. Isotopically enriched \(^{28}\mathrm{Si}\) provides a quiet nuclear environment, industrial electronics are unmatched, and a scanning-tunneling-microscope hydrogen lithography method can place phosphorus donors on chosen lattice sites.

An electron in silicon can sit in more than one equivalent momentum pocket. Those pockets interfere, so the exchange energy between two nearby donors depends fiercely on the direction of the displacement, not only on the distance.

That interference is a valley effect: the name is the shape of the energy surface in momentum space. [Experiment/Theory] Atomic-scale imaging and modeling show that aligning donors along favorable crystallographic directions suppresses, but does not abolish, exchange variability [R103].

Gate-defined silicon spin qubits already support electrically controlled two-qubit logic in devices that are not color centers. Their penalties, if what you wanted was an optical defect lattice, are millikelvin operation, elaborate gate stacks and reservoirs, and the lack of a naturally bright, cycling optical transition for standard phosphorus-donor nodes. If the job is a programmable electrical spin energy rather than a spin–photon network, silicon may be the drawer you open first.

Drop the optical requirement and silicon’s \(Q_{\mathrm{array}}\) case becomes the strongest in the chapter. Keep it, and the missing cycling transition is the bottleneck.

A drawer of oxides

“Oxide” is not one platform. The drawer includes chemically and structurally different hosts — MgO, ZnO, TiO\(_2\), Y\(_2\)O\(_3\), and many others.

Some host transition-metal defects, oxygen vacancies, or rare-earth dopants. Rare-earth oxides overlap the previous drawer.

[Theory/Experiment] Reviews identify low nuclear-spin abundance, large band gaps, and mature thin-film processing as useful search criteria, while also emphasizing charge-state stability, optical cycling, and reproducible defect formation as independent requirements [R073]. As of the evidence surveyed here, no generic wide-gap oxide combines deterministic single-spin placement, a high-fidelity optical lifecycle, preserved coherence after nanofabrication, and a demonstrated controlled interaction graph. Oxides are a discovery space, not one backup device waiting on a shelf.

Side by side

The following matrix is deliberately about interacting arrays. “High coherence” means only what the cited experiment measured under its stated conditions. Ratings are comparative judgments, not hidden numerical data.

Host and representative spin | Native/engineered coupling route | Placement and yield | Coherence evidence | Photonics and readout | Maturity and typical temperature | Toolbox note | |

4H-SiC: neutral divacancy, \(V_{\mathrm{Si}}^-\) | Nearby nuclear hyperfine demonstrated; electron dipolar/exchange at short range; cavity, strain, and electrical mediation plausible | Implantation, masks, annealing, commercial wafers; designed \(8\times8\) PL6 pattern demonstrated, but not an atomically registered interacting electron array [R099] | \(>1\) ms ensemble Hahn echo at low temperature [R096]; single-spin \(5.3\pm1.3\) s at 5 K with isotopic purification and 16,384-pulse decoupling [R097] | Near-infrared optical transitions, spin-to-charge readout, waveguides and SiC-on-insulator integration [R097]; [R098]; [R099] | Highest combined materials/device maturity here; room-temperature control exists, best resonant optical/readout records often cryogenic | Most complete optical-and-wafer toolbox here; activation statistics, final position, spectral disorder, and controlled electron–electron edges still open | |

hBN: boron vacancy and carbon-related spins | Short-range exchange/dipolar interactions are geometrically accessible in 2D; resonator coupling possible | Transfer, growth, irradiation and local writing are available; microscopic identity and reproducible spin-active yield remain weak | Room-temperature single-defect ODMR; about 5% ODMR-active yield in one >400-defect survey and roughly 35 MHz saturated linewidth [R100] | Bright visible emitters and easy planar integration; spectral and photodynamic variability substantial [R100] | Rapidly developing, room-temperature demonstrations | High-upside planar toolbox, not yet a reproducible many-spin component library | |

Rare-earth crystals: Eu:YSO, Yb:YVO\(_4\), Er:YSO | Weak direct ion–ion coupling; cavity-mediated and spectral-multiplexed links are natural | Dopants are usually dilute and spatially random; individual ions selected spectrally or by cavity overlap | Eu nuclear hyperfine \(370\pm60\) min at 2 K with decoupling [R101]; single Yb spin >30 ms in a cavity [R102] | Exceptional narrow optical lines; single-ion cavity readout >95% conditional fidelity [R102] | Mature memories and emerging nanophotonics; usually kelvin-scale | Memory and network toolbox; less natural for a dense prescribed local interaction graph | |

Silicon: P donors or gate-defined electron spins | Electrically tunable exchange is strong; capacitive and resonator links available | CMOS gates plus STM donor placement can approach lattice-site precision; exchange remains sensitive to valley phase and interfaces [R103] | Long coherence in enriched \(^{28}\)Si is established, but values depend strongly on electron versus nucleus, ensemble versus single device, and pulse sequence [R073] | Excellent electrical readout/control; standard donor architecture lacks a bright cycling optical interface | Most mature semiconductor control stack; generally dilution-refrigerator temperatures | Strongest electrical programmable-array toolbox; less suited to an optical color-center route | |

Wide-gap oxides: oxygen vacancies, transition-metal or rare-earth dopants | Dipolar/exchange possible in principle; oxide electronics and strain offer mediators | Thin-film processing is mature for some hosts, but quantum-active defect identity, charge state, activation and placement are host-specific [R073] | Isolated or ensemble coherence exists in selected systems; no transferable “oxide value” is meaningful [R073] | Some excellent emitters or microwave ensembles, rarely a complete single-spin lifecycle | Fragmented; temperatures range from ambient sensing to cryogenic spectroscopy | Discovery portfolio, not presently a validated interacting-array platform | |

Diamond baseline: NV and group-IV vacancies | Dipolar/exchange, nuclear registers, and strong nanophotonic interfaces | Implantation and delta doping mature but deterministic nanometer-scale coupled arrays remain difficult | Platform-leading single-node demonstrations, with defect- and temperature-dependent trade-offs [R073] | Most mature color-center networking evidence; nanofabrication and surfaces can degrade performance | Mature, spanning room-temperature NV control to cryogenic group-IV optics | Benchmark rather than automatic winner; SiC offers stronger wafer/electronics integration, not yet stronger end-to-end coupled-array evidence | |

The matrix separates two claims that are often quietly merged:

  • [Experiment] single-defect quality: SiC, rare-earth ions, silicon, diamond, and now hBN all contain individually controllable quantum systems, though with radically different evidence depth and conditions.

  • [Proposal] array suitability: none of these hosts has demonstrated a dense, designed, coherently interacting defect lattice.

Pick the drawer for the job. For an optically addressable interacting-defect program, SiC and diamond are the two primary toolboxes, with SiC favored when monolithic wafer electronics and photonics dominate; hBN is a high-risk planar alternative; rare-earth crystals favor cavity-mediated or spectral architectures rather than short-range lattices; and selected oxides remain discovery targets.

For an all-electrical exchange array, silicon moves to the front. The uncertainty is not cosmetic: a convincing two-dimensional hBN placement-and-yield result or a deterministic rare-earth implantation method could reorder the drawers.

Ways to get this wrong

The record-value collage. Combining a five-second SiC \(T_2\) at 5 K under 16,384 pulses [R097], a room-temperature implanted array [R099], and a separate nanophotonic linewidth [R098] does not describe one device.

Pattern equals placement. A lithographic aperture locates an ion trajectory.

Collision straggle, vacancy diffusion, annealing, charge conversion, and multi-defect occupancy determine the final active center. An optical spot at each mask location does not establish atomic coordinates.

Addressability equals coupling. Spectrally resolving two sites proves that controls can distinguish them. It does not measure \(J_{ij}\), coherent exchange, or entanglement.

Density equals a useful graph. Raising defect density increases desired coupling and unwanted couplings, implantation damage, spectral crowding, and charge noise together. The crystal does not know which edges were drawn in the grant proposal.

A long memory equals a fast processor. Rare-earth nuclear coherence can be extraordinary [R101], while direct local interactions remain weak. A useful array needs a favorable ratio of gate or coupling rate to error rate, not only a large \(T_2\).

Two-dimensional equals finished. hBN gives geometric access, not automatically chemical identity, uniformity, lifetime, or yield. The reported single-carbon-related ODMR evidence itself documents substantial variability [R100].

Semiconductor compatible equals process qualified. SiC can host electronics and photonics, but each implantation, etch, oxide, metal, and anneal step must be tested against charge stability and spin-optical coherence. Compatibility is a research program, not a sticker.

Coupled qubits equal a new phase of matter. Even a perfect SiC or silicon spin array would initially be an ordinary interacting quantum system. A gapped many-body phase with nonlocal observables does not follow from the host matrix alone.

How fast is fast enough

Let \(J\) be a desired coupling frequency, \(\Gamma_2=1/T_2\) an effective decoherence rate during the operation, \(\sigma_J\) the standard deviation of coupling disorder, \(\Omega\) the control rate, and \(\Delta_{\rm addr}\) the nearest unwanted spectral detuning. A useful regime asks, schematically,

\[ J\gg\Gamma_2,\qquad J\gg\sigma_J,\qquad \Gamma_2\ll\Omega\ll\Delta_{\rm addr}. \]

All symbols are frequencies in hertz, so the comparisons are dimensionally consistent. No host in the matrix has yet satisfied these inequalities across a large, designed defect array. They are the questions the next several chapters will quantify.

Check yourself

What fails if the host with the longest reported \(T_2\) is declared the winner?

Placement, coupling, addressability, readout, yield, and compatible operating conditions remain independent bottlenecks. \(Q_{\mathrm{array}}\) is limited by the weakest required operation.

What is SiC’s strongest array-level advantage?

The coexistence of optically addressable spins with commercial wafers, implantation, electronics, mechanics, and monolithic photonics.

Show that a 5.0 mT field on the cited PL6 center splits the two microwave lines to about 1.199 GHz and 1.481 GHz.

\(\gamma_e B_z=(2.82\ \mathrm{MHz\,G^{-1}})(50\ \mathrm G)=141\ \mathrm{MHz}\), so \(\nu_\pm=1340.4\pm141\) MHz.

What fails if the \(8\times8\) optical spots are treated as an interaction graph?

The pattern does not give nanometer-registered electron coordinates, and the 2024 entanglement was electron–nuclear, not selected electron–electron edges.

When might silicon outrank SiC?

When the target is an all-electrical, exchange-coupled programmable spin array and a direct optical interface is not required.

Show that the design-assumption crosstalk is \(10^{-2}\).

With \(\Omega=2\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and \(\Delta=20\ \mathrm{MHz}\), \(p_{\mathrm{xtalk}}\sim(\Omega/\Delta)^2=(1/10)^2=10^{-2}\). That leftover is not a measured array error; it is what the stated drive and detuning already predict.

Part V — Interacting defect systems

Two needles that feel each other, then three noisy bits pretending to be one quieter bit. Still local. Not yet a phase of matter.

Chapter 10 — Two needles that can feel each other

Lay two tiny compass needles on a table. Neither throws a particle at the other. Each still makes a magnetic field, so the second needle can feel the first.

Twist the line that joins them. The push can grow, shrink, change sign, or vanish. Distance matters, and so does angle.

The energy of one magnetic moment sitting in the field of another is dipole–dipole coupling. We take that as the definition.

What follows is that energy written for two electron spins in a crystal, and then a test of whether the number is large enough to use. A lonely megahertz is not a verdict.

The field of one needle

A magnetic moment is a tiny current loop. Far away, every loop with the same strength and direction looks the same.

Call the first moment \(\boldsymbol\mu_1\). Put a second moment a displacement \(\mathbf r\) away.

Write \(r\) for the length of \(\mathbf r\), in metres, and \(\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf r/r\) for the unit vector along the join.

The field the first moment makes at the second is

\[ \mathbf B_1(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3} \left[3(\boldsymbol\mu_1\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r})\hat{\mathbf r}-\boldsymbol\mu_1\right], \]

where \(\mu_0\) is the vacuum permeability, in \(\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}\). The energy of moment \(\boldsymbol\mu_2\) sitting in that field is \(-\boldsymbol\mu_2\cdot\mathbf B_1\). Multiply them and the two moments become an energy:

\[ H_{dd}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3} \left[ \boldsymbol\mu_1\!\cdot\!\boldsymbol\mu_2 -3(\boldsymbol\mu_1\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}) (\boldsymbol\mu_2\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}) \right]. \]

A localized moment’s field falls as \(1/r^3\). Energy is moment times field, so the coupling falls the same way. Hence the power is the product of those two facts, not a slogan pasted on later.

Drop localization and the \(1/r^3\) law is not a theorem. Overlapping electronic clouds are a different interaction, treated below. The far-field formula does not know about them.

Two electron spins

An electron spin is not a classical needle, but it still carries a magnetic moment. Write \(\mathbf S\) for the angular-momentum operator, in joule-seconds, and \(\hbar=h/(2\pi)\) for the reduced Planck constant.

The dimensionless spin is \(\mathbf s=\mathbf S/\hbar\). Its moment is \(\boldsymbol\mu=-g\mu_B\mathbf s\), where \(g\) is the electron’s dimensionless \(g\)-factor and \(\mu_B\) is the Bohr magneton, in \(\mathrm{J\,T^{-1}}\).

Plug those moments into the energy above. The two minus signs cancel. Dividing by Planck’s constant \(h\) turns joules into hertz:

\[ \boxed{ H_{dd}=h\,d(r) \left[ \mathbf s_1\!\cdot\!\mathbf s_2 -3(\mathbf s_1\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}) (\mathbf s_2\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}) \right]}, \qquad d(r)=\frac{\mu_0(g\mu_B)^2}{4\pi h r^3}. \]

The quantity \(d\) is a frequency, in hertz. The derivation supplies both the angular tensor and the \(1/r^3\) law. Neither is decorative.

Using \(g=2.0023\), \(\mu_B=9.2740101\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J\,T^{-1}}\), and \(h=6.62607015\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\), the CODATA constants give [R105]

\[ d(r)=\frac{52.04\ \mathrm{MHz\,nm^3}}{r^3}. \]

A units check: \(\mu_0\mu_B^2/r^3\) is joules. Divide by \(h\), in joule-seconds, and you have \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}=\mathrm{Hz}\). No leftover nanometres.

The table is that characteristic coefficient for two pointlike \(g\approx2\) electron spins. It does not include the angular factor or the matrix elements of a particular transition.

Separation \(r\) | \(d(r)\) | \(1/d\) | Noisy benchmark: \(d/\Delta\nu^*\) | Quiet benchmark: \(d/\Delta\nu^*\) | |

1 nm | 52.04 MHz | 19.2 ns | 164 | 16,400 | |

2 nm | 6.505 MHz | 154 ns | 20.4 | 2,044 | |

5 nm | 416.3 kHz | 2.40 µs | 1.31 | 131 | |

10 nm | 52.04 kHz | 19.2 µs | 0.164 | 16.4 | |

20 nm | 6.505 kHz | 154 µs | 0.0204 | 2.04 | |

50 nm | 416.3 Hz | 2.40 ms | 0.00131 | 0.131 | |

The two right columns are assumptions, not platform records. The noisy column takes free-induction coherence \(T_2^*=1\ \mathrm{\mu s}\); the quiet column takes \(T_2^*=100\ \mathrm{\mu s}\). For exponential loss of phase, the Lorentzian full width at half maximum is

\[ \Delta\nu^*=\frac{1}{\pi T_2^*}, \]

or 318 kHz and 3.18 kHz. A 52 kHz coupling at 10 nm sits above the quiet linewidth and inside the noisy one. Hence a bare “52 kHz” is not a gate verdict until it is compared with a linewidth measured under the same conditions.

At 1–2 nm the point-dipole arithmetic is still a useful reference, but electronic clouds may overlap. Then a different interaction, treated below, starts to matter, and the point-dipole-only model is incomplete.

At 50 nm the magnetic interaction still exists. Whether you can use it depends on coherence and on how much control you can afford.

From here on, every Hamiltonian is written in frequency units: \(H/h\) is in hertz. When two defects \(i\) and \(j\) have a coherent matrix element \(J_{ij}\), that number is whatever actually connects them. It is not automatically the same in every spin direction.

When the join is not along the field

An applied field picks a quantization axis. Call that axis \(z\), and let \(\theta\) be the angle between \(\hat{\mathbf r}\) and \(z\).

If the Zeeman or zero-field splitting is much larger than \(d\), terms that rotate quickly can be dropped. Write \(s^\pm=s^x\pm i s^y\) for the raising and lowering operators.

What remains is the energy-conserving piece:

\[ \frac{H_{dd}^{\mathrm{sec}}}{h} =d(r)(1-3\cos^2\theta) \left[s_1^z s_2^z-\frac14(s_1^+s_2^-+s_1^-s_2^+)\right]. \]

That leftover piece is the secular interaction. The name is worth keeping because ordinary English suggests “worldly,” while here it means only the part a high-field experiment actually sees: the rest averages away.

The first term is a conditional frequency shift. The second swaps one spin excitation when the two transitions match.

The angular factor is \(-2\) when the defects sit along \(z\), \(+1\) when they sit in the transverse plane, and zero at the magic angle \(\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\approx54.7^\circ\). Hence equal distances on a lattice can still give unequal, signed edges.

Suppose the useful two-state subspace is \(H/h=j(|10\rangle\langle01|+|01\rangle\langle10|)\), with \(j\) in hertz. Then a complete excitation swap takes \(t_{\mathrm{swap}}=1/(4|j|)\).

A rough gate condition is \(4|j|T_2\gg1\). Resolving the interaction in frequency generally needs \(|j|\) larger than the relevant linewidth.

Pulse sequences can refocus slow single-spin noise while keeping a chosen two-spin term, so \(T_2\), not \(T_2^*\), may govern a carefully designed gate.

Near the magic angle the terms you dropped, and any small tilt, start to matter. Drop the hypothesis that the splitting dwarfs \(d\), and the secular truncation is no longer justified. Pulse sequences cannot refocus relaxation, pulse error, or every fluctuating coupling.

Clouds that overlap

Press two electronic clouds close enough to share space. Electrons are indistinguishable fermions: swap them and the two-electron wavefunction changes sign. Different spin arrangements then cost different Coulomb energy.

Let \(\phi_i(\mathbf x)\) and \(\phi_j(\mathbf x)\) be the localized orbitals. The energy shift comes from the Coulomb matrix element in which their labels are crossed:

\[ J_{ij}^{\mathrm{ex}}\sim \iint d^3x\,d^3x'\, \phi_i^*(\mathbf x)\phi_j(\mathbf x) \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon|\mathbf x-\mathbf x'|} \phi_j^*(\mathbf x')\phi_i(\mathbf x'), \]

where \(e\) is the elementary charge and \(\epsilon\) is the host permittivity. That energy is direct exchange. Here the orbitals themselves overlap; later, virtual routes will not need that.

If an orbital envelope decays over a localization length \(a\), overlap is roughly \(e^{-r/a}\), so exchange commonly behaves like a polynomial times \(e^{-2r/a}\). Prefactor, sign, orbital orientation, and exponent are material-specific.

[Numerics] Atomistic calculations for several diamond spin-center pairs found exchange larger than magnetic dipolar coupling below roughly 3 nm for NV pairs, with strong crystallographic and defect-orientation dependence [R107]. That is a calculated trend, not a demonstrated reproducible NV–NV gate. Exchange buys strength by spending placement tolerance.

Drop overlap and this term vanishes; the dipolar term remains. The two mechanisms are not interchangeable names for “spins that talk.”

A hop that is not allowed

Take two half-filled sites. An electron would like to hop from one to the other with amplitude \(t\), in joules, but putting two electrons on one site costs \(U\), also in joules, and \(U\) is large.

Direct hopping is blocked in the low-energy subspace. A virtual doubly occupied state can still be visited and left.

Second-order perturbation theory then lowers the singlet relative to the triplet:

\[ H_{\mathrm{SE}}=J_{\mathrm{SE}}\,\mathbf s_1\cdot\mathbf s_2, \qquad J_{\mathrm{SE}}\approx\frac{4t^2}{U}. \]

This \(J_{\mathrm{SE}}\) is an energy. Its frequency is \(J_{\mathrm{SE}}/h\). Hence a blocked hop still generates an effective spin–spin coupling, of a size set by how expensive the virtual visit is.

This is superexchange. It is not a grander name for direct exchange.

Virtual charge hopping is the mechanism. If \(t\propto e^{-r/a}\), the scale again falls approximately as \(e^{-2r/a}\).

With an explicit bridge orbital it contains products of each defect-to-bridge hopping, so bond angles and bridge chemistry matter more than defect-to-defect distance alone.

The factor and sign can change for multiple orbitals, Hund coupling, or different filling, as Anderson’s original analysis makes clear [R108]. Drop the hypothesis that \(U\) is large compared with \(t\), and the low-energy spin-only description is no longer the right starting point.

Sharing a photon

Two optical transition dipoles talk through the electromagnetic field. In empty three-dimensional space the coherent near field scales as \(1/r^3\).

Retardation adds oscillatory \(1/r^2\) and \(1/r\) pieces once the separation is comparable to the optical wavelength. The same field also causes collective radiative decay, so a coherent level shift has to be compared with the optical homogeneous linewidth.

A resonator can replace free-space distance with a mode profile. Let \(a\) annihilate one cavity photon, \(\sigma_i^-\) lower emitter \(i\), \(g_i\) be its coupling frequency, and \(\Delta_i\) its detuning from the cavity. When \(|\Delta_i|\gg |g_i|\), the cavity is only virtually occupied. Eliminating it leaves the scale

\[ J_{12}^{\mathrm{cav}}\approx\frac{g_1g_2}{2} \left(\frac{1}{\Delta_1}+\frac{1}{\Delta_2}\right). \]

There is no universal \(1/r^n\): \(g_i\) follows the electric-field amplitude at each site. If the cavity energy-decay rate is \(\kappa\), it also contributes loss of order \((g_i/\Delta_i)^2\kappa\). Hence the useful test is \(|J_{12}^{\mathrm{cav}}|\) larger than emitter dephasing and cavity-induced decay, not merely nonzero.

This leftover interaction is cavity-mediated coupling. The range is now the mode, not the Euclidean distance.

[Experiment] Two SiV centers coupled to a common diamond nanocavity exhibited spectrally resolved superradiant and subradiant optical states [R086]. That is coherent photon-mediated emitter interaction. It is not, by itself, a high-fidelity gate between long-lived ground-state spin qubits.

Drop the large-detuning hypothesis and the cavity is occupied, not a virtual mediator. Reporting \(g_1g_2/\Delta\) without \(\kappa\), temperature, and emitter linewidth is half a calculation.

Sharing a vibration

Strain is the spatial derivative of displacement. A defect whose orbital or spin energy shifts with strain acts as an elastic dipole.

In an isotropic three-dimensional bulk solid, displacement from a point force scales approximately as \(1/r\). Differentiating at source and receiver gives a static elastic-dipole interaction that typically scales as \(1/r^3\).

[Theory] A 2024 lattice treatment derived this \(1/r^3\) phonon-mediated law for NV centers and identified a quadrupole–quadrupole spin structure [R111]. Crystal anisotropy, surfaces, and nanobeams can change the tensor and the power law.

A quantized mechanical mode is a shared vibration both defects can lean on. Let \(b\) annihilate one quantum of that vibration, \(g_i^{\mathrm{ph}}\) be the defect–mode coupling frequency, and \(\Delta_i^{\mathrm{ph}}\) the detuning. Dispersive elimination gives

\[ J_{12}^{\mathrm{ph}}\sim \frac{g_1^{\mathrm{ph}}g_2^{\mathrm{ph}}}{2} \left(\frac{1}{\Delta_1^{\mathrm{ph}}}+\frac{1}{\Delta_2^{\mathrm{ph}}}\right). \]

That shared quantum is a phonon. A waveguide Green function, rather than Euclidean distance alone, now sets the range.

An ideal single mode can link distant sites, but mechanical decay rate \(\kappa_m\) and thermal occupation \(\bar n=[\exp(hf_m/k_BT)-1]^{-1}\) add noise. Here \(f_m\) is the mode frequency, \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant, and \(T\) is temperature.

[Proposal] A quasi-one-dimensional diamond waveguide linking SiV centers by propagating phonons has been quantitatively analysed, including state emission and reabsorption [R109]. Treat this as a proposed network architecture, not evidence that a many-defect phonon bus already outperforms dipolar links.

Drop isotropy and the \(1/r^3\) bulk law need not survive. Drop low thermal occupation and the same mode that mediates \(J_{12}^{\mathrm{ph}}\) also injects noise of order \(\kappa_m(2\bar n+1)\).

Sharing a nucleus

An electron defect can feel a nearby nucleus. The coupling is a tensor \(\mathbf A\), in hertz, that ties the electron spin \(\mathbf s\) to the nuclear spin \(\mathbf I\):

\[ H_{\mathrm{hf}}/h=\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf I. \]

That tensor is the hyperfine interaction. It is how a nucleus becomes a mediator rather than just a memory.

If two electrons couple off-resonantly to the same nucleus, virtual nuclear flips generate an electron–electron scale \(J_N\sim A_{1\perp}A_{2\perp}/\delta_N\), where \(A_{i\perp}\) is a transverse hyperfine component and \(\delta_N\) is the detuning of the virtual nuclear transition. Exact factors depend on the selected levels.

Dipolar hyperfine terms scale as \(1/r_i^3\) with each electron–nucleus distance \(r_i\), so the product can scale as \(1/(r_1^3r_2^3)\) at fixed detuning. Contact hyperfine coupling instead follows electron density at the nucleus and is short-ranged. Hence there is no single law in the electron–electron separation.

The reverse architecture — dipolar-coupled NV electrons mediating an interaction between their nuclear memories — has been developed theoretically [R110]. [Proposal] It illustrates a mediator hierarchy, not experimental proof of a nuclear bus between arbitrary defects.

Nuclear spins offer long memory but slow coupling. Mediator initialization, spectral crowding, and electron back-action must sit in the linewidth budget.

Drop the off-resonance hypothesis and the nucleus is a real participant, not a virtual mediator. The product-of-hyperfines estimate then ceases to be the right starting point.

Electric needles

Magnetic moments are not the only pair that can feel each other at a distance. Some defect states carry a state-dependent electric moment \(\mathbf d\), measured in coulomb-metres. In an isotropic dielectric the electrostatic energy is

\[ H_{ee}=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon r^3} \left[\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2 -3(\mathbf d_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})(\mathbf d_2\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})\right]. \]

Same angular tensor. Same \(1/r^3\) near field. Only the constants changed: permittivity \(\epsilon\) instead of \(\mu_0\), electric moments instead of magnetic ones.

As an illustrative upper-scale calculation, two 1-debye dipoles in a dielectric with relative permittivity \(\epsilon_r=5.7\) have coefficient \(H_{ee}/h\approx26.5\ \mathrm{GHz\,nm^3}/r^3\). Here \(1\ \mathrm{D}=3.33564\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\,m}\).

At 10 nm that is 26.5 MHz. If each qubit state differs by only 0.01 D, the state-dependent product is smaller by \(10^{-4}\), giving 2.65 kHz at 10 nm.

Those dipoles are explicit assumptions, not measured NV values.

Ground-state spin levels usually couple to electric field only through spin–orbit, orbital, or strain admixture. Optical orbital transitions can couple much more strongly but decay faster.

The NV electric and strain response, and its symmetry, are reviewed in [R074]. Electric coupling must beat charge-noise-induced Stark linewidth and leakage.

A large electric susceptibility is both a control knob and a larger antenna for unwanted electric fields. Drop the assumption that the state-dependent moment is a full debye, and the megahertz-scale estimate collapses by the product of the two reductions.

What a lab pair actually did

The cleanest pairwise benchmark is dipolar-coupled NV centers. [Experiment] A pair separated by \(25\pm2\ \mathrm{nm}\) had a measured effective dipolar coupling of \(4.93\pm0.05\ \mathrm{kHz}\), and refocused optimal-control sequences produced electron-spin entanglement with reported fidelity above 0.82 at room temperature [R106].

Our point-dipole coefficient at 25 nm is \(52.04\ \mathrm{MHz}/25^3=3.33\ \mathrm{kHz}\); an orientation or matrix-element factor of order unity makes the measured value consistent with magnetic dipolar coupling. Hence the experiment used spin echo and control engineering because free-induction noise could mask the interaction.

It did not simply wait for a 4.93 kHz number to become a gate.

[Experiment] Millisecond-scale Hahn-echo coherence — up to 1.8 ms at room temperature in a specially isotopically engineered, low-spin-bath diamond sample — has been reported for single NV centers [R079]. That condition is not inherited automatically by dense implanted arrays. Damage, surfaces, unwanted paramagnetic defects, and inter-defect frequency disorder change both \(T_2\) and yield.

Mechanism | Range or placement law | Evidence level relevant here | Coherent-use comparison | |

Magnetic dipole | \(1/r^3\), angular tensor | Two-NV gates and entanglement demonstrated [R106] | \(j\) versus spin linewidth, \(1/T_2\), pulse error | |

Direct exchange | roughly exponential; atomistic orientation dependence | Diamond-pair dominance below about 3 nm is numerical [R107] | \(J/h\) versus dephasing, leakage, placement disorder | |

Superexchange | \(4t^2/U\); hopping often exponential | General mechanism established; defect implementation is material-specific [R108] | \(J/h\) versus charge/orbital noise and validity gap \(U/h\) | |

Free-space optical | near \(1/r^3\), retarded oscillatory tail | Collective optical effects are platform-specific | coherent shift versus optical linewidth and collective decay |

Cavity photon | cavity mode profile, not a simple power | Two-SiV coherent optical interaction demonstrated [R086] | \(J_{cav}\) versus emitter dephasing and induced \(\kappa\) loss | |

Static strain | often \(1/r^3\) for bulk elastic dipoles | Single-defect response established [R074]; NV pair interaction derived [R111] | shift versus strain disorder and spectral diffusion | |

Phonon bus | mechanical Green function/mode profile | Bulk NV theory [R111]; SiV waveguide proposal [R109] | \(J_{ph}\) versus \(\kappa_m(2\bar n+1)\) and spin dephasing | |

Nuclear bus | product of hyperfine couplings | Closely related electron-mediated nuclear scheme proposed [R110] | \(J_N\) versus nuclear/electron decoherence and control time | |

Electric dipole | near-field \(1/(\epsilon r^3)\) | Electric susceptibility established; pair gate is defect-specific [R074] | state-dependent shift versus Stark linewidth and leakage | |

This table refuses to rank mechanisms by coupling alone. A 10 MHz orbital interaction with a 100 MHz optical linewidth is not “stronger for quantum logic” than a 10 kHz spin interaction with a 100 Hz refocused linewidth.

Two coherently coupled defect spins are two interacting physical qubits. Several such spins projected onto a doublet may form one encoded qubit.

Neither fact establishes topological order. Emergent anyons need a many-body Hamiltonian, a gapped phase, and nonlocal observables — not merely an interaction graph that resembles a drawing in a theory paper.

Ways to get this wrong

Quote an angular rate \(\Omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) as if it were a cyclic frequency \(f\) in hertz. They differ by \(\Omega=2\pi f\). This chapter uses \(H/h\) and hertz throughout.

Treat \(52.04\ \mathrm{MHz\,nm^3}\) as every transition’s coupling. Drop the angular factor, or sit at the magic angle, and the secular term vanishes while \(d(r)\) is still finite.

Call every indirect interaction superexchange. Virtual charge hopping is superexchange. A virtual cavity photon is photon mediation. A virtual phonon is phonon mediation. Similar second-order algebra does not make the microscopic noise identical.

Eliminate a cavity or mechanical mode and report only \(g_1g_2/\Delta\). The same elimination generates inherited loss. Without \(\kappa\), temperature, and emitter linewidth the coherent piece is not a budget.

Prefer the largest available \(J\) at any cost. Very short-range exchange can beat dipolar coupling and still be wildly nonuniform across nominally identical pairs. A target Hamiltonian may prefer a weaker, predictable edge.

Use the best coherence from one sample and the densest spacing from another. A valid feasibility budget must combine coupling, linewidth, yield, addressability, and temperature under the same fabrication conditions. Cross-paper arithmetic is useful for bounds, not proof of an integrated device.

Check yourself

Show that magnetic dipolar coupling scales as \(1/r^3\).

A localized dipole’s field scales as moment divided by \(r^3\). The second dipole’s energy is its moment dotted into that field. The product therefore falls as \(1/r^3\).

Show that doubling an electron-spin separation divides \(d\) by eight.

\(d(r)\propto 1/r^3\), so \(d(2r)=d(r)/8\). For \(g\approx2\), that is 52.04 MHz at 1 nm and 6.505 MHz at 2 nm.

What fails if you take \(d=50\ \mathrm{kHz}\) as a coherence verdict?

The number alone cannot answer. Compare the selected matrix element with homogeneous linewidth, refocused \(T_2\), relaxation, detuning disorder, and control errors. A 52 kHz coupling at 10 nm sits inside a 318 kHz noisy linewidth and above a 3.18 kHz quiet one.

Show that the secular angular factor vanishes at \(\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt{3})\).

\(1-3\cos^2\theta=0\) when \(\cos^2\theta=1/3\), so \(\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt{3})\approx54.7^\circ\). Near that angle the terms dropped in the secular truncation, and any small tilt, start to matter.

What fails if you drop the distinction between direct exchange and superexchange?

Direct exchange needs overlapping orbitals and fermionic antisymmetry. Superexchange needs virtual hopping through energetically forbidden charge configurations, with the simplest scale \(4t^2/U\). Collapse the names and you inherit the wrong range law, the wrong noise, and the wrong placement tolerance.

What fails if a cavity-mediated \(J_{12}^{\mathrm{cav}}\) is quoted without \(\kappa\)?

Position enters through mode amplitudes \(g_i\), so there is no universal \(1/r^n\). Cavity loss still contributes \((g_i/\Delta_i)^2\kappa\). A nonzero coherent shift is not a gate if induced decay and emitter dephasing exceed it.

Those numbers and tensors are enough to write a small cluster Hamiltonian and ask whether it has an isolated low-energy doublet.
