Chapter 11 — Three noisy bits pretending to be one

Three compass needles sit on a table. Each jitters on its own. A truck goes by, a stray magnet swings past, the room warms a little — any of those can flip one needle, and the bit it was holding is gone.

Glue the three together with stiff springs. From across the room you no longer watch three independent jitters.

You watch a single object that can move in two slow ways. Every other motion bends a spring and costs more energy than you are willing to spend.

We have not invented a quieter needle. We have written an energy for three spins and kept only a two-dimensional low-energy piece. That piece is this chapter: isolate the pair, say what a physical operator does inside it, and then be honest about what the trick buys.

Eight states, two that matter

Take three real spin-\(1/2\) objects, numbered \(1,2,3\). Each can point up or down along a field, so the trio has eight product states.

We will not treat those eight as eight independent answers. We will tie the spins so that, at low energy, only two combinations matter.

Call that tied trio a cluster. Later we will couple several such trios, weakly, and treat each one as a single two-level object.

Let \(\mathbf S_i=(S_i^x,S_i^y,S_i^z)\) be the dimensionless spin of site \(i\), so \(S_i^z\) has eigenvalues \(\pm 1/2\). The energy inside one cluster is antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange plus a uniform field,

\[ H_C=J\sum_{i<j}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j-bS_{\mathrm{tot}}^z,\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z=\sum_{i=1}^3S_i^z. \]

The exchange \(J>0\) and the Zeeman coefficient \(b>0\) both have units of energy, so every term in \(H_C\) does too. If a lab quotes frequencies, use \(J/h\) and \(b/h\) in hertz, where \(h\) is Planck’s constant.

Three spins decompose into one total-spin \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}=3/2\) quartet and two copies of a total-spin \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}=1/2\) doublet. Restrict attention first to total magnetization \(m=S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z=+1/2\). In the product basis those two states can be written

\[ \begin{aligned} |\tilde 0\rangle &=\frac{|\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle}{\sqrt2},\\ |\tilde 1\rangle &=\frac{|\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle+|\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle-2|\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\rangle}{\sqrt6}. \end{aligned} \]

The first two arrows in \(|\tilde 0\rangle\) form a singlet. In \(|\tilde 1\rangle\) they occupy the triplet channel, coupled with spin 3 to total spin \(1/2\). Direct inner products give unit norm and \(\langle\tilde0|\tilde1\rangle=0\).

Using

\[ \sum_{i<j}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j =\frac12\left(S_{\mathrm{tot}}^2-\sum_i S_i^2\right), \]

and \(S_i^2=3/4\), both of those states have the same energy

\[ E_L=-\frac{3J}{4}-\frac b2. \]

Hence the two states span a two-dimensional eigenspace of \(H_C\). That is not yet a useful bit: it is a degeneracy waiting for a control story.

If \(J<0\), the quartet lies lower and this pair is not the ground piece. The antiferromagnetic hypothesis is doing work.

The pair we keep

A pair of low eigenvalues is not a computer. The two states have to be controllable and readable.

Unwanted states have to stay empty. Whatever we do to the three physical spins has to look, inside this pair, like the operation we meant.

When information is deliberately mapped into a chosen two-dimensional piece of a larger space, that piece is an encoded qubit. “Encoded” is a bookkeeping claim, not a compliment. The repetition state, this exchange-controlled pair, and an arbitrary pair of levels picked from a molecule are all encoded qubits if you put the information there on purpose.

Write the two kept states as \(|\tilde 0\rangle\) and \(|\tilde 1\rangle\). Everything else in the eight-dimensional space of the trio is a way to leave the encoding.

Encoding is not, by itself, protection. Protection is a later calculation about a named noise.

The climb out of the pair

Any motion that is not one of the two kept states costs extra energy. That extra cost is what keeps the extra states empty — but only if the pokes trying to fill them are smaller than the cost.

Collect the two kept states with

\[ P=|\tilde0\rangle\langle\tilde0|+|\tilde1\rangle\langle\tilde1|,\qquad Q=I-P, \]

where \(I\) is the identity on all eight states of the three spins. The complementary piece \(Q\) is every state we have declared to be an escape.

For an exactly degenerate pair, the upward cost of an escape is

\[ \Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}=\min_{|a\rangle\in Q}(E_a-E_L), \]

provided every excluded eigenstate sits above \(E_L\). That number is the leakage gap. It measures the climb out of the pair, not the quietness inside it.

If the intended pair itself has a small internal splitting, measure from the top of that pair to the nearest excluded level. Otherwise a large splitting inside the bit gets advertised as a large leakage gap, which it is not.

The other \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}=1/2\) states have \(m=-1/2\) and cost \(b\). The lowest member of the \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}=3/2\) quartet has \(m=+3/2\) and costs \(3J/2-b\). Therefore

\[ \boxed{\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}=\min\left(b,\frac{3J}{2}-b\right)},\qquad 0<b<\frac{3J}{2}. \]

At \(b=0\), the opposite-magnetization partners sit at the same energy as the chosen pair, so the fixed-\(m\) subspace is not energetically isolated. Raising \(b\) helps until the polarized quartet is pulled down. At \(b=3J/4\), the two candidate escape costs are equal at \(3J/4\).

If a perturbation has a characteristic matrix element \(v\), also in energy units, then \(v/\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}\) is dimensionless. The low-energy description needs that ratio small. A resonant control with angular Rabi rate \(\Omega\) similarly needs \(\hbar\Omega/\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}\ll 1\) unless a selection rule forbids the escape exactly.

A gap suppresses transitions only relative to the pokes trying to make them. It does not stop noise from acting within the pair. A perfectly isolated pair of levels can still dephase perfectly well.

What a physical operator looks like inside

We now need the rule that turns a real operation on the three spins into an operation on the pair. That rule is a two-by-two matrix, not a speech.

Define

\[ \begin{aligned} \bar Z&=|\tilde0\rangle\langle\tilde0|-|\tilde1\rangle\langle\tilde1|,\\ \bar X&=|\tilde0\rangle\langle\tilde1|+|\tilde1\rangle\langle\tilde0|,\\ \bar Y&=-i|\tilde0\rangle\langle\tilde1|+i|\tilde1\rangle\langle\tilde0|. \end{aligned} \]

For any physical operator \(O\), its first-order action on the pair is

\[ O_{\mathrm{eff}}=POP=c_0P+c_x\bar X+c_y\bar Y+c_z\bar Z. \]

The four coefficients are just the four matrix entries of \(O\) in the ordered basis \(\{|\tilde0\rangle,|\tilde1\rangle\}\). The machine that does this is the projector \(P\): sandwich the real operator, read the two-by-two.

For our three spins that calculation gives

\[ \begin{aligned} P(\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2)P &= -\frac14P-\frac12\bar Z,\\ P(\mathbf S_2\cdot\mathbf S_3)P &= -\frac14P+\frac14\bar Z-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\bar X,\\ P(\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_3)P &= -\frac14P+\frac14\bar Z+\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\bar X. \end{aligned} \]

Now let the three pairwise exchanges be independently tunable, \(J_{12},J_{23},J_{13}\). Inside the pair,

\[ PH_CP=E_{\mathrm{off}}P+h_x\bar X+h_z\bar Z, \]

where

\[ E_{\mathrm{off}}=-\frac{J_{12}+J_{23}+J_{13}}4-\frac b2,\quad h_x=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(J_{13}-J_{23}),\quad h_z=\frac{J_{13}+J_{23}-2J_{12}}4. \]

All three coefficients have energy units. Hence changing pairwise exchange rotates the encoded qubit about two nonparallel axes on its Bloch sphere.

Pulse sequences generate the third axis through noncommuting rotations. That is the core exchange-only idea proposed for three-spin qubits [R114] and later demonstrated in semiconductor quantum dots [R115].

[Theory/Experiment] Isotropic exchange also commutes with \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}^2\) and \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z\), so ideal exchange pulses do not couple this pair to the quartet. Real anisotropy, field gradients, timing errors, and coupling to higher orbital or defect levels restore leakage.

Once several clusters sit nearby, write the full energy as

\[ H=\sum_C H_C+\lambda\sum_{\langle C,D\rangle}V_{CD}. \]

Here \(C\) and \(D\) label clusters, \(H_C\) is the strong energy inside cluster \(C\), \(V_{CD}\) couples neighbors, and the dimensionless bookkeeping parameter \(\lambda\) says the coupling between clusters is weak. If each \(H_C\) has a well-isolated pair, the large microscopic space may reduce to one effective two-level system per cluster.

That word may is doing honest work. The states must be controllable and readable. Unwanted states must stay empty. Projected interactions must have the form you need. The fabrication process must reproduce the spectrum.

Projecting two clusters.

Let \(P_C\) project cluster \(C\) onto its pair and let \(P_{\mathrm{all}}=\prod_C P_C\).

To first order in weak intercluster coupling, \[ H_{\mathrm{eff}}=P_{\mathrm{all}}HP_{\mathrm{all}} =\sum_C P_CH_CP_C+\lambda\sum_{\langle C,D\rangle}(P_CP_D)V_{CD}(P_CP_D). \] Each projected pair term can be expanded in \(\bar\sigma_C^\mu\bar\sigma_D^\nu\), where \(\mu,\nu\in\{0,x,y,z\}\) and \(\bar\sigma^0=P\).

Virtual visits to \(Q\) add corrections of characteristic scale \(\lambda^2\|V\|^2/\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}\). Chapter 22 will derive that statement rather than asking it to pass on charm.

Drop the isolation of each cluster and the product projector is not a low-energy description. A nonzero \(QVP\) causes leakage and virtual corrections; the small parameter is a coupling matrix element divided by \(\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}\), not confidence divided by typography.

A bath that cannot tell them apart

Encoding alone makes no protection claim. Protection is a statement about a specific noise and a specific calculation.

Suppose the trio couples to a bath through

\[ H_{SB}=S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z\otimes B_z, \]

where \(B_z\) is an unspecified bath operator. In the fixed-\(m=+1/2\) pair,

\[ PS_{\mathrm{tot}}^zP=\frac12P. \]

The bath therefore cannot learn whether the encoded state was \(|\tilde0\rangle\) or \(|\tilde1\rangle\). It adds the same phase to both.

A subspace with that property, for that noise, is a decoherence-free subspace [R112]. [Theory] The name is worth keeping because ordinary English suggests that nothing decoheres, while the claim is always conditional: name the noise operators, then show that each acts as a scalar on the code.

It is not a decoherence-free subspace for independent noise \(\sum_i S_i^z\otimes B_i\). Different \(B_i\) operators can distinguish the spin patterns. “The environment is probably common-mode” is not that calculation.

A bath that can spin the box

Under fully collective noise the interaction can contain all three components,

\[ H_{SB}=\sum_{\alpha=x,y,z}S_{\mathrm{tot}}^\alpha\otimes B_\alpha. \]

A collective sideways rotation changes \(m\), so the fixed-\(m\) pair is not decoherence-free for this noise. Yet the entire total-spin-\(1/2\) sector factorizes as

\[ \mathcal H_{1/2}\cong \mathbb C^2_{\mathrm{logical}}\otimes\mathbb C^2_{\mathrm{gauge}}. \]

Collective spin operators act on the second factor and leave the first one alone. Information stored in that first factor is a noiseless subsystem [R113]. [Theory] The second factor — a gauge spin — may wander without erasing the logical state.

This is stronger than the fixed-magnetization decoherence-free subspace against longitudinal noise, but only for genuinely collective coupling.

Three equal-exchange spins have a four-dimensional \(S=1/2\) sector. A two-state projector therefore needs a fixed magnetization, another splitting mechanism, or this noiseless-subsystem reading. Forgetting the extra two states is how the gauge degeneracy sneaks back in.

Exchange as the only knob

An exchange-only qubit uses controllable pair exchanges rather than separately addressed single-spin rotations [R114]; [R115]. The hardware claim is about which knobs exist, not about how quiet the bit is.

Since exchanges commute with collective rotations, they naturally stir the logical factor of the three-spin noiseless subsystem and ignore its gauge orientation.

Magnetic dipolar coupling is anisotropic. Assuming exchange is available because “spins interact” confuses the operator you have with the operator the encoding asked for. Each physical interaction must be projected from its actual form.

When a symmetry forbids an escape

A different claim is that a symmetry, not a gap slogan, is doing the forbidding.

If a symmetry generator \(G\) commutes with \(H_C\), eigenstates can be labeled by symmetry sectors. A perturbation that also commutes with \(G\) has zero matrix elements between inequivalent sectors. That is symmetry protection: a vanishing matrix element, not a vibe.

In the toy model, isotropic exchange preserves total spin, while the longitudinal field preserves total magnetization. Those facts can close some leakage doors.

They do not automatically protect a logical splitting. Both logical states above share \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}=1/2\) and \(m=+1/2\), and unequal symmetry-allowed exchanges produce \(\bar X\) and \(\bar Z\) at first order. Hence to claim protection, identify the symmetry, the representation carried by the code, and the symmetry of the actual perturbation.

Drop the hypothesis that the perturbation commutes with \(G\), and the vanishing matrix element is gone. Anisotropy, field gradients, and orbital admixture are the usual ways it leaves.

Local operators still see the secret

The two states we kept live on three nearby spins. You can tell them apart by looking at a local pair: \(\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2\) is different in \(|\tilde 0\rangle\) and \(|\tilde 1\rangle\).

Unequal local exchange splits them at first order. A closed path among the three sites does not pick up a logical phase that depends on the shape of the path.

Hence the logical operators are supported on three nearby spins, and the degeneracy does not depend on the topology of a macroscopic surface.

That is encoding. It is not topological order.

Topological order, when it exists, is a property of a whole phase of matter: no small local poke can read the information or split it at first order, and the excitations that carry it can be moved around a large lattice. People later call those objects anyons.

Our cluster is not one of them. The three physical spins are ordinary qubits; the pair selected by \(P\) is one encoded qubit; driving those spins so their amplitudes reproduce a desired model is digital or analog emulation.

None of those facts is an emergent phase.

What the laboratory actually has

The exact Heisenberg triangle is a teaching model. Color-center hardware supplies spin-1 NV electrons, spin-\(1/2\) or larger nuclear memories, anisotropic dipolar and hyperfine tensors, optical reset, strain, and imperfect placement. Selecting two levels of a spin-1 center can make an effective physical qubit, but it does not turn magnetic dipolar coupling into isotropic exchange.

A literature search through August 2026 is most useful when it begins with inclusion criteria. For a direct realization of the worked example, ask for: (i) at least three deliberately used spins associated with color centers; (ii) a static strong intracluster Hamiltonian; (iii) a spectroscopically isolated logical doublet; and (iv) control through projected pair interactions. Related literature sorts into four bins.

Encoded center–nuclear registers exist. [Experiment] Reiserer et al. encoded a diamond network memory in two nearby \({}^{13}\mathrm C\) spins whose antiparallel states suppress common-mode phase shifts during repeated NV optical operations [R116].

Cramer et al. encoded a qubit across three \({}^{13}\mathrm C\) spins and repeatedly extracted and corrected error syndromes with an NV ancilla [R117]. These are genuine encoded color-center-associated clusters, but the protection comes respectively from a decoherence-free subspace and active error correction, not from the ground doublet of a three-center exchange Hamiltonian.

Spin-pair encodings have become strong experimental memories. [Experiment] Bartling et al. used pairs of \({}^{13}\mathrm C\) nuclei near NV nodes as antiparallel spin-pair qubits, reported intrinsic dephasing times exceeding one minute, and entangled two such encoded qubits [R118].

The “exceeding one minute” condition belongs to those measured nuclear pairs and protocols, not to arbitrary color-center clusters. This is compelling evidence for noise-selective encoding, not for passive many-body topological protection.

Large local registers and coupled centers are real, but they do not satisfy all four criteria. [Experiment] A ten-qubit diamond register combined one NV electron with its nitrogen nucleus and eight \({}^{13}\mathrm C\) nuclei under gate-based control [R119].

Separately, two NV electron spins have been entangled through their direct dipolar interaction [R106]. The former is a programmable register; the latter is an interacting pair.

Neither paper reports a three-color-center low-energy encoded qubit.

Multi-NV decoherence-free architectures have been proposed. [Proposal] Yun et al. proposed geometric gates in a decoherence-free subspace using NV centers coupled through cavity-QED resources [R120].

This is a genuine color-center decoherence-free-subspace proposal, but its logical space and gates are engineered by drives and a mediator; it is not evidence that a fabricated, strongly coupled NV triangle naturally has the spectrum and projected exchanges derived above.

The scoped verdict is therefore precise: the literature contains genuine encoded qubits built from spins around color centers, genuine coupled color centers, and genuine multi-center decoherence-free-subspace gate proposals. In the sources identified here, no experiment or proposal simultaneously establishes the particular chain “three deliberately positioned color-center electronic spins \(\rightarrow\) static exchange-dominated isolated doublet \(\rightarrow\) projected exchange-only qubit.” This is a search result, not a proof that no paper exists. It marks the missing link that a defect-cluster proposal must supply rather than quietly borrowing from semiconductor quantum dots.

Ways to get this wrong

Call any two low levels a protected qubit. The leakage gap concerns transitions out of the code. Noise projected as \(\bar Z\) still dephases inside it.

Forget the extra two states. Three equal-exchange spins have a four-dimensional \(S=1/2\) sector. A two-state projector requires fixed magnetization, another splitting mechanism, or the noiseless-subsystem reading.

Project and then discard \(Q\) forever. A nonzero \(QVP\) causes leakage and virtual corrections of scale \(\lambda^2\|V\|^2/\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}\).

Assume exchange is available because spins interact. Magnetic dipolar coupling is anisotropic. Hyperfine coupling joins unlike spins. Optical and strain mediators bring driven dynamics and loss. Each must be projected from its actual operator.

Treat a decoherence-free subspace as generic quietness. It cancels specified correlated noise. Independent fields, coupling mismatch, relaxation, optical back-action, and control error can remain.

Confuse active correction with a static energy gap. Repeated syndrome extraction can extend a logical lifetime, but the protection disappears if the correction cycle stops.

A leakage gap is a static spectral property. They can coexist; they are not the same mechanism.

Call the cluster an anyon, or call the encoding topological. Local pair correlations distinguish the two states.

Local exchange splits them at first order. That is a finite encoded object, not a deconfined excitation of a many-body phase.

Check yourself

Show that \(|\tilde0\rangle\) and \(|\tilde1\rangle\) are orthonormal.

Expanding in the product basis, \(\langle\tilde0|\tilde1\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}(1-1+0)=0\). Each coefficient list already has squared magnitudes adding to one. Equivalently, the singlet channel of the first two spins is orthogonal to the triplet channel.

Show that \(\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}=\min\bigl(b,3J/2-b\bigr)\) for \(0<b<3J/2\).

The \(m=-1/2\) partners cost \(b\). The lowest quartet member costs \(3J/2-b\). The leakage gap is the smaller of those two climbs.

What fails if \(b=0\)?

The opposite-magnetization partners sit at the same energy as the chosen pair, so the fixed-\(m\) subspace is not energetically isolated. The leakage gap formula assumed \(0<b<3J/2\).

Show that \(PS_{\mathrm{tot}}^zP=\frac12 P\) on the pair.

Both \(|\tilde0\rangle\) and \(|\tilde1\rangle\) have \(m=+1/2\), so \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z\) acts as the scalar \(1/2\) on the span of \(P\). That is why collective longitudinal noise cannot tell the encoded states apart.

What fails if the noise is \(\sum_i S_i^z\otimes B_i\) rather than \(S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z\otimes B_z\)?

Different \(B_i\) can distinguish the spin patterns. The pair is then not a decoherence-free subspace for that noise. “The environment is probably common-mode” is not a substitute for the calculation.

Why is this encoded qubit not topological?

Local pair operators distinguish \(|\tilde0\rangle\) from \(|\tilde1\rangle\), and unequal local exchange splits them at first order. The logical operators live on three nearby spins. That is a finite encoding, not a topologically ordered phase.

Part VI — Topology and anyons

A shoelace, a coffee cup, then two particles that trade places in a plane. Topology first. Strange particles after.

Chapter 12 — A shoelace through a coffee cup

Take a coffee cup and a shoelace. Thread the lace through the handle and tie the ends so you have a closed loop.

You can slide the lace around, stretch it into a circle, squash it into a potato, even wrap it twice around the handle. You cannot pull it off the cup without cutting the lace or breaking the handle.

The lace has a shape you can change, and it has a relationship to the hole that no polite tugging can change. We will count that relationship, see why one inch of lace cannot tell you the count, and then ask why a similar stubbornness might hide a bit.

Stretching is allowed, cutting is not

Treat the handle as a nail driven through a tabletop. Lay a closed loop of string on the table. The loop may be circular, triangular, or shaped like an indecisive potato.

You may slide and stretch the string while obeying three rules:

  • it must stay on the tabletop;

  • it must remain a closed loop;

  • it may not pass through the nail or be cut and rejoined.

If the loop does not surround the nail, you can shrink it to a tiny loop at an ordinary point. If it surrounds the nail once, shrinking gets stuck: the nail is in the way.

A loop wound twice is different again. The shape is flexible.

The relationship to the nail is not.

A movie of that allowed stretching is a deformation. We take this as the definition. The permitted moves, not the pretty shapes, are the object.

Suppose cutting the string is permitted. Then every loop can be undone, and the nail does no work.

Suppose the string may pass through the nail. Then the hole stops distinguishing anything.

A claim that something survives stretching is always relative to a space and a set of permitted moves.

The nail itself is not magical. We just refuse to let the string occupy one point of the table. That missing point is the hole.

Here is the whole toy world:

not wound wound once

____ ______
/ \ / \
\____/ • | • |
\______/

• = missing point

The left loop can contract without touching the missing point. The right loop cannot.

How many times around

Put the missing point at Cartesian coordinates

\[ \mathbf p=(a,b), \]

where \(a\) and \(b\) are lengths measured along the two axes. Describe the loop by

\[ \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t)), \qquad 0\leq t\leq 1. \]

The parameter \(t\) merely tells us where we are along the loop; it has no physical units. Closing the loop means \(\mathbf r(0)=\mathbf r(1)\). Missing the hole means \(\mathbf r(t)\neq\mathbf p\) for every \(t\).

From the hole, look toward the point \(\mathbf r(t)\). Let \(\theta(t)\) be the continuously unwrapped angle of that direction, measured in radians. “Unwrapped” means that after one counterclockwise turn the angle is allowed to increase from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), rather than jumping back to zero.

The net number of turns is

\[ w=\frac{\theta(1)-\theta(0)}{2\pi}. \]

Both angles and radians are dimensionless, so \(w\) is dimensionless. Because the loop ends where it began, its final direction from the hole must equal its initial direction. The unwrapped angle can therefore differ only by a whole number of turns:

\[ \theta(1)-\theta(0)=2\pi w, \qquad w\in\mathbb Z, \]

where \(\mathbb Z\) denotes the integers. Counterclockwise is positive by convention. Clockwise is negative.

That integer \(w\) is the winding of the loop about the hole. It is a count of turns, not a length or a curvature.

Take the circle of radius \(R>0\), where \(R\) has units of length:

\[ x(t)=a+R\cos(2\pi t), \qquad y(t)=b+R\sin(2\pi t). \]

Its direction angle is \(\theta(t)=2\pi t\). Thus

\[ w=\frac{2\pi-0}{2\pi}=1. \]

Reverse the direction by replacing \(t\) with \(-t\), interpreted modulo one, and \(w=-1\). Traverse the same circle twice with \(\theta(t)=4\pi t\), and \(w=2\). Put a small circle entirely to one side of the hole, and its direction first swings one way and then swings back; the net change is zero, so \(w=0\).

For a differentiable loop, the same quantity can be calculated directly from its coordinates:

\[ w=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^1 \frac{[x(t)-a]\,\dot y(t)-[y(t)-b]\,\dot x(t)} {[x(t)-a]^2+[y(t)-b]^2}\,dt. \]

A dot means differentiation with respect to the dimensionless parameter \(t\). The numerator and denominator both have units of length squared, so the integrand and \(w\) are dimensionless, as required.

For our circle,

\[ \dot x(t)=-2\pi R\sin(2\pi t),\qquad \dot y(t)=2\pi R\cos(2\pi t). \]

Substitution makes the fraction equal to \(2\pi\), because the numerator is \(2\pi R^2\) and the denominator is \(R^2\). Therefore

\[ w=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^1 2\pi\,dt=1. \]

Now squash the circle continuously into an ellipse. Its circumference and curvature change.

Its winding remains one, provided the ellipse never crosses the hole. Discard the detailed shape.

Keep the coarser count that is hard to change.

During a continuous deformation the loop changes continuously while remaining away from the hole, so \(w\) would have to change continuously. But \(w\) is restricted to integers.

A continuous function taking integer values cannot slide from \(1\) to \(0\); it would have to pass through nonintegers. The only escape is for the winding formula to stop being defined, which occurs when the loop hits the hole.

Hence an integer of this kind cannot drift.

Drop closedness and \(w\) need not be an integer: an open arc can change its direction by any real angle. Drop the rule that the loop miss the hole, and the formula is undefined at the instant of crossing. Either hypothesis is doing work.

One inch of string

Aim a microscope at one short segment of the right-hand loop. You can measure how bent it is.

You can measure how long that scrap is. You cannot tell whether the rest of the loop closes around the hole.

A property you can decide from a bounded neighborhood is local. The loop’s curvature at one point is local. A kink can be smoothed by changing only a short segment.

The opposite kind of property depends on the whole object, or on how it sits in the whole space. Winding is that kind. Inspecting a short segment cannot reveal whether the completed loop encloses the hole.

The contrast can be summarized without mysticism:

Question | Kind of information | Changed by | |

What is the loop’s length? | geometric, global | ordinary stretching | |

What is its curvature here? | geometric, local | smoothing nearby | |

Does it pass through this point? | geometric / incidence | moving one segment | |

What is its winding about the hole? | global, survives stretching | crossing the hole, cutting, or changing closure | |

Almost everything about the shape can change. Selected discrete information survives a specified class of continuous changes. Topology is the study of those surviving distinctions. It is about allowed moves, not about pretty lattices.

A honeycomb, a ring, or a device with a hole drilled in it can look suggestive. Coordinates and connectivity do not, by themselves, decide which counts survive.

Why a knot can protect a bit

Suppose the bit you care about is not “is this scrap of string bent?” but “does the closed loop go through the handle?”

A local tug changes a short segment. Under the rules above, a short segment cannot change the count.

To flip the bit you must cut the lace, break the handle, or walk the whole loop off the hole. Those are bigger jobs.

They get harder as the relevant distance grows.

A knot in a rope is the same stubbornness in three dimensions: you cannot untie it by stretching one inch. Our tabletop loop is the flatter cousin. Either way, the information lives in how the whole thing sits, not in any one inch.

That last sentence is the useful analogy for a protected quantum bit. It is only an analogy.

A classical string around a nail is not an entangled quantum state, and its winding is not yet a computer bit. After this section we will stop talking about shoelaces and start talking about labels.

The protection mechanism, if the analogy is going to earn its keep, has to look like this. A local disturbance resembles changing a short segment of string: it cannot change winding.

To alter a global quantum label, local errors must form an extended chain, an excitation must travel around a route that cannot be shrunk, or the perturbation must destroy the phase that made the label meaningful. The required process becomes harder as the relevant distance grows.

But “harder” is not “impossible.” Local errors can accumulate over time. Boundaries may shorten a dangerous path.

Thermal excitations can move. A finite device has residual splitting between labels.

Correlated noise need not be local. Initialization and measurement can fail.

A stubborn count changes the error mechanism. It does not repeal error mechanisms.

classical loop quantum many-body system
-------------- ------------------------
short reshaping local operator or local noise
winding count nonlocal quantum label
cross hole / cut loop extended error / gap-closing event
winding number loop measurement or charge label

The rest of the chapter puts names on those rows. The names are not the protection. The protection, when it exists, is that a local probe cannot read or flip the label.

A movie of two loops

Suppose we have an initial loop \(\mathbf r_0(t)\) and a final loop \(\mathbf r_1(t)\). A continuous deformation is a movie connecting them, frame by frame, without tearing the loop or touching the hole.

Such a movie is a homotopy. We write it as

\[ \mathbf H(t,s), \qquad 0\leq t\leq 1,\quad 0\leq s\leq 1. \]

Here \(t\) locates a point along the loop and \(s\) labels the movie frame. The conditions are

\[ \mathbf H(t,0)=\mathbf r_0(t),\qquad \mathbf H(t,1)=\mathbf r_1(t), \]

\[ \mathbf H(0,s)=\mathbf H(1,s), \]

and

\[ \mathbf H(t,s)\neq \mathbf p \]

for every \(t\) and \(s\). The last condition is the entire nail. The missing point \(\mathbf p\) is often called a puncture; the space is the punctured plane.

Two loops connected by such a movie are homotopic in the punctured plane. Their winding numbers are equal.

To change \(w\), some intermediate loop must cross the puncture, cease to be closed, or become discontinuous. In the stated rules, those are singular events.

Hence homotopy classes in the punctured plane are labeled by winding.

In the punctured plane, winding number completely classifies closed loops up to homotopy when a base point is handled appropriately. In more complicated spaces, one integer may not capture every distinction. “Find one invariant” is not the same as “classify the space.” Mathematicians keep that trap polished for visitors.

A label that local tugs cannot change

All loops with \(w=1\) form one family, all loops with \(w=0\) another, and so on. Allowed local stretching never moves a loop from one family to another.

A sector is a collection of configurations or quantum states sharing a global label that allowed local operations cannot change. It is a bin, not a shape.

For a quantum system, let \(\mathcal H\) denote its Hilbert space. A global label \(q\) can split that space schematically as

\[ \mathcal H=\bigoplus_q \mathcal H_q, \]

where \(\mathcal H_q\) is the set of states in sector \(q\), and \(\oplus\) means that the sectors are distinct subspaces.

In lattice models, a loop operator \(W(C)\) acts along a closed path \(C\). Its measured value can label a sector.

A short, contractible loop can often be assembled from local constraints. A loop that winds around a hole, or around a periodic direction of a torus, cannot be shrunk to a point, and its value can encode genuinely global information.

Kitaev’s toric-code model makes this correspondence exact: noncontractible loop operators distinguish degenerate ground states [R030].

This is the quantum echo of the tabletop example, not a proof that every loop operator creates the phase we want.

A global quantum sector can also arise from an ordinary symmetry or conservation law — for example, total particle-number parity. Such a label may be useful, but sector structure alone does not imply a topologically ordered phase. One must ask what enforces the sectors, whether local measurements distinguish them, and whether they remain robust when generic local perturbations are added.

Drop the requirement that local operations cannot change the label, and the bin is just a bookkeeping convenience. Drop robustness under generic local perturbations, and a symmetry-protected split can vanish the moment you add a term that breaks the symmetry.

When many particles share the stubbornness

Imagine many particles whose lowest-energy states come in a few versions that look identical if you only inspect a small patch. No local arrow tells you which version you have.

Distinguishing them takes an operator that wraps around the whole sample. Weak local noise should not mix the versions unless it first closes the energy gap that keeps them cheap to stay in.

That many-body property is quantum topological order. The name is worth keeping because the order lives in the phase, not in a drawing of a hole.

In the standard setting relevant here, it involves long-range entanglement and global organization that cannot be reduced to a local order parameter. Foundational work connected this order to topology-dependent ground-state degeneracy and robustness against local disorder [R122], and exactly solvable models show how nonlocal loop operators and unusual pointlike excitations realize it [R030]. Reviews [R015]; [R124] explain the broader framework and its qualifications.

No single beginner’s slogan is a complete definition for every modern setting. For a two-dimensional gapped phase intended to store quantum information, however, a practical diagnostic package is:

  • a local many-body Hamiltonian;

  • an energy gap above a low-energy ground-state manifold;

  • ground states that are locally indistinguishable in a large system;

  • nonlocal operators that distinguish or transform global sectors;

  • excitations with a conserved type and, in appropriate phases, unusual exchange and fusion behavior;

  • stability of the phase under sufficiently weak local perturbations that do not close the gap.

Those unusual pointlike excitations, when exchanging them can do more than attach a plus or minus sign, are anyons. They are not electrons with a prettier path; they are the mobile defects of the phase.

[Theory] In an ideal gapped topologically ordered system, matrix elements of an operator \(O_R\) supported in a bounded region \(R\) take the approximate form

\[ \langle \psi_a|O_R|\psi_b\rangle = c_O\,\delta_{ab}+\text{finite-size corrections}. \]

Here \(|\psi_a\rangle\) and \(|\psi_b\rangle\) are different ground states, \(c_O\) depends on the operator but not on the sector, and \(\delta_{ab}\) equals one when \(a=b\) and zero otherwise. In many gapped models the corrections are exponentially small in \(L/\xi\), where \(L\) is a system length and \(\xi\) is the correlation length [R123]; [R015]. Both have units of length, so \(L/\xi\) is dimensionless, as an exponential requires.

Hence a genuinely local probe cannot learn which global ground state was chosen, nor readily convert one ground state into another. A logical bit of information can therefore be stored nonlocally.

The four questions you should now be able to ask of any “topological protection” claim are separate:

  • What is the geometry — the actual lengths, angles, coordinates, and shape?

  • What classical surviving count remains unchanged under allowed continuous deformations?

  • What are the global quantum sectors — the quantum labels that no small local operation can change?

  • Does the system possess quantum topological order, rather than merely an interesting shape, a global conserved quantity, or a programmed simulation?

A loop with winding \(w=1\) has a classical surviving count. A quantum state labeled by a nonlocal loop measurement belongs to a global quantum sector.

A many-body phase with robust local indistinguishability and long-range entanglement may have quantum topological order. A logical qubit encoded in those sectors is a topological encoding.

A circuit on ordinary physical qubits that prepares the model state is a digital emulation unless the hardware’s own equilibrium Hamiltonian supplies the phase.

These statements are related. They are not synonyms.

When the shoelace stops helping

The analogy worked because both stories separate local deformation from global change. It stops because a classical loop is one configuration with a visible path.

A topologically ordered quantum ground state is a coherent superposition of many microscopic configurations, entangled across the system. Its order belongs to the wavefunction and Hamiltonian together, not to one attractive lattice sketch.

A literal hole can be useful in a topological code: logical operators may wind around it. Yet drilling a hole in an ordinary magnet does not manufacture topological order.

Likewise, arranging defect centers around an empty site creates geometry. Only their interactions and resulting many-body state could create the required quantum order.

What the laboratory actually has

A laboratory has a finite sample or processor, imperfectly local interactions, boundaries, disorder, controls, detectors, and a temperature. It does not have an infinite plane or an exact mathematical phase label taped to the cryostat.

Evidence therefore comes in layers.

[Experiment] Superconducting-qubit processors have prepared a toric-code ground state with a circuit, measured topological entanglement entropy, and simulated anyon interferometry [R125]. This demonstrates controlled preparation and probing of a topological model state. Because the state is circuit-prepared on a programmable processor, it does not by itself show that the processor material passively enters an equilibrium topologically ordered phase.

[Experiment] Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays have implemented frustrated dynamics and measured nonlocal string observables consistent with a toric-code-type spin-liquid regime [R126]. This is analog quantum-simulation evidence for the engineered model. Whether a particular implementation supplies long-lived passive protection is a separate experimental question.

[Theory] For an ideal local Hamiltonian, stability results show that topological ground-state structure persists under an appropriate range of weak local perturbations without a phase transition [R123]. The theorem does not say that any finite device is immune to temperature, loss, drive errors, long-range couplings, or a perturbation large enough to close the gap.

For defect-engineered matter, the evidence ladder should therefore be explicit:

  • fabricate and characterize the defects;

  • establish the intended microscopic couplings;

  • derive or measure the effective many-body Hamiltonian;

  • show a gapped regime and nonlocal sector structure;

  • demonstrate local indistinguishability or equivalent diagnostics;

  • create, move, and identify the predicted excitations;

  • test robustness as size, disorder, temperature, and evolution time are varied.

A regular defect pattern completes step one and part of step two. Calling the pattern “topological” does not quietly complete steps three through seven.

Ways to get this wrong

Take a pretty graph for a surviving count. A honeycomb, kagome, ring, or punctured device can be geometrically suggestive. The same graph can support a trivial product state or a topologically ordered state under different Hamiltonians.

Take one robust number for quantum order. Winding is robust under the rules of the toy problem.

It says nothing about entanglement, excitation statistics, an energy gap, or quantum coherence. A classical invariant is not quantum topological order.

Take a conserved global quantity for topological protection. A symmetry can divide a Hilbert space into sectors.

If protection disappears when a generic local symmetry-breaking perturbation is added, the mechanism is symmetry protection, not intrinsic topological order. That may still be useful engineering.

It is simply a different invoice.

Take an encoding for an emergent phase. Several physical spins can encode one logical qubit.

A surface-code patch can use nonlocal logical operators. Neither fact alone says the hardware Hamiltonian has an emergent topologically ordered ground state.

Active error correction, digital state preparation, and passive Hamiltonian protection must be reported separately.

Take a simulation for the simulated material. A programmable device may reproduce the amplitudes, string observables, or braiding protocol of a topological model.

Those are real experimental achievements [R125]; [R126]. They establish properties of the prepared or simulated dynamics under stated controls.

They do not automatically turn the underlying superconducting circuits or atoms into intrinsic anyonic matter.

Take “topological” for “error-free.” Topology suppresses particular local routes between sectors. It does not suppress leakage outside the modeled Hilbert space, readout mistakes, thermal population, correlated disturbances, fabrication failures, or control faults unless the architecture separately addresses them.

Even a noncontractible logical error can be assembled from many mundane local errors. The errors have no respect for branding.

Merge different meanings of “defect.” An atomic vacancy in diamond is a microscopic crystal defect. A vortex can be a classical topological defect of an order parameter.

An anyon is an emergent quantum excitation. A puncture or boundary in an error-correcting code is often called a defect as well.

These objects can interact in an architecture, but they are not interchangeable uses of one concept.

Check yourself

A circle is smoothly squashed into an ellipse without crossing the hole. What changes?

Its geometric length and curvature generally change; its winding number does not.

Show that \(w\) cannot change under a continuous deformation that misses the hole.

Along the movie, \(w\) would have to vary continuously, but \(w\) takes only integer values. A continuous integer-valued function is constant, so the winding of every frame equals the winding of the first.

What fails if the loop is allowed to pass through the hole?

The winding formula ceases to be defined at the crossing, and afterward \(w\) may jump. The hole no longer distinguishes families of loops.

Does a global quantum sector prove topological order?

No. The sector could come from an ordinary symmetry or imposed code constraint. One must also establish the many-body phase, local indistinguishability, nonlocal operators, a suitable gap, and stability.

What fails if a bounded operator \(O_R\) has matrix elements that distinguish two ground states at leading order?

Local indistinguishability has already failed. A local probe can then read or mix the supposed global labels, and the logical bit is not stored nonlocally.

What is the difference between digital emulation and emergence?

Digital emulation uses controlled gates to prepare or evolve a model state. Emergence means the hardware’s physical many-body Hamiltonian itself produces the low-energy phase and excitations.

You now have a deformation, a winding count, a local-versus-global habit, and a reason a stubborn loop can hide a bit. Next we replace one loop around one hole with worldlines of several indistinguishable particles in two dimensions. Their winding and exchange paths form braids, and in some systems those braids act as noncommuting operations on a degenerate quantum space.

  • [R122] X.-G. Wen and Q. Niu, “Ground-state degeneracy of the fractional quantum Hall states in the presence of a random potential and on high-genus Riemann surfaces,” Physical Review B 41, 9377–9396 (1990). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.41.9377.

  • [R030] A. Yu. Kitaev, “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons,” Annals of Physics 303, 2–30 (2003). DOI: 10.1016/S0003-4916(02)00018-0; arXiv: quant-ph/9707021.

  • [R123] M. B. Hastings and X.-G. Wen, “Quasi-adiabatic continuation of quantum states: The stability of topological ground-state degeneracy and emergent gauge invariance,” Physical Review B 72, 045141 (2005). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.72.045141; arXiv: cond-mat/0503554.

  • [R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das Sarma, “Non-Abelian anyons and topological quantum computation,” Reviews of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083; arXiv: 0707.1889.

  • [R124] X.-G. Wen, “Colloquium: Zoo of quantum-topological phases of matter,” Reviews of Modern Physics 89, 041004 (2017). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.041004; arXiv: 1610.03911.

  • [R125] K. J. Satzinger et al., “Realizing topologically ordered states on a quantum processor,” Science 374, 1237–1241 (2021). DOI: 10.1126/science.abi8378; arXiv: 2104.01180.

Chapter 13 — Two particles trade places

Two identical beads sit on a table. Slide them until each occupies the other’s old spot.

Photograph the table before and after. Because the beads have no names painted on them, the two photographs are the same picture.

The walk between the photographs is not a photograph. One bead can circle the other clockwise.

It can circle counterclockwise. It can go around twice.

The table offers no third direction in which to lift one path over the other and iron the trip flat.

If the beads are quantum objects, and if they are forbidden to sit on the same point, that leftover memory of the walk can be a plus one, a minus one, a leftover twist, or a small matrix. We will earn those options in that order.

Time drawn upward

A photograph hides the trip. Give the trip a picture of its own. Draw the table as a horizontal line and let time run up the page. Each bead now leaves a trail.

time
^ \ /
| X exchange
| / \
+------------> plane

The crossing is not a crash. One trail went around the other while both stayed on the table. If the beads may not occupy the same point, you are not allowed to pull one trail through the other.

That trail is a worldline. The object of study is no longer a pair of dots. It is a history.

Two histories count as the same if you can slide one drawing into the other without letting the lines meet, without moving the endpoints, and without running time backward.

Drop the collision ban and you may pull one trail through the other; the crossing becomes decoration. Keep the ban, and the drawing remembers how the beads walked.

A room would let you cheat

Stand the same two beads in a room instead of on a table. After they swap, you have an extra direction.

You can lift one path over the other and continuously undo a double swap. Under the usual rules for identical point particles, the leftover memory of the walk collapses to who sits where, not how many times they wound.

On a table that extra lift does not exist. Clockwise and counterclockwise are different movies.

Doing the same neighboring swap twice is a full winding of two worldlines. You cannot iron that winding flat while collisions stay forbidden.

Leinaas and Myrheim extracted this enlargement from the shape of the space of allowed arrangements. The extra possibilities are not a slogan. They are what two dimensions refuse to let you erase. [Theory] [R127]

Hence the same two photographs, in two spatial dimensions, may hide inequivalent walks.

The polite swap

The photographs match. The quantum state need not. After the two beads trade places counterclockwise, every amplitude can return exactly as it left. The whole state is multiplied by \(+1\).

That law belongs to a boson. Photons are bosons. Two of them are allowed to occupy the same condition.

Suppose instead the leftover were required to be a permutation of names and nothing more. Then \(+1\) would still be legal, but so would the next option, and nothing stranger.

In two dimensions the menu is longer. Plus one remains on it.

The rude swap

The other tidy option is a global minus sign. After the same counterclockwise trade, every amplitude flips. The whole state is multiplied by \(-1\).

That law belongs to a fermion. Electrons are fermions. The minus sign is why two electrons refuse the same condition.

Both laws are allowed on a table. A particle that lives in two dimensions is not automatically something stranger than a boson or a fermion.

Plus one and minus one still sit on the menu. In three or more spatial dimensions they are the menu.

Drop the two-dimensional restriction, and the extra leftover of a double swap can be ironed away. Keep it, and \(+1\) and \(-1\) are special cases, not a theorem that nothing else exists.

A leftover twist

On a table the state may come back multiplied by any phase

\[ e^{i\theta}, \]

where the real angle \(\theta\) is measured in radians and counted only modulo \(2\pi\). A clockwise trade gives \(e^{-i\theta}\). Plus one is \(\theta = 0\). Minus one is \(\theta = \pi\).

Wilczek called the general case an anyon, because the leftover phase can be any angle. [Theory] [R128] The name is a pun. It is also a claim: exchange writes a phase, and that phase is not required to be \(\pm 1\).

When the leftover is only a phase, every pair of exchanges commutes. Changing the order cannot rotate one internal basis state into another. The phase becomes visible only by comparing two paths, usually by interference. [Theory] [R128]; [R129]

One neighboring swap writes \(e^{i\theta}\). Sending one object all the way around the other is two swaps, and writes \(e^{i 2\theta}\). Those are different movies. Do not call a full winding “just the exchange.”

Hence Abelian anyonic statistics is a one-dimensional leftover, of which bosons and fermions are two points.

Shoelaces

Two strands are a boring lace. There is only one neighboring pair, so you cannot test whether the order of crossings matters.

Take three. Label the positions left, middle, and right.

Cross the left pair counterclockwise. Cross the right pair counterclockwise.

Those two movies do not look the same, and you can see the disagreement before any matrix appears.

left then right right then left

\ / | | \ /
X | | X
/ \ | | / \
| \ / \ / |
| X X |
| / \ / \ |

A tangle of this kind, up to sliding that never lets the laces pass through each other, is a braid. Stack two tangles by placing one above the other. The collection of all such tangles on \(N\) strands, with that stacking as the product, is the braid group.

Write \(B_N\) for the braid group on \(N\) strands. The neighboring counterclockwise crossings are its letters.

Call them \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{N-1}\). The generator \(\sigma_i\) exchanges the objects currently at neighboring positions \(i\) and \(i+1\).

Its inverse \(\sigma_i^{-1}\) does the same exchange clockwise, and

\[ \sigma_i\sigma_i^{-1} = 1. \]

Notice what is absent: \(\sigma_i^2 = 1\). A braid remembers winding, not only the final permutation. Adding that missing rule by hand would collapse the shoelaces back to ordinary permutations — the three-dimensional leftover.

Well-separated crossings do not interfere:

\[ \sigma_i\sigma_j = \sigma_j\sigma_i \quad\text{when }|i-j|\ge 2. \]

Neighboring crossings obey one more sliding rule. Pull one crossing past the junction of two others and the drawing changes, but the braid does not:

\[ \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}. \]

That is the whole presentation. Far-apart letters commute. Adjacent letters satisfy the three-strand sliding rule. Squares are not the identity.

Hence two generators may fail to commute even though both are “just neighboring swaps.”

Suppose we imposed \(\sigma_i^2=1\) after all. Then a double exchange would be trivial, clockwise would equal counterclockwise, and we would have returned to the permutation group. The relation we refused is the entire two-dimensional enlargement.

Forget the name tags

The braids are not a decoration drawn on top of physics. They are the collision-free histories, once you refuse to name the beads.

Start with \(N\) point-like objects in the plane. An ordered list of positions is

\[ (\mathbf r_1,\ldots,\mathbf r_N)\in(\mathbb R^2)^N, \]

where \(\mathbf r_j = (x_j,y_j)\) has units of length. Collision arrangements form the set

\[ \Delta = \{(\mathbf r_1,\ldots,\mathbf r_N):\mathbf r_j=\mathbf r_k \text{ for at least one }j\ne k\}. \]

Remove \(\Delta\), because an exchange path must keep the objects distinct. If the objects are identical, permuting their temporary labels changes no physical arrangement. The space that remains is the configuration space

\[ \mathcal C_N(\mathbb R^2) = \frac{(\mathbb R^2)^N\setminus\Delta}{S_N}, \]

where \(S_N\) is the group of all permutations of \(N\) labels.

A motion that starts and ends at the same physical arrangement is a loop in \(\mathcal C_N\). Loops that deform into one another without touching \(\Delta\) belong to the same class. Those classes form the fundamental group, and for particles in the plane the group is the braid group we just named from the laces:

\[ \pi_1\!\left(\mathcal C_N(\mathbb R^2)\right) = B_N. \]

[Theory] [R127]; [R129] This equation is the hinge of the chapter. In three or more spatial dimensions, the analogous ordinary-exchange classes reduce to the permutation group.

A wavefunction need not come back to the same complex value after such a loop. Equivalently, one may lift paths to a simply connected covering space and impose a unitary transformation when a path closes downstairs.

Consistency requires the transformation to depend only on the loop class and to preserve stacking. That is exactly a unitary representation of \(B_N\).

[Theory] [R127]; [R129]

Hence every later braid matrix is a linear action of a loop class in configuration space, not a doodle in the margin.

Drop identical-particle identification and you are studying ordered trajectories, which remember name tags the physics does not have. Drop the removal of \(\Delta\) and collisions become legal; the fundamental group collapses.

Three laces, two matrices

A machine that turns each tangle into a matrix, and turns stacking tangles into multiplying matrices, is a representation. Write \(\rho(b)\) for the matrix assigned to braid \(b\). Composition is preserved:

\[ \rho(b_1 b_2) = \rho(b_1)\rho(b_2). \]

Products of operators act on a ket from right to left. The symbol \(\rho\) names the representation. It is not a density matrix.

Overall phases can be unobservable for a closed isolated system. Relative phases between different paths can be measured by interference.

With two strands there is only one neighboring exchange, so there is no pair of generators whose order can be tested. Three strands are the smallest useful case. Consider a two-dimensional state space with orthonormal basis kets \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\). Define the Pauli matrices

\[ Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix},\qquad X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \]

and assign

\[ A \equiv \rho(\sigma_1) = e^{-i\pi Z/4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1-i & 0 \\ 0 & 1+i \end{pmatrix}, \]

\[ B \equiv \rho(\sigma_2) = e^{-i\pi X/4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ -i & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The imaginary unit satisfies \(i^2 = -1\). Both matrices are unitary: direct multiplication gives \(A^\dagger A = B^\dagger B = I\), where \(\dagger\) means conjugate transpose and \(I\) is the identity matrix.

Now calculate the two possible orders:

\[ AB = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 1-i & -1-i \\ 1-i & 1+i \end{pmatrix},\qquad BA = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 1-i & 1-i \\ -1-i & 1+i \end{pmatrix}. \]

They are not equal. Acting on \(|0\rangle\) gives, up to an overall phase,

\[ AB|0\rangle \sim \frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad BA|0\rangle \sim \frac{|0\rangle-i|1\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}. \]

The first state is certainly found in the \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\) outcome of an \(X\)-basis measurement. The second gives that outcome with probability \(1/2\). The different order is experimentally distinguishable, not merely different ink on paper.

Noncommutativity does not excuse the matrices from the sliding rule of the laces. They obey

\[ ABA = BAB = -\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

This is the three-strand braid relation. The matrices above are an Ising-type two-dimensional braid representation, up to basis and overall-phase conventions.

[Theory] [R015]; [R134] We have used them as a clean algebraic model. Writing these matrices into a pulse sequencer would not, by itself, manufacture Ising anyons.

Hence \(AB\neq BA\) is compatible with \(ABA=BAB\). The first fact is noncommutativity. The second is the braid relation. Both are required.

Four leftover laws

Collect the menu. A one-dimensional representation assigns each neighboring swap a single complex number of magnitude one.

A boson still has

\[ \rho(\sigma_i) = +1. \]

A fermion still has

\[ \rho(\sigma_i) = -1. \]

An anyon whose leftover is only a phase has

\[ \rho(\sigma_i) = e^{i\theta}. \]

Bosons and fermions are the special values \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = \pi\). All such complex numbers commute, so changing the order of exchanges cannot rotate one internal basis state into another.

The three-strand calculation was something else. The same positions supported a two-dimensional space, and the two neighboring swaps became matrices with

\[ AB \ne BA. \]

When the leftover is a matrix on a space of more than one state, and at least some pair of those matrices do not commute, the statistics are non-Abelian. The name is worth keeping because it describes the representation, not an electric charge that forgot how to commute and not the paths literally colliding.

One exchange matrix by itself cannot reveal this. You need enough strands and a pair of operations, as in the calculation above.

Arbitrary noncommuting matrices are not enough either. They must also satisfy the braid relations and unitarity.

Ours did.

Hence non-Abelian statistics is a property of a representation of \(B_N\), not a decorative phase on a single swap.

Parked particles still have leftovers

Where did that two-dimensional space come from? The beads are sitting still. Their positions are fixed. And yet \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) are two different states for the same photograph.

Imagine enclosing a pair and asking the outside world one coarse question: what kind of leftover does the pair look like from far away? Two anyons of the same kind can look like “nothing extra” or like “one leftover excitation.” Those are two answers, not a smoothie.

A prepared state may be a combination of the answers. A measurement of the pair picks one.

a a
\ /
\ /
?

The question mark is the leftover label. The list of allowed leftovers, for fixed positions and a fixed total leftover, is a fusion space.

Combining is already a quantum question. The particles do not have to move to own more than one state.

This chapter needs only the fact that the space has multiple basis states. The matrices \(A\) and \(B\) acted on one such space. The next chapter will name the leftover labels, draw the trees that organize them, and show how regrouping one tree into another produces the \(F\)-matrices behind concrete braid representations.

Drop the degeneracy and there is no room for a matrix leftover: every braid can at most write a phase. Keep the degeneracy without the braid relations, and you have a degenerate subspace, not statistics.

A slow walk around

Suppose a Hamiltonian \(H(\boldsymbol\lambda)\) depends on control parameters \(\boldsymbol\lambda\) that locate well-separated quasiparticles. If the system is moved slowly around a closed path while remaining in a degenerate low-energy subspace, its state can acquire a matrix-valued geometric leftover.

That leftover, after you strip off the ordinary dynamical phases that depend on how long you waited, is a holonomy. It is a transformation written by the shape of the walk, not by a clock. In an ideal topological phase the resulting unitary depends only on the braid class. [Theory] [R015]

“Slowly” and “well separated” hide physical inequalities. Motion must avoid exciting states across the many-body gap, but it must finish before decoherence and uncontrolled quasiparticle motion spoil the state.

The objects must be separated by distances large compared with the phase’s correlation length so that local couplings do not substantially split the intended degeneracy. Later chapters will turn those words into energy, length, and timing budgets.

No dimensional estimate is needed here. A braid operator and a statistical angle are dimensionless. Laboratory time is measured in seconds and gaps in joules or electronvolts, but their required inequalities depend on the chosen Hamiltonian rather than braid topology alone.

Drop adiabaticity and the walk populates excited states; the leftover is no longer a holonomy of the intended subspace. Drop large separation and the degeneracy splits; the walk is then ordinary dynamical evolution of a unique ground state.

A bump that thinks it is a particle

An emergent quasiparticle is a localized excitation of an interacting many-body Hamiltonian, described at low energy as an effective particle even though no matching fundamental particle appears in the microscopic inventory. A phonon is an emergent quasiparticle but not an anyon. An emergent anyon is the more specific case in which the excitation’s exchanges realize a nontrivial braid representation in an effectively two-dimensional topological phase.

A defect in diamond is a microscopic imperfection with electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom. It is not an anyon merely because it is point-like or can encode a qubit.

Defects might someday be the microscopic ingredients of a two-dimensional Hamiltonian whose collective excitations are anyons. That extra arrow — ingredients to emergent phase — is most of the engineering problem, wearing a small hat.

Fractional quantum Hall devices provide evidence for Abelian anyonic statistics. [Experiment] At filling factor \(\nu = 1/3\), collider measurements reported correlations consistent with fractional exchange statistics, while an electronic Fabry–Pérot interferometer reported a statistical phase associated with quasiparticle braiding.

[R130]; [R131] These are experiments on collective excitations of an interacting electron system, not software labels attached to ordinary particles. The inference from an interference or correlation signal to a statistical angle remains model- and device-dependent, so “evidence consistent with” is more accurate than “a braid matrix was directly photographed.”

Hence an anyon, when it is physical, is an excitation of a phase, not a renamed microscopic defect.

A braid the hardware does not own

A programmable processor can instead prepare an encoded many-qubit state and apply gates whose logical action realizes a braid representation. Call this an emulated braid when the braid is implemented by a designed gate, measurement, or code-deformation sequence rather than by adiabatically transporting persistent quasiparticle eigenstates of the hardware Hamiltonian.

[Experiment] In 2023, a superconducting processor implemented a generalized stabilizer code and unitary protocol for projective Ising-type graph defects, testing fusion and non-Abelian exchange effects. [R132] The paper explicitly notes that its mobile objects were not quasiparticles that persisted as eigenstates throughout Hamiltonian evolution; gates deformed the stabilizer graph. That is a substantive emulation of braid physics, but it is not evidence that the processor material sits passively in a non-Abelian topological phase.

For a defect-engineered platform, a braid matrix programmed into microwave pulses proves control of the encoded space. It does not prove an emergent excitation spectrum.

To make the stronger claim, the material or effective analog Hamiltonian must itself support the relevant phase and localized excitations, and exchanges must implement the representation while remaining inside its low-energy manifold. [Proposal] Engineered defect arrays could aim at this.

[Speculation] No conclusion follows merely from arranging defects on a planar lattice or drawing crossing paths between them.

Hence a programmed braid and an emergent anyon are different claims, even when they share a matrix.

Four labels that are not synonyms

A physical defect qubit is a controlled microscopic degree of freedom, such as a defect spin.

An encoded qubit is a selected subspace spread across multiple physical degrees of freedom.

An emulated braid is a protocol whose logical gates reproduce a braid representation.

An emergent quasiparticle is an excitation of the many-body Hamiltonian. It is an anyon only if physical exchanges have the required braid statistics.

Topological order is a property of the many-body phase, not of one clever gate sequence.

These descriptions can coexist in one experiment. None follows automatically from the preceding one.

Ways to get this wrong

“Only bosons and fermions exist.” That conclusion uses permutation topology appropriate to three or more spatial dimensions. The planar configuration space has braid-group topology. [R127]; [R129]

“Every two-dimensional excitation is an anyon.” Ordinary bosons and fermions also live in two dimensions. The exchange representation decides the statistics.

“Any unusual phase is non-Abelian.” A scalar \(e^{i\theta}\), however exotic \(\theta\) looks, is Abelian. Non-Abelian statistics requires a multidimensional state space and noncommuting braid operators.

“\(AB\) and \(BA\) are different matrices, so they are automatically valid braids.” Arbitrary noncommuting matrices are not enough. They must also satisfy the braid relations and unitarity. Our worked matrices passed both checks.

“A full winding is the same as one exchange.” One neighboring exchange is \(\sigma_i\); taking one object all the way around the other corresponds to \(\sigma_i^2\). For an Abelian anyon the phases are \(e^{i\theta}\) and \(e^{i 2\theta}\), respectively.

“A quasiparticle is a tiny constituent particle.” It is a collective low-energy excitation. Its usefulness does not depend on being microscopic. Its identity does depend on the Hamiltonian and phase.

“Executing the right unitary proves emergence.” A conventional processor can compile \(A\) and \(B\) exactly. That proves a braid representation was emulated. Emergent anyons require the representation to arise from exchanging excitations of the system’s many-body phase.

“Topological means perfect.” Topological dependence is an ideal low-energy statement. Finite separation, finite temperature, disorder, nonadiabatic motion, leakage, measurement error, and stray quasiparticles can all damage a braid.

[Theory] [R015]; [R030] Protection suppresses specified local errors under specified conditions. It does not negotiate with every error in the building.

Check yourself

Why can two-dimensional exchange be richer than three-dimensional exchange?

Because collision-free loops of identical-particle configurations form the braid group in two dimensions. A double exchange need not deform to the trivial path.

Show that imposing \(\sigma_i^2=1\) collapses the braid group to permutations.

That extra relation makes a double exchange trivial, so clockwise equals counterclockwise and winding is forgotten. What remains is the permutation of the final positions.

How are a boson, a fermion, and an Abelian anyon related?

All have one-dimensional exchange representations. Their exchange phases are respectively \(+1\), \(-1\), and general \(e^{i\theta}\); bosons and fermions are the \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = \pi\) cases.

What fails if \(AB\neq BA\) but \(ABA\neq BAB\)?

The matrices do not represent the braid group. Noncommutativity alone is not statistics; the three-strand sliding rule is required as well.

What makes an anyon non-Abelian?

Braids act as unitary matrices on a multidimensional degenerate state space, and at least some braid operations do not commute.

Does a gate sequence implementing \(A\) and \(B\) establish emergent anyons?

No. It establishes an emulated braid representation. Emergence additionally requires exchangeable quasiparticle excitations of the many-body Hamiltonian.

You now have worldlines, a menu of exchange laws, a braid group named from shoelaces, one pair of matrices that refuse to commute, and a fusion space for those matrices to act on. The next chapter builds that space from leftover labels and trees.
