Chapter 14 — Two particles in a bag

Put two particles in a bag and zip it. From outside you cannot see how they sit. You can only ask one coarse question: what kind of source is the whole bag?

Rattle them around inside. The answer must stay the same. Local rearrangements are invisible from outside. The bag has a label, and the label is stubborn.

Last chapter showed that exchanging two such particles can rotate a hidden state. This chapter says what that state is made of.

We will write a tiny multiplication table by hand. Then we will learn two moves on diagrams: one that regroups the bag, and one that swaps two particles.

A label the bag cannot change

Imagine a loop drawn around a few quasiparticles. Ask the outside world that same coarse question: “What kind of source is inside?” Anything you do locally, inside the loop, is not allowed to change the answer.

That answer is a charge. Physicists often say topological charge, because a poke in one place cannot flip it. For the rest of this chapter, charge means that bag label.

Give the possible charges names such as \(a\), \(b\), or \(c\). No allowed local operation can turn an isolated total charge \(a\) into a different total charge \(b\).

The empty bag — no leftover excitation — gets the special name \(1\). That \(1\) is a label, not the number one in an arithmetic drill.

Drop locality and a faraway operation may rewrite the bag from outside. Keep it, and the label is a sector in the sense of the last two chapters.

Adding two labels

Bring two bags together and treat them as one bigger bag. The combined label is not always unique. Charges \(a\) and \(b\) may be allowed to add up to several possible totals.

We write the list as a product,

\[ a\times b=\sum_c N_{ab}^{c}\,c. \]

Here \(N_{ab}^{c}\) is a nonnegative integer. Zero means “forbidden.” One means one way. Two means two independent ways to reach the same visible total \(c\).

The particles fuse. The name is worth keeping because they do not smash into debris the way billiard balls do.

They are still there. We have only asked what the bigger bag looks like from outside.

The plus sign lists alternatives. It is not a recipe for a half-and-half smoothie, and it does not say that every measurement returns both answers at once. A quantum state may superpose those alternatives only when the whole experimental setting permits it.

Hence the product is a list of allowed totals, not a prepared superposition and not a probability.

The smallest interesting table

The Ising model has three charge labels: \(1\), \(\psi\), and \(\sigma\). Its products are

\[ 1\times a=a,\qquad \psi\times\psi=1,\qquad \psi\times\sigma=\sigma,\qquad \sigma\times\sigma=1+\psi. \]

The symbol \(a\) in the first line means any of the three labels. Vacuum times anything is that thing.

Two \(\psi\) charges cancel. A \(\psi\) next to a \(\sigma\) is still a \(\sigma\).

Two \(\sigma\) charges may total either \(1\) or \(\psi\).

Write the same facts as a table. Each entry is the list of allowed totals:

\(\times\) | \(1\) | \(\psi\) | \(\sigma\) | |

\(1\) | \(1\) | \(\psi\) | \(\sigma\) | |

\(\psi\) | \(\psi\) | \(1\) | \(\sigma\) | |

\(\sigma\) | \(\sigma\) | \(\sigma\) | \(1+\psi\) | |

Every nonempty list in this table has length one, except the last cell. Each allowed total appears once.

The integer in front of a total — usually left unwritten when it equals one — is a fusion coefficient. It is a count of independent ways, not a probability.

All nonzero coefficients here equal one, so the model is multiplicity-free: one channel, or none.

The space of ways for \(a\) and \(b\) to total \(c\) is written

\[ V_{ab}^{c},\qquad \dim V_{ab}^{c}=N_{ab}^{c}. \]

Its dimension is exactly that integer. For two \(\sigma\) charges, \(V_{\sigma\sigma}^{1}\) and \(V_{\sigma\sigma}^{\psi}\) are each one-dimensional, and \(V_{\sigma\sigma}^{\sigma}\) is zero-dimensional: forbidden.

Suppose someone proposed \(N_{\sigma\sigma}^{\sigma}=1\) as well. Then two \(\sigma\) charges could total a third \(\sigma\), and the table would no longer be the Ising table. The missing channel is a fact, not an omission.

A fork with three legs

A basis vector in \(V_{ab}^{c}\) can be drawn as a fork. Read every diagram from top to bottom: incoming charges enter at the top, and their total leaves at the bottom.

a b
\ /
\ /
c

If \(N_{ab}^{c}>1\), put a label \(\mu=1,\ldots,N_{ab}^{c}\) beside the vertex. Then the triple \((a,b;c,\mu)\), not merely \(c\), specifies the channel.

Three or more charges need a sequence of pairwise combinations. Draw that sequence as a fusion tree.

Internal edges are intermediate charges. Choosing their labels chooses a basis.

The tree is bookkeeping for a many-particle state, not a claim that one collision literally happened before another.

Drop the multiplicity labels when \(N_{ab}^{c}>1\), and two independent ways to reach the same total are written as one vector. The shortcut “an internal edge specifies the state” works only when every relevant coefficient is zero or one.

Three particles, two pairings

Take three Ising \(\sigma\) charges and fix their total to \(\sigma\). First combine the left pair. Its intermediate charge \(x\) may be \(1\) or \(\psi\), and either result then combines with the third \(\sigma\) to total \(\sigma\):

Left pairing: ((σ σ)_x σ)_σ

σ σ σ
\ / |
\ / |
x |
\ /
\ /
σ

x = 1 or ψ

Alternatively, combine the right pair first. Its intermediate charge \(y\) may again be \(1\) or \(\psi\):

Right pairing: (σ (σ σ)_y)_σ

σ σ σ
| \ /
| \ /
| y
\ /
\ /
σ

y = 1 or ψ

The two trees have the same three external charges and the same total. They are two bases of one space, not two different physical systems.

Call that shared space the fusion space. It is the actual state space the last chapter’s braids act on.

Check the count from the table. Left pairing: the first pair may total \(1\) or \(\psi\), and both then combine with the remaining \(\sigma\) to give \(\sigma\).

Two states. Right pairing: the same two states, written in a different pairing.

Hence three \(\sigma\) charges of total charge \(\sigma\) support a two-dimensional fusion space. Changing the total-charge constraint changes the available space.

Sliding the pairing

The particles do not walk. Only the pairing slides:

σ σ σ σ σ σ
\ / | | \ /
x | --> | y
\ / \ /
σ σ

That slide is an F-move. Later we will need a different move that really does exchange positions.

Denote the orthonormal left-pairing states by \(|x\rangle_L\) and the right-pairing states by \(|y\rangle_R\). The slide is a change of basis,

\[ |x\rangle_L=\sum_{y\in\{1,\psi\}} \left[F^{\sigma\sigma\sigma}_{\sigma}\right]_{xy}|y\rangle_R. \]

In a standard gauge for Ising anyons,

\[ F^{\sigma\sigma\sigma}_{\sigma} =\frac{1}{\sqrt 2} \begin{pmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&-1 \end{pmatrix}, \]

where rows are \(x=(1,\psi)\) and columns are \(y=(1,\psi)\) [R015]; [R023]. The explicit recoupling is therefore

\[ |1\rangle_L=\frac{|1\rangle_R+|\psi\rangle_R}{\sqrt2}, \qquad |\psi\rangle_L=\frac{|1\rangle_R-|\psi\rangle_R}{\sqrt2}. \]

Suppose the first two charges are definitely in channel \(x=1\). If we instead measure the last two, the amplitudes are \(1/\sqrt2\) for \(y=1\) and \(1/\sqrt2\) for \(y=\psi\).

The Born rule therefore gives probability \(1/2\) for each result. That probability comes from the \(F\)-matrix.

The fusion table alone does not contain it.

The normalization checks itself:

\[ \left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^2+ \left|\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right|^2=1. \]

Also \(F^\dagger F=I\), where \(F^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose and \(I\) is the \(2\times2\) identity. Changing pairing must preserve inner products and probabilities.

Hence an \(F\)-move is a unitary change of basis on a fixed fusion space. It does not exchange positions.

What fails if \(F\) is not unitary? Inner products, and therefore Born probabilities, would depend on which pairing you used to write the state. The two trees would no longer be two bases of one physical space.

A partner that can cancel

Each simple charge \(a\) has a partner \(\bar a\) such that the empty bag occurs in their combination:

\[ N_{a\bar a}^{1}\ge 1. \]

That partner is the antiparticle. The two charges can disappear into vacuum, just as a particle and its antiparticle can.

In the common simple setting, the vacuum channel occurs once. A charge can be its own antiparticle: in the Ising table, \(\bar\sigma=\sigma\) and \(\bar\psi=\psi\).

A physical combination experiment can still have a probabilistic outcome even when every \(N_{ab}^{c}\) is only zero or one. The coefficient counts basis states, not outcome probabilities.

Probabilities depend on the prepared state. Conversely, \(N_{ab}^{c}=2\) means two orthogonal states share the same external labels \(a,b,c\).

A multiplicity label is then required even before anyone discusses amplitudes.

Drop the existence of \(\bar a\) and there is no way for \(a\) to disappear into vacuum. The empty bag would then be unreachable from that charge, and the theory would not have duals in the sense used later.

Two ways of counting must agree

For fixed total charge \(d\), the left pairing of three charges decomposes as

\[ V_{abc}^{d}\cong \bigoplus_e V_{ab}^{e}\otimes V_{ec}^{d}. \]

Here \(e\) runs over allowed intermediate charges, \(\oplus\) is a direct sum of alternatives, and \(\otimes\) combines the two vertex spaces along a chosen path. The same space has a right-pairing decomposition

\[ V_{abc}^{d}\cong \bigoplus_f V_{bc}^{f}\otimes V_{af}^{d}. \]

Equality of dimensions is an integer check you can run on the table before inventing any phases:

\[ \sum_e N_{ab}^{e}N_{ec}^{d} = \sum_f N_{bc}^{f}N_{af}^{d}. \]

If proposed coefficients fail this equation, no choice of clever phases will rescue them.

Run it on three \(\sigma\) charges with total \(\sigma\). Left pairing:

\[ N_{\sigma\sigma}^{1}N_{1\sigma}^{\sigma} + N_{\sigma\sigma}^{\psi}N_{\psi\sigma}^{\sigma} + N_{\sigma\sigma}^{\sigma}N_{\sigma\sigma}^{\sigma} = (1)(1)+(1)(1)+(0)(0) =2. \]

Right pairing is the same sum with the first pair replaced by the last pair, and it also equals \(2\). The table is at least consistent.

For \(n\) charges, repeat the construction. External edges record the \(n\) charges, internal edges record intermediate charges, and the root records total charge. The number of admissible labelings — counting vertex multiplicities — is the dimension of the fixed-total-charge fusion space.

That is why non-Abelian charges can store information. With the total fixed, several internal labelings can remain.

A local measurement around one separated particle cannot read the entire pattern. [Theory] In an ideal topological phase, operations supported far from one another act on this nonlocal fusion space according to the theory’s data, up to corrections from finite separation and unwanted excitations [R015]; [R017].

That is a statement about the effective theory. It is not a blanket promise about a fabricated device.

Hence associativity of fusion, at the level of dimensions, is a numerical identity on the coefficients. Fail it, and there is no fusion space for three charges.

How fast the space grows

The quantum dimension \(d_a\) measures the growth that charge \(a\) contributes to large fusion spaces. For a unitary theory, choose the positive numbers \(d_a\) satisfying

\[ d_a d_b=\sum_c N_{ab}^{c}d_c, \qquad d_1=1. \]

Equivalently, form a fusion matrix \((N_a)^c{}_{b}=N_{ab}^{c}\). Then \(d_a\) is its largest positive eigenvalue in the relevant sector. This is a Perron–Frobenius fact, not a fit parameter [R017]; [R016].

Apply the rule to the Ising table. From \(\psi\times\psi=1\), positivity gives \(d_\psi^2=1\), hence \(d_\psi=1\). From \(\sigma\times\sigma=1+\psi\),

\[ d_\sigma^2=d_1+d_\psi=2, \qquad d_\sigma=\sqrt2. \]

That irrational value is not the dimension of one ordinary on-site space. Finite vector spaces have integer dimensions.

It encodes growth. For \(2n\) Ising \(\sigma\) charges constrained to total charge \(1\), the fusion-space dimension is \(2^{n-1}\): two charges give one state, four give two, six give four, and so on.

The characteristic contribution per additional \(\sigma\) tends toward \(\sqrt2\).

A charge with \(d_a=1\) is Abelian in a unitary fusion theory. A charge with \(d_a>1\) supports non-Abelian fusion growth. The total quantum dimension is

\[ \mathcal D=\sqrt{\sum_a d_a^2}, \]

where the sum covers all simple charges. For Ising, \(\mathcal D=\sqrt{1+1+2}=2\).

Hence \(d_\sigma=\sqrt2\) is an asymptotic growth rate, not a local Hilbert-space dimension. Treating it as an on-site level count already contradicts the fact that vector-space dimensions are integers.

The same slide with more labels

Let \(a,b,c\) be three incoming charges and \(d\) their total. In the left tree, let \(e\) be the intermediate charge, \(\mu\) label a basis of \(V_{ab}^{e}\), and \(\nu\) label a basis of \(V_{ec}^{d}\). In the right tree, use \(f\), \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) the same way. Then

\[ \big|((ab)_e c)_d;\mu,\nu\big\rangle = \sum_{f,\alpha,\beta} \left[F^{abc}_{d}\right]_{(e,\mu,\nu)(f,\alpha,\beta)} \big|(a(bc)_f)_d;\alpha,\beta\big\rangle. \]

This equation is the \(F\)-matrix convention of this chapter. Other sources may reverse it, conjugate it, or place labels differently. That is harmless if the convention is stated and used consistently.

An \(F\)-move still does not exchange positions. Individual entries depend on phase choices for the vertex basis states.

That choice is a gauge. Observable probabilities and complete braid amplitudes do not depend on it.

Rephase a vertex basis and the individual \(F\)-symbols change. Closed-process probabilities, consistency relations, and physically defined interference signals do not. Mistaking a gauge-dependent entry for an observable is a bookkeeping error, not a new phase of matter.

Crossing two strands

Now let the particles walk. An R-move exchanges two neighbors. For a counterclockwise exchange of \(a\) and \(b\) in total channel \(c\), it is a unitary map

\[ R^{ab}_{c}:V_{ab}^{c}\longrightarrow V_{ba}^{c}. \]

On a diagram it is a crossing, not a slide:

a b b a
\ / --> \ /
c c

This is the move that actually braids. It is not an \(F\)-move wearing a small hat.

In a multiplicity-free theory, each allowed \(R^{ab}_{c}\) is a phase. In the same standard Ising gauge used above,

\[ R^{\sigma\sigma}_{1}=e^{-i\pi/8}, \qquad R^{\sigma\sigma}_{\psi}=e^{3i\pi/8} \]

for a chosen counterclockwise convention [R015]; [R023]. Reversing the exchange uses the inverse phases.

In the left-pairing basis of three \(\sigma\) charges, exchanging the first two is diagonal:

\[ B_{12}= \begin{pmatrix} R^{\sigma\sigma}_{1}&0\\ 0&R^{\sigma\sigma}_{\psi} \end{pmatrix}. \]

To exchange the last two, first slide into the basis where those two combine, apply their \(R\)-move, and slide back:

\[ B_{23}=F\,B_{12}\,F^{-1} \]

for the matrix convention of the worked example. Since \(F\) mixes the two channels and the two \(R\) phases differ, \(B_{12}\) and \(B_{23}\) do not commute. That is the small, concrete mechanism behind non-Abelian braid action.

Hence a braid of nonadjacent fusion partners generally requires both moves: \(F\) to regroup, \(R\) to exchange. Calling every basis change a braid confuses the two.

What fails if the two \(R\) phases are equal? Then \(B_{12}\) is a global phase, \(B_{23}\) is the same global phase, and they commute. Non-Abelian action on this two-dimensional space would disappear even though the fusion table was unchanged.

Why invented tables break

Regroup four charges through different sequences of \(F\)-moves. Both routes start and finish at the same trees, so they must give the same linear map.

This requirement is the pentagon equation. Likewise, regrouping and exchanging three charges in two equivalent ways produces the hexagon equations, which tie \(F\) and \(R\) together.

These coherence equations guarantee that a complicated diagram has a well-defined value independent of bookkeeping choices [R022].

Only now is it useful to name the algebraic package. A fusion category is a finite semisimple linear category whose simple objects are charge types, whose tensor product is fusion, whose unit object is \(1\), and whose associator is represented by \(F\)-matrices.

Dual objects represent antiparticles. A braided fusion category additionally has a braiding isomorphism represented by \(R\).

A bare fusion category need not possess \(R\)-moves at all. A unitary modular tensor category adds unitarity and a nondegeneracy condition on braiding, supplying the standard algebraic package for a fully fledged two-dimensional anyon theory [R017]; [R016].

The name arrived last on purpose. The table, the slide, and the crossing are the things you compute. The category is the filing cabinet.

The same coefficients \(N_{ab}^{c}\) can admit inequivalent consistent \(F\)- and \(R\)-data. Fusion rules are necessary input, not a complete fingerprint [R016]. Fail the pentagon or hexagon, and a larger diagram has no well-defined value: two bookkeeping routes disagree.

What the laboratory actually has

The symbols above define an effective theory. A laboratory has a finite sample, controls, detectors, unwanted excitations, boundaries, and a microscopic Hamiltonian. It never has a meter labeled “fusion category.”

[Experiment] Evidence for fusion data must come from operationally distinguishable outcomes: create or identify excitations, combine regions, measure total charge, and show that the observed channels match a consistent rule. Interferometry is one route to charge measurement because a probe can respond to the enclosed charge’s monodromy — the effect of winding around it [R023]. A single peak or degeneracy is not enough to reconstruct \(N\), much less \(F\) and \(R\).

[Experiment] Evidence for an \(F\)-matrix requires comparing incompatible fusion-tree measurements while preserving phase coherence well enough to recover amplitudes, not only a list of allowed outcomes. Evidence for \(R\) requires controlled exchanges or an operationally equivalent braid and must track channel-dependent phases. Multiple sequences should satisfy braid and coherence relations within measured uncertainty.

[Theory] Even perfect agreement with a few matrices establishes only the tested effective operations. To claim emergent anyons, the excitations should arise from a many-body phase, be deconfined over the relevant scale, and carry data stable against allowed local perturbations.

To claim topological protection, one must additionally bound non-topological errors, thermal excitation, finite-size splitting, and control faults. Those are physical claims beyond the algebra [R015]; [R017].

A circuit is not a crystal

A digital processor can encode the two Ising fusion-tree basis states in ordinary qubits and program the Hadamard matrix shown above. That is a digital emulation of an \(F\)-move.

A cluster of defect spins can likewise encode a two-dimensional subspace. Neither fact alone creates emergent \(\sigma\) anyons or topological order.

Extrinsic defects can also carry nontrivial projective fusion and braiding properties, but they must be distinguished from freely propagating intrinsic quasiparticles of the host phase [R021]. The same algebra can appear in several physical settings. The hardware evidence decides which setting applies.

A collection of defect spins does not become an anyon model because its levels can be given exotic names. The proposed microscopic Hamiltonian must produce emergent excitations whose low-energy states obey consistent fusion and braiding data. Later chapters will ask whether that demanding step is physically plausible.

Hence a programmed braid and an emergent anyon remain different claims when the algebra is fusion rather than exchange.

Ways to get this wrong

Reading “\(+\)” as a prepared superposition. The fusion rule lists allowed sectors. A state and its amplitudes require preparation information.

Treating \(N_{ab}^{c}\) as a probability. It is an integer dimension. Probabilities come from normalized state amplitudes and a measurement protocol.

Treating quantum dimension as an on-site level count. \(d_\sigma=\sqrt2\) cannot be the dimension of a finite local vector space. It summarizes asymptotic fusion-space growth.

Calling every basis change a braid. \(F\) regroups a fusion tree without exchanging positions. \(R\) exchanges two charges. A braid of nonadjacent fusion partners generally requires both.

Ignoring total charge. Three \(\sigma\) charges with total \(\sigma\) form the two-dimensional example above. Changing the total-charge constraint changes the available space.

Dropping multiplicity labels. The shortcut “an internal edge label specifies the state” works only when all relevant \(N_{ab}^{c}\le1\). General theories need vertex labels too.

Mistaking gauge-dependent entries for observables. Rephasing a vertex basis changes individual \(F\)- and \(R\)-symbols. Closed-process probabilities, consistency relations, and physically defined interference signals are gauge invariant.

Assuming fusion rules determine the phase. The same coefficients \(N_{ab}^{c}\) can admit inequivalent consistent \(F\)- and \(R\)-data. Fusion rules are necessary input, not a complete fingerprint [R016].

Promoting a simulator’s labels into material excitations. A circuit may reproduce fusion-space algebra accurately while every underlying carrier remains an ordinary physical qubit. Simulation is valuable; misnaming it is not.

Skipping the microscopic gap. A beautiful set of \(F\)- and \(R\)-tables does not prove that a proposed defect Hamiltonian realizes them. One still needs a gapped many-body phase, suitable excitations, and stability under realistic perturbations.

Check yourself

What does \(N_{ab}^{c}=2\) mean?

There are two linearly independent fusion channels from charges \(a,b\) to total charge \(c\). A multiplicity label is required.

Show that both pairings of three Ising \(\sigma\) charges with total \(\sigma\) have dimension two.

Left: \(N_{\sigma\sigma}^{1}N_{1\sigma}^{\sigma}+N_{\sigma\sigma}^{\psi}N_{\psi\sigma}^{\sigma}=1+1=2\). Right: the same sum on the last pair. The two trees are two bases of one two-dimensional fusion space.

What information does a fusion tree contain?

Its external edges contain the charges, internal edges contain intermediate charges, vertices may contain multiplicity labels, and the root contains total charge.

What fails if \(F\) is not unitary?

Inner products would depend on the pairing used to write the state. Born probabilities for the same physical question would then disagree.

What separates an \(F\)-move from an \(R\)-move?

\(F\) slides the pairing without exchanging positions. \(R\) exchanges neighboring charges in a specified fusion channel.

Does reproducing an \(F\)-matrix on defect-spin qubits demonstrate emergent anyons?

No. It demonstrates an encoded operation unless independent evidence establishes a many-body topological phase and its emergent excitations.

You now have a multiplication table, a way to regroup three charges, and a way to swap two of them. Next we fill the table with one lonely charge \(\tau\) and watch the Fibonacci numbers appear.

Part VII — Fibonacci anyons

One fusion rule, a growing pile of leftover labels, and why people got excited. A golden ratio is not a device.

Chapter 15 — Two answers for one pair

Here is a piece of arithmetic that should not work.

You have one leftover charge. Call it \(\tau\). Put two of them together. The pair is allowed to look like nothing at all, or like one more copy of \(\tau\):

\[ \tau\times\tau=1+\tau. \]

We take this as the definition of the Fibonacci fusion rule. The \(1\) is vacuum: the two leftovers cancel.

The plus sign does not add stuff to stuff. It is a fork.

When you ask what the pair is, you get one of two answers, never both at once.

A leftover that cancels itself

There are only two labels in this theory. Vacuum is \(1\). The leftover is \(\tau\).

Vacuum behaves as an identity. For either charge \(a\),

\[ 1\times a=a\times1=a. \]

A lone \(\tau\) is already itself. Two of them are the interesting case, and that is the fork above.

The leftover is its own antiparticle: fuse \(\tau\) with another \(\tau\) and vacuum is allowed. That is why a pair can disappear.

The charge is self-dual. Drop that, and the empty channel leaves the menu.

The plus sign still does not mean the particles break into two pieces. It means the pair has two orthogonal endings.

Those endings are the two fusion channels of \(\tau\times\tau\). Last chapter used that word for Ising anyons.

Here the channels are \(1\) and \(\tau\), and nothing else.

How many histories

A line of these leftovers carries a running total, either \(1\) or \(\tau\). Couple on one more \(\tau\).

A previous \(1\) has no choice: \(1\times\tau=\tau\). A previous \(\tau\) has the fork: \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\).

old total add τ new total
1 ------> τ
τ ------> 1 or τ

A valid history of labels is one basis state of the many-particle fusion space. More leftovers mean more valid histories. We count them before we name the sequence.

Let \(A_n\) be the number of histories for \(n\) copies of \(\tau\) that end with total charge \(1\). Let \(B_n\) count the histories that end with total charge \(\tau\). Adding one more \(\tau\) gives

\[ A_{n+1}=B_n, \qquad B_{n+1}=A_n+B_n. \]

The first equation is the forced move: only a previous \(\tau\) can fuse with the new \(\tau\) to make \(1\). The second adds the two ways to finish at \(\tau\). Hence the pair of counts is completely determined by the fusion rule and the starting data.

Start with one leftover. There is no way for a single \(\tau\) to be empty, and one way for it to be \(\tau\). So

\[ (A_1,B_1)=(0,1). \]

Now two:

\[ A_2=B_1=1, \qquad B_2=A_1+B_1=1. \]

Three:

\[ A_3=B_2=1, \qquad B_3=A_2+B_2=2. \]

Keep going through seven:

Number \(n\) of \(\tau\) anyons | total \(1\): \(A_n\) | total \(\tau\): \(B_n\) | sum of sectors | |

2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | |

3 | 1 | 2 | 3 |

4 | 2 | 3 | 5 |

5 | 3 | 5 | 8 | |

6 | 5 | 8 | 13 | |

7 | 8 | 13 | 21 | |

The last column is bookkeeping. It is a direct sum of different total-charge sectors, not one big coherent workspace.

A superselection rule forbids treating a blur between total \(1\) and total \(\tau\) as an ordinary qubit. Computation normally fixes the total charge and stays inside one column.

Look at either column: \(1,1,2,3,5,8,\ldots\) or \(1,2,3,5,8,13,\ldots\). Each entry is the sum of the two before it.

Those are the Fibonacci numbers. Define them by \(F_0=0\), \(F_1=1\), and \(F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1}\) for \(n\ge1\).

Then

\[ A_n=F_{n-1},\qquad B_n=F_n. \]

The table follows from the fusion rule alone [R135]. The theory is named for this count, not the other way around.

The same number three ways

The same recurrence can be written as a two-by-two step. In the ordered charge basis \((1,\tau)\),

\[ N_\tau = \begin{pmatrix} 0&1\\ 1&1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Acting with \(N_\tau\) updates the pair of path counts exactly as above. Powers of \(N_\tau\) therefore generate Fibonacci numbers. If \(V_c^{a_1\cdots a_n}\) is the complex vector space of fusion states in which charges \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) have fixed total charge \(c\), then

\[ \dim V_1^{\tau^n}=F_{n-1},\qquad \dim V_\tau^{\tau^n}=F_n. \]

Here \(\tau^n\) is shorthand for \(n\) copies of \(\tau\), not an ordinary numerical power. Every fusion multiplicity in this theory is either zero or one, so each valid labeling of a fusion tree is one basis vector.

The counts grow fast. The ratio of neighbors in the table settles down. The largest eigenvalue of \(N_\tau\) is the number that ratio approaches. The characteristic equation is \(\lambda^2-\lambda-1=0\), and the positive root is

\[ \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\approx1.618. \]

That is the golden ratio. It showed up as a growth rate, not as a mystic badge on the first page.

Last chapter already had a name for a growth rate of this kind. The quantum dimension \(d_a\) of a charge \(a\) is the positive number compatible with fusion,

\[ d_a d_b=\sum_c N_{ab}^{c}d_c. \]

Set \(d_1=1\). The rule \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\) becomes

\[ d_\tau^2=1+d_\tau. \]

Solving \(d_\tau^2-d_\tau-1=0\) gives \((1\pm\sqrt5)/2\). A unitary fusion theory keeps the positive Perron–Frobenius solution,

\[ d_\tau=\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\approx1.618. \]

Hence \(\varphi\) is three things at once: the largest eigenvalue of \(N_\tau\), the limit of \(F_{n+1}/F_n\), and the quantum dimension of \(\tau\). The state count therefore scales as a constant times \(\varphi^n\).

Quantum dimension is unitless and need not be an integer. It measures asymptotic fusion-space growth, not a number of on-site energy levels [R135]; [R015]. A single \(\tau\) does not have “1.618 states.”

Unequal phases after a slide

The histories are not little wires painted on the particles. They are nonlocal labels for a degenerate state space. Exchanging neighboring leftovers acts on that space.

If the exchanged pair already has a definite fusion channel, the exchange contributes a channel-dependent phase. If you exchange a different pair, first rewrite the state in a basis where that pair fuses first, apply the phases, and rewrite it back. In symbols that is the three-step recipe \(F^{-1}RF\) from the last chapter.

“Change basis” and “apply unequal phases” generally fail to commute. Two neighboring exchanges therefore generate different rotations of the encoded state.

Repeating them produces a large repertoire of rotations. That is why this particular fork is famous: the repertoire is large enough to approximate the gates a quantum computer wants.

The density argument below turns “large” into a careful word, and then immediately takes most of the slogan back.

An engineered Hamiltonian cannot earn the name of this theory by coughing up \(1.618\) somewhere. It has to reproduce the fusion spaces and the braid data. If someone claims passive protection, the same data have to be the low-energy physics of a gapped two-dimensional many-body phase.

Two paths for three leftovers

Take three \(\tau\) anyons and fix their total charge to \(\tau\). The table says \(B_3=2\). Two paths, one bit.

\[ \begin{aligned} |0_L\rangle&=|((\tau\tau)_1\tau)_\tau\rangle,\\ |1_L\rangle&=|((\tau\tau)_\tau\tau)_\tau\rangle. \end{aligned} \]

The subscript on parentheses is the total charge of that group. The logical qubit is which channel the first pair occupies, \(1\) or \(\tau\), while the three together stay at \(\tau\).

Locally each particle still looks like \(\tau\). The bit is not stored on any one leftover.

Four leftovers of total charge \(1\) also give a two-dimensional space, since \(A_4=2\). People often prefer that block so each encoded packet has vacuum total charge. Three of total \(\tau\) is the smallest picture, so we compute there.

Drop the total-charge constraint and the two paths are no longer a qubit. They sit in different superselection sectors, and a blur between those sectors is not an ordinary computational space.

Swap the first pair, then the second

Adopt the convention of Ref. [R135]: fusion trees point downward, basis channels are ordered \((1,\tau)\), and the positive generator is that review’s right-handed exchange with time pointing upward. Define

\[ r_1=e^{4\pi i/5},\qquad r_\tau=e^{-3\pi i/5}. \]

Exchanging anyons 1 and 2 is diagonal in our logical basis:

\[ \rho(\sigma_1)=R = \begin{pmatrix} r_1&0\\ 0&r_\tau \end{pmatrix}. \]

Here \(\sigma_i\) is the positive exchange of anyons \(i\) and \(i+1\), and \(\rho\) is its matrix representation on the fusion space. To exchange anyons 2 and 3, first change which pair is fused, using

\[ F = \begin{pmatrix} \varphi^{-1}&\varphi^{-1/2}\\ \varphi^{-1/2}&-\varphi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}. \]

This gauge makes \(F\) real, symmetric, and \(F^{-1}=F\). Therefore the three-step recipe collapses to

\[ \rho(\sigma_2)=FRF = \begin{pmatrix} \varphi^{-2}r_1+\varphi^{-1}r_\tau & \varphi^{-3/2}(r_1-r_\tau)\\ \varphi^{-3/2}(r_1-r_\tau)& \varphi^{-1}r_1+\varphi^{-2}r_\tau \end{pmatrix}. \]

Apply this braid once to \(|0_L\rangle\). Both entries in the first column are nonzero, so the braid creates a superposition of fusion outcomes. If the first pair is then fused and measured, this particular state yields

\[ P(1)=\varphi^{-2},\qquad P(\tau)=\varphi^{-1}. \]

They sum to one because \(\varphi^{-2}+\varphi^{-1}=1\). The probabilities are dimensionless, as probabilities must be.

They belong to this prepared state and this braid. They are not universal odds for every encounter of two \(\tau\) anyons.

Since \(R\) is diagonal while \(FRF\) has nonzero off-diagonal entries,

\[ \rho(\sigma_1)\rho(\sigma_2)\neq\rho(\sigma_2)\rho(\sigma_1). \]

Hence neighboring exchanges fail to commute on this two-dimensional space. That calculation is the smallest visible piece of non-Abelian statistics in this theory.

Suppose instead the two channel phases were equal, \(r_1=r_\tau\). Then \(R\) would be a global phase, \(FRF\) would equal that same phase, and the two neighboring braids would commute.

Unequal phases after a change of pairing are not decoration. Drop them and the non-Abelian action disappears.

A printed matrix is not yet physics

For three \(\tau\) anyons with total \(\tau\), the two bases are

\[ |((\tau\tau)_x\tau)_\tau\rangle, \qquad |(\tau(\tau\tau)_y)_\tau\rangle, \]

where \(x,y\in\{1,\tau\}\). The matrix \(F^{\tau\tau\tau}_\tau\) changes between them.

In the gauge above it equals the \(F\) we already used. All other allowed \(F\)-moves in this theory are scalars and can be chosen as one.

The pentagon equation says that every sequence of \(F\)-moves between two parenthesizations of four charges gives the same answer. It is the associativity audit. Even topology has paperwork.

The scalar \(R_c^{\tau\tau}\) is the phase for the chosen handed exchange of two \(\tau\) charges whose combined charge is \(c\). In our convention,

\[ R_1^{\tau\tau}=e^{4\pi i/5},\qquad R_\tau^{\tau\tau}=e^{-3\pi i/5}. \]

The hexagon equations enforce compatibility between recoupling and braiding. Together, the fusion rules, unitary \(F\)-symbols, and \(R\)-symbols define the braid representation used here [R135]; [R015].

These displayed entries are not convention-free observables. Rephasing the one-dimensional fusion and splitting vertices changes individual \(F\)-symbols and sometimes \(R\)-symbol representatives, while leaving complete diagrams and probabilities invariant. That freedom is a gauge, in the sense of the last chapter: a printed matrix is meaningless until you attach its basis order, fusion-tree orientation, gauge, and braid orientation.

Reversing braid handedness replaces \(R\) by \(R^{-1}=R^\dagger\). Taking the mirror theory complex-conjugates the braiding data.

Other books therefore print conjugate phases without disagreeing about the physics. Compare gauge-invariant braid words, fusion probabilities, and link amplitudes — not isolated signs.

Dense, not every gate

For \(n\) anyons the braid generators still obey the two rules from Chapter 13:

\[ \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i =\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}, \qquad \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\quad (|i-j|\ge2). \]

The \(F\)- and \(R\)-data turn these abstract generators into unitary matrices \(\rho(\sigma_i)\) on a fixed-total-charge fusion space.

[Theory] For this theory’s data, the resulting braid representations are dense, up to a physically irrelevant overall phase, in the unitary transformations on the computational fusion spaces. In particular, the two three-anyon matrices above generate a dense set of single-qubit rotations.

Suitable multi-anyon braids approximate entangling operations. That is the mathematical basis of braid universality [R015]; [R136].

Numerical compiling algorithms explicitly find braid words approximating target gates [R137].

Dense means: for a target unitary \(U\) and any tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), some finite braid word \(w\) satisfies

\[ \min_\alpha\|\rho(w)-e^{i\alpha}U\|<\varepsilon, \]

where \(\|\cdot\|\) is an operator norm and \(e^{i\alpha}\) is a global phase. It does not say every gate is one exchange. It does not say the shortest braid is known.

The ordinary English word for this density is universal. The name is worth keeping because it is the slogan people already know, and because that slogan will mislead unless it is fenced.

It does not mean every braid is a legal computational gate. It does not mean a laboratory already has a computer.

There is an important correction to the slogan that opened the “unequal phases” section. The fusion rule alone proves Fibonacci growth and fixes \(d_\tau\) in a unitary theory.

It does not by itself prove braid universality. Universality uses the particular consistent, unitary \(F/R\) data of this braided category.

A fusion ring is not yet a braid representation.

Extra states you did not order

For several encoded qubits, the full fixed-charge fusion space is generally larger than the chosen tensor-product computational subspace. A careless braid may populate the extra states.

That spill is leakage. “Universal” does not mean “every braid is leakage-free” [R015]; [R137]. Universal compilation can suppress it arbitrarily in the ideal theory. Initialization and fusion measurement are also required for a computer.

Drop the extra states from the accounting and a compiled braid that looks perfect on the intended bits may have left the computational subspace. The gate error you quoted is then the wrong invoice.

What the laboratory actually has

The equations above describe an ideal topological theory, not a specific material.

[Theory] The \(k=3\) Read–Rezayi fractional quantum Hall state was proposed to support a non-Abelian sector related to these anyons [R139]. Experimental observation of a Hall plateau at a compatible filling is not, by itself, a measurement of the full fusion and braiding data. In the literature surveyed through August 2026, intrinsic Fibonacci exchange and fusion have not been established in a defect crystal.

[Experiment] In 2024, Xu and collaborators used 27 superconducting transmon qubits to prepare and manipulate a digital representation of a Fibonacci Levin–Wen string-net state. They applied circuits representing creation, fusion, and braiding and measured signatures consistent with the target model [R138].

This is a substantial laboratory result. Its microscopic excitations were not passively emerging, mobile quasiparticles of a static transmon Hamiltonian.

The implemented string-net target is doubled Fibonacci order, and the operations were compiled gates on ordinary physical qubits [R138].

[Experiment] A 2026 trapped-ion experiment prepared a 54-qubit state of the \(S_3\) quantum double and demonstrated a universal gate set by combining braiding with fusion [R140]. It is relevant precisely as a control case: the anyons were digitally encoded, and the topological order was \(S_3\), not this theory. “Universal anyon computation” does not identify the anyon theory.

A processor that executes an \(F\) gate has simulated an algebraic move. It has not thereby acquired an equilibrium Fibonacci phase or passive topological memory.

Four things that are not the same

  • Encoded Fibonacci qubit: information stored in a fixed-charge fusion space of \(\tau\) anyons.

  • Emergent Fibonacci anyons: quasiparticles of a gapped two-dimensional many-body phase whose adiabatic exchange realizes the theory’s braid representation.

  • Doubled Fibonacci: the nonchiral Drinfeld-center theory produced by a Levin–Wen model with this chapter’s input data. Its full charge set and topological order are larger than the two-object chiral theory [R018].

  • Fibonacci-like digital simulation: ordinary hardware qubits encode fusion labels while programmed gates enact \(F\), \(R\), or string operators. It can test the algebra without supplying intrinsic quasiparticles or passive protection [R138].

Doubled Fibonacci is not “fake Fibonacci.” It is a genuine, distinct topological order containing computationally useful Fibonacci-type sectors. Nor is a digital simulation scientifically decorative: it can verify circuits and measurement protocols. The error is to erase which physical system carries the topological order and where protection comes from.

Ways to get this wrong

Inferring universality from \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\) alone. The rule fixes counting, not braid phases.

Pentagon- and hexagon-consistent unitary \(F/R\) data are essential. Drop the braid data and you still have Fibonacci growth; you do not have a density theorem.

Calling \(d_\tau=1.618\ldots\) a local degeneracy. A single anyon does not have “1.618 states.” Quantum dimension describes asymptotic growth of a nonlocal fusion space. Finding \(\varphi\) in a spectrum does not exhibit the fusion spaces.

Mixing total-charge sectors. The sum \(A_n+B_n\) is not automatically one coherent Hilbert space available for encoding.

Fix the boundary charge before counting logical states. What fails if you do not: you have counted a direct sum, not a qubit.

Quoting bare matrices. Changing basis phases, basis order, braid handedness, or mirror chirality changes their appearance. Compare gauge-invariant braid words, fusion probabilities, and link amplitudes — not isolated signs.

Equating braid universality with a fault-tolerant device. [Theory] Ideal adiabatic braids are insensitive to small path deformations when anyons remain separated in a gapped phase [R015].

Real systems can still suffer thermal anyon creation, quasiparticle poisoning, finite-separation splitting, diabatic transitions, control mistakes, and faulty readout. Universality says what gates can be approximated.

Protection says how errors scale. Different sentence, different invoice.

Ignoring leakage in multi-qubit encodings. The physical fusion space can contain states outside the computational tensor product. A compiler must control leakage as well as gate error [R137].

Replacing emergence with a circuit diagram. A processor that executes an \(F\) gate has simulated an algebraic move. It has not thereby acquired an equilibrium Fibonacci phase or passive topological memory.

Calling every non-Abelian platform Fibonacci. Ising anyons, finite-group quantum doubles, and Fibonacci anyons have different fusion and braid data. Non-Abelian is a family description, not a model number.

Check yourself

Show that \(A_{n+1}=B_n\) and \(B_{n+1}=A_n+B_n\) follow from the fusion rule.

Only a previous \(\tau\) can fuse with a new \(\tau\) to make \(1\), so \(A_{n+1}=B_n\). A new total \(\tau\) can come from previous \(1\) or previous \(\tau\), so \(B_{n+1}=A_n+B_n\).

Show that the positive solution of \(d_\tau^2=1+d_\tau\) is \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\).

Completing the quadratic gives \((1\pm\sqrt5)/2\). Unitarity keeps the positive root, which is the golden ratio. The same equation is the characteristic equation of \(N_\tau\).

Where is a three-anyon logical bit stored?

In the fusion channel \(1\) or \(\tau\) of the first pair, with the total charge of all three fixed to \(\tau\).

What fails if the two channel phases in \(R\) are equal?

Then \(R\) is a global phase on the two-dimensional space, \(FRF\) equals that same phase, and neighboring braids commute. The non-Abelian action is gone.

What fails if you infer universality from the fusion rule alone?

You have Fibonacci growth and, in a unitary theory, \(d_\tau=\varphi\). You do not have braid phases, and you do not have the density theorem. A fusion ring is not a braid representation.

Did a 27-transmon experiment create intrinsic chiral Fibonacci matter?

No. It digitally implemented a doubled-Fibonacci string-net state and associated operations on ordinary qubits [R138].

The next chapter takes a simpler phase that is not universal — the toric code — and shows how local Hamiltonian terms can create anyons and nonlocal logical sectors at all.

  • [R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das Sarma, “Non-Abelian anyons and topological quantum computation,” Reviews of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083. arXiv: 0707.1889.

  • [R136] M. H. Freedman, M. Larsen, and Z. Wang, “A modular functor which is universal for quantum computation,” Communications in Mathematical Physics 227, 605–622 (2002). DOI: 10.1007/s002200200645. arXiv: quant-ph/0001108.

  • [R137] L. Hormozi, G. Zikos, N. E. Bonesteel, and S. H. Simon, “Topological quantum compiling,” Physical Review B 75, 165310 (2007). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.75.165310. arXiv: quant-ph/0610111.

  • [R138] S. Xu et al., “Non-Abelian braiding of Fibonacci anyons with a superconducting processor,” Nature Physics 20, 1469–1475 (2024). DOI: 10.1038/s41567-024-02529-6. Stable article: nature.com/articles/s41567-024-02529-6.

Part VIII — Topological lattice models

Checks on a grid, a honeycomb of compasses, strings on a net. Then the difference between an actor playing a king and a king.

Chapter 16 — Checks that never look at the secret

A square lattice sits on a torus. Every edge carries one spin-\(1/2\).

At each vertex the four meeting edges are asked a single yes-or-no question. At each face a different four-edge question is asked.

The answers are local. They report whether that vertex or that face is violated. They do not report whether a loop of flipped edges winds through a hole of the torus.

A toric code is this lattice model: qubits on the edges, a vertex check and a face check of the two kinds below, and either a Hamiltonian or a code built from those checks. We take that as the definition.

A color-center spin is one physical qubit in a crystal. One defect per drawn edge supplies neither the checks nor a gap.

Eight qubits on a torus

Take a \(2\times 2\) square grid and identify opposite sides. Coordinates \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) run modulo \(2\). Let \(h_{x,y}\) be the horizontal edge from \((x,y)\) to \((x+1,y)\), and let \(v_{x,y}\) be the vertical edge from \((x,y)\) to \((x,y+1)\).

There are four horizontal edges and four vertical edges. The Hilbert space has dimension \(2^8=256\).

A flat drawing of the periodic patch is

h00 h10
(0,0) -----> (1,0) ------> (0,0)
| | |
v00| v10 | | periodic
v v v
(0,1) -----> (1,1) ------> (0,1)
h01 h11
| |
v01| v11 |
v v
(0,0) (1,0) (bottom = top)

The repeated vertices are identifications, not extra sites. A \(1\times 1\) periodic drawing is too cramped to show four distinct edges at a vertex. The \(2\times 2\) patch is the smallest that keeps the intended local pattern and still has two independent cycles.

Hence this is already a torus, not a crystal. The eight spins are labels on edges. They are not eight nitrogen-vacancy centers that inherited topology by sitting near one another.

Drop periodicity and the same local checks still make sense on a planar patch with boundary. The leftover-state count does not.

The four-edge product at a vertex

Four edges meet at a vertex: the horizontal edge going right, the horizontal edge coming in from the left, the vertical edge going up, and the vertical edge coming in from below.

Ask those four spins the \(X\) question and multiply. For the vertex at \((x,y)\),

\[ A_{x,y}=X_{h_{x,y}}X_{h_{x-1,y}}X_{v_{x,y}}X_{v_{x,y-1}}, \]

where \(X_e\) is the Pauli \(X\) operator on edge \(e\), and every index is modulo \(2\).

That four-edge product is a star. On a ground state the star returns \(+1\). A \(-1\) means that vertex is violated.

Suppose two stars share an edge. Both are products of \(X\), so they commute. Hence every star can be given a definite value at once.

If a later face check used \(X\) on a single shared edge instead of \(Z\) on two, that star and that face would anticommute. The split of Pauli type is part of the definition, not decoration.

The four-edge product on a face

Four edges bound a face: bottom, right, top, left.

Ask those four spins the \(Z\) question and multiply. For the square whose lower-left corner is \((x,y)\),

\[ B_{x,y}=Z_{h_{x,y}}Z_{v_{x+1,y}}Z_{h_{x,y+1}}Z_{v_{x,y}}, \]

where \(Z_e\) is Pauli \(Z\) on edge \(e\). Indices again run modulo \(2\).

That four-edge product is a plaquette. On a ground state the plaquette returns \(+1\). A \(-1\) means that face is violated.

Stars are made of \(X\). Plaquettes are made of \(Z\). That split is the local algebra of the model.

Replace the four-\(Z\) product by four \(X\) operators on the same face and the algebra with the stars changes: a star and that face then share edges of matching Pauli type, and two canceling minus signs are no longer guaranteed.

How a pair walks around a square

Start from any state \(|\psi_0\rangle\) on which every star and every plaquette already reads \(+1\). Apply \(Z\) on the single edge \(h_{0,0}\).

A star contains \(X\) operators. \(X\) and \(Z\) on the same edge anticommute. So this one \(Z\) anticommutes with the two stars that touch \(h_{0,0}\), the stars at \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\).

Those two eigenvalues flip from \(+1\) to \(-1\). The two violated vertices are \(e\) anyons.

The letter \(e\) labels a broken star. We keep it because the next construction breaks plaquettes instead.

Next apply \(Z_{v_{1,0}}\). The shared endpoint \((1,0)\) is flipped a second time and returns to \(+1\).

The other new endpoint appears at \((1,1)\). The pair has walked.

Then apply \(Z_{h_{0,1}}\), moving the walker to \((0,1)\). Finally apply \(Z_{v_{0,0}}\).

Both remaining endpoints disappear.

The four operations multiply to one plaquette:

\[ Z_{h_{0,0}}Z_{v_{1,0}}Z_{h_{0,1}}Z_{v_{0,0}}=B_{0,0}. \]

Because \(B_{0,0}|\psi_0\rangle=|\psi_0\rangle\), the finished trip around one square changed nothing the checks can see. Intermediate states held a pair. The closed path is itself a check.

There is a different ending. Keep walking around a periodic direction instead of around one square.

The endpoints meet and vanish, so every local check reads \(+1\). The leftover loop cannot shrink.

It is not a product of local plaquettes. Hence the checks have gone quiet, and a winding has moved.

Stop after three edges and one \(e\) remains. Energy is still paid, and you have not returned to the codespace.

Strings of the other kind

A path \(\gamma\) along the ordinary edges of the grid defines a \(Z\) string

\[ W_e(\gamma)=\prod_{e\in\gamma} Z_e. \]

At an interior vertex the path uses two of the four edges, so it anticommutes with that star twice and leaves no net sign. At each endpoint it uses one edge and flips the star. Those endpoints are the \(e\) anyons just walked.

Now draw a path \(\gamma^*\) on the dual lattice: it runs through the centers of faces and crosses a set of ordinary edges. Its \(X\) string is

\[ W_m(\gamma^*)=\prod_{e\perp\gamma^*}X_e. \]

This string flips the plaquette checks at its two endpoint faces. Those broken faces are \(m\) anyons.

Stars detect \(e\). Plaquettes detect \(m\). An open \(Z\) string makes \(e\). An open \(X\) string makes \(m\).

If both kinds of check are broken at once, the composite is \(\varepsilon=e\times m\). It carries one electric violation and one magnetic violation.

A \(Y\) error on one edge is not a third independent species. Since \(Y=iXZ\), it contributes to both syndromes at neighboring sites.

Why the checks commute

Each star \(A_v\) and each plaquette \(B_p\) is Hermitian and squares to the identity, so its only possible readings are \(+1\) and \(-1\). Here \(v\) labels a vertex and \(p\) a face.

Two stars commute because they are made only of \(X\). Two plaquettes commute because they are made only of \(Z\).

A star and a plaquette either share no edge or share two edges. On one shared edge, \(XZ=-ZX\). On two shared edges the two minus signs cancel:

\[ A_vB_p=(-1)^2B_pA_v=B_pA_v. \]

Hence every check can have a definite value at the same time. The local questions do not fight.

These checks are the stabilizers of the model: operators that leave the good states alone and return \(+1\) there.

What fails if a star and a plaquette share a single edge: they anticommute, they cannot be simultaneously sharp, and a Hamiltonian built from both is no longer a sum of commuting penalties.

Energy for a broken check

If the checks are standing energy penalties, the energy of the lattice is

\[ H_{\rm TC}=-J_e\sum_v A_v-J_m\sum_p B_p, \]

where \(J_e>0\) and \(J_m>0\) are energies. Pauli products have no units, so each \(J\) must carry energy and \(H_{\rm TC}\) does too.

A check itself is not a projector. Its eigenvalues are \(\pm 1\). The projectors onto those two answers are

\[ P^{\pm}_{v}=\frac{I\pm A_v}{2},\qquad P^{\pm}_{p}=\frac{I\pm B_p}{2}. \]

Write \(N_v\) and \(N_p\) for the numbers of vertices and faces. Then

\[ H_{\rm TC}=E_0+2J_e\sum_v P^-_v+2J_m\sum_p P^-_p, \qquad E_0=-J_eN_v-J_mN_p. \]

A violated star costs \(2J_e\). A violated plaquette costs \(2J_m\). On a closed torus the rules force either species to appear in pairs, so the cheapest pair costs \(4J_e\) or \(4J_m\).

Hence the model is a commuting-projector Hamiltonian: a sum of local penalties that all commute. The exact solution, and the anyon reading of the broken checks, is Kitaev’s construction [R030].

A diamond does not hand you \(H_{\rm TC}\). The four-body products have to be arranged, approximated, or compiled. Until they are, you have eight — or eight thousand — ordinary spins, not this energy.

Four quiet states

A ground state of \(H_{\rm TC}\) satisfies

\[ A_v|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle, \qquad B_p|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle \]

for every vertex and every face. On the \(2\times 2\) torus there are eight written checks. They are not all independent.

Every edge touches two vertices and borders two faces, so

\[ \prod_v A_v=I,\qquad \prod_p B_p=I. \]

There are therefore three independent stars and three independent plaquettes. Six independent yes-or-no constraints on an eight-qubit space leave

\[ \dim \mathcal H_0=2^{8-6}=4. \]

Equivalently, the patch encodes \(k=8-6=2\) logical qubits. The fourfold degeneracy is exact for the ideal Hamiltonian on a torus. More generally the toric code has \(4^g\) ground states on a closed orientable surface of genus \(g\); a torus is \(g=1\) [R030].

You can write one of the four states by hand. Begin with \(|0\rangle^{\otimes 8}\), which already has \(B_p=+1\) on every face, and average over products of stars:

\[ |\psi_{00}\rangle\propto \prod_{v\ne v_0}(I+A_v)|0\rangle^{\otimes 8}. \]

One star \(v_0\) is left out because the product of all stars is already \(I\). The state is an equal superposition of the contractible loop configurations. Applying either of two independent wrapping operators produces the other three sectors.

Hence four ground states survive, and they are locally indistinguishable.

Count eight independent checks and you would conclude there is no leftover state. The two global products equal the identity, so that count is wrong.

Loops that wrap

On our eight-edge patch, two \(Z\) loops that wrap the torus and cannot shrink are

\[ \bar Z_x=Z_{h_{0,0}}Z_{h_{1,0}},\qquad \bar Z_y=Z_{v_{0,0}}Z_{v_{0,1}}. \]

Two \(X\) loops that cross them once can be chosen as

\[ \bar X_x=X_{h_{0,0}}X_{h_{0,1}},\qquad \bar X_y=X_{v_{0,0}}X_{v_{1,0}}. \]

Each closed loop commutes with every star and every plaquette. Matching pairs share one edge and anticommute: \(\bar X_x\bar Z_x=-\bar Z_x\bar X_x\).

Mismatched pairs share zero edges or two, and they commute. That is exactly the Pauli algebra of two encoded qubits.

These wrapping products are the logical operators: the smallest operations that change the ground sector without leaving a local scar.

A local operator cannot measure a wrapping eigenvalue. It also cannot turn one quiet sector into another.

On an \(L\times L\) lattice it takes a string of at least \(L\) single-edge Pauli operations to complete a loop that cannot shrink. That smallest wrapping weight is the code distance, \(d=L\): the number of local mistakes you must stack before a winding moves and the checks still look fine.

Under weak enough local perturbations that leave a many-body gap, topological-order stability theorems say the local indistinguishability survives and the splitting among the four sectors is exponentially small in the system size, subject to their locality assumptions [Theory] [R142].

Drop the many-body gap and those theorems do not apply. Local perturbations can then mix the sectors at a scale that need not vanish with \(L\).

A phase, not a matrix

The fusion rules of the four charges are

\[ e\times e=1,\qquad m\times m=1,\qquad e\times m=\varepsilon, \]

\[ e\times\varepsilon=m,\qquad m\times\varepsilon=e,\qquad \varepsilon\times\varepsilon=1, \]

where \(1\) means vacuum, nothing left. Every pair of charges has exactly one fusion outcome. Every fixed-charge fusion space is therefore one-dimensional. There is no hidden basis for a braid to mix.

The string algebra is still not boring. Take an \(e\) around an \(m\). Their \(Z\) string and \(X\) string cross once, so

\[ W_eW_m=-W_mW_e. \]

The wavefunction picks up a phase \(-1\). Thus \(e\) and \(m\) have mutual semionic statistics. Taken alone, \(e\) and \(m\) have bosonic exchange statistics. Their composite \(\varepsilon\) is a fermion [R030].

These anyons are Abelian: every braid multiplies the state by a number, a phase. Non-Abelian anyons act with noncommuting matrices on a fusion space that has more than one dimension.

The toric code has topology. It does not have universal computation by braiding.

The name is worth keeping because ordinary English hears “Abelian” as “nothing happens.” A mutual phase \(-1\) happens. It is still a single number, so it cannot enact the matrix-valued braids of a non-Abelian fusion space.

Topological does not mean non-Abelian.

Endpoints a decoder can see

Suppose unwanted \(Z\) errors land on a set of edges \(E\). The error operator is \(Z(E)=\prod_{e\in E}Z_e\). Star checks return \(-1\) exactly on the boundary \(\partial E\): the vertices that touch an odd number of errored edges.

Those violated vertices are the syndrome: the data a decoder is allowed to see. The decoder never sees the path. It only sees the endpoints, and then has to guess a recovery.

A decoder chooses a recovery chain \(R\) with the same boundary. After recovery the net chain is the symmetric difference \(E\oplus R\), because applying \(Z\) twice is the identity. Since \(\partial(E\oplus R)=0\), the leftover is closed. Two things can happen:

  • If \(E\oplus R\) can shrink, it is a product of plaquettes and does nothing to the encoded sector.

  • If \(E\oplus R\) winds around the torus, it is a logical \(\bar Z\) and silently flips an encoded bit.

The same story with \(X\) errors, plaquette syndromes, and dual-lattice recovery produces logical \(\bar X\) failures. A general Pauli \(Y=iXZ\) contributes to both syndromes. Dennis and collaborators wrote this error-chain picture and tied it to statistical-mechanical decoding [R141].

Hence a vanished syndrome is not a proof of success. Both a harmless shrinkable loop and a damaging wrapping loop have no endpoints.

What fails if the decoder only cancels defects and never infers homology: it can “correct” into the wrong sector with a wrapping leftover.

A standing penalty versus asking again

The same operators appear in two physically different machines.

In passive Hamiltonian protection, the terms \(-J_eA_v\) and \(-J_mB_p\) sit in the device Hamiltonian all the time. Leaving the ground space costs energy.

At low temperature a bath must supply that energy to create a pair. A gap also supports stability against weak enough local perturbations [Theory] [R142].

This is genuine Hamiltonian protection only if the physical system actually realizes those interactions and lives in their gapped phase.

It is not a self-correcting quantum memory in two dimensions. Once a pair exists, either pointlike anyon can walk across the lattice without increasing the number of excitations.

The highest energy along a logical-string path therefore stays of order \(J_e\) or \(J_m\). It does not grow with \(L\).

At nonzero temperature, diffusion can finish a wrapping loop, so making the lattice bigger without bound does not make the passive lifetime bigger without bound [Theory] [R143]; [R144]. The gap makes pairs expensive to create.

It does not pin the pairs that already exist.

In active syndrome extraction, hardware measures the stars and plaquettes again and again, usually with extra ancilla qubits and a gate circuit. Classical software compares rounds, guesses space-time error chains, and updates a correction or a Pauli frame.

The checks need not be energy terms in the data-qubit Hamiltonian at all. Measurement errors make time another decoding direction, which is why one round of tidy-looking syndrome data is not enough [R141]; [R145].

A static \(H_{\rm TC}\) whose spectrum is thermally occupied is an analog many-body model. A circuit can prepare a toric-code wavefunction without making \(H_{\rm TC}\) the hardware’s equilibrium Hamiltonian.

Repeated check measurement is active quantum error correction, even if no four-body energy penalty exists. A material with a robust emergent \(\mathbb Z_2\) topological phase is stronger evidence than a prepared state or a short digital braid.

Eight defect spins on the eight edges of a drawing are still eight defect spins. They become this model only after the stars, the plaquettes, and a many-body gap are shown to exist.

The two strategies can be stacked, but their error models differ. Passive penalties change transition energies.

Active correction buys information and spends control, measurement, and decoding. Calling both “the toric code” is fine only after you say which machine you mean.

What the laboratory actually has

The ideal square-lattice Hamiltonian is built from weight-four products. Most elementary spin couplings in candidate hardware are one-body or two-body, so the exact commuting-projector Hamiltonian needs direct multiqubit interactions, perturbative stand-ins, extra constraints, or digital gates. Each route brings extra energy scales or control errors.

For a defect array, assigning one defect spin to each edge is only the first line of the recipe. One must still demonstrate the star and plaquette constraints and a many-body gap [Proposal]. A diamond device with tidy single-spin coherence is a different object than this lattice model.

[Experiment] Satzinger and collaborators prepared and characterized a toric-code ground state using 31 superconducting qubits, measured a topological entanglement signature, and performed anyon operations [R125]. That is strong evidence a programmable processor can synthesize and probe the state. It is not evidence that the processor’s native equilibrium material realizes a passive toric-code Hamiltonian.

[Experiment] Repeated stabilizer extraction has been demonstrated in planar surface-code devices, which use boundaries instead of a periodic torus but share the same local check algebra. Krinner and collaborators ran a distance-three, 17-qubit surface code through repeated correction cycles [R145]. That is evidence for active extraction and decoding, not for thermally passive storage.

[Experiment] A trapped-ion processor has also prepared toric-code topological order with measurement and feed-forward under periodic connectivity [R146]. Again the preparation protocol is the resource that did the work. Turning the controls off does not leave behind an autonomous topological material.

For defect-engineered crystals the toric code is therefore a benchmark, not a free inheritance. A convincing claim would need spectroscopy or dynamics that establish the intended effective terms, a separated low-energy manifold, nonlocal ground sectors, and controlled string excitations. Long coherence of individual defects, a few entangled neighbors, or a software-defined stabilizer graph answers a different question.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Calling every stabilizer a projector. \(A_v\) and \(B_p\) have eigenvalues \(\pm 1\). The projectors are \((I+A_v)/2\) and \((I+B_p)/2\). The distinction matters when you compare Hamiltonian coefficients.

  • Forgetting the global relations. Counting eight checks on eight qubits would predict no leftover state. Two products of checks equal the identity, leaving six independent constraints and two logical qubits.

  • Treating a vanished syndrome as proof of success. Both a harmless shrinkable loop and a damaging wrapping loop have no endpoints. Decoding has to infer the homology class, not merely cancel defects.

  • Equating an energy gap with a self-correcting memory. The two-dimensional toric code has a finite pair-creation cost and no energy barrier that grows with system size [R143]; [R144]. Passive suppression is useful. Indefinite thermal protection does not follow.

  • Equating Abelian braiding with triviality. The \(-1\) mutual phase is topological and measurable. It is still a single number, so it cannot enact the matrix-valued braids of a non-Abelian fusion space.

  • Equating digital preparation with emergence. A gate sequence may produce the exact wavefunction and the anyon algebra. Emergent topological order also requires that a local physical Hamiltonian make that sector its robust low-energy physics.

  • Assuming a torus demonstration is a device layout. A torus is mathematically clean. Laboratories usually use planar patches with boundaries. Boundaries change the degeneracy and the shape of the logical operators. They keep the local star and plaquette lesson.

  • Mistaking a diamond array for this model. One defect per edge is a hardware sketch. Without the four-body checks and a many-body gap, the crystal is still a pile of ordinary qubits.

Check yourself

Show that a star and a plaquette commute. Same-type checks use the same Pauli type. A star and a plaquette overlap on zero edges or two, so their \(XZ\) minus signs occur an even number of times.

Show that the eight-edge torus encodes two logical qubits. Eight physical qubits and six independent stabilizers: three stars plus three plaquettes, because \(\prod_v A_v=I\) and \(\prod_p B_p=I\). So \(k=n-r=8-6=2\), and there are four ground states.

What creates an \(e\) pair, and what creates an \(m\) pair? An open direct-lattice \(Z\) string flips star checks at its endpoints and creates \(e\) anyons. An open dual-lattice \(X\) string flips endpoint plaquettes and creates \(m\) anyons.

What fails if a decoder treats a vanished syndrome as success? Both a shrinkable leftover and a wrapping leftover have empty boundary. The wrapping leftover is a logical operator.

Why are the anyons Abelian if the braiding phase is not \(+1\)? Fusion outcomes are unique, so each fusion space is one-dimensional. Braiding multiplies the state by a phase such as \(-1\) rather than mixing a vector of fusion amplitudes.

What fails if you take the many-body gap for a self-correcting memory? Once a pair exists, either anyon can walk without raising the excitation number. The barrier along a wrapping path stays of order \(J_e\) or \(J_m\) and does not grow with \(L\).

Local commuting checks can open a gapped subspace whose leftover labels are nonlocal. Open strings make endpoint anyons.

Closed shrinkable strings are stabilizers. Closed wrapping strings are logical operators.

Crossing strings supply the braiding phase. A many-body gap is not by itself a scalable finite-temperature memory.

Active extraction is not passive Hamiltonian protection. One-dimensional fusion spaces make these anyons Abelian.

The next lattice we meet will try to get related order from two-body honeycomb bonds instead of four-spin checks.

  • [R141] E. Dennis, A. Kitaev, A. Landahl, and J. Preskill, “Topological quantum memory,” Journal of Mathematical Physics 43, 4452–4505 (2002). DOI: 10.1063/1.1499754. arXiv: quant-ph/0110143.

  • [R142] S. Bravyi, M. B. Hastings, and S. Michalakis, “Topological quantum order: stability under local perturbations,” Journal of Mathematical Physics 51, 093512 (2010). DOI: 10.1063/1.3490195. arXiv: 1001.0344.

  • [R143] R. Alicki, M. Fannes, and M. Horodecki, “On thermalization in Kitaev’s 2D model,” Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical 42, 065303 (2009). DOI: 10.1088/1751-8113/42/6/065303. arXiv: 0810.4584.
