Chapter 17 — A honeycomb of compasses

Draw a honeycomb. At every vertex sit a spin-\(1/2\). Three bonds leave each site, and those three bonds point along three different lattice directions. Color the directions \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\).

The neighbor rule is not “point the same way.” Along an \(x\)-colored bond the two spins couple only through their \(x\) components. Along a \(y\) bond, only \(y\).

Along a \(z\) bond, only \(z\). Each spin therefore hears three different instructions at once.

A classical arrow cannot obey all three. The \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) pieces of a quantum spin do not commute, so the same site cannot settle them independently.

This locked pairing of bond direction with spin direction is a compass interaction: on each nearest-neighbor bond of type \(\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}\), the energy contains \(\sigma_i^\alpha\sigma_j^\alpha\) and no other spin components. We take that as the definition. It is not the Heisenberg magnet, where every component talks to every component.

One hexagon that will not flip

The frustration is organized, not random. Walk around a single hexagon and pick one spin component at each corner. The product of those six operators is a loop the energy cannot change.

Label the six sites clockwise by \(1,2,\ldots,6\). Let the bond types around the perimeter be

1
y / \ z
6 2
x | | x
5 3
z \ / y
4

perimeter sequence: (1,2)=z, (2,3)=x, (3,4)=y,
(4,5)=z, (5,6)=x, (6,1)=y

Every vertex also has one bond leaving the hexagon. Its type is the missing member of \(\{x,y,z\}\). So the outward types at sites \(1\) through \(6\) are \(x,y,z,x,y,z\).

Put one spin-\(1/2\) at each vertex. Write \(\sigma_i^\alpha\) for the dimensionless Pauli operator of component \(\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}\) at site \(i\). The loop we want is

\[ W_p=\sigma_1^x\sigma_2^y\sigma_3^z \sigma_4^x\sigma_5^y\sigma_6^z . \]

Operators on different sites commute, and each Pauli operator squares to the identity. Therefore

\[ W_p^2=1, \]

so a measurement of \(W_p\) can return only \(w_p=+1\) or \(w_p=-1\). That two-valued loop eigenvalue is the flux through the hexagon. No ordinary magnetic field has to thread the ring.

Now check that the energy cannot change it. Take the \(z\)-bond term on sites \(1\) and \(2\),

\[ K_{12}=\sigma_1^z\sigma_2^z. \]

At site \(1\), \(\sigma^z\) anticommutes with the \(\sigma^x\) sitting in \(W_p\). At site \(2\), it anticommutes with \(\sigma^y\). Passing \(K_{12}\) through \(W_p\) therefore produces two minus signs:

\[ K_{12}W_p=(-1)^2W_pK_{12}=W_pK_{12}. \]

The same two-minus-sign argument works for every perimeter bond. An outward bond uses the same component as \(W_p\) at its hexagon endpoint, so it commutes there and acts as the identity on the other five plaquette sites. Every bond term commutes with \(W_p\), and so does their sum:

\[ [H,W_p]=0. \]

Hence every plaquette flux is conserved in the ideal model [R017]. The coloring is structural, not decoration. If a fabricator quietly replaces an \(x\) coupling by an isotropic one, the two-minus-sign argument may no longer apply.

A single spin operator generally flips two neighboring fluxes. For example, \(\sigma_i^\alpha\) anticommutes with the two plaquette operators adjacent to the \(\alpha\) bond from site \(i\), and commutes with the others.

Acting on a simultaneous flux eigenstate changes those two \(w_p\) signs. On a closed periodic lattice, fluxes are therefore created in pairs.

This is the honeycomb cousin of creating two toric-code anyons at the ends of a short string.

Three colored energies

Let \(\langle ij\rangle_\alpha\) mean a nearest-neighbor bond of type \(\alpha\). The Kitaev honeycomb energy is

\[ H_K=-J_x\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_x}\sigma_i^x\sigma_j^x -J_y\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_y}\sigma_i^y\sigma_j^y -J_z\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_z}\sigma_i^z\sigma_j^z . \]

The real numbers \(J_x,J_y,J_z\) have units of energy. Pauli products are dimensionless, so every term and \(H_K\) have units of energy.

When we draw the standard phase diagram we take \(J_\alpha\geq 0\). Many sign choices can be related by spin rotations or gauge choices.

Boundaries and finite geometries deserve separate care.

This is the compass interaction written as a Hamiltonian. It is not the isotropic Heisenberg interaction \(J\,\boldsymbol\sigma_i\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma_j\).

It also contains no explicit six-spin \(W_p\) term. The loop conservation law comes out of the algebra of the two-body terms.

Because all \(W_p\) commute with \(H_K\) and with one another, an energy eigenstate can be labeled by a set \(\{w_p\}\). Each complete assignment is a flux sector.

On a torus there are also two global Wilson-loop labels, and not every apparent sign assignment is independent. Those global constraints matter for exact state counting. The local lesson is that \(\{w_p\}\) is conserved.

For the translationally invariant model on the honeycomb lattice, the ground state lies in the flux-free sector, conventionally \(w_p=+1\) on every plaquette [R017]; [R148]. [Theory] “Flux-free” does not mean “feature-free.” The leftover spectrum can still be gapless or topological.

Chapter 16 obtained topology from explicit four-spin stabilizers. A proposed defect array is more likely to supply pairwise exchange, dipolar, or mediated couplings.

The honeycomb model is the existence proof that strictly local two-body spin interactions can generate flux sectors, fractionalized quasiparticles, and topological order collectively. [Theory] It is an exact result for a special Hamiltonian, not evidence that an arbitrary honeycomb-shaped array becomes topological [R017]; [R148].

Four halves for two answers

Inside any one sector the interacting spins can be rewritten as free fermions hopping through a frozen pattern of signs. The bookkeeping objects are Hermitian and square to one. Each is half of an ordinary complex fermion in the algebraic sense.

At each site introduce four of them,

\[ b_i^x,\quad b_i^y,\quad b_i^z,\quad c_i, \]

which anticommute when distinct and square to one. Represent the spin operators as

\[ \sigma_i^\alpha=i b_i^\alpha c_i. \]

A Majorana operator \(\gamma\) is exactly that kind of object: \(\gamma^\dagger=\gamma\) and \(\gamma^2=1\). The name is worth keeping because it marks an emergent variable used to solve a many-spin problem, not a microscopic electron literally sawn in half.

Four Majoranas span more states than one spin-\(1/2\). The physical subspace is selected by the local constraint

\[ D_i=b_i^x b_i^y b_i^z c_i=+1. \]

Changing all four Majoranas at a site by a minus sign changes no physical spin operator. That redundancy is a local \(\mathbb Z_2\) gauge freedom, not an extra laboratory knob.

Choose an orientation for every \(\alpha\) bond from site \(i\) to site \(j\), and define

\[ u_{ij}=i b_i^\alpha b_j^\alpha,\qquad u_{ij}=\pm1. \]

Substitution into one bond term gives

\[ -J_\alpha\sigma_i^\alpha\sigma_j^\alpha =iJ_\alpha u_{ij}c_i c_j, \]

with the displayed sign tied to the chosen bond orientation. Thus

\[ H_K=i\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_\alpha}J_\alpha u_{ij}c_i c_j. \]

Every \(u_{ij}\) commutes with this ideal Hamiltonian. Once their signs are fixed, \(H_K\) is quadratic in the \(c\) Majoranas and can be diagonalized as a free-fermion hopping problem.

The gauge-invariant product of \(u_{ij}\) around a plaquette equals \(W_p\) up to the fixed orientation convention. Individual \(u_{ij}\) signs depend on the gauge.

The loop product is physical.

The original sites carry physical spins. The \(b\) and \(c\) Majoranas live in an enlarged space subject to \(D_i=+1\).

A fixed-\(u\) solution before projection contains unphysical states. A flux is an emergent many-body label.

None of those facts demonstrates a localized, independently wired Majorana zero mode in a material, and none creates an encoded qubit by itself.

The reorganization splits two kinds of excitation:

  • fluxes, which change the loop eigenvalues; and

  • matter Majoranas, whose allowed energies depend on the flux background.

Their combination is the useful physics. Neither ingredient, treated as an unconstrained bookkeeping variable, is by itself a physical spin excitation.

When three lengths make a triangle

Use a two-site unit cell with sublattices \(A\) and \(B\). Let \(\mathbf a_1\) and \(\mathbf a_2\) be the translations connecting a chosen \(z\) bond to neighboring \(x\) and \(y\) bonds. In the flux-free gauge, the positive matter-Majorana excitation energy has the form

\[ E(\mathbf k)=2|f(\mathbf k)|, \qquad f(\mathbf k)=J_z+J_x e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a_1} +J_y e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a_2}, \]

where \(\mathbf k\) is crystal momentum. The factor of \(2\) depends on the Hamiltonian normalization. The condition for a zero does not.

The three complex terms in \(f\) can sum to zero exactly when the lengths \(J_x,J_y,J_z\) can form a triangle. Therefore the gapless \(B\) phase obeys

\[ J_x\leq J_y+J_z,\qquad J_y\leq J_z+J_x,\qquad J_z\leq J_x+J_y. \]

The name is Kitaev’s label for the interior of that triangle. The isotropic point \(J_x=J_y=J_z\) sits inside it and has two Majorana Dirac cones.

Outside the triangle are three gapped regions:

\[ \begin{aligned} A_x &: J_x>J_y+J_z,\\ A_y &: J_y>J_z+J_x,\\ A_z &: J_z>J_x+J_y. \end{aligned} \]

[Theory] At zero field the \(A\) phases have Abelian topological order. In a strongly anisotropic limit their low-energy theory becomes toric-code-like [R017]; [R148]. The unperturbed \(B\) phase is gapless, so it is not yet the gapped non-Abelian phase often advertised in one sentence too few.

Drop any one triangle inequality and \(f(\mathbf k)\) cannot vanish. The leftover spectrum then has a finite gap, and the isotropic cones are gone.

How pairs manufacture a loop

Take \(J_z\gg J_x,J_y>0\). A \(z\) bond has Hamiltonian \(-J_z\sigma_i^z\sigma_j^z\).

Its aligned states have energy \(-J_z\) and its anti-aligned states have energy \(+J_z\), leaving a low-energy doublet separated by \(2J_z\). Treat each aligned \(z\) dimer as one effective spin.

A single \(x\) or \(y\) bond leaves this subspace. The first process that returns every disturbed dimer while distinguishing a closed loop occurs at fourth order. Degenerate perturbation theory gives, in the standard convention,

\[ H_{\rm eff}=\text{constant}-J_{\rm eff}\sum_p \widetilde W_p+\cdots, \qquad J_{\rm eff}=\frac{J_x^2J_y^2}{16J_z^3}, \]

where \(\widetilde W_p\) is a four-effective-spin plaquette operator on the contracted lattice [R017]. The dimensional check is

\[ [J_{\rm eff}]=\frac{({\rm energy})^4}{({\rm energy})^3}={\rm energy}. \]

Hence nothing inserted a four-body microscopic force. Repeated virtual excursions generated it. The price is equally visible: if \(J_x,J_y\ll J_z\), the emergent topological scale is much smaller than the microscopic coupling.

What fails if the anisotropy is only moderate: higher-order terms and residual dimer-breaking processes are no longer small, and the effective toric-code description is not a controlled expansion.

A field, a gap, and Ising anyons

Break time-reversal symmetry with a weak Zeeman perturbation

\[ H_h=-\sum_i\left(h_x\sigma_i^x+h_y\sigma_i^y+h_z\sigma_i^z\right), \]

where each \(h_\alpha\) is an energy. For a physical magnetic field it contains the appropriate \(g\) factor and Bohr magneton. In third-order perturbation theory, nonzero \(h_xh_yh_z\) generates an effective three-spin interaction with scale

\[ \kappa\sim\frac{h_xh_yh_z}{J^2}, \]

where \(J\) denotes a representative Kitaev exchange. Again \([\kappa]=({\rm energy})^3/({\rm energy})^2={\rm energy}\). This term opens a mass gap at the Dirac cones.

[Theory] In the weak-field effective model, the resulting phase has Majorana-band Chern number \(\nu=+1\) or \(-1\) and vortices bind Majorana zero modes, producing non-Abelian Ising topological order [R017]; [R148]. A generic microscopic magnetic field also destroys exact flux conservation, so the all-field problem is not simply the same free-Majorana solution with a larger gap.

The word Ising now needs three separate boxes, because it has been asked to do three different jobs.

Conventional Ising magnetic order breaks a \(\mathbb Z_2\) symmetry and is diagnosed by a local order parameter such as magnetization. That is not the phase under discussion.

Ising topological order has topological charges \(1\) (vacuum), \(\sigma\) (vortex), and \(\psi\) (fermion), with \[ \sigma\times\sigma=1+\psi, \qquad d_\sigma=\sqrt2. \] Its degeneracy and braiding live in a nonlocal fusion space. No local magnetization is required.

Fibonacci topological order instead has \(1\) and \(\tau\), with \[ \tau\times\tau=1+\tau, \qquad d_\tau=\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}. \]

These fusion rules are not relabelings. Braiding Ising anyons alone does not provide a dense set of arbitrary qubit unitaries.

In standard encodings it supplies Clifford operations and needs an additional non-topological resource for universality. Fibonacci braiding is computationally universal in the sense developed in Chapter 15.

So the field-gapped honeycomb model is a rigorous route from two-body interactions to Ising-type non-Abelian anyons. It is not a realization, approximation, or synonym of Fibonacci order.

Do not call the honeycomb Fibonacci. The two phases disagree about the only data that define them.

What the laboratory actually has

The microscopic route most often discussed uses spin-orbit-entangled magnetic ions in edge-sharing octahedra. Interference between exchange paths can suppress ordinary Heisenberg exchange and favor bond-directional Kitaev coupling.

[Proposal] Jackeli and Khaliullin derived this mechanism for certain Mott insulators [R147]. It is a materials design principle, not a proof that every edge-sharing honeycomb implements \(H_K\).

Candidate compounds — including honeycomb iridates and \(\alpha\)-RuCl\(_3\) — also contain Heisenberg exchange, symmetric off-diagonal \(\Gamma\) terms, longer-range couplings, lattice distortions, phonons, stacking faults, and interlayer coupling [R149]; [R150]. \(\alpha\)-RuCl\(_3\) develops zigzag magnetic order near \(7\ \mathrm K\) at zero field, depending on sample and stacking history [R151]. [Experiment] That local symmetry-breaking order is direct evidence that the clean zero-field sample is not the ideal Kitaev spin liquid.

Neutron and Raman measurements have nevertheless found broad continua and field-dependent spectra compatible with substantial Kitaev interactions and fractionalized descriptions [R149]; [R150]; [R151]. [Experiment] Compatibility is weaker than unique identification: magnons, disorder, and multiparticle continua can overlap similar frequency ranges.

A sharper proposed signature is the thermal Hall conductance of one chiral Majorana edge mode. The ideal two-dimensional theory predicts

\[ \frac{\kappa_{xy}}{T} =\frac12\frac{\pi^2 k_B^2}{3h_{\rm P}} =\frac{\pi k_B^2}{12\hbar}, \]

where \(\kappa_{xy}\) is transverse thermal conductance, \(T\) is temperature, \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant, \(h_{\rm P}\) is Planck’s constant, and \(\hbar=h_{\rm P}/(2\pi)\). The units are \(\mathrm{W\,K^{-2}}\).

Kasahara and collaborators reported a half-quantized plateau-like signal in field-driven \(\alpha\)-RuCl\(_3\) and interpreted it as a Majorana edge contribution [R152]. [Experiment] Later measurements found strong sample dependence and substantial phonon or bosonic contributions [R150]; [R153].

A 2026 acoustic study directly inferred phonon Hall viscosity and attributed a substantial intrinsic thermal Hall response to phonons [R154]. [Experiment] As of 2026, the field-induced non-Abelian Kitaev phase in \(\alpha\)-RuCl\(_3\) remains actively disputed rather than experimentally settled [R150]; [R154].

No cited experiment has taken engineered color-center defects, arranged them into this exact compass Hamiltonian, and established intrinsic honeycomb-model Ising order. Still less has it obtained Fibonacci order.

For defect engineering, this chapter supplies a Hamiltonian target and a warning label: geometry, pairwise coupling, and a suggestive continuum are not sufficient. One must establish the interaction tensor, many-body gap, flux or gauge structure, and topological response.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Calling a honeycomb a Kitaev material because the graph has hexagons. A graph specifies who is connected. The Kitaev Hamiltonian also specifies which spin component couples on every edge and how large competing terms are. An isotropic Heisenberg magnet drawn on hexagons is a different model.

  • Seeing Majoranas in the algebra and announcing that the sample contains Majorana zero modes. The \(c_i\) operators form a delocalized matter band and live in an enlarged, gauge-redundant representation. A localized zero mode appears at a vortex only in the gapped topological regime and after the physical-state constraint is enforced. A numerical parton spectrum without gauge projection is not yet a physical excitation spectrum.

  • Assuming flux conservation survives realistic control fields. It is exact for \(H_K\) and for selected integrable extensions. Generic Zeeman, Heisenberg, \(\Gamma\), disorder, and drive terms can mix flux sectors. Small perturbations need not immediately destroy a gapped topological phase, but they do destroy the shortcut of labeling every eigenstate by exact \(w_p\) values.

  • Hearing “non-Abelian” and writing “Fibonacci.” Ising and Fibonacci anyons both have multidimensional fusion spaces, but their fusion rules, quantum dimensions, braid representations, and computational power differ. The honeycomb model’s canonical non-Abelian phase is Ising-type. Calling it Fibonacci discards the very topological data that define the phase.

  • Treating a finite programmed simulation as material emergence. A gate array can encode the Majorana Hamiltonian, prepare a flux sector, and measure the expected spectrum. That is a digital emulation by ordinary physical qubits unless the simulator’s own equilibrium Hamiltonian has the phase and protection. Simulation is valuable evidence about the model. It is not evidence that intrinsic anyons inhabited the processor between gate pulses.

  • Taking an exactly solvable point for a complete architecture. Exact solvability identifies the phase cleanly. An architecture must additionally initialize a sector, cool below the many-body gap, create and move excitations, read out fusion information, tolerate disorder, and scale boundaries and defects. The theorem does not route the wires.

Check yourself

Show that every plaquette flux commutes with the bond Hamiltonian. A perimeter bond anticommutes with two factors in \(W_p\), giving two canceling minus signs; an outward bond uses the same component as the plaquette factor at their shared site.

What is physical: \(u_{ij}\) or \(W_p\)? An individual \(u_{ij}\) depends on gauge choice. The loop product, equivalently the flux \(W_p\), is gauge-invariant.

Show that the zero-field matter spectrum is gapless precisely when \(J_x,J_y,J_z\) form a triangle. \(E(\mathbf k)=2|f(\mathbf k)|\) vanishes if and only if the three complex terms in \(f\) can sum to zero, which is the triangle inequalities. The isotropic point lies in this \(B\) region.

What fails if you take the ungapped \(B\) phase for protected non-Abelian anyons? The bulk is gapless. A weak time-reversal-breaking perturbation can gap its Dirac Majoranas and produce Ising topological order; the ungapped bulk is not the desired protected phase.

Why is the non-Abelian honeycomb phase not Fibonacci? Its vortices obey \(\sigma\times\sigma=1+\psi\) with \(d_\sigma=\sqrt2\), not \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\) with \(d_\tau=\varphi\). Their braid computational powers differ as well.

What fails if \(J_x,J_y\ll J_z\) is treated as a free topological scale? Virtual processes from two-body bonds can generate a loop interaction, but its scale \(J_x^2J_y^2/(16J_z^3)\) may be far smaller than the microscopic exchange.

You now have a two-body compass model that conserves flux, a free-fermion solution inside each sector, and a field-gapped phase whose anyons are Ising, not Fibonacci.

Chapter 18 — Strings that only meet in allowed ways

Draw colored strings on the edges of a honeycomb. A blank edge is empty. A colored edge carries one type of string. At each three-way meeting, not every trio is allowed.

Two of one color and one of another can be fine. Three of the same color can be fine. A single colored string arriving at two blanks is not.

Do not treat any one drawing as the state. The object we care about is a superposition of many legal drawings, with amplitudes. A local move can create a small closed loop, slide it across a meeting, and swallow it into the surrounding net.

A Levin–Wen model is this lattice Hamiltonian: a finite set of labels on the edges of a trivalent lattice, a local rule saying which three labels may meet, and a second local rule that inserts and recouples contractible loops. We take that as the definition. Enforcing the meeting rule alone is not a topological phase.

Which three labels may meet

The smallest useful color set is the one from Fibonacci fusion. Call the blank edge vacuum and write it \(1\). Call the nontrivial color \(\tau\). Both are their own reverse. Their fusion rules are

\[ 1\times a=a,\qquad \tau\times\tau=1+\tau, \]

where \(a\) may be \(1\) or \(\tau\). The plus sign still means two possible meeting channels, not two particles sitting in a pile.

On a lattice where three edges meet, the allowed unordered triples are

\[ (1,1,1),\qquad (1,\tau,\tau),\qquad(\tau,\tau,\tau), \]

including permutations. A vertex with exactly one \(\tau\) is forbidden. The triple \((\tau,\tau,\tau)\) is the interesting one: two \(\tau\) strings may meet and continue as \(\tau\).

That list is the branching rule. It is a local constraint on three incident labels. Enforcing it does not by itself make a topological phase.

Drop the triple \((\tau,\tau,\tau)\) and the remaining rule is Abelian: two \(\tau\) strings may meet only as vacuum. The later loop algebra then cannot reproduce Fibonacci fusion.

Superpositions of legal nets

The branching rule rejects illegal meetings. It does not decide which legal drawing is the ground state.

Stop treating any one legal drawing as the answer. The ground state we want is a coherent superposition of many of them.

A local move may create a small closed loop, slide it across a vertex, and absorb it into the surrounding net. Closed, branching drawings then appear at every length scale.

That fluctuating legal picture is a string-net. Levin and Wen showed that this picture can be written as the exact ground state of commuting local projectors [R018]. [Theory]

The toric code was the quieter cousin of this picture: local projectors, very simple string rules, and labels that commute past each other. Here a meeting can branch, and the rewrite amplitudes are not \(\pm 1\) bit flips.

An edge label is a microscopic basis state of the lattice. A closed labeled net is a component of a many-body wavefunction.

An endpoint or ribbon that survives all local equivalences can be an emergent quasiparticle. None of those is, merely by being written on paper, a defect-center spin or a digitally emulated anyon.

One hexagon, two drawings

Take a single hexagonal plaquette whose six outward legs all carry \(1\). The branching rule then leaves only two boundary configurations:

|0> : six boundary edges are 1
|R> : six boundary edges are τ, forming a ring

Insert a \(\tau\) loop into \(|0\rangle\) and push it outward until it lies on the boundary. Because \(\tau\times 1=\tau\), this gives \(|R\rangle\). Call this loop-insertion operator \(B^\tau\). In this two-state sector, fusing a second \(\tau\) loop uses \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\), so

\[ B^\tau|0\rangle=|R\rangle, \qquad B^\tau|R\rangle=|0\rangle+|R\rangle. \]

Therefore, in the ordered basis \((|0\rangle,|R\rangle)\),

\[ B^\tau= \begin{pmatrix} 0&1\\ 1&1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Let

\[ \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2} \]

be the golden ratio. The quantum dimensions are \(d_1=1\) and \(d_\tau=\varphi\), and the squared total quantum dimension of the input labels is

\[ \mathcal D^2=d_1^2+d_\tau^2=1+\varphi^2=\varphi+2. \]

Hence a loop did not get flipped like six independent bits. It was inserted and fused. The empty drawing and the ring are no longer separate classical pictures. They mix.

If the six outward legs are not all vacuum, this two-by-two matrix is not the whole story. Intermediate fusion channels appear, and the isolated-hexagon calculation cannot leave its sector without an \(F\)-move.

Weighting the loops

The empty net is not the ground state. Average over loop types, weighted by their quantum dimensions:

\[ B_p=\frac{1}{\mathcal D^2}\sum_{s\in\{1,\tau\}}d_s B_p^s =\frac{I+\varphi B_p^\tau}{\varphi+2}, \]

where \(B_p^1=I\). This weighted average is the plaquette projector. It is not a six-bit flip. It is a filter that accepts the particular superposition the input data demand.

In our two-state sector,

\[ B_p=\frac{1}{\varphi+2} \begin{pmatrix} 1&\varphi\\ \varphi&\varphi^2 \end{pmatrix} =|g\rangle\!\langle g|, \]

with

\[ |g\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle+\varphi|R\rangle}{\sqrt{\varphi+2}}. \]

This calculation does three useful things. It shows that \(B_p^2=B_p\), that a ground-state component is not just the empty net, and that the relative amplitude \(\varphi\) is fixed by the input labels. A loop was inserted, fused, and coherently recoupled.

This tiny sector hides the interesting bookkeeping. If outward legs carry \(\tau\), several intermediate fusion channels are possible.

Moving the inserted loop through a vertex then changes the parenthesization of three fusions. That is an \(F\)-move, and we will need it as soon as the hexagon is no longer isolated.

Equal weights in place of \(d_s\) would generally destroy idempotence. The empty net and the ring would then not sit in a rank-one projector.

Labels on every edge

Zoom out from one hexagon. Choose an oriented trivalent lattice, often a honeycomb.

Each oriented edge \(e\) carries a label \(i_e\) from a finite set \(I=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). The label \(0\), also written \(1\), is vacuum.

Reversing an edge replaces \(i\) by its dual \(i^*\). Fibonacci labels are self-dual, so orientation is visually quiet there.

It matters for a general set of labels.

A basis vector is a complete assignment

\[ |\{i_e\}\rangle=\bigotimes_e |i_e\rangle. \]

The fusion multiplicity \(N_{ij}^{k}\) is the number of independent ways labels \(i\) and \(j\) can fuse to \(k\). For the multiplicity-free models used here, \(N_{ij}^{k}\) is either zero or one.

A trivalent vertex with appropriately oriented labels \(i,j,k\) is allowed when \(N_{ij}^{k^*}>0\). Input data with multiplicities need an extra vertex-channel index.

Suppressing that index is a simplification, not a theorem that nature dislikes indices.

The quantum dimension \(d_i>0\) is the positive solution of

\[ d_i d_j=\sum_k N_{ij}^{k}d_k. \]

For Fibonacci fusion this gives \(d_\tau^2=1+d_\tau\), whose positive root is \(\varphi\). Those are the same numbers that weighted the hexagon.

Hence the honeycomb labels are the microscopic basis of the many-body Hilbert space, not a drawing laid over some other degrees of freedom.

A projector at each vertex

Define \(Q_v\) to be diagonal in the edge-label basis:

\[ Q_v|i,j,k\rangle= \begin{cases} |i,j,k\rangle,&N_{ij}^{k^*}>0,\\ 0,&N_{ij}^{k^*}=0. \end{cases} \]

Thus \(Q_v^2=Q_v\). A state with \(Q_v=0\) violates the local fusion rule.

This operator is the vertex projector: the branching rule written as an energy term. It accepts allowed meetings and kills forbidden ones.

In the Hamiltonian, changing a satisfied vertex from eigenvalue one to zero raises the energy by \(J_v\), before accounting for any linked plaquette violations.

One could instead define a penalty \(J_v(1-Q_v)\). It differs from \(-J_v Q_v\) only by an additive constant. The physics is less impressed by constants than accountants are.

What fails if \(Q_v\) is omitted: illegal triples such as a single \(\tau\) at a vertex remain in the low-energy space, and the later loop operators no longer act inside a fusion-consistent subspace.

Changing the order of fusion

Fusion can be performed in different orders:

\[ ((a\times b)\to x)\times c\to d \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad a\times((b\times c)\to y)\to d. \]

The unitary change of basis is

\[ |((ab)x c)d\rangle =\sum_y [F^{abc}_{d}]_{xy} |a(bc)y;d\rangle. \]

Here \(a,b,c,d\) are labels, while \(x,y\) are allowed intermediate fusion channels. The matrices \(F^{abc}_{d}\) obey the pentagon equation.

That consistency condition says that two sequences of recouplings around a five-leg tree give the same answer. It is precisely what makes neighboring plaquette operations mutually compatible [R018]; [R155].

[Theory]

In a common unitary gauge, the only nontrivial two-dimensional Fibonacci matrix is

\[ F^{\tau\tau\tau}_{\tau}= \begin{pmatrix} \varphi^{-1}&\varphi^{-1/2}\\ \varphi^{-1/2}&-\varphi^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \]

where rows and columns are ordered by intermediate channel \((1,\tau)\). The matrix is real, symmetric, and unitary. Its signs and phases depend on gauge, but consistent gauge changes do not alter measurable topological data.

When a \(\tau\) loop is pushed through a vertex whose outward legs already carry \(\tau\), this matrix is the amplitude book. Without it, the hexagon calculation does not know how to leave the two-state sector.

Drop the pentagon equation and neighboring \(B_p\) need not commute. The model then ceases to be a commuting-projector Hamiltonian.

How a loop joins the net

For each possible string type \(s\), define \(B_p^s\) by a graphical algorithm:

  • insert a closed loop of type \(s\) just inside plaquette \(p\);

  • fuse that loop into the boundary edges;

  • apply an \(F\)-move at each boundary vertex to recouple it through the existing net;

  • sum coherently over every allowed intermediate channel.

For a hexagon this is a circuit of six local recouplings, not a statement that the final operator is a simple product of six Pauli matrices. Its matrix elements also depend on labels on the legs leaving the plaquette.

The loop operators reproduce the fusion algebra,

\[ B_p^r B_p^s=\sum_t N_{rs}^{t}B_p^t. \]

The special weighted sum

\[ B_p=\frac{1}{\mathcal D^2}\sum_s d_s B_p^s, \qquad \mathcal D=\sqrt{\sum_s d_s^2}, \]

is a projector. Quantum-dimension identities establish \(B_p^2=B_p\); the pentagon equation establishes \([B_p,B_{p'}]=0\), including for adjacent plaquettes. The branching and recoupling data also give \([Q_v,B_p]=0\) [R018]; [R155].

There is a short reason the weights work. Let \(\Omega=\sum_s d_s s\) denote the formal weighted loop. Fusion with a label \(r\) gives

\[ r\times\Omega=\sum_{s,t}d_s N_{rs}^{t}t=d_r\Omega. \]

Fusing two weighted loops therefore gives \(\Omega\times\Omega=\mathcal D^2\Omega\). Dividing loop insertion by \(\mathcal D^2\) makes it idempotent. The plaquette projector is a normalized vacuum-flux filter.

A six-edge bit flip with convenient coefficients is a different Hamiltonian. It need not reproduce this fusion algebra.

Energy for both rules

Call each vertex \(v\) and each plaquette \(p\). Let \(Q_v\) be the dimensionless projector that accepts allowed labels at vertex \(v\), and let \(B_p\) be the dimensionless projector that applies the plaquette rule at \(p\). Let the positive energies \(J_v\) and \(J_p\) set the cost of violating those rules. The many-body Hamiltonian is

\[ H=-J_v\sum_v Q_v-J_p\sum_p B_p. \]

Every term has units of energy. Authors often set \(J_v=J_p=1\); that chooses an energy unit rather than discovering free electricity.

The vertex terms reject illegal meetings. The plaquette terms declare locally equivalent legal nets to be parts of one quantum state.

The jobs line up like this:

microscopic edge degree of freedom
↓
allowed fusion at every vertex Q_v = 1
↓
coherent loop fluctuations B_p = 1
↓
nonlocal ground sectors and emergent anyons

That is an exact theoretical construction, not a material recipe. The difference between those two sentences is much of the remaining book.

When every projector agrees

Because all terms commute, the model is frustration free. A ground state \(|\Psi_0\rangle\) satisfies

\[ Q_v|\Psi_0\rangle=|\Psi_0\rangle, \qquad B_p|\Psi_0\rangle=|\Psi_0\rangle \]

for every \(v\) and \(p\). [Theory] These equations say, respectively, that the wavefunction has support only on legal nets and is invariant under the weighted insertion and recoupling of a contractible loop [R018]. Tensor-network constructions make this coherent superposition explicit [R159].

“Condensed” does not mean every edge is likely occupied. It means closed nets can fluctuate over arbitrarily large scales in the ideal ground state, with local reconnections related by the input data.

That proliferation of closed, branching nets at all length scales is string-net condensation [R018]. The name is worth keeping because it names a phase of the wavefunction, not a box of threads, and because it is not the same job as taking an already-emergent bosonic particle and identifying it with the vacuum.

On a surface with noncontractible cycles, a local move cannot always erase the global winding information. Distinct global sectors form the topological ground space.

Enforcing only \(Q_v=1\) produces a constrained Hilbert space of legal drawings. Without coherent \(B_p\) dynamics it can remain a classical collection of nets.

Leftover ends

A local operator can violate one or more projectors. A failed vertex constraint resembles an electric charge.

A failed plaquette constraint resembles flux. In a non-Abelian string net, however, the fully mobile quasiparticles are generally charge–flux composites.

Ribbon operators create them in pairs, move them along paths, and reveal fusion and braiding through the algebra of intersecting ribbons.

The input label \(\tau\) on an edge is not itself one of those quasiparticles. It is a microscopic basis state. An emergent anyon is an excitation of the collective Hamiltonian that survives all local equivalences.

The systematic home of those bulk superselection sectors is the Drinfeld center \(Z(\mathcal C)\) of the input fusion category \(\mathcal C\) [R156]; [R157]. [Theory] The center equips an object with consistent information about how it passes every string type.

That extra passing rule is the emergent braiding data. One does not have to put a microscopic braid operator on every edge.

What fails if the edge label is treated as the anyon: you have counted input data, not excitations of \(H\).

The mirror that comes for free

For modular Fibonacci input,

\[ Z(\mathrm{Fib})\simeq \mathrm{Fib}\boxtimes\overline{\mathrm{Fib}}, \]

where the overline denotes the mirror, with opposite braiding chirality. The four bulk charges may be labeled

\[ (1,\bar1),\quad(\tau,\bar1),\quad(1,\bar\tau),\quad(\tau,\bar\tau), \]

with quantum dimensions \(1,\varphi,\varphi,\varphi^2\), respectively. On a torus the ideal doubled-Fibonacci model consequently has four topological ground sectors [R156]; [R158]. [Theory]

This is doubled-Fibonacci order: a Fibonacci sector paired with its time-reversed partner. Its net chirality cancels.

The input label \(\tau\) is not itself an emergent anyon, and the bulk is not a single chiral Fibonacci theory. Chapter 19 will examine what that does — and does not — mean for computation.

Drop the mirror sector and you have described a different phase. Ordinary two-dimensional Levin–Wen with Fibonacci input does not produce a lone chiral Fibonacci liquid.

What a crystal does not give you

The Levin–Wen Hamiltonian is an exact existence proof and a precise benchmark. It is not a list of naturally available couplings in diamond, sapphire, or silicon carbide.

A proposed defect implementation would first need an isolated local Hilbert space for every effective edge, with \(|1\rangle\) and \(|\tau\rangle\) encoded in two reliably controlled states. It would then need a large energy penalty implementing the three-edge branching projector \(Q_v\). Harder still, it would need the plaquette matrix elements dictated by a product of \(F\)-moves and the exact ratio \(d_1:d_\tau=1:\varphi\).

Microscopic defect interactions are commonly pairwise at leading order, whereas \(B_p\) is a correlated, label-dependent operation around an entire plaquette and its attached legs. It is not merely a uniform ring exchange.

[Proposal] Ancilla-mediated perturbative gadgets, periodic drives, or digital circuits could synthesize such an operator, but each route must separately establish the effective coefficients, unwanted terms, many-body gap, and regime of validity. The code and Turaev–Viro literature establishes mathematical and computational constructions [R155]; [R158]; it does not thereby establish a passive defect-material phase.

[Speculation] A defect-cluster architecture might encode one edge label per cluster and use mediators to generate \(Q_v\) and \(B_p\). The microscopic challenge is not “make spins on a honeycomb.” It is to reproduce the category-consistent multi-edge recoupling amplitudes strongly enough that residual two-body terms, disorder, leakage, and temperature do not close the topological gap. No result in the sources used for this chapter demonstrates that hierarchy in a crystalline defect array.

Exact commutation is not required throughout an entire topological phase. Suitable commuting-projector topological order is stable to sufficiently weak local perturbations while its gap remains open [R142]. [Theory] But “sufficiently weak” is a condition to derive or measure for the proposed effective Hamiltonian, not permission to ignore a term because it makes the diagram untidy.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Calling the edge label an anyon. The microscopic \(\tau\) label is input data. Emergent anyons are excitations of the collective Hamiltonian and belong to \(Z(\mathrm{Fib})\).

  • Equating branching with topological order. Enforcing \(Q_v=1\) produces a constrained Hilbert space. Without coherent \(B_p\) dynamics, it can remain a classical collection of legal nets.

  • Replacing recoupling with a bit flip. Fibonacci \(B_p\) depends on fusion channels and \(F\)-symbols. A six-edge flip with convenient coefficients is generally a different Hamiltonian.

  • Calling every superposition a condensate. String-net condensation includes scale-spanning closed-net fluctuations and topological equivalences. A prepared superposition of two drawings does not prove a phase.

  • Confusing string-net condensation with anyon condensation. The former constructs a ground-state liquid of fluctuating nets. The latter changes topological order by condensing an emergent bosonic sector.

  • Dropping the mirror sector. A Fibonacci input to the ordinary two-dimensional Levin–Wen construction gives doubled Fibonacci, not a lone chiral Fibonacci phase.

  • Treating digital enforcement as passive emergence. Measuring projectors and applying corrections can emulate or stabilize a code space. Passive topological order requires the material Hamiltonian itself to energetically select the phase.

  • Assuming exact solvability is the protection mechanism. Commuting projectors make analysis clean. Protection instead depends on locality, a persistent many-body gap, system size, temperature, and control of perturbations. Exact algebra is the map; it is not the weather.

Check yourself

Show that \(Q_v\) is a projector. It is diagonal in the edge-label basis with eigenvalues \(1\) on allowed triples and \(0\) on forbidden ones, so \(Q_v^2=Q_v\).

What does \(B_p^s\) do? It inserts an \(s\)-type loop into plaquette \(p\), fuses it into the boundary, and recouples the resulting fusion trees with \(F\)-moves.

Show that the weights \(d_s/\mathcal D^2\) make \(B_p\) a projector. The formal loop \(\Omega=\sum_s d_s s\) obeys \(\Omega\times\Omega=\mathcal D^2\Omega\). Dividing by \(\mathcal D^2\) makes insertion idempotent, so \(B_p^2=B_p\).

What fails if you enforce \(Q_v=1\) without coherent \(B_p\)? You obtain a constrained space of legal nets. Without loop recoupling they need not form a topological liquid.

What topological order follows from Fibonacci input? The bulk is \(Z(\mathrm{Fib})\), equivalent to Fibonacci times mirror Fibonacci: doubled-Fibonacci order.

What fails if the edge label \(\tau\) is treated as an emergent anyon? \(\tau\) is microscopic input. The bulk charges live in \(Z(\mathrm{Fib})\) and include the mirror sector.

  • [R155] Lukasz Fidkowski, Michael Freedman, Chetan Nayak, Kevin Walker, and Zhenghan Wang, “From string nets to nonabelions,” Communications in Mathematical Physics 287, 805–827 (2009). DOI: 10.1007/s00220-009-0757-9; arXiv: cond-mat/0610583.

Chapter 19 — A dance and its mirror

Two dancers circle clockwise. Film them. Play the film: the same steps, the same handedness. Stand a mirror next to the floor. In the glass, clockwise has become counterclockwise.

One film has a handedness. The pair of films has both. The pair is not a third, handedness-free dance. Two opposite corkscrews in the same drawer do not become spoons.

Chapter 15 gave one fusion rule. Chapter 18 built a lattice Hamiltonian from that rule. Neither sentence said whether you bought the dance, the mirror, or both.

A braid that notices a mirror

A braid of two non-Abelian quasiparticles is a dance with a direction. Play it normally and the fusion state is transformed by a unitary matrix \(U\).

Reflect the laboratory. Clockwise has become counterclockwise, and — after consistent choices of basis — the matrix is the complex conjugate \(U^*\).

A medium that supplies only one orientation of that movie is chiral. Reverse space and the braiding data change. That is a physical claim, not a nickname.

The chiral Fibonacci theory, written \(\mathcal F\), is that one-orientation medium. Its nontrivial charge is \(\tau\).

We will not use Fibonacci by itself as the name of a phase or a quasiparticle. That word is the family name.

It does not say which member you are holding.

Drop the orientation and you have not specified a theory. The fusion rule \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\) is shared by the dance and the glass. The braid matrices are not.

The reverse braid

Stand the laboratory in a mirror and you get a second theory. Call it the mirror chiral Fibonacci theory, written \(\overline{\mathcal F}\). Its corresponding charge is \(\bar\tau\).

The bar means reversed braiding, not antiparticle. Both \(\tau\) and \(\bar\tau\) are self-dual: each is its own partner under fusion.

Hence \(\mathcal F\) and \(\overline{\mathcal F}\) are not the same phase. One is a left-handed dance.

The other is the dance you see in the glass. A Hamiltonian that realizes one need not realize the other.

What fails if you read the bar as “antiparticle”? You will look for a charge that annihilates \(\tau\) and miss that \(\tau\) already annihilates itself.

A pair of labels

Put the two theories side by side as independent bookkeeping layers. An excitation must then carry a pair of labels:

\[ (\text{charge in }\mathcal F,\ \text{charge in }\overline{\mathcal F}). \]

That pair is the useful picture of doubling. It is not yet the definition, and it need not mean that a device literally contains two physical films.

The formal construction packages a theory together with all consistent ways its strings can pass around other strings. For a modular input, that package happens to factor as theory times mirror [R160].

The result is the doubled-Fibonacci theory, written \(\mathrm{DFib}\):

\[ \mathrm{DFib}=\mathcal F\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal F}. \]

The name is worth keeping because ordinary English hears a copy, or a cancellation into something dull. The construction packages a theory with its reverse.

You still have two corkscrews. You do not have spoons.

[Theory] A Levin–Wen model whose input is the Fibonacci fusion category has bulk anyons described by the Drinfeld center of that category. Because the chiral Fibonacci category is modular, its center is equivalent to a product of the chiral theory and its reverse-braided mirror [R018]; [R160]. The standard commuting-projector construction therefore targets \(\mathrm{DFib}\), not \(\mathcal F\) alone.

That distinction is not decoration. It changes the bulk charge list, the torus degeneracy, the edge, the thermal Hall response, and the operations you must control if you want a computer. A defect lattice aimed at the wrong member of the family may be beautifully engineered and still answer a different question.

Four charges, not two

The chiral theory \(\mathcal F\) has \(1\) and \(\tau\). Its mirror \(\overline{\mathcal F}\) has \(\bar 1\) and \(\bar\tau\). Therefore \(\mathrm{DFib}\) has four simple bulk charges. Give them names that keep their sector:

Doubled-Fibonacci charge | Pair label | Quantum dimension | Topological spin | |

vacuum \(\mathbf 1\) | \((1,\bar1)\) | \(1\) | \(1\) | |

left-handed charge \(x\) | \((\tau,\bar1)\) | \(\varphi\) | \(e^{4\pi i/5}\) | |

right-handed charge \(y\) | \((1,\bar\tau)\) | \(\varphi\) | \(e^{-4\pi i/5}\) | |

diagonal charge \(b\) | \((\tau,\bar\tau)\) | \(\varphi^2\) | \(1\) | |

Here \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\) is the golden ratio. The displayed spin convention chooses \(\theta_\tau=e^{4\pi i/5}\); reversing every braid conjugates it. The quantum dimension of a pair is the product of the component dimensions [R160]; [R015].

Hence the doubled-Fibonacci theory is not the two-object theory \(\{1,\tau\}\) with a longer name. It contains two simple charges, \(x\) and \(y\), each carrying one chiral Fibonacci fusion subtheory, plus the diagonal charge \(b\).

The symbol \(b\) is a label, not a claim that this non-Abelian charge is an ordinary pointlike boson. It has trivial topological spin but quantum dimension \(\varphi^2>1\). Drop that distinction and you will treat \(b\) as a spare copy of vacuum.

Fuse one side at a time

Pair labels make the arithmetic almost clerical. Fuse each factor on its own:

\[ (a,\bar c)\times(a',\bar c') =(a\times a',\ \bar c\times\bar c'). \]

For example,

\[ x\times y =(\tau,\bar1)\times(1,\bar\tau) =(\tau,\bar\tau)=b. \]

There is only one outcome. Now fuse that result with itself:

\[ \begin{aligned} b\times b &=(\tau\times\tau,\ \bar\tau\times\bar\tau)\\ &=(1+\tau,\ \bar1+\bar\tau)\\ &=\mathbf1+x+y+b. \end{aligned} \]

The complete nontrivial fusion rules are therefore

\[ \begin{aligned} x\times x&=\mathbf1+x, & y\times y&=\mathbf1+y,\\ x\times y&=b, & x\times b&=y+b,\\ y\times b&=x+b, & b\times b&=\mathbf1+x+y+b. \end{aligned} \]

Hence \(x\) fuses with itself exactly as \(\tau\) did in Chapter 15, and \(y\) does the same job in the mirror. The diagonal charge \(b\) is the new object. It is not a spare copy of \(\tau\).

What fails if you fuse only the first components and ignore the bars? You recover the chiral table and lose \(y\) and \(b\) as distinct bulk charges.

Add the squared sizes

For any anyon theory, add up the squared sizes of the simple charges. The total quantum dimension \(\mathcal D\) is defined by

\[ \mathcal D^2=\sum_a d_a^2, \]

where the sum runs over simple charges and \(d_a\) is the quantum dimension of charge \(a\). In this example,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal D_{\mathrm{DFib}}^2 &=1+\varphi^2+\varphi^2+\varphi^4\\ &=(1+\varphi^2)^2,\\ \mathcal D_{\mathrm{DFib}}&=1+\varphi^2=\varphi+2. \end{aligned} \]

The last equality uses \(\varphi^2=\varphi+1\). Hence \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{DFib}}\) is the square, in categorical dimension, of one chiral sector — as a double should be [R160].

On a torus, the ideal doubled-Fibonacci theory has four ground-state sectors, one per simple bulk charge. The chiral Fibonacci theory has two. If someone hands you a ground-space count of two and calls it doubled, they have miscounted.

Opposite braids do not cancel every rotation

If only \(x\) charges are braided, the mirror component is vacuum. Their fusion spaces, \(F\)-moves, and braid matrices are exactly those of \(\mathcal F\). If only \(y\) charges are braided, the matrices are their complex conjugates.

For diagonal charges, both components move. A braid word represented by \(U\) in \(\mathcal F\) is represented schematically by

\[ U\otimes U^* \]

on the factorized doubled fusion space.

This does not make every braid the identity. Opposite chiralities cancel net handedness.

They do not cancel every rotation. Suppose the two factors were forced to move together as an inseparable pair.

Then the computational action would be that of \(U\otimes U^*\), not of \(U\), and the usual chiral-sector argument would no longer apply.

You also cannot point to the fusion rule of \(b\) and silently reuse that argument. Which charge is mobile and measurable is part of the computer specification.

A leftover you can heat

A topological phase is chiral when its low-energy topological data have a net handedness. Reversing spatial orientation replaces its braiding by the reverse braiding.

You can give that leftover a number. Call it the chiral central charge \(c_-\), defined modulo the appropriate invertible phase. At an interface with the vacuum it controls the universal low-temperature thermal Hall coefficient [R015]

\[ \frac{\kappa_{xy}}{T}=c_-\frac{\pi^2 k_B^2}{3h}, \]

where \(\kappa_{xy}\) is thermal Hall conductance in watts per kelvin, \(T\) is temperature in kelvin, \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant, and \(h\) is Planck’s constant. The dimensions work: \(k_B^2/h\) has units \(\mathrm{W\,K^{-2}}\), the same as \(\kappa_{xy}/T\).

The chiral Fibonacci theory has nonzero \(c_-\). The mirror chiral Fibonacci theory has the opposite value.

In the doubled-Fibonacci theory the sum vanishes [R160]; [R015]. Equivalently, the topological spins of \(x\) and \(y\) are complex conjugates, while the diagonal charge has spin one.

Hence zero \(c_-\) does not imply trivial topological order, and it does not prove that a microscopic Hamiltonian respects time reversal. It says that the doubled topological data have no net chiral anomaly.

How a string slides past every partner

A Levin–Wen edge may carry only the input labels \(1\) or \(\tau\). The bulk theory has four charges.

The extra objects are not a counting error. They are input labels that have been told how to slide past every other string.

That extra rule is a half-braiding: a consistent recipe for sliding one string past every possible partner. The consistency condition is what promotes recoupling data into genuine two-dimensional bulk braiding data.

For an input fusion category \(\mathcal C\), package every object together with every consistent half-braiding. The resulting theory is the Drinfeld center \(Z(\mathcal C)\).

[Theory] Levin–Wen edge labels are input labels, while deconfined bulk quasiparticles are simple objects of \(Z(\mathcal C)\) [R018]; [R161]. For \(\mathcal C=\mathcal F\), modularity gives

\[ Z(\mathcal F)\simeq\mathcal F\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal F} =\mathrm{DFib}. \]

Hence microscopic edge labels are not a census of emergent quasiparticles. Drop the half-braiding and you are left with a grammar of meetings, not a list of bulk charges.

Commuting projectors pick both

In the ideal string-net Hamiltonian,

\[ H=-\sum_v Q_v-\sum_p B_p, \]

all local projectors commute. The ground state is assembled by local recouplings without selecting a net direction of propagation.

The center supplies every consistent over-crossing together with the reverse-braided information needed for a nonchiral bulk. This is why the construction naturally yields doubled orders [R018]; [R161].

This is a statement about this construction, not a ban on chiral phases in lattice systems. Noncommuting local Hamiltonians can realize chiral topological order. “Lattice” does not mean “doubled.” “Standard Levin–Wen commuting projector” does.

An edge that cannot sit still

At a boundary between a standalone chiral Fibonacci phase and the trivial vacuum, the nonzero net chirality obstructs a completely gapped edge [R156]; [R015]. Low-energy modes must carry the anomaly. Edge disorder may complicate them, but it cannot simply erase the net chiral energy flow while the bulk phase remains unchanged.

The doubled-Fibonacci theory is different. Opposite edge chiralities can couple and gap one another. [Theory] It admits gapped boundaries described by suitable boundary data; in one categorical description the condensable diagonal combination is built from \(\mathbf1\oplus b\) [R156].

“Admits” is the important verb. A particular termination may still be gapless because of its couplings or symmetries. A sketch with a circle around it is not a boundary condition.

A gapped doubled-Fibonacci boundary can also rearrange which charges are distinguishable or confined at that boundary. A proposal that uses holes, punctures, or boundary quasiparticles must specify its boundary type.

Which charge you can move

Consider four \(x=(\tau,\bar1)\) charges constrained to total charge \(\mathbf1\). There are two fusion paths. If \(a\) is the intermediate charge of the first pair, define

\[ |0_L\rangle:\ a=\mathbf1, \qquad |1_L\rangle:\ a=x. \]

This two-dimensional fusion space is a logical qubit. Braiding the \(x\) charges acts with the same dense braid-group representation as braiding charges in the chiral Fibonacci theory.

[Theory] Those representations can approximate arbitrary logical unitaries, up to overall phase and with standard encoding and compilation qualifications [R136]; [R015]. The \(y\) sector offers the complex-conjugate construction.

Hence an ideal doubled-Fibonacci phase can support universal topological quantum computation, provided the architecture can create, move, braid, fuse, and measure a selected chiral simple-object sector — \(x\) or \(y\) — while controlling leakage and unwanted sector mixing. The presence of the mirror sector does not cancel those gates.

Three limitations belong with that verdict.

  • The fusion rule alone is insufficient; universality uses the \(F\)- and \(R\)-data and access to the correct charge sector.

  • If hardware exposes only the diagonal charge \(b\), or forces mirror charges to move as inseparable pairs, universality does not follow from the ordinary chiral-sector argument.

  • Universal braid representations do not supply initialization, charge measurement, low thermal anyon density, or an adequate many-body gap. Those are physical requirements, not categorical corollaries.

[Theory] Turaev–Viro codes make the computational statement constructive: under suitable access to encoded surfaces and topological operations, doubled theories derived from universal modular data can implement quantum computation [R158]. This is support for the ideal-model verdict, not evidence that a proposed defect Hamiltonian realizes those operations.

Keep the four layers separate. A physical spin or transmon is a microscopic qubit.

A fusion space of several \(x\) charges can encode a logical qubit. A circuit that stores the amplitudes of that fusion space digitally emulates the doubled-Fibonacci model.

An emergent \(x\) charge requires a many-body phase whose low-energy bulk superselection sectors are those of \(\mathrm{DFib}\). Only the last case makes braiding passive geometric motion inside an intrinsic topological medium.

Twenty-seven qubits, no crystal

The mathematical distinction is settled. Its material realization is not.

[Experiment] In 2024, Xu and collaborators used 27 superconducting transmon qubits to digitally prepare a three-plaquette state of the Levin–Wen model built from Fibonacci fusion-category data, then implemented open-string, recoupling, and braid circuits [R138]. They reported average vertex- and plaquette-projector expectation values of \(0.94\) and \(0.58\) for their optimized prepared state, under the device and measurement conditions given in that paper. The target string-net is a doubled-type topological model even though the paper uses a shorter anyon label.

The same experiment explicitly states that its braids involved no Hamiltonian dynamics of quasiparticle excitations and therefore did not inherit protection from a many-body energy gap [R138]. The transmons executed gates that emulated the desired fusion-space transformations.

That is an important experimental result. It is not evidence of an intrinsic chiral Fibonacci material phase, nor of an equilibrium doubled-Fibonacci phase passively stabilized in defect matter.

[Proposal] A static defect-spin architecture based on a Levin–Wen target should therefore write \(\mathrm{DFib}\) in its requirements. It must derive a low-energy Hamiltonian with the correct center, gap, ribbon operators, and controllable sector-resolved excitations. No result cited in this chapter establishes that diamond, sapphire, silicon carbide, or another defect host currently meets those conditions.

A chiral Fibonacci target would be a different engineering program. It would need a mechanism for broken time-reversal symmetry and nonzero net chirality. It would not be obtained merely by deleting the word “doubled” from a commuting-projector string-net proposal.

Ways to get this wrong

Call every object \(\tau\). In the doubled-Fibonacci bulk, \(x\), \(y\), and \(b\) are inequivalent. Writing \(\tau\) for all three discards topological spin and fusion information.

Confuse input strings with output anyons. The two Levin–Wen edge labels \(1,\tau\) define local Hilbert-space states.

The four charges \(\mathbf1,x,y,b\) classify emergent bulk excitations. They live at different descriptive levels.

Think “doubled” means trivial. Net thermal Hall response cancels, but non-Abelian fusion spaces remain. The doubled-Fibonacci theory has four bulk sectors, total quantum dimension \(\varphi+2\), and nontrivial braiding.

Think opposite chirality cancels every gate. It cancels net chiral central charge. A braid confined to the \(x\) sector is not accompanied by a \(y\)-sector braid, so its computational action remains that of the chiral Fibonacci theory.

Assume a gappable edge is already gapped. Existence of a consistent gapped boundary does not specify the boundary Hamiltonian or its gap.

Equate a prepared wavefunction with an equilibrium phase. A circuit may prepare a small state with ideal-model correlations and may enact an ideal braid matrix.

An analog topological phase additionally requires a local Hamiltonian, a robust many-body gap, scalable bulk, and adiabatic quasiparticle motion. Digital simulation tests the model; it does not cause the processor’s microscopic excitations to become doubled-Fibonacci anyons.

Check yourself

What topological order does a standard Levin–Wen model with the Fibonacci fusion category as input produce?

The doubled-Fibonacci order \(Z(\mathcal F)\simeq\mathcal F\boxtimes\overline{\mathcal F}\), not a single chiral Fibonacci order.

Show that \(x\times y=b\) and \(b\times b=\mathbf1+x+y+b\).

Fuse the pair labels independently: \((\tau,\bar1)\times(1,\bar\tau)=(\tau,\bar\tau)=b\), and \((\tau\times\tau,\bar\tau\times\bar\tau)=(1+\tau,\bar1+\bar\tau)=\mathbf1+x+y+b\).

Show that \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{DFib}}=\varphi+2\).

\(\mathcal D^2=1+\varphi^2+\varphi^2+\varphi^4=(1+\varphi^2)^2\), so \(\mathcal D=1+\varphi^2\). Then \(\varphi^2=\varphi+1\) gives \(1+\varphi^2=\varphi+2\).

What fails if hardware exposes only the diagonal charge \(b\)?

The ordinary chiral-sector universality argument does not apply. The fusion rule of \(b\) is not the fusion rule of \(\tau\), and a braid of inseparable pairs acts as \(U\otimes U^*\), not as \(U\).

What fails if a digital braid is offered as evidence of an intrinsic doubled-Fibonacci phase?

The braid demonstrates controlled emulation of the model’s state and operations. It does not establish a protecting many-body Hamiltonian or emergent quasiparticles.

Why is the doubled-Fibonacci theory nonchiral but nontrivial?

The two sectors have opposite chiral central charges, so the net value vanishes, while their non-Abelian fusion and braiding data remain.

A Levin–Wen model with the Fibonacci fusion category as input targets \(\mathrm{DFib}\). Its four bulk charges are \(\mathbf1,x,y,b\).

The charges \(x\) and \(y\) carry opposite chiral Fibonacci braid data. The doubled edge can be gapped even though a single chiral edge cannot.

Ideal universal computation is available by controlling one chiral charge sector, not merely by observing the fusion rule. Chapter 20 will use those distinctions to audit what programmable hardware has actually prepared, fused, braided, and protected.

  • [R160] M. Müger, “From subfactors to categories and topology II: The quantum double of tensor categories and subfactors,” Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 180, 159–219 (2003). DOI: 10.1016/S0022-4049(02)00248-7; arXiv: math/0111205.

Chapter 20 — An actor playing a king

An actor walks onstage in a crown. He speaks the king’s lines.

He makes the king’s choices. The audience follows the plot.

After the curtain he takes the crown off. He is still an actor.

The castle is still plywood.

A programmable chip can do the same job with anyons. It can hold the labels vacuum and \(\tau\).

It can apply the braid matrix. It can return the fusion histogram the theory wrote down.

That is a real experiment. It is not a crystal whose own energy landscape is those anyons.

Four things that look alike

When a paper says “we braided Fibonacci anyons,” four different objects may be hiding under that one sentence.

The first object is the actual two-level thing in the fridge: a superconducting circuit bit, a trapped ion, a nuclear spin in a drop of chloroform. Nobody braided that object around another object. It sat on a chip, or in a trap, and waited for a pulse.

The second object is a pattern of several of those bits that we choose to read as a charge. The charge lives in the bookkeeping. The fridge still contains transmons, or ions, or nuclei.

The third object is a snapshot of the whole register. At one instant the entanglement can be real, the loops can have the right answers, and the fusion table can match the model.

The snapshot was written by a circuit. It starts rotting the moment the circuit stops.

The fourth object is an excitation the material itself would produce if you just cooled it. No circuit standing over the wavefunction with a script. The energy landscape does the selecting.

Those four pictures need four names, or the next paper will glue them together. The hardware bit is a physical qubit.

A pattern of several bits, read through a target model, is an encoded anyonic degree of freedom. A snapshot with the right model observables is a digitally prepared topological wavefunction.

An excitation of the laboratory Hamiltonian is an intrinsic anyon.

The name encoded is worth keeping because it marks the gap between “the theory is on the chip” and “the chip is the theory.”

[Experiment] Superconducting and trapped-ion processors have prepared wavefunctions with Fibonacci, finite-group quantum-double, and twist-defect structure. They have also run circuit operations that stand for fusion and braiding [R162]; [R132]; [R163]; [R164]; [R138]; [R165]; [R140]; [R166]. None of that shows that the processor’s own Hamiltonian has a Fibonacci phase, a protecting many-body gap, or thermally stable quasiparticles.

A future defect array can still be useful as a digital processor even if it never becomes Fibonacci matter. Digital success is a real capability. It is not the same capability as a material that hosts the anyons by itself.

Braid two, then ask how they fuse

Let \(\mathbf 1\) denote vacuum and \(\tau\) a Fibonacci charge, with

\[ \tau\times\tau=\mathbf 1+\tau . \]

Four \(\tau\) anyons whose total charge is vacuum encode a two-dimensional logical space. Define \(|\bar 0\rangle\) as the state in which the first pair and the last pair each fuse to \(\mathbf 1\). Define \(|\bar 1\rangle\) as the state in which those pairs each fuse to \(\tau\), while all four still have total charge \(\mathbf 1\).

Create the pairs from vacuum, so the initial state is \(|\bar 0\rangle\). Exchange the middle two anyons once. In a common phase convention, the braid generator \(\sigma_2\) gives

\[ \sigma_2|\bar 0\rangle = \phi^{-1}e^{4\pi i/5}|\bar 0\rangle + \phi^{-1/2}e^{-3\pi i/5}|\bar 1\rangle, \]

where

\[ \phi=\frac{1+\sqrt 5}{2} \]

is the golden ratio. The phases depend on chirality and convention. The probabilities in this experiment do not. Fuse the original pairs and measure their channels:

\[ P(\mathbf 1)=\left|\phi^{-1}\right|^2=\phi^{-2}\approx0.382, \qquad P(\tau)=\left|\phi^{-1/2}\right|^2=\phi^{-1}\approx0.618. \]

The normalization works because \(\phi^2=\phi+1\), so \(\phi^{-2}+\phi^{-1}=1\). The ratio is especially convenient:

\[ \frac{P(\tau)}{P(\mathbf 1)}=\phi . \]

Hence a single braid of the middle pair, followed by fusion of the original pairs, must return the golden ratio. That is the logic behind the fusion signature used in recent superconducting experiments [R138]; [R165]. It is more informative than merely applying a precomputed \(2\times2\) braid matrix, because creation, motion in an encoded string-net, and fusion readout are all represented on a spatial many-qubit register.

What fails if you keep only the final \(2\times2\) matrix and skip the spatial register? You can still match the histogram. You have not shown that intermediate states represented spatially separated quasiparticles.

The digital implementation still has a mundane circuit underneath:

initialize physical qubits
|
prepare target vacuum wavefunction U_prep
|
create two encoded anyon pairs U_create
|
move/exchange middle pair U_braid
|
change to a fusion basis U_fuse
|
measure physical qubits ----------> fusion histogram

The anyon worldlines describe the logical action of these gates. No transmon literally walks around another transmon.

A circuit is not a cooling step

Let \(N\) be the number of physical qubits. A digital experiment typically begins with the product state \(|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\) and applies a compiled circuit

\[ |\psi_{\mathrm{prep}}\rangle =U_{\mathrm{prep}}|0\rangle^{\otimes N}. \]

The target may be the ground state \(|G\rangle\) of an ideal Hamiltonian

\[ H_{\mathrm{target}}=-\sum_v Q_v-\sum_p B_p, \]

where \(Q_v\) enforces an allowed fusion or branching rule at vertex \(v\), and \(B_p\) enforces the desired flux around plaquette \(p\). For a Fibonacci Levin–Wen model, \(Q_v\) can involve three edge qubits and \(B_p\) can involve many qubits around a plaquette [R138].

The circuit can be exact, variationally synthesized, measurement-assisted, or adaptive. The experiment then measures quantities such as \(\langle Q_v\rangle\), \(\langle B_p\rangle\), Wilson loops, or entanglement combinations.

Agreement says that the prepared state resembles the target. It does not say that the laboratory Hamiltonian equals \(H_{\mathrm{target}}\).

In equilibrium preparation, by contrast, one would engineer \(H_{\mathrm{physical}}\approx H_{\mathrm{target}}\), cool below its gap, and let the Hamiltonian select and stabilize the phase. That stronger test belongs to Chapter 21.

Suppose the circuit is exact, so \(|\psi_{\mathrm{prep}}\rangle=|G\rangle\). The snapshot can still be perfect.

The idle Hamiltonian of the chip can still be something else. A prepared ground-state wavefunction is not a phase.

Moving a label with gates

An open string operator \(W_a(\gamma)\) of charge type \(a\) acts along a path \(\gamma\). Ideally it creates a pair of charges at the endpoints while leaving the intervening region locally in the code space:

\[ |a,\bar a;\gamma\rangle=W_a(\gamma)|G\rangle. \]

For digital string nets, a local rewrite of the graph can change how fusion is parenthesized, or slide a string, without changing the topological content. That rewrite is an \(F\)-move. Every compiled braid on a string-net is mostly a pile of these local rewrites, not a transmon taking a walk.

An \(R\)-move supplies the exchange phase when strings cross. Both moves become multi-qubit gates and are finally decomposed into native one- and two-qubit operations.

A compiled braid is therefore a product

\[ U_{\mathrm{braid}} =U_mU_{m-1}\cdots U_2U_1, \]

where each \(U_j\) is a local graph deformation, string extension, or crossing operation. The order matters. Showing that two such products give different final observables is the operational signature of non-Abelian behavior.

What fails if two compiled words that differ by a local deformation give different histograms? Then the hardware is not implementing the topological move you named. It is implementing some other circuit that happens to share a label.

Fusion is a measurement

The symbol \(a\times b=\sum_c N_{ab}^{c}c\) lists allowed total charges \(c\). A fusion experiment must resolve which channel occurred. Let \(\Pi_c^{(ab)}\) be the projector onto channel \(c\) for the chosen pair. For density matrix \(\rho\),

\[ P(c)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho\,\Pi_c^{(ab)}\right). \]

Hardware rarely measures \(\Pi_c^{(ab)}\) directly. Instead, a circuit maps the fusion basis to computational-basis bit strings, after which physical-qubit readout estimates \(P(c)\).

Other experiments measure stabilizers or a nonlocal string whose eigenvalue identifies the charge. Error mitigation can improve the estimate.

It must be reported separately from raw protection.

Hence a fusion histogram is a statement about a measurement circuit and a readout channel, not automatically a statement about an anyon the material produced.

Four kinds of “protected”

Four mechanisms get sold under the same adjective.

First: the material’s own energy gap slaps your hand if you wander off the code space. Local perturbations split logical states only weakly as the system grows.

Nobody has to keep typing corrections. That is passive protection, and it is the strongest mode in this chapter.

The Hamiltonian is doing the work, not the control software.

Second: you keep measuring syndromes, decoding, and correcting. The protection is real. It is also a job. That is active error correction.

Third: you run the experiment several noisy ways and guess what a quieter machine would have said. Dynamical decoupling, readout correction, zero-noise extrapolation, twirling, and postselection all live here.

They improve an estimate. They do not create a protected logical memory.

Fourth: inside the ideal model, some selected pretend-errors act as a global phase. That demonstrates the model’s algebra. It does not make the hardware immune to its own uncontrolled noise.

The 2024 Fibonacci experiment states the point unusually clearly: its braids used no Hamiltonian dynamics of quasiparticle excitations and therefore lacked the topological protection supplied by an energy gap [R138]. The 2025 IBM experiment likewise required deep circuits and composite error mitigation [R165].

A correct final braid is still not enough by itself. Suppose calibration produces a direct unitary \(V\) equal to the desired logical braid on the encoded two-dimensional subspace.

Measuring the expected fusion probabilities proves that \(V\) was implemented there. It does not prove that intermediate states represented spatially separated quasiparticles, nor that local path deformations leave the operation unchanged.

Stronger evidence combines several tests: model constraints before and after the operation, localized endpoint excitations, path or order dependence, fusion-channel readout, noncommuting braid sequences, and negative controls. Even that package establishes a digital realization unless a native Hamiltonian and protection test are also present.

What the laboratory actually has

The table is current through 24 August 2026. It includes direct Fibonacci demonstrations and the closest non-Abelian digital comparators, because “non-Abelian,” “universal,” and “Fibonacci” are not interchangeable. Qubit counts distinguish the active experimental register from the total chip where the paper makes that distinction.

Date and primary source | Hardware and qubits | Target model and preparation | Fusion measurement | Braid operation and evidence | Protection mode | Intrinsic-versus-emulated verdict | |

May 2023, Xu et al. [R162] | Programmable square-lattice superconducting processor; up to 68 transmons | Toric/surface-code states with twist defects; finite-depth gate circuits prepare stabilizer ground states | Stabilizers and logical/string observables distinguish \(\sigma\times\sigma=\mathbf1+\varepsilon\) channels | Pauli-string operations and graph deformations implement Ising-type logical gates and noncommuting/projective braids | No passive gap; circuit preparation and readout mitigation | Emulated projective Ising anyons, not Fibonacci and not native transmon excitations | |

May 2023, Andersen et al. [R132] | Google superconducting processor; 25 transmons in a \(5\times5\) register | Generalized surface-code stabilizer state; four CZ layers prepare the ground state | Destructive stabilizer and nonlocal Pauli-string measurements reveal vacuum or fermion after fusing twist vertices | Local two-qubit Clifford graph-deformation gates move and braid degree-3 vertices; fusion after crossing reveals changed fermion parity | No repeated error correction and no passive gap; paper identifies future error correction as necessary | Encoded twist defects with projective Ising statistics; spatial digital braid, but not intrinsic or Fibonacci | |

July 2023, Fan et al.

July 2025, Minev et al.

Two trends matter. First, the hardware has progressed from direct matrix emulation on two nuclear spins to spatial many-qubit string nets and adaptive non-Abelian wavefunctions.

Second, the interpretation has not crossed the digital–intrinsic boundary. Larger registers and better topological observables do not, by themselves, change what Hamiltonian the laboratory built.

The two superconducting Fibonacci experiments are complementary. Xu et al. used 27 transmons to represent a three-plaquette fixed-point string-net state and measured entanglement and braid/fusion data [R138].

Minev et al. reduced the local graph resources, used exact graph moves, and made fusion readout economical, but relied on very deep circuits and extensive mitigation [R165]. Both are significant experiments.

Neither is a passively protected topological computer.

The 2026 ion results broaden the lesson. Lo et al. obtained universality from \(S_3\) anyons by combining braid operations with fusion measurements [R140].

That is not the Fibonacci claim that braiding alone densely generates logical gates.

Hayata, Hidaka, and Kikuchi encoded the Fibonacci fusion algebra in a non-Abelian lattice-gauge simulation and pushed long sequences of \(F\)-moves, but did not braid or fuse localized anyon pairs [R166]. “Contains Fibonacci mathematics” is therefore a wider category than “demonstrates Fibonacci fusion and braiding.”

Ways to get this wrong

Call every non-Abelian object Fibonacci. Ising twist defects obey \(\sigma\times\sigma=\mathbf1+\varepsilon\), not \(\tau\times\tau=\mathbf1+\tau\). \(D_4\) and \(S_3\) quantum doubles have still richer charge sets.

They are valuable comparators, but their braid representations and computational power differ. A universal protocol using \(S_3\) braiding and fusion is not evidence of Fibonacci braid universality.

Treat a snapshot as a stable phase. A finite-depth or adaptive circuit can prepare a state with target stabilizers and long-range entanglement.

Once the circuit stops, the hardware evolves under its own control and noise Hamiltonian. Without a sustained target Hamiltonian or repeated error correction, the state is not passively stabilized.

Confuse a better estimate with a better memory. Zero-noise extrapolation estimates a hypothetical low-noise observable from several noisy runs.

Readout mitigation inverts a calibrated measurement channel. Postselection discards detected bad shots.

None produces a logical qubit that remains correct in an individual run. They improve scientific inference, not stored quantum information.

Ask “protected against what?” The NMR experiment showed robustness against a programmed class of local disturbances inside its encoded model [R163]. That is a legitimate test of a theoretical invariant.

It does not mean the liquid-state nuclear spins were protected against RF miscalibration, relaxation, or dephasing; the measured gate error was in fact dominated by ordinary hardware decoherence [R163]. Always ask: protected against which physical errors, for how long, and relative to what unencoded control?

Infer a material from a compiled answer. A direct logical unitary can reproduce the same final fusion histogram as a spatial braid.

Better demonstrations localize endpoints, move them with local operations, compare braid orders, and perform fusion or interferometric readout. Still, digital locality is programmed locality.

Intrinsic emergence additionally requires the physical Hamiltonian to generate and stabilize the quasiparticle sector.

Ignore how small the chip is. Three plaquettes can display exact algebraic relations, but cannot establish asymptotic degeneracy splitting, a correlation length well below system size, a stable phase under generic perturbations, or a logical-error rate that improves with code distance. Small systems are excellent microscopes for topological data and poor rulers for thermodynamic protection.

Check yourself

What is the clean operational sequence for a digital braid experiment?

Prepare a target vacuum wavefunction, create encoded anyon pairs, move/exchange them with compiled local gates, map to a fusion basis, and measure the fusion channel.

Show that \(P(\tau)/P(\mathbf1)=\phi\) after braiding the middle pair of four Fibonacci anyons.

The braid amplitudes have squared magnitudes \(\phi^{-2}\) and \(\phi^{-1}\). Their ratio is \(\phi\), and \(\phi^2=\phi+1\) makes the two probabilities add to one.

Did the superconducting experiments contain physically intrinsic Fibonacci anyons?

No. Ordinary transmon qubits digitally represented doubled-Fibonacci string-net states and operations. The experiments did not realize a native Fibonacci Hamiltonian with passive protection.

What fails if adaptive measurement and feed-forward is called passive?

Adaptive circuits can prepare or actively maintain a state. Passive protection comes from the physical Hamiltonian and gap without continual corrective intervention. The label then names the wrong agent.

What fails if every non-Abelian digital result is filed under Fibonacci?

Ising, \(D_4\), and \(S_3\) have different fusion rules, braid representations, and computational power. A universal \(S_3\) protocol that uses braiding and fusion is not evidence of Fibonacci braid universality.

What can a defect-spin array borrow from these results without becoming topological matter?

State-preparation circuits, encoded fusion spaces, compiled \(F/R\) moves, stabilizer or Wilson-loop measurements, adaptive feedback, and error-mitigation methods.

You can now read a braid paper and ask which of the four objects it actually built. Next we replace the compiled preparation \(U_{\mathrm{prep}}|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\) with the stronger demand that the laboratory Hamiltonian itself look like the target.
