Chapter 21 — A recipe versus a landscape

A recipe is a list of moves. Cream the butter.

Add the eggs. Bake for forty minutes.

When you follow it, a cake appears. The cake is real.

If you leave the kitchen, the recipe does not keep the cake from going stale.

A landscape is not a list. Water sits at the bottom of a valley because every nearby step is uphill.

You can walk away. The water stays.

The ground is doing the work, not a cook standing over the pot.

A circuit that prepares a toric-code state is a recipe. A crystal whose own energy prefers that state is a valley.

Both can put the same wavefunction on the table. Only one of them is still doing the job after you stop typing gates.

Two jobs with the same snapshot

The last chapter was the recipe. A processor applies timed gates, writes a snapshot, and measures it. That is digital simulation. The hardware is following instructions about a model, not becoming the model.

The stronger claim is that the material itself is the valley. Local interactions stay on.

The desired long-range-entangled sector sits lower than everything nearby. Excitations cost a fixed energy.

Fabrication errors do not flatten the valley. The environment does not hand out enough anyons, and move them far enough, to enact a logical operator.

That is an analog realization. The hardware is the landscape, not a script about the landscape.

A defect spin can still be a physical qubit. Several defects can still encode a logical bit.

A processor can still write a Fibonacci-like snapshot. None of those facts says an undriven array sits in a topologically ordered phase.

The energy landscape of a closed quantum system is a Hermitian operator \(H\), the Hamiltonian. Every later inequality in this chapter is a statement about \(H\), not about one pretty wavefunction.

The analog target is a family of materials

\[ H_{\mathrm{physical}}=H_{\mathrm{topological}}+V, \]

where the unwanted term \(V\) is local enough and weak enough that it does not change the phase. An encoded logical qubit may live in either a digital snapshot or an analog Hamiltonian. Emergent anyons and equilibrium topological order require the Hamiltonian.

Only then can one discuss passive protection supplied by energy and locality, rather than by a controller that keeps measuring syndromes.

Four edges of one square

Put one qubit on each edge of a square lattice. Let \(X_e\) and \(Z_e\) denote Pauli operators on edge \(e\). For every vertex \(v\) and plaquette \(p\), define

\[ A_v=\prod_{e\ni v}X_e, \qquad B_p=\prod_{e\in\partial p}Z_e. \]

Each product contains four edges on the square lattice. A star and a plaquette share either zero or two edges, so all \(A_v\) and \(B_p\) commute. The static toric-code Hamiltonian is

\[ H_{\mathrm{TC}}=-J_s\sum_v A_v-J_p\sum_p B_p, \tag{21.1} \]

where \(J_s>0\) and \(J_p>0\) are energies, measured in joules (J) or electronvolts (eV). A ground state obeys \(A_v=B_p=+1\) for every term. On a torus, the ideal model has four ground states distinguished by noncontractible loop operators [R030]. [Theory]

Now isolate one plaquette, label its edges \(1,2,3,4\), and define \(B=Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4\). During a digital time step of duration \(\delta t\), the target evolution from the plaquette term \(-J_pB\) is

\[ U_p(\delta t)=\exp\!\left(+i\frac{J_p\delta t}{\hbar}B\right), \tag{21.2} \]

where \(\hbar\) has units J·s. The exponent is dimensionless because \(J_p\delta t/\hbar\) has units \((\mathrm{J})(\mathrm{s})/(\mathrm{J\,s})=1\).

A gate processor can synthesize this four-body evolution using parity computation. Let

\[ W=\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\rightarrow4} \operatorname{CNOT}_{2\rightarrow4} \operatorname{CNOT}_{3\rightarrow4}. \]

Conjugation gives \(W^\dagger Z_4W=Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4=B\). With \(R_z(\phi)=\exp(-i\phi Z/2)\), choose \(\phi=-2J_p\delta t/\hbar\). Then

\[ W^\dagger R_z(\phi)_4W =\exp\!\left(+i\frac{J_p\delta t}{\hbar}B\right). \tag{21.3} \]

Repeating corresponding gate blocks for all stars and plaquettes implements evolution under Eq. (21.1).

At the exactly commuting point the ideal factors commute, so this particular decomposition has no Trotter error. Real gates still have control errors, decoherence, and an idle Hamiltonian that is not Eq.

(21.1).

Compare that circuit with a material containing a permanent term \(-J_pB\). If \(b=\pm1\) is the measured eigenvalue of \(B\), its energy contribution is \(-J_pb\).

Changing \(b\) from \(+1\) to \(-1\) costs \(2J_p\). A local \(X_e\) anticommutes with the two adjacent plaquettes, so in a periodic bulk it creates two magnetic anyons and costs \(4J_p\).

Similarly, a local \(Z_e\) creates two electric anyons and costs \(4J_s\). Thus the periodic model’s lowest bulk pair-creation gap is

\[ \Delta_{\mathrm{pair}}=4\min(J_s,J_p), \tag{21.4} \]

while the energy assigned to one well-separated anyon is \(\epsilon_a=2J_s\) or \(2J_p\). Boundaries can permit a single excitation, so one must state which gap convention and geometry are being quoted [R030]; [R141]. [Theory]

Hence the circuit and the static Hamiltonian can produce the same unitary or the same state. Only the static Hamiltonian supplies the energy penalty continuously. If the circuit prepares \(|\psi_{\mathrm{TC}}\rangle\) and then the hardware idles under a trivial \(H_{\mathrm{idle}}\), the target state was prepared, not made into an equilibrium phase.

The hill a local shovel must climb

Order the eigenenergies of the full interacting Hamiltonian as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). If the topological ground manifold occupies the lowest \(q\) levels, define the bulk many-body gap

\[ \Delta(L)=E_q(L)-E_{q-1}(L), \qquad \Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}=\liminf_{L\rightarrow\infty}\Delta(L), \tag{21.5} \]

where \(L\) is the sample’s linear size in metres and \(\Delta\) is an energy. Material topological order requires \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}>0\), not merely a nonzero level spacing in a small cluster.

That number \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\) is the many-body gap. The name is worth keeping because it is a property of the whole interacting spectrum in the large-sample limit, not of one defect or one cluster. A defect’s optical gap, a cluster’s leakage gap, and the collective topological gap are three different numbers.

The gap sets a microscopic response time \(\tau_\Delta=\hbar/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\). Slow, weak changes compared with this scale can avoid exciting the bulk. They still need not preserve the logical state if they split the ground manifold or move real anyons.

What fails if you quote only a two-site splitting and call it \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\)? You have measured a cluster, not the thermodynamic gap above the topological manifold.

A shove that stays nearby

Write a lattice Hamiltonian as

\[ H=\sum_X h_X, \]

where \(X\) is a bounded set of nearby sites and \(h_X\) acts only on those sites. “Local” normally means finite range or sufficiently fast decay with the diameter of \(X\). It does not mean that the global operator norm \(\|H\|\) is small.

That norm generally grows with the number of sites.

For an unwanted perturbation \(V=\sum_X V_X\), a useful local strength is

\[ g_{\mathrm{loc}}=\max_i\sum_{X\ni i}\|V_X\|, \tag{21.6} \]

which has units of energy. The engineering ratio is \(g_{\mathrm{loc}}/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\), not \(\|V\|/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\).

That per-site number is the local strength. An extensive perturbation can look huge in the global norm while remaining weak at every site — and one strong local defect can be dangerous despite a small average.

Stability theorems prove that broad classes of local commuting-projector Hamiltonians retain separated spectral bands and exponentially narrow ground bands below a nonzero local perturbation threshold, subject to topological-order conditions [R142]. [Theory] The theorem does not supply one universal threshold such as “ten percent” for every material.

Defect arrays make locality subtle. Dipolar interactions fall as \(1/r^3\), rather than ending at a chosen neighbor.

In spatial dimension \(D\), the shell sum scales as \(\int dr\,r^{D-1}/r^\alpha\), so it converges at long distance only for \(\alpha>D\). A \(1/r^3\) tail is summable in two dimensions, but that fact alone does not put it under every finite-range stability theorem.

The real tail, crosstalk, and disorder must be retained or bounded, not erased with a hopeful nearest-neighbor sketch.

How far a local change is felt

For local observables \(O_i\) and \(O_j\) separated by distance \(r\), define their connected ground-state correlation

\[ C(r)=\langle O_iO_j\rangle-\langle O_i\rangle\langle O_j\rangle. \]

A gapped short-range system generally has

\[ |C(r)|\le C_0e^{-r/\xi}, \tag{21.7} \]

where \(C_0\) carries the observable’s units and \(\xi\) is the correlation length in metres [R167]. [Theory] It is the reach of ordinary local questions, not the length of the nonlocal entanglement that topological order is allowed to keep.

A dimensional estimate is \(\xi\sim\hbar v_{\mathrm{LR}}/\Delta\), where \(v_{\mathrm{LR}}\) is a characteristic information-propagation velocity in m/s: \((\mathrm{J\,s})(\mathrm{m/s})/\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{m}\).

Finite \(\xi\) does not contradict topological order. Ordinary local correlators can decay rapidly while the ground state contains nonlocal entanglement and loop information.

At the exact toric-code fixed point, many connected local correlations vanish beyond zero range. Generic perturbations make \(\xi\) finite rather than destroying the phase.

The practical requirement is

\[ L\gg\xi, \tag{21.8} \]

and, for localized non-Abelian anyons, their separation \(R\gg\xi\). Otherwise their topological sectors overlap appreciably and “nonlocal encoding” is mostly a label on a small device.

Two ground states that look the same up close

Topological ground states are locally indistinguishable in the thermodynamic limit: a bounded local operator cannot reliably tell which logical sector the system occupies. Weak local perturbations then dress the states rather than immediately selecting one sector [R142]. This is zero-temperature phase stability, not a lifetime theorem.

On a finite torus, virtual anyons can wind around a noncontractible cycle and annihilate. The process couples logical sectors. For a gapped local phase, its characteristic splitting has the form

\[ \delta E_0(L)\sim C\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}e^{-L/\xi}, \tag{21.9} \]

up to model-dependent powers, paths, and coefficients. Fusion-state splitting for anyons separated by \(R\) is similarly exponentially small in \(R/\xi\) [R015]. [Theory] Here \(C\) is dimensionless, so \(\delta E_0\) has energy units.

During storage time \(t_{\mathrm{store}}\), this splitting produces a relative phase of order \(\delta E_0t_{\mathrm{store}}/\hbar\). A necessary condition is

\[ \frac{\delta E_0t_{\mathrm{store}}}{\hbar}\ll1. \tag{21.10} \]

For controlled adiabatic motion, a familiar ideal window is \(\hbar/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\ll t_{\mathrm{op}}\ll\hbar/\delta E_0\): slow relative to bulk excitation, fast relative to resolving the unwanted splitting [R015]. [Theory] Real control adds diabatic errors, noise, and timing constraints.

What fails if you treat \(\delta E_0=0\) at finite \(L\)? The relative phase still accumulates. Over a long enough \(t_{\mathrm{store}}\) the sectors are resolved, and “exact degeneracy” was a finite-size slogan.

Heat keeps handing out anyons

At nonzero temperature, the environment keeps creating excitations.

At temperature \(T\) in kelvin, a weakly coupled equilibrium system has density matrix

\[ \rho_T=\frac{e^{-H/(k_BT)}}{\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-H/(k_BT)})}, \]

where Boltzmann’s constant \(k_B\) has units J/K. A dilute anyon species of energy \(\epsilon_a\) has an equilibrium occupation proportional to

\[ n_a\sim \frac{g_a}{a^2}e^{-\epsilon_a/(k_BT)} \tag{21.11} \]

in two dimensions, where \(a\) is the lattice spacing and \(g_a\) is a dimensionless degeneracy factor. This expression is only the dilute, noninteracting estimate.

The expected number also grows with area. Thus \(k_BT\ll\epsilon_a\) is necessary for suppression but does not guarantee an anyon-free macroscopic sample [R141]; [R169]; [R143].

[Theory]

As a scale exercise, suppose — not claim — that \(J_s=J_p=h\times1\,\mathrm{GHz}\). Since \(h\times1\,\mathrm{GHz}/k_B\approx48\,\mathrm{mK}\), one anyon costs \(2J\approx k_B\times96\,\mathrm{mK}\), and a bulk pair costs \(4J\approx k_B\times192\,\mathrm{mK}\).

At \(T=20\,\mathrm{mK}\), the pair Boltzmann factor is \(e^{-192/20}\approx6.8\times10^{-5}\), but the single-anyon density factor is \(e^{-96/20}\approx8.2\times10^{-3}\). The arithmetic is favorable and still not magic: area, bath spectral density, and motion determine the logical error rate.

In two-dimensional toric-code-like memories, the environment can create an anyon pair for a fixed energy and then move one anyon across the sample without climbing a taller hill. A large sample is therefore not automatically a better passive memory.

Creation is only half a fault

Once an anyon exists, local hopping can extend its error string. If motion is diffusive in two dimensions with diffusion constant \(D\) in m\(^2\)/s, its root-mean-square distance after time \(t\) is

\[ \ell_{\mathrm{diff}}(t)=\sqrt{4Dt}, \tag{21.12} \]

which has units \(\sqrt{(\mathrm{m^2/s})(\mathrm{s})}=\mathrm{m}\). A code of distance \(d\) and spacing \(a\) needs, roughly, \(\ell_{\mathrm{move}}(t_{\mathrm{store}})\ll da\), together with a sufficiently low creation rate.

Static disorder can Anderson-localize ideal toric-code defects, giving wavefunctions that decay over a localization length \(\xi_{\mathrm{loc}}\) [R170]. [Theory] [Numerics] This can slow coherent propagation.

It does not raise the creation gap, and a thermal bath can supply inelastic hops between localized states. At finite density, anyon interactions also invalidate a one-particle localization argument.

Hence localization is a kinetic aid to be demonstrated under the actual noise model, not a synonym for topological protection. Deliberate pinning also conflicts with operations that require controlled anyon motion.

What fails if you treat localization as a gap? Creation remains cheap. A bath can still hop the anyon from well to well. The energy barrier never grew.

What is actually in the fridge

A fabricated defect array has more than the target Hamiltonian:

\[ H_{\mathrm{lab}}=H_{\mathrm{target}}+V_{\mathrm{static}}+H_{\mathrm{drive}}(t) +H_{\mathrm{bath}}+H_{\mathrm{system\text{-}bath}}. \tag{21.13} \]

The terms represent fabrication disorder and unwanted couplings, time-dependent control, environmental modes, and their coupling to the spins. An analog claim must survive the first correction and quantify the last two. Turning on drives that Floquet-engineer an effective Hamiltonian can be valuable, but then heating, micromotion, calibration, and drive failure belong in the protection claim.

A persuasive material demonstration would not stop at preparing a target state.

It would establish a bulk gap and its size scaling; show that local observables cannot distinguish candidate ground sectors beyond finite-size corrections; measure nonlocal loop or braiding data; and demonstrate that weak local perturbations do not close the gap or change the topological data. Thermal measurements must separately estimate excitation creation and transport.

No single finite-device signature proves the thermodynamic phase.

For defect-cluster architectures, \(H_{\mathrm{physical}}\approx H_{\mathrm{string\text{-}net}}\) remains a [Proposal] until the derived microscopic terms, corrections, gap, and diagnostics are supplied. Agreement between a programmed circuit and target fusion data is evidence for control and simulation, not evidence that the undriven material has emergent anyons.

Immortality is a taller claim

A self-correcting quantum memory has a storage lifetime that grows without bound with system size at fixed nonzero temperature, without active syndrome measurement and feedback [R169]. That is stronger than a long lifetime in one finite sample.

The ordinary two-dimensional toric code has a constant energy barrier. Create an anyon pair for a fixed cost, move one endpoint across the lattice with no additional growing energy cost, then annihilate the pair.

The resulting string can be a logical operator. Under the assumptions of geometrically local two-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians, the Bravyi–Terhal no-go theorem proves an \(O(1)\) energy barrier, ruling out conventional self-correction in that class [R168].

[Theory] This theorem is powerful but not a license to make claims about every non-Abelian, long-range, driven, or nonequilibrium model.

Accordingly, a gapped 2D topological phase can suppress local matrix elements, exponentially reduce finite-size splitting, and lower thermal anyon density, yet still need active error correction for arbitrarily long storage. Analyses of the toric code coupled to thermal reservoirs likewise distinguish stability against static perturbations from thermal stability [R143]. [Theory] “Passive protection” should therefore be reported as a measured improvement over specified time, temperature, size, and bath — not as an unqualified promise of immortality.

A useful necessary-condition sheet is

\[ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}>0,\qquad L/\xi\gg1,\\ &g_{\mathrm{loc}}/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}<c_{\mathrm{stab}},\\ &k_BT/\epsilon_a\ll1,\\ &\delta E_0t_{\mathrm{store}}/\hbar\ll1,\\ &\ell_{\mathrm{move}}(t_{\mathrm{store}})\ll da. \end{aligned}} \tag{21.14} \]

Here \(c_{\mathrm{stab}}\) is a model-dependent dimensionless stability threshold. These inequalities are necessary, not jointly sufficient. One must also count creation sites, include leakage out of encoded clusters, establish the target topological data, and model the bath.

Ways to get this wrong

A prepared ground-state wavefunction is not a phase. A phase is a stable property of a Hamiltonian family and its low-energy sector, not one state produced by a pulse sequence.

A single-particle or cluster gap is not the topological gap. The required \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\) is the many-body gap above the topological manifold after all effective corrections are included.

Global perturbation norm is the wrong criterion. An extensive perturbation can have large \(\|V\|\) while remaining weak per site. Conversely, one strong local defect can be dangerous despite a small average.

Finite correlation length is not short-range entanglement. Topological phases have short-ranged ordinary connected correlations but long-range entanglement.

Exponential splitting is not exact degeneracy. At finite \(L\), \(\delta E_0\) is generally nonzero and matters over long enough time.

Localization is not a gap. Localization slows motion; it does not prevent thermal creation and may fail under bath-assisted or interacting dynamics.

Perturbative stability is not thermal self-correction. The former concerns a weak static change of Hamiltonian near zero temperature. The latter concerns open-system dynamics for growing size at nonzero temperature.

Active digital correction is not passive material protection. Useful error correction remains useful. The category label is what changes.

Check yourself

A circuit exactly implements \(e^{-iH_{\mathrm{TC}}t/\hbar}\). Has it realized an analog toric-code phase?

No. The idle physical Hamiltonian must itself lie in the phase; a timed gate sequence implements dynamics but need not supply an equilibrium energy landscape.

Show that a local \(X_e\) on the periodic toric code costs \(4J_p\).

\(X_e\) anticommutes with the two adjacent plaquettes. Each flipped plaquette changes its energy by \(2J_p\), so the pair costs \(4J_p\).

What fails if you use \(\|V\|\) instead of \(g_{\mathrm{loc}}\)?

\(\|V\|\) usually grows with array size even when every site remains weakly perturbed. The engineering ratio then looks fatal while the local theory is still in the phase — or, conversely, one strong defect is hidden by a small average.

Show that if \(J_s=J_p=h\times1\,\mathrm{GHz}\), the pair Boltzmann factor at \(T=20\,\mathrm{mK}\) is about \(6.8\times10^{-5}\).

\(h\times1\,\mathrm{GHz}/k_B\approx48\,\mathrm{mK}\), so a pair costs \(4J\approx k_B\times192\,\mathrm{mK}\) and \(e^{-192/20}\approx6.8\times10^{-5}\).

What fails if \(k_BT\ll\Delta_{\mathrm{pair}}\) is taken as passive fault tolerance?

The number of creation sites, the bath, anyon mobility, code geometry, and the constant energy barrier can still produce logical errors. Diluteness is not emptiness, and a large sample is not automatically safer.

What does the 2D stabilizer no-go theorem actually rule out?

A growing energy barrier — and hence conventional self-correction — within its assumptions of geometrically local two-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians. It does not classify every conceivable topological material.

You can now tell a compiled circuit from a Hamiltonian in the phase, and you have a short list of inequalities that phase still has to satisfy. Next we ask whether a microscopic defect Hamiltonian actually produces the required low-energy terms — and how large the leftover corrections become.

Part IX — Engineering topology from defect clusters

The expensive states still whisper. Two-body crystals try to fake four-body rules. Pretty arrows get audited.

Chapter 22 — The expensive states still whisper

A cluster has more states than you will keep. The coupling that joins two clusters does not stay inside the pair you came for: it mixes that pair with expensive levels and returns. The return trip is a new operator on the cheap pair.

Suppose the cheap states sit at energy zero, the expensive ones sit at least \(\Delta\) above them, and the mixing has scale \(g\), with \(|g|/\Delta\) small. Then any leftover operator that starts cheap and ends cheap must use the mixing at least twice. The first such term has scale \(g^2/\Delta\).

That leftover is the working Hamiltonian of this chapter. Delete the expensive states before recording the return trips and you lose it. Keep every state and the page is too large to read.

A trip that starts cheap and ends cheap

Picture two subspaces. The cheap one holds the states you will keep.

The expensive one costs at least an extra energy \(\Delta\). A weak coupling of strength \(g\) joins them.

Both \(g\) and \(\Delta\) are energies, and we take \(|g|/\Delta\) small.

One use of the coupling cannot start cheap and finish cheap: it lands in the expensive subspace. Two uses can:

\[ \text{cheap }a \xrightarrow{g} \text{expensive }m \xrightarrow{g} \text{cheap }b. \]

The leftover amplitude has the scale

\[ \frac{g\,g}{E_{\rm low}-E_m}\approx -\frac{g^2}{\Delta}. \]

Three facts sit in that expression. Two couplings produce \(g^2\).

A large expensive gap suppresses the process as \(1/\Delta\). If the intermediate state lies above the states you kept, the denominator is negative.

The expensive state appears as an intermediate amplitude, not as a final state you would find if you measured energy. That kind of contribution is virtual.

Hence a second-order leftover on the cheap subspace is an energy of order \(g^2/\Delta\), not of order \(g\).

If the coupling becomes strong enough to populate the expensive state for real, calling the contribution virtual is wishful accounting. The visit is virtual only while \(|g|/\Delta\) is small.

The final sign of a particular spin coupling also depends on matrix-element phases and on how you write the leftover operator. “Second order is negative” is therefore too crude. The energy correction from coupling only to higher states is negative-semidefinite.

An exchange coefficient extracted after you subtract a constant can still be positive. The two-site example later will do exactly that.

The same scale, drawn as a chain:

cheap states

Three states, one expensive

Take three orthonormal states: two cheap ones \(|L\rangle\) and \(|R\rangle\), and one expensive one \(|e\rangle\). Let the unperturbed Hamiltonian be

\[ H_0=\Delta |e\rangle\langle e|, \]

where \(\Delta>0\) has units of energy. The cheap states sit at energy zero. Let a coupling of strength \(g\), also an energy, join each cheap state to the expensive one:

\[ V=g\bigl(|e\rangle\langle L|+|e\rangle\langle R|+\text{h.c.}\bigr). \]

Here “h.c.” means the Hermitian conjugate, which supplies the return paths. We assume \(|g|/\Delta\ll1\).

The machine that keeps the cheap pair is

\[ P=|L\rangle\langle L|+|R\rangle\langle R|. \]

Everything you threw away is

\[ Q=|e\rangle\langle e|. \]

They add to the whole space, \(P+Q=I\). Applied twice, each is itself. They kill each other:

\[ P^2=P,\qquad Q^2=Q,\qquad PQ=QP=0. \]

\(P\) is a projector. You have already used projectors as measurement questions. Here the same machine just means “keep this subspace.” \(Q\) is the complementary projector: the expensive states you threw off the working page.

Because \(PVP=0\), there is no first-order cheap-to-cheap door. The second-order leftover is

\[ H_{\rm eff}^{(2)} =-PVQ\frac{1}{\Delta}QVP =-\frac{g^2}{\Delta} \begin{pmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&1 \end{pmatrix}_{\{|L\rangle,|R\rangle\}}. \]

A microscopic coupling that never directly joins \(|L\rangle\) to \(|R\rangle\) still generates

\[ \langle L|H_{\rm eff}|R\rangle=-\frac{g^2}{\Delta}. \]

Hence a virtual path through a single expensive state writes an off-diagonal cheap coupling that the original \(V\) did not contain.

The antisymmetric combination \((|L\rangle-|R\rangle)/\sqrt2\) is dark: it stays at zero energy. The symmetric combination couples to \(|e\rangle\) and slides down by \(-2g^2/\Delta\).

This toy can be solved exactly. Its lower bright energy is

\[ E_- = \frac{\Delta-\sqrt{\Delta^2+8g^2}}{2} =-\frac{2g^2}{\Delta}+\frac{4g^4}{\Delta^3} +O\!\left(\frac{g^6}{\Delta^5}\right). \]

The expansion displays control rather than merely asserting it. The leading retained shift is of order \(g^2/\Delta\).

Here symmetry kills the cubic term, so the first omitted energy correction is fourth order. Drop that symmetry and a second-order truncation leaves third-order leftovers.

Split the space before you expand

Write the full Hamiltonian as

\[ H=H_0+\lambda V. \]

The operator \(H_0\) is the part you can solve. \(V\) has units of energy and holds the perturbation. The number \(\lambda\) is a dimensionless bookmark: set it to \(1\) after you have decided that the physical ratio is small.

The projector \(P\) selects the retained subspace. Its partner \(Q=I-P\) selects every eliminated state. Choose \(P\) from eigenstates of \(H_0\), so \(PH_0Q=0\). In blocks,

\[ H= \begin{pmatrix} PHP & PHQ\\ QHP & QHQ \end{pmatrix}. \]

The diagonal blocks stay inside one subspace. The off-diagonal blocks join cheap to expensive. A first-order projection, \(PHP\), simply deletes those blocks. We are going to record the return trips instead.

Let \(E_a\) be an unperturbed energy in \(P\) and \(E_m\) one in \(Q\). The separation is

\[ \Delta=\min_{a\in P,\,m\in Q}|E_m-E_a|. \]

For a genuinely cheap \(P\), the relevant differences \(E_m-E_a\) are positive. The useful small parameter is not “\(V\) is small” by itself. It is

\[ \epsilon=\frac{|\lambda|v}{\Delta}\ll1, \]

where \(v\) is the off-diagonal coupling scale — for example a suitable operator norm of \(PVQ+QVP\). Both \(v\) and \(\Delta\) are energies, so \(\epsilon\) is a pure number.

Hence the expansion is controlled by a ratio of two energies, not by the mere existence of a splitting of \(H\) into \(H_0+V\).

If a level in \(Q\) approaches a level in \(P\), then \(\Delta\) shrinks, \(\epsilon\) grows, and the cheap model you chose has to grow with it. The divergence is a warning label, not free coupling strength.

The exact leftover after you throw them out

Write an exact eigenstate as \(|\psi\rangle=|p\rangle+|q\rangle\), with \(|p\rangle=P|\psi\rangle\) and \(|q\rangle=Q|\psi\rangle\). Projecting \(H|\psi\rangle=E|\psi\rangle\) gives two equations:

\[ PHP|p\rangle+PHQ|q\rangle=E|p\rangle, \]

\[ QHP|p\rangle+QHQ|q\rangle=E|q\rangle. \]

If \(E-QHQ\) can be inverted, the second line solves for the expensive piece:

\[ |q\rangle=(E-QHQ)^{-1}QHP|p\rangle. \]

Feed that back into the first line and you get an exact, energy-dependent cheap operator

\[ H_{\rm eff}(E)=PHP+PHQ(E-QHQ)^{-1}QHP. \]

That is the projection logic associated with Feshbach [R171]. The inverse is the denominator you already met. Replacing \(E\) and \(QHQ\) by their unperturbed values starts the series.

For a degenerate cheap manifold of energy \(E_0\), the result through second order is

\[ \boxed{ H_{\rm eff} =E_0P+\lambda PVP +\lambda^2PVQ\frac{1}{E_0-QH_0Q}QVP +O\!\left(\frac{|\lambda|^3v^3}{\Delta^2}\right) } \]

on a bounded finite problem whose relevant perturbation scales are represented by \(v\). Equivalently, when every eliminated state lies above \(E_0\),

\[ H_{\rm eff}^{(2)} =-PVQ\frac{1}{QH_0Q-E_0}QVP. \]

The two forms are the same. The second makes the minus sign hard to drop, because \(QH_0Q-E_0\) is positive.

Hence the cheap leftover through second order is the first-order block \(PHP\), plus a sum of virtual paths through \(Q\), plus a remainder of order \(v^3/\Delta^2\).

In a basis \(|a\rangle,|b\rangle\in P\) and \(|m\rangle\in Q\),

\[ \langle a|H_{\rm eff}^{(2)}|b\rangle = \sum_{m\in Q} \frac{\langle a|V|m\rangle\langle m|V|b\rangle} {E_0-E_m}. \]

Every allowed virtual path contributes. Paths may add or cancel. A small denominator fattens a term and, at the same time, threatens the expansion.

A small twist that almost splits the blocks

There is another way to write the same folding. Choose an anti-Hermitian generator \(S^\dagger=-S\), taken to be off-diagonal, and transform

\[ \widetilde H=e^SHe^{-S}. \]

Because \(e^S\) is unitary, \(H\) and \(\widetilde H\) have the same exact spectrum. Expand \(S=\lambda S_1+\lambda^2S_2+\cdots\) and use

\[ e^SHe^{-S}=H+[S,H]+\frac12[S,[S,H]]+\cdots. \]

Split \(V=V_{\rm d}+V_{\rm od}\) into the part that stays inside a subspace and the part that joins cheap to expensive. Cancelling the first-order off-diagonal block requires

\[ [S_1,H_0]=-V_{\rm od}. \]

Therefore

\[ \langle a|S_1|m\rangle =\frac{\langle a|V|m\rangle}{E_a-E_m}. \]

Project the twisted Hamiltonian back into \(P\) and you recover

\[ H_{\rm eff}=PH_0P+\lambda PV P +\frac{\lambda^2}{2}P[S_1,V_{\rm od}]P+O(\lambda^3). \]

If the retained states are not exactly degenerate, the second-order matrix element uses the Hermitian average of the two denominators:

\[ \frac12\sum_m V_{am}V_{mb} \left(\frac{1}{E_a-E_m}+\frac{1}{E_b-E_m}\right). \]

Hence the same second-order leftover can be written as a change of basis that removes the cheap-to-expensive block order by order.

Different honest choices of cheap basis can make two leftover Hamiltonians look different while leaving their cheap predictions unitarily equivalent [R025]. State the convention before you compare coefficients.

This small twist is the Schrieffer–Wolff transformation. The name is worth keeping because it is the standard label for this particular folding, written by Schrieffer and Wolff for a different cheap problem and now used wherever a cluster or a many-body system has a cheap block that still hears the expensive states [R024]; [R025]. It is degenerate perturbation theory dressed as a change of basis.

Two sites that hop and then pay

The Hubbard model describes fermions that hop between sites and pay an on-site energy for double occupancy [R172]. Take two sites, labeled \(1\) and \(2\), occupied by exactly two electrons. Let \(c_{i\sigma}^\dagger\) create an electron of spin \(\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}\) on site \(i\), and write \(n_{i\sigma}=c_{i\sigma}^\dagger c_{i\sigma}\). The pieces are

\[ H_0=U\sum_{i=1}^{2}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}, \]

\[ V=-t\sum_{\sigma} \left(c_{1\sigma}^\dagger c_{2\sigma} +c_{2\sigma}^\dagger c_{1\sigma}\right). \]

Here \(U>0\) is the double-occupancy bill and \(t\) is the hopping matrix element; both are energies. We set \(\lambda=1\) and assume \(|t|/U\ll1\).

The retained sector \(P\) has one electron per site:

\[ |\uparrow,\uparrow\rangle, \quad |\uparrow,\downarrow\rangle, \quad |\downarrow,\uparrow\rangle, \quad |\downarrow,\downarrow\rangle. \]

All four have unperturbed energy \(E_0=0\). The thrown-away sector \(Q\) holds the two doublon-hole states

\[ |D_1\rangle=|\uparrow\downarrow,0\rangle, \qquad |D_2\rangle=|0,\uparrow\downarrow\rangle, \]

both at energy \(U\). In this two-site problem the gap is \(\Delta=U\), and \(PVP=0\): one hop always creates a doublon and a hole.

Use total-spin states

\[ |S\rangle=\frac{|\uparrow,\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow,\uparrow\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \]

\[ |T_0\rangle=\frac{|\uparrow,\downarrow\rangle+|\downarrow,\uparrow\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \quad |T_+\rangle=|\uparrow,\uparrow\rangle, \quad |T_-\rangle=|\downarrow,\downarrow\rangle. \]

A doubly occupied single orbital must be a spin singlet. The polarized triplets are Pauli blocked. The two hopping paths from \(|T_0\rangle\) cancel. With a consistent choice of fermionic phases,

\[ V|S\rangle=-\sqrt2t\left(|D_1\rangle+|D_2\rangle\right), \qquad V|T_\mu\rangle=0. \]

The total squared matrix element from the singlet into \(Q\) is \(4t^2\). The denominator is \(0-U=-U\), so

\[ \delta E_S^{(2)}=-\frac{4t^2}{U}, \qquad \delta E_T^{(2)}=0. \]

The singlet drops relative to the triplets. That is antiferromagnetic exchange: positive \(J\) favors antiparallel spins. In operator form inside the singly occupied sector,

\[ \boxed{ H_{\rm eff}^{(2)} =J\left(\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2-\frac14 n_1n_2\right), \qquad J=\frac{4t^2}{U}>0, } \]

where \(\mathbf S_i\) is the spin-\(1/2\) operator at site \(i\), and \(n_i=n_{i\uparrow}+n_{i\downarrow}\). At half filling inside \(P\), \(n_1n_2=1\). Since \(\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2=-3/4\) in the singlet and \(+1/4\) in a triplet, the formula gives \(-J\) and \(0\), respectively.

Hence the leftover of two hops through a doubly occupied intermediate is an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg coupling whose coefficient is \(4t^2/U\).

People often drop the constant \(-J/4\) and write \(J\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2\). That shifts every retained energy by \(+J/4\) but keeps the singlet-triplet splitting \(J\). Confusing the two conventions produces apparent disagreements of exactly one constant.

Dimensional check. Because \([t]=[U]=\text{energy}\),

\[ [J]=\frac{[t]^2}{[U]}=\text{energy}. \]

For a deliberately hypothetical example, take \(t=1\ \text{meV}\) and \(U=10\ \text{meV}\). Then \(t/U=0.1\) and

\[ J^{(2)}=4\frac{(1\ \text{meV})^2}{10\ \text{meV}} =0.4\ \text{meV}. \]

These are teaching numbers, not a claim about a particular defect.

The two-site problem also shows the error. The exact singlet-triplet splitting is

\[ J_{\rm exact}=\frac{\sqrt{U^2+16t^2}-U}{2} =\frac{4t^2}{U}-\frac{16t^4}{U^3} +O\!\left(\frac{t^6}{U^5}\right). \]

At the illustrative ratio \(t/U=0.1\), \(J_{\rm exact}\approx0.385\ \text{meV}\), about \(3.9\%\) below the second-order value. Odd orders vanish in this specific two-site, half-filled model.

That is a symmetry and path-counting bonus, not a general Schrieffer–Wolff rule. Drop the two-site restriction, or leave half filling, and those odd orders need not vanish.

Systematic \(t/U\) expansions for the Hubbard model generate further-neighbor and multi-spin terms at higher order [R026]. The superexchange mechanism and its antiferromagnetic sign have a broader history beyond this minimal model [R173].

When “small” is actually small

For a finite cluster with characteristic off-diagonal matrix element \(v\), the hierarchy is

\[ \underbrace{|\lambda|v}_{\text{mixing}} \ll \underbrace{\Delta}_{\text{leakage cost}}. \]

Then the thrown-away amplitude inside a dressed cheap eigenstate is generally of order \(\epsilon=|\lambda|v/\Delta\). A generated second-order energy is of order

\[ \epsilon^2\Delta=\frac{|\lambda|^2v^2}{\Delta}, \]

and a generic third-order remainder is of order

\[ \epsilon^3\Delta=\frac{|\lambda|^3v^3}{\Delta^2}. \]

These are scaling estimates, not universal coefficient-one error bars. Multiple bonds, near-degeneracies, and many virtual paths supply combinatorial factors.

In an array of clusters with coordination number \(z\), a conservative local check is often \(zv/\Delta\ll1\), followed by an explicit bound or a convergence study for the actual local Hamiltonian. A global operator norm grows with system size and can be an unnecessarily blunt criterion.

Local Schrieffer–Wolff and linked-cluster formulations organize extensive systems more carefully [R025].

Hence a useful derivation reports at least four items: the retained space \(P\), the smallest relevant gap \(\Delta\), the dimensionless expansion parameter, and the leading omitted operators with their scale.

Reporting only the attractive term is not perturbation theory. It is advertising.

What a laboratory still has to measure

The Schrieffer–Wolff transformation is [Theory]. A laboratory has energy levels, transition matrix elements, drives, disorder, dissipation, and finite temperature. To claim that a measured defect cluster realizes a leftover Hamiltonian derived this way, you have to connect those observables to \(H_0\), \(V\), \(P\), and \(Q\).

For a defect cluster, \(P\) might be an isolated spin doublet. The gap \(\Delta\) might be a many-spin excitation gap, an orbital splitting, or a charge-transfer energy.

Those are physically different denominators and they can have different noise sensitivity. The coupling \(V\) might be magnetic dipole coupling, direct exchange, strain coupling, or a driven interaction.

A magnetic dipole term that already acts inside the doublet contributes at first order through \(PVP\); do not relabel it “superexchange.” A charge-transfer or mediator-assisted path that leaves \(P\) and returns can contribute at second or higher order.

For real superexchange through a ligand or an extra defect orbital, several intermediate energies and hopping amplitudes replace the single \(U\). Their contributions can compete.

Orbital occupancy plus Hund coupling can even flip the leftover sign. The two-site formula \(4t^2/U\) is a derivation template, not a universal materials formula [R173].

A credible check is spectroscopic: measure or calculate the cheap manifold and the leakage levels, estimate the matrix elements that join them, diagonalize at least the smallest microscopic cluster, and compare its cheap spectrum and projected observables with the truncated leftover model. [Numerics] Exact diagonalization is especially useful here, because it tests coefficients and truncation errors without assuming the series is already accurate. Agreement at one tuned point is weaker than agreement across a range of \(v/\Delta\).

[Proposal] Later cluster constructions may use this expansion to ask whether the two-body defect couplings you actually have generate the encoded interactions you want. The transformation itself does not guarantee that the desired term is large, that unwanted terms cancel, or that the leftover phase is topological.

Eliminating expensive states does not create a new physical device. The crystal still contains every microscopic defect and mediator state. \(H_{\rm eff}\) describes an encoded cheap sector of that same system.

A generated spin interaction does not establish emergent anyons or topological order; those are many-body properties that need the right phase, the right gap, and the right nonlocal observables. A digitally programmed gate sequence that looks second-order is yet another category: it may emulate the same operator without owning the static microscopic hierarchy derived here.

Ways to get this wrong

Wrong denominator sign. For a retained energy \(E_0\) and a higher intermediate energy \(E_m\), use \(E_0-E_m<0\). Equivalently, write an explicit minus sign and the positive cost \(E_m-E_0\). Do not do both.

Throwing the expensive states away before the return trips. Replacing \(H\) by \(PHP\) loses \(PVQ(E_0-QH_0Q)^{-1}QVP\). First-order projection and second-order elimination answer different questions.

No spectral separation. If a \(Q\) level approaches \(P\), its denominator becomes small, mixing becomes large, and the cheap model you chose has to grow. The divergence is a warning label, not free coupling strength.

Comparing gauges term by term. Leftover Hamiltonians related by a unitary rotation inside \(P\) can share out coefficients differently while predicting the same spectrum. Compare invariant predictions, or transform operators consistently [R025].

Forgetting dressed observables. Physical cheap states contain a \(Q\)-sector admixture of order \(v/\Delta\). An observable \(O\) should be transformed as \(Pe^SOe^{-S}P\), not merely replaced by \(POP\), when that correction matters.

Hiding lower-order unwanted terms. A desired interaction generated at fourth order may be much smaller than an allowed first- or second-order nuisance. Symmetry must forbid, cancel, or let you tune those terms. Notation cannot.

Calling a small coefficient accurate because it exists. If virtual paths nearly cancel, the desired coefficient can be smaller than the nominal remainder. Control of the full Hamiltonian does not guarantee a small relative error in a specially suppressed term.

Using a closed-system Hamiltonian to claim coherence. Block diagonalization does not remove phonons, fluctuating fields, thermal activation, or control noise. Coupling to a bath can cause real leakage, and leftover noise operators have to be projected too.

Equating generated interactions with a topological phase. A two-body microscopic model may generate multi-body operators, but correct operator content, coefficient hierarchy, system size, temperature, and perturbative stability still have to be established.

Check yourself

What do \(P\) and \(Q\) mean? \(P\) projects onto the cheap states retained in the leftover model; \(Q=I-P\) projects onto the expensive states you threw away.

Show that a virtual process that leaves \(P\) and returns at second order has scale \(v^2/\Delta\). It uses the coupling twice to leave and return, and the intermediate resolvent supplies one inverse excitation energy, so the leftover is \(v\cdot(1/\Delta)\cdot v\).

What fails if an intermediate energy \(E_m\) approaches the cheap energy \(E_0\)? The denominator \(E_0-E_m\) becomes small, \(\epsilon=v/\Delta\) is no longer small, and the cheap model you chose has to grow. The leftover formula is not a source of free coupling.

Show that Hubbard exchange is antiferromagnetic even though the singlet correction is negative. Only the singlet gains the energy \(-4t^2/U\); the triplets remain at zero. Writing this splitting as \(J(\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2-1/4)\) gives \(J=4t^2/U>0\).

What must accompany a second-order leftover Hamiltonian? The definition of \(P\), the leakage gap \(\Delta\), a dimensionless small parameter such as \(v/\Delta\), and the scale and operator form of the leading omitted corrections.

What fails if a Schrieffer–Wolff-generated plaquette term is taken as proof of topological order? The term is one leftover operator. The many-body phase and its gap, excitations, robustness, and finite-size behavior still need separate evidence.

Sources

  • [R024] J. R. Schrieffer and P. A. Wolff, “Relation between the Anderson and Kondo Hamiltonians,” Physical Review 149, 491–492 (1966). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.149.491.

  • [R025] S. Bravyi, D. P. DiVincenzo, and D. Loss, “Schrieffer–Wolff transformation for quantum many-body systems,” Annals of Physics 326, 2793–2826 (2011). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2011.06.004; arXiv: 1105.0675.

  • [R171] H. Feshbach, “Unified theory of nuclear reactions,” Annals of Physics 5, 357–390 (1958). DOI: 10.1016/0003-4916(58)90007-1.

  • [R172] J. Hubbard, “Electron correlations in narrow energy bands,” Proceedings of the Royal Society A 276, 238–257 (1963). DOI: 10.1098/rspa.1963.0204.

  • [R026] A. H. MacDonald, S. M. Girvin, and D. Yoshioka, “\(t/U\) expansion for the Hubbard model,” Physical Review B 37, 9753–9756 (1988). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.37.9753.

  • [R173] P. W. Anderson, “New Approach to the Theory of Superexchange Interactions,” Physical Review 115, 2–13 (1959). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.115.2.

Chapter 23 — Perturbative gadgets

Four spins sit around a square. Topology wants them to pay an energy only when their four answers multiply to the wrong sign.

The crystal, left to itself, will not write that rule. It knows how to couple two neighbors.

It does not know how to couple four at once.

So we add a fifth spin and make it expensive to flip. Each of the four can knock that helper, weakly, two at a time. A process that knocks all four and then puts the helper back where it started leaves a four-body term on the cheap subspace.

That term is the whole trick. It is also a bill.

The helper is extra hardware. The four-body energy is tiny compared with the two-body knocks that produced it.

And the first leftovers are not four-body at all — they are ordinary pair terms, larger, and they have to be cancelled by hand.

Four neighbors and one expensive helper

Picture the square with the helper in the middle:

target 1
|
target 4 -- ancilla -- target 2
|
target 3

strong cost to excite ancilla: Δ
weak two-body links: g_i

The helper has a large excitation energy \(\Delta\). One weak knock can send it into the expensive subspace.

A process that stays cheap must eventually bring it home. If all four targets take part before that return, the leftover amplitude can remember the product of four spin operators.

The expensive helper is a mediator. It never stays excited in the process we care about. It only carries the visits.

Those visits are virtual: they live in an amplitude, not as a stable population that an energy measurement would find. Each visit contributes a weak coupling in the numerator and an energy denominator. Four visits therefore suggest

\[ K\sim \frac{g^4}{\Delta^3}, \]

where \(g\), \(\Delta\), and the effective coupling \(K\) are energies. The units check is \(E^4/E^3=E\), as a Hamiltonian coefficient must be.

Hence a four-body leftover generated by four two-body knocks has scale \(g^4/\Delta^3\), not scale \(g\).

The rule of thumb is useful. It hides combinatorial factors and lower-order debris. We now expose both.

The first leftover is a pair, not a square

Let the four targets be spin-\(1/2\) particles numbered \(i=1,2,3,4\). The Pauli operator \(Z_i\) has eigenvalues \(z_i=\pm1\). Let the mediator have ground state \(|0\rangle_a\), excited state \(|1\rangle_a\), and excitation cost \(\Delta>0\). Define

\[ H_0=\Delta |1\rangle_a\langle1|, \qquad V=X_a S, \qquad S=\sum_{i=1}^{4}g_i Z_i . \]

Here \(X_a\) flips the mediator, and \(g_i\) is the energy of a two-body \(X_aZ_i\) coupling. Every term in \(V\) is two-local. The projector onto the low-energy mediator state is

\[ P=|0\rangle_a\langle0|\otimes I_{1\ldots4}. \]

This toy is unusually friendly because all \(Z_i\) commute. For fixed target eigenvalues, the mediator Hamiltonian is the matrix

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 0&S\\ S&\Delta \end{pmatrix}. \]

Its lower eigenvalue, now read as an operator on the targets, is

\[ E_-(S)=\frac{\Delta-\sqrt{\Delta^2+4S^2}}{2} =-\frac{S^2}{\Delta}+\frac{S^4}{\Delta^3} -\frac{2S^6}{\Delta^5}+O\!\left(\frac{S^8}{\Delta^7}\right). \]

The first nonconstant term appears at second order, not fourth. Expanding it gives

\[ -\frac{S^2}{\Delta} =-\frac{\sum_i g_i^2}{\Delta}I -\sum_{i<j}\frac{2g_i g_j}{\Delta}Z_iZ_j. \]

The identity merely shifts every energy. The six pair couplings are unwanted and parametrically larger than the term we want. At fourth order, however,

\[ \frac{S^4}{\Delta^3} \supset \frac{24g_1g_2g_3g_4}{\Delta^3}Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4. \]

The factor \(24=4!\) counts the orders in which the four links can act. Choosing the sign of one \(g_i\) sets the sign of the four-body term. Direct two-body counterterms can cancel the pair terms through fourth order. For completeness, the fourth-order coefficient multiplying a particular \(Z_iZ_j\) is

\[ \frac{4g_ig_j(g_i^2+g_j^2) +12g_ig_j\!\sum_{k\ne i,j}g_k^2}{\Delta^3}. \]

A calibrated counterterm must negate this coefficient together with the second-order coefficient. After that cancellation,

\[ H_{\mathrm{eff}}=K Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4 +O(g^6/\Delta^5), \qquad K=\frac{24g_1g_2g_3g_4}{\Delta^3}. \]

An adapter of this kind is a gadget. The name is worth keeping because it is an engineering part, not a new law of nature: two-body couplings in, a hoped-for many-body term out, and a loss of scale in between.

Hence the four-body term is real, but it is not the first leftover. The first leftover is a pair, larger by two powers of \(g/\Delta\), and it must be cancelled before the four-body term is the leading cheap operator.

This construction is explicit. One mediator. Four mediator–target links. Six nominal target–target counterterm links. It is a derivation, not a promise that a particular crystal supplies those ten links.

The mediator and the four targets are physical or cluster-encoded spins. The operator \(Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4\) is an effective interaction.

Neither fact alone creates an emergent anyon. Only an extended, gapped lattice Hamiltonian in the correct phase has toric-code quasiparticles.

Digitally applying a four-qubit gate would simulate the same operator in time. It would not provide a passive static Hamiltonian.

How small the four-body piece is

For equal magnitudes \(|g_i|=g\), define the dimensionless expansion parameter \(\eta=g/\Delta\). Then

\[ \frac{|K|}{\Delta}=24\eta^4. \]

The sixth-order contribution to the same four-body operator is \(-960g^6/\Delta^5\), so its magnitude relative to the leading \(K\) is \(40\eta^2\).

At \(\eta=0.05\), the leading four-body scale is only \(1.5\times10^{-4}\Delta\), the sixth-order correction is 10% of it, and the leading unwanted pair scale \(2g^2/\Delta=5\times10^{-3}\Delta\) is about 33 times larger.

Holding the residual pair term below \(0.1K\) consequently requires roughly 0.3% cancellation in this illustrative cell. At \(\eta=0.025\), the sixth-order fraction falls to 2.5%, but \(K/\Delta\) falls to \(9.375\times10^{-6}\).

Hence perturbation theory sends an invoice either way: make \(\eta\) smaller and the series improves while \(K\) collapses. [Theory] These numbers follow directly from the expansion above; they are not measured device performance.

As a units example, suppose — not claim — that \(\Delta/h=1\ \mathrm{GHz}\), where \(h\) is Planck’s constant. At \(\eta=0.05\), \(K/h=150\ \mathrm{kHz}\), and the dynamical time \(\hbar/K=1/[2\pi(K/h)]\approx1.1\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). The arithmetic shows why a large microscopic gigahertz number need not imply a large topological gap.

To make a toric-code plaquette, use \(Z_i\) on its four edges. To make a star, replace each target \(Z_i\) by \(X_i\).

On a periodic square lattice with \(E\) target edges, there are \(V+P=E\) stabilizers, so this naive design uses one mediator per stabilizer: \(E\) mediators for \(E\) targets, four mediator-link incidences and six counterterm incidences per stabilizer. Each target must participate in four gadgets.

This count excludes routing devices and whatever encoding turns a defect cluster into one target spin.

From one cell to a lattice

Write a gadget Hamiltonian as

\[ H=H_0+V, \]

where \(H_0\) has a low-energy subspace \(P\), its complement is \(Q=I-P\), and the smallest \(P\)-to-\(Q\) excitation energy is \(\Delta\). A sequence contributing at order \(n\) has the schematic form

\[ PVQ\frac{1}{E_0-QH_0Q}QVQ\cdots QVP, \]

with \(n\) copies of \(V\) and \(n-1\) resolvents. If every weak matrix element has scale \(g\), its scale is \(g^n/\Delta^{n-1}\).

Jordan and Farhi give systematic gadgets at arbitrary perturbative order, while Bravyi, DiVincenzo, Loss, and Terhal show how bounded-strength local target Hamiltonians can be simulated with an extensive error \(O(\epsilon N)\) without making simulator couplings grow with the number \(N\) of target spins [R174]; [R175]. [Theory] Those are Hamiltonian-simulation results.

They do not remove device connectivity or coherence requirements.

Three separate gaps must not be conflated.

  • Penalty gap \(\Delta\): the cost of leaving a gadget’s encoded subspace.

  • Effective stabilizer coefficient \(K\): typically suppressed as \(g^n/\Delta^{n-1}\).

  • Topological many-body gap \(\Delta_{\rm top}\): the lowest allowed excitation energy of the extended effective model.

For the ideal toric-code Hamiltonian

\[ H_{\rm TC}=-K_A\sum_v A_v-K_B\sum_p B_p, \]

an individual violated stabilizer costs \(2K_A\) or \(2K_B\). On a closed surface, local operations create violations in pairs, so the smallest such pair costs \(4\min(K_A,K_B)\). Thus the simulator’s useful low-energy gap is of order \(K\), not \(\Delta\). A basic hardware budget is

\[ \max\!\left(k_BT,\;\hbar/T_2,\;|\delta J|,\;|\delta K|\right) \ll \Delta_{\rm top}\sim K\ll g\ll\Delta. \]

Here \(k_B T\) is thermal energy, \(T_2\) is the relevant coherence time, \(\delta J\) is a residual unwanted two-body energy, and \(\delta K\) denotes stabilizer disorder. Every entry has energy units.

Hence the useful protection is set by the suppressed coefficient \(K\), not by the mediator penalty that produced it.

The inequality is a design criterion, not a universal phase boundary. One gadget cell is not an extensive proof.

Shared targets permit mixed virtual paths involving neighboring mediators. The number of paths grows with coordination, and operator-norm bounds based on the whole \(V\) can grow with system size.

Parallel-gadget constructions, locality-based Schrieffer–Wolff analyses, or exact subsystem symmetries are needed to keep local errors controlled [R175]; [R177]. Finally, proving that an approximate effective Hamiltonian has the right ground space is weaker than proving a stable thermodynamic gap and the correct excited anyons.

What the papers actually built

Target | Microscopic construction | First target order / resource cost | What is established | Important limit | |

Toric-code phase from the honeycomb model | Nearest-neighbor \(XX\), \(YY\), or \(ZZ\) bonds; strong \(J_z\) dimers encode effective spins | Fourth order; two physical spins per effective dimer | In the anisotropic limit, \(K=J_x^2J_y^2/(16|J_z|^3)\) multiplies an effective four-dimer plaquette operator [R017]; [R176]. [Theory] | Natural and exactly solvable, but its non-Abelian phase is Ising type, not Fibonacci. | |

Toric code by code gadgets | Each target edge qubit is encoded into four physical qubits; inter-gadget couplings are two-body | Fourth order on a square lattice; four physical qubits per target qubit | Encoded star and plaquette terms arise; odd orders vanish and second order is a constant because the gadget detects single-qubit errors [R177]. [Theory] | The low-energy model is approximate, frustrated, and has a suppressed gap. | |

Finite-group quantum doubles \(D(G)\) | Two-body code gadgets using \(|G|\)-level qudits | Four physical qudits per target edge in the square-lattice construction [R177] | Includes non-Abelian anyonic models when \(G\) is non-Abelian. [Theory] | A non-Abelian quantum double is not automatically Fibonacci; local dimension and operator control grow with group structure. | |

Simplified quantum doubles | A hopping/clock gadget generates an ordered operator product | Order follows the clock path; König reduces quantum-double interactions to simpler local terms [R178]. [Theory] | Ordered noncommuting products demand more structure than the commuting parity toy above. | | |

String-net PEPS | Strong two-body terms define an encoded PEPS subspace; weak bonds generate a parent Hamiltonian | Finite order set by the local interaction region; additional virtual degrees of freedom per PEPS tensor | A two-body parent construction is proved for a broad PEPS class, with an explicit double-semion string-net example [R018]; [R179]. [Theory] | Double semion is Abelian. The paper is not an experimental doubled-Fibonacci defect design. | |

Exact two-body alternative | Enlarged “composite particles” and two-body interactions | Extra local Hilbert space rather than a small perturbation parameter | Ocko and Yoshida construct nonperturbative two-body models for toric-code and quantum-double topological codes [R180]. [Theory] | Avoids perturbative gap suppression but retains substantial local-state and coupling complexity. | |

The honeycomb result is a particularly clean reality check. In the strong-\(J_z\) limit, each \(z\)-bond has a two-dimensional low-energy doublet.

A closed sequence of two \(J_x\) and two \(J_y\) bond operations returns all dimers to that subspace. Lower orders only shift energies; fourth order produces the plaquette term with coefficient \(J_x^2J_y^2/(16|J_z|^3)\) [R017]; [R176].

This is the same numerator-and-denominator logic as the toy mediator, but lattice symmetry and exact solvability organize the unwanted terms for us.

The distinction between “non-Abelian” and “Fibonacci” is load-bearing. König’s and Brell et al.’s group-based constructions reach quantum doubles of finite groups, some with non-Abelian excitations [R177]; [R178].

Levin–Wen models are broader categorical string nets [R018]. The PEPS gadget framework explicitly treats double semion and argues for a broad class of suitable PEPS [R179], but that is not the same as a worked, defect-mapped two-body Hamiltonian for doubled Fibonacci.

[Proposal] Extending such machinery to a particular doubled-Fibonacci tensor and then to a fabricable defect interaction graph remains an architecture problem, not a solved consequence of citing “string nets.”

What a defect has to answer

A defect device does not begin with abstract Pauli symbols. It begins with electronic and nuclear levels, selection rules, dipolar tensors, exchange paths, strain, optical excited states, and disorder. Mapping a gadget requires answers to six concrete questions.

Where does \(\Delta\) come from? It may be a crystal-field splitting, a driven dressed-state gap, or an intra-cluster penalty.

Whichever it is, the same control fields and strain that set \(\Delta\) must leave a well-isolated low-energy doublet. Leakage levels turn the simple two-level denominator into several denominators, possibly with opposite signs.

Can each required operator be implemented? The parity cell needs \(Z_iX_a\); a complete toric code also needs the basis-rotated star analogue.

A fixed magnetic dipole interaction generally supplies a geometry-dependent tensor, not independently switchable clean Pauli products. Echo or dressing can average terms, but then the Hamiltonian becomes Floquet-engineered rather than simply static.

Can one mediator reach four targets without reaching unwanted neighbors? Dipolar couplings decay rather than stop.

Exchange is shorter-ranged but highly sensitive to atomic placement. The toy’s six counterterms include diagonal target pairs that may be harder to realize than the four radial links.

Published code-gadget constructions solve locality in an abstract lattice, not defect implantation and routing [R177]; [R179].

Are signs and magnitudes calibratable? At \(\eta=0.05\), our toy needed sub-percent cancellation merely to make residual pair terms one tenth of \(K\).

Spatial disorder changes both \(g_i\) and denominators. A small fractional error relative to \(g\) can therefore be a large error relative to \(K\).

Can the system be initialized and cooled into \(P\)? The penalty suppresses real mediator excitation only when thermal energy, drive-induced transitions, and linewidths are small compared with \(\Delta\). Topological defects are controlled by the much smaller \(\Delta_{\rm top}\), so satisfying \(k_BT\ll\Delta\) is not enough.

Does coherence outlast the effective dynamics? The relevant time is \(\hbar/K\), not \(\hbar/g\).

Mediator dephasing can also be inherited by the effective term because the virtual admixture is nonzero. A useful calculation must project both the Hamiltonian and the noise operators.

[Experiment] None of the gadget papers reviewed in this chapter reports a crystal-defect array that realizes its full two-body simulator Hamiltonian and diagnoses the resulting topological phase [R175]; [R177]; [R178]; [R179]; [R180]. Their results are theory constructions. Defect hardware may eventually supply ingredients, but combining the required connectivity, anisotropy, scale hierarchy, cooling, and calibration is presently a proposal-level mapping exercise.

Ways to get this wrong

Quoting the penalty gap as protection. The mediator may cost \(\Delta\), while anyons cost only order \(K\). Thermal and coherent protection must be budgeted against the latter.

Ignoring lower orders. Our desired term first appeared at fourth order, but larger pair terms appeared at second order. “First desired order” does not mean “first nonzero order.”

Cancelling on paper, not in hardware. A counterterm is another physical interaction with its own noise, range, and calibration error.

Extrapolating one cell to a lattice. Shared-spin virtual paths can create cross-gadget operators. Extensivity and a thermodynamic gap need separate analysis.

Calling an encoded target spin topological. The four-qudit code gadget of Brell et al. is a local error-detecting encoding; topology belongs to the extended low-energy phase [R177].

Calling every non-Abelian model Fibonacci. Non-Abelian quantum doubles and the honeycomb Ising phase have different fusion and braid data from Fibonacci anyons.

Confusing an effective ground Hamiltonian with its excitations. Correct ground-space order does not automatically guarantee the desired quasiparticle dispersion, localization, or braiding under higher-order corrections.

Taking \(g/\Delta\) vanishingly small. This improves the series while collapsing \(K\), slowing operations and tightening temperature and coherence requirements.

Check yourself

Show that an order-\(n\) virtual process usually scales as \(g^n/\Delta^{n-1}\). It contains \(n\) weak matrix elements and \(n-1\) intermediate energy denominators.

What did the one-mediator example cost? One ancilla, four mediator–target links, six nominal pair counterterms, and fourth-order gap suppression for one four-spin term.

What fails if \(\Delta\) is quoted as the toric-code gap? \(\Delta\) penalizes leaving the gadget subspace; stabilizer violations live inside the low-energy theory and cost order \(K\ll\Delta\). Thermal and coherent protection must be budgeted against \(K\).

Show that reducing \(g/\Delta\) improves the relative sixth-order error while collapsing \(K\) faster. For equal \(|g_i|\), the relative sixth-order piece is \(40\eta^2\) while \(|K|/\Delta=24\eta^4\). Halving \(\eta\) quarters the relative error and multiplies \(K\) by \(1/16\).

Do existing non-Abelian quantum-double gadgets establish doubled Fibonacci defect hardware? No. They establish Hamiltonian reductions for a different family; the category, local Hilbert space, physical couplings, and phase diagnostics still have to be mapped.

What must be shown after deriving one plaquette term? Controlled parallel composition, small local errors compared with \(K\), a stable thermodynamic gap, and the correct extended ground and excitation structure.

A two-body gadget can generate a four-body term. Its coefficient is generally high order in \(g/\Delta\).

Mediators, counterterms, and shared-cell paths are real resources. The useful topological gap is order \(K\), not the penalty \(\Delta\).

Toric-code and finite-group quantum-double reductions are established theoretically. A defect-specific doubled-Fibonacci construction is not.

  • [R017] A. Kitaev, “Anyons in an exactly solved model and beyond,” Annals of Physics 321, 2–111 (2006). DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2005.10.005; arXiv:cond-mat/0506438.

  • [R177] C. G. Brell, S. T. Flammia, S. D. Bartlett, and A. C. Doherty, “Toric codes and quantum doubles from two-body Hamiltonians,” New Journal of Physics 13, 053039 (2011). DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/13/5/053039; arXiv:1011.1942.

Chapter 24 — Eight arrows that are not a machine

Here is the nicest picture in the book.

host crystal
-> addressable defect spins
-> strongly coupled cluster
-> isolated two-state pseudospin
-> edge label {1, tau}
-> vertex and plaquette operators
-> doubled-Fibonacci phase
-> emergent anyons and a logical qubit

Each arrow looks like a finished step. It is not.

The words are hypotheses. We will take them one at a time, name the object sitting on each side, and write down a measurement that would make the arrow fail.

The first honest calculation is three spins and one coupling. Everything after that is a bill.

A defect electron or nucleus is a physical spin. A cluster doublet is an encoded leftover: two slow states built out of several real spins.

Calling those two states \(1\) and \(\tau\) is a dictionary, not an anyon. A lattice whose Hamiltonian really is the Levin–Wen one can have emergent quasiparticles.

A processor that prepares the same amplitudes is a digital copy. Only the many-body phase supplies intrinsic topological order.

The diagram above mixes all four of those objects as if they were the same noun.

Three defects, not twenty

Someone will ask for five to twenty defects. That interval is not a result.

The evidence below does not show a designed, mutually coupled array of five to twenty optically addressable centers that forms a protected low-energy edge. So we start with three effective spin-\(1/2\) objects: the smallest open antiferromagnetic chain with a spinful ground doublet.

That is modesty demanded by the algebra, not a secret optimum.

Let \(\mathbf S_i=(S_i^x,S_i^y,S_i^z)\) be the dimensionless spin-\(1/2\) operator at site \(i\), with \(\mathbf S_i^2=3/4\). Energies live in the coupling \(J\), measured here in joules. A spectroscopist may quote \(J/h\) in hertz, where \(h\) is Planck’s constant. Consider

\[ H_C=J\left(\mathbf S_1\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_2+ \mathbf S_2\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_3\right), \qquad J>0. \]

This is an ideal isotropic exchange model. [Theory] It is a worked target, not a claim that three nearby NV, SiV, or SiC centers naturally realize equal antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange.

Exchange-only encodings based on three spins are established theoretically, and controlled three-electron versions have been pursued in quantum dots [R114]. That does not hand the same Hamiltonian to color centers.

Define the end-spin sum \(\mathbf S_{13}=\mathbf S_1+\mathbf S_3\) and the total spin \(\mathbf S=\mathbf S_{13}+\mathbf S_2\). Then

\[ H_C=\frac{J}{2}\left(\mathbf S^2-\mathbf S_{13}^2-\mathbf S_2^2\right). \]

The spectrum follows without diagonalizing an \(8\times8\) matrix:

End spin \(S_{13}\) | Total spin \(S\) | Energy | Degeneracy | |

1 | \(1/2\) | \(-J\) | 2 | |

0 | \(1/2\) | \(0\) | 2 | |

1 | \(3/2\) | \(J/2\) | 4 | |

The ground manifold is a doublet. The smallest climb out of it is

\[ \Delta_C=0-(-J)=J. \]

A convenient basis, in site order \(1,2,3\), is

\[ |\tilde\uparrow\rangle= \sqrt{\frac23}|\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle -\sqrt{\frac16}\left(|\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\rangle+ |\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle\right), \]

with \(|\tilde\downarrow\rangle\) obtained by flipping every spin. Let

\[ P_C=|\tilde\uparrow\rangle\langle\tilde\uparrow|+ |\tilde\downarrow\rangle\langle\tilde\downarrow| \]

keep only this pair, and let \(\widetilde{\mathbf S}=P_C\mathbf S P_C\) be the leftover spin-\(1/2\) operator. That leftover pair is a pseudospin. The name is worth keeping because it is two slow states made of three real spins, not a fourth particle that appeared in the crystal.

Angular-momentum addition gives

\[ P_C\mathbf S_1P_C=P_C\mathbf S_3P_C=\frac23\widetilde{\mathbf S}, \qquad P_C\mathbf S_2P_C=-\frac13\widetilde{\mathbf S}. \]

Hence the three-spin chain, if it really is this Hamiltonian, has a unique ground doublet whose local magnetic answers stand in the ratio \(2:-1:2\).

The signs are an experiment. If you do not see the predicted spectrum and those matrix elements, this cluster model is already dead. There is no reason to draw a lattice around it.

One link between two leftover pairs

Take two clusters, \(A\) and \(B\), with an endpoint interaction

\[ V_{AB}=j\,\mathbf S_{3,A}\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_{1,B}, \]

where \(j\) is an energy. With \(P=P_A P_B\), first-order projection writes

\[ PV_{AB}P=\frac{4j}{9}\, \widetilde{\mathbf S}_A\!\cdot\!\widetilde{\mathbf S}_B. \]

Virtual leakage adds corrections of order \(j^2/J\), so the controlled regime is \(|j|/J\ll1\). The units check: \(j^2/J\) is still an energy.

[Theory] This derivation establishes a two-body leftover exchange and nothing more. It does not generate a string-net vertex projector, a plaquette recoupling operator, or Fibonacci statistics.

Hence the first honest intercluster leftover is a Heisenberg coupling of two pseudospins, smaller than the microscopic endpoint coupling by \(4/9\), plus a leakage correction of order \(j^2/J\).

Each reduction swallows internal motion and leaves a slower pair. A later gadget swallows mediator motion and leaves a still slower vertex or plaquette term.

The output is useful only if every reduction has a clean input and less leftover junk than the thing it is supposed to produce. Here the junk is leakage, disorder, leftover lower-order interactions, and decoherence.

Each reduction also shrinks the energy. That is the whole tension: a hierarchy can simplify the space while making the desired physics too faint to see.

Nor is the leftover pair automatically quiet. Uniform magnetic noise couples to \(\widetilde{\mathbf S}\) at first order because

\[ P_C(\mathbf S_1+\mathbf S_2+\mathbf S_3)P_C= \widetilde{\mathbf S}. \]

The cluster suppresses leakage when noise lacks energy near \(J\). It does not suppress ordinary logical dephasing. Encoded and decoherence-free are not synonyms.

Two names on two states

A Fibonacci string-net edge admits two labels: vacuum \(1\) and the nontrivial label \(\tau\), with the fusion rule

\[ \tau\times\tau=1+\tau. \]

A cluster doublet has the right local dimension, so we may define

\[ |1\rangle_e\equiv|\tilde\uparrow\rangle_e, \qquad |\tau\rangle_e\equiv|\tilde\downarrow\rangle_e \]

for edge \(e\). [Proposal] This is a dictionary between two bases. The physical spin operator does not acquire Fibonacci fusion data by being given a Greek name.

On a trivalent graph, the allowed unordered vertex triples are

\[ (1,1,1),\quad (1,\tau,\tau)\text{ and permutations},\quad (\tau,\tau,\tau). \]

Let \(Q_v\) project the three edges that meet at vertex \(v\) onto those allowed states. That is a three-edge constraint.

Hence dimension two does not write the vertex rule for you. Drop the constraint and the two names are only a relabeling of a spin.

A plaquette that is not a product of Paulis

Let \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\) be the golden ratio, the quantum dimension of \(\tau\). The total squared quantum dimension is

\[ \mathcal D^2=1+\varphi^2. \]

For plaquette \(p\), let \(B_p^s\) mean “insert a loop carrying label \(s\) and recouple it into the surrounding edges using the Fibonacci \(F\)-symbols.” The doubled-Fibonacci plaquette projector is [R018]

\[ B_p=\frac{B_p^1+\varphi B_p^\tau}{1+\varphi^2}. \]

The ideal Levin–Wen Hamiltonian is

\[ H_{\rm LW}=-K_v\sum_v Q_v-K_p\sum_p B_p, \qquad K_v,K_p>0, \]

where \(K_v\) and \(K_p\) are energies. [Theory] The projectors commute in the ideal construction and realize doubled, not single chiral, Fibonacci order [R018].

The plaquette operator changes superpositions of edge labels with precise irrational relative amplitudes. An arbitrary six-spin interaction is not “close enough” merely because it touches a hexagon.

Generic perturbative constructions can reduce locality for broad classes of encoded PEPS parent Hamiltonians, and an explicit double-semion string-net example exists [R179]. [Theory] That result is an existence argument in an abstract two-body model, not a defect-specific doubled-Fibonacci blueprint. For a gadget whose desired term first appears at order \(n\), dimensional analysis gives a scale of the form

\[ K_{\rm eff}\sim c\,j\left(\frac{j}{\Delta_m}\right)^{n-1}, \]

where \(\Delta_m\) is a mediator excitation energy and \(c\) is a dimensionless, construction-dependent coefficient. Every extra perturbative order reduces the output when \(|j|/\Delta_m\ll1\). Lower-order unwanted terms must be canceled or shown harmless.

Hence producing one desired term in perturbation theory is not producing \(H_{\rm LW}\). Nature is allowed to notice the orders you erased from the blackboard.

Two inequalities that have to hold

Define \(\delta_C\) as the energy norm of intra-cluster disorder, \(\Gamma\) as a logical decoherence rate in s\(^{-1}\), \(\sigma_{\rm eff}\) as the energy scale of spatial variation in effective couplings, and \(H_{\rm err}\) as all unwanted effective terms. Here \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant, \(T\) is temperature in kelvin, \(\hbar=h/(2\pi)\), and \(\|\cdot\|\) is the operator norm. Let \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) be the actual many-body gap above the intended ground sector, not simply the coefficient printed before one projector. A minimally viable passive hierarchy is

\[ J\gg \max(|j|,\delta_C,k_BT), \]

and

\[ \Delta_{\rm topo}\gg \max(k_BT,\hbar\Gamma,\sigma_{\rm eff},\|H_{\rm err}\|). \]

Both sides of each inequality have energy units. These are necessary, not sufficient.

You still need locality, a system larger than the correlation length, a way to initialize, and a way to identify topological sectors. Stability theorems protect suitable topologically ordered commuting-projector models against sufficiently weak local perturbations [R142].

They do not say that a badly approximated microscopic Hamiltonian lies in that phase.

Hence a large cluster coupling \(J\) does not, by itself, protect a logical qubit. The many-body gap after every projection and gadget suppression is the scale that has to beat temperature, decoherence, disorder, and leftover junk.
