This table is the architecture. The arrow diagram was only its table of contents.

What the laboratory actually has

[Experiment] Small interacting diamond systems exist. Neumann and colleagues coherently controlled a pair of color centers at a measured separation of \(98\pm3\) Å [R181].

Dolde and colleagues generated entanglement between individual defect electron spins [R080]. Rosenfeld and colleagues observed coherent dynamics involving an NV center and two dark electronic spins [R182].

These results establish that “defects can interact coherently” is not fantasy. They do not establish equal antiferromagnetic Heisenberg bonds, repeatable cluster spectra, or a two-dimensional array.

[Experiment] Cluster-sized registers also exist in a different sense. Bradley and colleagues controlled a ten-qubit diamond register consisting of one NV electron spin and nine nuclear spins, at 3.7 K, and entangled as many as seven spins [R119].

That is impressive evidence for multispin control. It is not ten engineered defect centers, not a passive exchange cluster, and not an analog string-net Hamiltonian.

The electron-mediated, pulse-controlled register belongs in the digital/control column.

[Experiment] Programmable processors have now dynamically prepared Fibonacci string-net states and exercised fusion and braiding protocols [R165]. This demonstrates control of the encoded mathematics, not spontaneous emergence from a static defect Hamiltonian.

It is valuable as a measurement recipe and a source of target data. It does not validate the material hierarchy.

For sapphire, corundum, SiC, or diamond, the selection must be made from measured interaction tensors, fabrication distributions, charge stability, and readout — not from the beauty of the host crystal. [Speculation] No source cited here supports treating a five-to-twenty-defect cluster in any of these hosts as an available component. The count is a resource hypothesis to be optimized after a microscopic Hamiltonian exists.

Eight tests that can still kill it

The proposal survives only if all of the following can be tested and retained.

  • A1 — Repeatable local object [Proposal]. The selected defect and charge state behave as the same effective spin across a dense array. Spectroscopy must bound site-to-site Hamiltonian variation.

  • A2 — Cluster window [Proposal]. A reproducible cluster has one doublet separated by \(\Delta_C\), with \(\Delta_C\) exceeding \(k_BT\), disorder, the energy scale of leakage-driving controls, and intercluster coupling by stated margins.

  • A3 — Useful projection [Theory → experiment]. Measured microscopic operators project to the predicted leftover tensors. For the worked model, endpoint exchange must approach \(4j/9\) and corrections must scale as \(j^2/J\).

  • A4 — No cluster-count assumption [Speculation]. Three, five, or twenty spins are acceptable only if they improve a measured objective such as gap, addressability, noise susceptibility, or gadget order. More spins are otherwise more fabrication opportunities for the universe to express an opinion.

  • A5 — Operator completeness [Proposal]. Available interactions plus mediators generate both \(Q_v\) and \(B_p\) with the Fibonacci matrix elements. Hamiltonian tomography must include unwanted terms; fitting only the desired coefficients fails this assumption.

  • A6 — Surviving energy scale [Proposal]. The measured \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\), obtained after every projection and gadget suppression, exceeds \(k_BT\), \(\hbar\Gamma\), coupling disorder, and residual interactions.

  • A7 — Phase evidence [Numerics → experiment]. Finite-size calculations using measured parameters show convergence toward doubled-Fibonacci topological data, and success persists across the measured disorder distribution. One carefully tuned small patch is insufficient.

  • A8 — Operational topology [Proposal]. Excitations can be created, moved, and fused without closing the gap, and a nonlocal observable is less sensitive to local perturbations as system size grows.

A sensible experimental ladder is therefore: one cluster spectrum; two-cluster projection; one three-edge vertex; one plaquette operator; then several connected plaquettes. Stop at the first failed inequality.

A tiny patch can falsify a microscopic mapping. It cannot by itself prove a thermodynamic phase.

End-to-end verdict — [Assessment]. The hierarchy is highly speculative but physically coherent.

No link violates a known principle, and the first projection is explicit. Experimental support presently reaches only small coherent spin systems and digitally controlled registers.

The defect-specific cluster Hamiltonian, Fibonacci vertex and plaquette operators, surviving topological gap, and protected logical operation are all unestablished. Neither a five-to-twenty-defect component nor defect-based Fibonacci feasibility may be used as an input assumption.

Ways to get the chain wrong

The local-dimension fallacy. Two levels can encode \(1\) and \(\tau\), a coin toss, or whether lunch happened. Fusion rules live in constraints and recoupling amplitudes, not in the number two.

The five-to-twenty fallacy. No scaling law in this chapter selects that interval.

Increasing cluster size may create a cleaner code space, but it also increases spectral crowding, placement burden, control cross-talk, and the number of disorder parameters. Until a calculation and experiment identify an optimum, the interval has status [Speculation].

The gadget-equals-phase fallacy. Producing one desired term in perturbation theory is not producing the target Hamiltonian.

Lower-order terms can dominate; higher-order terms can be smaller than linewidths; the perturbative parameter can be too large for the expansion and too small for observation. Annoyingly, nature is permitted to notice all orders.

The digital-equals-emergent fallacy. Pulse sequences can prepare a string-net wavefunction and compile braids [R165].

That is [Experiment: digital emulation]. Passive order requires the material Hamiltonian, its gap, and its perturbative stability to do the work between pulses.

The gap-label fallacy is this: \(J\) is a cluster leakage gap, not a topological gap.

\(K_p\) is a Hamiltonian coefficient, not automatically the many-body gap.

Only the spectrum of the full disordered effective model determines \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\).

The protection fallacy. The worked cluster is spinful, so magnetic noise acts within its logical doublet.

Even a genuine two-dimensional topological phase at nonzero temperature contains thermally activated anyons. Topological order does not repeal thermodynamics.

The chirality fallacy. The Levin–Wen target here is doubled Fibonacci. Calling it simply “Fibonacci” hides the time-reversed sector and can lead to incorrect edge and control claims.

Check yourself

Why use three defects rather than assume five to twenty? Three is the smallest exactly tractable cluster with a spinful ground doublet, while the larger count has no demonstrated defect-cluster basis in the cited evidence.

Show that endpoint exchange between two such clusters projects to \((4j/9)\widetilde{\mathbf S}_A\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf S}_B\). Each endpoint spin projects as \(P_C\mathbf S_{\mathrm{end}}P_C=(2/3)\widetilde{\mathbf S}\), so the product of the two leftover factors is \(4/9\). Corrections of order \(j^2/J\) sit outside this first-order statement.

What fails if you map \(|\tilde\uparrow\rangle\) to \(|1\rangle\) and stop? You have named a local basis.

Vertex constraints, plaquette recoupling, a gapped phase, and emergent excitations are still required. Dimension two does not write fusion.

What is the decisive energy scale? The full model’s measured or reliably calculated \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\), after projection and gadget suppression — not the bare cluster coupling \(J\).

What fails if the first cluster does not show the predicted doublet and the \(2:-1:2\) local response? The cluster model is already dead. There is no reason to fabricate a lattice around it.

Chapter 25 — Three graphs that disagree

Draw a honeycomb and put a label on every edge. A string-net vertex term checks the three labels that meet at a corner.

A plaquette term recouples the six labels around a hexagon. That is one drawing.

Now move each label to the midpoint of its edge, and join two midpoints whenever the original edges share a vertex. The new drawing is not a honeycomb. It is a lattice of triangles and hexagons.

Now let every pair of midpoints couple as the laboratory Hamiltonian couples them, including the slow \(1/r^3\) tail and any helper parked at a vertex. The energy sees a third drawing still.

A pretty tiling is not a Hamiltonian. The energy written in the crystal must know the same meetings as the string net, or the operators copied from Levin and Wen act on the wrong graph.

The map the operators were written for

A string-net Hamiltonian asks two adjacency questions: which labels meet at a vertex, and which labels surround a plaquette. That asked-for adjacency is the target graph.

Call it \(G=(V,E)\). Here \(V\) is the set of vertices and \(E\) is the set of edges.

In the primary drawing, every vertex of \(G\) is trivalent: three edges meet there. Those three edges are the three labels that a vertex term will later check.

Hence the operators were written for \(G\), not for a photograph of the chip.

The host crystal does not automatically supply \(G\). It supplies defects at whatever positions fabrication can hold, and couplings that depend on distance, orientation, crystal axis, and leftover damage. Between \(G\) and those couplings sit two more drawings, and they are allowed to disagree.

The chain is

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{topological data} &\longrightarrow \text{target graph} \longrightarrow \text{cluster positions}\\ &\longrightarrow \text{physical couplings} \longrightarrow \text{effective operators}. \end{aligned} \]

Drop any middle arrow and the remaining ones do not compose. That is how a lattice proposal quietly acquires magic wires.

Clusters at the midpoints

Chapter 24 put several physical defects into one low-energy cluster, and asked that cluster to carry a string-net edge label. So put one encoded cluster \(C_e\) at the midpoint of each target edge \(e\). The cluster stores the label — say \(1\) or \(\tau\) for the Fibonacci input theory — not a microscopic defect spin directly.

Those midpoints, with an edge between two clusters whenever the corresponding target edges share a vertex, form the placement graph.

The distinction is easiest to see one graph at a time. The first panel below is the logical honeycomb: labels live on its edges.

The second moves one encoded cluster to every edge midpoint; joining clusters whose honeycomb edges share a vertex produces kagome triangles and hexagons. The third adds the couplings and helpers that the laboratory Hamiltonian may actually contain.

The target, placement, and interaction graphs are different objects. Honeycomb edge labels become kagome-positioned encoded clusters; mediators and unwanted long-range couplings then enlarge the physical interaction graph.

The six central cluster sites alone are incomplete. Each \(C_i\) also belongs to a triangle of three edge centers near each end of its original honeycomb edge. Repeat the construction and the clusters occupy a kagome lattice.

Two clusters are neighbors in the placement graph precisely when their target edges share an endpoint. That construction is the line graph \(L(G)\) of \(G\): the vertices of \(L(G)\) are the edges of \(G\). The name is worth keeping because a line graph is not a plot of a line; it is this mechanical swap of vertices for edges.

An edge of a degree-three graph has two endpoints and meets two other edges at each endpoint, so every cluster has

\[ z_{L(G)}=2(3-1)=4 \]

nearest constraint-neighbors. Hence “honeycomb target” and “kagome device” can both describe the same architecture without contradiction. They are two of the three drawings, not two competing crystals.

If you drop the shared-vertex rule and join every pair of nearby clusters, you have already left \(L(G)\). That larger drawing is the next object, not this one.

Who actually couples

If each nearby pair of clusters coupled only along placement-graph edges, the placement graph would also be the pair graph of the Hamiltonian. Dipolar tails, leftover exchange, cavities, drives, and perturbative gadgets do not stop at the pencil line. Who actually couples is the interaction graph.

The ideal Levin–Wen energy has a vertex term \(Q_v\) and a plaquette term \(B_p\),

\[ H_{\mathrm{SN}}=-\sum_{v\in V} J_v Q_v-\sum_{p}J_p B_p, \]

where \(J_v\) and \(J_p\) are energies.

\(Q_v\) checks the allowed fusion of the three labels incident on vertex \(v\).

\(B_p\) inserts and recouples a loop around plaquette \(p\). On a honeycomb plaquette, \(B_p\) acts on six boundary edge labels and also depends on nearby labels through the recoup

The exact commuting-projector construction is [Theory], not an interaction already known to occur among color centers [R018].

Hence drawing \(G\) does not write \(H_{\mathrm{SN}}\). The Hamiltonian can see only the interaction graph.

The defects inside \(C_e\) are physical spins. The doublet of \(C_e\) is an encoded local degree of freedom.

The labels on \(G\) are string-net variables. Excitations are emergent anyons only if the many-body Hamiltonian actually enters the topological phase.

Programming a circuit, or measuring a few fusion-like outcomes, does not by itself make intrinsic anyons.

One length, then a factor of 0.19

Give each logical honeycomb edge length \(a\), measured in metres. Two incident edge midpoints are separated by

\[ d_1=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a. \]

The numerical factor is dimensionless, so \([d_1]=[a]=\mathrm{m}\). All four nearest placement-graph bonds of a cluster have this same length in the regular embedding. That equality is the main geometric advantage of the primary choice.

Suppose, only to expose the tail, that pair coupling magnitudes scale as \(J(r)=C/r^3\), where \(C\) has units of energy times cubic metres. The next kagome distance is \(d_2=\sqrt{3}\,d_1\). Then

\[ \frac{J(d_2)}{J(d_1)}=\left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^3 =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\approx0.19. \]

Hence a fifth of the nearest-neighbor scale already sits on the next kagome shell. Chapter 26 must retain such non-target terms or provide a demonstrated refocusing mechanism.

This is a derived geometric estimate, not a universal defect coupling. Magnetic dipoles also have angular factors.

Exchange need not follow a power law. Driven interactions can have another range entirely.

Still, \(0.19\) is too large to erase with a hopeful adjective. Drop the \(r^{-3}\) hypothesis and the number changes; do not drop the extra edges.

A vertex helper \(M_v\) may sit near each original honeycomb vertex and couple to the three surrounding \(C_e\). A plaquette helper \(M_p\) may sit at each hexagon center and couple radially to six boundary clusters.

The spokes meet only at their helper, so a planar layout needs no geometric crossing. A six-neighbor helper and an effective six-edge operator are not the same thing.

The latter still requires a controlled gadget or projection.

The geometry has five jobs:

  • keep the logical vertex degree compatible with the branching rule;

  • provide usable and sufficiently uniform separations;

  • avoid unwanted interaction edges or make them correctable;

  • leave physical room for vertex and plaquette helpers without wire crossings;

  • tolerate placement error, missing defects, annealing, surfaces, and crystal-axis constraints.

Fail any one of those and the remaining four do not rescue the Hamiltonian.

Why three edges at a vertex

Let \(z\) denote vertex degree: the number of target edges incident on a target vertex. The standard Levin–Wen construction is naturally expressed on a trivalent graph, \(z=3\), where a local branching constraint tests three labels [R018].

Higher-degree vertices can be resolved into trees of trivalent vertices using additional short edges and choices of fusion basis. That resolution adds degrees of freedom and operators.

It is not free simplification.

If edge clusters are used on a regular degree-\(z\) graph, their line graph has degree

\[ z_{\mathrm{edge\ clusters}}=2(z-1). \]

A triangular target (\(z=6\)) therefore gives degree 10 among edge clusters. A square or kagome target (\(z=4\)) gives degree 6.

A trivalent target gives degree 4. Hence lower degree usually means fewer intended pair channels, fewer spectral collisions, and fewer ways for one bad site to be everyone’s problem.

Drop the trivalent hypothesis and you have not merely redrawn the wallpaper. You have changed the local algebra the vertex term was written to test.

A five-percent wobble

For a distance-dependent coupling, fabrication error becomes coupling disorder. If \(J(r)=C r^{-3}\) and a bond length changes by a small amount \(\delta r\), differentiation gives

\[ \frac{\delta J}{J}\approx -3\frac{\delta r}{r}. \]

The quantities \(\delta r\) and \(r\) must use the same length unit, so the ratio is dimensionless. A 5% radial error therefore means roughly 15% coupling error before angular and defect-to-defect variation are counted. This is geometry, not a forecast for a particular wafer.

Equal drawing lengths also do not guarantee equal spin couplings. For magnetic dipoles the bond direction relative to quantization axes matters.

Defects in crystallographically inequivalent orientations may therefore turn a one-length lattice into a several-coupling Hamiltonian. Pulse engineering might average that anisotropy.

Until derived for the selected defects, that is [Proposal].

Drop the power-law hypothesis and the factor of three changes. Keep it, and a millimetre-scale drawing error is not a rounding error in \(J\).

Drawn edges versus real couplings

Write a target adjacency matrix \(A_{ij}\), equal to one when clusters \(i\) and \(j\) should couple at the leading pairwise level and zero otherwise. Let the realized pair coupling be \(J_{ij}\). A useful geometry makes large \(|J_{ij}|\) coincide with \(A_{ij}=1\), while keeping

\[ \epsilon_{\mathrm{graph}} =\frac{\max_{A_{ij}=0}|J_{ij}|} {\min_{A_{ij}=1}|J_{ij}|} \]

small. This dimensionless ratio does not prove topological stability. It reveals graph mismatch before a heroic many-body calculation begins.

Long-range dipolar coupling means \(A_{ij}=0\) rarely implies \(J_{ij}=0\). Hence \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{graph}}\) is a diagnostic, not a license to delete the tail. If you count only drawn edges, you have already answered a different question from the one the Hamiltonian asks.

A helper in the middle

Every named tiling below is planar, so nearest-neighbor target edges can be drawn without crossings. The harder question is whether the operator-incidence graph is still planar after helpers are added.

One helper per vertex is easy. One helper per face is geometrically natural but may demand coordination equal to face size: six on honeycomb, three and twelve on decorated honeycomb, and four or eight on square–octagon.

A central helper can share a site, cavity, or mode among several bonds. Pairwise microscopic couplings do not automatically become the required product operator.

[Theory] Perturbative constructions can generate multi-body terms only with energy denominators, unwanted corrections, and a reduced effective scale. Chapter 23 supplied that warning.

A lattice cannot repeal perturbation theory.

Hence a six-leg star of pair couplings is not \(B_p\). Drop the gadget derivation and you are left with six ordinary bonds, not a plaquette recoupling.

A drawn dot is not a defect

A drawn coordinate is not a guaranteed active defect. The fabrication stack includes pattern registration, aperture or beam size, ion straggle, vacancy diffusion during annealing, conversion yield, depth distribution, and damage-induced noise.

[Experiment] Toyli and colleagues used electron-beam-defined apertures plus nitrogen implantation to fabricate patterned single-spin and spin-array sites in diamond; for 20 keV \(^{15}\mathrm N\), their modeling gave about 9 nm lateral straggle, under those implantation conditions [R189].

[Experiment] In a different 2017 experiment, focused Si implantation produced SiV centers with approximately 32 nm lateral standard deviation and \(48\pm21\) nm accuracy relative to nanocavities; the measured conversion yield reached about 2.5% at 100 keV before an added electron-irradiation step [R190]. Those are not interchangeable “placement precision” numbers.

They concern different ions, energies, devices, and reported metrics.

A geometry should therefore permit repeated masks or direct-write coordinates, post-fabrication characterization, and spare sites or repair strategies. None of the cited experiments demonstrates a dense, uniformly coupled lattice of encoded clusters realizing a string-net Hamiltonian.

Drop the distinction between beam width and annealed endpoint spread, and you have already understated the disorder that enters \(J_{ij}\).

Which graphs are even on the table

The table separates the target graph from the edge-cluster graph. “Mediator burden” means local vertex and face operators, not merely nearest-neighbor drawing lines.

Candidate target | Target degree | Edge-cluster degree | Spacing/graph issue | Crossing or mediator issue | Fabrication verdict | |

Honeycomb | 3 | 4; positions are kagome | One intended midpoint spacing in regular embedding; dipolar tails remain | No planar crossings; 3-leg vertex and 6-edge face | Primary: simplest trivalent incidence and a single repeated coordinate motif | |

Triangular | 6 | 10 | Dense, strongly overconnected for edge encoding | No geometric crossings, but a six-label vertex must be decomposed | Reject as direct string-net graph; useful only for a different derived model | |

Kagome | 4 | 6 if its edges carry labels | Triangles and hexagons create two face scales; degree exceeds trivalent target | 4-label vertices require resolution; 3- and 6-face mediators | Keep as the placement graph of honeycomb edge clusters, not the primary logical graph | |

Decorated honeycomb / star \((3,12^2)\) | 3 | 4 | Intra-triangle and inter-triangle bonds naturally form at least two classes | 3-edge and 12-edge faces; large face operator or mediator tree | Interesting for Kitaev-type physics, but too many scales for the first defect prototype | |

Ruby | 4 | 6 | Crowded local triangles and colored bond classes | Higher local degree and mediator congestion | Strong theoretical precedent for two-body color-code physics, not a direct Fibonacci edge-label map | |

Square–octagon \((4.8.8)\) | 3 | 4 | Incident midpoint distances are unequal in regular embedding | 3-leg vertices; separate 4- and 8-edge face machinery | Fallback: orthogonal registration is attractive, but two bond/face scales must be calibrated | |

Square | 4 | 6 | One site spacing but wrong degree for direct trivalent branching | 4-label vertex resolution and 4-edge faces | Natural for toric-code stabilizers, not the cleanest doubled-Fibonacci map | |

Brick-wall honeycomb | 3 | 4 | Graph-equivalent to honeycomb but geometrically anisotropic | Same incidence as honeycomb | A mask-friendly deformation of the primary, not a distinct topological candidate | |

The verdict column is a choice of graph, not a report of a material. Each later section earns one of those rows.

Honeycomb

The honeycomb wins by being boring in the correct places. It is trivalent, bipartite, planar, and has one face size.

Levin and Wen’s construction directly uses trivalent string-net branching [R018]. Kitaev’s exactly solved honeycomb model further shows that a simple trivalent interaction graph can support emergent gauge structure and non-Abelian Ising-type excitations for suitable bond-dependent interactions, although that phase is not Fibonacci order [R017].

[Theory] This precedent validates the importance of the graph, not the proposed defect Hamiltonian.

Hence the primary target is honeycomb because the local algebra matches, not because hexagons are fashionable.

Its disadvantage is already sitting in the worked example. Edge encoding turns the cluster positions into degree-four kagome.

Plaquette terms still span six clusters, and long-range tails add unwanted edges. Borrow Kitaev’s anyons and you have borrowed the wrong phase.

Six neighbors

A triangular lattice places six nearest neighbors around every vertex. That is useful for frustrated magnets and quantum dimer models; a gapped resonating-valence-bond phase was established theoretically in the triangular-lattice quantum dimer model [R187]. [Theory] It does not follow that triangular geometry implements the Fibonacci string net needed here.

As a direct target it replaces each trivalent branching check with a six-way junction. Resolving that junction needs internal fusion-tree edges.

With edge clusters, the local pair graph has degree ten. Dense coordination may strengthen connectivity, but it also multiplies unintended dipolar paths and addressability demands.

We reject it for the first architecture. Keep the triangular lattice for a different derived model; do not rename its dimers \(\tau\).

Kagome is not the target

Kagome has four edges meeting at each vertex and contains triangular and hexagonal faces. It is famous for frustration; theory has found fractionalized phases in specific kagome Hamiltonians [R188]. Again, “supports a spin liquid in some model” is not “supports this string net with available couplings.”

Kagome nevertheless has a privileged role here: it arises automatically as the physical midpoint lattice of honeycomb edge variables. In that role, each kagome triangle corresponds to one logical honeycomb vertex and each kagome hexagon corresponds to one logical honeycomb plaquette.

Hence the exact incidence match is more valuable than using kagome as the target graph itself. Take kagome as the target and you have already given up trivalent branching and accepted two face scales.

Decorated honeycomb

Replace every honeycomb vertex by a triangle and one obtains the decorated honeycomb, or star, lattice with face sequence \((3,12,12)\). It remains trivalent.

[Theory] Yao and Kivelson solved a Kitaev-type model on this lattice and found a chiral spin liquid with non-Abelian anyons in part of its phase diagram [R184]. Those excitations are associated with Kitaev/Majorana physics, not doubled Fibonacci string-net order.

For fabrication, decoration provides internal triangles that could coincide with strongly coupled mini-clusters. It also creates two geometric bond classes — within and between triangles — and faces of size three and twelve.

That may be useful if the microscopic Hamiltonian naturally has two scales. It is a liability if uniformity is already the scarce resource.

A twelve-boundary plaquette operation also needs a helper tree or several perturbative stages.

We retain it as a research variant, not the primary layout. Drop the two-scale hypothesis and the decoration is a cost with no corresponding microscopic gift.

Ruby

The ruby lattice is four-valent and uses colored bond types in the best-known topological construction. [Theory] Kargarian, Bombin, and Martin-Delgado gave a two-body spin Hamiltonian on the ruby lattice whose low-energy sector realizes topological color-code order [R185]. This is genuine and relevant evidence that microscopic two-body interactions can encode richer low-energy stabilizers.

It is not evidence for a ruby-lattice Fibonacci phase in defect clusters. Ruby’s degree-four junctions, small triangles, and several bond classes raise control and placement burdens. Its main value to this architecture is methodological: study whether a two-body parent Hamiltonian can generate the required low-energy constraints.

Do not borrow the color-code result and relabel its anyons \(\tau\). The anyons belong to the Hamiltonian that produced them.

Squares mixed with octagons

The Archimedean square–octagon tiling has face sequence \((4,8,8)\) and degree three, so it preserves trivalent branching. Kitaev-type models on it support a rich set of Abelian and non-Abelian phases in theory [R186], though those results again do not establish Fibonacci order or defect feasibility.

Its straight, orthogonal square motif is friendly to lithographic registration. The price appears even before materials physics. At a vertex, the angles between incident edges are \(90^\circ,135^\circ,135^\circ\). For equal target-edge length \(a\), adjacent midpoint distances are

\[ d_{90}=a\sin45^\circ=\frac{a}{\sqrt2},\qquad d_{135}=a\sin67.5^\circ\approx0.924a. \]

A pure \(r^{-3}\) interaction would differ by

\[ \left(\frac{d_{135}}{d_{90}}\right)^3\approx2.23 \]

between those two intended bond lengths. The square and octagonal plaquettes also require four-edge and eight-edge operations. Calibration, geometric distortion, or driven equalization is therefore mandatory.

Hence the fallback is viable because its logical degree and planarity are right — not because the regular embedding is uniform. Drop the equal-edge hypothesis and you might flatten the 2.23; you then owe a derivation of the distortion that did it.

A square, and a brick-wall honeycomb

The square lattice hosts many toric-code drawings, but its degree-four vertices do not directly match a trivalent Fibonacci fusion tree.

A brick-wall embedding is graph-isomorphic to honeycomb: bend the edges until rows and columns look rectangular without changing which vertices connect. Topological lattice models tolerate such graph-preserving deformation at the ideal level.

Physical coupling strengths do not. Brick-wall coordinates may simplify a write pattern, but unequal bond lengths or orientations must be carried into the Hamiltonian.

We regard it as a fabrication variant of the primary honeycomb, not the fallback phase graph. Isomorphism of \(G\) is not isomorphism of the interaction graph.

What the laboratory can put down

[Experiment] Patterned arrays and individual nanostructure targets have been implanted [R189]; [R190]. These capabilities support coordinate lists at tens-to-hundreds-of-nanometres scales in particular experiments, not arbitrary interaction matrices.

The proposed string-net prototype needs substantially more:

  • several defects must form each reproducible cluster doublet;

  • intra-cluster couplings must dominate inter-cluster couplings;

  • every intended edge must have the correct sign, tensor structure, and strength;

  • unwanted long-range couplings must be included or suppressed;

  • missing or wrong-charge defects must be found and repaired;

  • vertex and plaquette terms must emerge with a gap larger than disorder and decoherence.

No cited experiment meets that list. The geometry decision is therefore [Proposal]: use a shallow planar patterned layer in a host whose chosen defect species can be created and read out, first testing isolated triangles and hexagons.

Diamond has direct patterned-implantation evidence [R189]; [R190]. Silicon carbide may offer wafer-scale fabrication advantages, but this chapter does not assume equal placement yield, coherence, or coupling without host- and defect-specific evidence.

A graph-first sequence should test one logical vertex, then two vertices sharing an edge cluster, then one hexagonal plaquette with neighboring legs. Measure each projected constraint before tiling the coordinate cell.

Ways to get this wrong

Confusing target and placement lattices. Call the device “kagome” without saying that kagome sites encode honeycomb edges, and the branching map is already lost. Call it “honeycomb” and you can conceal the degree-four physical neighbor graph.

Counting drawn edges, not couplings. Dipolar interactions do not stop at the nearest-neighbor pencil line.

Evaluate \(J_{ij}\), angular factors, and \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{graph}}\). What fails if you set every \(A_{ij}=0\) entry to \(J_{ij}=0\) is the tail that Chapter 26 still has to write.

Equating equal distance with equal interaction. Crystal orientation, strain, charge state, and quantization axis remain. Geometry controls only part of \(J_{ij}\).

Treating a helper as a many-body term. A six-leg star of pair couplings is not \(B_p\). The effective operator and its correction terms must be derived.

Borrowing an anyon from another Hamiltonian. Decorated-honeycomb and square–octagon Kitaev models provide non-Abelian precedents [R184]; [R186]; ruby models provide color-code order [R185]. None thereby realizes Fibonacci anyons in the proposed defects.

Using nominal beam size as final defect uncertainty. Straggle, annealing, registration, and stochastic conversion survive the beam specification [R189]; [R190].

Optimizing only nearest-neighbor spacing. Making \(a\) small strengthens desired and undesired interactions, crowds clusters and helpers, and can merge damage volumes.

Making \(a\) large improves addressability while weakening local interactions. Chapter 28 must optimize the full error and coupling budget.

Assuming planarity removes crossings in Hilbert space. A planar drawing can still require nonplanar control connectivity or a high-degree cavity mode. “No crossed ink” is a necessary convenience, not a Hamiltonian theorem.

Which graph we keep

Primary — honeycomb logical graph, kagome cluster positions. It matches trivalent branching without auxiliary fusion-tree vertices; all nearest edge-midpoint separations are equal in the regular embedding; its line graph has degree four; vertex and hexagonal plaquette helpers fit without planar crossings; and the pattern repeats with one coordinate motif. Fabrication remains challenging because clusters, yields, long-range tails, and six-edge effective terms are unproved.

Fallback — square–octagon logical graph. It preserves degree three and planarity while offering an orthogonal square motif that may suit registration, routing, or device boundaries.

It loses on uniform spacing: its regular edge-midpoint layout has two intended distances and two face sizes, so it demands calibration or engineered couplings. Choose it only if fabrication tests show that orthogonal patterning and access outweigh the factor-of-about-2.23 geometric spread in a nominal \(r^{-3}\) bond scale.

Both choices are proposals, not reports of an observed topological material. The selected target graph is trivalent honeycomb.

One encoded cluster occupies each edge midpoint. The physical nearest-constraint graph is degree-four kagome.

A vertex term addresses three clusters and a hexagonal plaquette term at least six boundary clusters. The regular nearest midpoint spacing is \(\sqrt{3}\,a/2\).

Long-range pair terms stay in the Hamiltonian. Square–octagon is the fallback, with two intended midpoint distances and four- and eight-edge faces.

The next job is no longer to choose a tiling. It is to write the zero-field, Zeeman, dipolar, exchange, strain, phonon, and drive terms that can actually produce that graph and its required operators.

Check yourself

Show that honeycomb edge clusters occupy a kagome lattice of degree four.

Two cluster sites are adjacent when their honeycomb edges share a vertex. That line-graph construction is kagome, and \(z_{L(G)}=2(3-1)=4\).

What are the three graphs that must not be conflated?

The string-net target graph, the physical placement graph, and the realized interaction graph including unwanted and mediated couplings.

Show that a pure \(r^{-3}\) tail on the next kagome shell is about \(0.19\).

The next distance is \(d_2=\sqrt{3}\,d_1\), so \(J(d_2)/J(d_1)=(d_1/d_2)^3=1/(3\sqrt{3})\approx0.19\).

What fails if you take planarity as a proof that mediators are easy?

Geometric edge crossings disappear, but high-degree mediators and effective multi-body operators still require a physical derivation. A six-leg star is not \(B_p\).

What is the primary/fallback decision?

Primary: honeycomb target with kagome edge-cluster positions. Fallback: square–octagon target, accepted only with compensation for its two spacing and face classes, including the factor-of-about-\(2.23\) spread in a nominal \(r^{-3}\) bond scale.

What fails if beam width is used as “placement accuracy”?

Beam width, lateral straggle, final defect distribution, and registration to a device are different quantities. None of the cited numbers may be used without its definition and conditions.

A pretty tiling is not a Hamiltonian. Honeycomb is the target graph because it is trivalent and has one face size.

Kagome is where the clusters sit. Who couples is a third drawing, and the \(0.19\) dipolar tail is already enough to keep the extra edges.

Chapter 26 — What diamond actually writes

Three red points sit a few nanometres apart inside a diamond. Each is an NV\(^-\): one carbon gone, a nitrogen next door, an extra electron that glows.

You already know the 2.87 GHz split and the microwave that parks that electron in \(m_s=0\) or \(m_s=-1\). The leftover \(m_s=+1\) is leakage, not a third answer.

Those three electrons can feel one another. A magnetic dipole falls as \(1/r^3\).

At five nanometres that is hundreds of kilohertz, not gigahertz. Diamond also gives each defect a crystal axis, a nitrogen nucleus, strain, phonons, and whatever microwave you shine in.

A host-supported microscopic Hamiltonian is the operator whose every term is either a thing diamond supplies or a thing we write down in order to set it to zero. We take that as the definition.

Then we throw unused states away twice: first each spin-1 down to a driven qubit, then each triangle down to two cluster states. The shopping list becomes an operator only after we have a picture we can actually solve.

Three vacancies in a triangle

Take three NV\(^-\) centers with the same crystal axis, and call that axis local \(z\). Put them, ideally, at the vertices of an equilateral triangle in the plane perpendicular to \(z\).

A diamond (111) plane has that symmetry. Fabricating many identical nanometre-scale triangles is a proposal, not a demonstrated device.

Each ground-state NV electron has spin \(S=1\). Write \(|0\rangle\) for \(m_s=0\) and \(|1\rangle\) for \(m_s=-1\). Define Pauli operators \(\tau^\alpha\), for \(\alpha=x,y,z\), by

\[ \tau^z|0\rangle=|0\rangle,\qquad \tau^z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle. \]

The omitted \(m_s=+1\) state is leakage, not a third qubit value.

Use a static field \(B_0\) along \(z\), and apply a microwave near the \(|0\rangle\leftrightarrow|1\rangle\) line. Sit in a frame that rotates with that microwave.

Fast leftover oscillations can be dropped if the leftover frequencies are huge compared with the couplings. That drop is the rotating-wave approximation.

What remains of the dipole is called secular: the part that does not shake at gigahertz.

For two identical, resonant NV qubits the secular pair energy is

\[ \frac{H_{ij}^{\rm sec}}{h} = \frac{c_{ij}}{4}(1-3\cos^2\theta_{ij}) \left(\tau_i^z\tau_j^z-\tau_i^x\tau_j^x-\tau_i^y\tau_j^y\right) +\text{one-body shifts}. \]

Here \(h\) is Planck’s constant, \(c_{ij}>0\) is a frequency defined below, and \(\theta_{ij}\) is the angle between the pair displacement and \(z\). For the planar triangle, \(\theta_{ij}=\pi/2\). If all three sides are equal, write \(c_{ij}=c\). The cluster Hamiltonian is then

\[ \frac{H_C}{h}=\frac{c}{4}\sum_{i<j\in C} \left(\tau_i^z\tau_j^z-\tau_i^x\tau_j^x-\tau_i^y\tau_j^y\right). \tag{26.1} \]

This toy is small enough to solve. In the one-excitation basis \(\{|100\rangle,|010\rangle,|001\rangle\}\), every diagonal entry is \(-c/4\), and every off-diagonal hop is \(-c/2\). Therefore the symmetric state

\[ |W_1\rangle=\frac{|100\rangle+|010\rangle+|001\rangle}{\sqrt3} \]

has quasienergy \(-5hc/4\), while the two states with phases \(1,e^{\pm2\pi i/3},e^{\mp2\pi i/3}\) have quasienergy \(+hc/4\). Those rotating-frame numbers are quasienergies: they are defined only while the drive and its clock are on, and they are defined only up to the drive frequency. The name is worth keeping because a quasienergy is not a laboratory energy; turn the drive off and the number is no longer the splitting you will measure.

Flip every qubit and the two-excitation state

\[ |W_2\rangle=\frac{|011\rangle+|101\rangle+|110\rangle}{\sqrt3} \]

also has quasienergy \(-5hc/4\). The fully polarized states have quasienergy \(+3hc/4\). Thus, in the ideal resonant rotating frame, \(|W_1\rangle\) and \(|W_2\rangle\) form a doublet separated from the nearest cluster states by

\[ \Delta_C/h=\frac{3c}{2}. \tag{26.2} \]

Hence the cluster gap of the ideal triangle is \(3c/2\) in frequency units, between the symmetric \(W\)-state doublet and the chiral states.

Define cluster Pauli operators \(X_C,Y_C,Z_C\) with \(Z_C|W_1\rangle=|W_1\rangle\) and \(Z_C|W_2\rangle=-|W_2\rangle\). If \(P_C\) projects onto this doublet, direct evaluation gives, for any site \(i\) in the symmetric triangle,

\[ P_C\tau_i^zP_C=\frac13 Z_C,\qquad P_C\tau_i^xP_C=\frac23 X_C,\qquad P_C\tau_i^yP_C=\frac23 Y_C. \tag{26.3} \]

Equation (26.3) is the microscopic-to-encoded dictionary. It is also a warning.

A physical pair interaction remains an encoded pair interaction at first order. Projection shrinks and rotates coefficients.

It does not spontaneously manufacture a plaquette operator.

Drop the equal-side, equal-axis hypotheses and the doublet of (26.2) splits. The dictionary (26.3) is then a different matrix, not a small footnote.

Every term diamond actually writes

We write \(H/h\), so every coefficient is in hertz. Electron spin operators \(S_i^\alpha\) are dimensionless and have eigenvalues \(m_s=0,\pm1\).

Each NV has a local orthonormal frame \((x_i,y_i,z_i)\), with \(z_i\) along the nitrogen–vacancy axis. The selected array uses only one of diamond’s four NV orientations.

Mixing orientations would produce different splittings and interaction tensors.

Now the shopping list becomes an operator. A host-supported microscopic Hamiltonian is

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{H}{h}={}& \sum_i\Big[D_i\big((S_i^{z_i})^2-\tfrac23\big) +E_{x,i}\big((S_i^{x_i})^2-(S_i^{y_i})^2\big) +E_{y,i}\{S_i^{x_i},S_i^{y_i}\}\Big] \\ &+\sum_i\gamma_e\mathbf B_i\cdot\mathbf S_i +\sum_i\left(\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf A_i\cdot\mathbf I_i +P_i(I_i^{z_i})^2-\gamma_{n,i}\mathbf B_i\cdot\mathbf I_i\right)\\ &+\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}\left[\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j -3(\mathbf S_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij})(\mathbf S_j\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij})\right]\\ &+\sum_{i<j}J^{\rm ex}_{ij}\,\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j +\frac{H_{\rm strain}(t)+H_{\rm ph}+H_{\rm drive}(t)}{h}. \tag{26.4} \end{aligned} \]

The anticommutator is \(\{A,B\}=AB+BA\). Every line is a thing diamond actually supplies, or a thing we write down in order to set it to zero.

Zero-field and static strain. \(D_i\) is the axial zero-field splitting. For the NV\(^-\) ground state near room temperature, \(D\approx2.87\ \mathrm{GHz}\) [R074].

Subtracting \(2/3\) only removes an irrelevant trace. The frequencies \(E_{x,i}\) and \(E_{y,i}\) describe transverse symmetry breaking from static strain and electric fields.

The NV ground-state spin Hamiltonian and its electric response are experimentally established [Experiment] [R074]; [R191].

It is useful to separate controllable or fluctuating strain:

\[ \frac{H_{\rm strain}(t)}{h}=\sum_i\left[ \delta D_i(t)(S_i^{z_i})^2+ \epsilon_{x,i}(t)((S_i^{x_i})^2-(S_i^{y_i})^2)+ \epsilon_{y,i}(t)\{S_i^{x_i},S_i^{y_i}\}\right]. \tag{26.5} \]

The coefficients already include the appropriate spin–strain susceptibility and therefore have units of hertz. Mechanical control of NV spin transitions has been demonstrated [Experiment] [R192]; [R193]. Equation (26.5) does not assume a strain-mediated interaction between distant defects.

Zeeman term. \(\gamma_e=g_e\mu_B/h\approx28\ \mathrm{GHz/T}\) is the electron gyromagnetic ratio in frequency units, \(\mathbf B_i\) is the magnetic field in tesla, and \(\mathbf S_i\) is dimensionless. Thus \(\gamma_eB\) has units \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), as required.

Hyperfine term. \(\mathbf I_i\) is the dimensionless \(^{14}\mathrm N\) or \(^{15}\mathrm N\) nuclear spin; \(\mathbf A_i\) is its hyperfine tensor in hertz.

\(P_i\) is the \(^{14}\mathrm N\) quadrupole coefficient, and \(\gamma_{n,i}\) is the nuclear gyromagnetic ratio. Nearby \(^{13}\mathrm C\) nuclei add terms of the same form.

Hyperfine coupling is not optional bookkeeping: its megahertz-scale structure can exceed the dipolar coupling in the example below [R074]. The proposal therefore requires isotopic \(^{12}\mathrm C\) enrichment and preparation of every nitrogen nucleus in a specified state.

Otherwise “identical NVs” is false.

Magnetic dipole–dipole term. \(\mathbf r_{ij}\) points from defect \(i\) to \(j\), \(r_{ij}=|\mathbf r_{ij}|\), and \(\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}=\mathbf r_{ij}/r_{ij}\). Its coefficient is

\[ c_{ij}=\frac{\mu_0(g_e\mu_B)^2}{4\pi h\,r_{ij}^3}. \tag{26.6} \]

The units check is \((\mathrm{T\,m/A})(\mathrm{J/T})^2/(\mathrm{J\,s\,m^3})=\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Numerically, \(c_{ij}\approx52\ \mathrm{MHz}(1\ \mathrm{nm}/r_{ij})^3\).

Coherent coupling and entanglement between separate NV electron spins have been demonstrated [Experiment] [R080]. This supports the term, not the proposed array yield.

Exchange. \(J^{\rm ex}_{ij}\) is an isotropic overlap-mediated exchange frequency. Diamond does not provide a verified, lithographically tunable long-range NV–NV exchange bus.

Because electronic wave-function overlap decays rapidly with separation, the 5–10 nm toy array below sets \(J^{\rm ex}_{ij}\approx0\). We retain the symbol in (26.4) to state what was discarded, not to borrow a convenient Heisenberg interaction.

In particular, the antiferromagnetic open-chain Hamiltonian sometimes used for an abstract three-spin encoded qubit does not follow from this NV geometry.

Phonons. Let \(b_q\) destroy a phonon in normal mode \(q\), with frequency \(\nu_q\). A compact supported form is

\[ \frac{H_{\rm ph}}h=\sum_q\nu_q b_q^\dagger b_q+ \sum_{i,q}(b_q+b_q^\dagger) \left[g_{iq}^{\parallel}(S_i^{z_i})^2+g_{iq}^{x}Q_i^x+g_{iq}^{y}Q_i^y\right], \tag{26.7} \]

where \(Q_i^x=(S_i^{x_i})^2-(S_i^{y_i})^2\), \(Q_i^y=\{S_i^{x_i},S_i^{y_i}\}\), and each \(g\) is a frequency. Phonons can coherently drive a selected mechanical mode [R192]; [R193], but an uncontrolled bath produces relaxation and dephasing.

Measured NV longitudinal relaxation depends strongly on temperature [Experiment] [R194]. We do not replace that bath with a noiseless interaction.

Drive. A microwave magnetic field \(\mathbf B_{1,i}(t)\) gives

\[ \frac{H_{\rm drive}(t)}h=\sum_i\gamma_e\mathbf B_{1,i}(t)\cdot\mathbf S_i. \tag{26.8} \]

Optical fields can initialize and read the NV through excited electronic states [R074], but those states are outside (26.4). Adiabatic elimination would add light shifts, Raman couplings, scattering, and optical decay together. We do not keep the useful term and misplace the decay under the rug.

Hence every symbol in (26.4) is either measured, estimated, or set to zero on purpose. Drop the “set to zero” column and you have changed the host.

From spin 1 to a driven qubit

Let \(P_i=|0\rangle\langle0|+|1\rangle\langle1|\). In this subspace,

\[ P_iS_i^zP_i=\frac{\tau_i^z-\mathbb1}{2},\qquad P_iS_i^xP_i=\frac{\tau_i^x}{\sqrt2},\qquad P_iS_i^yP_i=\frac{\tau_i^y}{\sqrt2}. \tag{26.9} \]

For a field along the NV axis, the two transition frequencies from \(m_s=0\) are approximately \(\omega_-=D-\gamma_eB_0\) and \(\omega_+=D+\gamma_eB_0\). A drive near \(\omega_-\), with \(\omega_-\), \(\omega_+\), and their separation all much larger than couplings and Rabi frequencies, permits the rotating-wave and leakage expansions. Projecting (26.6) and discarding terms oscillating near gigahertz frequencies gives the secular pair Hamiltonian used in the triangle.

This derivation is [Theory]. It describes a Floquet quasienergy Hamiltonian sustained by a phase reference.

Turning off the resonant drive restores the large laboratory energy difference between \(|W_1\rangle\) and \(|W_2\rangle\). The encoded doublet is therefore not a passive ground-space doublet.

Hence the first projection is a driven two-level truncation, not a spontaneous encoding. The three microscopic NV spins are still physical spins.

The two states retained at each NV are still physical qubit levels. Nothing in (26.9) has invented an anyon.

What fails if the leftover frequencies are not huge compared with the couplings is the rotating-wave step itself: gigahertz terms that were dropped come back, and (26.1) is no longer the pair energy.

From a triangle to two cluster states

Let \(P=\prod_C P_C\) project every triangle onto the doublet of (26.2), and let \(V\) contain intercluster dipolar bonds, detuning disorder, and weak drives. Schrieffer–Wolff perturbation theory — the downstairs-and-upstairs expansion of Chapter 22 — gives

\[ \frac{H_{\rm eff}}h=P\frac{H_C+V}{h}P -P\frac{V}{h}Q\left(Q\frac{H_C-E_0}{h}Q\right)^{-1}Q\frac{V}{h}P +O\!\left(\frac{v^3}{(\Delta_C/h)^2}\right), \tag{26.10} \]

where \(Q=\mathbb1-P\), \(E_0\) is the ideal doublet energy, and \(v\) bounds the frequencies in \(V\). Hidden states still matter: a traveler can briefly leave the retained space, take a shortcut, and return. Those virtual excursions are the second-order terms.

For a physical bond between site \(i\) of cluster \(C\) and site \(j\) of cluster \(D\), (26.3) yields

\[ P\,\tau_{i}^{\alpha}T_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}\tau_j^\beta P =M_\alpha M_\beta\, \Sigma_C^\alpha T_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}\Sigma_D^\beta, \quad (M_x,M_y,M_z)=\left(\frac23,\frac23,\frac13\right), \tag{26.11} \]

with repeated \(\alpha,\beta\) summed, \(T_{ij}\) the physical dipolar tensor in hertz, and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_C=(X_C,Y_C,Z_C)\). A uniform resonant transverse drive projects as \(P_C\Gamma\sum_i\tau_i^xP_C=2\Gamma X_C\).

A detuning \(\sum_i\delta_i\tau_i^z/2\) gives \((\sum_i\delta_i)Z_C/6\) at first order. Unequal detunings also mix the doublet with the chiral states and generate corrections of order \(\sigma_\delta^2/(\Delta_C/h)\).

Consequently the toy model is

\[ \frac{H_{\rm eff}}h= \sum_C(2\Gamma_C X_C+\bar\delta_C Z_C) +\sum_{\langle C,D\rangle}\sum_{\alpha,\beta} \widetilde J_{CD}^{\alpha\beta}\Sigma_C^\alpha\Sigma_D^\beta +\delta H^{(2)}/h, \tag{26.12} \]

not a string-net Hamiltonian. Here \(\widetilde J=M T M\), and \(\delta H^{(2)}/h\) contains shifts and additional two-cluster or, when two bonds share a virtual cluster excitation, small multicluster terms of scale at most roughly \(u^2/(\Delta_C/h)\).

Their coefficients are fixed by geometry and denominators. They are not automatically Fibonacci \(F\)-symbols.

Hence a first-order intercluster bond remains a bilinear bond between cluster Pauli operators, with projection factors \((2/3,2/3,1/3)\). A cluster doublet is an encoded pseudospin.

A periodically driven array of those pseudospins is an analog emulator. Neither label, alone or together, establishes emergent anyons or equilibrium topological order.

Choose \(B_0=20\ \mathrm{mT}\). Using \(D=2.87\ \mathrm{GHz}\) and \(\gamma_e=28\ \mathrm{GHz/T}\) gives \(\omega_-\approx2.31\ \mathrm{GHz}\) and \(\omega_+\approx3.43\ \mathrm{GHz}\).

For an illustrative triangle side \(r=5\ \mathrm{nm}\), (26.6) gives \(c\approx52/5^3\ \mathrm{MHz}=0.416\ \mathrm{MHz}\), so \(\Delta_C/h\approx0.624\ \mathrm{MHz}\). At a representative \(10\ \mathrm{nm}\) intercluster separation, the unprojected dipolar scale is \(u\lesssim52\ \mathrm{kHz}\) before angular and projection factors.

A weak drive \(\Gamma\sim20\ \mathrm{kHz}\) would satisfy \(u,\Gamma\ll\Delta_C/h\ll\omega_\pm\).

The dimensional hierarchy is therefore plausible on paper. The complete regime is stricter: \[ \omega_\pm\gg c\gg u,\Gamma,\sigma_\delta,\Gamma_{\rm decoh}, \qquad k_BT/h\ll\Delta_{\rm desired}/h, \tag{26.13} \] while nuclear states must be fixed and the rotating-frame phases synchronized.

The last thermal inequality refers to a desired many-body gap, which (26.12) has not been shown to possess.

Nanoscale aperture masks with sub-10 nm features have confined implanted NV clusters, including clusters of up to three centers [Experiment] [R195]; ion straggle and conversion statistics mean this is not deterministic placement of the specified 5 nm equilateral triangle, much less a honeycomb-edge array.

The numbers are a falsifiable design point [Proposal], not an experimental device claim.

The leading controlled corrections are now explicit:

\[ \left\|\delta H^{(2)}/h\right\| =O\!\left(\frac{u^2+\Gamma^2+\sigma_\delta^2}{\Delta_C/h} +\frac{c^2+\Omega^2}{\min(\omega_-,\omega_+)} +\frac{c^2+\Omega^2+E_\perp^2}{\Delta_{\rm leak}/h}\right), \tag{26.14} \]

where \(\Omega\) is a physical microwave Rabi frequency, \(E_\perp^2=E_x^2+E_y^2\), and \(\Delta_{\rm leak}\) is the relevant separation to \(m_s=+1\). The first fraction is cluster leakage, the second is the nonsecular or Bloch–Siegert correction, and the third is spin-1 leakage.

Equation (26.14) is scaling, not an equality. A device calculation must diagonalize its actual tensor geometry.

What fails if \(u\) is not small compared with \(\Delta_C/h\) is the Schrieffer–Wolff truncation: the traveler does not return, and the retained doublet is no longer the slow space.

What the operator still is not

The hoped-for chain is NV electron spins, then coupled three-NV clusters, then cluster pseudospins, then a honeycomb-edge model, then topological order. The last step is a question mark.

A low-energy projector only translates the microscopic interactions that are present. It does not award extra interactions for architectural enthusiasm.

The doubled-Fibonacci Levin–Wen target has a local branching constraint \(Q_v\) at every trivalent vertex and a plaquette operator \(B_p\) that inserts a loop and recouples edge labels with the Fibonacci \(F\)-symbols [R018]. For the honeycomb-edge architecture, (26.12) is missing:

  • a three-edge vertex projector with the correct allowed Fibonacci fusion channels;

  • the conditional, many-edge off-diagonal plaquette action with the correct relative amplitudes and phases;

  • a mechanism canceling larger one-body and two-body terms without also closing the intended gap;

  • evidence that residual terms in (26.14) lie inside the doubled-Fibonacci phase’s stability region;

  • a passive laboratory-frame ground manifold. The present doublet is resonantly dressed.

Higher-order gadgets could be proposed to address items 1–3, but they require mediators and produce amplitudes suppressed by products of \(u/\Delta_C\). Those mediators are not in the selected microscopic Hamiltonian. Therefore [Theory] the derived model is an anisotropic, driven pseudospin model; [Speculation] it might become an ingredient of a separately engineered gadget construction; it is not presently a derivation of Fibonacci order.

Three questions, answered in order. What roads does diamond provide?

Known. Which roads remain inside the chosen subspace?

Calculable. Do the remaining roads have the pattern required by the target topological model?

No. That is a successful derivation, not a failed sales pitch.

What the laboratory actually has

[Experiment] Single-NV zero-field, Zeeman, hyperfine, electric/strain, microwave, optical, and phonon-relaxation physics are well characterized [R074]; [R191]; [R192]; [R193]; [R194]. [Experiment] Dipolar coupling has been used to entangle two individually addressed NV electron spins [R080]. These facts justify the terms in (26.4).

What is not established is equally specific. References [R074]; [R191]; [R192]; [R193]; [R080]; [R194]; [R018]; [R195] do not report a mesoscopic array of identical 5 nm three-NV triangles with fixed orientation, initialized nuclear states, uniform detunings, and individually phased drives.

They do not measure the cluster gap in (26.2), nor a many-body topological gap, topological degeneracy, string operator, or anyonic excitation in this material architecture. The microscopic ingredients and the proposed architecture therefore remain separated by a fabrication-and-control gap.

A measured pair coupling is a physical bond. A projected cluster doublet is an encoded leftover. Neither object is a vertex projector, a plaquette recoupling, or a topological gap.

Ways to get this wrong

Calling a rotating frame a passive phase. Quasienergy degeneracy depends on a drive and a clock.

It is not thermal ground-state protection. What fails if the drive is turned off is the doublet of (26.2) itself: the laboratory splitting between \(|W_1\rangle\) and \(|W_2\rangle\) returns.

Replacing dipole coupling with friendly exchange. Isotropic antiferromagnetic exchange makes elegant encoded-spin algebra, but it is not a supported 5–10 nm NV coupling here. Keep \(J^{\rm ex}_{ij}\) in (26.4) and set it to zero on purpose; silently restoring it changes the host.

Ignoring the nitrogen nucleus. An unresolved hyperfine manifold is not a small footnote compared with a sub-megahertz cluster gap.

Treating phonons only as a bus. The same coupling permits relaxation and dephasing. A coherent-mode proposal must include loss and thermal occupation.

Confusing first-order projection with a gadget. Equations (26.3) and (26.11) preserve operator locality. Multibody terms require virtual processes and arrive with denominators and competitors.

Inferring a phase from a Hamiltonian’s vocabulary. “Honeycomb,” “cluster,” and “plaquette” are nouns. The spectrum, gap, ground-state degeneracy, and quasiparticle data carry the physics.

Using the toy numbers as tolerances. Five and ten nanometres are assumed separations, not achieved placement distributions or yields.

Check yourself

Why is exchange written and then set to zero?

To make the microscopic audit explicit. Long-range tunable NV–NV exchange is not a supported resource for the chosen spacing; silently using it would change the host.

Show that the ideal triangle has cluster leakage gap \(\Delta_C/h=3c/2\).

In the one-excitation basis the symmetric \(W\)-state sits at \(-5c/4\) and the chiral states at \(+c/4\), so the gap is \(3c/2\). The two-excitation partner \(|W_2\rangle\) matches.

What fails if you replace the dipole with isotropic antiferromagnetic exchange?

The secular pair energy is no longer the XXZ form of (26.1), and the abstract three-spin Heisenberg encoding of Chapter 24 does not follow from this NV geometry.

Show that an intercluster dipolar bond remains bilinear at first order.

Equation (26.3) sends each physical Pauli to a cluster Pauli times \((2/3,2/3,1/3)\), so (26.11) is still a two-cluster coupling \(\widetilde J=MTM\).

Which target terms are absent?

The Fibonacci branching projector and the conditional \(F\)-symbol plaquette recoupling operator, along with a demonstrated passive topological gap.

What fails if the resonant drive is turned off?

Quasienergy degeneracy of \(|W_1\rangle\) and \(|W_2\rangle\) disappears. The laboratory-frame splitting returns, and the encoded doublet is no longer a passive ground-space pair.

A same-orientation NV array is described by (26.4). Spin-1 projection gives (26.9) and a secular dipolar tensor.

An ideal resonantly driven three-NV triangle has the doublet (26.2). Local operators project according to (26.3).

Intercluster bonds produce (26.11) with corrections scaling as (26.14). None of that is a static encoded doublet, isotropic exchange, a vertex projector, a plaquette recoupling, or a topological gap.

Part X — Numbers, noise, and other kitchens

Energy, distance, gaps, noise, protection, and two other labs trying the same dream. A number travels with a passport.

Chapter 27 — A number that travels with a passport

Someone writes 13 ms on the whiteboard and sits down. The room now has a coherence time for silicon vacancies. It does not.

The 13 ms is real, and it is narrower than that sentence. It was recorded on one SiV\(^-\) electron spin, near 100 mK, after a CPMG-32 pulse train, in diamond with \(10^{-3}\%\) \(^{13}\)C [R083]. Warm the stone, skip the pulses, or put the carbon-13 back, and you are measuring a different object.

A recorded number together with those conditions is a passport. We take this as the definition.

The rest of the chapter treats a frequency, a time, or a fidelity without a passport as unusable in a Hamiltonian. The number can still tell a story.

It should not cross an engineering border.

Three objects, one unit

A slide can show 2.87 GHz, 4.93 kHz, and 12.7 kHz in the same column. Hertz is a crowded room. Those three numbers are not three sizes of one thing.

The first is a static level splitting: it picks a local basis. The NV\(^-\) ground-state zero-field splitting is one of those. It tells \(m_s=0\) from \(m_s=\pm1\) before a magnet is turned on.

The second is a coupling: it moves information or makes entanglement. The fitted dipolar matrix element of a 25 nm NV pair is one of those.

The third is a decay or a linewidth: it erases phase. A Ramsey width, an echo width, and a phonon-broadened optical line are three of those, and they are not interchangeable with each other either.

All three can be quoted in megahertz. The shared unit does not make them the same object.

Hence a large on-site splitting does not rescue a tiny intercluster coupling, and a millisecond echo does not promise a millisecond of undriven many-body evolution. “Works at room temperature” does not mean thermal equilibrium prepares the spin you wanted.

Two comparisons will keep coming back:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{useful coupling} &> \text{uncontrolled broadening and drift},\\ \text{effective gap} &> \text{thermal and disorder scales}. \end{aligned} \]

This chapter fills the left- and right-hand sides with numbers that still have their passports. Filling those sides does not produce a topological gap. That object is a spectrum, and it is not on this page.

Treat each entry as a record with mandatory fields:

quantity | platform and charge state | sample | temperature
| field/strain/drive protocol | measurement definition | source

Drop any field and the number is free to wander into the wrong inequality.

Hertz become kelvin once you name the map

Laboratories speak frequency. Thermometers speak kelvin. A Hamiltonian, strictly, speaks joules. Those are three names for the same interval once the conversion is named.

Let \(\nu\) be ordinary cyclic frequency, in hertz. Let \(\omega=2\pi\nu\) be angular frequency, in radians per second. Let \(E\) be energy, in joules or electronvolts. Define

\[ E=h\nu=\hbar\omega, \qquad T_E=\frac{E}{k_{\mathrm B}}=\frac{h\nu}{k_{\mathrm B}}, \]

where \(h\) is Planck’s constant, \(\hbar=h/(2\pi)\), and \(k_{\mathrm B}\) is Boltzmann’s constant. The number \(T_E\) is the equivalent temperature of that energy.

The name is worth keeping because it is not the temperature of the cryostat. It is the temperature at which \(k_{\mathrm B}T\) would match \(E\).

The constants \(h=6.62607015\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\), \(k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\), and the elementary charge are exact in the SI [R196]. Therefore

\[ \begin{aligned} 1\ \mathrm{GHz}&\leftrightarrow 4.135667696\ \mu\mathrm{eV}\leftrightarrow 47.9924307\ \mathrm{mK},\\ 1\ \mathrm{MHz}&\leftrightarrow 0.004135667696\ \mu\mathrm{eV}\leftrightarrow 47.9924307\ \mu\mathrm{K},\\ 1\ \mathrm{kHz}&\leftrightarrow 4.135667696\times10^{-6}\ \mu\mathrm{eV}\leftrightarrow 47.9924307\ \mathrm{nK},\\ 1\ \mathrm{K}&\leftrightarrow 86.1733326\ \mu\mathrm{eV}\leftrightarrow 20.8366191\ \mathrm{GHz}. \end{aligned} \]

The arrows are conversions. They are not a license to call a gigahertz an energy.

Gigahertz is cyclic frequency. Microelectronvolts are energy.

Millikelvin here is equivalent temperature. Write \(E=h\nu\) or \(E/h=\nu\) when you mean the Hamiltonian coefficient.

The dimensional check is visible: \((\mathrm{J\,s})(\mathrm{s^{-1}})=\mathrm J\), and \(\mathrm J/(\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}})=\mathrm K\).

We will quote Hamiltonian coefficients as cyclic frequencies. If a term has energy \(J\), the table gives \(J/h\) in hertz.

If a paper writes \(H=\hbar g(\cdots)\), then \(g\) is normally angular frequency and the cyclic frequency is \(g/(2\pi)\). Lose that factor of \(2\pi\) and every later comparison is off by six.

Drop the distinction between \(T_E\) and the cryostat set point, and a 100 mK refrigerator looks “cold” for a 5 kHz splitting. It is not. The splitting’s equivalent temperature is a fraction of a microkelvin.

Three measured numbers through that map

NV zero-field splitting. For the NV\(^-\) ground-state triplet near room temperature, \(D/h\approx2.87\ \mathrm{GHz}\) [R197]. The energy and equivalent temperature are

\[ E_D=h(2.87\ \mathrm{GHz})=11.87\ \mu\mathrm{eV}, \qquad T_D=0.1377\ \mathrm K. \]

At 300 K, \(k_{\mathrm B}T/h\approx6.251\ \mathrm{THz}\), far above \(D/h\). Hence room-temperature optical polarization works because the driven optical cycle is out of thermal equilibrium, not because the \(m_s=0\) state is thermally frozen out.

A measured NV–NV coupling. In an implanted pair separated by \(25\pm2\ \mathrm{nm}\) at room temperature, the fitted secular dipolar coupling was \(4.93\pm0.05\ \mathrm{kHz}\) [R080]. Its energy and equivalent temperature are

\[ E_{dd}=2.039\times10^{-5}\ \mu\mathrm{eV}, \qquad T_{dd}=2.366\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm K. \]

That tiny equivalent temperature does not forbid a driven gate at 300 K. It does say that thermal equilibrium cannot select states separated only by this bare pair coupling.

A cryostat set point. At \(T=100\ \mathrm{mK}\),

\[ k_{\mathrm B}T=8.617\ \mu\mathrm{eV}, \qquad \frac{k_{\mathrm B}T}{h}=2.084\ \mathrm{GHz}. \]

An SiV orbital splitting whose cyclic frequency is 46 GHz has equivalent temperature 2.21 K, so its upper branch is strongly suppressed at 100 mK. A 5 kHz dipolar splitting is not. One thermometer reading can therefore be cold for one degree of freedom and effectively infinite-temperature for another.

Suppose you quote only the refrigerator temperature. Then you have said nothing about which splittings equilibrium can see.

A decay time is not a gap

Let \(T_2\) be a coherence time. For a purely exponential coherence envelope \(\exp(-t/T_2)\), the corresponding Lorentzian full width at half maximum is

\[ \Delta\nu_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=\frac{1}{\pi T_2}. \]

This is a model-dependent conversion, not a definition of every linewidth. Gaussian Ramsey decay, spectral diffusion, stretched exponentials, and pulse-filtered noise do not obey the same formula. Keep both the protocol and the envelope whenever you can.

A gate duration \(t_g\) gives an operation rate \(1/t_g\). It is not automatically a Hamiltonian gap.

For example, \(t_g=20\ \mathrm{ns}\) gives \(1/t_g=50\ \mathrm{MHz}\); the resonant Rabi frequency for a \(\pi\) rotation may differ by factors set by the pulse convention. Write “inverse duration” rather than relabel it as an energy.

What fails if you drop the exponential hypothesis? The same \(T_2\) number can be assigned to a quasi-static, calibratable detuning and to an irreversible Markovian linewidth. Those two noises last the same time on a Ramsey plot and disagree about whether a later pulse can undo them.

Who sits in the upper level

For two nondegenerate levels separated by energy \(\Delta\), thermal equilibrium gives

\[ \frac{p_1}{p_0}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right), \]

where \(p_0\) and \(p_1\) are the lower- and upper-level probabilities. The dimensionless ratio

\[ R_T=\frac{\Delta}{k_{\mathrm B}T} \]

is the thermal-resolution ratio. It answers one question only: does equilibrium even notice the split?

When \(R_T\ll1\), the two levels are nearly equally populated unless a drive, a measurement, or a reservoir engineers a nonequilibrium state. When \(R_T\gg1\), thermal excitation is exponentially suppressed. Degeneracy multiplies the Boltzmann factor, so the equation must be amended when several states share an energy.

For an architecture we also need

\[ R_C=\frac{|J|/h}{\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{noise}}}, \qquad N_{\mathrm{coh}}=\frac{|J|T_{2,\mathrm{relevant}}}{h}. \]

Here \(J\) is the coupling energy, \(\Delta\nu_{\mathrm{noise}}\) is the relevant cyclic-frequency broadening, and \(N_{\mathrm{coh}}\) is roughly the number of coupling cycles available inside the applicable coherence time. “Applicable” means free-induction or Hamiltonian-compatible protection, not whichever decoupling record is largest.

Hence \(R_T\) is not \(R_C\), and neither is a many-body gap. A system can be thermally blind to a splitting and still gate it, or thermally resolved and still too noisy to use.

What the laboratory actually wrote down

The table below is not a leaderboard. It contains conditional brackets from identifiable experiments or, where marked, a transparent conversion anchored by a measurement.

A range may represent tensor components, inequivalent defect configurations, or protocols on the same sample; the “conditions” column says which. It is not silently promoted to a population-wide distribution.

The rows favor samples relevant to interacting defects: bulk or nanostructured hosts, implanted pairs where coupling was actually measured, and protocols whose temperature is stated. Records based on aggressive dynamical decoupling are retained but quarantined from undriven analog evolution. Absence of a comparable single-defect metric is recorded as absence, not replaced with an ensemble number from a different task.

All frequency-valued Hamiltonian entries are \(E/h\). “Equivalent \(T_E\)” means \(E/k_{\mathrm B}\), not the operating temperature. Uncertainties and ranges keep their source-specific meaning.

Readout and initialization fidelity | NV\(^-\): electron initialization \(\ge99.7\pm0.1\%\); single-shot electron readout \(93.2\pm0.5\%\) using a 40 \(\mu\)s window | Readout inverse duration \(25\ \mathrm{kHz}\), not an energy splitting | Single NV in bulk diamond below 10 K using resonant, spin-selective optical excitation. Room-temperature off-resonant fluorescence normally requires repeated averaging and must not inherit this fidelity [R199]. | [Experiment] [R199] | |

Slow cryogenic optical operations | SiV\(^-\): optical pumping timescale about 30 ms; single-shot readout about 89% with 20 ms integration | Inverse durations about 33 Hz and 50 Hz | Single SiV near 100 mK with field aligned to the defect axis; the long coherence experiment used still longer preparation/readout pulses. These durations concern optical cycling and collection, not microwave gate speed [R083]. | [Experiment] [R083] |

The table deliberately contains awkward comparisons. That is the point.

NV centers can be controlled quickly at room temperature, yet a demonstrated 25 nm dipolar coupling sits in the kilohertz range. SiV centers offer narrow, stable optical transitions, yet their orbital phonons force millikelvin operation for the longest spin memory.

SiC can show millisecond Hahn echoes at 20 K, but that datum comes from isolated defects in high-quality material, not a densely implanted interacting lattice.

Ruby supplies a robust ensemble transition at \(E/h=11.493\ \mathrm{GHz}\), while modern evidence for individually initialized, coupled Cr\(^{3+}\) defect arrays with the complete control stack remains missing [R088].

One pair, three ledgers

Use the measured room-temperature NV pair as a deliberately honest example. Let the coupling be \(J/h=4.93\ \mathrm{kHz}\). For the two centers, take \(T_2^*=22.6\)–\(27.8\ \mu\mathrm s\) and echo times 150–514 \(\mu\mathrm s\), all from the same sample and protocol family [R080]. Then

\[ N_{\mathrm{coh}}^*=\frac{J}{h}T_2^*=0.11\text{–}0.14, \]

whereas

\[ N_{\mathrm{coh}}^{\mathrm{echo}}=0.74\text{–}2.53. \]

Hence the free-induction result is below one coupling cycle. Echo improves the ledger, and the actual entangling sequence used tailored double-quantum phase accumulation plus refocusing [R080].

A static many-body Hamiltonian cannot automatically borrow that pulse sequence. The pulses may average away the interaction one hoped to retain.

For thermal equilibrium at 300 K,

\[ R_T=\frac{h(4.93\ \mathrm{kHz})}{k_{\mathrm B}(300\ \mathrm K)} \approx7.9\times10^{-10}. \]

The same experiment can demonstrate driven entanglement while being nowhere near passive thermal polarization in the interaction eigenbasis. There is no contradiction. Driven quantum control and equilibrium many-body protection are different products.

If an exponential \(T_2^*=25\ \mu\mathrm s\) were the correct model, then \(\Delta\nu=1/(\pi T_2^*)=12.7\ \mathrm{kHz}\). Comparing a 4.93 kHz coupling gives \(R_C\approx0.39\).

This estimate is conservative only for that line shape and protocol. A quasi-static, calibratable detuning and an irreversible Markovian linewidth can yield the same Ramsey timescale but have very different consequences for control.

The cure is a measured noise spectrum, not a more decorative decimal place.

Ways to get this wrong

Compare \(D\) to the noise and call the coupling safe. Suppose \(D/h=2.87\ \mathrm{GHz}\) and the linewidth is a kilohertz.

Then the on-site splitting is safe, and the interaction that would generate a topological stabilizer has not been mentioned. The relevant comparison is the projected intercluster term against projected noise.

Borrow an optical width for a spin width. Suppose the optical D line is 100 MHz.

That number can matter for photon indistinguishability and resonant readout. Drop the distinction of operators, and you have assigned the optical noise spectrum to the spin.

Optical and microwave transitions sample different operators.

Call an inverse time an energy. Suppose a pulse lasts 20 ns.

Then \(1/(20\ \mathrm{ns})=50\ \mathrm{MHz}\) is useful bookkeeping. What fails if you call it a 50 MHz gap?

You have skipped the Hamiltonian. The resonant Rabi frequency for a \(\pi\) rotation may differ by the pulse convention.

Confuse the cryostat with the sample. Suppose the refrigerator reaches 20 mK.

In the ruby experiment that did not imply a 20 mK optically illuminated spin ensemble; the inferred local temperature was \(143\pm7\ \mathrm{mK}\) at low optical power [R088]. Laser heating, imperfect thermal anchoring, and microwave dissipation belong in the passport.

Import protection that changes the Hamiltonian. Dynamical decoupling extends memory by reversing selected couplings.

What fails if the same toggling-frame average cancels \(J\)? The longer \(T_2\) is numerically impressive and architecturally weightless.

High-fidelity resonant NV readout below 10 K does not imply passive low-temperature order [R199]. Conversely, weak thermal polarization does not prevent active optical initialization.

Call a driven pair a topological qubit. A pulse sequence creating entanglement between two NVs is an experiment on driven physical qubits.

It is not an encoded topological qubit, an emergent anyon, or evidence for topological order. A future cluster projection would produce new effective couplings and new effective noise; those scales must be derived rather than copied from the physical-spin table.

Cherry-pick records. A record coherence time often combines an unusually pure host, a deep defect, low defect density, low temperature, and many refocusing pulses.

A dense implanted array tends to move several of those conditions in the wrong direction. What fails if you combine the best coherence from one sample, the best optical linewidth from another, and the closest pair from a third?

You have described a crystal that was never grown. Keep \(T_2^*\), echo \(T_2\), and dynamically decoupled \(T_2\) as separate columns, and keep local temperature under illumination, not merely refrigerator temperature.

[Proposal] Until a candidate cluster is fabricated, use scenario ranges rather than a single “best” input: a pessimistic case tied to implanted or shallow data, a base case tied to reproducible bulk or device data, and an optimistic case that requires every enabling condition to be stated. Do not combine the best coherence from one sample, the best optical linewidth from another, and the closest pair from a third as though they were one crystal. That imaginary sample is always excellent.

[Experiment] Across demonstrated defect platforms, local cyclic frequencies \(E/h\) span roughly 1–12 GHz in the specific NV, 4H-SiC divacancy, and ruby cases tabulated here, while directly measured tens-of-nanometres electron dipolar interactions can sit at kilohertz scales [R197]; [R080]; [R096]; [R088]. Optical strain susceptibilities can be enormous, but static optical tuning is not itself a coherent interdefect interaction [R200]. Phonon processes can change linewidths strongly between 4 and 20 K for SiV centers [R201].

[Theory] These facts establish a hierarchy problem, not impossibility. Projection and perturbative gadgets usually reduce useful intercluster scales further, while disorder and leakage remain. Any viable proposal must calculate the effective \(J_{\mathrm eff}\), the effective linewidth, and the many-body gap from the same conditional parameter set.

[Speculation] It is possible that strain-enhanced, phonon-mediated, exchange-assisted, or cavity-mediated designs move beyond bare dipolar kilohertz scales. This chapter supplies no experimental basis for assigning such a design a particular topological gap. A proposed coupling belongs in a separate row until measured.

Check yourself

Show that if \(H=\hbar g\,S_x\) with \(g=2\pi\times5\ \mathrm{MHz}\), the cyclic frequency in this ledger is 5 MHz.

\(g/(2\pi)=5\ \mathrm{MHz}\); the energy is \(\hbar g=h(5\ \mathrm{MHz})\).

What are the energy and equivalent temperature of 1 MHz?

\(0.0041357\ \mu\mathrm{eV}\) and \(47.992\ \mu\mathrm K\).

Show that an NV splitting with \(D/h=2.87\ \mathrm{GHz}\) does not thermally polarize the spin at 300 K.

Its equivalent temperature is only \(0.1377\ \mathrm K\). Optical pumping produces the useful nonequilibrium polarization.

What fails if you insert the 13 ms SiV coherence into a static analog simulation?

It used CPMG-32 near 100 mK in isotopically purified diamond. The pulse sequence and isotope conditions must be compatible with the intended Hamiltonian; the protection can average away the interaction one hoped to keep.

What must accompany a readout fidelity?

Platform, sample, temperature, optical protocol, integration time, state definition, and whether the result is single-shot.

What fails if you compare the zero-field splitting to the noise and declare the coupling safe?

\(D\) is an on-site splitting. The relevant comparison is the projected useful coupling, and ultimately the many-body gap, against projected noise.

A number without a passport is a rumor with units. Hamiltonian coefficients are cyclic frequencies \(E/h\).

Equivalent temperature is \(E/k_{\mathrm B}\), not the cryostat. The laboratory’s local cyclic frequencies span roughly 1–12 GHz in the tabulated NV, 4H-SiC divacancy, and ruby cases, while a measured 25 nm electron dipolar coupling sits at 4.93 kHz.

Driven entanglement at 300 K and thermal resolution of that same coupling are different products. The next chapter asks how far apart the defects actually are.
