Chapter 28 — How far apart, and did the right atom land there?

Two NV centers, ten nanometres apart, would have a point-dipole coefficient of 52 kHz if they sat exactly on the dots you drew. Draw the dots, fire a nitrogen through a hole, anneal, and look for the glow.

You have specified a target. You have not specified a pair.

The energy is set by the actual displacement and by whether the intended charge-stable spin formed at each end. If the two centers land 10 nm apart on average but wander by several nanometres, the couplings smear. If only a few sites hold the intended spin, the picture is mostly holes.

A commanded spacing is not a device. We take this as the problem: the Hamiltonian cares about the measured positions of centers that pass optical, spin, charge, and coherence tests. Everything else is a proxy.

The beam is not the stop

An ion is told a coordinate. The crystal answers with at least five lengths, and they are not five names for resolution.

  • Where the incoming ion crosses the surface. That is the beam spot, or the hole in the mask.

  • Where the ion actually stops, after rattling through the solid.

  • How far a mobile vacancy wanders during the anneal before it is captured, recombines, clusters, or dies at a surface.

  • The chance that the delivered ion or created vacancy becomes the named structural defect, in the named charge.

  • The measured position after you keep only the centers that also pass optical, spin, charge, and coherence tests.

The sideways and downward spray in (2) is implantation straggle. The name is worth keeping because the brochure quotes the beam, and the crystal answers with this extra scatter.

A sub-10-nm beam can feed a 20-nm straggle distribution. A sharply stopped implanted nitrogen can capture a vacancy that has wandered.

A center can sit in the right place and still be optically dark. The instrument brochure normally quotes the first number, because that is the number the instrument controls.

The Hamiltonian cares about the fifth.

A useful schematic is

commanded site
|
+-- surface entry: beam/aperture distribution
|
+-- stopping point: entry convolved with ion straggle
|
+-- annealed complex: vacancy migration and capture
|
+-- created center: structural/charge conversion succeeds
|
`-- usable center: position measured; spin passes acceptance tests

“Convolved” means that independent random displacements add as random variables, not as marketing adjectives. For independent Gaussian one-dimensional errors with standard deviations \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots\), the total standard deviation is

\[ \sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\cdots}. \]

Hence independent errors combine under a square root. Systematic registration offsets must instead be added as biases and calibrated. They do not disappear under that square root.

What fails if you quote only the beam? You have specified entry, not stopping, not capture, and not the conditional distribution of centers that later pass a spin test.

Two spins and a cube of distance

Take two localized electron spins separated by a displacement vector \(\mathbf r\). Its length is \(r\), and \(\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf r/r\) is its direction. Let \(\mathbf S_1\) and \(\mathbf S_2\) be dimensionless spin operators, so their eigenvalues are pure numbers. For electron Landé factors \(g_1\) and \(g_2\), the point-dipole energy is

\[ H_{dd}=h\nu_d(r) \left[ \mathbf S_1\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_2 -3(\mathbf S_1\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}) (\mathbf S_2\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}) \right], \]

where \(h\) is Planck’s constant and

\[ \nu_d(r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{g_1g_2\mu_B^2}{h r^3}. \]

Here \(\mu_0\) is the vacuum permeability and \(\mu_B\) is the Bohr magneton. The frequency \(\nu_d\) is the dipolar coefficient.

It is not automatically the observed transition splitting or gate rate. Those additionally contain the angular factor, spin-state matrix elements, detuning, and pulse-sequence conventions.

For two electron-like spins with \(g_1=g_2=2.0023\), using rounded 2022 CODATA values [R208],

\[ \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\approx10^{-7}\ {\rm N\,A^{-2}},\qquad \mu_B=9.274010\times10^{-24}\ {\rm J\,T^{-1}}, \]

\[ h=6.62607015\times10^{-34}\ {\rm J\,s}, \]

we obtain

\[ \nu_d(r)\approx \frac{52.04\ {\rm MHz\,nm^3}}{r^3}. \]

A tesla is \({\rm T=N\,(A\,m)^{-1}}\). Therefore

\[ \left({\rm N\,A^{-2}}\right) \frac{\left({\rm J\,T^{-1}}\right)^2} {\left({\rm J\,s}\right){\rm m^3}} = \left({\rm N\,A^{-2}}\right) \frac{\left({\rm A\,m^2}\right)^2} {\left({\rm N\,m\,s}\right){\rm m^3}} ={\rm s^{-1}}. \]

So \(\nu_d\) is a frequency. Substituting \(r=1\,{\rm nm}=10^{-9}\,{\rm m}\) gives \(5.204\times10^7\ {\rm s^{-1}}=52.04\ {\rm MHz}\). The cubic scaling then supplies every other row.

Separation \(r\) | \(r^3\) (nm\(^3\)) | Dipolar coefficient \(\nu_d\) | Square-lattice density proxy \(1/r^2\) (sites/µm\(^2\)) | |

1 nm | 1 | 52.0 MHz | 1,000,000 | |

2 nm | 8 | 6.50 MHz | 250,000 | |

5 nm | 125 | 416 kHz | 40,000 | |

10 nm | 1,000 | 52.0 kHz | 10,000 | |

20 nm | 8,000 | 6.50 kHz | 2,500 | |

50 nm | 125,000 | 416 Hz | 400 | |

The density column is only the geometric value for one site per square of side \(r\). Real honeycomb, kagome, cluster, routing, and optical-access layouts have different areas per site.

The dipolar values agree in scale with [Experiment] coherent coupling of two NV electron spins whose inferred separation was \(9.8\pm0.3\) nm; the observed coupling was in the tens-of-kilohertz range after geometry was included [R181]. That experiment established a coupled pair, not a deterministic 10,000-site-per-square-micrometre array.

The angular operator matters. With both spin moments quantized along a unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf z}\), a common secular coefficient contains

\[ A(\theta)=1-3\cos^2\theta, \]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\hat{\mathbf r}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf z}\). It ranges from \(-2\) to \(+1\) and vanishes at the magic angle \(\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\approx54.7^\circ\).

Hence “10 nm gives 52 kHz” means a coefficient scale. It does not promise a 52 kHz usable edge.

Drop the angular factor, and a pair sitting at the magic angle looks like a missing coupling rather than a geometry. Keep it, and 52 kHz is an envelope, not a delivered gate.

When two nanometres is not a dipole

At 1–2 nm, treating each defect as a point magnetic dipole is no longer a complete microscopic model. Electronic wavefunctions can overlap. Charge configuration, relative crystallographic orientation, strain, and the exact atomic realization matter.

The leftover short-range piece is exchange. It is not a polite correction to the table: it often changes roughly exponentially rather than as a universal power law. [Numerics] Atomistic calculations for diamond spin centers found strongly orientation-dependent exchange that can exceed dipolar coupling for some NV-pair geometries below roughly 3 nm [R107].

This does not mean that every 2 nm pair receives a convenient, strong, identical exchange link. It means the 6.50 MHz dipolar entry is only the long-range term in a site-specific Hamiltonian.

At these distances one must calculate or measure the actual pair, check that two recognizable defects and their desired charge states remain stable, and include exchange, tunnelling, altered orbital levels, and implantation damage. Adding a guessed “exchange bonus” to the table would be fiction with units.

What fails if you keep only the \(r^{-3}\) term below 2 nm? You have kept the piece that is universal and dropped the piece that can dominate.

How a wobble becomes a noisy coupling

Let the intended separation be \(r_0\), and let \(\delta r\) be a small error in the separation along the bond direction. Because \(\nu_d=C r^{-3}\), where \(C=52.04\ {\rm MHz\,nm^3}\) for the electron-like case,

\[ \frac{d\nu_d}{dr}=-3Cr^{-4}=-\frac{3\nu_d}{r}. \]

To first order,

\[ \frac{\delta\nu_d}{\nu_d}\approx-3\frac{\delta r}{r_0}. \]

Suppose each endpoint has an independent one-axis placement standard deviation \(\sigma_{\rm site}\) along the bond. The relative displacement then has

\[ \sigma_r=\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\rm site}, \qquad \frac{\sigma_\nu}{\nu_d}\approx \frac{3\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\rm site}}{r_0}. \]

This is an optimistic radial-only estimate. It omits angular-factor disorder, non-Gaussian tails, missing sites, and exchange variability. Requiring radial dipolar disorder below 10% gives

\[ \sigma_{\rm site}<\frac{0.10}{3\sqrt2}r_0\approx0.0236r_0. \]

Target spacing | Maximum independent per-site \(\sigma_{\rm site}\) for 10% radial coupling scatter | |

1 nm | 0.024 nm | |

2 nm | 0.047 nm |

5 nm | 0.118 nm | |

10 nm | 0.236 nm | |

20 nm | 0.471 nm | |

50 nm | 1.18 nm | |

These are not claimed fabrication capabilities. They are derived tolerances.

Even a 2 nm per-site standard deviation would produce an estimated \(3\sqrt2(2/10)\approx0.85\), or 85%, radial coupling scatter around a 10 nm design. Moving to 50 nm relaxes the relative tolerance, but the bare coefficient has fallen to 416 Hz.

Hence spatial design has no free lunch. It does provide an itemized bill.

The linear expression fails when \(\sigma_r/r_0\) is not small. It can also assign probability to negative scalar distances if used carelessly.

A proper disorder model samples three-dimensional endpoint positions, computes \(\mathbf r\), evaluates the full dipolar tensor and any short-range terms, and rejects atomically impossible or merged-defect configurations. Report quantiles of \(J\), not just \(J\) at the mean distance: because \(r^{-3}\) is convex, rare close pairs create a long strong-coupling tail.

What fails if you quote only \(J\) at the mean distance? Convexity of \(r^{-3}\) puts extra weight on the close tail, so the typical coupling and the mean coupling need not agree.

Usable only if every yes holds

A site is usable only if several things happen in a row. Define the following events for one target site: \(A\), the intended ion or vacancy is delivered; \(C\), the desired structural complex forms; \(Q\), it has the usable charge state; \(O\), it can be initialized and read out; \(S\), its spin and coherence pass specification; and \(G\), its final geometry lies inside tolerance. The usable-site probability is exactly

\[ p_{\rm use}=P(A)P(C\mid A)P(Q\mid A,C)P(O\mid A,C,Q) P(S\mid A,C,Q,O)P(G\mid A,C,Q,O,S). \]

That product is a yield. It is a chain of conditional probabilities, not a single success.

The factors need not be independent. “Single-ion detected” addresses \(A\), not the rest.

“20% conversion” addresses a version of \(C\) under stated processing conditions, not \(p_{\rm use}\).

“33 nm placement” is meaningful only after specifying whether it is lateral, depth, one standard deviation,

If \(N\) sites were independent and every one were required, the defect-free array yield would be \(p_{\rm use}^N\). At \(p_{\rm use}=0.96\), even 100 sites give \(0.96^{100}\approx1.69\%\).

At 1,000 sites the value is about \(1.9\times10^{-18}\). Repair, repeated implantation, movable qubits, redundant layouts, or tolerance of missing sites can change this conclusion.

Silently replacing site yield by array yield cannot.

A related trap appears when the number of created centers per target is Poisson distributed with mean \(\lambda\). The probability of exactly one center is

\[ P(1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda}, \]

which is largest at \(\lambda=1\), where \(P(1)=e^{-1}\approx36.8\%\). Dose tuning alone cannot beat that ceiling under a Poisson model. Feedback or postselection changes the process rather than winning an argument with the exponential.

Hence a cheerful percentage is not a device yield until the denominator, the conditioning, and the array size are named.

What the laboratory actually has

The following rows deliberately preserve different definitions. They should not be compressed into a leaderboard called “resolution.”

Host and process | Surface-entry control | Straggle/stopping distribution | Vacancy motion | Reported creation yield | Final measured placement or usability statement | |

Diamond, focused Si implantation for SiV | Typical beam FWHM below 40 nm | [Numerics] 19 nm lateral straggle; combining a 40 nm FWHM beam (\(\sigma\approx17\) nm) and straggle predicted \(\sigma\approx26\) nm | High-temperature anneal; vacancy capture controls conversion | [Experiment] up to about 2.5% at 100 keV; electron irradiation plus re-anneal raised a tested bulk-sample value to about 20% [R190] | [Experiment] created single SiVs had 32 nm one-axis standard deviations; radial offset \(40\pm20\) nm. Diamond, delta-doped N plus localized electron irradiation used a 200 keV electron beam with a 20 nm spot.

Electrons create vacancies along a narrow path; the N layer, rather than ion stopping, sets depth.

850 °C, 11 min anneal; [Numerics] diffusion-capture modeling accompanied the measurement.

[Exper

4H-SiC, 30 keV carbon implantation through a lithographic mask | Mask-defined target arrays | [Numerics] implantation selected shallow silicon vacancies at roughly 40 nm depth | Host- and defect-specific activation; diamond diffusion numbers do not transfer | [Experiment] \(19\pm4\)% silicon-vacancy generation efficiency and \(34\pm4\)% probability of a single emitter at optimized dose [R205] | Predetermined arrays were demonstrated, but those yield figures do not by themselves establish sub-10-nm final pair-spacing distributions [R205] | |

The SiV row is the bookkeeping done out loud. Suppose the beam FWHM is 40 nm.

Converting to a Gaussian standard deviation gives \(40/2.355\approx17\) nm. Combining that with 19 nm straggle gives \(\sqrt{17^2+19^2}\approx25.5\) nm, consistent with the paper’s predicted 26 nm.

The measured created-center distribution was broader, at 32 nm per axis [R190]. Hence a “below 40 nm” beam was not a below-40-nm final location.

The discrepancy is why the endpoint has to be measured.

The CN-mask row supplies another propagation, not a measurement. If entry points were uniform across a circular aperture of radius \(a=40\) nm, one Cartesian coordinate would have \(\sigma_x=a/2=20\) nm.

Combining that idealized aperture distribution with 9 nm straggle gives \(\sqrt{20^2+9^2}\approx22\) nm before adding alignment, diffusion, channeling tails, or optical-localization uncertainty. This is an illustrative use of the reported inputs, not a measured final NV standard deviation [R202].

A narrow pitch between apertures does not make centers within an aperture narrowly spaced.

Vacancy diffusion can create the center or erase the intended geometry. [Experiment] In nitrogen-rich type-Ib diamond implanted with focused Ar ions, Räcke and colleagues measured 0.04–0.79 created NV centers per implanted Ar ion over 12–132 keV [R206].

[Numerics] Their model of vacancy loss to the surface placed an upper bound of about 300 nm on the single-vacancy diffusion length for an 800 °C anneal [R206]. That upper bound is not a claim that every NV moves 300 nm, nor can it be inserted as a Gaussian placement error.

The implanted nitrogen is comparatively immobile; a mobile vacancy must reach a neighboring lattice site to form the complex. The result is a reaction-and-capture distribution conditioned on nitrogen density, depth, surfaces, damage, charge state, temperature, and time.

The methods do different jobs. Delta doping can make depth thin while leaving lateral position random.

A focused beam can target lateral coordinates while ion scattering broadens depth and lateral position. Laser feedback can raise center-creation yield without providing atomic-scale three-dimensional registration.

[Experiment] By 2025, delta doping combined with localized electron-created vacancies had demonstrated about 4 nm depth confinement and 46(1) nm lateral confinement in 280 nm diamond pillars, but not the sub-nanometre relative placement required for a uniform 10 nm dipolar graph [R207].

Using such hybrid methods for a dense interacting lattice remains [Proposal] until the final pair distribution and usable-array yield are measured.

A regularly spaced fluorescence image is an array of physical emitters. It is not yet an array of coherently coupled qubits.

A few coupled defects are not an encoded cluster. A fabricated interaction graph is not evidence of a topological phase.

Spatial success supplies one necessary input to the microscopic Hamiltonian. It does not certify emergence, a many-body gap, or a logical qubit.

Ways to get this wrong

Quote the beam and forget the crystal. Suppose the ion-optical spot is 10 nm.

That specifies entry, not stopping. The reported SiV experiment had a nominal beam smaller than 40 nm, 19 nm calculated lateral straggle, and a 32 nm measured one-axis created-center spread [R190].

Drop any of the three and the remaining number is a different object.

Treat a transport simulation as an endpoint measurement. Transport simulations are valuable [Numerics].

They model ion trajectories and damage under assumptions about an initially ideal target. What fails if you stop there?

Charge-state stability, annealed-complex location, channeling tails in a particular crystal, and usable-spin yield have not been measured. Validate simulated distributions with microscopy, spectroscopy, or coupling-based localization.

Call conversion yield deterministic placement. A detected single ion can still fail to form the requested center.

Conversely, a 96% laser-feedback creation result does not mean that 96% of sites land inside a 1 nm tolerance or pass a coherence threshold [R203]. Drop the denominator, the conditioning, or the acceptance tests, and the percentage is free to wander.

Ignore tails and nearest unwanted neighbours. Mean and standard deviation are insufficient when rare close pairs dominate \(r^{-3}\) coupling.

Damage-related paramagnetic defects may also sit nearer than the intended qubit and couple more strongly. What fails if you report only the mean distance?

Convexity of \(r^{-3}\) puts extra weight on the close tail. Report a three-dimensional point-process distribution, tail quantiles, and identities of dark spins where possible.

Import diamond statistics into another host. Stopping distributions depend on ion species, energy, crystal orientation, density, channeling, and target composition.

Vacancy migration and complex formation depend on the host’s defect chemistry. The 300 nm diamond upper bound [R206], 7% CN-to-NV result [R202], and SiC yield [R205] are separate conditioned experiments, not interchangeable constants.

For sapphire in particular, a proposed array has no defensible spatial budget until the chosen defect, charge state, implantation species, anneal, and final spin acceptance measurement are specified.

Assume stronger is automatically better. At 1–2 nm, exchange, tunnelling, altered defect identity, and damage may defeat the intended isolated-spin model [R107].

At 50 nm, placement is easier but 416 Hz bare dipolar coupling may lose to linewidth and decoherence. The viable window is where a measured distribution of useful couplings outruns the Chapter 27 noise rates without leaving the Hamiltonian model’s domain.

Check yourself

What fails if a focused beam has a 10 nm spot and you take that as the final defect uncertainty?

Ion straggle, registration bias, annealing/capture physics, and the conditional distribution of successfully created usable centers remain.

Show that the electron-spin dipolar coefficient at 20 nm is 6.50 kHz.

\(52.04\ {\rm MHz\,nm^3}/20^3=6.50\ {\rm kHz}\), before angular and matrix-element factors.

What fails if you treat the 1 nm table entry as a complete coupling prediction?

Wavefunction overlap and site-specific exchange, tunnelling, charge, and structural changes can rival or dominate the point-dipole term.

Show that independent 1 nm bond-direction placement errors at a 10 nm pitch give about 42% radial dipolar scatter.

\(3\sqrt2(1/10)\approx0.42\) in the small-error approximation; angular disorder is additional.

Does a 20% conversion yield imply a 20% usable-site yield?

No. Charge state, readout, coherence, and geometric-tolerance probabilities remain, with potentially correlated conditioning.

What must a fabrication paper report for this architecture?

Three-dimensional final-position distributions, non-Gaussian tails and biases, exact creation-yield denominator, charge/spin acceptance, missing and extra defects, pair-coupling distribution, and array-level yield under stated processing conditions.

A 10 nm drawing is a wish. For electron-like spins the point-dipole coefficient is \(52.04\ {\rm MHz\,nm^3}/r^3\), giving 52.0 MHz, 6.50 MHz, 416 kHz, 52.0 kHz, 6.50 kHz, and 416 Hz at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, and 50 nm.

Angular factors and short-range exchange stay separate. Small radial errors give \(\sigma_J/J\approx3\sqrt2\sigma_{\rm site}/r\), so 10% coupling uniformity wants per-site bond-direction error below about \(0.0236r\).

The laboratory has useful pieces — coupled 10 nm-class pairs, nanometre-scale stopping calculations, tens-of-nanometre measured final placement, and process-dependent creation yields — but not a dense, defect-free, sub-nanometre-tolerance interaction graph. Spacing is not a device.

Chapter 29 — A coupling wearing a nicer hat

Write \(J\) next to two defects. Write \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) on the same line. The second symbol has not been earned.

\(J\) is a coupling between neighbors — maybe fifty megahertz if you write it as a frequency. A many-body gap is the energy of the first excitation that leaves the ground-state family of the whole lattice.

Those are different objects. Projection, a fourth-order gadget, temperature, disorder, and decoherence can only reduce what you may spend.

They cannot mint the gap from \(J\) by renaming.

We will write every cut in the same units. There is no measured material \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) to insert at the end.

Same units, or the comparison is empty

Several scales compete in one spectrum. A ledger forces every scale into the same units and stops you from counting the same joule twice.

Energies are not literally spent. They still have to be ordered.

We will usually quote an energy \(E\) as a frequency \(E/h\), where \(h\) is Planck’s constant. A table entry of \(1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) means the energy \(h\times 10^6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), not an angular frequency. Temperature converts by

\[ \frac{k_B T}{h}=20.8366\ \frac{\mathrm{GHz}}{\mathrm{K}}T =20.8366\ \frac{\mathrm{MHz}}{\mathrm{mK}}T. \]

Here \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant and \(T\) is thermodynamic temperature in kelvin. The numerical conversion follows from the exact SI values of \(k_B\) and \(h\) [R196]. Writing energies as ordinary frequencies keeps stray factors of \(2\pi\) from breeding.

Hence 1 mK is 20.8366 MHz in these units, and a kilohertz coupling is \(4.8\times10^{-5}\) mK. Mix cyclic frequency with angular frequency, or mix the cryostat with the sample, and the ledger is already lying.

One tile is not a phase

Start with an ideal effective term

\[ H_p=-K B_p, \]

where \(K>0\) is an energy and \(B_p\) is a dimensionless operator with eigenvalues \(+1\) and \(-1\). Calling \(p\) a plaquette is suggestive. One tile is still not a topological phase.

Its two energies are \(-K\) and \(+K\), so reversing its eigenvalue costs

\[ \Delta_p=(+K)-(-K)=2K. \]

That subtraction, not the symbol \(K\) by itself, is the excitation energy. In a closed lattice, constraints can require excitations to appear in pairs, in which case the lowest allowed bulk process may cost \(4K\).

Boundaries can change that factor. A genuine value of \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) has to come from the spectrum and boundary conditions of the stated model.

Now suppose \(K\) is not sitting on the table. In the strongly anisotropic limit of Kitaev’s honeycomb model, fourth-order perturbation theory generates a plaquette coefficient of the form [R017]

\[ K=\frac{J_x^2J_y^2}{16\Lambda^3}. \]

Here \(J_x\) and \(J_y\) are weak bond energies and \(\Lambda\) denotes the strong bond scale (called \(J_z\) in the original model). Setting \(J_x=J_y=J\) gives

\[ K=\frac{J^4}{16\Lambda^3} =\frac{J}{16}\left(\frac{J}{\Lambda}\right)^3. \]

The dimensions check: \([J^4/\Lambda^3]=\mathrm{energy}\). If \(J/\Lambda=0.1\), the coefficient is \(J/16{,}000\), before disorder or other corrections enter.

[Theory] This fourth-order result is established for the specified honeycomb limit [R017]. It is not a derived coefficient for a diamond, SiC, or sapphire defect array, and the honeycomb phase in this limit is not doubled Fibonacci order.

For a conservative toy ledger below, we define

\[ \Delta_{\rm topo}=2K. \]

[Assumption] That factor of two represents one violated effective term. It is deliberately less favorable than a periodic pair threshold of \(4K\). It remains an illustrative assumption, not a material gap claim.

What fails if you quote \(K\) as the gap? You have named the coefficient of a local term, not the first allowed excitation of the lattice. Pair creation and boundaries can change the factor, and a crystal does not inherit \(K\) from a paper that chose it freely.

The first state that is not family

Let \(E_0\le E_1\le E_2\le\cdots\) be the eigenenergies of the finite effective Hamiltonian. A topologically ordered system may have several nearly degenerate ground states. Let \(\mathcal G\) denote that low-energy family. Define

\[ \Delta_{\rm topo}=E_{\rm first\ outside\ \mathcal G}-E_{\rm top\ of\ \mathcal G}. \]

That difference is the topological gap. The name is worth keeping because it is a many-body spectral object, not a new hat for \(J\).

The finite-size width inside \(\mathcal G\) is a different quantity,

\[ \delta_{\rm fs}=E_{\rm top\ of\ \mathcal G}-E_{\rm bottom\ of\ \mathcal G}. \]

Both have units of joules. We will quote \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/h\) and \(\delta_{\rm fs}/h\) in hertz.

A cluster leakage gap \(\Lambda\), an optical transition energy, and a bare nearest-neighbor coupling \(J\) are not \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\). They constrain the derivation of the effective Hamiltonian.

Only diagonalization, a controlled analytic solution, or defensible many-body numerics can supply its gap. Exactly solvable commuting-projector string-net models demonstrate how a local Hamiltonian can possess topological order [R018], but their overall energy scale is freely chosen in the abstract model.

A crystal does not inherit that normalization.

A defect spin is a physical degree of freedom. A cluster doublet is an encoded local degree of freedom.

A circuit that prepares a string-net wavefunction is a digital emulation unless the undriven hardware Hamiltonian already has the phase. \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) is a property of the many-body Hamiltonian and its spectrum. A logical qubit additionally requires controlled initialization, operations, and readout inside that family.

Measuring a two-spin avoided crossing establishes none of the last three items by itself.

Drop the distinction between \(\delta_{\rm fs}\) and \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\), and a small splitting inside the family looks like a small gap. Small \(\delta_{\rm fs}\) is good. Small \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) is bad.

Each virtual hop takes a cut

Write the microscopic Hamiltonian as

\[ H=H_0+V, \]

where \(H_0\) separates a retained cluster subspace from leakage states by energy \(\Lambda\), and \(V\) contains weaker intercluster couplings of characteristic local strength \(J\). The dimensionless ratio

\[ \epsilon=\frac{J}{\Lambda} \]

is the expansion parameter. Every later power of it is a cut you can see.

For an interaction first generated at perturbative order \(n\), dimensional analysis gives

\[ K_n=c_n\frac{J^n}{\Lambda^{n-1}} =c_nJ\epsilon^{n-1}, \]

where \(c_n\) is a dimensionless coefficient fixed by the actual graph, matrix elements, denominators, and interference among virtual paths. Perturbative gadgets can generate higher-body interactions from two-body couplings, but their target terms and errors must be bounded together [R209]. [Theory] The scaling law is a bookkeeping form; neither \(n\) nor \(c_n\) may be guessed after looking at a desired answer.

Suppose the first omitted contribution is approximately

\[ R_{n+1}=c_{n+1}J\epsilon^n. \]

Then

\[ \frac{|R_{n+1}|}{|K_n|} \approx \left|\frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}\right|\epsilon. \]

A small \(\epsilon\) improves control but shrinks \(K_n\). A large \(\epsilon\) increases the nominal term while undermining the expansion. This is a real optimization problem, not permission to set \(\epsilon=0.9\) and write “perturbative” in the caption.

A crooked bond becomes a crooked \(K\). For \(K=cJ^n\Lambda^{1-n}\), logarithmic differentiation gives

\[ \frac{\delta K}{K} =n\frac{\delta J}{J}-(n-1)\frac{\delta\Lambda}{\Lambda}+\frac{\delta c}{c}. \]

A spatially common drift in \(J\) is amplified by \(n\). If \(n\) independent bond factors each have the same small fractional standard deviation \(s\), their product instead has fractional standard deviation approximately \(\sqrt n\,s\) to leading order.

Correlation therefore matters. Quoting one implantation-position standard deviation is not yet a distribution of \(K\).

Hence fourth order is not a free improvement. It is a cut of order \(\epsilon^3\) on \(J\), paid for in validity, and then amplified again if the bonds wobble.

Temperature, disorder, forgetfulness, and size

Temperature. Thermal excitation is governed by \(k_BT\). In a dilute, noninteracting estimate, the occupation of an excitation of energy \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) carries a Boltzmann factor

\[ p_1\sim e^{-\Delta_{\rm topo}/k_BT}. \]

[Theory] This captures activation but not diffusion, entropy, boundaries, or interaction among anyons. Reviews of finite-temperature quantum memories emphasize that a nonzero gap alone does not make a two-dimensional memory self-correcting [R169]. For \(N\) approximately independent places where an excitation can occur, the crude expected count is \(Np_1\). Requiring it below a target \(p_\star\) gives

\[ \frac{\Delta_{\rm topo}}{k_BT}\gtrsim \ln\!\left(\frac{N}{p_\star}\right). \]

This system-size condition is stricter than merely \(\Delta_{\rm topo}>k_BT\).

Disorder. Define \(\sigma_J\) here as the root-mean-square energy variation of the relevant projected local terms after static calibration.

This definition matters. Raw microscopic coupling variation can partly renormalize \(K\), generate random effective fields at lower perturbative order, or mix the retained and leakage subspaces.

The dangerous comparison is local:

\[ \sigma_J\ll\Delta_{\rm topo}. \]

A total operator norm that grows with the number of sites is not the right local yardstick. Nor is an RMS value sufficient when distributions have long tails or spatial correlations.

[Theory] Stability theorems prove persistence of spectral bands for certain topologically ordered commuting-projector Hamiltonians under sufficiently weak, bounded, short-range local perturbations [R142]. They do not provide a universal percentage tolerance for a proposed defect device.

Decoherence broadening. Define the effective decoherence rate by

\[ \Gamma=\frac{1}{T_{2,\rm eff}}, \]

where \(T_{2,\rm eff}\) is the decay time, in seconds, of the projected degree of freedom under the stated control sequence. Then the associated energy scale is \(\hbar\Gamma\), with \(\hbar=h/(2\pi)\). In ordinary frequency units,

\[ \frac{\hbar\Gamma}{h}=\frac{1}{2\pi T_{2,\rm eff}}. \]

This convention must not be confused with a spectroscopic full width at half maximum, which can carry a different factor. Also, one scalar \(T_2\) cannot describe leakage, non-Markovian noise, or correlated errors. The comparison \(\hbar\Gamma\ll\Delta_{\rm topo}\) is necessary for resolving coherent many-body dynamics, not sufficient for fault tolerance.

Finite size. For a gapped local topological phase, virtual processes that wind around the sample can split the nominal ground-state family. A common asymptotic form is

\[ \delta_{\rm fs}\sim A\Delta_{\rm topo}e^{-L/\xi}, \]

where \(L\) is the shortest noncontractible linear size, \(\xi\) is a correlation length in the same units, and \(A\) is dimensionless. [Theory] Exponentially narrow low-energy bands under appropriate weak local perturbations are supported by stability results [R142], but the prefactor and even the useful asymptotic regime are model-dependent. Exactly solvable commuting-projector points can have zero splitting; generic perturbations restore a nonzero one.

What fails if you keep only \(\Delta_{\rm topo}>k_BT\)? You have ignored entropy, system size, local disorder, linewidth, and the splitting inside the family. Any one of those can eat the leftover.

The leftover has to beat all four

The compact screening criterion is

\[ \boxed{ \Delta_{\rm topo}\gg k_BT,\quad \sigma_J,\quad \hbar\Gamma,\quad \delta_{\rm fs} } \]

with two additions:

  • unwanted projected terms and perturbative remainders must also be locally much smaller than \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\); and

  • thermal performance should be tested against \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/k_BT\gtrsim\ln(N/p_\star)\), not only against one.

For a numerical screen, define

\[ \mathcal M=\frac{\Delta_{\rm topo}} {\max(k_BT,\sigma_J,\hbar\Gamma,\delta_{\rm fs})}. \]

\(\mathcal M<1\) fails even the scale-ordering test. \(\mathcal M>1\) only passes that test. The symbol \(\gg\) demands a margin tied to a target error probability and system size; it is not a decorative greater-than sign.

Hence a ratio of 4.86 is not a comfortable gap. It is a number that still has to face \(\ln(N/p_\star)\).

Three toy ledgers

The following is a sensitivity calculation, not a prediction. Every uncited number in the input block is deliberately labeled as an assumption.

[Proposal; Assumptions] We use the fourth-order toy coefficient \(K=J^4/(16\Lambda^3)\) motivated by the specified honeycomb limit [R017], set \(\Delta_{\rm topo}=2K\), set the finite-size prefactor \(A=1\), and assume the quantities in this table after projection:

Input | Optimistic | Base | Pessimistic | |

cluster separation \(\Lambda/h\) | \(1000\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(250\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(50\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

weak coupling \(J/h\) | \(300\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(50\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(5\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

expansion ratio \(\epsilon=J/\Lambda\) | \(0.30\) | \(0.20\) | \(0.10\) | |

physical temperature \(T\) | \(0.010\ \mathrm{mK}\) | \(1.0\ \mathrm{mK}\) | \(100\ \mathrm{mK}\) |

residual effective disorder \(\sigma_J/h\) | \(0.100\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.025\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.001\ \mathrm{MHz}\) |

projected \(T_{2,\rm eff}\) | \(1\ \mathrm{ms}\) | \(0.10\ \mathrm{ms}\) | \(0.010\ \mathrm{ms}\) | |

linear size \(L/\xi\) | \(10\) | \(5\) | \(2\) | |

The “optimistic” temperature is \(10\ \mathrm{\mu K}\). That is an aggressive assumed spin temperature, not a cited capability of a dense defect array.

The other temperatures, couplings, disorder values, and projected coherence times are likewise scenario inputs. Experiments have separately demonstrated coherent coupling between individual diamond defect spins [R080] and long electronic-spin coherence under specialized material and decoupling conditions [R211]; those results do not validate simultaneous achievement of this table.

Using ordinary frequency units avoids repeated factors of \(h\):

\[ \frac{K}{h}=\frac{1}{16} \frac{(J/h)^4}{(\Lambda/h)^3},\qquad \frac{\Delta_{\rm topo}}{h}=2\frac{K}{h}. \]

For the base row,

\[ \frac{K}{h} =\frac{1}{16}\frac{(50\ \mathrm{MHz})^4}{(250\ \mathrm{MHz})^3} =0.025\ \mathrm{MHz}, \]

so \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/h=0.050\ \mathrm{MHz}=50\ \mathrm{kHz}\). The units reduce as \(\mathrm{MHz}^4/\mathrm{MHz}^3=\mathrm{MHz}\).

Applying the same arithmetic to all rows gives:

Derived quantity | Optimistic | Base | Pessimistic | |

\(K/h\) | \(0.50625\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.025\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.0003125\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

\(\Delta_{\rm topo}/h\) | \(1.0125\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.050\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.000625\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

\(k_BT/h\) | \(0.20837\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(20.8366\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(2083.66\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

\(\sigma_J/h\) | \(0.100\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.025\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.001\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

\(\hbar\Gamma/h\) | \(0.000159\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.001592\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.015915\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

assumed \(\delta_{\rm fs}/h\) | \(0.0000460\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.000337\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | \(0.0000846\ \mathrm{MHz}\) | |

scale margin \(\mathcal M\) | \(4.86\) | \(2.40\times10^{-3}\) | \(3.00\times10^{-7}\) | |

All displayed digits are arithmetic outputs, not measurement precision. The temperature conversion uses the SI constants [R196].

Decoherence uses \(1/(2\pi T_{2,\rm eff})\). Finite-size splitting uses the explicit assumption \(A=1\) and the listed \(L/\xi\).

Verdict. [Proposal] The base and pessimistic scenarios fail because \(k_BT\) exceeds the toy gap; the pessimistic scenario also has decoherence broadening and effective disorder above the gap. The optimistic scenario passes only the weakest ordering test, with temperature setting \(\mathcal M=4.86\). For a toy array with \(N=1000\) excitation locations and an assumed target \(p_\star=0.01\), the dilute estimate demands

\[ \frac{\Delta_{\rm topo}}{k_BT}\gtrsim \ln(1000/0.01)=11.51, \]

whereas the optimistic ratio is \(4.86\). It therefore fails that stated thermal target too.

These conclusions trace only to the displayed toy formula, the exact unit conversion, and the labeled assumptions. They are not claims that a real defect architecture has any of the three gaps.

The exercise also reveals a design trap. Reducing \(J/\Lambda\) from \(0.30\) to \(0.10\) makes fourth-order perturbation theory more comfortable, but—together with the assumed absolute scales—collapses the toy gap from megahertz to hundreds of hertz. A feasibility proposal must optimize validity and gap simultaneously, then include the leading unwanted terms.

What the laboratory actually has

[Experiment] Coupled individual defect spins and long coherence have each been demonstrated in diamond [R080]; [R211]. They are important ingredients. They are not a measurement of a bulk topological gap, a correlation length, or a topological ground-state family.

For the defect-cluster architecture assessed here, the gap budget currently lacks four experimentally connected objects:

  • a fabricated lattice with the required interaction graph;

  • spectroscopy validating the projected many-body Hamiltonian and its unwanted terms;

  • finite-size scaling that separates a ground-family splitting from the excitation gap; and

  • evidence that the fitted phase has the claimed topological data rather than merely a similar low-energy spectrum.

Consequently, there is no supported material value of \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) to insert. [Proposal] A defensible program would first measure small-cluster spectra and distributions, fit a microscopic Hamiltonian without discarding inconvenient terms, compute its phase diagram and gap with uncertainty propagation, and then compare increasingly large patches. A gap should be reported with host, defect species, charge state, geometry, field, strain, temperature, boundary conditions, and model-fitting procedure attached.

Temperature also needs care. Refrigerator temperature, phonon-bath temperature, and the effective temperature of driven spins need not coincide.

Similarly, a single-defect echo \(T_2\) measured under a pulse train is not automatically the \(T_{2,\rm eff}\) of a continuously interacting cluster lattice. Combining the best coupling from one device, the best coherence from another, and the lowest cryostat temperature from a third produces a brochure, not a budget.

Ways to get this wrong

Call the largest energy the gap. Suppose the zero-field splitting is a gigahertz and the fourth-order topological term is a kilohertz.

Then the largest energy is safe, and the gap of the phase has not been mentioned. The gap is spectral and phase-specific.

Use the target Hamiltonian’s normalized gap. Writing a string-net Hamiltonian with unit coefficients sets a convention.

It does not show that a defect implementation supplies one joule, one kelvin, or one megahertz [R018]. Drop the conversion and the crystal inherits a paper’s choice of one.

Ignore lower-order unwanted terms. A desired fourth-order plaquette term loses if a symmetry-breaking field survives at first or second order. Compare local projected remainder norms with \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\).

Treat RMS disorder as a complete model. Rare bad bonds can nucleate low-energy excitations.

Correlated drift and heavy tails are different from independent Gaussian variation. What fails if you quote only an RMS?

You have described a typical bond, not the worst one the lattice actually has.

Equate a nonzero gap with passive memory. Thermally created anyons can diffuse and enact a logical operator without paying an energy proportional to their travel distance. Two-dimensional topological order can be stable as a phase while being a poor self-correcting memory at nonzero temperature [R169].

Confuse ground-state splitting with the bulk gap. Small \(\delta_{\rm fs}\) is good; small \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) is bad.

A finite patch may show both. What fails if spectroscopy swaps their labels?

A narrow family looks like a small gap, and the architecture is declared dead for the wrong reason — or alive for the wrong reason.

Use \(T_2\) as an energy gap. \(T_2\) gives a linewidth scale only after a convention and noise model are specified. It says nothing by itself about topological order.

Promote digital evidence to an analog gap. A programmable device can prepare and manipulate states with anyonic fusion rules while its native Hamiltonian remains an ordinary qubit Hamiltonian. The relevant analog claim is that the material’s low-energy spectrum and phase realize the order without a gate sequence continually synthesizing it.

Extrapolate a perturbation series outside control. Increasing \(J/\Lambda\) raises the target coefficient and every omitted order. The remainder must be calculated or bounded, not wished smaller.

Report a single favorable point. A phase needs a finite region of parameter space. Fabrication produces a distribution, so uncertainty propagation and finite-size scaling belong in the claim.

Check yourself

What defines \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\)?

The energy from the top of the finite-size ground-state family to the first state outside it, for a stated Hamiltonian and boundary condition.

Show that if \(K=J^4/(16\Lambda^3)\) and \(J/\Lambda=0.1\), then \(K=J/16{,}000\).

Substitute: \(K=(J/16)(J/\Lambda)^3=J/16\times10^{-3}=J/16{,}000\). Projection and perturbative order can reduce the effective coefficient to \(c_nJ(J/\Lambda)^{n-1}\), and the spectral gap adds a model-dependent factor. A bare coupling \(J\) is not the gap.

Show that \(1\ \mathrm{mK}\) is \(20.8366\ \mathrm{MHz}\) in these units.

\(k_BT/h=20.8366\ \mathrm{MHz}\), using exact SI constants [R196].

Show that if \(T_{2,\rm eff}=100\ \mathrm{\mu s}\) and \(\Gamma=1/T_{2,\rm eff}\), then \(\hbar\Gamma/h=1.59\ \mathrm{kHz}\).

\(1/(2\pi T_{2,\rm eff})=1.59\ \mathrm{kHz}\).

What fails if you only require \(\Delta_{\rm topo}>k_BT\)?

Entropy and system size matter; a dilute estimate requires roughly \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/k_BT\gtrsim\ln(N/p_\star)\) for the stated target. Disorder, decoherence, finite-size splitting, and leftover projected terms remain.

What evidence would turn a budgeted gap into a gap claim?

A derived or fitted effective Hamiltonian with quantified errors, followed by controlled analytic or numerical spectroscopy and finite-size scaling; experimental spectroscopy is stronger still.

A coupling is a handshake. A gap is a spectrum.

The screening inequality is \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\gg k_BT,\sigma_J,\hbar\Gamma,\delta_{\rm fs}\), plus small projected remainders and a logarithmic thermal penalty. The three ledgers in this chapter are scenarios only.

There is no measured material \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\) to put in the last cell.

  • [R211] N. Bar-Gill, L. M. Pham, A. Jarmola, D. Budker, and R. L. Walsworth, “Solid-state electronic spin coherence time approaching one second,” Nature Communications 4, 1743 (2013). DOI: 10.1038/ncomms2771.

Chapter 30 — The same shove, a different filter

A truck rolls past the building. Three nearby defects all feel the same magnetic shove. Those three spins were taught to impersonate one quiet pair: two levels we keep, and a crowd of others we promised not to visit.

The shove does not wait outside the encoding. It is an operator on the three physical spins.

Sandwich it with the projector onto the quiet pair and you get a two-by-two matrix acting inside that pair. Sandwich the leftover piece and you get a ticket out.

So a cluster is not a wall. It is a filter.

More physical spins do not automatically mean less noise. They mean different signs and different gains on baths that were already in the crystal.

Three places a shove can go

Imagine three microphones wired to report one number. Average their outputs and independent hiss partly cancels.

Shake all three together and averaging does nothing. Reverse one sign and the common shove may cancel — but now a gradient becomes the signal.

A cluster encoding is that wiring. After this paragraph the microphones are gone: the microscopic defects are the sites, and the matrix elements inside the chosen pair are the signs and the gains.

There are three places a perturbation can go.

  • It can shift the two kept levels differently. The relative twist smears. That is dephasing, the same failure Chapter 4 measured as a fading off-diagonal, now written on the encoded pair.

  • It can mix the two kept levels. Population moves inside the pair. That is relaxation or excitation of the encoded qubit.

  • It can leave the pair. That is leakage, the climb into \(Q\) from Chapter 11.

Static fabrication errors add a fourth practical problem: different clusters implement different Hamiltonians. Slow drift makes that disorder time dependent.

A cluster can reject a uniform magnetic field and still be painfully sensitive to a field gradient, a fluctuating exchange bond, or a pulse that addresses several constituent defects at once. Drop the hypothesis that “more spins average the bath,” and a perfectly common shove survives the filter unchanged. The universe has read the wiring too.

Three spins and a local field

Take three spin-\(1/2\) defects with strong, approximately isotropic exchange. Let \(|\uparrow\rangle\) and \(|\downarrow\rangle\) be eigenstates of the single-spin operator \(S^z\), with eigenvalues \(+1/2\) and \(-1/2\). We use dimensionless spin operators. An energy-valued field \(\xi_i(t)\), measured in joules (J), couples as

\[ \delta H_z(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_i(t)S_i^z . \]

Within the total-magnetization sector \(S^z_{\rm tot}=+1/2\), choose the logical states

\[ |0_L\rangle=\frac{|\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \]

\[ |1_L\rangle=\sqrt{\frac23}|\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\rangle -\frac{|\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle+|\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle}{\sqrt6}. \]

These are the same kind of three-spin pair Chapter 11 kept. Let \(P=|0_L\rangle\langle0_L|+|1_L\rangle\langle1_L|\) project onto this doublet. Define logical Pauli operators

\[ \tau_z=|0_L\rangle\langle0_L|-|1_L\rangle\langle1_L|, \qquad \tau_x=|0_L\rangle\langle1_L|+|1_L\rangle\langle0_L|. \]

Direct multiplication gives

\[ \begin{aligned} P S_1^zP&=\frac16 I-\frac16\tau_z-\frac{\sqrt3}{6}\tau_x,\\ P S_2^zP&=\frac16 I-\frac16\tau_z+\frac{\sqrt3}{6}\tau_x,\\ P S_3^zP&=\frac16 I+\frac13\tau_z . \end{aligned} \]

Therefore

\[ P\delta H_zP=h_0 I+h_x\tau_x+h_z\tau_z, \]

where

\[ h_0=\frac{\xi_1+\xi_2+\xi_3}{6},\qquad h_x=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}(-\xi_1+\xi_2), \]

\[ h_z=\frac{-\xi_1-\xi_2+2\xi_3}{6}. \]

The identity term \(h_0I\) supplies a common phase and does not damage the logical state. Low-frequency \(h_z\) noise dephases it. Noise in \(h_x\) near the logical angular frequency \(\omega_L\), measured in radians per second, drives logical transitions.

Now set \(\xi_1=\xi_2=\xi_3=\xi_c\). Both \(h_x\) and \(h_z\) vanish because

\[ P(S_1^z+S_2^z+S_3^z)P=\frac12 I. \]

Hence a perfectly common longitudinal fluctuation is rejected to first order. [Theory] That is decoherence-free behavior for one specified operator, not immunity to magnetic noise in general. Drop uniformity — let \(\xi_3\) differ from \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\) — and \(h_z\) returns at once.

For equal, mutually uncorrelated site noise, define the two-sided energy-noise spectrum

\[ S_\xi(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\,e^{i\omega t} \langle\xi_i(t)\xi_i(0)\rangle . \]

Its units are \({\rm J^2\,s}\): the integrand has \({\rm J^2}\), and \(dt\) contributes seconds. The projected spectra are

\[ S_{h_x}(\omega)=S_{h_z}(\omega)=\frac16S_\xi(\omega). \]

That factor of six is useful. It is not a blanket sixfold lifetime improvement. Dephasing depends on the low-frequency filter function. Relaxation samples noise near \(\omega_L\). Leakage samples higher frequencies near the cluster gap.

The state

\[ |Q\rangle=\frac{|\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\rangle+|\downarrow\uparrow\uparrow\rangle+|\uparrow\uparrow\downarrow\rangle}{\sqrt3} \]

belongs to the spin-\(3/2\) manifold rather than the encoded doublet. Local field gradients have nonzero matrix elements \(\langle Q|S_i^z|0_L\rangle\) and \(\langle Q|S_i^z|1_L\rangle\), so noise at the cluster excitation energy can cause leakage.

A uniform longitudinal field, proportional to total \(S^z\), cannot make that transition. Clustering has suppressed one correlation channel while exposing gradient and leakage channels.

Every bath, the same sandwich

Let the ideal cluster Hamiltonian be \(H_C\), and let its logical doublet be separated from all other cluster states by a minimum energy \(\Delta_C\), measured in J. Define \(Q=I-P\) as the projector onto those unwanted states. Write the microscopic disturbance as

\[ \delta H(t)=\sum_a \xi_a(t)O_a. \]

The label \(a\) includes site, Cartesian component, and physical mechanism. For example, \(O_a\) might be a spin component, an orbital or strain operator, a local charge projector, or a bond operator \(\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j\). The coefficient \(\xi_a(t)\) carries whatever units make \(\xi_aO_a\) an energy.

Every operator, once trapped inside the pair, has the form

\[ PO_aP=c_{a0}I+\frac12\sum_{\mu=x,y,z}g_{a\mu}\tau_\mu. \]

Here \(c_{a0}\) is an irrelevant common shift. The numbers \(g_{a\mu}\) are the cluster’s noise susceptibilities. The name is worth keeping because they are the wiring gains: how much this physical operator, after projection, looks like each logical Pauli.

The effective logical field is

\[ b_\mu(t)=\sum_a g_{a\mu}\xi_a(t), \qquad P\delta H P=\text{common shift}+\frac12\sum_\mu b_\mu\tau_\mu. \]

If the logical splitting points along \(z\), slow \(b_z\) produces phase wander. Components \(b_x,b_y\) at \(\omega_L\) cause transitions. Hence which physical disturbance is “longitudinal” is decided after projection, not by its name in the laboratory.

How two baths covary at a frequency is written as a cross-spectrum,

\[ S_{ab}(\omega)=\int dt\,e^{i\omega t} \langle\delta\xi_a(t)\delta\xi_b(0)\rangle. \]

The diagonal is each bath’s power at frequency \(\omega\). The off-diagonal is whether two baths shake together. Then

\[ S^{(L)}_{\mu\nu}(\omega)= \sum_{a,b}g_{a\mu}g_{b\nu}S_{ab}(\omega). \]

This equation is the noise model. The diagonal entries describe logical noise power.

The off-diagonal entries retain correlations between logical axes. A Markovian weak-noise calculation would make the logical relaxation rate proportional to \([S^{(L)}_{xx}(\omega_L)+S^{(L)}_{yy}(\omega_L)]/\hbar^2\).

The dimensions check: \({\rm J^2s}/({\rm J^2s^2})={\rm s^{-1}}\). Exact prefactors depend on one-sided versus two-sided spectral conventions, so a simulator must state its convention rather than smuggling in a factor of two.

The output is not a single coherence time. It is this frequency-dependent matrix, plus whatever still lives in \(Q\). Drop the off-diagonal blocks of \(S_{ab}\) and you can reverse the predicted benefit of the encoding.

When hiss cancels and when it does not

Suppose the same operator acts at \(N\) sites with logical coefficients \(g_i\). If site noises are independent and have the same spectrum \(S_0\), then

\[ S_L=S_0\sum_i g_i^2. \]

If they are perfectly correlated, then

\[ S_L=S_0\left(\sum_i g_i\right)^2. \]

For a delocalized average, \(g_i=1/N\): independent noise falls as \(1/N\), while common noise stays unchanged. For a decoherence-free sign pattern with \(\sum_i g_i=0\), common noise cancels. Conversely, if every \(g_i\) has the same order-one sign, common noise power grows as \(N^2\).

Hence correlation is neither automatically good nor automatically bad. It must be contracted with the projected susceptibility vector. [Theory] What fails if you quote only \(\sum_i g_i^2\) is the common-mode case: the encoding that looked like averaging becomes an antenna.

The states we promised not to visit

Projection onto \(P\) is only half the story. The discarded block \(QO_aP\) is the ticket out of the pair.

For an unwanted eigenstate \(|m\rangle\) with energy difference \(E_m-E_L=\hbar\omega_{mL}\), the weak-noise transition rate contains

\[ \Gamma_{L\rightarrow m}\propto \frac{1}{\hbar^2}\sum_{a,b} \langle L|O_a|m\rangle \langle m|O_b|L\rangle S_{ab}(\omega_{mL}). \]

Those matrix elements \(\langle m|O_a|L\rangle\) are exactly the contents of \(QO_aP\). A large \(\Delta_C\) helps only when the environment has little spectral weight at \(\Delta_C/\hbar\) and controls are slow or spectrally narrow compared with that frequency.

Strong pulses, resonant phonons, and charge switching do not promise to be polite. Every microscopic noise operator therefore needs both pieces: \(PO_aP\) for what it does inside the pair, and \(QO_aP\) for how it leaves. Quoting one \(T_2\) throws both pieces away.

A ledger of named baths

Keep “source,” “channel,” and “cluster consequence” on separate lines. The names below are physical objects, not synonyms for “decoherence.”

Microscopic source | Typical microscopic coupling | Main channel after projection | Clustering can suppress when… | Clustering can worsen when… | |

Host nuclear spins, including \(^{13}\mathrm C\) in diamond | Hyperfine fields and nuclear flip-flops | Quasistatic dephasing, spectral diffusion; sometimes resonant relaxation | the nuclear field is common across a fixed-magnetization encoding, or isotopic purification removes most bath spins | each constituent samples a different Overhauser field, and the cluster contains more strongly coupled nuclei | |

Paramagnetic impurities and unintended defects | Magnetic dipolar fields, bath flip-flops, cross-relaxation | Dephasing, relaxation, correlated magnetic bursts | symmetry rejects common field; detuning avoids bath resonances | high defect density supplies both desired coupling and a denser spin bath | |

Surface spins | Fluctuating magnetic dipoles at interfaces | Dephasing and relaxation, often depth dependent | the cluster is deep and compact compared with the field’s correlation length | shallow fabrication exposes every constituent and a nearby fluctuator acts nonuniformly | |

Charge noise | Electric/Stark shifts; modulation of orbital energies and exchange | Dephasing, bond noise, optical spectral diffusion | a clock point makes the logical splitting first-order insensitive | one trap modulates several bonds or shifts the cluster through an avoided crossing | |

Strain and electric-field noise | Crystal-field, spin-orbit, Stark, and spin-strain terms | Dephasing, relaxation, coupling disorder | symmetry makes uniform strain an identity operation | long-wavelength strain drives all sites coherently with non-cancelling matrix elements | |

Phonons | Dynamic strain and orbital/spin-phonon coupling | \(T_1\), orbital relaxation, leakage, temperature-dependent dephasing | the encoded transition has a vanishing matrix element or no resonant phonon density | collective matrix elements add, or a phonon matches \(\Delta_C\) |

Implantation/processing damage | Vacancies, interstitials, strain fields, traps, paramagnetic complexes | Static disorder plus magnetic, charge, and strain noise | annealing and materials processing remove or passivate damage | adding more implanted constituents multiplies nearby damage and broadens \(J\) and \(\Delta_C\) | |

Charge-state instability | Ionization/recombination of the active defect | Leakage or erasure; abrupt Hamiltonian change | redundant heralding detects the event | one constituent changing charge destroys the encoded Hamiltonian and perturbs neighbors | |

Nuclear and paramagnetic baths. In diamond NV systems, coherent evolution coupled to \(^{13}\mathrm C\) nuclei and nitrogen-related electron-spin baths has been directly observed, and dynamical decoupling can reshape rather than remove the bath spectrum [Experiment] [R214]; [R215].

The same lesson carries to a cluster: isotopic purification attacks nuclear abundance, while pulse filtering attacks selected frequencies. Neither guarantees small leakage matrix elements.

A deliberately dense array also risks converting spectators, residual implantation products, and off-target charge states into a correlated electron-spin bath.

Surfaces. Measurements with shallow NV centers support a substantial surface-related magnetic-noise contribution [Experiment] [R216].

A compact cluster much smaller than the source distance may see nearly common field noise and reject it. Place one defect much closer to the interface, however, and the common-mode approximation fails.

Nanostructuring for optical access can therefore change both noise strength and its spatial covariance. A single-defect \(T_2\) does not determine the encoded \(T_2\).

Charge, electric field, and optical spectral diffusion. NV experiments have separated regimes dominated by magnetic and electric-field noise [Experiment] [R217], while electric coupling of an individual NV spin has been measured directly [Experiment] [R191].

Charge traps also move optical transition frequencies and can change the defect’s charge state. In a cluster, electric noise may shift each logical level, modulate the intra-cluster exchange \(J_{ij}\), or modulate inter-cluster coupling.

Those are three different operators and require three sets of \(g_{a\mu}\). Charge conversion is more severe than ordinary phase noise: if a constituent ceases to occupy the required charge/spin manifold, it is leakage or erasure, not a small Pauli error.

Near-surface NV ensembles exhibit coupled charge dynamics and density-dependent charge-state behavior [Experiment] [R218].

Strain and phonons. Static strain is disorder; time-dependent strain is noise.

Spin-strain coupling has been driven and measured in NV–mechanical systems [Experiment] [R219]. Phonons can also relax orbital branches and spins.

For inversion-symmetric group-IV vacancy centers, orbital phonon processes are central to temperature-dependent coherence models [Theory/Experiment] [R201]. A long-wavelength acoustic mode can be highly correlated across a nanometre-scale cluster.

That helps only if the projected uniform-strain operator is proportional to \(I\); otherwise the coherent sum can amplify logical drive or leakage.

Implantation damage. Ion implantation provides placement but creates collision cascades, vacancies, interstitials, local strain, and charge traps; annealing converts only part of that landscape into the desired centers [Experiment/Review] [R212].

Damage is therefore not a single named decay channel. It is a generator of static \(J_{ij}\) disorder and of magnetic, electric, and strain fluctuators.

A credible array model must correlate damage statistics with placement statistics rather than drawing them independently.

Spectral diffusion. The transition frequency wanders as surrounding spins or charges switch.

That wandering is a behavior, not an extra microscopic substance. Slow nuclear flip-flops, electron-spin flips, and charge-trap telegraph processes can all produce it [R213]; [R214]; [R217].

Gaussian white noise is often a poor description: one nearby trap yields discrete, non-Gaussian jumps; a broad ensemble of switching rates can yield an approximate \(1/f\) spectrum. Echo may refocus slow wander during idle evolution, yet the same drift can detune optical initialization, readout, or cluster-mediated gates.

Bonds that wander

Let the intended microscopic coupling on bond \(ij\) be \(J_{ij}\), in J, and write its error as

\[ J_{ij}(t)=\bar J_{ij}+\delta J_{ij}^{\rm static}+\delta J_{ij}^{\rm dyn}(t). \]

The static term produces a distribution of cluster splittings, leakage gaps, and projected inter-cluster couplings. The dynamic term is bond noise.

Because a dipolar coupling depends on distance and orientation, positional disorder enters multiplicatively. Exchange is generally even more sensitive to atomic-scale geometry.

Projecting \(\delta J_{ij}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j\) may create a logical \(\tau_z\) field, a transverse logical term, or leakage, depending on the encoding.

At array level, retain at least four kinds of correlation:

  • Local independent noise: separate nuclei or traps near each constituent.

  • Intra-cluster common mode: long-wavelength magnetic, electric, or strain fluctuations.

  • Inter-cluster correlations: a surface patch, electrode, laser, or acoustic mode affects several encoded qubits.

  • Control correlations: pulse-amplitude error, detuning, crosstalk, and global-drive phase noise act coherently by design.

The last item is where clustering can be especially treacherous. A global pulse intended to rotate every constituent can have a matrix element that adds as \(N\), giving error power proportional to \(N^2\).

Fast control can also populate \(Q\). Symmetry that cancels passive common-mode noise may make desired control impossible at the same order, forcing gradient fields or symmetry-breaking pulses that reintroduce sensitivity.

A cluster doublet is an encoded qubit made from physical defect spins. Projecting microscopic noise into Pauli operators does not create topological order.

Even if a later many-body Hamiltonian has emergent anyons, errors that change a defect’s charge state or leave a cluster doublet occur below the anyon description. They cannot be assumed to become harmless local anyon pairs.

A digital simulation that inserts a chosen Pauli channel likewise does not demonstrate the material’s native noise correlations.

What the laboratory actually has

For individual color centers and ensembles, laboratories can measure Ramsey and echo decay, relaxation, noise spectra under pulse sequences, optical spectral diffusion, charge-state switching, strain response, and sometimes spatial dependence near surfaces [R213]; [R214]; [R215]; [R216]; [R217]; [R191]; [R218]; [R219]; [R201]. [Experiment] These measurements establish that the named mechanisms are real. They do not yet establish a complete covariance matrix \(S_{ab}(\omega)\) for a fabricated, strongly coupled 5–20-defect cluster, much less for a large cluster array.

A responsible characterization sequence would be:

  • Measure each constituent where individual addressability survives: resonance, charge state, \(T_1\), Ramsey, echo, and optical stability.

  • Spectroscopically identify the cluster doublet and every nearby leakage level, obtaining \(\omega_L\) and \(\Delta_C/\hbar\).

  • Apply calibrated common-mode and gradient magnetic, electric, and strain perturbations to determine the coefficients \(g_{a\mu}\).

  • Measure simultaneous time traces or cross-spectra on multiple constituents/clusters rather than inferring independence.

  • Fit static bond disorder separately from dynamic noise.

  • Use the measured spectra and leakage matrix elements in many-body simulations; do not replace them with one average \(T_2\).

[Proposal] No cited experiment demonstrates that clustering color centers produces a topologically ordered array with a measured passive-protection advantage. The projection framework gives a falsifiable test: measured susceptibilities and spectra must predict logical and leakage rates below the relevant interaction and topological-gap scales. Until that comparison exists, “noise-resilient cluster” is a design hypothesis.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Quoting only \(T_2\). \(T_2\) folds together a pulse sequence, a noise spectrum, and an operating point. It omits charge erasure, optical instability, correlated errors, and leakage. One number cannot be the noise model.

  • Calling every fluctuation independent. Common electrodes, surfaces, laser fields, strain waves, and fabrication damage create correlations. Setting \(S_{ab}=0\) for \(a\ne b\) can reverse the predicted benefit of an encoding.

  • Calling every common fluctuation harmless. Cancellation requires \(\sum_a g_{a\mu}=0\) for the actual operator. Common exchange or transverse fields need not satisfy it.

  • Projecting and forgetting \(Q\). The effective Pauli model is incomplete when noise or control has spectral weight near \(\Delta_C/\hbar\). Leakage can grow with the number of constituent levels.

  • Confusing disorder with decoherence. Static disorder does not by itself destroy phase in one isolated device, but it changes Hamiltonian parameters, closes local gaps, frustrates calibration, and causes ensemble dephasing. Drift is dynamic disorder.

  • Assuming echo fixes the architecture. Echo can reject selected low-frequency terms while also averaging desired interactions. It does not reverse irreversible \(T_1\), charge conversion, or unobserved leakage.

  • Optimizing single defects instead of clusters. The best individual coherence site may yield the wrong interaction graph. The strongest-coupled cluster may sit amid the worst implantation bath. Feasibility is a joint distribution.

  • Treating topological protection as a solvent. Topological order can suppress particular local processes under particular energy and temperature conditions. Correlated faults spanning multiple effective sites, leakage below the effective model, and time-dependent Hamiltonian disorder can bypass that argument.

Independent and correlated components contract differently with the cluster susceptibilities. Static bond and onsite disorder, dynamic dephasing and relaxation, charge erasure, and leakage are distinct channels.

Clustering suppresses a source only when the relevant symmetry and correlation pattern make its projected logical matrix element small. That, not a borrowed single-center lifetime, is the minimum model needed to test whether an apparent many-body gap survives a realistic defect array.

Check yourself

What decides whether a microscopic perturbation dephases or relaxes the cluster qubit?

Its projected coefficients: logical \(\tau_z\) noise near zero frequency dephases, while \(\tau_x\) or \(\tau_y\) noise near \(\omega_L\) drives transitions.

Show that a perfectly common longitudinal field is invisible inside the three-spin doublet.

Both logical states have \(S^z_{\rm tot}=+1/2\), so \(P(S_1^z+S_2^z+S_3^z)P=\frac12 I\). The projected operator is a common phase.

What fails if the three site noises are perfectly correlated rather than independent?

The independent formula \(S_L=S_0\sum_i g_i^2\) is replaced by \(S_L=S_0(\sum_i g_i)^2\). Averaging disappears; a decoherence-free sign pattern still cancels, while same-sign coefficients amplify as \(N^2\).

What is leakage in this setting?

A transition from the logical doublet \(P\) into another cluster state in \(Q\), driven by microscopic noise or control at the appropriate energy. The matrix elements live in \(QO_aP\).

Is spectral diffusion a separate elementary bath?

No. It is observed frequency wandering that can arise from nuclear, paramagnetic, or charge dynamics.

What fails if you treat charge-state switching as a small Stark shift?

A Stark shift may project as dephasing. Changing charge can remove the constituent’s required spin and alter the whole cluster Hamiltonian, producing leakage or erasure rather than a Pauli error inside \(P\).
