Chapter 31 — Topological protection is not magic

One edge of the lattice flips. The two checks that touch that edge both change their minds. Two anyons sit a lattice spacing apart.

Is this a disaster? Not yet. The pair can walk toward each other and vanish. Every local alarm goes quiet. The secret stored in the winding may still be intact.

Or they walk the long way around the doughnut, meet, and vanish just as quietly. Every local alarm still goes quiet. The secret has flipped.

One local accident is not yet a logical disaster. Topology makes the disaster take a long history. It does not make the history impossible. Protected is not immortal.

Four words get asked to wear the same hat: gap, decoder, threshold, error-free. They are not synonyms. This chapter follows one local fault from its first scream to its possible logical consequence, and refuses to let those four words trade places.

A footprint is not a lap

Imagine fresh snow on a circular running track. One footprint is local.

A continuous trail that goes all the way around the track is global. Inspecting any short segment does not tell you whether the trail eventually closes around the circle.

A topological code works the same way, with less snow and more Pauli matrices. After this paragraph the snow is gone.

A local operator normally creates nearby excitations. Further local operators move them.

If the excitations meet and disappear, every local alarm can return to normal. Yet their complete path may wind around a hole or handle.

That winding acts on the logical state.

This is the central limitation: topology makes a logical fault require an extended history, not an impossible history. Locality buys distance.

An energy gap buys a Boltzmann penalty for creating excitations. Neither automatically buys a growing energy barrier against moving them.

The spacetime version is even more useful. A data error draws a segment in space.

Persistence draws it through time. A faulty syndrome bit draws a time-like segment.

Decoding asks which collection of segments most plausibly explains the observed endpoints. A logical failure occurs when the inferred history and the real history differ by a topologically nontrivial loop.

Drop the word “history” and you are left staring at a quiet syndrome, announcing that nothing happened. The quiet syndrome is compatible with both the short walk and the lap.

Four flips around the doughnut

Use the toric code on a square lattice wrapped periodically in both directions. Put one physical qubit on every edge. Let

\[ A_v=\prod_{e\ni v}X_e, \qquad B_p=\prod_{e\in \partial p}Z_e, \]

where \(v\) labels a vertex, \(p\) labels a plaquette, \(e\) labels an edge, and \(X_e\) and \(Z_e\) are Pauli operators on edge \(e\). The ground space has eigenvalue \(+1\) for every vertex operator \(A_v\) and plaquette operator \(B_p\). A \(-1\) result is a syndrome defect, interpreted in the ideal model as an anyonic excitation [R030].

Take a periodic row containing four horizontal edges, \(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4\). Apply \(Z\) errors consecutively:

\[ E_j=Z_{e_1}Z_{e_2}\cdots Z_{e_j},\qquad j=1,2,3,4. \]

A single \(Z_e\) anticommutes with the two vertex checks at the ends of \(e\). Therefore \(E_1\) creates two violated vertex checks.

Multiplying by \(Z_{e_2}\) restores the shared vertex and violates the next one: one endpoint has moved. The same happens at \(e_3\).

After \(e_4\), the moving endpoint meets the first endpoint and both disappear.

Step | Physical action | Visible syndrome | Topological result | |

0 | identity | none | identity | |

1 | \(Z_{e_1}\) | two endpoints | pair created | |

2 | \(Z_{e_1}Z_{e_2}\) | two endpoints | one endpoint moved | |

3 | \(Z_{e_1}Z_{e_2}Z_{e_3}\) | two endpoints | one endpoint moved again | |

4 | \(\bar Z=\prod_{i=1}^{4}Z_{e_i}\) | none | noncontractible logical loop | |

Why is the last row not the identity? Choose a noncontractible \(X\) loop \(\bar X\) crossing this row once. At the one crossing, \(XZ=-ZX\), while all other factors commute. Hence

\[ \bar X\bar Z=-\bar Z\bar X. \]

An operator that anticommutes with a logical observable changes the encoded state. The syndrome is empty, but the logical qubit has suffered \(\bar Z\). This is the local-error-chain mechanism in its least decorative form [R030]; [R141].

For an \(L\times L\) periodic lattice, the shortest such loop has \(L\) edges. The code distance is therefore \(d=L\), and ideal decoding can guarantee correction of at most \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) adversarial Pauli errors.

That statement is a worst-case combinatorial guarantee. A threshold, later in this chapter, is a different kind of claim: an asymptotic statement about a probability distribution over faults and a specified decoder.

The edge spins above may be physical qubits, cluster-encoded pseudospins, or digitally emulated variables. The algebra of an error chain is the same.

The protection is not. A simulator can execute the code Hamiltonian while its underlying hardware remains protected only by ordinary active error correction.

An analog material realizes passive topological protection only if its own low-energy spectrum, excitations, and local perturbations implement this structure.

The gap charges for birth, not for walking

The Hamiltonian can do some of the work without anyone measuring a syndrome and feeding back. That is passive suppression: the device itself is doing the suppressing. No decoder, no recovery pulse, just the spectrum.

Two mechanisms matter.

First, a many-body gap makes excitation creation energetically costly. Define \(\Delta_a\) as the energy to create one well-separated anyon, in joules (J), and \(T\) as absolute temperature, in kelvin (K). A pair costs approximately \(2\Delta_a\) in the ideal dilute model. Its thermal weight contains

\[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{2\Delta_a}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right), \]

where \(k_{\mathrm B}\) is Boltzmann’s constant in J/K. The exponent is dimensionless because J divided by \((\mathrm{J/K})\mathrm{K}\) is one.

This suppresses creation when \(k_{\mathrm B}T\ll\Delta_a\) [R169]. It is a price of birth, not a fence around motion.

Second, nonlocal encoding makes a weak local perturbation poor at distinguishing logical sectors. In suitable gapped topologically ordered Hamiltonians, sufficiently weak local perturbations preserve the phase, and finite-size logical splitting can scale schematically as

\[ \delta E(L)\sim E_0 e^{-L/\xi}. \]

Here \(\delta E\) and \(E_0\) are energies, \(L\) is a linear system size, and \(\xi\) is a correlation length in the same length unit. [Theory] This stability is conditional on locality, a spectral gap, topological-order assumptions, and perturbations small enough not to leave the phase [R142]. It is not a blanket theorem about a fabricated, driven, open array.

Passive suppression does not infer an error chain or apply a recovery. If an anyon already exists, moving it can cost little or no additional energy.

The toric-code string above never needs more than two endpoints, so its maximum energy above the ground space is constant as \(L\) grows. Two-dimensional local stabilizer Hamiltonians therefore lack a macroscopic energy barrier under the assumptions of the Bravyi–Terhal no-go theorem [R168].

Thermal analyses of the ideal two-dimensional Kitaev model likewise show that its encoded information is not a self-correcting memory merely because the ground state is topological [R143]. [Theory] The theorem has a scope — two-dimensional stabilizer-code Hamiltonians with local interactions — and should not be inflated into a proof about every non-Abelian phase.

The warning, however, travels well: calculate the barrier; do not infer it from the gap.

Someone has to read the alarms

The four-flip loop left every check quiet. If you want to catch the walk before it closes, you have to look, guess a history, and undo it.

That looking-and-guessing is a decoder. The hardware does not magically know which pair of endpoints belong together. Someone, or some circuit, has to pick a history.

Active correction measures local checks, repeats measurements when they are noisy, decodes the spacetime syndrome, and applies or tracks a recovery. Its ingredients are operational:

  • extract enough syndrome information without uncontrolled backaction;

  • attach time stamps to repeated rounds;

  • use a decoder matched well enough to the actual noise;

  • complete recovery before errors accumulate beyond the decoder’s capacity.

Active correction can remove thermally created pairs before their worldlines become logical. It can also distinguish a transient detector fault from a persistent data fault by comparing rounds.

None of that is passive. The refrigerators do not run minimum-weight matching in their spare time.

What fails if you skip the decoder is exactly the four-flip loop: the alarms go quiet after the lap, and the logical observable has already changed sign.

A percentage that is not a promise

A fault-tolerance threshold is conditional. The name is worth keeping because it is a crossing, not a blessing: below it, growing the code helps; above it, growing the code can make things worse.

Roughly, for a family of growing codes, a specified fault model, syndrome circuit, decoder, and operation schedule, there may be a critical physical-fault parameter \(p_{\mathrm{th}}\) such that for \(p<p_{\mathrm{th}}\), increasing distance drives the logical error per operation downward [R141]. This does not say that every component’s quoted “fidelity” may be compared with one universal percentage.

In the canonical independent stochastic model studied by Dennis and collaborators, the toric/surface-code transition is about \(10.9\%\) when syndrome measurements are perfect; a phenomenological model with repeated noisy measurements and equal data/measurement error rates gives about \(2.9\%\) [R141]. [Theory/Numerics] Those are properties of those models, not acceptable error specifications for a defect device. Change leakage, correlations, geometry, boundaries, decoder, or circuit, and the number changes.

Threshold statements must name:

  • what counts as a location and a fault;

  • whether faults are independent, local stochastic, biased, leaking, or correlated;

  • whether state preparation and measurement are noisy;

  • whether qubits can disappear or change charge state;

  • the decoder and its latency;

  • the logical task and error metric.

A gap budget such as \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}>k_{\mathrm B}T\) is an energy-scale margin, not an error-correction threshold. A braid’s adiabatic condition is also not a threshold theorem. Vocabulary is cheaper than dilution; use the right noun.

Zero is a different word

Error-free means the logical channel is exactly the intended one. It is a mathematical identity, not a compliment you award a small number.

An ideal commuting-projector model at zero temperature, initialized exactly in its ground space and acted on by exact operators, can have zero error by assumption. A finite laboratory run instead has a nonzero logical-error probability, even when that probability is impressively small.

Below threshold means suppressible with increasing resources, not zero. Passive protection means reduced sensitivity to selected local faults, not zero.

So the four hats, in one place:

  • A gap charges for creating excitations. It need not charge for moving them.

  • A decoder guesses a history from alarms and tries to undo it.

  • A threshold is a crossing for a named noise model, circuit, and decoder.

  • Error-free is exactly the intended logical channel.

Protected is not immortal. The rest of the chapter is the ways a local accident still becomes a logical disaster.

Created is not the same as moved

Thermal errors have two stages. Creation pays an energy cost; diffusion may not.

Let \(a\) be the lattice spacing in metres and suppose a dilute equilibrium anyon density per site scales as \(n_a\sim e^{-\Delta_a/(k_{\mathrm B}T)}\). In two dimensions, the characteristic separation then scales as

\[ \ell_a\sim \frac{a}{\sqrt{n_a}} \sim a\,e^{\Delta_a/(2k_{\mathrm B}T)}. \]

Both \(\ell_a\) and \(a\) have units of metres; the exponential is dimensionless. [Theory] This estimate omits species degeneracy, interactions, boundaries, nonequilibrium baths, and kinetic bottlenecks, but it exposes the relevant competition: system size must not be confused with mean thermal separation [R169].

For a hypothetical \(10\,\mathrm{GHz}\) anyon energy \(\Delta_a/h\) at \(T=0.10\,\mathrm K\), use \(k_{\mathrm B}T/h\approx2.08\,\mathrm{GHz}\). Then \(\Delta_a/(k_{\mathrm B}T)\approx4.8\), so the ideal single-anyon Boltzmann factor is about \(8\times10^{-3}\), while a pair factor is about \(7\times10^{-5}\).

This is an illustrative calculation, not a defect-array forecast: the attempt rate, number of creation sites, bath spectrum, and actual many-body gap are still required. Ten thousand opportunities can make a small per-site weight operationally noticeable.

Once present, an anyon can random-walk, be pushed by disorder gradients, or be moved by control crosstalk. A boundary can absorb one member of a pair, leaving a charge whose history is difficult to infer.

For non-Abelian anyons, diffusion is worse than a misplaced classical particle: unrecorded exchanges and fusion events act on the fusion space [R015]. Active syndrome extraction and decoding must beat this kinetic process, not merely the initial Boltzmann factor.

What fails if you stop at “the temperature is below the gap” is the second stage. The Boltzmann factor prices birth. It does not pin the walkers.

Bigger helps one thing and hurts another

A real patch is finite, so three lengths compete: its linear size \(L\), the correlation length \(\xi\), and the characteristic spacing or travel length of unwanted quasiparticles. Increasing \(L/\xi\) can exponentially reduce virtual tunnelling between boundaries or around a handle.

The associated coherent phase rate is \(\delta E/\hbar\), because energy divided by \(\hbar\) has units s\(^{-1}\). But a larger area also supplies more places to create thermal pairs and more hardware that can fail. “Bigger” helps one mechanism and hurts another.

Disorder is not one scalar. Weak, bounded, static local perturbations may deform a stable topological phase without destroying it [R142].

[Theory] Fabrication disorder can nevertheless vary local gaps, couplings, cluster projectors, and measurement responses. A rare low-gap region becomes a thermal doorway.

A sign error or missing interaction may change the effective Hamiltonian rather than merely perturb it. Sufficiently strong disorder can close the mobility or spectral gap and drive the system out of the target phase.

Localization of unwanted quasiparticles can slow diffusion and therefore help memory in some models [R169]. [Theory/Numerics] It is not a free upgrade.

The same pinning can obstruct intended braids, strand poison quasiparticles near computational anyons, broaden spectroscopy, and invalidate a decoder that assumes homogeneous motion. A protection claim must specify the disorder distribution — including tails — and simulate both equilibrium and dynamics.

Leaving the space you promised

Two ways to leave the promised description look similar from far away and are not the same accident.

Quasiparticle poisoning means an uncontrolled topological charge enters, leaves, or changes the computational region. The poison is an extra anyon, not a slightly wrong pulse.

A thermally created anyon is one source, but poisoning also includes injection from an edge, a reservoir, a driven hotspot, or a nonequilibrium defect. In a non-Abelian device, a stray anyon can fuse with a computational anyon and change its fusion channel.

Subsequent nominal braids then implement the wrong unitary [R015]. The error is not necessarily visible to local charge measurements until information has already escaped.

Leakage means a physical constituent leaves the two-level space used by the code. The site is no longer the qubit the decoder was promised.

For a defect cluster, define \(P\) as the projector onto its intended low-energy doublet and \(Q=I-P\) as the projector onto all other cluster states. An ordinary encoded error has support within \(P\).

Leakage produces population in \(Q\). Then the projected Pauli model no longer describes the site, and its couplings can spread an error with amplitudes absent from the decoder’s model.

Topological distance does not suppress a single-site leakage event merely because the intended code is topological. Active leakage-reduction schemes periodically remove, reset, swap, or explicitly detect leaked population.

Surface-code studies show that untreated leakage can propagate through syndrome circuits and require dedicated handling [R220]. [Theory/Numerics] That result is evidence about an active code architecture, not proof that the same protocol works in an interacting defect phase.

For an analog cluster array, resetting one cluster may itself quench local couplings and create anyons.

Charge-state switching is especially treacherous. It may simultaneously be leakage from the cluster doublet, a missing or altered coupling in the many-body Hamiltonian, and an optical-readout failure. Counting it once in a Pauli error budget understates the damage.

Before, during, and after

Topology protects information after the system occupies the intended phase and logical sector. Cooling below the gap does not guarantee a known ground state: a finite sample may retain trapped quasiparticles, freeze into the wrong flux sector, or cross a small gap nonadiabatically. Initialization therefore needs a verified preparation protocol — cooling, pumping, syndrome measurement, boundary charge removal, or some combination — and a test of total topological charge.

Control has a window rather than a blessing. A pulse with spectral weight near a leakage transition can populate \(Q\).

A local control field strong enough to close the gap along a path can nucleate excitations. An intended adiabatic braid must be slow relative to relevant inverse-gap scales, but making it slower increases exposure to poisoning, drift, and dephasing.

The crude timescale \(\hbar/\Delta\) has seconds because \((\mathrm{J\,s})/\mathrm J=\mathrm s\); it is only a necessary scale, not a complete adiabatic bound, which also depends on matrix elements and the path’s minimum gap [R015]. Topology can make the ideal braid unitary insensitive to smooth geometric deformation.

It does not make arbitrary pulse errors, unintended braids, or dynamical phases harmless.

Readout has two layers. Local syndrome readout asks where excitations appear.

Logical readout asks for a nonlocal loop, boundary parity, or fusion outcome. A local detector can have assignment error, backaction, crosstalk, and dead time.

Repeating a noisy check turns decoding into a three-dimensional spacetime problem; it does not make the check perfect [R141]. A readout result also needs a confidence model conditioned on leakage and charge state.

Destructive optical readout may be adequate at the end of a computation while being useless for repeated error correction.

A useful laboratory report therefore gives separate confusion matrices for local checks and logical readout, leakage-conditioned statistics, backaction measurements, cycle time, and decoder latency. Quoting only the best single-defect readout fidelity does not characterize the many-body protocol.

When many sites fail together

Threshold estimates are often generous only because the model is local. One formal local-stochastic condition bounds the probability that every location in a set \(S\) is faulty by a quantity that falls exponentially with \(|S|\). Correlations may exist, but high-weight events must become rapidly rarer.

A global magnetic transient, laser-intensity excursion, strain wave, shared microwave phase slip, or calibration error can act on many clusters at once. If one event writes a length-\(L\) string with probability proportional to a single-event rate rather than that rate raised to the \(L\)th power, increasing code distance may provide little benefit.

Long temporal correlations likewise make repeated syndrome rounds agree for the wrong reason. Work on correlated environments shows that fault-tolerance behavior depends on the correlations’ spatial and temporal decay rather than on a single per-qubit error probability [R221].

[Theory]

Correlations are not automatically fatal. Short-range, sufficiently weak correlations can remain compatible with threshold results under appropriate assumptions.

The audit task is to measure or bound the correlation function, map it through the cluster projector, and use that model in decoding and logical-level simulation. Averaging a covariance matrix down to one “error rate” discards exactly the information topology needs.

What the laboratory actually has

For a defect-cluster proposal, the protection stack should be demonstrated in order:

Layer | Required evidence | What it does not establish | |

Cluster encoding | isolated doublet, measured leakage gap, projected controls | topological order | |

Many-body phase | gap, correlations, topological-sector or anyon evidence | useful logical lifetime | |

Passive suppression | scaling against local perturbations, temperature, and size | active correction or zero error | |

Syndrome system | repeated check/fusion measurements with backaction characterized | operation below threshold | |

Active logical memory | logical-error scaling versus distance and rounds under measured noise | universal protected computation | |

Braiding/control | correct process on the fusion space with poisoning/leakage bounds | error-free gates | |

[Proposal] A fabricated defect array will have placement disorder, missing or wrong charge states, cluster leakage, local drives, and imperfect optical or microwave readout. The ideal Hamiltonian contains none of these unless they are explicitly added.

Consequently, exact diagonalization of a clean patch can establish a model property; it cannot establish passive laboratory protection. Likewise, successful decoding of synthetically injected independent Pauli errors establishes a decoder benchmark; it cannot establish that the material noise is independent or Pauli.

The decisive experiment is a scaling experiment. Vary a meaningful code distance or quasiparticle separation while holding relevant physical conditions fixed, characterize the microscopic noise, and show how logical error changes.

Repeat versus temperature to separate thermal activation from control-limited floors, and versus syndrome cadence to separate passive from active benefit. If larger samples only add more poison sources, the data will say so.

That is useful science, even when the line slopes the inconvenient way.

Ways to get this wrong

  • “The ground-state splitting is exponentially small, so the memory is self-correcting.” No. Small virtual splitting addresses coherent sector mixing. Thermal creation and diffusion are different processes.

  • “The temperature is below the gap, so no anyons exist.” No. Boltzmann suppression is finite, the sample has many sites, and nonequilibrium injection can dominate.

  • “The physical error rate is below the surface-code threshold.” Incomplete. Which rate, code, circuit, leakage model, correlations, decoder, and measurement model?

  • “The braid is topological, so control errors do not matter.” Smooth path deformations within the same gapped sector may be harmless. Leaving that sector, braiding the wrong charge, or poisoning the fusion space is not.

  • “Weak disorder localizes anyons, therefore disorder helps.” Sometimes one kinetic channel improves. Gaps, controls, readout, and intended motion can worsen.

  • “No syndrome was observed, so no logical error occurred.” The worked noncontractible loop has empty syndrome.

  • “Repeated measurement is passive protection.” It is active error correction, even if software tracks the recovery rather than physically applying it.

  • “Below threshold means error-free.” It means logical error can decrease with increasing resources under stated assumptions. Every finite implementation retains residual risk.

Check yourself

Show that four local \(Z\) errors on a noncontractible row can leave no syndrome and still flip the logical qubit.

Their endpoints annihilate after the chain closes. The closed chain winds nontrivially and anticommutes with a crossing logical \(X\) loop, so \(\bar X\bar Z=-\bar Z\bar X\).

What fails if you treat the gap as a fence against motion?

The gap prices creation. Once two endpoints exist, sliding one of them around the lattice need not cost more energy. The two-dimensional stabilizer no-go is exactly that missing barrier.

What is the difference between passive protection and active correction?

Passive protection comes from the Hamiltonian and encoding without syndrome feedback. Active correction measures, decodes, and recovers or tracks errors.

Why is a published threshold not automatically a hardware specification?

It belongs to a particular code, noise model, syndrome circuit, decoder, and operation definition; leakage and correlations can change or invalidate it.

How do poisoning and leakage differ?

Poisoning changes uncontrolled topological charge in the computational region. Leakage moves a constituent outside its intended local encoded subspace. One physical event can cause both.

What fails if a finite below-threshold device is called error-free?

Below threshold describes favorable scaling under stated assumptions. A finite noisy run still has a nonzero logical-error probability. Error-free means the logical channel is exactly the intended one.

A logical fault is a topologically nontrivial spacetime history. A gap suppresses creation but not automatically diffusion.

Finite size trades exponentially small virtual splitting against extensive fault opportunities. Disorder can preserve a phase yet create dangerous weak spots.

Poisoning and leakage leave the intended computational description. Initialization, control, and readout require separate error models.

Correlations can defeat distance-based suppression. Passive suppression, active correction, threshold operation, and error-free operation are four distinct claims.

Protected is not immortal.

  • [R141] E. Dennis, A. Kitaev, A. Landahl, and J. Preskill, “Topological quantum memory,” Journal of Mathematical Physics 43, 4452–4505 (2002). DOI: 10.1063/1.1499754. arXiv:quant-ph/0110143.

  • [R168] S. Bravyi and B. Terhal, “A no-go theorem for a two-dimensional self-correcting quantum memory based on stabilizer codes,” New Journal of Physics 11, 043029 (2009). DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/11/4/043029. arXiv:0810.1983.

  • [R143] R. Alicki, M. Fannes, and M. Horodecki, “On thermalization in Kitaev’s 2D model,” Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical 42, 065303 (2009). DOI: 10.1088/1751-8113/42/6/065303. arXiv:0810.4584.

  • [R169] B. J. Brown, D. Loss, J. K. Pachos, C. N. Self, and J. R. Wootton, “Quantum memories at finite temperature,” Reviews of Modern Physics 88, 045005 (2016). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.045005. arXiv:1411.6643.

  • [R142] S. Bravyi, M. B. Hastings, and S. Michalakis, “Topological quantum order: stability under local perturbations,” Journal of Mathematical Physics 51, 093512 (2010). DOI: 10.1063/1.3490195. arXiv:1001.0344.

  • [R015] C. Nayak, S. H. Simon, A. Stern, M. Freedman, and S. Das Sarma, “Non-Abelian anyons and topological quantum computation,” Reviews of Modern Physics 80, 1083–1159 (2008). DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1083. arXiv:0707.1889.

  • [R220] A. G. Fowler, “Coping with qubit leakage in topological codes,” Physical Review A 88, 042308 (2013). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.88.042308. arXiv:1308.6642.

  • [R221] E. Novais, E. R. Mucciolo, and H. U. Baranger, “Resilient quantum computation in correlated environments: A quantum phase transition perspective,” Physical Review Letters 98, 040501 (2007). DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.040501. arXiv:quant-ph/0607155.

Chapter 32 — A peak is not a braid

Two other labs want the same thing we want: a leftover you can walk around another leftover, so the memory they share rotates in a way a local bump cannot fake.

The first lab starts with a thin semiconductor wire, an ordinary superconductor glued along it, and a magnet. They hope leftover pieces of electron sit at the two ends and refuse to be ordinary electrons. Those leftovers, if they are what the theory hopes, braid like Ising anyons.

The second lab starts with a flat sheet of electrons, colder than almost anything in the building, in a magnet strong enough to freeze their motion into Landau levels. They hope the electrons lock into a liquid whose leftover swirls, at one particular filling, braid like Fibonacci anyons.

Neither platform is a crystal full of defects. That is ours.

Theirs are older, louder, and further along in some rooms. We are going to steal their scorecard: what the braids can compute on paper, what the laboratory has actually seen, and which nouns they are still not allowed to skip.

A zero-bias peak is not a braid. A resistance plateau is not a Fibonacci anyon. Nature is under no obligation to read the press release.

Allowed, identified, controlled

Imagine finding footprints, identifying the animal, and training it to carry a package. These are three experiments, not one.

  • A phase is allowed. A Hamiltonian has a topological region on an ideal phase diagram.

  • An excitation is identified. Several independent measurements rule out ordinary states and determine charge, fusion, and statistics.

  • A computational operation is controlled. Initialization, a braid or parity-measurement sequence, and readout implement a reproducible unitary on an encoded space.

After this paragraph the footprints are gone. The three layers are the scorecard.

Majorana nanowires have strong work at layer one and parts of two. Fractional quantum Hall fluids have conclusive demonstrations of Abelian fractional charge and statistics at some filling factors.

That does not identify Fibonacci quasiparticles at filling factor \(12/5\). Neither substitution is permitted.

The leftovers themselves are not one object wearing four hats.

A leftover sitting at the end of a one-dimensional superconducting segment is an extrinsic defect mode. The ends were put there by the fabricator.

A vortex in a suitable two-dimensional topological superconductor can behave as an Ising anyon. A digitally programmed Majorana operator is an emulation.

A quasihole of an intrinsic quantum Hall fluid is an emergent excitation of the liquid. These objects can share braid mathematics without sharing physical evidence or passive protection.

What the Ising braid can compute

We first compare the ideal anyon theories. This is a pencil-and-paper experiment. Laboratory status comes later.

The Ising theory has three charges: \(1\) (vacuum), \(\psi\) (a fermion), and \(\sigma\). Two \(\sigma\) leftovers fuse according to

\[ \sigma\times\sigma=1+\psi. \]

Encode one qubit in four \(\sigma\) anyons whose total charge is \(1\). Define \(|0\rangle\) as the state in which the first pair fuses to \(1\), and \(|1\rangle\) as the state in which it fuses to \(\psi\). Let \(B_1\) exchange the first two anyons counterclockwise, and let \(B_2\) exchange the middle two. In a common phase convention, after dropping one common global phase,

\[ B_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad B_2=\frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 1+i&1-i\\ 1-i&1+i \end{pmatrix}. \]

Now multiply:

\[ B_1B_2B_1=\frac{1+i}{2} \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} =e^{i\pi/4}H, \]

where \(H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is the Hadamard gate. Thus Ising braids give the phase gate \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\) and \(H\), up to global phases. These belong to the Clifford gate set [R015].

The missing gate is easy to name:

\[ T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4}). \]

No braid of Ising anyons approximates \(T\) arbitrarily well. Ising braiding generates only a finite projective Clifford image, not a dense subset of all one-qubit rotations. Universal computation therefore needs an added non-topological resource, commonly a specially prepared magic state, a non-topological phase operation, or an appropriate measurement protocol [R015].

Hence non-Abelian is not the same as universal. Drop that distinction and an Ising leftover is asked to do Fibonacci work.

What the Fibonacci braid can compute

The Fibonacci theory has charges \(1\) and \(\tau\), with

\[ \tau\times\tau=1+\tau. \]

Encode one qubit in three \(\tau\) anyons with total charge \(\tau\). Define \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) by whether the first pair fuses to \(1\) or \(\tau\). Let

\[ \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt 5}{2} \]

be the golden ratio. A standard choice of the basis-change and exchange matrices is

\[ F= \begin{pmatrix} \varphi^{-1}&\varphi^{-1/2}\\ \varphi^{-1/2}&-\varphi^{-1} \end{pmatrix},\qquad R= \begin{pmatrix} e^{-4\pi i/5}&0\\ 0&e^{3\pi i/5} \end{pmatrix}. \]

The first exchange is \(B_1=R\). To exchange the second and third anyons, first change fusion basis, exchange, and change back:

\[ B_2=F^{-1}RF=FRF, \]

because this convention has \(F^{-1}=F\). The relative phase of the two eigenvalues of \(B_1\) is

\[ \frac{e^{3\pi i/5}}{e^{-4\pi i/5}}=e^{7\pi i/5}=e^{-3\pi i/5}, \]

which is not a Clifford \(Z\)-rotation. More importantly, \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) rotate about different axes.

Their braid words form a dense representation on the computational space: longer words can approximate an arbitrary one-qubit unitary, and suitable braids of larger encodings supply entangling gates [R015]. Phase conventions can change signs and common phases in these matrices, but not this gate-set conclusion.

Here is the compact result:

Anyon model | Elementary fusion | Braiding supplies | Braiding alone universal? | Missing engineering | |

Ising/Majorana | \(\sigma\times\sigma=1+\psi\) | Clifford gates such as \(H\) and \(S\) | No; no dense gate set | non-Clifford resource, parity control, leakage control | |

Fibonacci | \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\) | dense single-qubit rotations and entangling braids | Yes, ideally | compilation, initialization, fusion readout, thermal and leakage control | |

Universality is a property of the braid representation, not proof that the anyons exist in a sample.

A wire that wants two leftover ends

Consider a one-dimensional semiconductor with strong spin–orbit coupling, sitting against an ordinary \(s\)-wave superconductor, in a magnetic field. Cooper pairing leaks into the semiconductor through the interface.

People say the wire is proximitized. The name is worth keeping because the pairing is borrowed, not grown in the semiconductor itself.

A minimal Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian is

\[ H(p)=\left(\frac{p^2}{2m^*}-\mu\right)\tau_z +\alpha p\,\sigma_y\tau_z +V_Z\sigma_x +\Delta\tau_x. \]

Here \(p\) is momentum in kg m s\(^{-1}\); \(m^*\) is the electron effective mass in kg; \(\mu\) is chemical potential in joules or electronvolts; \(\alpha\) is the spin–orbit coefficient in energy-times-length; \(V_Z\) is Zeeman energy; and \(\Delta\) is the induced superconducting pairing energy. The Pauli matrices \(\sigma_a\) act on spin, while \(\tau_a\) act on particle–hole space. Every term has units of energy: for example, \(\alpha p\) is energy-times-length times inverse length.

For the ideal, uniform, single-band model, the bulk gap closes and reopens at

\[ V_Z^2=\Delta^2+\mu^2. \]

The region \(V_Z>\sqrt{\Delta^2+\mu^2}\) is topological and supports a leftover mode near each end of a sufficiently long segment [Theory] [R222]. Spin–orbit coupling, Zeeman splitting, and ordinary pairing have together manufactured an effective spinless \(p\)-wave channel.

That leftover is a Majorana operator \(\gamma_j\). It is its own partner,

\[ \gamma_j^\dagger=\gamma_j,\qquad \{\gamma_i,\gamma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}, \]

where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) for \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Two Majoranas define one ordinary fermion,

\[ f=\frac{\gamma_1+i\gamma_2}{2},\qquad i\gamma_1\gamma_2=2f^\dagger f-1. \]

The occupation \(f^\dagger f\) is stored nonlocally between the two ends. Four Majoranas at fixed total parity provide a qubit. An ideal counterclockwise exchange is represented, up to orientation convention, by

\[ U_{ij}=\exp\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\gamma_i\gamma_j\right). \]

These are the same Ising operations used in the worked example.

If the end modes decay over a localization length \(\xi\), their overlap in a clean wire of length \(L\) is roughly proportional to \(e^{-L/\xi}\), often with an oscillatory prefactor. Increasing \(L/\xi\) can suppress coherent splitting.

It does not suppress quasiparticle poisoning, a stray low-energy state near one end, a bad tunnel barrier, or a control pulse that closes the gap. Nonlocal encoding protects against a specified class of local perturbations, not against the laboratory as a whole.

Other leftover-end platforms

Semiconductor nanowires are not the only proposal. Two-dimensional semiconductor–superconductor heterostructures can form gate-defined networks; magnetic-atom chains on superconductors can produce effective topological bands; and vortices or boundaries in candidate intrinsic topological superconductors can host zero-energy states [Proposal/Theory] [R223].

The distinction between intrinsic and engineered matters. In an intrinsic topological superconductor, the superconducting bulk itself carries the relevant topological invariant.

In a hybrid, ordinary components collectively realize an effective topological phase under tuned conditions. A sharp zero-energy spectroscopic feature is compatible with a Majorana in either setting, but ordinary Andreev bound states, disorder, and inhomogeneous potentials can imitate important signatures [R223].

Spectroscopy locates a suspect. It does not conduct the trial.

Electrons in a flat magnet

A two-dimensional electron gas in a perpendicular magnetic field \(B\) forms Landau levels. Define the dimensionless filling factor

\[ \nu=\frac{nh}{eB}, \]

where \(n\) is the areal electron density in m\(^{-2}\), \(h\) is Planck’s constant in J s, and \(e\) is the elementary charge in C. The units cancel because \(eB/h\) has units of inverse area.

Interactions can stabilize incompressible fractional quantum Hall liquids at rational \(\nu\). The \(k=3\) Read–Rezayi state occurs at partial filling \(3/5\) in its simplest spin-polarized form and contains a Fibonacci topological sector [Theory] [R139].

With two lower Landau levels filled, that corresponds to total filling \(13/5\). Particle–hole conjugation within the active Landau level maps it to partial filling \(2/5\), hence total filling \(12/5\).

The conjugate reverses appropriate chiral data but retains Fibonacci fusion content. “Read–Rezayi at \(12/5\)” is therefore often shorthand for this candidate family, not an experimentally stamped label.

The microscopic Coulomb problem does not promise to choose that family. Landau-level mixing, finite quantum-well thickness, disorder, spin polarization, and charge-density order compete.

Exact diagonalization and density-matrix-renormalization studies have found regimes consistent with Read–Rezayi or its particle–hole conjugate [Numerics] [R225]; [R227]; [R228]. Finite systems and model-dependent corrections leave room for competing Abelian or symmetry-broken interpretations.

Agreement with a trial-state overlap or entanglement spectrum is powerful numerical evidence, not a quasiparticle braid.

Why a Fibonacci leftover would be special

A quasihole in the Fibonacci sector carries charge and topological charge. Its electromagnetic charge affects transport and interferometer phase; its topological charge determines the fusion space. Exchanging quasiholes acts on that space by the \(F\) and \(R\) matrices above. A decisive program must therefore connect several observables:

  • a robust incompressible plateau and activated longitudinal resistance;

  • fractional quasiparticle charge;

  • edge or thermal measurements compatible with the candidate topological order;

  • fusion-channel-dependent interference or projective fusion outcomes;

  • noncommuting, order-dependent braid operations consistent with the predicted matrices.

No single item substitutes for the list. A plateau without fusion, or an interferometer without an identified phase, is still only layer one or a fragment of layer two.

What the laboratory actually has

The evidence snapshot below follows peer-reviewed literature through 2026 and states the strongest justified conclusion, not the most exciting possible interpretation.

Claim | Status | Platform | What was measured or established | Verdict | |

The ideal spin–orbit nanowire has a topological phase and endpoint Majoranas above the phase boundary | [Theory] established | semiconductor–superconductor | BdG invariant and gap closing/reopening in model Hamiltonians [R222] | candidate mechanism, not material identification | |

Hybrid and candidate intrinsic superconductors show zero-energy and related signatures | [Experiment] partial | nanowires, planar hybrids, chains, vortex systems | tunnelling and spatial spectroscopy; trivial states can imitate key features [R223] | compatible evidence, platform-dependent and not a braid | |

Single-shot interferometric parity readout is feasible in an InAs–Al device | [Experiment] demonstrated operation | gate-defined InAs–Al hybrid | up to 1 fF capacitance shift, signal-to-noise ratio 1 in 3.6 µs, state dwell time above 1 ms near 2 T, and 1% assignment error [R224] | a strong readout primitive; the paper analyzes both trivial and topological origins | |

Majorana fusion rules and non-Abelian exchange have been conclusively demonstrated in these solid-state devices | not established | Majorana candidates | no accepted controlled exchange establishing the Ising braid representation [R223]; [R224] | remains a required experiment | |

An incompressible \(12/5\) fractional quantum Hall state exists in high-quality GaAs | [Experiment] demonstrated | GaAs quantum well | activated transport; one 30-nm-well study reported a zero-tilt activation gap near 30 mK [R226] | establishes the plateau, not its topological order | |

The \(12/5\) state is the particle–hole-conjugate \(k=3\) Read–Rezayi phase | [Numerics/Theory] supported candidate | second Landau level | finite-size spectra, entanglement data, and competing-order studies [R225]; [R227]; [R228] | plausible but not uniquely identified experimentally | |

Fractional statistics can be measured in an electronic quantum Hall interferometer | [Experiment] demonstrated for Abelian anyons | \(\nu=1/3\) Laughlin state | phase slips consistent with quasiparticles encircling localized fractional charge [R131] | validates an important method, but not Fibonacci statistics | |

Fibonacci fusion and braiding have been observed at \(12/5\) | not established | fractional quantum Hall | no conclusive quasiparticle-identification-and-braid sequence [R139]; [R225]; [R226]; [R227]; [R228] | theoretical candidate, not demonstrated Fibonacci hardware | |

The thermal scale illustrates the quantum-Hall difficulty. A reported \(12/5\) activation gap of \(30\ \mathrm{mK}\) corresponds to

\[ k_B T=(8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}})(0.030\ \mathrm{K}) \approx2.6\ \mu\mathrm{eV}, \]

where \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant [R226]. Energy-per-kelvin times kelvin gives energy, as required.

This is an activation scale extracted from transport, not necessarily the pristine many-body gap. Either way, wiring, filtering, and local electrostatic control must avoid heating a fluid whose useful scale is tiny.

What each platform cannot skip

The wire

  • Identity before arrays. Disorder and smooth confinement can create low-energy Andreev states that resemble end Majoranas. Scaling an ambiguous unit cell produces a larger ambiguity.

  • A hard, uniform gap. Gates, magnetic field, semiconductor density, and superconductivity must coexist across every segment and junction. The ideal inequality \(V_Z>\sqrt{\Delta^2+\mu^2}\) is not a factory acceptance test.

  • Networks and motion. One-dimensional endpoints cannot literally pass each other. Braiding needs junction networks or measurement-only parity sequences, each with calibrated tunnel couplings and protected paths.

  • Parity lifetime and readout. Quasiparticle poisoning changes the encoded sector. Fast, repeatable, quantum-nondemolition parity measurements are therefore part of the qubit, not an optional oscilloscope attachment.

  • Non-universal braids. Even perfect Ising braiding still needs a high-quality non-Clifford resource. That resource can dominate overhead and weaken the slogan “all gates are topological.”

The fluid

  • Phase identification. A \(12/5\) plateau must be distinguished from competing orders before its quasiparticles become computational inventory.

  • Small operating scale. The fragile state demands ultralow electron temperature, extremely clean material, and low-noise gates [R226].

  • Controlled quasiparticles. Gates must create, position, move, and fuse individual quasiholes without closing the gap or unintentionally reconstructing the edge.

  • Interferometer stability. Coulomb charging, changing device area, localized quasiparticles, and edge equilibration can alter phase signals. A scalable processor needs many such elements calibrated simultaneously.

  • Readout and leakage. Fusion charge must be measured without accidentally adding quasiparticles. Universal braid mathematics does not provide a cable plan.

Five gates a defect array still has to pass

A defect array may offer site-by-site fabrication and familiar spin readout that a quantum Hall fluid lacks. It pays elsewhere: the desired topological Hamiltonian and anyons have not yet emerged. The comparison suggests five milestone gates.

  • Derive a many-body topological phase from measured microscopic defect parameters, not only from an intended interaction graph.

  • Measure the bulk gap and topological diagnostics while ruling out a prepared but unprotected state.

  • Create localized excitations and establish their fusion channels.

  • Demonstrate order-dependent braid operations or an equivalent measurement-only protocol.

  • Show that logical error decreases when separation, code distance, or another predicted protection parameter increases.

The right benchmark is not “does the platform show a two-level system?” Majorana devices did that long ago. It is whether the full chain from Hamiltonian to protected operation survives alternative explanations.

Ways to get this wrong

  • “A zero-bias peak is a Majorana.” A peak is a spectroscopic observation. Majorana identification requires correlated spatial, gap, parity, fusion, and ultimately statistics evidence; trivial bound states can contribute similar peaks [R223].

  • “Parity readout proves what carries the parity.” The 2025 InAs–Al experiment demonstrated an excellent measurement primitive and explicitly treated topologically trivial and non-trivial interpretations [R224]. Instrument capability is not quasiparticle identity.

  • “The \(12/5\) plateau proves Fibonacci order.” Quantized Hall response and activated transport establish an incompressible phase. They do not uniquely determine its fusion category [R225]; [R226]; [R227]; [R228].

  • “Quantum Hall anyons have been braided, therefore Fibonacci anyons have been braided.” The direct interferometric result in Ref. [R131] concerns Abelian Laughlin anyons at \(\nu=1/3\), not the non-Abelian candidate at \(12/5\).

  • “Non-Abelian means universal.” Ising anyons are non-Abelian but their braids produce Clifford operations only. Fibonacci anyons are computationally universal by braiding in the ideal theory [R015].

  • “Universal means scalable.” Universality says a gate set is dense. It says nothing about gap size, poisoning, control wiring, braid time, readout fidelity, fabrication yield, or heat load.

  • “A simulated braid settles the material question.” A processor can enact the same matrices without hosting the corresponding emergent quasiparticles. That validates control and theory, not intrinsic topological order.

Keep four nouns apart as you climb. Candidate phase: an ideal or numerically studied Hamiltonian supports the order.

Compatible signature: data agree with a prediction but also admit alternatives. Quasiparticle identification: independent observables establish charge, fusion, and statistics.

Topological qubit: an encoded state is initialized, operated, and read out with an error advantage tied to topology. Do not skip a noun while climbing this ladder.

Check yourself

Why are Majorana zero modes associated with Ising rather than Fibonacci computation?

Their fusion space and exchange operators realize the Ising braid representation, which generates Clifford gates but not a dense universal gate set.

Show that the Ising product \(B_1B_2B_1\) is a Hadamard, up to a global phase.

Direct multiplication gives \(\frac{1+i}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}=e^{i\pi/4}H\). Braiding alone still cannot supply the non-Clifford \(T\) gate.

Why does \(12/5\) attract Fibonacci interest?

Its active Landau-level filling is \(2/5\), the particle–hole conjugate of the \(k=3\) Read–Rezayi state at \(3/5\), whose topological order contains a Fibonacci sector.

What did the 2025 InAs–Al experiment establish?

Fast single-shot interferometric fermion-parity measurement with 1% assignment error under reported conditions, not conclusive Majorana identity, fusion, or braiding [R224].

What fails if an activated \(12/5\) plateau is treated as a Fibonacci qubit?

The plateau establishes an incompressible phase, not unique fusion content, controlled quasiparticles, fusion-channel readout, a non-Abelian braid test, or scaling of protected logical operations.

What is the central lesson for defect-engineered proposals?

Measure each link — microscopic Hamiltonian, phase, excitation, statistics, and logical operation — and preserve alternative explanations until an experiment removes them.

The wire has a simple effective Hamiltonian and a live fight over whether the leftover is the leftover it claims. The fluid has a real incompressible liquid and a live fight over which liquid it is.

Neither has shown a controlled non-Abelian braid in the solid-state device they want to sell. A defect array is not ahead of them.

It has not yet entered the same fight.

Chapter 33 — Programmable competitors

A superconducting chip can already fire a short list of microwave pulses and then measure. A cloud of cold atoms, parked by lasers and puffed into giant orbits, can be rearranged into a new graph overnight. Both platforms have prepared states that look like the models of the last few chapters.

A lattice of implanted spins might hide a Fibonacci anyon, but only after growth, placement, and a many-body gap. Every year spent waiting for that Hamiltonian is a year not spent on a processor that can already run a braid circuit. That unpaid bill is opportunity cost: the value of the route you did not take.

We will not pick a winner. We will put the same four-spin square on three platforms and compute what each one pays.

Two different jobs

There are two different jobs. Mix them up and every table in the chapter will lie.

The first job is to learn the model. Prepare states, make excitations, measure a braid or a correlation, watch a small system move.

The second is to build protected hardware. Make the low-energy sector of the physical system itself topologically ordered, so a local bump barely touches the encoded information.

Suppose a circuit prepares the exact ground-state wavefunction of a topological model and then leaves the hardware governed by an unrelated Hamiltonian. Then the state may display topological entanglement at the measurement time, while possessing no energetic protection against later local errors. Hence a prepared state is not a protected phase.

Superconducting processors and Rydberg arrays already have strong evidence for the first job. [Experiment] Superconducting processors have prepared toric-code states and moved their excitations [R125], and have digitally simulated Fibonacci string-net states, fusion, and braiding [R138].

[Experiment] A Rydberg array has shown signatures of a toric-code-type spin liquid in a programmable analog simulator [R126]. None of those statements, by itself, says that a stored logical qubit enjoyed passive topological protection.

A defect architecture is interesting for the second job only if its nearly static microscopic Hamiltonian produces the model at useful strength. Flexible imitation and passive protection are different products.

Drop the distinction and you will credit a digital braid matrix with a material anyon. That is the counterexample the rest of the chapter is written to prevent.

The same four-spin square

Place four two-level systems on the edges of one square and label them \(1,2,3,4\). For system \(i\), the Pauli operator \(Z_i\) has eigenvalue \(+1\) on \(|0\rangle_i\) and \(-1\) on \(|1\rangle_i\). The plaquette operator is the product of those four questions,

\[ P_\square=Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4, \]

and the target Hamiltonian is

\[ H_\square=-K P_\square, \]

where \(K>0\) is an energy, measured in joules or electronvolts.

Because \(P_\square^2=I\), the only possible eigenvalues are \(p=\pm1\). The \(p=+1\) sector has energy \(-K\), the \(p=-1\) sector has energy \(+K\), and the separation is \(2K\). Hence a single square already has a parity constraint and a gap.

It does not have topological order. There is no thermodynamic phase, no noncontractible loop, and no pair of locally indistinguishable ground-state sectors.

The square is useful because the same term appears as one ingredient in stabilizer Hamiltonians. Fair comparison means all three platforms receive this same small target, the same accounting of controls and ancillas, and the same test for protection.

Drop the last sentence and a platform that can fire six gates will look like a platform that has grown a phase. The gates are real. The phase is a different claim.

Six gates and a twist

For a short time \(\delta t\), with units of seconds, the desired evolution is

\[ U_\square(\delta t) =\exp\!\left(-\frac{iH_\square\delta t}{\hbar}\right) =\exp\!\left(+i\frac{K\delta t}{\hbar}P_\square\right), \]

where \(\hbar\) is Planck’s reduced constant in joule-seconds. The ratio \(K\delta t/\hbar\) is dimensionless.

Let \(R_z^{(4)}(\phi)=\exp(-i\phi Z_4/2)\) rotate qubit 4 through angle \(\phi\), measured in radians. A CNOT with control \(j\) and target 4 transforms \(Z_4\) into \(Z_jZ_4\) under conjugation. Therefore the sequence

1: ──■────────────────────────────■──
│ │
2: ──┼──■──────────────────────■──┼──
│ │ │ │
3: ──┼──┼──■────────────────■──┼──┼──
│ │ │ │ │ │
4: ──X──X──X──Rz(φ)─────────X──X──X──

implements \(\exp(-i\phi P_\square/2)\). Choosing

\[ \phi=-\frac{2K\delta t}{\hbar} \]

produces \(U_\square(\delta t)\) exactly in the ideal gate model. Hence the digital cost of one plaquette step is six two-qubit gates plus one single-qubit rotation.

Sparse connectivity can add routing gates. A parity-measurement construction can instead use an ancilla, but then reset, readout, and feedforward belong in the bill. The circuit is not free just because it is short.

Suppose the target is \(H=A+B\), where \(A\) and \(B\) contain terms that do not commute. A first-order product formula uses \[ e^{-iH\delta t/\hbar}\approx e^{-iA\delta t/\hbar}e^{-iB\delta t/\hbar}. \] The leading operator error per step is proportional to \(\delta t^2[A,B]/\hbar^2\).

More, shorter steps reduce this digitization error but require more imperfect gates. Commuting stabilizer terms avoid the product-formula error, not the hardware errors.

Defects have to invent the four-body term

A defect-spin array normally supplies one-spin terms and two-spin interactions — dipolar, exchange, superexchange, strain-mediated, or photon-mediated — not a clean \(Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4\) term. There are two routes.

The digital route compiles the CNOT sequence into whatever entangling gates the defects support. It works only if the four spins can be initialized, individually or selectively controlled, and read out, and if the six entangling operations fit inside the error budget.

A fixed sparse graph may require a central electron spin, nuclear ancillas, or swaps. [Experiment] Pairwise entanglement between individual diamond defect spins has been demonstrated [R080], and a seven-qubit diamond register has implemented fault-tolerant logical operations and flagged stabilizer measurements [R234].

Those results establish valuable primitives. They do not demonstrate a dense, static four-body topological Hamiltonian.

The analog route introduces mediator levels or a defect cluster. Virtual excursions can then generate a low-energy four-body interaction. To see the cost without pretending to have a materials design, suppose a particular fourth-order gadget has microscopic coupling energy \(J\), mediator penalty \(\Delta\), and a dimensionless coefficient \(c\). Dimensional analysis permits

\[ K_{\mathrm{eff}}=c\frac{J^4}{\Delta^3}. \]

Both sides have units of energy. Control of the expansion requires \(|J/\Delta|\ll1\), which also makes \(K_{\mathrm{eff}}\ll|J|\). Hence a gadget that is honest about perturbation theory is honest about a small gap.

Lower-order shifts and unwanted couplings must be cancelled or tolerated. [Proposal] Defects become competitive for passive Hamiltonian engineering only if the resulting \(K_{\mathrm{eff}}\) exceeds decoherence, disorder, temperature, leakage, and finite-size scales established in earlier chapters. No pulse diagram can rescue a static gap that is too small.

A chip that already ran the model

A superconducting implementation maps the exact circuit to calibrated microwave pulses and native two-qubit gates. Planar processors commonly provide a fixed or tunable local coupling graph; all-to-one connectivity for this square may be native, mediated by a coupler, or compiled with swaps. Nanofabrication makes repeated layouts possible, while frequency crowding, crosstalk, wiring, leakage beyond the computational doublet, and calibration remain system-level costs [R229].

This is the most direct route to digital plaquette evolution. It is also easy to change \(K\), reverse its sign, omit a plaquette, or measure a different string operator in software.

[Experiment] This control style supported preparation and probing of topologically ordered states on a superconducting processor [R125] and a later digital demonstration of Fibonacci fusion and non-Abelian braid action [R138]. In the Fibonacci experiment, ordinary superconducting qubits simulated the string-net Hilbert space and applied gates representing braids.

The hardware did not contain intrinsic material Fibonacci anyons [R138].

A tunable coupler can also engineer driven effective interactions, but “analog superconducting” does not automatically mean passive. If periodic drives, active calibration, or a finite-depth preparation circuit are required, turning them off generally returns a different native Hamiltonian. [Experiment] Separately, below-threshold surface-code scaling on a 105-qubit superconducting processor is evidence for active quantum error correction, not evidence for a self-correcting topological material [R230].

Hence the chip that ran the model is a superb instrument for the first job. It is not, by that fact, a casting of the second.

Atoms that refuse to sit next to each other

Park a neutral atom with optical tweezers. A laser can lift its outer electron into a huge orbit.

That puffed-up atom is a Rydberg atom. The name is worth keeping because the giant orbit is what makes the next atom feel it from far away.

For one commonly used model, the computational state \(|1\rangle_i\) is coupled by a laser toward a Rydberg level. Define \(n_i=(I-Z_i)/2\) as its occupation projector, \(\Omega_i\) as a laser Rabi angular frequency in radians per second, \(\delta_i\) as a detuning in radians per second, and \(V_{ij}\) as an interaction angular frequency. A useful rotating-frame Hamiltonian is

\[ \frac{H_{\mathrm R}}{\hbar} =\sum_i\left(\frac{\Omega_i}{2}X_i-\delta_i n_i\right) +\sum_{i<j}V_{ij}n_in_j, \qquad V_{ij}=\frac{C_6}{r_{ij}^{6}}. \]

Here \(X_i\) flips the two states, \(r_{ij}\) is the atom separation in metres, and \(C_6\) has units \(\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}m^6}\). The strong \(r^{-6}\) interaction creates a blockade: nearby atoms cannot all be resonantly excited. Geometry, detuning, and drive strength are therefore programmable Hamiltonian parameters [R231].

The native interaction is pairwise \(n_in_j\), not the product \(Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4\). The plaquette can be produced digitally by compiling the same parity circuit into blockade-mediated entangling gates.

A purpose-built multiqubit blockade pulse or an ancilla constraint can reduce depth, but its phase and leakage still require calibration. [Experiment] Parallel two-qubit gates with reported 99.5% fidelity on up to 60 atoms, together with low-error three-qubit gates, demonstrate that this route is more than a chalkboard possibility [R232].

They do not establish a native four-body plaquette term.

Rydberg arrays also offer the closest of the three platforms to a rapidly reconfigurable analog simulator. The atoms can be rearranged and the physical Hamiltonian above can act continuously rather than as a gate list.

[Experiment] A constrained 219-atom array reported signatures of a topological spin liquid [R126]. That was a finite, driven atomic simulator with engineered blockade physics.

Its evidence is stronger than a classical simulation of the same Hamiltonian. It is not evidence that the apparatus stores an indefinitely passive topological qubit after the lasers are removed.

Drop the lasers and you generally drop the Hamiltonian. That is the remark, not a complaint.

Count the parts, not the slogans

Who can talk to whom

Connectivity means which pairs can interact strongly enough, selectively enough, and at the same time. It is not the number of lines in a vendor diagram.

Suppose two sites share a long-range tail. Then they are connected in the Hamiltonian, but they are not independently programmable unless the tail can be switched or compiled away. Hence “connected” and “wired on demand” are different predicates.

Defect geometry is largely fixed after fabrication. Dipolar interactions are long-ranged but fall as \(r^{-3}\) and carry angular dependence; exchange is shorter-ranged and exponentially sensitive to wavefunction overlap. A beautiful graph on average can still be a poor graph sample by sample.

Superconducting circuits use lithographic nearest-neighbour or coupler graphs that are reproducible, and bus resonators or tunable couplers add options. Long-range logical edges usually consume routing, chip area, frequency allocation, or extra modes.

Rydberg tweezers permit two- and three-dimensional rearrangement, while the blockade radius supplies many-neighbour interactions. Long tails and simultaneous-addressing constraints remain. The graph is programmable. It is not an arbitrary adjacency matrix written in software.

How many useful operations you get

Raw coherence time is a poor scoreboard. A slower qubit can win if its gates are proportionally cleaner, and a long-lived memory can lose if initialization takes most of the experiment. The useful dimensionless quantities are operations per coherence time, error per circuit layer, leakage, and duty cycle.

Superconducting gates are electronically fast and support rapid repetition, but relaxation, dephasing, leakage, and calibration drift operate on the same chip [R229]. Neutral-atom entangling gates exploit strong Rydberg interactions; atom loss, Doppler effects, laser noise, spontaneous emission, rearrangement, and imaging enter the cycle [R231]; [R232]. Defect electron or nuclear spins can be excellent memories, but entangling remote defects, collecting photons, or addressing dense spectra can become the bottleneck.

Comparing one platform’s best memory with another’s full algorithm would be an especially athletic category error. Drop the duty-cycle accounting and the longest-lived spin always wins a race it was not entered in.

Making, resetting, and reading

Superconducting qubits are fabricated as circuits and measured through microwave resonators and amplifiers in a dilution refrigerator. Fabrication is repeatable enough for large processors, but every additional control and readout channel adds cryogenic and calibration load [R229]; [R230].

Rydberg platforms assemble identical atoms from a reservoir rather than fabricating each atom. Rearrangement repairs vacancies before a run; loss can recur during it.

State-selective fluorescence gives highly parallel readout, generally destructively for the detected atom, so reloading and sorting matter. [Experiment] Reconfigurable arrays have operated an encoded processor with up to 280 physical qubits and 48 logical qubits in sampling circuits [R233].

Those counts describe a logical experiment, not 280 permanently available, error-free atoms.

Defect hosts can hold spins in a compact solid and sometimes permit optical readout, but creating the desired defect, charge state, position, orientation, and spectral line are separate yields. The seven-spin diamond logical experiment [R234] used a local register around one optically active center. It should not be silently redrawn as a wafer-scale lattice of equivalent electronic defect clusters.

Four meanings of scalable

“Scalable” has at least four meanings: more physical sites, more simultaneously high-quality sites, more executable circuit depth, and more logical performance after overhead. Atom count chiefly demonstrates assembly.

Chip count chiefly demonstrates integration. Neither alone demonstrates a protected computation.

Superconducting processors require dilution refrigeration and dense classical control. Rydberg processors require ultrahigh vacuum, laser cooling, optical access, stable lasers, and repeated atom handling, though not a millikelvin solid-state stage [R231]. Defects span very different regimes: some spins can operate at room temperature, while high-quality optical interfaces or particular defect species require cryogenic operation.

“Defects need no cryogenics” is therefore not a platform-level fact. Drop the species and the interface, and the slogan becomes a counterexample waiting for a citation.

Changing the energy without compiling

Analog programmability asks which coefficients in \(H\) can be changed without decomposing time evolution into gates.

Rydberg arrays offer tunable geometry, local or global detuning, drive amplitude, and strong finite-range constraints. Their native Hamiltonian family is rich but not arbitrary.

Superconducting circuits offer tunable frequencies, drives, and couplers, with excellent waveform control but substantial calibration and a tendency toward digital compilation. Defects offer the least post-fabrication reconfiguration; local fields and drives can tune them, but microscopic exchange paths and positions remain fixed.

That inflexibility is a disadvantage for discovery. It is a possible advantage only after the right static Hamiltonian has actually been found. An unchangeable wrong \(H\) is not a feature.

What the laboratory actually has

Evidence in this chapter is assessed through August 2026. The cited experiments are milestones, not purchasing advice; each platform changes faster than a cryostat’s delivery estimate.

The compact comparison is:

Criterion | Crystalline defects | Superconducting processor | Rydberg array | |

Native interactions | Dipolar, exchange, optical/phonon mediated; strongly materials-dependent | Circuit-mediated two-body gates and tunable couplers | Laser drive plus strong distance-dependent blockade interactions | |

Graph | Fixed and fabrication-disordered | Lithographic, usually local; routing/couplers extend it | Reconfigurable geometry with interaction tails | |

Control style | Local microwave/optical control; static interactions possible | Highly developed fast digital pulse control | Strong digital gates and unusually natural analog control | |

Readout | Species-dependent optical or electrical interface | Multiplexed microwave readout | Parallel fluorescence imaging, with atom-loss/reload cost | |

Environment | Host- and transition-dependent; room temperature is not universal | Dilution refrigerator and cryogenic wiring | Ultrahigh vacuum, laser cooling, optical infrastructure | |

Present topological evidence cited here | Defect entanglement and small logical registers, not a material topological phase [R080]; [R234] | Digital toric-code and Fibonacci simulations [R125]; [R138] | Analog spin-liquid signatures in a finite driven array [R126] | |

Plaquette route | Gate compilation or weak gadget-generated \(K_{\mathrm{eff}}\) | Short digital circuit; driven analog options | Blockade-compiled gate or constrained analog construction | |

Passive-protection opportunity | Static host Hamiltonian could qualify if all scale tests pass | Usually active QEC or driven simulation | Emergent analog phase possible during drive; passive memory not automatic | |

This table does not crown a universal winner because the answer changes with the job.

[Experiment] For programmable exploration today, superconducting processors have directly executed topological-state circuits and digital non-Abelian braid protocols [R125]; [R138], while Rydberg arrays combine flexible geometry with an analog Hamiltonian that has produced topological-spin-liquid signatures [R126]. [Experiment] Defect platforms have compelling local control, entanglement, networking, and small-register results [R080]; [R234], but the cited evidence does not include a defect lattice realizing an emergent non-Abelian phase.

[Proposal] For a static, material Hamiltonian, defects retain a logically distinct opportunity: once fabricated, the interaction network might remain on without a long gate schedule. That statement is an incentive to calculate and measure \(K_{\mathrm{eff}}\), disorder, and thermal stability — not evidence that the opportunity has been realized.

Ways to get this wrong

1. Calling a prepared state a protected phase

A circuit can prepare the exact ground-state wavefunction of a topological model and then leave it governed by an unrelated hardware Hamiltonian. The state may have topological entanglement signatures at the measurement time, while possessing no energetic protection against later local errors.

2. Calling active correction passive protection

Surface-code cycles can suppress logical error through repeated syndrome extraction, decoding, and feedback. That is genuine protection and an engineering triumph [R230].

It is active protection. A static Hamiltonian gap suppressing local transitions without continual syndrome cycles is passive protection.

Neither should borrow the other’s adjective.

3. Calling a Rydberg analog experiment “just digital”

Also wrong. When the laser-driven many-atom Hamiltonian itself realizes a phase over its coherent evolution window, its correlations and excitations are emergent properties of that analog Hamiltonian, not a classical playback of stored answers. But finite lifetime, drive dependence, boundaries, preparation, and readout still limit memory claims.

4. Treating connectivity as free

A long-range interaction can create unwanted edges as readily as wanted ones. A movable atom consumes transport time.

A resonator bus adds modes and crowding. A dipolar tail adds disorder and crosstalk.

Every graph must be compiled into simultaneous, calibrated operations or into a quantitatively controlled static Hamiltonian.

5. Comparing a proposed defect array with demonstrated competitors

A projected defect gap should be labelled [Proposal] or [Speculation], not placed in the same table cell as a measured gate or correlation. Conversely, present programmable hardware should not be credited with passive Fibonacci protection merely because it displayed a Fibonacci braid matrix.

The superconducting Fibonacci experiment [R138] used physical superconducting qubits to digitally emulate Fibonacci string-net states and braids. The Rydberg spin-liquid experiment [R126] probed correlations emerging from a driven analog Hamiltonian in a finite atomic array.

A defect spin is a physical qubit; a register code such as [R234] is an encoded logical qubit. A static defect lattice would possess topological order only if its many-body Hamiltonian, spectrum, correlations, and excitations met the phase criteria.

None of the first three observations implies the fourth.

Check yourself

Show that \(P_\square^2=I\) forces a gap of \(2K\).

The only eigenvalues of a square-one Hermitian operator are \(\pm1\). Then \(H_\square=-KP_\square\) takes the values \(-K\) and \(+K\), so the sectors are separated by \(2K\).

Why is one plaquette not topological order?

It lacks an extended many-body phase, nonlocal logical sectors, and the scaling properties that make local perturbations ineffective.

What fails if you treat a digitally displayed Fibonacci braid as a material anyon?

The hardware Hamiltonian need not contain the anyon at all. Ordinary qubits can represent the Hilbert space and apply gates. The braid matrix is then a circuit output, not an excitation of the chip.

Show that the six-CNOT sequence with \(\phi=-2K\delta t/\hbar\) produces \(U_\square(\delta t)\) in the ideal gate model.

Conjugation by the three CNOTs turns \(R_z^{(4)}(\phi)\) into \(\exp(-i\phi P_\square/2)\). That choice of \(\phi\) is exactly \(\exp(+i K\delta t\,P_\square/\hbar)\), which is \(U_\square(\delta t)\).

What would make a defect implementation scientifically distinct?

A quantitatively verified static low-energy Hamiltonian with a many-body gap and perturbative stability could provide passive physics without replaying a circuit. Long-lived isolated spins alone do not meet that condition.

What fails if you compare one platform’s best memory with another’s full algorithm?

The useful scores are operations per coherence time, error per layer, leakage, and duty cycle. A long-lived spin that cannot be entangled or read on schedule loses the race it was not entered in.
