Chapter 34 — The coordinate that is not the atom

You type a coordinate. The beam fires. A nitrogen ion punches into diamond and does not stop at the number you typed.

It rattles through the lattice, dumps energy into electrons and nuclei, and comes to rest somewhere nearby. Then you heat the stone.

A vacancy wanders. Maybe it finds the nitrogen.

Maybe it finds the surface. The glowing center, if one appears, sits where the chemistry finished — not where the file said “here.”

That gap is the whole chapter. A map of commanded sites is not a Hamiltonian.

The Hamiltonian you actually get is drawn by missing centers, extra centers, wrong charges, dark emitters, damaged spins, and bonds that landed a few nanometres off. Chapter 28 already showed why a few nanometres is not a rounding error: electron-spin dipolar coupling scales as \(J\propto r^{-3}\), so a small fractional error in bond length is tripled as a fractional error in coupling. A 20 nm graph that wants 20% coupling scatter has almost no room left.

Several processes can pattern emitters, grow a thin dirty layer, or count ions one by one. None cited here has made a dense, uniformly coupled, defect-complete cluster lattice at the sub-nanometre relative tolerance that graph demands.

Seven inspections, not one aim

Think of building a row of workshops. The truck crosses a property line.

The cargo ploughs through the ground. A mobile part wanders during heating.

The workshop may or may not assemble, receive the right number of electrons, open its door, or run the machine inside specification.

Those pictures name seven different questions. After this paragraph they die.

Beam accuracy says where the ion crosses the surface. Straggle says where it stops after ploughing through the crystal.

Diffusion says where a mobile vacancy wanders during heating. Creation yield says whether the intended complex assembles.

Charge-state yield says whether it receives the right number of electrons. Optical usability says whether initialization and readout work.

Spin usability says whether the machine inside initializes, stays coherent, and answers within specification.

A bright spot at the right map coordinate can fail the last test. A beautiful spin can fail the map. A complete array needs every indispensable site to pass every inspection, unless the architecture explicitly includes spares and repair.

The picture below follows one nine-site coordinate file through delivery and annealing to the endpoint audit. Dashed rings are commanded positions, green circles are accepted spin-active centers, and offsets or failed sites remain part of the device description.

Commanded coordinates do not determine the final defect array. Ion stopping, vacancy diffusion, structural conversion, charge state, and spin acceptance separate the coordinate file from the realized interaction graph.

Every fabrication and acceptance step has a conditional probability. Multiplying a beam-position number by a conversion yield is not enough. One has units of length. The other is a probability. The device needs both.

Nine spins and a 0.94 nanometre budget

Consider [Proposal] three triangular encoded clusters, each containing three electron-spin defects. This nine-site patch is not a topological phase. It is a fabrication coupon: can you place the same intra-cluster interactions more than once?

Let the intended nearest-neighbour separation inside each cluster be \(r=20\ \mathrm{nm}\). Require root-mean-square radial dipolar-coupling disorder below 20%.

Let \(\sigma_{\rm site}\) be the independent one-dimensional standard deviation of each endpoint along a bond. For \(J=C/r^3\), first-order propagation gives

\[ \frac{\sigma_J}{J}\approx \frac{3\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_{\rm site}}{r}. \]

The ratio is dimensionless because both \(\sigma_{\rm site}\) and \(r\) are lengths. Hence the placement allocation is

\[ \sigma_{\rm site}\le \frac{0.20(20\ \mathrm{nm})}{3\sqrt2} =0.94\ \mathrm{nm}. \]

This is a derived requirement, not a reported capability. It also omits angular-factor disorder, crystallographic site discreteness, exchange variation, and correlated registration error. Drop those omissions and the budget shrinks further.

Now compare it with a measured endpoint distribution. Focused Si implantation followed by annealing produced single SiV centers with a one-axis standard deviation of about \(32\ \mathrm{nm}\) around target coordinates [R190]. [Numerics] If, only for a scale estimate, that distribution were an unbiased Gaussian and the acceptance window were \(|x|<0.94\ \mathrm{nm}\), then

\[ P(|x|<0.94\ \mathrm{nm}) =\operatorname{erf}\!\left( \frac{0.94}{\sqrt2(32)}\right) \approx0.0235. \]

Requiring the same window independently in two lateral coordinates gives approximately \((0.0235)^2=5.5\times10^{-4}\) per site before depth is tested. Raising that toy number to nine gives about \(4.8\times10^{-30}\).

The calculation is not a forecast — the measured distribution need not be Gaussian into its central nanometre, and the SiV process was not optimized for this coupon. Its purpose is to expose the orders-of-magnitude mismatch between “tens of nanometres” and a sub-nanometre coupling-disorder allocation.

A ledger, not a single yield

Placement is only half the budget. Define the events

  • \(A\): the requested ion or vacancy is delivered;

  • \(C\): the desired structural complex forms;

  • \(Q\): the desired charge state is occupied;

  • \(O\): initialization and optical readout pass;

  • \(S\): spin coherence and control pass;

  • \(G\): the final three-dimensional position passes.

The usable-site probability is the conditional product

\[ p_{\rm use}=P(A)P(C|A)P(Q|A,C)P(O|A,C,Q) P(S|A,C,Q,O)P(G|A,C,Q,O,S). \]

This identity does not assume independence. Each factor is conditional on previous acceptance.

Hence a single published “yield” is almost never \(p_{\rm use}\). It is some prefix of the product, taken under the experiment’s own acceptance cuts.

In a deterministic \(^{15}\mathrm N\) implantation experiment, counted molecular ions were focused with \(121(35)\ \mathrm{nm}\) lateral resolution and produced about 0.6% optically identified \(^{15}\mathrm{NV}^{-}\) centers after annealing [R258]. [Experiment] That 0.6% is already a composite of delivery, structural conversion, negative charge, and optical detection — not a separate value for each factor. Even treating \(0.006\) as an optimistic upper bound on \(p_{\rm use}\) would give

\[ Y_9\le(0.006)^9\approx1.0\times10^{-20}, \]

before imposing the 0.94 nm geometry requirement.

For planning, suppose a future same-process line reaches the following explicitly hypothetical conditional values: \(0.995\) delivered, \(0.50\) structural conversion, \(0.90\) desired charge, \(0.85\) optical acceptance, \(0.90\) spin acceptance, and \(0.80\) geometric acceptance. [Proposal] Then

\[ p_{\rm use}=0.995(0.50)(0.90)(0.85)(0.90)(0.80)=0.274, \]

and, if sites are independent, \(Y_9=p_{\rm use}^9=8.7\times10^{-6}\). Correlated wafer damage or anneal drift could make the array yield still worse. Conversely, measured correlations, spares, repeated implantation, or post-fabrication selection require a different yield model. With no repair, even a 50% nine-site array yield requires

\[ p_{\rm use}\ge0.5^{1/9}=0.926. \]

That 92.6% is the useful fabrication target. “One ion on command” is merely its first factor. Drop the later factors and a counted arrival looks like a finished spin.

Shoot an ingredient, then wait for a workshop

Conventional implantation accelerates an ion species into a crystal, often through a lithographic aperture. The surface-entry distribution is set by aperture geometry, alignment, beam divergence, and vibration.

The ion then loses energy through electronic and nuclear collisions. Its stopping depth and lateral displacement are distributions, called longitudinal and lateral straggle.

The name is worth keeping because it is leftover scatter, not a typo in the aim. Crystal channeling can add non-Gaussian tails.

The implanted atom is not automatically the desired center. Nitrogen must acquire a neighbouring vacancy to become an NV center.

An implanted silicon atom must reach the appropriate split-vacancy configuration for SiV. Annealing supplies mobility and repairs some collision damage, but can also move vacancies to surfaces, aggregates, or unintended impurities.

In one masked CN\(^-\) implantation experiment, roughly 50 nitrogen atoms per 80 nm aperture produced a mean 3.5 NV centers — about 7% N-to-NV conversion under an 800 °C, two-hour anneal [R202]. [Experiment] It demonstrated patterned ensembles, not exactly one usable NV at each commanded atomic coordinate.

Implant energy presents a recurring trade. Lower energy gives shallower stopping and usually smaller straggle, but near-surface charge noise, vacancy loss, and damage can reduce conversion and coherence.

Higher energy can improve vacancy production and conversion while broadening depth and lateral distributions [R260]. [Experiment] There is no host-independent “implantation precision”: ion mass, energy, crystal orientation, target composition, and anneal recipe belong beside every number.

Take the mask off, keep the collisions

A focused ion beam raster-writes coordinates, which helps registration to pillars, waveguides, and cavities. It does not abolish stopping straggle.

For focused silicon implantation into diamond, the beam full width at half maximum was typically below 40 nm, calculated lateral straggle was 19 nm, and the measured created-center distribution had a 32 nm one-axis standard deviation [R190]. [Experiment] The measured Si-to-SiV conversion reached about 2.5% at 100 keV; electron irradiation and a second anneal raised a tested bulk-sample value to about 20% [R190]. Those values attach to that SiV process, not to NV, SiC, or sapphire.

Focused writing is attractive for sparse photonic devices because each coordinate can be registered independently. For dense interacting lattices, beam tails, dose calibration, redeposition, cumulative damage, stage drift, and write time become array variables. A nominal beam spot is a creation aim, not a final center covariance matrix.

Suppose the beam were infinitely sharp. The ion would still stop according to a collision distribution, and the vacancy would still wander. Hence a vanishing entry width does not imply a vanishing Hamiltonian error.

A thin layer with no street address

During growth you can open the impurity tap for only a thin interval, then close it. That thin dirty sheet is delta doping: a depth trick, not a street address.

In diamond, nitrogen layers about 1–2 nm thick were grown, then vacancies were supplied by irradiation and annealing; cap thickness selected nominal NV depths from about 5 to 100 nm [R204]. [Experiment] This is powerful depth engineering and avoids the implanted nitrogen’s stopping distribution. It does not choose a lateral lattice site: dopants remain random within the plane.

Delta doping is therefore complementary to a localized vacancy source. It narrows one coordinate while another process selects \(x\) and \(y\).

A 2025 experiment combined a nitrogen delta layer with a localized 200 keV electron beam and reported about 4 nm depth confinement and lateral standard deviation \(46(1)\ \mathrm{nm}\) in 280 nm diamond pillars [R207]. [Experiment] Characterized NVs had mean Hahn-echo \(T_2=98(37)\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) under those conditions [R207].

This is unusually complete endpoint evidence — position plus a spin metric — but it is not yet a 20 nm-pitch coupled lattice.

Drop the lateral process and you have a well-defined sheet of random sites. That is a useful sample. It is not a graph.

Write vacancies, not impurity atoms

Energetic electrons transfer momentum to lattice atoms and create vacancies with much less chemical implantation than a heavy ion beam. Uniform irradiation can raise the probability that pre-existing or implanted dopants find vacancies.

A focused electron beam can localize vacancy generation laterally, while a delta-doped layer supplies depth selection [R207]. The vacancy-generation volume is still three-dimensional, and mobile vacancies react during annealing.

Electron irradiation therefore changes \(P(C|A)\) and the damage landscape. It does not by itself guarantee \(A\) for a chosen impurity, \(Q\) for the final charge, or \(S\) for the spin.

In the SiV work, irradiation plus re-annealing improved conversion in a separate tested sample [R190]. Combining its improved yield with another sample’s best placement as though both occurred simultaneously would be a record-value collage.

Stop when one light appears

A tightly focused femtosecond pulse can create vacancies inside diamond without implanting a foreign atom. Subsequent local heating or furnace annealing lets a vacancy bind to native nitrogen. Optical feedback can stop the write-and-anneal sequence after a single emitter appears, rather than accepting the Poisson limit of one center per blindly dosed site.

Chen and colleagues reported approximately 96% single-NV creation yield with feedback and about 33 nm in-plane positioning deviation [R203]. [Experiment] This is a major creation-yield result.

It is not 96% sub-nanometre three-dimensional placement, 96% NV\(^-\) charge occupancy under every optical condition, or 96% spin acceptance. The method also requires suitable pre-existing nitrogen near the written vacancy.

Feedback raises \(P(C|A)\) for a bright center by watching and stopping. It does not write the covariance matrix of the finished spin. Those remain different columns in the ledger.

Align through the last hole

A scanning probe can carry a nanometre-scale aperture in its cantilever. The probe images surface markers, aligns locally, and admits ions through the aperture.

Persaud and colleagues integrated such a piezoresistive probe with an ion beam and demonstrated single highly charged-ion hits in resist; the terminal aperture limited the spot size [R259]. [Experiment] This solves an important registration problem and can bring a stencil close to the surface.

It does not remove aperture convolution, ion straggle, vacancy diffusion, or stochastic conversion. The cited instrument paper did not demonstrate a complete lattice of charge-stable, coherent color centers. “Scanning probe” names the alignment and collimation strategy.

It is not a yield certificate.

Heat until something wanders

Vacancy engineering chooses how many vacancies are generated, where they are generated, and which sinks compete for them. Heavy ions, electrons, neutrons, and lasers create different damage profiles. Annealing temperature and time control vacancy mobility, recombination, aggregation, surface loss, and capture by dopants.

In nitrogen-rich diamond implanted with focused Ar ions, Räcke and colleagues measured 0.04–0.79 created NV centers per implanted Ar ion over 12–132 keV [R206]. [Experiment] Their diffusion-and-surface-loss model placed an upper bound of roughly 300 nm on the single-vacancy diffusion length for an 800 °C anneal [R206].

[Numerics] That upper bound is not a statement that every final NV is displaced by 300 nm: nitrogen was already distributed in the crystal, and the endpoint is a reaction-and-capture process. It does prove that annealing cannot be represented honestly as “damage erased, position unchanged.”

Annealing can also change charge compensation and optical linewidth by altering residual defects. The correct optimization target is not maximum luminescence alone. It is the joint distribution of final position, desired charge, optical linewidth and stability, spin coherence, and nearby dark paramagnets.

Suppose you treat the furnace as a reset button. Then you will count a bright center as a well-placed spin and miss the capture walk that placed it. The 300 nm bound is the counterexample.

Count the arrivals, then audit the leftovers

The apparatus can detect or prepare a known number of incident ions and stop at the requested count. That is deterministic delivery: it names the count, not the fate.

It removes dose-number uncertainty. It does not make the collision trajectory deterministic, nor does it force an implanted atom into a particular complex or charge state.

Groot-Berning and colleagues extracted single laser-cooled \(^{15}\mathrm N_2^+\) ions at 5.9 keV, implanted without a mask, and verified \(^{15}\mathrm{NV}^{-}\) centers by ODMR after annealing [R258]. [Experiment] The lateral resolution was \(121(35)\ \mathrm{nm}\) and conversion about 0.6% [R258].

This is genuinely deterministic ion-number delivery and genuinely stochastic usable-center creation in the same experiment. The distinction is the central lesson of this chapter.

What the laboratory actually has

The table keeps unlike metrics in separate columns. A dash means the cited experiment did not establish that quantity as an array-level probability.

Process and conditions | Beam or creation accuracy | Straggle or diffusion | Structural/charge result | Optical/spin usability | Compound-array verdict | |

CN\(^-\) through 80 nm apertures; diamond; 800 °C, 2 h [R202] | Mask-defined 80 nm entry aperture | About 9 nm simulated straggle for the 20 keV N component [R202] | About 7% N-to-NV conversion | Fluorescent NV arrays; no complete spin-acceptance distribution | Patterned sites, not deterministic single centers | |

Focused Si, diamond, up to 100 keV [R190] | Beam FWHM below 40 nm | 19 nm calculated lateral straggle; 32 nm measured one-axis endpoint spread | Up to about 2.5% SiV conversion; separate irradiation/re-anneal test about 20% | Nearly lifetime-limited emitters occurred in nanostructures; not every site qualified | Useful photonic targeting; insufficient evidence for dense complete clusters | |

N delta layer plus focused electrons, diamond [R207] | 20 nm electron spot | About 4 nm depth confinement; \(46(1)\) nm lateral standard deviation | Dose-tunable NV count, not absolute deterministic conversion | Mean Hahn-echo \(T_2=98(37)\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) for characterized NVs | Depth and spin evidence coexist; lateral graph remains broad | |

Femtosecond vacancy writing with feedback, diamond [R203] | Diffraction-scale write focus | Vacancy creation and local annealing set endpoint | About 96% single-NV creation under feedback | Optical detection closes the feedback loop; full charge/spin pass rate separate | High creation yield, about 33 nm in-plane deviation | |

Counted \(^{15}\mathrm N_2^+\) at 5.9 keV, diamond [R258] | \(121(35)\) nm lateral resolution | Included in measured resolution, not eliminated | About 0.6% \(^{15}\mathrm{NV}^{-}\) conversion | ODMR and coherence characterized for created centers | Deterministic arrivals, very low nine-site compound yield | |

30 keV C implant through mask, 4H-SiC [R205] | Predetermined array coordinates | Simulated shallow \(V_{\rm Si}\) depth about 40 nm [R205] | \(19\pm4\)% generation efficiency; \(34\pm4\)% probability of a single emitter at optimized dose | Single emitters identified optically | Host-specific patterned array; no demonstrated sub-10-nm pair distribution | |

The strongest evidence is complementary rather than cumulative. Delta doping gives thin depth.

Focused beams and scanning apertures give lateral registration. Electron beams and lasers place vacancy generation.

Feedback raises the probability of exactly one bright center. Counted-ion implantation fixes arrival number.

Annealing activates complexes. No demonstrated process stack cited here simultaneously supplies sub-nanometre relative placement, near-unity desired-center formation, near-unity desired charge, array-wide optical and spin qualification, and a complete interaction graph.

A counted ion is a fabrication event. A fluorescent color center is a physical emitter.

An ODMR-active center is a physical spin qubit candidate. Several coupled spins may form an encoded qubit only after a low-energy subspace is demonstrated.

A regular image of bright points is not an interaction graph, and an interaction graph is not an emergent topological phase or a logical topological qubit. Fabrication supplies microscopic degrees of freedom and disorder distributions.

It does not supply topological order by vocabulary.

Ways to get this wrong

Beam width called placement accuracy. Entry width, simulated stopping straggle, annealed endpoint spread, and device-registration error answer different questions. Report each with axis, statistic, and conditions.

Creation yield called deterministic implantation. Counted-ion delivery controls \(A\). The 0.6% \(^{15}\mathrm{NV}^{-}\) result [R258] shows directly that \(C\), \(Q\), and detection remain stochastic.

Brightness called charge or spin yield. A fluorescence threshold can reject dark sites, but it does not by itself establish charge stability during control, \(T_2\), gate fidelity, or absence of nearby dark spins.

Annealing treated as a reset button. It mobilizes the vacancies needed for creation and changes damage; it can also broaden capture positions, lose vacancies at a surface, or form unwanted aggregates [R206].

Record values assembled across incompatible samples. The 96% laser-feedback yield [R203], 1–2 nm delta layer [R204], 32 nm SiV endpoint spread [R190], and a separate long-coherence sample do not describe one fabrication line.

Site yield substituted for array yield. If every one of \(N\) sites is indispensable and independent, \(Y_N=p_{\rm use}^N\). Correlations require a measured joint model, not permission to omit the exponent.

A Gaussian standard deviation treated as the whole disorder model. Channeling and diffusion create tails; rare close pairs dominate \(r^{-3}\) coupling. Supply three-dimensional endpoints, biases, covariance, tail quantiles, missing and extra centers, and dark-defect statistics.

Importing diamond processing into another host. The 4H-SiC result [R205] has its own ion, energy, vacancy, charge, and anneal physics. Sapphire or hBN needs a new conditioned ledger, not renamed diamond numbers.

A lithography file is a list of commanded coordinates. The Hamiltonian is the joint distribution of the centers that actually formed, charged, glowed, spun, and sat still. Those are different documents.

Check yourself

What does deterministic implantation determine?

The number of delivered ions, when individual arrivals are prepared or detected. It does not determine stopping point, complex formation, charge, optical usability, or spin quality.

Show that a 20 nm dipolar graph with 20% radial coupling scatter needs \(\sigma_{\rm site}\lesssim0.94\) nm.

First-order propagation gives \(\sigma_J/J\approx 3\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_{\rm site}/r\). Set the left side to \(0.20\) and \(r=20\ \mathrm{nm}\). Then \(\sigma_{\rm site}\le 0.20\times20/(3\sqrt{2})=0.94\ \mathrm{nm}\).

What does delta doping do especially well?

It confines dopants in depth during growth. By itself it does not assign lateral coordinates.

What fails if you treat annealing as a reset button?

Vacancies move. Capture positions broaden, surfaces steal vacancies, and unwanted aggregates can form. The 300 nm single-vacancy diffusion bound for an 800 °C anneal is the existence proof that “damage erased, position unchanged” is false.

Show that independent \(p_{\rm use}=0.90\) on nine indispensable sites yields about 38.7%, and that a 50% array target needs at least 92.6%.

Under independence, \(Y_9=0.90^9\approx0.387\). The inverse is \(p_{\rm use}\ge0.5^{1/9}=0.926\).

What data should enter a Hamiltonian simulation?

Sampled three-dimensional center coordinates and species, missing/extra-site indicators, charge and spin acceptance, covariance and tails, and the resulting distribution of intended and unintended couplings — not a nominal pitch alone.

Chapter 35 — One microscope, three neighbors

You park a green laser on one diamond. A single red point answers. In an earlier chapter that was the whole experiment: one missing atom, one spin, one microscope.

Move the defects closer until they can talk. The same microscope still sees a red point.

The point is now three neighbors sharing one spot. The microwave that would flip your target also lands on the two next door.

The red flash does not say whose flash it is. A frequency shift that would label your site is, when the pulse is off, just disorder. You need a way to pick one cluster without wrecking the reason you packed them this tight.

Five jobs, not one flash

An isolated defect that behaves under a microscope is not a controllable array. In a dense patch every laser spot contains neighbors, every microwave line radiates past its intended site, and every frequency shift changes part of the Hamiltonian you were trying to keep uniform.

Five jobs have to be named separately.

  • Initialize charge, spin, and encoded-cluster state.

  • Select a site or cluster in space or frequency.

  • Drive a desired physical or encoded transition.

  • Measure it with a stated degree of destructiveness.

  • Calibrate the controls without quietly replacing the many-body model you came to test.

The spectral differences that make sites distinguishable are on-site disorder when the control is off. That is the trade, not a footnote.

Previous chapters asked for localized defect states, coherent coupling, a low-energy cluster doublet, the right graph, effective multi-spin terms, and a many-body gap. None of that answers the lab question: which cluster did that pulse hit?

For an analog topological Hamiltonian the knobs are not clerical. A magnetic gradient changes Zeeman energies.

Strain and electric fields shift optical and spin transitions and can change the encoded wavefunctions. A focused optical reset can ionize, heat, or project neighboring defects.

Local control perturbs the same system whose symmetry and uniformity are supposed to support a phase.

[Experiment] Optical initialization, coherent microwave control, and optical readout are mature for isolated diamond NV centers, and multi-spin registers around individual centers have been controlled [R074]; [R119]. [Proposal] Integrating those primitives with dense defect clusters and an intrinsic topological Hamiltonian remains an architecture, not a demonstrated machine.

Drop the last distinction and a beautiful single-center register will be redrawn as a lattice. It is a register.

Four ways to pick one

A conductor can cue an orchestra all at once. Singling out one player needs a label: position, pitch, timing, polarization, or a private wire. After this paragraph the orchestra is gone.

In a quantum array that label often is a Hamiltonian term. Assign cluster \(i\) a distinctive frequency \(\omega_i\) and you have added a site-dependent energy. That may spoil the equivalence the model requires.

There are four common selectors.

  • Spatial: focus light or a near field on one location.

  • Spectral: drive only the transition resonant with one tone.

  • Internal: use polarization or selection rules to choose an orientation or transition.

  • Temporal: refocus unwanted evolution with pulse sequences.

Real devices combine them. A modest gradient separates frequencies, a shaped microwave pulse narrows the addressed bandwidth, and an optical channel supplies readout.

Each selector has an error budget. The phrase “individually addressable” without that budget is a brochure, not a specification.

Suppose two sites share a line within the driven bandwidth. Then no amount of spatial slogans will keep the spectator idle. Hence a selector is a quantitative window, not a drawing of a beam.

A neighbor that almost flips

Let target cluster \(C\) have an encoded two-level transition at angular frequency \(\omega_C\), in radians per second. Let a neighboring spectator \(S\) have frequency \(\omega_S\). Their detuning is

\[ \Delta_S=\omega_S-\omega_C. \]

Drive both with a microwave field resonant with \(C\). Keep only the part of the drive that stays in step with the spin. Let the target Rabi angular frequency be \(\Omega\), also in radians per second: how fast the resonant pulse rotates the target. A square pulse of duration

\[ t_\pi=\frac{\pi}{\Omega} \]

rotates the target by \(\pi\). The units check: radians are dimensionless, so \((\mathrm{s}^{-1})^{-1}=\mathrm{s}\).

For an ideal two-level spectator that starts in its lower state, the largest possible off-resonant excitation under a constant drive is bounded by

\[ P_{S,\max}=\frac{\Omega^2}{\Omega^2+\Delta_S^2} \approx\left(\frac{\Omega}{\Delta_S}\right)^2 \quad\text{when }|\Delta_S|\gg\Omega. \]

That unwanted leftover on the neighbor is crosstalk. The name is worth keeping because it is an operation error on a victim, not a picture of how fat the beam looked.

Suppose the design permits at most \(10^{-3}\) spectator excitation from this mechanism. The ideal bound requires

\[ \frac{|\Delta_S|}{\Omega}\gtrsim\sqrt{10^3}\approx31.6. \]

This is a dimensionless ratio, as it must be. It is not a device promise.

Pulse edges, extra levels, inhomogeneous broadening, calibration drift, and interactions add errors. Smooth pulses can reduce spectral sidelobes.

They generally take longer.

Now add the cluster’s unwanted excited states. Let \(\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}\) be the energy gap from the encoded doublet to the nearest leakage state, in joules, and define \(\omega_{\mathrm{leak}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{leak}}/\hbar\), in radians per second. Selective control needs a window resembling

\[ \Gamma_C\ll\Omega\ll \min\left(|\Delta_S|,\omega_{\mathrm{leak}}\right), \]

where \(\Gamma_C\) is the target transition linewidth in radians per second. The left inequality makes the pulse faster and clearer than the linewidth. The right inequalities suppress spectator excitation and leakage.

That window is selectivity: a bandwidth, not a slogan. If the window is empty, pulse optimization cannot manufacture one.

Faster gates want larger \(\Omega\). Selectivity and leakage suppression want smaller \(\Omega\).

Decoherence objects to waiting while the engineers discuss it. Drop any one of the three inequalities and the remaining two do not define a gate.

Charge, then spin, then the cluster

A defect cluster can have at least three initialization layers.

Charge and configuration. The intended optical and spin levels exist only in the desired charge state and structural configuration.

Optical illumination may both prepare and disturb charge. A bright spot is not proof that every member of a cluster is in the right charge state.

Physical spins. Spin-dependent intersystem crossing allows nonresonant optical pumping of an NV electronic spin.

Resonant cryogenic protocols can provide more selective preparation [R074]. These mechanisms are platform-specific.

A group-IV vacancy or a defect in SiC has a different level structure and different temperature requirements.

Encoded cluster state. Polarizing each constituent does not automatically prepare a particular eigenstate of an interacting cluster.

You may need a sequence of physical-spin rotations, dissipative pumping, measurement and feedback, or an adiabatic ramp from an easily prepared Hamiltonian. The relevant success probability is the overlap with the encoded state, not the brightness of one constituent.

Initialization also has a time at which it is allowed. Resetting a constituent after a correlated many-body phase has been prepared is a local dissipative operation.

It can create excitations and erase entanglement. Global reset before preparation is therefore much less invasive than arbitrary mid-run local reset.

Suppose you polarize every physical spin and stop. Then the cluster occupies a product state that may have almost no overlap with the encoded doublet. Brightness is not that overlap.

Light that cannot pick one

Optical control can select by position, transition frequency, polarization, or a photonic mode. Ordinary far-field focusing is diffraction limited, so several nanometre-spaced defects can occupy one spot. Super-resolution methods use a nonlinear optical response to narrow the effective point-spread function.

[Experiment] Pezzagna and colleagues combined implantation with stimulated-emission-depletion microscopy to optically distinguish closely spaced NV centers [R235]. That is evidence for nanoscale optical selection. It is not evidence for simultaneous low-crosstalk control of a many-body cluster lattice.

Spectral optical addressing uses differing zero-phonon-line frequencies. It can be powerful at cryogenic temperature, where narrow resonant transitions permit spin-selective excitation and single-shot protocols.

It is also vulnerable to spectral diffusion, strain variation, electric-field noise, and charge rearrangement. Nanophotonic fabrication can shift and broaden emitters even while improving collection.

[Experiment] Integrated diamond nanophotonics has coupled multiple silicon-vacancy centers to optical modes, and two emitters in a cavity have shown photon-mediated interactions after spectral tuning [R086]; [R238]. Separately, a 2025 platform optically resolved and manipulated more than 100 NV centers in parallel while using shared coherent control [R239].

These results advance routing and multiplexing. They do not demonstrate a uniform, strongly interacting cluster lattice.

Optical frequency differences are useful labels for photon routing. They may be unwelcome disorder if the same orbital states mediate spin interactions.

Tuning emitters into mutual optical resonance helps indistinguishable-photon protocols. Tuning them apart helps frequency-selective local addressing.

The operating schedule must say which condition is required at each moment.

A resolved optical line is not a resolved cluster. Several cluster transitions may appear, or several defects may share one line. Assignment needs controlled perturbations.

A field that covers the whole chip

Microwave wavelengths are enormous compared with defect spacing, so a conventional antenna supplies a nearly global magnetic field. Individual selection then comes from frequency differences, local near-field conductors, magnetic gradients, or pulse refocusing.

[Experiment] A microcoil-generated gradient of about \(0.1\ \mathrm{G\,nm^{-1}}\) frequency-encoded four NV sites separated by about \(100\ \mathrm{nm}\), enabling site-selective Rabi control; each site contained multiple NVs at smaller separations [R236]. Here \(\mathrm{G}\) is gauss, with \(1\ \mathrm{G}=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T}\), and \(\mathrm{nm}\) is nanometre. Those values and that geometry belong to a sensing-oriented device, not a demonstrated strongly coupled topological patch.

A local static magnetic gradient changes Zeeman splittings. A local wire can supply a stronger near field but introduces wiring density, dissipation, fabrication variation, and possibly magnetic noise. Frequency multiplexing reduces wire count, yet the minimum separation between channels must exceed linewidths, drive bandwidth, drift, and interaction-induced shifts.

For an encoded cluster, the microwave field couples through a projected physical operator. Let \(P_C\) project onto the encoded doublet and let \(S_j^x\) be the transverse spin operator of constituent \(j\). The encoded drive is governed by

\[ P_C\left(\sum_j g_j S_j^x\right)P_C, \]

where \(g_j\) is the local field coupling, with energy units if the drive Hamiltonian is written directly in joules. A highly symmetric cluster under a spatially uniform field may have a vanishing matrix element between its logical states.

That can protect against uniform magnetic noise — and make the same uniform microwave field unable to perform the desired gate. Local gradients or deliberately asymmetric couplings can restore control.

They also open noise and leakage channels.

Hence symmetry has two faces. It can suppress the noise you fear. It can also suppress the matrix element you need. Drop either face and the remaining slogan is incomplete.

Looking is also a shove

Room-temperature NV readout usually maps spin-dependent optical dynamics to different fluorescence statistics and averages many repetitions [R074]. Cryogenic resonant excitation can give single-shot, projective electron-spin readout, as demonstrated for an NV center [R199]. Spin-to-charge conversion maps spin information onto a longer-lived charge distinction and can improve the photon budget under suitable conditions [R237].

Every method has a measurement volume and a back-action volume. Excitation light can pump nearby defects, change charge states, and heat a nanostructure.

Collected photons from several centers can overlap at one detector. Spectral filters, confocal or super-resolution collection, cavities, and separate waveguides help.

None of them makes back-action disappear.

Three measurement claims must be kept separate.

  • Destructive local readout: the target state may be lost, and neighbor effects are bounded.

  • Repeatable local readout: the target can be measured again with a stated quantum-nondemolition fidelity.

  • Phase-preserving many-body readout: the measurement extracts the intended observable without uncontrolled projection or excitation of the surrounding phase.

The first has strong single-defect precedents. The third is an architectural requirement and remains [Proposal] for the defect-cluster topological system considered here. Ordinary fluorescence of one spin is not automatically a stabilizer measurement, and it is not a reading of a logical topological charge.

Suppose you call a bright photon stream a nondemolition loop. Then you have named the detector, not the operator. Repeatability and the measured observable still have to be specified.

Every knob, written down

A scalable calibration record needs more than one resonance frequency. For each physical defect and encoded cluster it should include:

  • charge-state preparation and survival probabilities;

  • spin initialization and readout confusion matrices;

  • microwave and optical transition frequencies and linewidths;

  • Rabi-rate response versus control amplitude;

  • pulse phase and timing offsets;

  • leakage spectra and encoded-state matrix elements;

  • pairwise interaction shifts;

  • optical and microwave crosstalk matrices; and

  • drift versus time, temperature, and preceding illumination.

An unconstrained \(N\)-cluster crosstalk matrix has \(N(N-1)\) off-diagonal entries, so exhaustive measurement scales quadratically. Verified locality and repeated geometry can reduce this burden.

Calibration still consumes shots. Practical runs need sacrificial and interleaved references that track both common drift and local outliers.

A crosstalk number is not a beam diameter. It must name the victim subsystem, the unwanted observable or operation, the control sequence, the neighbor state, and the measurement conditions. Drop any of those and the number cannot be audited.

Everyone at once, or one at a time

Global pulses use fewer channels and can preserve lattice symmetries. They suit polarization, echoes, and repeated bulk sequences. They cannot identify defects or correct local errors unless the Hamiltonian maps those errors to collective signals.

Local controls add routing and calibration freedom. They also add disorder, wiring, heat, and crosstalk. A hybrid with global bulk operations and sparse local controls is [Proposal], not proof that sparse controls suffice.

Driving every cluster through the same programmed pulse can digitally or Floquet-engineer an effective evolution. It does not prove that the undriven material has an intrinsic topological phase.

Conversely, local optical readout of physical defect spins does not by itself read a logical topological charge. Always name the physical operator, the encoded operator it projects to, and whether the phase exists only under active control.

Two inequalities that cannot both be true

Let \(\sigma_\omega\) be the root-mean-square spread of cluster transition angular frequencies when all addressing controls are off. Let \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) be a characteristic intended intercluster coupling energy and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mb}}\) the many-body gap, both in joules. A rough uniformity requirement is

\[ \hbar\sigma_\omega\ll\min(|J_{\mathrm{eff}}|,\Delta_{\mathrm{mb}}). \]

The left side has units \((\mathrm{J\,s})(\mathrm{s}^{-1})=\mathrm{J}\), so the comparison is dimensionally valid. Spectral addressability, however, asks neighboring transition spacings to exceed the driven bandwidth and linewidth:

\[ |\omega_i-\omega_j|\gg\max(\Omega,\Gamma_i,\Gamma_j). \]

Permanent random detunings generally cannot satisfy both inequalities when the transition energy participates directly in the target Hamiltonian. Possible escapes are all conditional:

  • apply a switchable local shift only during control and return to a uniform idle point;

  • encode the logical transition so its address frequency changes while the relevant static Hamiltonian coefficient does not;

  • compensate known offsets in a rotating frame or with echo pulses, accepting active rather than passive operation; or

  • use spatial selection without large spectral disorder.

Switchability is not free. Turning a local shift on and off can excite leakage states, accumulate unknown phases, or close the local many-body gap. A symmetry-protected encoded state may also be dark to the control operator.

The correct question is not “uniform or addressable?” It is whether a verified control path connects a uniform idle Hamiltonian to a selective operation and back with errors below the phase’s tolerance. Drop the return trip and you have addressed a different Hamiltonian than the one you came to test.

Nine steps for one cluster

Consider target cluster \(C\) inside a dense patch of spectator clusters. The schedule below is for a prepare–probe–read experiment. It does not assume that fluorescence can reset or measure \(C\) nondestructively in the middle of an established topological state.

Stage | Control action | Required observation or bound | Phase status | |

  1. Sacrificial map | In separate calibration shots, sweep weak microwave/optical probes and fit \(\omega_C\), linewidth, leakage transitions, neighbor detunings, and readout confusion matrix. | Stable confidence intervals over the planned run time; crosstalk matrix measured, not inferred from beam size. | Target phase not claimed. | |

  2. Global reset | Prepare charge states and optically polarize all clusters using the platform-specific sequence. Herald or reject runs with wrong charge where possible. | Per-cluster and whole-patch initialization yield reported separately. | No many-body phase yet. |

  1. Encoded preparation | Apply calibrated global and local pulses, or an adiabatic cluster ramp, to place each cluster in its low-energy encoded state. | Leakage of \(C\) and representative spectators bounded by spectroscopy. | Cluster encoding prepared; topology not yet established. | |

  2. Hamiltonian ramp | Turn on the intended intercluster Hamiltonian with a globally specified ramp. | Ramp time justified against the measured finite-patch spectrum and coherence window. | Candidate many-body state prepared. | |

  3. Select \(C\) | Apply a reversible local Stark, strain, or Zeeman shift \(\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}(t)\), or activate a calibrated gradient. Use a smooth envelope. | During the pulse, \(|\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}|\gg\Omega,\Gamma\) for spectators; after it, residual shift obeys the uniformity budget. | Local Hamiltonian is perturbed; induced excitations must be counted. | |

  4. Drive \(C\) | Apply a shaped encoded microwave pulse with area \(\int\Omega(t)dt=\pi\) for a \(\pi\) rotation, or the smaller angle required by the probe. | \(\Omega\ll\omega_{\mathrm{leak}}\); measured spectator error and target leakage satisfy the experiment’s budget. | Intentional local excitation/rotation; not automatically a logical topological gate. | |

  5. Restore and refocus | Reverse the selection envelope and use a calibrated echo only if it preserves the intended interaction terms. Track the dynamical phase \(\phi_C=\int\delta_{\mathrm{sel}}(t)dt\). | Residual frequency and interaction changes return within idle tolerances; \(\phi_C\) is compensated or included in the model. | Candidate bulk Hamiltonian restored. | |

  6. Evolve | Let the patch evolve for the protocol’s dwell time, using global refocusing only when its effective Hamiltonian has been derived. | Total schedule shorter than the relevant encoded coherence time; control-induced heating and drift bounded. | Target dynamics under test. | |

  7. Read at endpoint | Stop or reverse the phase-preparation ramp if required, then map the encoded observable onto a readable physical spin and perform optical or spin-to-charge readout. | Report target confusion matrix and neighbor state changes. Repeat over many shots. | Readout may be destructive; no claim of phase survival afterward. | |

Every invasive step occurs either before phase preparation or is labeled as a perturbation. To claim nondestructive in-phase control, an experiment would need to show that stages 4–6 neither close the local gap nor create uncontrolled quasiparticles, and that stage 8 measures the desired encoded observable through an ancilla or equivalent channel. That evidence does not yet exist for this architecture.

What the laboratory actually has

The strongest evidence is modular rather than integrated.

Capability | Status through August 2026 | What it establishes | What it does not establish | |

Optical spin preparation and fluorescence readout of single NV centers [R074] | [Experiment] | A single defect can be initialized and observed. | Dense-cluster, phase-preserving reset/readout. | |

Nanoscale optical distinction of implanted NVs [R235] | [Experiment] | Far-field super-resolution can beat ordinary diffraction for selected centers. | Parallel, low-back-action control at the spacing of a strongly interacting lattice. | |

Four-site gradient/frequency encoding [R236] | [Experiment] | Microwave site selection and coherent control in a small NV array. | Uniform interacting clusters or topological dynamics. | |

Entanglement of two separated NV electronic spins [R080] | [Experiment] | Selective control can coexist with a measured two-spin interaction in a small device. | Scaling to a dense, calibrated many-body patch. | |

Cryogenic single-shot NV readout and spin-to-charge conversion [R199]; [R237] | [Experiment] | Stronger measurement primitives than averaged fluorescence exist. | Neighbor-safe logical topological measurement. | |

Ten-qubit register around one NV [R119] | [Experiment] | Sophisticated calibration and control of a local electron–nuclear register. | A lattice of equivalent defect clusters with intercluster topology. | |

Multi-emitter nanophotonics [R086]; [R238] | [Experiment] | Optical routing, tuning, and emitter integration are advancing. | Intrinsic defect-array topological order. | |

Parallel control and readout of more than 100 resolved NVs [R239] | [Experiment] | Spatially selective optical manipulation and shared coherent control scale beyond a few sites. | Independent local microwave control or a strongly interacting uniform lattice. | |

The missing integration matters. Isolated-emitter methods may place defects too far apart for strong direct coupling, while dense creation can broaden spectra and confound assignment.

Gradients aid selection but split supposedly identical sites. Fabrication, interaction, optical, microwave, thermal, and calibration budgets must therefore be modeled together.

Ways to get this wrong

A resolved line is not a resolved cluster. Several cluster transitions may appear, or several defects may share one line. Assignment needs controlled perturbations.

Disorder is not an address bus. Accidental frequency labels drift and alter the target Hamiltonian.

Spot size is not crosstalk. Measure unwanted rotations, phases, charge changes, or Hamiltonian shifts on neighbors.

Optical readout is not automatically nondestructive. Repeatability and the measured observable must be specified.

Physical control is not encoded control. Project the drive into the logical doublet and bound leakage.

Compensation is active operation. Continuous echoes or per-site corrections may synthesize useful dynamics, but they do not establish passive protection.

Symmetry breaking can break protection. A useful gradient may remove degeneracy or noise cancellation. Returning to the symmetric idle point is part of the gate.

Check yourself

What fails if permanent site-dependent frequencies are used both to address and to keep a uniform Hamiltonian?

Addressing wants \(|\omega_i-\omega_j|\gg\max(\Omega,\Gamma_i,\Gamma_j)\). Uniform many-body physics may require \(\hbar\sigma_\omega\ll\min(|J_{\mathrm{eff}}|,\Delta_{\mathrm{mb}})\). Permanent random detunings generally cannot satisfy both when the transition energy sits in the target Hamiltonian.

Show that \(P_{S,\max}\le10^{-3}\) requires \(|\Delta_S|/\Omega\gtrsim31.6\) for the ideal two-level bound.

When \(|\Delta_S|\gg\Omega\), \(P_{S,\max}\approx(\Omega/\Delta_S)^2\). Set the right side to \(10^{-3}\) and invert: \(|\Delta_S|/\Omega\gtrsim\sqrt{10^3}\approx31.6\).

Why is initializing each physical spin not enough?

An interacting cluster’s encoded state is a particular collective eigenstate or subspace. A product of polarized constituents may have poor overlap with it.

What must a crosstalk number specify?

The victim subsystem, unwanted observable or operation, control sequence, neighbor state, and measurement conditions. Beam geometry alone is insufficient.

Show that a uniform field on a highly symmetric encoded cluster can refuse to drive the logical transition.

The encoded drive is \(P_C(\sum_j g_j S_j^x)P_C\). If the \(g_j\) are equal and the logical states are opposite under a symmetry that flips the sum, the matrix element vanishes. Protection against uniform noise is then also darkness to a uniform microwave.

Does driving one encoded cluster implement a topological logical gate?

Not generally. A local operator may create quasiparticles or probe a local degree of freedom. A logical topological action requires the appropriate nonlocal or braided operation and evidence that the phase survives.

Control is not free. Initialization must separately establish charge, physical-spin, and encoded-cluster state.

A selective drive needs a nonempty bandwidth window between linewidth and spectator or leakage scales. Crosstalk is an operation error, not a picture of the beam.

Optical, microwave, spectral, and local selectors all perturb the device. Global protocols preserve symmetry and reduce wiring but lack arbitrary routing.

Local protocols improve routing while adding disorder and calibration overhead. Local spin readout is not logical topological readout.

Chapter 36 — Reading topological information

You have one spin. A green flash, a handful of red photons, and you call the answer up or down.

That is a real question with a real detector. It is also the smallest question in the building.

Someone now claims the crystal is storing a bit that no single spin owns. The information is supposed to live in a nonlocal sector: two globally different patterns that look the same under every local check.

You cannot walk over and ask the sector how it feels. You have to climb.

Start with the one spin. Then ask whether four neighbors obey a local rule.

Then ask what energy a drive can spend. Then drag an open string and see whether charges appear at the ends.

Then close a loop that cannot shrink, and ask which sector you are in. Then bring two excitations together and ask what total charge comes back.

Each question is a different operator. A claim that does not name one is not yet a claim.

The questions, in order

A microscope can name the color of one thread. A four-thread check can tell whether a local weaving rule was broken.

Neither tells you whether a colored strand winds around the whole tapestry. For that you have to follow an extended path, or compare two globally different patterns.

After this paragraph the tapestry is gone.

The quantum version is the same hierarchy, written as operators:

one-site readout -> physical spin or edge label
local parity -> stabilizer / nearby excitation
spectral response -> energy and transition matrix element
open string endpoints -> created or moved charges
closed loop -> enclosed charge or logical sector
fusion experiment -> possible total-charge channels
many-basis data -> tomography or selected correlators

A quantum measurement is an operator with a probability distribution. Let the data system sit in a state \(\rho\), a density operator. For an observable \(M\) with eigenvalues \(m\), the ideal projective odds are

\[ P(m)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\Pi_m), \]

where \(\Pi_m\) projects onto the eigenspace with eigenvalue \(m\). A readout protocol earns its keep only when the actual detector record can be mapped, with calibrated errors, onto those ideal outcomes.

One distinction will keep coming back. A local stabilizer checks whether a small neighborhood satisfies one term of a code Hamiltonian.

A nonlocal logical loop distinguishes globally different states that can satisfy every local term. Their circuits can look almost identical — both can be parity measurements — while their meanings are not interchangeable.

Attach a short dossier to every claimed signal: the operator, the preparation assumptions, the measurement circuit, the calibration, the error model, and the competing explanations. If any of those is missing, you have a plot, not an identification.

Four nearby edges

Use the toric-code convention: one physical two-level system on each edge of a square lattice with periodic boundaries. Periodic boundaries turn the sheet into a torus. For edge \(e\), let \(X_e\) and \(Z_e\) be Pauli operators. Define a plaquette operator

\[ B_p=\prod_{e\in\partial p} Z_e, \]

where \(\partial p\) is the set of four edges around plaquette \(p\). Its eigenvalues are \(b_p=+1\) and \(-1\). At each vertex \(s\), also define the star operator

\[ A_s=\prod_{e\ni s}X_e, \]

where \(e\ni s\) means the four edges that meet at \(s\). The ideal ground space has \(A_s=+1\) and \(B_p=+1\) for every star and plaquette [R030]. [Theory]

To measure \(B_p\), bring in an extra two-level system \(a\), an ancilla, initialized in \(|0\rangle_a\). This spin is not part of the code. It is a helper that is allowed to forget everything except one parity.

For each of the four data edges in \(\partial p\), apply a controlled-NOT with the data edge as control and the ancilla as target. Then measure \(Z_a\). In the computational basis the ancilla records the parity of the four data bits:

\[ m_a=z_1z_2z_3z_4=b_p, \]

where each \(z_j=\pm1\) is the corresponding \(Z\)-eigenvalue and \(m_a\) is the ancilla outcome. Thus \(m_a=-1\) reports a violated plaquette check in the ideal circuit.

For a coherent superposition the same circuit measures the operator \(B_p\), not four pre-existing classical bits. It projects the data into a \(B_p\) eigenspace without revealing the individual \(Z_e\) values.

Repeated ancilla-mediated stabilizer extraction is a working technique in superconducting surface-code experiments [R230]. [Experiment] That fact establishes a measurement primitive.

It does not establish passive topological order in the processor.

Drop the ancilla and measure the four edges directly, and you still learn the product — but you also learn the factors, and you generally destroy coherence in incompatible bases. The circuit is not a formality.

A loop that will not shrink

Now choose a closed path \(C_x\) that winds once around the torus in the \(x\) direction. Define

\[ \overline Z_x=W_Z(C_x)=\prod_{e\in C_x}Z_e. \]

Use a fresh ancilla and the same style of parity circuit, but couple it to every edge along \(C_x\), then measure the ancilla. The result \(\overline z_x=\pm1\) distinguishes two logical sectors. The loop commutes with every stabilizer, so states with different \(\overline z_x\) can have identical local stabilizer outcomes.

There is a trap. If a closed path \(C\) can be shrunk to a point, then in the ideal code its \(Z\) loop is a product of the enclosed plaquette stabilizers.

It is not an independent logical measurement. A path becomes logical only because it is noncontractible on the torus — it cannot be pulled down to a point — or, on a planar surface code, because it connects the appropriate boundaries or encircles a puncture.

The name is worth keeping because length is not the point. Topology of the path is the point.

The contrast is now a table:

Measurement | Support | Ideal question | A \(-1\) result means |

\(B_p\) | four nearby edges | Is this local constraint satisfied? | a local syndrome/excitation is present |

\(\overline Z_x\) | a system-spanning noncontractible path | Which logical sector is occupied? | logical eigenvalue \(-1\), not necessarily a local defect | |

The two operators can be measured with similar hardware. One is a Hamiltonian term.

The other is a logical observable. Measuring all \(B_p=+1\) does not determine \(\overline Z_x\).

Measuring \(\overline Z_x\) once does not certify that all local constraints hold.

A destructive alternative is to measure every data edge along the chosen path in the \(Z\) basis and multiply the outcomes. That estimates the same parity for that shot, but it also reveals individual values and generally destroys coherence in incompatible bases.

Destructive measurement is often simpler and can be excellent for a final readout. It is a poor choice if the state must survive for another braid.

Suppose you call every long correlator a logical loop. Then a contractible product of plaquettes will be promoted to a sector label. Length was never the definition.

Photons are not Pauli Z

A local readout maps a microscopic state onto photons, charge, current, resonator phase, or another classical record. In diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers, confocal fluorescence combined with magnetic resonance enabled detection of individual defect centers [R240], and spin-selective optical protocols later achieved projective readout of a solid-state spin register [R199]. [Experiment] Related platforms use spin-dependent tunnelling, spin-to-charge conversion, cavity transmission, or dispersive frequency shifts.

The raw observable is platform-specific. A fluorescence count is not itself \(Z\).

Calibration supplies conditional distributions \(P(r|z=+1)\) and \(P(r|z=-1)\) for detector record \(r\). Preparation errors, state changes during readout, background counts, crosstalk, and threshold choice belong in the inference.

Reporting only a thresholded bit discards the information needed to audit that inference.

Local spin readout answers local questions: occupation, polarization, a basis-rotated component, or correlations assembled across repeated shots. It can reconstruct an extended operator by multiplying many local outcomes. It cannot make that operator robust against the growing number of readout errors.

Hence a calibrated transducer is necessary and not sufficient. The operator still has to be named, and the error still grows with the support.

An extra spin that keeps a secret

For a Pauli product

\[ S=P_1P_2\cdots P_w, \]

where each \(P_j\) is \(X\), \(Y\), or \(Z\) on one data system and \(w\) is the operator weight, an ancilla can acquire the eigenvalue of \(S\). Basis rotations convert \(X\) or \(Y\) parity to a \(Z\)-parity circuit. Measuring the ancilla then reveals \(s=\pm1\) while ideally preserving superpositions inside the same eigenspace.

The schedule matters. One ancilla fault can propagate through several two-body gates into a correlated data error.

Fault-tolerant layouts therefore constrain gate order, add flag ancillas, repeat rounds, and decode a history rather than trusting one bit. Modern surface-code experiments demonstrate repeated stabilizer extraction and below-threshold logical-error scaling in engineered superconducting circuits [R230].

[Experiment] These are active error-correction results. They should not be relabelled as evidence for a naturally occurring topological phase.

Stabilizer expectation values also provide an energy estimate for an ideal commuting Hamiltonian such as

\[ H=-J\sum_s A_s-J\sum_p B_p, \]

where \(J\) is an energy, \(A_s\) is a star operator, and \(B_p\) is a plaquette operator. Measuring \(\langle A_s\rangle\) and \(\langle B_p\rangle\) estimates \(\langle H\rangle\). It does not, alone, determine the gap, long-range entanglement, or robustness to unmeasured perturbations.

An energy estimate is not a phase identification. Drop the rest of the dossier and a well-satisfied stabilizer looks like a topological certificate.

A gap is not a name

Spectroscopy drives the system at angular frequency \(\omega\) and measures absorption, fluorescence, resonator response, or state transfer. Resonance near

\[ \hbar\omega=E_n-E_0 \]

connects the initial energy \(E_0\) to an excited energy \(E_n\), provided the drive operator has a nonzero transition matrix element. Both sides have units of joules. By varying momentum, position, polarization, and drive operator, an experiment can probe gaps, dispersions, selection rules, bound states, and continuum thresholds.

A spectral gap is necessary for many topological-protection arguments, but a gap is not topological. Ordinary magnets, molecules, and kitchen cupboards can all be gapped; only two of those are routinely diagonalized. Spectroscopy becomes persuasive when the observed states also have the predicted charge, fusion, nonlocal response, and perturbation dependence.

What fails if you stop at the gap? You have shown an energy difference under the probed conditions. You have not shown a nonlocal sector, anyonic statistics, or logical-sector robustness.

Strings that open and loops that close

An open string operator is a product of local operators along a path with endpoints. In the toric code, applying an open string creates, moves, or annihilates excitations at its ends while commuting with stabilizers away from them [R030]. Measuring endpoint syndromes before and after the string checks this rule.

A closed Wilson loop \(W_a(C)\) represents transporting or testing a charge type \(a\) around a closed contour \(C\). The loop is the question, and the charge label \(a\) is part of the question.

Depending on the model, its expectation value diagnoses confinement, enclosed topological charge, or a logical sector. A contractible loop and a noncontractible logical loop must always be labelled separately.

There are three practical routes:

  • Ancilla accumulation: coherently couple one ancilla to every term in the product and read its phase or parity.

  • Destructive multiplication: measure all sites in suitable local bases and multiply outcomes shot by shot.

  • Interferometry: coherently split a probe path, make one branch encircle a region, recombine the branches, and infer the acquired Abelian phase or non-Abelian action from output probabilities.

Interferometry is conceptually closest to asking what charge lies inside a loop. In an Abelian theory, encircling can add a phase.

In a non-Abelian theory, braiding acts as a matrix on a fusion space, so one output intensity is generally insufficient; state preparation and a final fusion-channel measurement are required [R015]. [Theory] Visibility loss may arise from dephasing, path distinguishability, leakage, thermal quasiparticles, or a mixture of charges.

It is not automatically a non-Abelian signature.

A dim fringe is not a braid matrix. Drop the competing explanations and any lost contrast will be sold as statistics.

Bringing two charges together

To measure a fusion rule, prepare identified quasiparticles, move them together or implement the equivalent code deformation, and measure the total topological charge of the enclosing region. For Fibonacci charge \(\tau\),

\[ \tau\times\tau=1+\tau \]

permits vacuum charge \(1\) or charge \(\tau\). A useful experiment must show not merely two histogram peaks but a calibrated mapping from those peaks to charge projectors, repeatability or controlled destructiveness, and the dependence on preparation and braid history.

A region’s total charge can be read by a Wilson loop around its boundary, by interferometry, or by converting the charge to local degrees of freedom through a known fusion circuit and then measuring those degrees of freedom. The last option is often called destructive fusion readout: bring the anyons together, measure the resulting local syndrome, and accept that the original encoded state is gone.

Digital superconducting-processor experiments have implemented code deformations and non-Abelian graph-vertex braiding [R132], and a 27-transmon experiment prepared a Fibonacci string-net state and measured creation, fusion, and braiding signatures [R138]. [Experiment: digital simulation] These are important demonstrations of protocols and controlled Hilbert spaces. They did not observe intrinsic Fibonacci quasiparticles emerging in an unprogrammed defect material; the operations were compiled into gates on ordinary processor qubits [R132]; [R138].

Logical-charge measurement asks the same question at the encoding scale. If logical information is stored in the total charge of a set of anyons or holes, measure a loop enclosing exactly that set, or fuse according to the encoding tree and read the final channel.

The loop geometry, orientation, charge label, and chosen fusion basis are part of the observable. “Measure the anyons” is not yet a circuit.

Two peaks alone are spectroscopy with ambitious branding. What fails if you stop there is every test that would distinguish fusion from a pair of ordinary resonances.

Asking every question

Full state tomography measures enough observables to reconstruct \(\rho\). It is a census, not a phase label.

For \(N\) two-level systems, \(\rho\) is a \(2^N\times 2^N\) matrix, so unrestricted reconstruction scales exponentially. Small patches can support full tomography.

Larger arrays require selected correlators, stabilizer sampling, reduced density matrices, randomized measurements, or classical-shadow protocols [R241]. [Theory/Protocol]

Reconstructing a small state close to an ideal code state verifies preparation on that patch. It does not by itself establish thermodynamic ground-state degeneracy or stability as system size grows. Conversely, carefully chosen nonlocal and entanglement observables may test a specific hypothesis more efficiently than full reconstruction.

A complete census of four spins is still a four-spin fact. Drop the scaling tests and a beautiful density matrix will be asked to certify a phase it cannot see.

What the laboratory already has

The relevant techniques already exist, but not all in one platform. Single defects can be optically located and spin-read [R240]; [R199].

Superconducting processors repeatedly measure high-weight parity checks with ancillas [R230]. A superconducting experiment prepared a toric-code state and probed excitations and topological observables [R125].

[Experiment: digital state preparation] A programmable Rydberg array measured signatures consistent with a toric-code-type spin liquid [R126]. [Experiment: analog quantum simulation] Non-Abelian and Fibonacci protocols have been digitally implemented on superconducting processors [R132]; [R138].

Those achievements answer different questions. In a gate processor, the operator being measured is usually known because the experimenter compiled it.

The challenge is fidelity, scaling, and whether the prepared state retains the predicted structure. In an analog simulator, the Hamiltonian is less directly scripted and phase identification leans more heavily on a dossier of observables.

In a defect lattice, additional interfaces are required: local optical or microwave addressability, ancillas or mediator modes for parity, sufficiently nondestructive cycling, and a way to implement loops without the error probability becoming overwhelming.

A credible defect experiment should report at least: raw and corrected outcomes; detector calibration; leakage and loss; control sequence; operator support; error bars; blind or held-out model comparisons where practical; and results versus system size, temperature, preparation time, and controlled perturbations. Readout correction should be shown both applied and unapplied. Otherwise a large “corrected” Wilson loop can become a portrait of the calibration model.

The same measurement words get used in four different rooms. A stabilizer circuit on programmed qubits is active syndrome extraction.

A prepared code state is a digital emulation unless it is the equilibrium or dynamically stable phase of the physical Hamiltonian under study. An analog simulator may realize an engineered many-body Hamiltonian, but signatures on one finite patch are not automatically thermodynamic topological order.

An emergent anyon is an excitation of such a many-body phase; a logical qubit is information encoded in its nonlocal sector. State the room.

The vocabulary will not do it for you.

Ways to get this wrong

One stabilizer becomes “topology.” A local constraint can be satisfied by a trivial product state or by a state prepared to pass that one check. Measure the full constraint pattern and independent nonlocal observables.

A long correlator becomes a logical loop. Length is not enough. The path must have the correct topology and operator content. A contractible loop may be only a product of stabilizers.

Postselection manufactures perfection. Discarding shots with leakage or unwanted syndromes changes the sampled ensemble. Report acceptance rates and conclusions without postselection.

Readout mitigation assumes the answer. Independent single-site confusion matrices may fail under correlated crosstalk. Validate the correction on states with known multi-site parity.

A gap becomes a phase identification. Spectroscopy can show an energy gap. Topological order additionally requires nonlocal structure and robustness.

Fusion-looking populations become fusion rules. Fusion evidence requires controlled charges, a defined fusion basis, charge-projector calibration, and history-dependent tests. Two peaks alone are spectroscopy with ambitious branding.

Finite prepared-state signatures become passive protection. The toric-code and Fibonacci processor demonstrations [R125]; [R132]; [R138] measured deliberately prepared or digitally evolved states. [Experiment] They do not show that the same hardware passively relaxes into, or protects, that phase.

A Wilson-loop value becomes universal proof. Loop behavior depends on contour, state, temperature, boundaries, matter content, and noise. Combine it with local syndromes, gap data, entanglement diagnostics, sector structure, and perturbation tests.

Destructive parity is called nondemolition. Multiplying individually measured spins can estimate a loop but destroys incompatible coherence. A quantum-nondemolition claim requires repeated agreement beyond what state re-preparation or detector memory explains.

A useful evidence hierarchy is cumulative:

Evidence | What it supports | What remains open | |

Local spin contrast | controllable/readable constituents | interactions and collective phase | |

Stabilizers near target values | local code constraints | nonlocal sector and long-range entanglement | |

Gap spectroscopy | energetic isolation | topology of the gapped state | |

Open-string endpoint rule | candidate quasiparticle motion | statistics and deconfinement |

Noncontractible loops | global sector information | robustness and thermodynamic scaling | |

Fusion and braid matrices | anyonic process within calibrated space | intrinsic emergence versus compiled simulation | |

Size/perturbation/temperature trends plus entanglement data | coherent phase-identification dossier | ultimate scalability and protection | |

No row erases the need for the rows beneath it. Strong phase identification combines local checks, independent nonlocal observables, spectral and entanglement information, controlled creation and fusion, scaling, and exclusion of plausible trivial models.

Satzinger et al. and Semeghini et al. illustrate complementary digital and analog dossiers rather than a single decisive meter [R125]; [R126]. [Experiment]

Check yourself

What does an ancilla stabilizer measurement reveal?

The eigenvalue of a specified local operator product, ideally without revealing individual data values inside that eigenspace.

Show that a contractible \(Z\) loop on the torus is not an independent logical observable.

In the ideal code it is a product of the enclosed plaquette operators \(B_p\). Any two ground states that satisfy every \(B_p=+1\) therefore agree on that loop. A noncontractible loop cannot be written that way and can distinguish those states.

What is the difference between destructive and nondestructive loop readout?

Destructive readout measures constituent sites and multiplies outcomes; nondestructive ancilla readout extracts only the loop eigenvalue while ideally preserving coherence within its eigenspace.

What fails if you identify a spectral gap with topological order?

You have shown an energy difference under the probed conditions. Ordinary magnets are gapped too. Nonlocal entanglement, anyonic statistics, and logical-sector robustness remain unshown.

What fails if two histogram peaks are called a fusion rule?

Fusion evidence needs identified input charges, a defined fusion basis, calibrated charge projectors, and history-dependent tests. Two peaks are spectroscopy until those are attached.

What is the minimum honest label for a gate-compiled Fibonacci experiment?

A digital simulation or emulation of Fibonacci states and operations, unless independent evidence establishes intrinsic emergent Fibonacci order in the hardware Hamiltonian.

Local spins are read through calibrated transducers. Pauli products can be extracted with ancillas or destructive snapshots.

Spectroscopy measures energy differences. Open strings test endpoint charges.

Closed loops and interferometers probe enclosed or logical charge. Fusion readout projects a defined total-charge channel.

Tomography supplies selected state information at exponential full-state cost. None of those tools is a topology meter.

A claim needs an observable, and the observable needs a dossier.
