Part XI — Verdict

The strongest case, the load-bearing joints, the written nos, the smallest calculation with an exit, and a grade.

Chapter 37 — The strongest case, not the loudest

A colleague grants every measurement in the book. Two nearby defect spins can entangle.

A crystal plane can make dipoles agree on a sign. A molecule can drop three nitrogens at once.

A nucleus next door can remember a state for more than a minute. None of that is a topological phase.

Then she asks what, exactly, is still worth building.

The strongest honest version of the answer is a steelman. The name is worth keeping because the opposite — a straw man — is what you build when you want to win a fight.

We are not here to win a fight. We are here to see whether grouping defects into clusters gives knobs that a lonely spin does not.

The move that is specific to this architecture is the grouping. A cluster can hide a messy handful of physical spins behind one leftover two-state object.

Those leftovers can talk. If the talk is the right shape, and the same from cell to cell, a phase can appear that no single defect ever had.

Every “can” in that paragraph has a different evidence status. Keeping the statuses attached is the whole job.

[Experiment] Several pieces exist separately: coherent coupling of nearby defect spins, small multi-defect motifs, dense two-dimensional dipolar ensembles, local electron–nuclear registers, controlled optical interfaces, and improving three-dimensional placement. [Theory] Local two-body Hamiltonians can support emergent topological phases, and cluster projection can generate interactions not obvious in the microscopic model. [Speculation] No defect-cluster array has been shown to realize a topologically ordered phase, doubled-Fibonacci order, or intrinsic Fibonacci quasiparticles as of August 2026.

A leftover, not a nicer spin

Long coherence is useful on many platforms. Bright fluorescence is useful for many experiments. Neither by itself explains why grouping defects should help produce emergent topological order.

Suppose a cluster prices out its expensive motions. What remains is a two-state object sitting behind a gap.

The microscopic teeth are physical spins and orbitals. The leftover is a low-energy doublet.

The cluster does three jobs: it exposes one useful motion, it makes unwanted motions costly, and it translates available forces into that leftover motion.

For cluster \(C\), write

\[ H=\sum_C H_C+\sum_{\langle C,D\rangle}V_{CD}. \]

The internal energy \(H_C\) defines a two-state manifold with projector \(P_C\). The jump from that manifold to the nearest leftover state is the cluster gap \(\Delta_C\), measured in joules or electronvolts.

The talk between clusters, \(V_{CD}\), has a characteristic matrix element \(v\), also an energy. If \(v/\Delta_C\ll1\), the array may be described by leftover two-state objects — pseudospins — sitting inside \(P=\prod_C P_C\).

The object is not a physical spin. It is what the cluster pretends to be after the expensive motions have been priced out.

Hence the structural promise is not that projection makes interactions better by magic. It is that the cluster spectrum, wavefunctions, symmetry, and placement become design variables. A microscopic term that is awkward in the physical-spin basis may project to a useful leftover operator:

\[ P V_{CD}P =J_x\tau_C^x\tau_D^x +J_y\tau_C^y\tau_D^y +J_z\tau_C^z\tau_D^z +\text{local terms}, \]

where \(\tau_C^{x,y,z}\) are Pauli operators acting on cluster \(C\)’s doublet. Virtual leakage can add terms proportional to \(v^2/\Delta_C\) or higher powers. The “instruction set” is the projected Hamiltonian.

Drop reproducibility and the case fails at once. Random spectra and random projected operators give a small box of trouble, not an array. The case succeeds only if cluster-to-cluster spectra and projected operators are reproducible enough that one calibration strategy covers an array.

Two clusters and one leftover coupling

Take two identical three-spin clusters, \(A\) and \(B\). Assume each has a low-energy doublet \(\{|\tilde0\rangle,|\tilde1\rangle\}\) separated by \(\Delta_C\) from other cluster states.

This doublet is the encoded leftover. It is not yet a topological qubit.

Suppose a physical dipolar or exchange interaction joins one spin in \(A\) to one spin in \(B\):

\[ V_{AB}=v\,S_{A,3}^zS_{B,1}^z. \]

Here \(S^z\) is a dimensionless spin operator and \(v\) is an energy. Within the encoded doublets, assume the cluster matrix elements are

\[ P_A S_{A,3}^zP_A=a_0I_A+a_z\tau_A^z, \qquad P_B S_{B,1}^zP_B=b_0I_B+b_z\tau_B^z. \]

The dimensionless coefficients \(a_0,a_z,b_0,b_z\) are determined by the cluster eigenstates. First-order projection gives

\[ PV_{AB}P =v(a_0I_A+a_z\tau_A^z)(b_0I_B+b_z\tau_B^z). \]

The useful coupling is

\[ J_{zz}^{(1)}=v a_zb_z. \]

The same expression also produces local fields \(va_0b_z\tau_B^z\) and \(va_zb_0\tau_A^z\), plus a constant. Hence the microscopic interaction is fixed, but the projected coefficients are controlled by the cluster wavefunctions. Change the internal coupling graph or symmetry, and the effective operator changes without requiring a new fundamental force.

Symmetry may force \(a_0=b_0=0\). If it does not, the nuisance terms are real. That is the remark, not a footnote: a designed leftover is useful only if the operators you did not want are either forbidden or pushed to higher order.

At second order, virtual cluster excitations add terms of scale

\[ J^{(2)}\sim\alpha\frac{v^2}{\Delta_C}, \]

where the dimensionless coefficient \(\alpha\) is a signed sum over matrix elements and denominators. [Theory] Schrieffer–Wolff perturbation theory makes this statement controlled when \(v/\Delta_C\ll1\) [R025].

[Proposal] Repeating such clusters could synthesize an interaction graph unavailable from bare defects. The two-cluster calculation does not establish that a two-dimensional array has topological order.

Five knobs grouping might turn

The pro case rests on five linked features. Each is a structural knob, not a compliment to diamond.

  • A cluster can convert a messy microscopic space of states into a designed low-energy leftover.

  • Crystal orientation and patterned density can shape the sign and dimensionality of dipolar interactions.

  • Short-range and mediated couplings can, in principle, occupy different levels of the hierarchy.

  • Nearby nuclear spins and optical transitions provide local control and measurement without being the encoded topological degree of freedom.

  • A static solid-state array could realize an always-on analog Hamiltonian, rather than merely compiling its time evolution into gates.

The next five sections take those knobs one at a time. A knob that has been turned in a different sample is not a knob that has been turned here.

The leftover, the gap, and the jobs they keep

A bare spin provides one local space of states. A cluster can provide an isolated doublet, a leakage gap, selection rules, and projected operators. Those are exactly the objects needed for controlled Hamiltonian reduction.

This could be structurally valuable in two ways.

First, strong couplings inside a cell and weaker couplings between cells can be assigned different jobs. Inside, the interactions create the leftover and its gap.

Between cells, they create the many-body model. Geometric separation supplies a natural hierarchy for dipolar coupling because it scales as \(r^{-3}\); exchange supplies an even sharper short-range dependence.

Second, symmetries can suppress selected local fields or matrix elements. That can move an unwanted operator to higher perturbative order while retaining a useful one.

[Theory] This is standard encoded-subspace reasoning, not a defect-specific discovery. [Speculation] No experimentally validated color-center cluster is currently known to project realistic couplings into the complete doubled-Fibonacci string-net operator set.

Hence the best version of the proposal starts with spectroscopy and exact diagonalization of one repeatable cluster. It does not start by drawing anyons over a lithography image. Drop the isolation of the doublet, and there is nothing left to project.

Tilting the crystal to pick a sign

Dipolar coupling depends on both separation and angle. That is usually presented as a nuisance. It can also be a design resource.

[Experiment] Hughes and collaborators grew dense, preferentially aligned, two-dimensional NV ensembles in (111)-oriented diamond and showed that this geometry gives the in-plane dipolar interactions a common positive sign in their convention [R242]. The observed interaction-dependent line-shape asymmetry changed with spin polarization, supporting the dipolar interpretation. A 2026 erratum corrected density and sensitivity calculations, so those corrected metrology numbers should not be borrowed casually; the structural point used here is the orientation-dependent interaction sign [R242].

This result is stronger than “diamond hosts NV centers.” It shows that the host plane, defect axis, and dimensionality can jointly select an interaction pattern. The limitation is equally important: the experiment used an ensemble, not an individually patterned cluster graph, and same-sign dipoles are not a string-net Hamiltonian.

Drop the common orientation and the sign is no longer a knob. Keep the ensemble average and you still have not built a lattice of leftovers.

Making a cluster in one shot

If a cluster requires three defects within a few nanometres, placing each defect independently compounds yield and registration errors. Correlated implantation offers a different primitive: deliver several dopant atoms from one molecular ion, then let their common straggle define a local motif.

[Experiment] Haruyama and collaborators used a nitrogen-bearing molecular ion to create triple NV centers. Their calculated implanted-nitrogen separation was \(9\pm4\) nm; among 7,116 implantation events they identified nine optical triples, one strongly coupled triple and one weakly coupled triple. The total NV creation yield was 7.4%, and the longest reported Hahn-echo \(T_2\) in the measured population was 428 \(\mu\)s [R243].

The steelman is not that these yields scale. They plainly do not.

The structural lesson is that “cluster creation” need not always mean three independent atomic placement operations. A future process could target the yield and internal spectrum of a motif as a unit.

That hypothesis is testable before attempting a lattice.

What fails if the motif is not the fabrication primitive? Then every extra defect multiplies independent placement error, and the cluster spectrum is an accident of three uncorrelated landings.

Helpers that are not the leftover

Dense analog arrays are hard to interrogate. Defect platforms offer a possible division of labor: electron spins participate in faster interactions; nearby nuclear spins store state or act as helpers; optical transitions initialize and read an electron; photonic structures route selected signals.

[Experiment] A diamond NV register containing one electron spin, one nitrogen nuclear spin, and eight \(^{13}\)C nuclear spins demonstrated pairwise control across ten qubits and protected an arbitrary single-qubit state for more than 75 s at about 3.7 K under dynamical-decoupling control [R119]. This does not demonstrate a cluster of electron-spin defects or passive protection. It demonstrates that a single defect neighborhood can contain addressable helper and memory resources far richer than one two-level system.

[Experiment] Optical photon-mediated interactions have also been induced between two silicon-vacancy centers in a diamond nanocavity [R086]. Such mediation could repair missing graph edges or separate interaction and readout channels. It brings spectral matching, cavity fabrication, drive, and loss requirements; it is not automatically an equilibrium, short-range Hamiltonian.

Hence the structural opportunity is heterogeneity within a repeated cell: data leftover, leakage monitor, readout helper, and photonic port can be physically nearby while serving distinct roles. Call the nuclear memory passive protection and you have renamed a control resource.

Start lower than Fibonacci

The strongest research program is a ladder, not a leap.

[Theory] Kitaev’s honeycomb model proves that local two-body, bond-dependent spin interactions can yield emergent Majorana fermions and a non-Abelian Ising phase [R017]. Levin–Wen string-net Hamiltonians provide commuting-projector targets for doubled topological orders, including doubled non-Abelian theories [R018]. These are existence proofs for Hamiltonians, not materials demonstrations.

A defect-cluster platform could first test a projected bond-dependent model, then a generated stabilizer, then a small topological patch. Success at an Abelian or Ising-type model would validate the architecture’s Hamiltonian engineering without being renamed “Fibonacci.” The ultimate doubled-Fibonacci claim remains a separate, higher bar.

Drop that order and you test the hardest noun first. A failed Fibonacci headline then cannot say whether the leftover, the graph, or the recoupling data was the missing piece.

A stack of numbers that have never met

Use frequency units to keep the arithmetic readable. For any energy \(X\), define \(\nu_X=X/h\), where Planck’s constant \(h\) has units joule-seconds. Consider this deliberately optimistic design point:

Layer | Best-case input | Status | Depends on | |

Cluster leakage gap | \(\nu_{\Delta}=1\) GHz | [Proposal] design target | reproducible cluster spectrum | |

Intercluster matrix element | \(\nu_v=100\) MHz | [Speculation] as an array-wide value | distance, orientation, mediator, disorder | |

Expansion ratio | \(\epsilon=\nu_v/\nu_\Delta=0.10\) | derived | two rows above | |

Desired perturbative order | \(q=2\) | [Proposal] | selection rules and projected matrix elements | |

Path coefficient | \(\alpha=1\) | optimistic assumption | interference among virtual paths | |

Effective interaction | \(\nu_{\rm eff}=\alpha\nu_v\epsilon^{q-1}=10\) MHz | derived | all rows above | |

Generic next-order scale | \(\nu_{\rm corr}\sim\nu_{\rm eff}\epsilon=1\) MHz | scaling estimate | no enhanced coefficients or small denominators | |

Gap fraction | \(c=\Delta_{\rm topo}/J_{\rm eff}=0.2\) | [Speculation] model assumption | verified many-body phase | |

Topological gap | \(\nu_{\rm topo}=c\nu_{\rm eff}=2\) MHz | derived, not measured | correct Hamiltonian and thermodynamic extrapolation | |

Comparator coherence | \(T_2=100\ \mu\)s, so \(1/T_2=10\) kHz | [Experiment, borrowed] approximately the mean Hahn-echo scale of positioned NVs in one 2025 process [R207] | incompatible sample and control conditions may apply | |

Disorder target | \(\sigma_J/h\lesssim0.2\) MHz | [Proposal] ten-percent-of-gap rule | placement, strain, charge, calibration | |

The dimensional check is

\[ \nu_{\rm eff}=\frac{\nu_v^2}{\nu_\Delta} =\frac{(100\ \text{MHz})^2}{1000\ \text{MHz}} =10\ \text{MHz}. \]

At this point the optimistic gap exceeds the borrowed decoherence rate by a factor of 200:

\[ \nu_{\rm topo}T_2=(2\times10^6\ \text{s}^{-1})(10^{-4}\ \text{s})=200. \]

That is the steelman’s central numerical opening: a low-order generated interaction could, in principle, outrun a single-defect coherence rate. It is not a device prediction, because the 1 GHz cluster gap, 100 MHz array-wide coupling, coefficient \(\alpha=1\), gap fraction \(c=0.2\), disorder target, and borrowed \(T_2\) have never been co-realized.

Order is decisive. Holding the same \(\epsilon=0.1\), a fourth-order target would have

\[ \nu_{\rm eff}^{(4)}\sim\nu_v\epsilon^3=0.1\ \text{MHz}, \qquad \nu_{\rm topo}^{(4)}\sim20\ \text{kHz}, \]

only twice the borrowed \(1/T_2\), before disorder or control errors. Hence the best case depends on finding a first- or second-order parent model, or an exact symmetry mechanism, rather than brute-forcing a high-order Fibonacci plaquette.

Temperature is harsher. Since \(k_B/h\approx20.84\) GHz/K,

\[ \frac{k_BT}{h}\approx208\ \text{MHz}\quad\text{at }T=10\ \text{mK}. \]

That exceeds the assumed 2 MHz gap by roughly two orders of magnitude. Equilibrium passive suppression would require a substantially larger gap or an effective temperature well below

\[ T_{\rm gap}=\frac{h\nu_{\rm topo}}{k_B}\approx96\ \mu\text{K}. \]

No cited defect-cluster experiment supplies this full thermal stack. The strongest near-term case is therefore preparation and spectroscopy of an analog phase on coherent timescales, not a passively self-correcting memory. Calling the former the latter would improve the headline and damage the science.

The dependency chain is unforgiving but useful:

This diagram is the strongest case because each box is experimentally or numerically attackable. The architecture can be falsified in modules before a heroic full-array fabrication run. Drop any box and the boxes below it become theatre.

What the laboratory actually has

The evidence stack is broad but not integrated:

Structurally relevant claim | Status | What was actually shown | What remains missing | |

Nearby defect electron spins can interact coherently | [Experiment] | Room-temperature entanglement between two diamond defect spins [R080] | repeatable large graph and uniform couplings | |

A multi-defect motif can be fabricated | [Experiment] | one strongly coupled triple NV motif found in a 7,116-event molecular-implantation data set [R243] | deterministic yield, target spectrum, replication | |

Crystal orientation can shape dipolar sign | [Experiment] | aligned 2D (111) NV ensembles with same-sign in-plane dipolar geometry [R242] | individually defined cluster lattice and topological Hamiltonian | |

Defects can be registered to nanostructures | [Experiment] | 2025 \(\delta\)-doping plus electron irradiation gave about 4 nm depth precision, 46(1) nm lateral precision in 280 nm pillars, and mean Hahn-echo \(T_2=98(37)\ \mu\)s [R207] | nanometre-scale relative placement required for a chosen direct-coupling graph | |

One defect neighborhood can host control helpers | [Experiment] | ten-qubit electron–nuclear register and long protected nuclear memory [R119] | parallel operation inside an interacting analog array | |

A cavity can mediate emitter interactions | [Experiment] | two SiV emitters interacted through one nanocavity [R086] | low-loss, uniform, many-cell Hamiltonian regime | |

Cluster projection can synthesize leftover operators | [Theory] | controlled effective-Hamiltonian formalism [R025] | measured defect-cluster coefficients | |

Local spin models can host non-Abelian order | [Theory] | solvable honeycomb and string-net models [R017]; [R018] | mapping from available defect terms with a usable gap | |

Defect clusters realize doubled-Fibonacci order | [Speculation] | no experimental or numerical defect-specific demonstration cited here | essentially the entire integrated chain | |

A separate proposal showed how NV registers and optical links might be organized into a scalable solid-state processor [R244]. That work supports modular engineering concepts, not the claim that the material Hamiltonian is topologically ordered.

A coupled defect triple is a physical spin cluster. Its isolated doublet may be an encoded leftover.

A lattice of such leftovers can digitally emulate or analogously realize a model. Only if the many-body Hamiltonian is in the appropriate phase do emergent anyons exist.

Only a demonstrated nonlocal encoding with the relevant error suppression is a topological logical qubit. These nouns describe successive tests, not interchangeable marketing settings.

Ways the case falls apart

Assembling best values from incompatible samples. The parameter stack above intentionally does this once and labels it. A final claim may not combine the coherence of a dilute bulk spin, the coupling of a damaged close pair, the placement of a nanostructure process, and the optical linewidth of a cryogenic center as though one device possessed all four.

Treating disorder tolerance as no geometry requirement. Topological phases can tolerate bounded local perturbations. They do not tolerate an interaction graph that never approximates the target Hamiltonian.

Calling a helper-rich register passive protection. Nuclear memories and repeated control can improve preparation and readout. They remain active resources unless the static many-body spectrum itself supplies protection.

Counting a generated term but not its competitors. The desired \(v^q/\Delta^{q-1}\) term must exceed lower-order local fields, anisotropies, leakage corrections, disorder, and decoherence. A nonzero coefficient is not a victory condition.

Assuming a demonstrated pair interaction scales uniformly. Dipolar coupling magnifies relative placement error: for \(J\propto r^{-3}\), small radial error gives \(\delta J/J\approx-3\delta r/r\). A 10% coupling tolerance requires roughly 3% relative distance control before angular errors.

Using “Fibonacci-like” to bridge a missing phase. Ising non-Abelian order, doubled-Fibonacci string-net order, digital braid emulation, and genuine chiral Fibonacci order have different excitations and computational power.

Ignoring temperature because coherence is long. \(T_2\) concerns phase memory under specified control. Thermal excitation depends on \(k_BT/\Delta_{\rm topo}\). One inequality cannot substitute for the other.

Overlooking the real structural advantage. The credible pro case is co-design of motif, spectrum, interaction, helper, and measurement — not an assertion that one host material is universally superior.

Five things you can test

The steelman is not a finished device. It is five hypotheses, each attackable before anyone fabricates a heroic array.

  • Correlated fabrication can produce a reproducible cluster motif.

  • One motif has an isolated doublet with useful projected operators.

  • Crystal orientation plus local or mediated coupling can realize the required low-order interaction graph.

  • The resulting many-body gap can exceed disorder and decoherence under one set of conditions.

  • Available ancillas can measure phase-defining local and nonlocal observables without replacing analog emergence by digital emulation.

The case succeeds only as a staged, falsifiable research program. The next chapter should attack the dependencies with the greatest leverage — especially uniform coupling, perturbative order, thermal scale, and fabrication yield.

Check yourself

What is the strongest cluster-specific advantage?

A cluster’s spectrum and wavefunctions can translate available microscopic couplings into designed leftover operators while placing leakage behind a measurable gap.

Show that first-order projection of \(V_{AB}=v S_{A,3}^z S_{B,1}^z\) produces a leftover coupling \(J_{zz}^{(1)}=v a_z b_z\).

Inside the doublets, \(P_A S_{A,3}^z P_A=a_0 I_A+a_z\tau_A^z\) and \(P_B S_{B,1}^z P_B=b_0 I_B+b_z\tau_B^z\). Expanding the product, the \(\tau^z\tau^z\) coefficient is \(v a_z b_z\). Local fields survive unless symmetry forces \(a_0=b_0=0\).

What fails if the same \(\epsilon=0.1\) is used at fourth order rather than second?

Then \(\nu_{\rm eff}^{(4)}\sim\nu_v\epsilon^3=0.1\) MHz and \(\nu_{\rm topo}^{(4)}\sim20\) kHz, only twice the borrowed \(1/T_2\), before disorder. The optimistic stack outruns coherence only at low perturbative order.

Which number has the greatest leverage in the worked stack?

The perturbative order \(q\). At \(v/\Delta_C=0.1\), moving from second to fourth order suppresses the effective term by \(10^{-2}\).

Show that \(\nu_{\rm topo}T_2=200\) at the optimistic point, and state what that does not establish.

\((2\times10^6\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})(10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s})=200\). At most, coherent dynamics might resolve a gap under matched conditions. It does not establish thermal protection, the correct phase, or scalable readout.

What claim remains speculative?

That a fabricated defect-cluster array can realize a gapped doubled-Fibonacci Hamiltonian and host its emergent quasiparticles.

Grouping defects is a design move, not a compliment to diamond. The leftover two-state object, the crystal plane, the one-shot motif, the nearby helpers, and the always-on analog Hamiltonian are five knobs that have been turned one at a time.

They have never been turned together. The optimistic stack can outrun a borrowed coherence rate only at low perturbative order, and even then it loses to \(10\) mK by two orders of magnitude.

The honest best case is a staged program, not a passively self-correcting Fibonacci crystal.

Chapter 38 — The strongest case against

You do not attack a tower by listing every cracked window. You find the columns.

A color center can be a beautiful sensor, a network node, or a physical qubit and still be a useless brick for an analog topological phase. The proposal in this book is not “put defects in diamond.” It is a chain of arrows, and every arrow has to fire in the same sample, in the same parameter window:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{defects} &\to\text{clusters}\to\text{pseudospins}\to\text{target graph}\\ &\to\text{many-body terms}\to\text{gapped phase} \to\text{logical protection}. \end{aligned} \]

That chain is conjunctive. The name is worth keeping because the logic is ordinary and unforgiving: every arrow must hold at once.

Ten separate papers demonstrating ten separate arrows do not demonstrate the chain. The strongest case against is not “diamond is hard.” It is that several individually demanding requirements multiply, while the perturbative steps that create the desired Hamiltonian divide the useful energy.

After that picture, call the missing pieces columns only if they sit under the whole claim. Interaction strength, cluster isolation, placement, and graph fidelity are columns.

The effective plaquette term is built from them. The topological gap is built from that term.

Preparation and thermal stability are judged against that gap. Scaling repeats the entire structure hundreds or thousands of times.

Two axes, not a complaint list

That picture gives two axes for ranking a crack.

The first axis asks how close the evidence sits to the hardware you actually want. Is the claim measured in a relevant defect array, established only for a component, derived for an ideal model, or merely proposed?

Call that closeness evidence proximity. A theorem about an ideal Hamiltonian is not a measurement of a fabricated patch.

The second axis asks how many later requirements die if this one fails. A problem with a workaround can be expensive. A failed inequality at the base can be fatal. Call that reach leverage.

A low ranking does not mean easy. It means that, today, another obstacle is more likely to make solving it irrelevant. Rank a later protocol first and you polish a roof while the first floor is missing.

One weak scale and a falling tower

Take a deliberately favorable toy. Each cluster has a low-energy leftover doublet, separated from unwanted cluster states by an energy \(\Delta_c\), measured in joules. Neighboring defects or clusters interact with a two-body energy \(J\). The small number that decides whether you may forget the leftover cluster states is

\[ \epsilon=\frac{J}{\Delta_c}. \]

Projection into the doublet requires \(\epsilon\ll1\). Suppose a desired four-body plaquette coefficient \(K\) first appears at fourth order. Perturbative-gadget theory shows the general problem: a \(k\)-body term assembled from two-body couplings can first arise at order \(k\) [R174]. Ignoring a dimensionless geometry coefficient \(c\),

\[ K\sim c\,J\epsilon^3 =c\frac{J^4}{\Delta_c^3}. \]

Hence the same small ratio that protects the encoded doublet suppresses the interaction meant to protect the topological state.

Here is how the failures hang together.

fabrication and charge-state yield
|
+-- positions and orientations ------> pair couplings J_ij and graph
| |
| +--> coupling disorder sigma_J
|
+-- cluster spectrum ----------------> isolated doublet, gap Delta_c
|
+-- require epsilon = J/Delta_c K ~ J epsilon^3
|
+----------------------------+------------------+
| | |
unwanted terms topological gap preparation gap
delta H Delta_topo Delta_min
| | |
+---------- require --------+--------+---------+
|
Delta_topo >> sigma_K, ||delta H||, hbar Gamma, k_B T
|

|
repeat with adequate yield and control

Now assign hypothetical, not measured, values. Let

\[ \frac{\Delta_c}{h}=5\ \mathrm{GHz},\qquad \frac{J}{h}=100\ \mathrm{MHz},\qquad c=1, \]

where \(h\) is Planck’s constant. Then \(\epsilon=0.02\), and

\[ \frac{K}{h}=100\ \mathrm{MHz}\times(0.02)^3=800\ \mathrm{Hz}. \]

This passes the projection test comfortably and fails to produce a comfortable many-body scale. If the coherence time is a hypothetical \(T_2=1\ \mathrm{ms}\), define \(\Gamma=1/T_2=10^3\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). The associated energy linewidth in frequency units is

\[ \frac{\hbar\Gamma}{h}=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}=159\ \mathrm{Hz}. \]

Thus \(K/(\hbar\Gamma)\approx5\), not a robust \(\gg1\) hierarchy. A dimensionless factor smaller than our optimistic \(c=1\), extra perturbative order, or correlated noise can erase the margin.

Placement error is amplified too. For magnetic dipolar coupling, \(J\propto r^{-3}\), where \(r\) is separation in metres. A small radial error \(\delta r\) gives

\[ \frac{\delta J}{J}\approx-3\frac{\delta r}{r}. \]

Because \(K\propto J^4\) in this toy path,

\[ \frac{\delta K}{K}\approx4\frac{\delta J}{J} \approx-12\frac{\delta r}{r}. \]

A 5% separation spread therefore produces about a 60% spread in \(K\) in this simplified common-coupling estimate. The arithmetic is a sensitivity calculation, not a universal disorder law; independent bonds and angular errors require the actual Hamiltonian.

Preparation inherits the small gap. Let the minimum many-body gap along an interpolation be optimistically \(\Delta_{\min}=h\times800\ \mathrm{Hz}\), and let the norm of the Hamiltonian change with dimensionless interpolation coordinate \(s\) be \(\lVert dH/ds\rVert=h\times100\ \mathrm{MHz}\). A common sufficient adiabatic scale is [R245]

\[ t_f\gg\frac{\hbar\lVert dH/ds\rVert}{\Delta_{\min}^2} =\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{10^8}{800^2}\ \mathrm{s} \approx25\ \mathrm{s}. \]

That is roughly \(2.5\times10^4\) hypothetical coherence times. The bound is schedule- and theorem-dependent, but the inverse-gap penalty is not a decorative detail.

Finally, at \(T=10\ \mathrm{mK}\),

\[ \frac{k_BT}{h} =(20.84\ \mathrm{GHz/K})(0.010\ \mathrm{K}) \approx208\ \mathrm{MHz}, \]

which overwhelms an 800 Hz equilibrium gap. Driven preparation can evade thermal equilibrium for a while, but then the claim has changed from a passive thermal phase to a controlled nonequilibrium experiment.

The hierarchy did not collapse because 800 Hz is intrinsically absurd. It collapsed because the same 800 Hz had to beat disorder, decoherence, temperature, and an inverse-gap preparation time simultaneously.

Drop any one of those inequalities and the toy still looks promising. Keep all of them and it does not.

Ten obstacles, ranked

The ranking below is an assessment of the defect-cluster route to an analog, emergent, gapped topological Hamiltonian, not of defect qubits in general. “Direct” means evidence exists for the relevant ingredient; no cited experiment integrates all ingredients. Leverage runs from 1 (localized cost) to 5 (failure blocks the central claim).

Rank | Obstacle | Evidence proximity | Leverage | Why it sits here | |

1 | Generate the required high-order terms | strong theory; architecture-specific implementation is a proposal | 5 | Without the stabilizer/plaquette algebra, there is no target phase to protect. | |

2 | Retain a usable topological gap | rigorous stability theory starts from an already gapped target; defect value unmeasured | 5 | Every noise, preparation, and thermal inequality is paid from this one scale. | |

3 | Scale yield and calibration | direct component evidence; no phase-scale array | 5 | Per-site and per-link imperfections compound with system size. | |

4 | Place the right defects at the right coordinates | direct fabrication evidence | 5 | Position controls coupling, graph, cluster spectrum, and disorder at once. | |

5 | Make interactions coherent and strong enough | direct pair-level evidence | 5 | \(J\lesssim\hbar\Gamma\) kills coherent Hamiltonian engineering before topology enters. | |

6 | Control disorder | direct evidence for inhomogeneity sources; phase-level tolerance model-dependent | 4 | Disorder perturbs denominators and effective terms and can close or fill the gap. | |

7 | Realize the right interaction graph | microscopic interactions known; graph conversion is a proposal | 4 | Extra long-range and angular couplings are Hamiltonian terms, not merely wiring inconvenience. | |

8 | Survive finite temperature | strong theory; thermalization rates platform-dependent | 4–5 | It is existential for passive memory, but can be deferred for a short proof-of-principle state. | |

9 | Prepare the phase before it decoheres | strong adiabatic theory; no integrated demonstration | 4 | A small minimum gap can make a formally valid Hamiltonian experimentally unreachable. | |

10 | Initialize, address, drive, and read the array | direct small-register evidence; array extrapolation uncertain | 3–4 | Severe, but global protocols and improved interfaces offer more workaround space than missing terms do. | |

Ranks 3–7 are close. A host with mediator-enhanced coupling could move interaction downward while adding control or loss problems.

If the goal is an equilibrium passive memory rather than a finite-time phase demonstration, thermal stability rises to rank 3. The table is a decision order, not a law of nature.

The algebra that may never appear

String-net Hamiltonians require local constraints and plaquette recoupling operations with a precise algebra [R018]. Available defect interactions are predominantly two-body.

Perturbative gadgets can produce many-body terms [Theory], but higher order suppresses the desired coefficient and also generates lower-order shifts and unwanted operators [R174]. Symmetry can cancel some terms, yet the cancellation itself becomes sensitive to strain, orientation, and coupling imbalance.

The decisive question is not “can a four-body term be written in perturbation theory?” It is

\[ \lVert H_{\mathrm{unwanted}}\rVert, \ \sigma_K, \ \hbar\Gamma \ll K \]

throughout a manufacturable patch. No defect-cluster experiment cited here has measured that hierarchy. [Proposal] Until it does, the central analog-Hamiltonian step is an engineering hypothesis.

What fails if you stop at a nonzero coefficient? You have shown that a term exists in an expansion. You have not shown that it is the Hamiltonian.

A gap that theorems will not invent

Topological-order stability theorems show that certain already-gapped, local ideal Hamiltonians retain separated spectral bands under sufficiently weak local perturbations [R142]. [Theory] This is encouraging only after the engineered Hamiltonian lies inside the phase and its perturbations are below the theorem’s threshold. It does not say that a weak approximate plaquette term overcomes larger parasitic terms.

Define \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\) as the many-body energy gap above the relevant ground-state manifold. The useful requirement is

\[ \Delta_{\mathrm{topo}} \gg \max(k_BT,\sigma_K,\lVert H_{\mathrm{unwanted}}\rVert, \hbar\Gamma,\delta_{\mathrm{fs}}), \]

where \(\sigma_K\) is effective-coupling disorder, \(T\) is temperature in kelvin, \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant, \(\Gamma\) is a decoherence rate in inverse seconds, and \(\delta_{\mathrm{fs}}\) is a finite-size splitting in joules. An experimentally visible spectral gap is still not, by itself, proof of topological order; its excitations, nonlocal operators, and robustness must match the target.

Invoke the stability theorem before the target term dominates, and you have used the conclusion as a hypothesis.

Multiplication as an enemy

Suppose every required site independently works with probability \(p\). An all-good \(N\)-site patch then has yield

\[ Y_N=p^N. \]

This toy model ignores correlated fabrication and repair. It nevertheless exposes the tax: for \(N=1000\), \(p=0.99\) gives \(Y_N\approx4.3\times10^{-5}\), while \(p=0.999\) gives \(Y_N\approx0.368\). Links, orientations, charge states, optical usability, and cluster spectra add separate conditions unless the architecture tolerates vacancies and reroutes around them.

Scaling also means calibrating an extensive number of nonidentical frequencies and couplings. A scheme that needs a separate analog cancellation tone for every parasitic bond may scale in component count while failing in calibration entropy. This is why scaling ranks above several spectacular single-device limitations.

Drop independence and the number can be kinder. Keep it, and \(p=0.99\) is already a closed door at a thousand sites.

The right defect in the right place

[Experiment] A 2025 diamond experiment combined nitrogen delta doping and localized electron irradiation in prefabricated nanopillars, reporting about 4 nm depth precision and 46(1) nm lateral precision in 280 nm-diameter pillars, with mean Hahn-echo \(T_2=98\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) for the created single NV centers [R207]. Those are important fabrication advances under the paper’s conditions. They do not provide arbitrary three-dimensional, few-nanometre, orientation-selected interacting lattices.

The comparison must be made to the architecture’s tolerance, not to the word “nanoscale.” If a dipolar design uses separation \(r\) and permits relative coupling spread \(q\), radial placement alone needs roughly \(\sigma_r/r\lesssim q/3\). Exchange-mediated proposals can be more position-sensitive because exchange often changes exponentially with wave-function overlap. Post-fabrication mapping can identify what was built, but topology requires the mapped graph to remain in the desired phase or be repairable.

A 46 nm lateral number does not refute every future process. It does refute treating that 2025 process as already inside a few-nanometre interacting lattice.

A pair is not a lattice

[Experiment] Two engineered NV electron spins separated by approximately 25 nm were entangled at room temperature using their roughly 5 kHz magnetic dipolar coupling [R080]. This is decisive evidence that coherent defect–defect interaction is real, not evidence that the same coupling supplies a clean high-order gap across a large lattice. The experiment used control sequences and a selected pair.

Dipolar interaction offers no independent knobs for strength, angle, and range:

\[ J_{ij}\propto\frac{1-3\cos^2\theta_{ij}}{r_{ij}^3}, \]

where \(\theta_{ij}\) is the angle between the separation vector and quantization axis. Bringing defects closer increases \(J\) but generally worsens fabrication damage, spectral crowding, unwanted exchange, and individual addressability.

Optical, phononic, or cavity mediators can extend range, but add loss, fabrication, and mode-crowding budgets. They move the bottleneck; they do not delete it.

Hence \(J/\hbar=10\Gamma\) for a pair clears only that pair-level comparison. The topological gap, not bare \(J\), is the later test.

Disorder walks in twice

Microscopic disorder first changes bare frequencies, orientations, and \(J_{ij}\). It then enters perturbative denominators, so it changes effective coefficients nonlinearly. A cluster may cease to have a clean doublet before the array-level topological phase is tested.

Local disorder below a stable phase’s threshold need not be fatal [R142]. The hostile case is not weak generic disorder around a healthy gap.

It is disorder comparable to a gap already reduced by projection. Echo can refocus certain single-spin frequency offsets but cannot refocus a static error in the Hamiltonian one is trying to realize without also modifying the target dynamics.

Drop the second entrance — the denominators — and disorder looks like a local-field problem. Keep it, and a clean doublet can vanish before anyone asks about anyons.

Extra edges are operators

A string-net or bond-directional model specifies which degrees of freedom couple and which operator acts on each edge or plaquette [R018]. A three-dimensional crystal supplies crystallographic orientations, long-range dipolar tails, and surfaces — not a freely editable graph.

One can encode graph structure into clusters, frequency selection, pulse sequences, or mediators. Each technique adds either smaller effective scales, time-dependent control, or hardware. [Proposal] A digitally toggled average Hamiltonian may emulate the graph, but then its protection is control-dependent and should not be advertised as an autonomous material Hamiltonian.

An extra dipolar tail is not wiring inconvenience. It is a term in \(H\).

Heat does not ask permission

At nonzero temperature, excitations appear with rates that depend on the gap and bath dynamics. They can diffuse and enact logical operators.

The finite-temperature quantum-memory literature shows that dimensionality, energy barriers, kinetics, and decoding matter, not merely the existence of a zero-temperature gap [R169]. [Theory] Two-dimensional local stabilizer Hamiltonians cannot provide a self-correcting quantum memory with a macroscopic energy barrier under the assumptions of the Bravyi–Terhal no-go theorem [R168].

That theorem is not a blanket impossibility result for every non-Abelian, driven, long-range, or actively corrected architecture; it does block casual claims that a 2D local Hamiltonian automatically stores forever.

A short-lived ground-state experiment may operate with active cooling and rapid measurement even when \(k_BT>\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\). That can demonstrate aspects of a model. It is not passive thermal protection.

The comparison is \(k_BT/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\), not the refrigerator temperature alone. A millikelvin number is unimpressive beside a hertz-scale emergent gap.

Getting there before the clock runs out

Even if the final Hamiltonian is in the desired phase, an adiabatic path can pass through a smaller gap \(\Delta_{\min}\). Adiabatic bounds depend on the full schedule, derivatives of the Hamiltonian, and matrix elements, not only the final gap [R245]. [Theory] Increasing system size can shrink \(\Delta_{\min}\) near a phase transition, while decoherence and calibration drift accumulate for longer.

Measurement-assisted or dissipative preparation may be faster. Those are new protocols with ancilla, reset, measurement, and verification requirements. Preparing a wavefunction once also does not prove an equilibrium phase: the subsequent Hamiltonian and response must carry the evidence.

A formally valid Hamiltonian with no experimental window is not a device. It is a matrix.

Control is last because it has more doors

[Experiment] A seven-spin diamond processor has demonstrated fault-tolerant protocol primitives for a five-qubit-code logical qubit, including flagged stabilizer measurements and real-time processing [R234]. The authors explicitly noted that fidelity and qubit number still needed improvement to suppress logical errors below physical errors. This shows sophisticated control in a selected local register, not dense analog control of an extensive defect lattice.

Color-center network reviews likewise identify simultaneous demands on spin coherence, optical interfaces, spectral stability, and integrated fabrication [R246]. Local tuning can correct disorder but may break cluster symmetry; spectral distinguishability helps addressability but creates detuning; dense packing strengthens interaction but increases crosstalk. These are not ten independent knobs.

Control ranks last because workarounds exist. Missing plaquette algebra does not have a workaround that still yields the proposed phase.

What the laboratory actually has

The evidence through 2026 is asymmetric.

  • [Experiment] Individual defects, small registers, coherent pair coupling, logical-protocol primitives, and improving registered fabrication are real [R207]; [R080]; [R234].

  • [Theory] Perturbative generation, stability of ideal topological phases, adiabatic conditions, and finite-temperature limitations are well developed [R174]; [R245]; [R018]; [R142]; [R169]; [R168].

  • [Proposal] Mapping a particular manufacturable defect-cluster Hamiltonian to a clean non-Abelian string-net model remains a proposal.

  • [Numerics] Small-model numerics can validate a chosen effective Hamiltonian, but they cannot supply fabrication distributions or decoherence parameters that have not been measured.

  • [Speculation] Extrapolating current defect components to a scalable, passively protected Fibonacci-like material is scientifically coherent but unsupported as an integrated hardware claim.

The negative verdict is therefore not “impossible.” It is “the central conjunction has no demonstrated margin.” The most impressive experimental results support the bottom edges of the dependency tree, while the claim lives at the top.

Ways to get this wrong

Counting ingredients instead of checking simultaneous inequalities. A long \(T_2\), a strong pair coupling, accurate implantation, and a topological model in four different samples do not form one device. The relevant object is the joint distribution of \(J\), \(\Delta_c\), disorder, coherence, yield, and control in the same fabricated patch.

Calling any effective interaction a plaquette term. An observed four-spin spectral shift is not enough.

The operator, sign, competing terms, spatial pattern, and perturbative validity must match the target Hamiltonian. Otherwise a higher-order effect has been demonstrated, not the needed algebra.

Treating a digital workaround as proof of passive emergence. Pulse synthesis can cancel extra edges and generate multi-body average Hamiltonians.

That may be excellent digital or Floquet simulation. If continuous calibration and periodic drive are essential, the protection mechanism is not simply an autonomous equilibrium Hamiltonian.

Using topological stability circularly. The theorem says a suitable topological phase survives sufficiently weak perturbations. It cannot be invoked before showing that the target term dominates and the system begins inside that phase.

Hiding yield behind postselection. Selecting one successful pair from a large implanted field demonstrates pair physics. A scalable architecture must count failed sites, unusable charge states, missing links, calibration time, and the effect of repair on the graph.

Confusing a cold refrigerator with a cold effective Hamiltonian. The comparison is \(k_BT/\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\), not the refrigerator temperature alone. A millikelvin number is unimpressive beside a hertz-scale emergent gap.

Collapsing five different claims into one word. A physical defect qubit can be coherent.

A cluster can encode a leftover. A controlled array can digitally emulate a string-net Hamiltonian.

An analog material can possess emergent topological order. An encoded state can be actively error-corrected.

Failure of the analog defect-cluster route would not negate the other four.

Check yourself

Why is high-order-term generation ranked above control complexity?

Because control has possible architectural workarounds, while absence of the target plaquette/stabilizer algebra removes the proposed phase itself. High-order synthesis also sets the small scale inherited by several downstream tests.

Show that the toy numbers give \(K/h=800\) Hz and \(K/(\hbar\Gamma)\approx5\).

With \(J/h=100\) MHz and \(\epsilon=0.02\), \(K/h=100\,\mathrm{MHz}\times(0.02)^3=800\) Hz. For \(T_2=1\) ms, \(\Gamma=10^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(\hbar\Gamma/h=\Gamma/2\pi=159\) Hz, so the ratio is about 5, not \(\gg1\).

What fails if cluster isolation \(\Delta_c/J\) is increased to protect the doublet?

A fourth-order coefficient scales as \(J(J/\Delta_c)^3\). The projection becomes cleaner while the desired term becomes smaller. Better isolation can make the topological gap worse.

Show that a 5% radial spread produces about a 60% spread in \(K\) on this fourth-order dipolar path.

\(\delta J/J\approx-3\delta r/r\) and \(K\propto J^4\), so \(\delta K/K\approx-12\delta r/r\). Then \(12\times0.05=0.60\). Independent bonds and angles need the actual Hamiltonian.

Does 46 nm lateral positioning precision refute a few-nanometre architecture?

It refutes neither future improvement nor every fabrication method. It shows that one advanced, high-yield 2025 process did not yet meet that hypothetical tolerance. The architecture must state its tolerance and compare like with like.

What fails if \(k_BT>\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\)? Is every experiment pointless?

Fast, driven, cooled, measured, or postselected experiments may reveal model dynamics. The result would not establish a passive equilibrium memory at that temperature.

The attack is on the joints, not the windows. Improving a later protocol cannot rescue a missing column.

Chapter 39 — Write the no first

You are about to spend years cooling a crystal so a bit can sit still without anyone watching. Before you book the helium, write the number that would make you stop.

Not the number you hope for. The number that, if the data land on the wrong side of it, ends this particular claim. Write it now, while the cartoon still looks clean.

That written no is a kill criterion. The name is worth keeping because it is a door you can actually fall through. A wish list has no door.

A design target says we would like a larger gap. A kill criterion says: if the upper bound you still believe on the activation gap is below this value after measurement X, stop pursuing a memory that sits still at temperature \(T\).

The constraints do not take turns. They hold at the same time.

A poor cluster yield reduces patch yield. A weak coupling reduces the gap.

A smaller gap makes preparation slower. Slower preparation gives decoherence more time.

The product, not the nicest factor, is the project.

This is not theatrical pessimism. It is arithmetic you agree to before you like the answer.

Five parts of a useful no

A useful trapdoor has five parts:

  • a claim you can still point to after the measurement;

  • a metric with units and a measurement or calculation protocol;

  • a threshold derived from that claim;

  • an uncertainty rule decided before seeing the result;

  • an action: continue, redesign, pivot, or stop.

That fourth part is preregistration. The threshold is a promise, not a mood. You do not move the line after you like the plot.

There is no universal magic ratio such as \(J/\Gamma>10\). The required ratio depends on how many interaction times the protocol consumes and how much error is allocated to decoherence.

Likewise, \(\Delta>k_{\mathrm B}T\) is not enough for a thousand-site sample if the allowed probability of even one thermal seed is tiny. The criterion must know the model and the task.

Drop the predeclared action and a missed number becomes a discussion. Keep it, and a missed number is a decision.

A table that can say no

Consider a deliberately hypothetical target, not a claim about any existing material. [Proposal] One thousand cluster leftovers form a two-dimensional analog topological memory with \(N_s=1000\) required sites and \(N_b=1500\) required bonds.

The effective interaction frequency is estimated as \(\nu_{\mathrm{eff}}=J_{\mathrm{eff}}/h=20\,\mathrm{MHz}\), with a credible interval of \(10\)–\(40\,\mathrm{MHz}\). The measured dephasing time under the intended controls is \(T_2=100\,\mu\mathrm{s}\), interval \(50\)–\(200\,\mu\mathrm{s}\).

Here \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is an energy in joules (J), \(h\) is Planck’s constant in J·s, and \(T_2\) is in seconds.

The project writes four decisions before the numbers arrive:

  • Continue: the conservative bound you still believe passes.

  • Resolve: the intervals cross; obtain the measurement or larger simulation that controls the decision.

  • Redesign: the present implementation fails, but a named change could alter the controlling equation.

  • Stop/pivot: even the optimistic bound fails. Stop claiming the stated target; a different target, such as active digital simulation, is a new project.

The numbers below are invented to show the arithmetic. Replace them with the parameter ledger and the model calculations you already have. The table is a rehearsal, not a verdict on a real crystal.

Gate | Hypothetical estimate, including uncertainty | Preregistered threshold | Decision | Required action | |

Coherent interaction \(R_J=J_{\mathrm{eff}}/(\hbar\Gamma)\) | \(1.26\times10^4\) \([3.1\times10^3,5.0\times10^4]\) | \(R_J\ge2.0\times10^4\) | Resolve | Measure \(T_2\) under the complete pulse schedule; do not scale the array yet | |

Thermal activation \(x_T=E_{\mathrm{act}}/(k_{\mathrm B}T)\) | \(0.0048\) \([0.0010,0.015]\) at \(10\,\mathrm{mK}\) | \(x_T\ge\ln(N_s/10^{-3})=13.8\) | Stop/pivot | Abandon passive equilibrium memory for this scale unless the gap or temperature changes by orders of magnitude | |

Coupling-disorder quantile \(q_J/J\) | \(0.08\) \([0.04,0.15]\) | model phase boundary \(\eta_c=0.05\) \([0.03,0.08]\) | Resolve | Simulate measured disorder tails and missing bonds; RMS alone is insufficient | |

Placement spread for direct dipolar bonds | \(\sigma_r=1.0\,\mathrm{nm}\) \([0.5,2.0]\) at \(r=10\,\mathrm{nm}\) | \(\sigma_r\le0.17\,\mathrm{nm}\) for 5% coupling spread | Redesign | Add tunability or change coupling mechanism; direct fixed dipolar layout fails this tolerance | |

Unhandled leakage per control location \(p_u\) | \(2\times10^{-4}\) \([5\times10^{-5},8\times10^{-4}]\) | \(p_u\le10^{-6}\) for 1000 locations and \(10^{-3}\) budget | Redesign | Demonstrate detection/reset before accepting more locations | |

Preparation window | \(t_{\mathrm{ad}}=100\,\mu\mathrm{s}\) \([30,500]\) | \(t_{\mathrm{ad}}\le0.01T_2=0.5\)–\(2\,\mu\mathrm{s}\) | Stop/pivot | Change preparation path or use dissipative/active preparation; present ramp has no window | |

Site-only patch yield \(Y_s=y_s^{N_s}\) | \(0.0067\) \([4.3\times10^{-5},0.368]\) for \(y_s=0.995\,[0.990,0.999]\) | \(Y_s\ge0.10\), before bond losses | Resolve | Measure correlated yield and test repairable layouts; monolithic scale-up is not justified | |

Logical scaling, \(p_L(d+2)/p_L(d)\) | \(0.80\) \([0.60,1.10]\) | upper credible bound \(<1\) at fixed physical conditions | Resolve | Add distances and blind decoder analysis; do not extrapolate an improving lifetime yet | |

Let us check two rows. Define \(\Gamma=1/T_2\), in s\(^{-1}\), and \(\hbar=h/(2\pi)\). Then

\[ R_J=\frac{J_{\mathrm{eff}}}{\hbar\Gamma} =2\pi\nu_{\mathrm{eff}}T_2 =2\pi(20\times10^6\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})(100\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s}) \approx1.26\times10^4. \]

The units cancel. If the protocol consumes \(\alpha=20\) inverse-interaction times and receives a decoherence budget \(\epsilon_J=10^{-3}\), the exposure estimate \(\Gamma t\approx\alpha/R_J\) requires \(R_J\ge\alpha/\epsilon_J=2.0\times10^4\).

The central estimate fails, but the interval crosses. The correct action is measurement, not rhetoric.

For the thermal row, suppose a small-patch calculation gives an activation energy \(E_{\mathrm{act}}/h=c_{\mathrm{act}}\nu_{\mathrm{eff}}\), with \(c_{\mathrm{act}}=0.05\,[0.02,0.08]\). The central activation frequency is \(1\,\mathrm{MHz}\).

At \(T=10\,\mathrm{mK}\), \(k_{\mathrm B}T/h\approx208\,\mathrm{MHz}\), so \(x_T\approx1/208=0.0048\). Even combining the optimistic endpoints gives only \(3.2/208\approx0.015\).

The best case misses 13.8 by nearly three orders of magnitude. More precise fitting cannot rescue the stated passive-memory target.

This table tests an analog memory that is supposed to sit still. A digital simulator may operate with \(E_{\mathrm{act}}<k_{\mathrm B}T\) because its effective Hamiltonian is enacted by calibrated gates and active error correction rather than thermal equilibrium.

Passing a digital circuit benchmark does not pass the analog thermal gate. Conversely, failing passive memory does not prove the hardware useless as physical qubits, sensors, or an emulation platform.

Hence two different claims share the same hardware and not the same door.

How many ticks before the spin forgets

Define \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) as the coefficient, in J, of the effective term that actually performs the needed low-energy dynamics — not the bare intra-cluster splitting and not the largest microscopic coupling. Define \(\Gamma\) as the measured decay rate, in s\(^{-1}\), under the operating point and control schedule relevant to that term. The dimensionless coherent ratio is

\[ R_J=\frac{J_{\mathrm{eff}}}{\hbar\Gamma}. \]

If a protocol requires time

\[ t_{\mathrm{req}}=\alpha\frac{\hbar}{J_{\mathrm{eff}}}, \]

where \(\alpha\) is a dimensionless path or circuit cost obtained from simulation, then first-order Markovian exposure is \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{dec}}\approx\Gamma t_{\mathrm{req}}=\alpha/R_J\). Allocating at most \(\epsilon_J\) to this channel gives the falsifiable criterion

\[ \boxed{R_J\ge\frac{\alpha}{\epsilon_J}}. \]

This is why a bare rule \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}>\hbar\Gamma\) is weak: it buys only order-one dynamics before decay. It also explains why \(T_2\) measured on an isolated defect cannot be inserted automatically. Clustering, continuous drives, optical cycling, and correlated noise change \(\Gamma\).

Kill rule. Stop the specified protocol if the upper bound you still believe on \(R_J\) remains below the lower bound you still believe on \(\alpha/\epsilon_J\) after the effective coupling and driven coherence are measured in the same device. If a different protocol reduces \(\alpha\), that is a redesign with a new gate.

What fails if you borrow an isolated-spin echo? You have compared \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) to someone else’s \(\Gamma\). The inequality is then a collage, not a test.

One seed is already too many

Define \(E_{\mathrm{act}}\), in J, as the lowest energy barrier for a locally accessible harmful excitation process. It need not equal the clean spectral gap \(\Delta_{\mathrm{topo}}\). Boundaries, weak bonds, disorder, and multi-step paths can lower it. For \(N_c\) approximately independent creation opportunities, a dilute equilibrium estimate gives

\[ P_{\mathrm{seed}}\lesssim N_c g\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{act}}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right), \]

where \(g\) is a dimensionless species or channel factor and \(P_{\mathrm{seed}}\) is the probability of at least one harmful seed. Requiring \(P_{\mathrm{seed}}\le\epsilon_T\) yields

\[ \boxed{\frac{E_{\mathrm{act}}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\ge \ln\!\left(\frac{N_c g}{\epsilon_T}\right)}. \]

The exponent is dimensionless: J divided by \((\mathrm{J/K})\mathrm K\). Finite-temperature topological memories require kinetic analysis as well as this occupancy estimate; in two-dimensional local stabilizer Hamiltonians, a constant energy barrier prevents passive self-correction under the no-go theorem’s assumptions [R168]; [R169]. [Theory]

Kill rule. For passive equilibrium memory, stop if the optimistic disorder-renormalized \(E_{\mathrm{act}}\), the lowest temperature you still believe, and the smallest useful \(N_c\) still fail the logarithmic bound.

If active removal is proposed, replace this gate with a measured creation rate, diffusion model, syndrome cadence, and logical-error target. Do not silently keep the word passive.

\(\Delta>k_{\mathrm B}T\) is not the same test. The required ratio grows as \(\ln(N_c g/\epsilon_T)\), and diffusion can still dominate after occupancy looks small.

The weakest bond, not the average

Write the realized Hamiltonian as

\[ H=H_{\mathrm{target}}+\delta H, \qquad \delta H=\sum_b \delta J_b O_b, \]

where \(b\) labels bonds or local terms, \(\delta J_b\) is a coupling error in J, and \(O_b\) is a dimensionless operator. Topological phases can be stable to sufficiently weak local perturbations, but the theorem assumes a gapped target and bounded local perturbations; it does not convert an RMS fabrication number into a universal tolerance [R142]. [Theory]

The proper threshold \(\eta_c\) must come from the candidate model’s disordered phase diagram or a conservative local-gap bound. A minimal simulation sweeps the measured distribution, including missing terms and spatial correlations, and estimates where the gap, topological diagnostic, or logical scaling fails. The fabrication metric should be a high quantile

\[ q_J=Q_{1-\alpha/N_b}(|\delta J_b|), \]

not merely the standard deviation. Here \(Q_p\) is the \(p\)-quantile, \(N_b\) is the number of required bonds, and \(\alpha\) is the allowed probability that any bond exceeds the quoted value. The \(1/N_b\) makes the tail requirement tighten with scale.

Kill rule. Stop monolithic scale-up if even the lower tail you still believe of \(q_J/J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) lies beyond the upper model tolerance \(\eta_c\) you still believe, or if missing or sign-flipped terms put the realized Hamiltonian in a different phase. A calibratable static offset is not automatically harmless; demonstrate that calibration preserves the many-body gap and does not add control noise.

Report the average and a large patch can still die on one weak bond. The quantile is the object; the RMS is a summary of a different question.

How far the atoms may wander

Positioning is fatal only through a model-dependent transfer function. Let \(r\) be nominal separation and \(\sigma_r\) a small radial uncertainty, both in metres. For a dipolar interaction \(J(r)=C r^{-3}\), differentiation gives

\[ \left|\frac{\sigma_J}{J}\right|\approx \left|\frac{d\ln J}{dr}\right|\sigma_r =3\frac{\sigma_r}{r}. \]

Thus an allowed fractional coupling spread \(\eta_J\) requires

\[ \boxed{\sigma_r\le\frac{\eta_J r}{3}}. \]

At \(r=10\,\mathrm{nm}\) and \(\eta_J=0.05\), this is \(0.17\,\mathrm{nm}\). Length divided by length makes the fractional error dimensionless. Angular uncertainty must be added because dipolar coupling also contains an orientation factor.

For exchange-like coupling \(J(r)=J_0e^{-r/\lambda}\), where \(\lambda\) is a decay length in metres, the corresponding result is \(\sigma_J/J\approx\sigma_r/\lambda\). The relevant tolerance may then be much smaller than a nanometre. Defect-platform reviews document that creation, charge-state control, coherence, and placement are separate yields, so a nominal beam diameter is not a complete position distribution [R074]. [Experiment]

Kill rule. Stop the fixed-coupling layout if the best demonstrated final-position distribution, propagated through the full angular and radial coupling law, exceeds \(\eta_c\). Tunable couplers, spectroscopy-based calibration, or a less sensitive geometry are redesigns and must include their added noise and wiring costs.

A beam diameter is not \(\sigma_r\). Straggle, diffusion, conversion, charge selection, and registration enter the realized coupling distribution.

A leak that stays leaked

Let \(p_\ell\) be leakage probability per relevant control or syndrome location. Let \(p_u\le p_\ell\) be the probability that leakage remains undetected and unremoved long enough to spread. For \(N_{\mathrm{loc}}\) locations in a task, the dilute approximation gives

\[ P_{\mathrm{leak}}\approx N_{\mathrm{loc}}p_u. \]

Allocating \(\epsilon_\ell\) to unhandled leakage requires

\[ \boxed{p_u\le\frac{\epsilon_\ell}{N_{\mathrm{loc}}}}. \]

A reset every \(m\) cycles changes \(p_u\), but it may also interrupt the analog Hamiltonian. Surface-code studies show that long-lived leakage creates time-correlated, propagating faults and that dedicated leakage-reduction circuitry can restore threshold behavior in particular active circuits [R220]. [Theory] [Numerics] That is a method to test, not permission to assume the same threshold for clusters.

Kill rule. Stop scaling if the optimistic unhandled leakage probability exceeds the task allocation and no compatible detection or reset operation has been demonstrated. Count charge-state switching, departure from the cluster doublet, and loss of a constituent separately before combining them.

Treat leakage as a Pauli error and you have left the modeled local Hilbert space without noticing.

A window that has to exist

Let the preparation path be \(H(s)\), with dimensionless schedule coordinate \(s\in[0,1]\). Define \(A=\max_s\|\partial_sH\|\), in J, and \(\Delta_{\min}\), in J, as the minimum many-body gap along the actual path. A schematic leading adiabatic estimate is

\[ \epsilon_{\mathrm{ad}}\sim \left(\frac{\hbar A}{t_p\Delta_{\min}^2}\right)^2, \]

where \(t_p\) is preparation time in seconds. The combination \(\hbar A/\Delta_{\min}^2\) has units \((\mathrm{J\,s})\mathrm J/\mathrm J^2=\mathrm s\). Rigorous bounds include endpoint smoothness, higher derivatives, matrix elements, and system-size dependence [R247]. [Theory] Solving for an allocated diabatic error \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{ad}}^*\) gives a lower bound

\[ t_p\ge t_{\min}= \frac{\hbar A}{\Delta_{\min}^2\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{ad}}^*}}. \]

Decoherence supplies an upper bound \(t_p\le t_{\max}\approx\epsilon_{\mathrm{dec}}^*/\Gamma\) in the small-error Markovian estimate. A viable ramp needs

\[ \boxed{t_{\min}<t_{\max}}. \]

Kill rule. Stop the adiabatic preparation route if the bounds you still believe leave no overlap, including the size dependence of \(\Delta_{\min}\). A dissipative or measurement-assisted route is a new protocol; give it a mixing or convergence time, residual excitation density, and its own decoherence and readout budget.

What fails if the ramp may be arbitrarily slow? Diabatic error falls and open-system error rises. When \(t_{\min}>t_{\max}\), slower is not a solution.

Almost every site is not every site

Let \(y_s\) be the probability that a required site has the correct position, species, charge state, local spectrum, and addressability. Let \(y_b\) be the probability that a required bond lies within tolerance. If these events were independent, an unrepairable patch yield would be

\[ Y_{\mathrm{patch}}=y_s^{N_s}y_b^{N_b}. \]

This is dimensionless. At \(y_s=0.995\) and \(N_s=1000\), the favorable site-only result is \(0.995^{1000}\approx0.0067\).

Adding bond failures only lowers it. Independence is not guaranteed: implantation damage, annealing, strain, and optical collection can correlate failures.

Known-loss topological-code thresholds can be high in specifically designed active codes; for example, the idealized surface-code analysis of Stace and collaborators connects tolerable heralded loss to lattice percolation [R248]. [Theory] [Numerics] That value must not be borrowed for a string-net Hamiltonian whose interaction graph and terms disappear with a site. A reroutable design passes only after the defective graph is shown to remain in the target phase and the readout identifies losses reliably.

Kill rule. Set an economic or experimental minimum yield \(Y_{\min}=1/N_{\mathrm{attempt,max}}\).

Stop monolithic fabrication when the upper \(Y_{\mathrm{patch}}\) you still believe is below \(Y_{\min}\). Continue a repairable architecture only if measured defect maps, an explicit repair algorithm, and phase simulations pass together.

Multiply advertised yields with no denominators and you have multiplied different conditional events as if they were one.

Bigger has to get better

Small patches can imitate a gap or a topological degeneracy. The extrapolation must be stated. For linear size \(L\), one gapped ansatz is

\[ \Delta(L)=\Delta_\infty+a e^{-L/\xi}, \]

where all \(\Delta\) and \(a\) are in J and \(L\) and correlation length \(\xi\) share units. A phase claim needs a \(\Delta_\infty>0\) you still believe and competing finite-size fits. A logical-memory claim under fixed physical noise might use

\[ p_L(d)=A_0e^{-\alpha d}, \]

where code distance \(d\), prefactor \(A_0\), and exponent \(\alpha\) are dimensionless. Improvement requires \(\alpha>0\), or equivalently \(p_L(d+\delta d)/p_L(d)<1\).

Kill rule. Stop claiming scalable protection if the upper improvement ratio you still believe is at least one across preregistered larger sizes under the same noise distribution, or if extrapolation excludes a nonzero thermodynamic gap.

Do not let postselection, better control on larger samples, a different decoder, or a lower temperature masquerade as distance scaling. Those may be useful experiments, but they test another curve.

A kill here is not total failure of the hardware. It is failure of the stated scaling claim under the stated noise.

What the lab has to write down

A kill criterion is only as honest as its uncertainty. Each input should retain a distribution and a condition:

  • \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\): inferred from the low-energy spectrum with corrections and fit covariance;

  • \(\Gamma\): measured under the complete operating schedule, not copied from isolated-spin echo;

  • \(E_{\mathrm{act}}\) and \(\Delta_{\min}\): minimized over boundaries, disorder samples, leakage sectors, and preparation path;

  • placement and coupling disorder: joint spatial distributions and tail confidence, not only RMS values;

  • leakage: state-resolved rate, dwell-time distribution, propagation, and reset efficacy;

  • yield: denominators for creation, correct species, charge, coherence, addressability, and bonds;

  • scaling: raw logical counts, decoder frozen before unblinding, and uncertainty on fit and model choice.

[Numerics] Exact diagonalization can establish these quantities only for the Hamiltonian, sizes, boundary conditions, and disorder ensemble actually simulated. [Experiment] Spectroscopy can establish a finite-device gap, not by itself thermodynamic topological order. [Proposal] Combining the two requires posterior predictive checks: feed measured distributions into the model and ask whether it predicts held-out spectra, dynamics, and logical observables.

Use one-sided intervals for decisions. If passing requires a quantity to be large, compare its lower bound with the threshold.

If passing requires it to be small, compare its upper bound. A hard stop is justified when even the optimistic bound fails after the measurement has enough power to resolve the decision.

An imprecise experiment usually earns “resolve,” not “go” and not “stop.”

Ways to get this wrong

  • Universalizing a model threshold. The roughly 11% perfect-syndrome toric-code threshold belongs to a stochastic Pauli model and decoder assumptions [R141]. It is not a disorder, leakage, or fabrication threshold.

  • Comparing unlike units. \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}/h\) is in hertz; \(\Gamma=1/T_2\) is in s\(^{-1}\); the energy comparison uses \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}/(\hbar\Gamma)=2\pi(J_{\mathrm{eff}}/h)T_2\). Dropping \(2\pi\) can move a marginal gate.

  • Using \(\Delta/k_{\mathrm B}T>1\) as a binary test. The required ratio grows as \(\ln(N_cg/\epsilon_T)\), and diffusion can still dominate.

  • Reporting average disorder for a large patch. Rare weak bonds, missing sites, and spatially correlated regions govern failure.

  • Calling nominal implantation precision the final placement error. Straggle, diffusion, conversion, charge selection, and registration enter the realized coupling distribution.

  • Treating leakage as a Pauli error. Leakage leaves the modeled local Hilbert space and can persist or spread.

  • Optimizing preparation against only one bound. Adiabaticity imposes a minimum time; decoherence imposes a maximum.

  • Multiplying advertised yields with no denominators. Creation yield, correct charge, optical usability, cluster completion, and bond tolerance are different conditional events.

  • Changing conditions while claiming scaling. Logical improvement with distance must hold at fixed physical noise and analysis rules.

  • Interpreting a kill as total failure. A passive-memory kill may motivate an active simulator, sensor, network node, or smaller proof of principle. That pivot must receive a new claim and new criteria.

Check yourself

Show that \(R_J=2\pi\nu_{\mathrm{eff}}T_2\approx1.26\times10^4\) for the hypothetical numbers, and why \(R_J>1\) is usually insufficient.

\(2\pi(20\times10^6\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})(100\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s})\approx1.26\times10^4\). That permits many interaction cycles, but a protocol costing \(\alpha\) interaction times with error budget \(\epsilon_J\) needs \(R_J\ge\alpha/\epsilon_J\). Here \(\alpha/\epsilon_J=2.0\times10^4\).

What fails if you use \(\Delta>k_{\mathrm B}T\) as a binary test?

The required ratio grows as \(\ln(N_c g/\epsilon_T)\). For \(N_s=1000\) and \(\epsilon_T=10^{-3}\), that logarithm is 13.8, and diffusion can still dominate after occupancy looks small.

Show that a 5% dipolar-coupling tolerance at \(r=10\) nm forces \(\sigma_r\le0.17\) nm.

Since \(J\propto r^{-3}\), \(\sigma_J/J\approx3\sigma_r/r\), so \(\sigma_r\le\eta_J r/3=0.05\times10/3\approx0.17\) nm.

What fails if \(t_{\min}>t_{\max}\) even when arbitrarily slow ramps are available?

The adiabatic lower time bound exceeds the decoherence upper time bound. Slower then reduces diabatic error but increases open-system error. The window does not exist.

Why can 99.5% site yield be poor?

An unrepairable thousand-site patch has site-only yield \(0.995^{1000}\approx0.0067\), before bond failures.

What makes a result a hard stop rather than “more data needed”?

A preregistered threshold is missed even by the optimistic bound you still believe after a measurement or calculation capable of resolving the gate.

The eight inequalities are go/no-go gates, not aspirations. A stage advances only when the conservative bounds pass.

Intervals that cross trigger the cheapest resolving calculation. Optimistic bounds that fail terminate the stated route or force an explicit redesign.
