Chapter 40 — Calculations with exits

You sit down with two defects and a four-by-four matrix. You diagonalize it. You look at the two lowest states. If they are not a useful pair, you stop.

That is the whole method. The rest of the chapter is the same door, four more times, each time a little more expensive.

The sequence is cheap at the front on purpose:

\[ \text{two defects} \rightarrow \text{one cluster leftover} \rightarrow \text{three-to-six-cluster plaquette} \rightarrow \text{small patch}. \]

At each arrow you name the inputs, compute the observables, test whether the answer moved when you tightened the calculation, and then either pass a gate you wrote down beforehand or walk out. The aim is not the prettiest picture. It is to kill an unworkable architecture before you rent a supercomputer to decorate it.

A plausible pair does not guarantee an isolated cluster doublet. A plausible doublet does not guarantee the plaquette operator you wanted.

A recognizable plaquette term does not guarantee a topological phase. A small patch with a close pair of eigenvalues does not prove topological degeneracy.

Every later calculation eats artifacts from the earlier one: calibrated matrices, projectors, uncertainty ranges, effective couplings, leftover error. Enthusiasm is not an artifact.

Two spins on a page

We begin with a screening calculation, not with a claim about a particular material.

Represent each defect by a spin-\(1/2\). Let \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) be the dimensionless Pauli matrices, and let \(I\) be the two-dimensional identity. In units where \(\hbar=1\),

\[ H_2= \frac{\omega_1}{2}Z\otimes I+ \frac{\omega_2}{2}I\otimes Z+ J_x X\otimes X+J_y Y\otimes Y+J_z Z\otimes Z. \]

The coefficients \(\omega_1,\omega_2,J_x,J_y,J_z\) must all use the same angular-frequency unit, such as radians per second. Then every eigenvalue of \(H_2\) has that unit. Multiplying by \(\hbar\) converts it to energy.

The following Julia program writes the four-by-four matrix, asks for every eigenvalue, keeps the two lowest eigenvectors as columns of a projector \(P\), calculates the leakage gap, projects three physical control operators, and checks the eigensolver leftover. It prints no invented benchmark values. You have to supply cited, condition-specific parameters.

using LinearAlgebra

I₂ = Matrix{ComplexF64}(I, 2, 2)
X = ComplexF64[0 1; 1 0]
Y = ComplexF64[0 -im; im 0]
Z = ComplexF64[1 0; 0 -1]

function pair_spectrum(ω₁, ω₂, Jx, Jy, Jz)
H = 0.5 * ω₁ * kron(Z, I₂) + 0.5 * ω₂ * kron(I₂, Z)
H += Jx * kron(X, X) + Jy * kron(Y, Y) + Jz * kron(Z, Z)

decomposition = eigen(Hermitian(H))
E = decomposition.values # ascending
U = decomposition.vectors
P = U[:, 1:2] # candidate leftover basis
Δ_leak = E[3] - E[2]

physical_ops = Dict(
"Z1" => kron(Z, I₂),
"Z2" => kron(I₂, Z),
"X1" => kron(X, I₂),
)
projected_ops = Dict(
name => P' * op * P for (name, op) in physical_ops
)

scale = max(norm(H), 1.0)
residual = norm(H * U - U * Diagonal(E)) / scale
return E, Δ_leak, projected_ops, residual
end

Writing the whole matrix and asking for every eigenpair is exact diagonalization. The name is worth keeping because nothing is thrown away except the digits the computer cannot hold. People shorten it to ED.

This program is a pipeline test, not a color-center model. Real defects may need a larger spin, orbital, hyperfine, strain, or charge basis. Replace the toy matrix with the cited microscopic Hamiltonian from Chapters 7–10 and 26.

The output already asks the right questions. Are the two lowest states a useful doublet?

Is \(\Delta_{\rm leak}=E_2-E_1\) large compared with intercluster coupling, drive bandwidth, disorder, and decoherence expressed in the same units? Do the projected physical operators span useful controls on the encoded pair, or does projection turn them into multiples of the identity?

A low pair of eigenvalues with no addressable transition is an elegant paperweight.

Freeze the numbers first

Before diagonalizing anything, create one machine-readable parameter record. It should contain:

  • defect species, charge state, spin and retained orbitals;

  • magnetic-field vector, strain tensor, electric field, and temperature;

  • pair positions and crystal orientations;

  • every Hamiltonian coefficient, unit, sign convention, source, sample conditions, and uncertainty interval;

  • which interactions are measured, calculated, fitted, or assumed;

  • the architecture’s predeclared kill criteria from Chapter 39.

Use one internal unit. If Hamiltonian coefficients are angular frequencies, convert every linewidth and inverse coherence time to angular frequency before comparison.

If they are energies, convert temperature through \(k_B T\). A comparison between megahertz and microelectronvolts without conversion is not multidisciplinary research.

It is two columns standing near each other.

Stop rule 0. Stop the material-specific calculation if a term essential to the target interaction has neither a cited physical mechanism nor a bounded parameter range. An unconstrained fitting knob can reproduce nearly any tiny spectrum and predict none.

Hence the record is not paperwork. It is the Hamiltonian you are actually studying. Drop a coefficient’s provenance and later “agreement with experiment” has nothing to agree with.

Two defects

Use dense ED for the smallest basis. If the same small model later needs pulses, collapse operators, or correlation functions, a package built for that job is QuTiP [R249]. For a closed Hermitian matrix, NumPy, SciPy, or Julia’s standard linear algebra is enough.

Sweep the full fabrication uncertainty, not only a best-fit point. For each sample of position, orientation, field, and coupling, store:

  • the low-energy spectrum \(E_n\);

  • level splittings and avoided crossings;

  • eigenstate composition in the microscopic basis;

  • derivatives \(\partial E_n/\partial p\) with respect to uncertain parameter \(p\);

  • matrix elements of physically available drives and readout operators;

  • leakage under a representative pulse or weak interpair coupling;

  • solver residuals and symmetry quantum numbers.

Convergence test. Enlarge the local basis — for example, add the nearest omitted orbital or hyperfine state — and compare the retained eigenvalues and projected operators.

The relevant error is not just an energy shift. A stable spectrum paired with unstable control matrix elements is not converged.

Stop rule 1. Reject the pair design if no connected region of the cited uncertainty range supports the required ordering of states, or if the needed coupling exists only at an isolated fine-tuned point narrower than the fabrication and control tolerance. Also stop if the leakage gap fails the model-specific inequality set in Chapter 39.

What fails if you keep only the best-fit point? You have shown that a Hamiltonian exists in a set of measure zero. The architecture lives in a distribution.

The whole cluster

Let a cluster contain \(m\) defects, each with retained local dimension \(d\). The raw Hilbert-space dimension is \(d^m\). Use all exact symmetries to block-diagonalize it, but check that the perturbations you later add do not break those symmetries.

Dense ED returns every eigenpair and is ideal while the largest symmetry block comfortably fits memory. Sparse Lanczos or Davidson methods return a selected low-energy window once the full matrix is too large.

A custom sparse implementation is justified when the Hamiltonian has repeated local terms and exact bit-level structure. In Julia, sparse matrices plus KrylovKit are a direct route; ITensors.jl becomes attractive when a matrix-product representation is natural [R250].

From the two lowest cluster eigenstates, build the rectangular projector

\[ P=|\tilde 0\rangle\langle 0|+|\tilde 1\rangle\langle 1|, \]

understood as a map from a two-state leftover basis \(\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}\) into the microscopic cluster space. For each microscopic operator \(O\), compute

\[ O_{\rm eff}=P^\dagger O P. \]

Expand the resulting two-by-two matrix as

\[ O_{\rm eff}=c_0 I+c_xX+c_yY+c_zZ, \]

with coefficients \(c_\mu=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\mu O_{\rm eff})\), where \(\sigma_\mu\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}\). This tells us what local fields, noise, readout, and intercluster couplings become inside the encoded subspace.

Compute the cluster splitting, leakage gap, projected control strengths, and projected noise operators across the uncertainty ensemble. Then couple two complete clusters microscopically and compare their exact low-energy spectrum with the predicted encoded interaction.

[Theory] A Schrieffer–Wolff expansion is controlled only when coupling between retained and discarded sectors is small relative to the relevant energy denominators; direct low-energy diagonalization provides the necessary finite-system benchmark [R025].

Convergence tests. Increase the number of retained cluster states; tighten sparse-eigensolver residuals; compare results with and without each nominally small microscopic term; and verify that phase choices within the doublet do not change basis-invariant conclusions.

Stop rule 2. Stop the cluster architecture if the doublet disappears over realistic disorder, if required controls project nearly to identity while noise projects strongly onto Pauli operators, or if exact two-cluster spectra cannot be reproduced within the predeclared effective-model error budget.

A leftover is certified by isolation, usable projected controls, tolerable projected noise, and agreement between exact coupled-cluster spectra and the effective model. A pretty doublet in an isolated cell is not that list.

Three to six clusters make a plaquette

This is the decisive gadget test and is still an ED problem. If each cluster is first truncated to a leftover, six clusters span only \(2^6\) states. Run two versions:

  • the effective calculation, using one leftover per cluster;

  • the leakage-aware calculation, retaining additional cluster states and the microscopic intercluster couplings.

Let \(n\) be the number of clusters around the candidate plaquette. Project the leakage-aware Hamiltonian into the encoded space and expand it in all Pauli strings,

\[ H_{\rm fit}=\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha}c_{\boldsymbol\alpha} \,\sigma_{\alpha_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\sigma_{\alpha_n}, \]

where each \(\alpha_j\) is \(0,x,y,\) or \(z\), and \(\sigma_0=I\). Because Pauli strings are orthogonal under the trace inner product,

\[ c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}=2^{-n} \operatorname{Tr}\!\left( \sigma_{\boldsymbol\alpha}^\dagger H_{\rm fit} \right). \]

This calculation does not merely ask whether the target plaquette coefficient \(K\) is nonzero. It reports every unwanted one-body, two-body, and higher-body coefficient generated at the same time. Compare the full exact low-energy spectrum and eigenvectors with the fitted operator, not just \(K\).

Sweep the intercluster scale \(\lambda\). The useful window must satisfy two conditions simultaneously: the target term is large enough to beat the relevant noise and temperature criteria, and the effective description remains accurate. If perturbation theory predicts the plaquette at a particular order in \(\lambda\), fit the scaling only inside a range where exact and effective spectra agree; do not select the fitting interval after seeing the desired exponent [R025].

Calculate spectrum, plaquette gap, target coefficient, norm of unwanted terms, leakage weight, and response to each physically allowed local perturbation. QuTiP remains useful for small driven or open plaquettes [R249].

A sparse ED implementation is usually simpler for closed spectra. Tensor-network methods add approximation without buying useful size here.

Stop rule 3. Abandon this gadget if no parameter interval simultaneously passes the hierarchy, leakage, disorder, and decoherence gates; if cancellation of unwanted terms requires unattainable precision; or if the target operator appears only after projecting away states that strongly mix in the exact calculation.

Hence a nonzero \(K\) is not the gate. The gate is \(K\) together with every competitor, in a window where leakage-aware ED still agrees.

A small patch

Start with the least ambitious topological target capable of testing the interaction architecture — typically an Abelian stabilizer or gauge-theory proxy before a doubled-Fibonacci claim. The purpose is to validate emergence from the proposed couplings, not to win the final noun on the first run.

Use ED while the symmetry-reduced Hilbert space and required Krylov vectors fit memory. For \(N\) encoded spins, one complex state vector has \(2^N\) entries.

If each entry is stored as a 16-byte complex number, its storage is \(16\times2^N\) bytes; an iterative solver needs several such vectors plus operator workspace. Do this dimensional estimate before choosing ED.

For long strips and cylinders, write the state as a chain of tensors with a bond that remembers the cut. Growing that bond until the leftover weight stops moving is the density-matrix renormalization group, or DMRG, in its matrix-product-state form.

ITensor and TeNPy implement it [R035]; [R250]; [R251]. DMRG is strongest when entanglement across the one-dimensional ordering remains manageable.

A two-dimensional lattice mapped onto a cylinder becomes harder as circumference increases; one narrow cylinder is not a two-dimensional thermodynamic limit [R035]; [R252].

For genuinely two-dimensional patches beyond ED, use finite or infinite projected entangled-pair states — PEPS — when the target state admits a tractable bond dimension and contractions can be converged [R252]; [R253]. In Julia, TensorKit.jl with MPSKit.jl or PEPSKit.jl provides symmetry-aware tensor infrastructure; ITensors.jl is a mature choice for matrix-product calculations [R250].

Report package versions and contraction algorithms. “Used tensor networks” is not a reproducible method.

Quantum Monte Carlo belongs only where weights are nonnegative or a demonstrated sign-problem treatment applies. Frustrated, complex, or non-Abelian effective interactions commonly remove that advantage. Do not recommend Monte Carlo merely because the lattice has many sites.

Method names do not allocate entanglement capacity. A wide two-dimensional cluster with high entanglement may be worse for DMRG than a smaller ED calculation.

What to measure, in order

Compute observables in an order that prevents advanced diagnostics from laundering a failed spectrum.

Spectrum, gap, and degeneracy. For each size and boundary condition, obtain several lowest states.

Define \(\Delta\) as the separation between the candidate ground-state manifold and the first excitation, and \(\delta\) as the splitting within that manifold. Track both with linear size.

A small \(\delta\) at one size may be accidental.

Local indistinguishability and perturbation response. Compare local expectation values and reduced density matrices across candidate ground states.

Add each realistic local perturbation separately and in sampled combinations. Track \(\Delta\), \(\delta\), sector mixing, leakage, and observable drift.

The phase claim fails if a generic weak local term distinguishes or mixes the supposed sectors at a scale incompatible with the architecture’s kill criteria.

Entanglement entropy. For a region \(A\), compute

\[ S(A)=-\operatorname{Tr}[\rho_A\log\rho_A], \]

where \(\rho_A\) is its reduced density matrix. Converge the Schmidt spectrum, not only the reported scalar entropy.

Topological entanglement entropy. Use Kitaev–Preskill or Levin–Wen subtraction geometries to cancel boundary contributions [R254]; [R255].

Regions must be large relative to the correlation length and small relative to the whole system. On a tiny patch, the subtraction is a finite-size diagnostic, not a measured universal constant.

Wilson loops. Define the loop operator from the model’s actual gauge or string algebra.

Measure contractible loops of several shapes and noncontractible loops when the boundary permits them. Check scaling with perimeter or enclosed area and compare sectors.

One loop expectation value is insufficient.

Fusion. Create separated candidate excitations with open strings, combine them through alternative paths, and project onto charge sectors.

Record allowed channels, state counts, and path dependence. On a small patch this tests the intended operator algebra; it does not establish asymptotic quasiparticles.

Modular \(S\) and \(T\). Attempt these only after obtaining a resolved quasi-degenerate ground manifold on a torus or equivalent geometry.

Construct minimally entangled states, implement or infer the relevant modular transformations, fix arbitrary ground-state phases, and bootstrap uncertainty from numerical truncation. Ground-state entanglement can in principle reveal quasiparticle statistics [R256], but a poorly resolved manifold makes \(S\) and \(T\) gauge-dependent numerology.

What fails if you extract modular data from accidental degeneracy? Any nearly degenerate finite matrix admits arbitrary basis rotations. The matrices then depend on a phase convention you have not earned.

Every method has knobs

Every reported point needs more than one knob:

Method | Must vary | Must report | Invalid use |

Dense/sparse ED | basis truncation, eigensolver tolerance, symmetry sectors | residuals, number of eigenpairs, omitted levels | claiming a phase from one size | |

MPS-DMRG | bond dimension, sweeps, initial states, cylinder length/circumference | energy variance, discarded weight, sector, observable drift | treating an unconverged wide cylinder as exact | |

PEPS/iPEPS | bond dimension, environment dimension, optimizer starts, unit cell | energy/observable convergence and contraction error | reporting one bond dimension | |

Open-system QuTiP | local basis, time step/solver tolerance, collapse operators | trace preservation, positivity checks, parameter provenance | scaling to a many-body patch by dense matrices | |

Monte Carlo | size, temperature, sampling length, autocorrelation | sign, effective sample size, finite-size scaling | ignoring a sign problem | |

For DMRG, use multiple initial states and explicit sector constraints; a variational optimizer may repeatedly find the easiest sector rather than the full ground manifold. For PEPS, vary both state bond dimension and contraction environment dimension.

For every method, compare at least one overlapping size against ED. Agreement in the overlap is the handoff certificate.

One PEPS run is not convergence. Bond dimension, environment dimension, unit cell, and initial state all need variation [R252]; [R253]. Low energy alone does not certify the correct sector.

The run book

The following run book is executable at the level a research repository should implement. It specifies calculations and data products. It asserts no numerical outcome.

Run A — pair audit. Load the parameter record; construct the full two-defect matrix; diagonalize it densely; export sorted eigenvalues, eigenvectors, operator matrix elements, residuals, and parameter derivatives.

Repeat over the fabrication-uncertainty ensemble. Cross-check the toy-to-full-model transition by adding omitted local levels.

Decision A. Pass only if a connected robust parameter region survives Stop rule 1. Freeze the retained microscopic basis; do not retune it later to improve the plaquette.

Run B — cluster projection. Assemble the complete intra-cluster Hamiltonian.

Compute enough low states to include the candidate doublet and leakage multiplets. Export \(P\), \(P^\dagger O_iP\) for every drive, noise, readout, and coupling operator \(O_i\), plus uncertainty samples.

Couple two clusters and export the exact-versus-effective spectral error.

Decision B. Pass only if Stop rule 2 is avoided and the error fits the predeclared projection budget.

Run C — plaquette decomposition. Build three-, four-, five-, and six-cluster candidates only when their geometry is physically placeable.

Diagonalize both encoded and leakage-aware Hamiltonians. Export all Pauli-string coefficients, low spectra, leakage weights, and perturbation sweeps.

Rank designs by a vector of target strength, unwanted-term norm, robustness, and fabrication cost; do not hide tradeoffs in one hand-tuned score.

Decision C. Choose at most one primary and one fallback plaquette. If none passes Stop rule 3, terminate the topological-patch branch and report the best lower-level result.

Run D — ED patch. Tile the chosen plaquette into the smallest open patch, cylinder, and periodic cluster that each answer a distinct question.

Export the low-energy manifold, \(\Delta\), \(\delta\), local reduced states, Wilson loops, excitation and fusion tests, and perturbation response. Repeat for every ED-accessible size and boundary.

Decision D. Continue only if the trends are compatible with a stable gap, decreasing sector splitting, and local indistinguishability. A single favorable size is “unresolved,” not “pass.”

Run E — size extension. If geometry is cylindrical, reproduce the largest ED point with ITensor or TeNPy DMRG, then increase length, circumference, and bond dimension [R035]; [R250]; [R251].

If genuinely two-dimensional scaling is essential, reproduce an ED point with finite PEPS before enlarging the patch [R252]; [R253]. Compute entanglement and Wilson diagnostics first.

Attempt modular matrices only after the ground-manifold prerequisites are met [R256].

Decision E. Label the result positive, negative, or numerically unresolved. Failure to converge is not evidence for the phase and not evidence against it. It is evidence that this calculation did not decide.

Preserve inputs, package versions, random seeds, symmetry sectors, solver logs, and immutable outputs. Label direct microscopic ED, projected ED, and tensor-network approximations separately.

Move a stop rule after seeing results and you have renamed calibration as goalpost relocation. Thresholds may be revised when new experimental evidence changes the input contract. They may not be revised merely because the favorite model missed them.

What the laboratory actually has

The simulation begins from laboratory-conditioned parameters, not symbols selected for convenience. Defect positions are distributed, orientations may be discrete, charge states can change, couplings have sample conditions, and coherence data depend on temperature and pulse sequence.

[Experiment] supplies distributions and bounds: spectra, linewidths, placement statistics, coupling measurements, control matrix elements, and noise correlations.

[Theory] supplies the microscopic Hamiltonian, projection, perturbative expansion, and ideal phase diagnostics.

[Numerics] supplies finite-system spectra, fitted effective operators, wavefunctions, response curves, and controlled extrapolations.

A numerical phase in a Hamiltonian outside experimental uncertainty is a result about that Hamiltonian. It is not evidence that the defect platform realizes the phase.

Conversely, a failed toy Hamiltonian does not rule out every defect architecture; it rules out the declared model and parameter domain. Scope is part of the result.

Before any open-system simulation, first prove that the closed-system Hamiltonian has the desired low-energy structure. Lindblad evolution of a model with no topological sector can calculate decay very accurately. It cannot decay into topology.

Ways to get this wrong

Starting with the largest patch. This hides whether failure came from the defect model, cluster truncation, gadget, boundary, or solver. The staged overlaps are not bureaucracy; they locate the broken arrow.

Using DMRG because the system is “large.” DMRG is a matrix-product variational method, strongest for one-dimensional and quasi-one-dimensional geometries [R035]. A wide two-dimensional cluster with high entanglement may be worse for DMRG than a smaller ED calculation. Method names do not allocate entanglement capacity.

Calling one PEPS run convergence. PEPS optimization and contraction are approximate. Bond dimension, environment dimension, unit cell, and initial state all need variation [R252]; [R253]. Low energy alone does not certify the correct sector.

Measuring topological entropy too early. The subtraction formulas assume a scale separation among lattice spacing, correlation length, region size, and system size [R254]; [R255]. A tiny-patch value can be suggestive but not asymptotic evidence.

Extracting modular data from accidental degeneracy. Any nearly degenerate finite matrix admits arbitrary basis rotations. Modular matrices become meaningful only after the candidate ground manifold, topology, symmetry action, and phase conventions are controlled [R256].

Confusing fitted and emergent interactions. If a target plaquette term is manually inserted, the simulation tests that term.

If it is derived from two-body defect couplings and validated against leakage-aware ED, the simulation tests emergence. Plot these as different models.

Discarding negative uncertainty samples. A design that works only at nominal couplings but fails across measured placement or strain distributions has failed its engineering objective. Sampling uncertainty is part of the Hamiltonian study, not cosmetic error bars.

Moving stop rules after seeing results. Thresholds may be revised when new experimental evidence changes the input contract.

They may not be revised merely because the favorite model missed them. That maneuver is called calibration when done before the run and goalpost relocation when done after it.

Check yourself

Why begin with two defects rather than a topological patch?

Because the pair cheaply tests the microscopic interaction, basis, and uncertainty range on which every later projection depends.

Show that Pauli-string coefficients on \(n\) leftovers are \(c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}=2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\boldsymbol\alpha}^\dagger H_{\rm fit})\).

Pauli strings are orthogonal under the trace inner product, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(I)=2^n\). The factor \(2^{-n}\) is the inner-product normalization, not a fitting choice. The expansion exists to reveal unwanted terms, not to report only \(K\).

What fails if you start with the largest patch?

Failure cannot be located. The defect model, cluster truncation, gadget, boundary, and solver are then one lump. The staged overlaps exist to name the broken arrow.

Show that one complex state vector on \(N\) encoded spins occupies \(16\times 2^N\) bytes if each entry is 16 bytes, and say what that decides.

There are \(2^N\) amplitudes. Storage is \(16\times 2^N\) bytes before the solver’s extra vectors. Do this estimate before choosing ED.

When is DMRG appropriate?

For one-dimensional or quasi-one-dimensional matrix-product-friendly geometries, with convergence in bond dimension, sweeps, sector, and cylinder dimensions.

What fails if modular \(S\) and \(T\) are extracted from accidental degeneracy?

The matrices become gauge-dependent numerology. A resolved quasi-degenerate ground manifold on suitable geometry, controlled truncation, minimally entangled states, and fixed basis phases must come first.

You now have a versioned parameter record, a pair spectrum, a projector you can defend, a plaquette you can refuse, and three allowed answers at every door. The last gate you actually passed is the result. The most ambitious calculation you attempted is not.

Chapter 41 — The grade

Here is the grade. No ceremony.

The full idea — a crystal packed with defect clusters that become a doubled-Fibonacci phase and quietly protect a logical qubit — is speculation. Coherent speculation: nothing in it breaks a known law.

It is not established. It is not a straightforward extension of a device anyone already builds.

It is not yet a credible proposal, the kind of difficult program you fund because the missing pieces are listed and the first measurement can say no. The interaction that would have to exist and the geometry that would have to be made have not been shown together.

It is also not incompatible. Incompatible would be cleaner.

You could close the notebook.

The nearest honest job is smaller than the dream. Four triangles.

Twelve spins. One question: can the pair interactions we already know how to write generate a useful four-body term, or do the ordinary pair terms simply win?

The first link that is not automatic

The architecture is a chain of arrows:

defects -> cluster doublet -> interacting encoded spins
-> many-body projector -> topological phase -> useful logical qubit

Testing the last arrow first is expensive and muddy. A failed large device can blame fabrication, initialization, control, readout, or the phase itself. The better experiment is a tensile test: isolate the first nontrivial link that ordinary pair interactions do not automatically provide.

A three-defect cluster can form a two-state low-energy manifold in a controlled model. That result is interesting.

It is not topological. Projecting a physical pair interaction into two cluster doublets normally produces another pair interaction.

A toric-code stabilizer needs a product acting on four encoded spins. A doubled-Fibonacci plaquette is more demanding still, because its amplitudes must implement particular recoupling data [R175]; [R018]; [R030].

So the first paper asks a smaller question: is a four-cluster plaquette term generated at a useful scale, with a tolerable list of unwanted operators?

This is deliberately not a Fibonacci paper. A negative answer would prevent years of polishing a Hamiltonian that never existed. A positive answer would earn — not assume — the right to study a patch.

Drop that order and a failed headline cannot say which arrow broke.

Four triangles, twelve spins

Use negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy centers, NV\(^-\), in diamond, because their spin Hamiltonian and coherent control are unusually well characterized [R074]. Make four nominal clusters, labeled \(C=1,2,3,4\).

Each cluster contains three same-orientation NV electron spins arranged as a triangle. Keep the physical levels \(|0\rangle=|m_s=0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle=|m_s=-1\rangle\).

The omitted \(m_s=+1\) level remains a leakage state.

For a symmetric, resonantly dressed triangle, define Pauli operators \(\tau_i^\alpha\) on physical defect \(i\), where \(\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}\). A useful ideal cluster Hamiltonian is

\[ \frac{H_C}{h}=\frac{c}{4}\sum_{i<j\in C} \left(\tau_i^z\tau_j^z-\tau_i^x\tau_j^x-\tau_i^y\tau_j^y\right), \tag{41.1} \]

where \(h\) is Planck’s constant and \(c\) is the intracluster dipolar frequency. Its low states are

\[ |W_1\rangle=\frac{|100\rangle+|010\rangle+|001\rangle}{\sqrt3},\qquad |W_2\rangle=\frac{|011\rangle+|101\rangle+|110\rangle}{\sqrt3}, \]

separated from the nearest ideal cluster states by \(\Delta_C/h=3c/2\). Call this pair an encoded leftover, with encoded Pauli operators \(X_C,Y_C,Z_C\). The two states are a qubit written on three defects, not an anyon.

Place the four triangles on a loop and include every physical dipolar bond, not only the bonds a diagram finds agreeable. Twelve two-level defects give dimension \(2^{12}=4096\), small enough for exact diagonalization.

A full spin-1 cross-check has dimension \(3^{12}=531{,}441\), still reachable with sparse methods for a few low-energy states. These dimensions are exact counts, not performance forecasts.

The target observable is one encoded weight-four coefficient, for example

\[ K_4 Z_1Z_2Z_3Z_4, \]

where each \(Z_C\) acts on one cluster doublet and \(K_4\) has units of frequency. A single weight-four term does not establish topological order. It establishes only that the proposed microscopic mechanism can cross the pairwise-to-many-body bottleneck.

Hence four encoded spins are the smallest system that can expose a weight-four coefficient and every lower-weight competitor. Three clusters cannot ask the question.

What the first paper may assume

A defensible title is:

Can dipolar NV triangles generate a useful encoded plaquette interaction? A four-cluster microscopic benchmark.

The paper should report success or failure with equal enthusiasm. It should not contain “Fibonacci phase” in the title, because neither a branching constraint nor a Fibonacci plaquette has yet been derived.

Declare the assumptions before anyone fits a number.

  • Host and charge state. Use same-axis NV\(^-\) electron spins in isotopically enriched diamond. Include the measured zero-field, Zeeman, strain/electric, hyperfine, drive, and magnetic dipole terms summarized by the established NV Hamiltonian [R074].

  • Geometry. Use nominal equilateral three-NV clusters with intracluster side \(r_C\) and a four-cluster loop with separation \(R\). Treat both as variables and sample position errors. Do not present \(r_C=5\,\mathrm{nm}\) as fabricated fact.

  • No borrowed exchange. Set long-range, lithographically tunable NV–NV exchange to zero unless a separate microscopic calculation or measurement supplies it. Dipolar coupling and microwave control are the supported resources. Entanglement through direct dipolar coupling between two NV electron spins has been demonstrated [Experiment] [R080].

  • Driven status. Equation (41.1) is a rotating-frame model sustained by a microwave reference. It is an analog driven emulator, not a passive equilibrium ground-state Hamiltonian.

  • Nuclei and disorder. Either include the nitrogen and selected \(^{13}\)C nuclear spins explicitly or fix their states and state the preparation assumption. Sample detuning, strain, angular, amplitude, and position disorder separately so their effects remain diagnosable.

  • No post-selection of the answer. Fix the cluster basis from isolated-cluster spectroscopy. If local basis rotations are optimized, constrain them to calibrated single-cluster controls and report the unrotated ledger too.

  • Two protocols, two labels. Analyze (a) continuous static-in-the-rotating-frame couplings and (b) a predeclared periodic refocusing sequence. Call the second result Floquet engineering, not passive protection.

Fabrication evidence does not yet satisfy these assumptions simultaneously. Nanoaperture work localized implanted NV clusters on roughly the 10-nm scale and reported separations down to about 40 nm [Experiment] [R257].

A deterministic single-ion source later demonstrated a \(5\times5\) pattern at \(2\,\mu\mathrm m\) pitch, with \(121(35)\,\mathrm{nm}\) lateral resolution and about \(0.6\%\) NV conversion in that shallow-implantation experiment [Experiment] [R258].

These are valuable but different achievements: localization, exact ion count, conversion, charge stability, orientation, and coherent yield have not been demonstrated together for repeated 5-nm triangles.

What fails if a different encoded basis is chosen for every disorder sample? A large-looking target coefficient that no fixed control realizes. That is optimization of the conclusion.

The Hamiltonian you actually write

The calculation should begin from physical spin-1 operators \(\mathbf S_i\), not from the hoped-for stabilizer. Write

\[ \begin{aligned} H(t)=&\sum_i\Big[D_i(S_i^z)^2+g_e\mu_B\mathbf B_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_i +H_{\mathrm{hf},i}+H_{\mathrm{strain},i}+H_{\mathrm{drive},i}(t)\Big]\\ &+\sum_{i<j}\frac{\mu_0(g_e\mu_B)^2}{4\pi r_{ij}^3} \left[\mathbf S_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_j -3(\mathbf S_i\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij})(\mathbf S_j\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij})\right]. \end{aligned} \tag{41.2} \]

Here \(D_i\) is the zero-field splitting energy, \(g_e\) is the electron \(g\) factor, \(\mu_B\) is the Bohr magneton, \(\mu_0\) is vacuum permeability, \(\mathbf r_{ij}=r_{ij}\hat{\mathbf r}_{ij}\) joins defects \(i\) and \(j\), and the three named \(H\) terms describe hyperfine, strain/electric, and microwave interactions. Every term has units of joules. The NV\(^-\) ground-state value \(D/h\approx2.87\,\mathrm{GHz}\) and its spin Hamiltonian are experimentally established [R074].

After transforming to the declared rotating frame and checking the rotating-wave approximation against the full model, project onto the four cluster doublets. Let \(P\) be that \(2^4\)-dimensional projector and \(Q=I-P\). A Schrieffer–Wolff calculation yields an effective Hamiltonian, while exact low-energy eigenvectors provide a nonperturbative comparison. Expand the result in the complete encoded Pauli basis:

\[ \frac{H_{\mathrm{eff}}}{h}=\sum_{P_a\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes4}}k_aP_a, \qquad k_a=\frac1{16}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(P_a\frac{H_{\mathrm{eff}}}{h}\right). \tag{41.3} \]

The coefficient \(k_{ZZZZ}\) is \(K_4\). All other \(k_a\) are competitors, not rounding errors. Perturbative gadgets can generate many-body interactions from two-body resources, but desired terms arrive with energy denominators and with unwanted corrections [Theory] [R175].

An illustrative scale check shows why the ledger matters. Electron dipoles have a frequency scale near \(52\,\mathrm{MHz}(1\,\mathrm{nm}/r)^3\).

At the proposed, not demonstrated, values \(r_C=5\,\mathrm{nm}\) and \(R=10\,\mathrm{nm}\), this gives \(c\approx0.416\,\mathrm{MHz}\), \(\Delta_C/h\approx0.624\,\mathrm{MHz}\), and an unprojected intercluster scale \(u\lesssim52\,\mathrm{kHz}\) before geometry factors.

Those bare coefficients, about 416 kHz inside a triangle and 52 kHz between triangles, are inputs. They are not the much smaller plaquette scale generated later.

If the first surviving connected ring process is fourth order, dimensional analysis gives

\[ K_4\sim\frac{u^4}{(\Delta_C/h)^3}\sim 30\,\mathrm{Hz}. \tag{41.4} \]

The units are \(\mathrm{Hz}^4/\mathrm{Hz}^3=\mathrm{Hz}\). The coefficient and even the leading order depend on symmetry and pulse design, so \(30\,\mathrm{Hz}\) is [Proposal] scale analysis, not a prediction.

Its temperature equivalent is \(hK_4/k_B\approx1.4\,\mathrm{nK}\), where \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant. A passive phase at that scale would be implausible.

A driven spectroscopic signal might still be measurable if coherence, calibration, and averaging allow it. The computation decides whether lower-order constructive routes exist or whether larger pair terms simply win.

No demonstrated process repeatedly produces charge-stable, coherent 5-nm NV triangles with acceptable compound yield. Linewidth, disorder, temperature, and perturbative suppression have to be carried together.

The geometry and distributions above remain explicit study parameters. They sit inside the book’s screening ranges.

They are not demonstrated fabrication resources.

Hence \(K_4\neq0\) is a mechanism check. It is not a phase.

Six calculations, then stop if you must

The paper can be completed without fabricating twelve precisely placed NV centers.

  • Calibrate one cluster. Diagonalize the full \(3^3\) spin-1 Hamiltonian over magnetic field, drive, strain, hyperfine state, and triangular distortion. Record the doublet splitting, gap \(\Delta_C\), leakage matrix elements, and projected single-spin operators.

  • Audit two clusters. Diagonalize six spins and compare exact low energies with first- and second-order Schrieffer–Wolff results. This fixes the regime where an encoded Hamiltonian is controlled and reveals the dominant one- and two-cluster Pauli terms.

  • Fit four clusters. Use exact diagonalization of the 4096-state physical-qubit model, with selected full-spin-1 cross-checks. Construct \(H_{\mathrm{eff}}\) by a specified quasi-degenerate projection, expand all 256 encoded Pauli strings using (41.3), and publish the full coefficient table.

  • Test the drive honestly. For a periodic sequence of duration \(T_d\), compute the one-period propagator \(U(T_d)\) and its quasienergies. Track micromotion, leakage, sensitivity to pulse errors, and the branch choice in \(H_F=(i\hbar/T_d)\log U(T_d)\). Do not interpret a quasienergy gap as a thermal gap.

  • Sample fabrication distributions. Vary each defect position, orientation, detuning, strain, and drive amplitude. Report medians, tails, failure fractions, and correlations rather than one immaculate geometry.

  • Attempt a patch only after the gate passes. If a dominant, robust \(K_4\) exists, place the fitted operators on the smallest periodic stabilizer patch and compute spectrum, low-energy degeneracy, Wilson loops, and response to local perturbations. If the isolated plaquette fails, stop. A topological diagnostic cannot rescue a missing interaction.

Define

\[ R_4=\frac{|K_4|}{\sum_{a\in\mathcal U}|k_a|}, \]

where \(\mathcal U\) is the predeclared set of symmetry-allowed, noncommuting unwanted terms after removing calibratable one-cluster fields. Also define \(\epsilon_{\rm spec}\) as the maximum error of the effective model’s sixteen low energies, divided by \(|hK_4|\), and \(p_{\rm leak}\) as the largest \(Q\)-space weight among those states.

A minimum theoretical success is: \(R_4>1\), \(\epsilon_{\rm spec}<0.1\), \(p_{\rm leak}<0.01\), and the inequalities remain true across a declared fabrication distribution. A promising result is \(R_4>10\) plus \(|K_4|\) larger than independently measured logical decoherence and quasistatic disorder rates. The values 1, 0.1, 0.01, and 10 are project decision thresholds, not universal constants.

Stop or redesign when any of the following occurs:

  • no isolated cluster doublet survives realistic hyperfine and geometric disorder;

  • eliminating leakage requires \(u/\Delta_C\) so small that \(K_4\) falls below relevant linewidths;

  • lower-weight noncommuting terms remain larger than \(K_4\) after physically allowed calibration;

  • a refocusing sequence works only with pulse errors below demonstrated control capability;

  • the fitted patch lacks a stable gap or the expected topological-sector structure;

  • success depends on exchange, mediators, placement, or cooling not included in the declared platform.

The numerical paper is difficult but tractable. The Hilbert spaces are modest.

The real work is gauge-consistent low-energy projection, disorder sampling, and refusing post hoc cancellations. A two-person theory effort could reproduce it from public Hamiltonian parameters without a new fabrication line.

The physical twelve-defect demonstration is substantially harder. It combines nanometre geometry, same-axis and charge-state yield, nuclear-state preparation, individual or patterned microwave phases, spectral discrimination, and long enough coherence.

Existing experiments establish important pieces, not their conjunction [R074]; [R080]; [R257]; [R258]. A doubled-Fibonacci material would add correct vertex constraints, conditional recoupling amplitudes, a many-body gap, and phase diagnostics [R018].

That is not the next experiment.

If the four-cluster ledger fails, identify whether geometry, a mediator, or another host changes the scaling before adding system size. If it passes, the physical sequence is one triangle for spectroscopy, then two coupled triangles, and only then the twelve-defect plaquette.

A larger topological patch is justified only after the desired term dominates. A Fibonacci claim waits until branching constraints, recoupling amplitudes, a stable gap, and non-Abelian diagnostics are all present.

A Floquet quasienergy gap depends on a clock, drive stability, and continued power. It does not thermalize like a static ground-state gap. Call it passive protection and the claim has changed.

What the laboratory actually has

Claim | Status | Platform | Evidence | Reference | |

Single NV spin Hamiltonian, initialization, readout, and microwave control are understood | experimentally demonstrated | Diamond NV\(^-\) | Extensive spectroscopy and control literature | [R074] | |

Two separated NV electron spins can be entangled through their interaction | experimentally demonstrated | Diamond NV\(^-\) | Room-temperature two-spin entanglement experiment | [R080] | |

Nanometre-localized implanted NV clusters exist | experimentally partial | Diamond NV\(^-\) | Nanoaperture localization; not repeated deterministic 5-nm triangles | [R257] | |

Joint exact ion delivery, NV conversion, and nanoscale coherent-array yield | experimentally partial | Diamond NV\(^-\) | Individual fabrication ingredients exist, but the deterministic-delivery experiment retained coarse focus and low conversion under its stated conditions | [R257]; [R258] | |

Two-body interactions can perturbatively produce encoded many-body terms | theoretically established | Abstract spin gadgets | Controlled expansions with denominators and error bounds | [R175] | |

The required Fibonacci string-net projectors define doubled-Fibonacci order | theoretically established | Ideal lattice model | Exact commuting-projector construction | [R018] | |

Digital processors can prepare and braid Fibonacci-model excitations | experimentally demonstrated | Superconducting processors | State preparation, fusion, and digital braiding simulate the target model; they do not establish an autonomous material phase | [R138]; [R165] | |

A defect lattice could host genuine Fibonacci quasiparticles | speculative | Diamond, sapphire, SiC, others | The cited literature establishes defect qubits, ideal models, and digital simulations, but no defect-material realization | [R074]; [R018]; [R138]; [R165] | |

Ruby supplies some control ingredients relevant to defect clusters | experimentally partial | Cr\(^{3+}\):Al\(_2\)O\(_3\) | Ensemble spin–cavity coupling has been measured; deterministic single-ion arrays have not | [R089] | |

Ways to get this wrong

  • Optimizing away the conclusion. Choosing a different encoded basis for every disorder sample can manufacture a large-looking target coefficient that no fixed control realizes.

  • Calling \(K_4\neq0\) a phase. One local term is a mechanism check. Topological order requires a thermodynamic phase or convincing finite-size scaling with the right degeneracy and nonlocal diagnostics.

  • Calling Floquet quasienergy passive protection. A driven frame depends on a clock, drive stability, and continued power. It does not thermalize like a static ground-state gap.

  • Comparing placement records from incompatible processes. Beam focus, implantation straggle, conversion yield, charge yield, and coherent yield are separate columns.

  • Using digital Fibonacci demonstrations as material evidence. Experiments have digitally prepared and braided Fibonacci-model anyons [Experiment] [R138]; [R165]. They establish control protocols and model behavior, not native Fibonacci quasiparticles in the processor substrate.

  • Hiding the denominator. A high-order gadget can be mathematically correct and physically useless because its desired coefficient shrinks faster than decoherence and disorder.

Fifteen questions

  1. Can multiple defects act as one effective qubit? Yes, in theory and in controlled few-spin encodings, provided a two-dimensional manifold is spectrally isolated and controls and readout act predictably within it. For the specific three-NV triangle, the ideal driven model supplies a doublet; fabrication and disorder robustness remain unproved. Verdict: plausible, platform-specific, not yet an array fact.

  2. Can multiple effective defect qubits emulate anyons? Yes. Gates or driven interactions can reproduce string operators, fusion measurements, and braiding statistics. That is an emulator whose underlying errors remain those of the defect controls.

  3. Can defect systems digitally simulate Fibonacci anyons? In principle, yes if they provide a universal enough gate set, initialization, and readout. Superconducting processors have already demonstrated digital Fibonacci-model braiding [R138]; [R165], so no known principle excludes a defect processor. The missing evidence is competitive defect-array scale and fidelity, not the algorithm.

  4. Could a static or driven defect Hamiltonian genuinely possess Fibonacci topological order? Known physics permits it, but the cited defect interactions do not derive it. A static realization needs the correct low-energy projectors and a stable gap; a driven realization additionally needs Floquet stability and controlled heating. Current status: speculative.

  5. What is the difference between simulating an anyon and having an emergent anyon? Simulation programs physical qubits to reproduce selected anyon observables. Emergence means the system’s own many-body low-energy excitations carry the fusion and braiding structure robustly throughout a phase. Exact output from a circuit can still lack autonomous Hamiltonian protection.

  6. Would clustering defects provide meaningful additional protection? Sometimes. A symmetric encoding can reject a common-mode field or reduce a chosen matrix element, but it can amplify gradients, add leakage, and multiply fabrication channels. Protection must be computed from projected noise operators, not inferred from defect count.

  7. Is diamond actually the best substrate? Not categorically. Diamond currently offers the strongest evidence package for optically addressable individual color-center spins, but it is difficult to place and activate dense, identical interacting arrays. “Best” depends on whether the limiting metric is coherence, deterministic fabrication, coupling, optical networking, or passive interaction strength.

  8. Is corundum/sapphire competitive? As a low-loss host with mature ensemble spin spectroscopy, potentially; as the specific dense, individually controlled defect-cluster platform studied here, the evidence is weaker. The 2025 ruby result demonstrates Cr\(^{3+}\) ensemble–cavity physics, not deterministic single-defect plaquettes [R089]. Sapphire should remain a comparison arm, not be promoted by analogy.

  9. What physical interaction is the biggest bottleneck? A strong, controllable, correctly signed many-body encoded interaction that dominates ordinary one- and two-body terms. Dipolar coupling exists; the missing step is converting it into the required projector without suppressing the target below noise.

  10. What fabrication capability is the biggest bottleneck? Repeated three-dimensional placement and activation of the correct defect species, orientation, charge state, and local environment at the interaction length scale, with high coherent yield. Deterministic ion arrival alone is insufficient [R257]; [R258].

  11. What energy scales would be required? The hierarchy must satisfy

\[ \frac{\Delta_C}{h}\gg u,\Omega,\sigma,\Gamma_{\rm decoh}, \qquad \frac{\Delta_{\rm topo}}{h}\gg \frac{k_BT}{h},\Gamma_{\rm decoh},\sigma_{\rm eff}, \]

where the quantities compared are frequencies. Here \(u\) is intercluster coupling, \(\Omega\) a drive scale, \(\sigma\) disorder, \(\Gamma_{\rm decoh}\) a decoherence rate, \(\Delta_C/h\) the cluster-gap frequency, and \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/h\) the many-body-gap frequency.

The illustrative NV geometry gives sub-megahertz cluster scales and may yield only hertz-scale high-order terms. Those numbers are a warning to calculate, not a device requirement.

  1. At what temperature would such a system probably need to operate? There is no honest temperature before there is a measured gap. A passive target needs \(k_BT\) comfortably below the energy \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\); choosing a tenfold Boltzmann margin gives \(T<\Delta_{\rm topo}/(10k_B)\). Thus \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/h=1\,\mathrm{MHz}\) implies \(T<4.8\,\mu\mathrm K\), while \(\Delta_{\rm topo}/h=1\,\mathrm{GHz}\) implies \(T<4.8\,\mathrm{mK}\). These are design inequalities, not forecasts, and a driven quasienergy gap does not satisfy them automatically.

  2. How many physical defects might be needed per effective degree of freedom? Three in the scoped triangle model. More elaborate symmetry, leakage suppression, or gadget mediators could raise that count substantially. No evidence presently identifies an optimum, so a universal “5–20” estimate would be decoration rather than calculation.

  3. What is the smallest experiment capable of falsifying the idea? Spectroscopy of one fabricated three-NV triangle can falsify the assumed cluster doublet. To falsify the many-body mechanism, the smallest decisive physical device is four such clusters — twelve defects — because it can extract a weight-four coefficient and its competitors. The four-cluster numerical experiment should come first and can already falsify the Hamiltonian mechanism.

  4. What result would make this direction genuinely promising? A reproducible cluster doublet followed by a measured or microscopically validated many-body coefficient that dominates noncommuting residual terms, exceeds disorder and decoherence, survives realistic position distributions, and produces the expected gap and nonlocal diagnostics on a larger patch. A visually plausible lattice or a digitally scripted braid is not enough.

How sure we can be

Proposition | Confidence | Explanation | |

Defect clusters can form encoded leftovers | Medium | Few-spin encoding is standard theory and the ideal NV triangle is solvable, but the specified symmetric cluster array is not demonstrated. | |

Dense interacting defect arrays are manufacturable | Low | Placement, conversion, charge, orientation, and coherent yield have not been combined at the required repeated nanometre geometry [R257]; [R258]. | |

Effective many-body interactions can be engineered | Low | Gadget theory permits them [R175], but the desired term is suppressed by denominators and competes with larger native terms in this platform. | |

Toric-code-like phases are plausible | Medium | They require simpler Abelian stabilizer data than Fibonacci order and can be digitally or Floquet emulated; a passive defect realization remains unshown. | |

Non-Abelian phases are plausible | Low | No derived defect Hamiltonian, gap, or phase diagram supports one here. Digital non-Abelian behavior does not raise the material rating. | |

Doubled-Fibonacci phase is physically realistic | Low | The ideal target is established [R018], but its branching and recoupling projectors have no supported microscopic defect derivation. | |

Passive topological protection improves coherence | Low | Conditional theory is sound, but this architecture has neither a demonstrated passive topological gap nor evidence that thermal and leakage errors lie below it. | |

Diamond is superior to competing platforms | Low | Diamond leads on several single-defect capabilities, not on every system metric; fabrication and coupling may favor another host or a hybrid platform. | |

The five ranks, used once more so the words stay honest:

  • established — measured or derived in the relevant system.

  • extension — a straightforward next device, using existing technology.

  • proposal — a credible but difficult research program, with a first measurement that can fail.

  • speculation — physically coherent, but the indispensable pieces are unshown.

  • incompatible — in conflict with known physics.

For the complete proposal — dense defect clusters producing a genuinely topologically ordered, potentially doubled-Fibonacci material and a passively improved logical qubit — the only justified classification is

\[ \boxed{\textbf{highly speculative but physically coherent}}. \]

It is not incompatible with known physics: local Hamiltonians with doubled-Fibonacci order exist, effective interactions can arise perturbatively, and defect spins can be controlled. It is not yet a credible but difficult research program at the full architecture level, because the central microscopic interaction and manufacturable geometry have not been demonstrated or even numerically validated together. The scoped four-cluster paper is a proposal in the narrower sense: it is credible precisely because it can return “no” and still succeed scientifically.

The nearest fallback

The nearest fallback is a digitally controlled defect-spin network with active error correction, using single defects or small clusters only where they improve a measured control or noise metric. It would prepare stabilizer or small string-net states with gates, measure syndromes, and treat anyon operations as quantum simulation. Optical links or a cavity may connect sparse modules, relaxing the demand for a perfect dense crystal lattice.

This fallback gives up autonomous Fibonacci topological order and passive self-protection. It retains useful defect coherence, local memories, distributed entanglement, active logical encoding, and a platform for studying anyon protocols.

If dense NV fabrication fails, SiC defects, donors, rare-earth ions, trapped ions, neutral atoms, or superconducting circuits should compete on the same measured ledger rather than on substrate loyalty. Digital Fibonacci experiments already show that scientifically meaningful anyon work does not require claiming a native Fibonacci material [R138]; [R165].

Keep digital simulation, driven emulation, and equilibrium emergence in separate columns. Mixing those columns is how a grade inflates.

Check yourself

Why is a four-cluster calculation the first paper?

Because four encoded spins are the smallest system that can expose a weight-four plaquette coefficient and every lower-weight competitor.

Show that the ideal triangle (41.1) has gap \(\Delta_C/h=3c/2\), and that a fourth-order \(K_4\) at the proposed 5 nm / 10 nm geometry is about \(30\,\mathrm{Hz}\).

The isolated-cluster splitting of (41.1) is \(3c/2\). With \(c\approx0.416\) MHz one has \(\Delta_C/h\approx0.624\) MHz and \(u\lesssim52\) kHz, so \(K_4\sim u^4/(\Delta_C/h)^3\sim30\) Hz, or \(hK_4/k_B\approx1.4\) nK. That is a warning to compute, not a measured coupling.

What fails if \(K_4\neq0\) is treated as a phase?

One local term is a mechanism check. Dominance, robustness, a gapped phase, and topological diagnostics remain separate tests. A nonzero coefficient does not establish topological order.

Why not begin with doubled Fibonacci?

Its vertex and recoupling projectors require more structure than the proposed microscopic Hamiltonian has earned. The simpler stabilizer bottleneck can falsify the route first.

What fails if a different encoded basis is chosen for every disorder sample?

A large-looking target coefficient that no fixed control realizes. The cluster basis must be fixed from isolated-cluster spectroscopy, or constrained to calibrated single-cluster controls, with the unrotated ledger reported too.

What is the honest fallback?

Use defects as controllable physical or cluster-encoded qubits in an actively corrected digital architecture, and call anyon experiments simulations unless the hardware Hamiltonian itself produces the phase.

Mathematical appendices

Tool drawers. Open one when a chapter points at it.

Appendix A — Arrows you can add and stretch

Take a pencil and draw an arrow on a scrap of paper. Draw a second arrow.

Lay the second at the tip of the first and call the new path their sum. Stretch either by \(2\), shrink it by \(1/2\), or reverse it by multiplying by \(-1\).

High-school geometry already knows both operations.

Now let the stretch factor be a complex number. Multiplying by \(i\) rotates the arrow a quarter turn.

Multiplying by \(3+4i\) stretches it by \(5\) and turns it. The arrows still add tip to tail.

Nothing physical has been assumed. The set of allowed stretches has simply grown.

Two operations

A set of objects you can add and complex-scale — with a zero, an opposite for every object, and the rule that \(1\) times anything is itself — is a vector space. We take this as the definition.

The objects may be pencil arrows, columns of two complex numbers, or the internal states of a silver atom. The two operations are the whole structure.

Write \(\mathbb C\) for the complex numbers and \(V=\mathbb C^2\) for the space of columns of height two. Addition and scaling act entrywise.

For vectors \(u,v,w\in V\) and scalars \(a,b\in\mathbb C\), the operations associate and commute where they should, and they distribute over one another. There is no hidden geometry yet.

Coordinates are not the arrow

The ket \(|\psi\rangle\) is the abstract vector. The column you write down depends on which reusable directions you picked.

In the standard pair

\[ |0\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad |1\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}, \]

a normalized state is

\[ |\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle, \qquad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1. \]

Here \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C\), and \(|\alpha|\) is the complex modulus. Define another pair,

\[ |+\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}, \qquad |-\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle-|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}. \]

Substitution — not a new physical assumption — gives

\[ |\psi\rangle=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\sqrt2}|+\rangle +\frac{\alpha-\beta}{\sqrt2}|-\rangle. \]

The state stayed put. Only its coordinates changed. If \(U\) is the matrix whose columns are the new directions written in the old ones, the coordinate columns obey

\[ [\psi]_{\rm new}=U^\dagger[\psi]_{\rm old}. \]

The dagger \(\dagger\) will mean conjugate transpose once we have earned it. This particular \(U\) will turn out to preserve lengths, so the state stays normalized.

A finite list \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) is linearly independent when

\[ a_1v_1+\cdots+a_kv_k=0 \]

forces \(a_1=\cdots=a_k=0\). Its span is every weighted sum you can form from the list.

A basis is a linearly independent list whose span is all of \(V\). Every basis of a finite-dimensional space has the same length; that length is the dimension \(\dim V\).

A subspace \(W\subseteq V\) contains \(0\) and is closed under addition and complex scaling. The logical doublet of a defect cluster is a two-dimensional subspace of a much larger space. Calling it a subspace says nothing yet about whether the energy operator or the noise keeps a state inside it.

The direct sum \(V=W\oplus W'\) means every \(v\in V\) has one and only one split \(v=w+w'\), with \(w\in W\) and \(w'\in W'\). Projection methods write the whole space as the desired low-energy piece plus whatever is left.

Remark. Linear independence is a property of a list, not of any one arrow. Drop it and the same vector may acquire several coordinate columns in the same spanning set.

A pairing that makes length

Addition and scaling still do not know length or angle. Suppose we are given a machine that eats two vectors and returns a complex number \(\langle u|v\rangle\). We use the physics convention: conjugate-linear in the first argument and linear in the second,

\[ \langle au+bw|v\rangle=a^*\langle u|v\rangle+b^*\langle w|v\rangle, \]

\[ \langle u|av+bw\rangle=a\langle u|v\rangle+b\langle u|w\rangle. \]

It also satisfies conjugate symmetry, \(\langle u|v\rangle=\langle v|u\rangle^*\), and positive definiteness: \(\langle v|v\rangle\ge0\), with equality only for \(v=0\). The star is complex conjugation.

That pairing is an inner product. Length, angle, orthogonality, and later probability all sit inside it.

The length is \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v|v\rangle}\). Two vectors are orthogonal when their pairing vanishes. A list \(\{|e_j\rangle\}\) is orthonormal when \(\langle e_j|e_k\rangle=\delta_{jk}\), where the Kronecker delta \(\delta_{jk}\) equals one for \(j=k\) and zero otherwise.

A ket \(|v\rangle\) is a vector. Its associated bra \(\langle v|\) is the linear functional that maps \(|w\rangle\) to \(\langle v|w\rangle\). In an orthonormal coordinate basis, taking a ket column to its bra means transpose and complex-conjugate it.

For any orthonormal basis \(\{|e_j\rangle\}_{j=1}^d\),

\[ I=\sum_{j=1}^{d}|e_j\rangle\langle e_j|, \qquad |v\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{d}|e_j\rangle\langle e_j|v\rangle. \]

The first equation is the resolution of the identity. The second says that coordinates are inner products with basis vectors.

Hence, once an orthonormal basis is chosen, the abstract vector and its coordinate column determine each other.

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

\[ |\langle u|v\rangle|\le \|u\|\,\|v\|, \]

ensures that the overlap of normalized states has modulus at most one. One proof considers the nonnegative length of \(|u\rangle-z|v\rangle\) and chooses the complex number \(z\) that minimizes it. That is the algebra beneath the statement that Born probabilities lie between zero and one.

In finite dimensions, a complex vector space with a positive-definite inner product is automatically complete in the induced norm, so people also call it a Hilbert space. You do not need that second name to finish a matrix calculation. You need the pairing.

Remark. Drop positive-definiteness and you may still have a Hermitian form. You no longer have a length that vanishes only at zero, and the last step of Cauchy–Schwarz fails.

Machines that do not break addition

A map \(A:V\to W\) is linear when

\[ A(au+bv)=aA(u)+bA(v). \]

Once bases are chosen, \(A\) is a matrix. Its entry in row \(j\), column \(k\) is \(A_{jk}=\langle e_j|A|e_k\rangle\). Matrix multiplication represents composition: \((AB)|v\rangle=A(B|v\rangle)\), so the rightmost operator acts first.

The kernel \(\ker A\) contains vectors mapped to zero. The image \(\operatorname{im}A\) contains outputs \(A|v\rangle\). The rank–nullity theorem states

\[ \dim V=\dim(\ker A)+\dim(\operatorname{im}A) \]

for a linear map whose domain \(V\) is finite dimensional. Nothing is lost and nothing is invented. The missing directions go to zero; the rest span the outputs.

Asking the machine backwards

Given a linear machine \(A\), there is a unique partner \(A^\dagger\) defined by

\[ \langle u|A v\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u|v\rangle \]

for all vectors \(u,v\). In orthonormal bases its matrix is the conjugate transpose. That partner is the adjoint. Lengths, measurement averages, and time evolution all compare \(A\) with \(A^\dagger\).

Several classes recur.

  • \(A\) is Hermitian when \(A=A^\dagger\). Observables and energy operators are represented by Hermitian operators.

  • \(U\) is unitary when \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\). Unitary operators preserve inner products.

  • \(P\) is an orthogonal projector when \(P=P^\dagger=P^2\). Its image is the retained subspace.

  • \(A\) is positive semidefinite, written \(A\ge0\), when \(\langle v|A|v\rangle\ge0\) for every \(|v\rangle\).

  • \(A\) is normal when \(AA^\dagger=A^\dagger A\). Hermitian and unitary operators are normal.

The trace is the basis-independent number

\[ \operatorname{Tr}A=\sum_j\langle e_j|A|e_j\rangle. \]

It obeys cyclicity, \(\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)\), whenever the finite-dimensional products are defined. Cyclicity does not mean arbitrary reordering: generally \(\operatorname{Tr}(ABC)=\operatorname{Tr}(BCA)\), not \(\operatorname{Tr}(ACB)\).

Remark. Drop the inner product and the adjoint is not defined. You can still transpose a matrix of numbers, but that operation then depends on the basis you used to write the numbers down.

Directions the machine does not mix

A nonzero vector \(|v\rangle\) is an eigenvector of \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\in\mathbb C\) when

\[ A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle. \]

The machine only stretches that arrow. It does not knock it sideways. The eigenvalue is degenerate if its eigenspace has dimension greater than one.

Suppose \(A=A^\dagger\) and \(A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle\) with \(\|v\|=1\). Then

\[ \lambda=\langle v|A|v\rangle=\langle A v|v\rangle=\lambda^*, \]

so \(\lambda\) is real. Hence every eigenvalue of a Hermitian operator is real.

The finite-dimensional spectral theorem says that a normal operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis [R001]; [R002]. In particular, a Hermitian operator can be written

\[ A=\sum_r \lambda_r P_r, \]

where \(\lambda_r\) are its distinct real eigenvalues and \(P_r\) are mutually orthogonal projectors satisfying \(P_rP_s=\delta_{rs}P_r\) and \(\sum_rP_r=I\). Degeneracy is handled by allowing \(P_r\) to project onto a multidimensional eigenspace.

A function of \(A\) is then defined spectrally:

\[ f(A)=\sum_r f(\lambda_r)P_r. \]

For a Hamiltonian \(H\), measured in joules (J), unitary time evolution for time \(t\), measured in seconds (s), is

\[ U(t)=e^{-iHt/\hbar}=\sum_r e^{-i\lambda_rt/\hbar}P_r. \]

The exponent is dimensionless because \((\mathrm J)(\mathrm s)/(\mathrm{J\,s})=1\). Here \(\hbar\) is the reduced Planck constant.

Hence \(U(t)\) is unitary: in the spectral basis every eigenvalue becomes a phase of modulus one, so \(U(t)^\dagger U(t)=I\).

Over \(\mathbb C\), the characteristic polynomial of a finite matrix has a root, so a normal operator has at least one eigenvector. Normalize it.

Normality makes the orthogonal complement of that eigenvector invariant under both \(A\) and \(A^\dagger\). Restrict \(A\) to that smaller space and repeat.

Induction supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis. This sketch hides no physics, but a complete proof carefully establishes the invariant-complement step [R001]; [R002].

Remark. Drop normality and a finite matrix may lack an orthonormal eigenbasis.

It may even be defective: too few independent eigenvectors to span the space. The spectral formula for \(f(A)\) is then unavailable in that form.

The most general two-level energy matrix

Define the Pauli matrices

\[ \sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Every \(2\times2\) Hermitian Hamiltonian can be written

\[ H=cI+h_x\sigma_x+h_y\sigma_y+h_z\sigma_z =cI+\mathbf h\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma, \]

where \(c,h_x,h_y,h_z\in\mathbb R\) have units of J, \(\mathbf h=(h_x,h_y,h_z)\), and \(\boldsymbol\sigma=(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z)\). Define \(h=\sqrt{h_x^2+h_y^2+h_z^2}\). For \(h\ne0\), define the unit vector \(\mathbf n=\mathbf h/h\).

The Pauli multiplication rule is

\[ \sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}I+i\sum_\ell\varepsilon_{jk\ell}\sigma_\ell, \]

where \(\varepsilon_{jk\ell}\) is the antisymmetric Levi-Civita symbol. The symmetric product \(n_jn_k\) kills the antisymmetric term, so

\[ (\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2=I. \]

An operator squaring to \(I\) has eigenvalues \(\pm1\). Its projectors are

\[ P_\pm=\frac12(I\pm\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma), \]

because \(P_\pm^2=P_\pm\), \(P_+P_-=0\), and \(P_++P_-=I\). Therefore the spectral decomposition is

\[ H=(c+h)P_+ +(c-h)P_-. \]

The two energies are \(E_\pm=c\pm h\), and their separation is \(2h\). Applying a function spectrally gives

\[ \begin{aligned} e^{-iHt/\hbar} &=e^{-i(c+h)t/\hbar}P_+ +e^{-i(c-h)t/\hbar}P_-\\ &=e^{-ict/\hbar}\left[ \cos\!\left(\frac{ht}{\hbar}\right)I -i\sin\!\left(\frac{ht}{\hbar}\right)\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma \right]. \end{aligned} \]

This one result covers Zeeman precession, driven qubits in a rotating frame, and effective cluster pseudospins. At \(h=0\), the direction \(\mathbf n\) is undefined but harmless: \(H=cI\), and evolution is only a common phase.

A two-dimensional subspace is mathematically capable of representing a qubit. It is not automatically a controllable physical qubit, an error-corrected logical qubit, or a topological ground space. Those labels add dynamical and operational conditions that linear algebra alone cannot supply.

Four rewrites that are not the same

Authors may place vectors as columns without kets, use the mathematics convention in which the inner product is linear in its first argument, or set \(\hbar=1\). Check conventions before moving a complex scalar through an inner product. Also distinguish:

  • a basis change, which changes coordinates;

  • a unitary physical evolution, which changes the state relative to fixed measurement operators;

  • a similarity transformation \(A'=U^\dagger AU\), which represents the same abstract operator in a new orthonormal basis;

  • a projected operator \(PAP\), which generally discards information and is not a basis change.

For infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the spectral theorem becomes a statement about projection-valued measures. Unbounded operators also require domains: the expression \(AB\) may not be defined on every vector. The finite-dimensional matrix version is sufficient for the defect clusters and finite lattice models in this book, but continuum papers may need the stronger functional-analytic machinery [R003]; [R005].

Ways to get this wrong

  • Forgetting complex conjugation. Bras are conjugate-transposed kets; otherwise norms need not be real or positive.

  • Diagonalizing every matrix as if it were Hermitian. A non-normal matrix may lack an orthonormal eigenbasis and may even be defective.

  • Treating degeneracy as a unique basis. The eigenspace is fixed, but any orthonormal basis inside it is allowed.

  • Confusing \(PAP\) with \(A\). Projection omits coupling through the complementary subspace; perturbation theory restores some of those virtual effects.

  • Using trace cyclicity as commutativity. Operators remain order sensitive outside the cyclic trace identity.

  • Ignoring units in exponentials. \(e^{-iHt}\) silently assumes \(\hbar=1\); restore \(tH/\hbar\) before numerical work.

Check yourself

What is basis independent: a ket or its coordinate column? The ket is abstract and basis independent; its coordinate column depends on the basis.

Show that every eigenvalue of a Hermitian operator is real. If \(A=A^\dagger\) and \(A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle\) with \(\|v\|=1\), then \(\lambda=\langle v|A|v\rangle=\langle Av|v\rangle=\lambda^*\).

What extra structure turns a complex vector space into a Hilbert space in finite dimensions? A positive-definite inner product. Finite-dimensional spaces are automatically complete in the induced norm.

Show that \(e^{-iHt/\hbar}\) is unitary when \(H=H^\dagger\). In the spectral basis every eigenvalue of \(H\) is real, so every eigenvalue of the exponential is a phase of modulus one.

What fails if you drop normality? A finite matrix need not have an orthonormal eigenbasis, and the spectral formula for \(f(A)\) need not apply.

What is lost in replacing \(A\) by \(PAP\)? Matrix elements connecting the retained subspace to its complement and all action wholly within that complement.

Later chapters may use without rederivation that orthonormal bases resolve the identity; Hermitian operators possess real spectral decompositions; projectors isolate possibly degenerate subspaces; operator functions act eigenvalue by eigenvalue; unitary changes of orthonormal basis preserve inner products; and a projected two-dimensional operator is a linear combination of \(I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z\). Appendix B adds composite systems, incomplete information, and irreversible channels.
