Appendix G — Checks that never read the secret

Three coins sit on a table. They are supposed to show the same face.

You may look at whether coin 1 matches coin 2, and whether coin 2 matches coin 3. If both checks pass, all three agree.

You still do not know whether they are heads or tails.

That unknown is the secret. The checks never read it.

A general state of \(n\) qubits needs \(2^n\) complex amplitudes. Some important states can be named the way those coins were named: by a short list of agreement rules, not by writing every amplitude. “All three bits agree” is shorter than listing eight strings and setting six of them to zero.

An operator that leaves the good states alone

Suppose a state \(|\psi\rangle\) is already one of the allowed ones. There is an operator \(S\) that does nothing to it:

\[ S|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle. \]

The operator leaves the state fixed. That is a stabilizer. The good states are the ones this check has already passed: the answer is \(+1\), as if the coins already matched.

A stabilizer code is the common \(+1\) eigenspace of a commuting set of Pauli operators. The compression is what makes error correction, the toric code, and efficient classical simulation of Clifford circuits possible [R028]; [R031].

It does not efficiently describe every quantum state or every gate. Magic remains expensive.

Four matrices on one qubit

On one qubit the four matrices are

\[ I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. \]

They obey \(X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I\) and, for example, \(XZ=-ZX\). The \(n\)-qubit Pauli group \(\mathcal P_n\) contains tensor products of these matrices multiplied by phases \(\{+1,-1,+i,-i\}\). We abbreviate the tensors: \(Z_1Z_2\) means \(Z\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes\cdots\).

Two Pauli strings either commute or anticommute. Count the qubit positions at which their nonidentity factors anticommute.

The strings commute when that count is even and anticommute when it is odd. Hence commutation is a parity, not a continuum of possibilities.

A family that must commute, and must not contain \(-I\)

A stabilizer group \(\mathcal S\subset\mathcal P_n\) must be Abelian — its elements commute — and must not contain \(-I\). If it contained \(-I\), a stabilized state would have to satisfy both \(|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle\) and \(-|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle\), leaving only the zero vector.

Suppose \(\mathcal S\) has \(r\) independent generators \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\). “Independent” means no nonempty product of generators equals \(I\). The code projector is

\[ \Pi_{\mathcal C}=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{I+S_j}{2}. \]

Each independent commuting constraint halves the space, so

\[ \dim\mathcal C=2^{n-r}. \]

The code therefore encodes

\[ k=n-r \]

logical qubits and is denoted \([[n,k,d]]\) once its distance \(d\) is known.

The rank of a projector equals its trace. Expanding \(\Pi_{\mathcal C}\) gives \(2^{-r}\) times a sum of stabilizer elements.

Every nonidentity Pauli has trace zero, while \(\operatorname{Tr}I=2^n\). Independence ensures that only the empty product gives \(I\).

Therefore

\[ \operatorname{Tr}\Pi_{\mathcal C}=2^{-r}2^n=2^{n-r}. \]

Drop independence and you overcount the constraints. Redundant checks do not remove another qubit.

Three qubits that must agree

Take three physical qubits and two generators

\[ S_1=Z_1Z_2,\qquad S_2=Z_2Z_3. \]

They commute. The simultaneous \(+1\) condition says qubits 1 and 2 agree and qubits 2 and 3 agree. Thus

\[ \mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{|000\rangle,|111\rangle\}. \]

There are \(n=3\) physical qubits and \(r=2\) independent generators, so \(k=1\). Choose logical basis states

\[ |0_L\rangle=|000\rangle, \qquad |1_L\rangle=|111\rangle. \]

A physical bit flip \(X_1\) anticommutes with \(S_1\) and commutes with \(S_2\). Measuring the two stabilizers returns eigenvalues called the syndrome. You see only the symptoms — which checks flipped — not the secret those checks were built to ignore. Write \(+1\) as bit 0 and \(-1\) as bit 1:

error | \(S_1\) | \(S_2\) | syndrome | |

\(I\) | \(+1\) | \(+1\) | 00 | |

\(X_1\) | \(-1\) | \(+1\) | 10 | |

\(X_2\) | \(-1\) | \(-1\) | 11 |

\(X_3\) | \(+1\) | \(-1\) | 01 | |

The syndrome identifies any single \(X\) error without measuring whether the logical state is \(|0_L\rangle\) or \(|1_L\rangle\). Stabilizer measurement extracts an error relation, not the encoded amplitudes.

Logical Pauli operators must preserve the code space while acting nontrivially inside it. One choice is

\[ \overline X=X_1X_2X_3, \qquad \overline Z=Z_1. \]

The bar marks a logical operator. Both commute with \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), and \(\overline X\overline Z=-\overline Z\overline X\). Multiplying a logical operator by a stabilizer changes its physical representative but not its action on code states; for example, \(Z_1\), \(Z_2\), and \(Z_3\) are equivalent logical \(\overline Z\) representatives.

This code corrects one bit flip if the noise is restricted to \(X\) errors. As a quantum code against arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors, however, it has distance one: \(Z_1\) is already a weight-one undetectable logical operation.

Its full label is \([[3,1,1]]\) [R028]. Calling it a “single-error-correcting quantum code” without naming the noise model would mix two different jobs.

Operators that sneak past the checks

The normalizer of \(\mathcal S\) within the Pauli group is

\[ N(\mathcal S)=\{P\in\mathcal P_n:PS=SP\ \text{for every }S\in\mathcal S\}. \]

These are the Pauli strings that commute with every check. For Pauli operators, commuting with every stabilizer is equivalent to normalizing the group, up to the irrelevant global phases we usually quotient out. A normalizer element can walk past every local check without setting off an alarm.

A Pauli error \(E\) has three possibilities:

  • If \(E\) anticommutes with at least one generator, it changes a syndrome and is detectable.

  • If \(E\in\mathcal S\), it acts trivially on every code state.

  • If \(E\in N(\mathcal S)\setminus\mathcal S\), it is an undetectable nontrivial logical Pauli.

The weight \(\operatorname{wt}(E)\) is the number of qubits on which \(E\) is not \(I\). The code distance is

\[ d=\min_{E\in N(\mathcal S)\setminus\mathcal S}\operatorname{wt}(E). \]

A distance-\(d\) code detects all Pauli errors of weight less than \(d\) and corrects arbitrary errors on at most \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) qubits, assuming ideal syndrome extraction and a suitable decoder [R028]; [R029]. Degeneracy means distinct physical errors can have the same action on the code because they differ by a stabilizer.

Drop the set difference \(N(\mathcal S)\setminus\mathcal S\) and you will count stabilizers themselves as logical operators. They are in the normalizer and they act as the identity on the code.

Asking the checks, or charging energy for them

The projectors onto the \(s_j=\pm1\) eigenspaces of generator \(S_j\) are

\[ \Pi_{s_j}=\frac{I+s_jS_j}{2}. \]

In a circuit, an ancilla can acquire the parity associated with \(S_j\) and then be measured. In an analog Hamiltonian

\[ H_{\rm stab}=-\sum_jK_jS_j, \]

with energies \(K_j>0\), violating stabilizer \(S_j\) changes its term from \(-K_j\) to \(+K_j\), a cost \(2K_j\). Passive energetic enforcement and active repeated syndrome extraction are different mechanisms even though they use the same operators.

A stabilizer is an algebraic constraint. A measured stabilizer code is active quantum error correction.

A static stabilizer Hamiltonian energetically favors a code space. Topological order additionally requires locality, system-size-dependent logical operators, and the appropriate many-body phase.

One word does not perform all four jobs.

Two binary lists instead of a matrix

Phases do not affect Pauli commutation, so encode a Pauli string by two binary vectors \(\mathbf x,\mathbf z\in\mathbb F_2^n\), where \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) with arithmetic modulo two:

\[ P\longleftrightarrow(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z). \]

At qubit \(j\),

\[ (0,0)\leftrightarrow I,\quad (1,0)\leftrightarrow X,\quad (0,1)\leftrightarrow Z,\quad (1,1)\leftrightarrow Y \]

up to phase. Multiplication becomes binary vector addition. Two Paulis \(u=(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z)\) and \(v=(\mathbf x'\mid\mathbf z')\) commute exactly when their symplectic inner product vanishes:

\[ [u,v]_{\rm sp} =\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z' +\mathbf z\cdot\mathbf x' =0\pmod 2. \]

The word is just a pairing that notices when two strings anticommute. Software will compute this pairing, not stare at matrices.

Place the \(r\) generator rows into a binary check matrix

\[ H=(H_X\mid H_Z). \]

Commutation of all generator pairs is the matrix condition

\[ H_XH_Z^T+H_ZH_X^T=0\pmod 2. \]

For an error vector \(e=(\mathbf x_e\mid\mathbf z_e)\), the syndrome bits are symplectic products with the generator rows. Gaussian elimination over \(\mathbb F_2\) finds the rank \(r\), redundant checks, logical representatives, and inconsistencies. This is the practical bridge from operator notation to software.

Stars and plaquettes, written as checks

Place one qubit on each edge of a square lattice with periodic boundaries. For each vertex \(v\), define a star operator

\[ A_v=\prod_{e\ni v}X_e, \]

and for each plaquette \(p\), define

\[ B_p=\prod_{e\in\partial p}Z_e. \]

A star and plaquette either share zero edges or two edges. Each shared edge contributes one \(XZ=-ZX\), so two minus signs cancel.

Therefore every \(A_v\) commutes with every \(B_p\) [R030]. Products of all stars and of all plaquettes equal identity on a periodic connected square lattice, giving two generator dependencies.

For an \(L\times L\) torus there are \(n=2L^2\) edge qubits and \(r=2L^2-2\) independent stabilizers, hence \(k=2\). [Theory] The two logical qubits correspond to noncontractible loop operators [R030].

A shortest logical loop has weight \(L\), so the ideal periodic square-lattice code has distance \(d=L\). Boundaries and lattice defects change the counting and must be specified.

An open \(Z\) string anticommutes with the two star operators at its endpoints, producing a pair of electric syndromes. Extending the string moves an endpoint without creating a trail of violated checks.

A closed contractible string is a stabilizer; a closed noncontractible string is logical. This is the algebraic core of Chapter 16’s error-chain picture.

What a check list cannot prove

Stabilizer algebra proves exact commutation, ground-space dimension, syndromes, and logical-loop structure of the ideal toric code. It does not by itself establish that a microscopic defect Hamiltonian realizes that code.

A gadget may aim to generate \(-K_jS_j\) in a low-energy subspace. The Schrieffer–Wolff calculation must also report unwanted terms.

If a correction anticommutes with stabilizers, it can create excitations; if it lies in the normalizer but outside the stabilizer, it can split or rotate the logical manifold. Classifying corrections by commutation is more informative than listing coefficients alone.

For a proposed small patch, software should first build the binary check matrix and verify: pairwise commutation, rank, encoded-qubit count, logical representatives, and distance where tractable. Sparse exact diagonalization can then confirm the predicted ground-space dimension and excitation energies. Under non-Pauli perturbations, stabilizer labels need not remain exact; measure expectation values \(\langle S_j\rangle\), Wilson loops, and overlap with the ideal code subspace rather than forcing every state into a perfect syndrome box.

The Gottesman–Knill theorem permits efficient classical simulation of stabilizer states under Clifford gates, Pauli measurements, and classical feed-forward [R028]; [R031]. [Theory] That efficiency is a property of this restricted computational family, not evidence that the corresponding quantum material is easy to simulate under arbitrary interactions.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Including \(-I\). Then the purported code space is empty.

  • Counting listed generators instead of independent ones. Redundant checks do not remove another qubit.

  • Ignoring phases during state definition. Binary vectors suffice for commutation, but generator signs choose the \(+1\) eigenspace.

  • Calling every normalizer element logical. Stabilizers themselves are in the normalizer and act trivially.

  • Quoting distance without boundaries. A planar patch, torus, puncture, and rough/smooth edge have different logical operators.

  • Confusing code distance with an energy gap. Distance counts support size; a Hamiltonian gap has energy units.

  • Assuming a syndrome identifies a unique error. Decoding chooses among equivalence classes and noise-weighted possibilities.

Check yourself

Show that if \(-I\in\mathcal S\), then the code space is \(\{0\}\).

A stabilized state would have to satisfy both \(|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle\) and \(-|\psi\rangle=|\psi\rangle\).

Show that \(r\) independent stabilizers on \(n\) qubits encode \(k=n-r\) logical qubits.

The projector \(\Pi_{\mathcal C}\) has trace \(2^{n-r}\), which equals \(\dim\mathcal C\). Hence \(k=n-r\).

What makes a Pauli error detectable?

It anticommutes with at least one stabilizer generator and flips that syndrome bit.

Show that \(Z_1\), \(Z_2\), and \(Z_3\) are equivalent logical \(\overline Z\) representatives for the three-qubit code.

They differ by products of \(S_1=Z_1Z_2\) and \(S_2=Z_2Z_3\), so they agree on every code state.

Why is the repetition code only \([[3,1,1]]\) as a full quantum code?

A weight-one \(Z\) operator is an undetectable logical operation.

Show that toric-code stars and plaquettes commute.

Their supports overlap on an even number of edges, so the minus signs from \(XZ=-ZX\) cancel in pairs.

Appendix H — Boxes and wires

Draw three boxes in a row. Each box has a wire sticking up. Neighboring boxes share a horizontal wire.

s1 s2 s3 physical indices
| | |
[A]---a1----[A]---a2----[A]
| |
boundary boundary

joined line a1: sum over a1
open line s1: coefficient still depends on s1

That picture is the whole notation. A box is a table of numbers.

An open wire is a label you still care about. A wire joining two boxes means: add over that label until it disappears.

The diagram is not decoration. Connectivity specifies the summations.

A giant table, then smaller ones

A wavefunction for \(N\) local degrees of freedom is a table

\[ \psi_{s_1s_2\cdots s_N}, \]

with one physical index \(s_i\) per site. If each index takes \(d\) values, the table has \(d^N\) complex entries. That is already too big to store for a modest chain.

We replace the one giant table by smaller multidimensional arrays whose shared indices are summed. Those smaller arrays are tensors. The word covers a scalar (no index), a vector \(v_i\) (one index), a matrix \(M_{ij}\) (two), and a rank-\(r\) object \(T_{i_1\ldots i_r}\) (\(r\) indices) in one breath.

Here “rank” means number of indices, not matrix rank. Mathematics enjoys reusing words. Context has to do some work.

This is like factoring an integer, except the factors have several index slots and may still be difficult to find. The compression works when the state’s correlations fit through moderately sized internal indices. A tensor network is an ansatz family and a notation, not a guarantee of cheap or accurate computation.

Joined wires are sums

If \(A_{ij}\) and \(B_{jk}\) share the index \(j\), glue the \(j\) wires and add:

\[ C_{ik}=\sum_jA_{ij}B_{jk}. \]

That sum is a contraction. The shared label is gone.

Indices \(i\) and \(k\) remain free. Every term in an equation must have the same free indices.

An index should normally appear at most twice in one monomial: once means free, twice means summed. We will write sums explicitly when ambiguity is possible.

Contraction order changes computational cost but not the exact scalar or tensor obtained. For an approximate contraction, order and truncation do affect the numerical error. Drop exactness and the diagram still names a network; it no longer names a unique number.

Wires nobody measures

For a quantum state, the open wires that label basis states are physical. The extra wires we invented to factor the table have no local measurement attached.

Those internal wires are virtual indices. An auxiliary label is not something a magnet could read.

How wide is the pipe

If a virtual index takes \(\chi\) values, \(\chi\) is its bond dimension. That number is the width of the pipe between two boxes. It is not yet an error bar.

A chain of matrices

Line the boxes up along an open chain of \(N\) sites. At site \(i\), write a small matrix \(A_i^{s_i}\) of size \(\chi_{i-1}\times\chi_i\). Multiply them, and the leftover number is the amplitude of the bit string \(s_1\cdots s_N\).

That product is a matrix product state, or MPS:

\[ |\psi\rangle= \sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_N} \left(A_1^{s_1}A_2^{s_2}\cdots A_N^{s_N}\right) |s_1s_2\cdots s_N\rangle. \]

Open boundaries have \(\chi_0=\chi_N=1\), so the matrix product is a scalar. In fully indexed form,

\[ \psi_{s_1\cdots s_N} = \sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1}} (A_1)^{s_1}_{1a_1} (A_2)^{s_2}_{a_1a_2}\cdots (A_N)^{s_N}_{a_{N-1}1}. \]

The physical index \(s_i\) has dimension \(d_i\); neighboring virtual indices have dimensions \(\chi_{i-1}\) and \(\chi_i\). Site-dependent dimensions are legal and often useful.

The same state, different numbers

Insert any invertible matrix \(G\) and its inverse on a bond:

\[ A_i^{s_i}A_{i+1}^{s_{i+1}} = (A_i^{s_i}G)(G^{-1}A_{i+1}^{s_{i+1}}). \]

The state is unchanged. Tensor entries are therefore not unique physical observables.

This gauge freedom can be used to place an MPS in a canonical form. You may slide an invertible matrix through a wire.

Drop invertibility and the insertion need not be undoable; the state can change.

How much one cut can carry

Across a chosen bond, a state has a Schmidt decomposition

\[ |\psi\rangle=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{r} \lambda_\alpha |\alpha_L\rangle|\alpha_R\rangle, \]

where the Schmidt coefficients \(\lambda_\alpha\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha^2=1\), and the left and right Schmidt states are orthonormal. The Schmidt rank \(r\) cannot exceed the MPS bond dimension \(\chi\) on that cut. The bipartite von Neumann entropy is

\[ S=-\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_\alpha^2 \ln\lambda_\alpha^2 \le\ln\chi. \]

Hence bond dimension is an entanglement capacity. It is not a direct accuracy certificate: a state can require large \(\chi\) for one cut, and a poorly optimized MPS can waste its available dimension.

Two matrices that make GHZ

For \(N\) qubits, define the Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state

\[ |\mathrm{GHZ}_N\rangle =\frac{|00\cdots0\rangle+|11\cdots1\rangle}{\sqrt2}. \]

Use bond dimension \(\chi=2\) and the same two matrices at every site:

\[ A^0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Choose a left boundary row and right boundary column

\[ \ell=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1), \qquad r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}. \]

The amplitude of a bit string \(s_1\cdots s_N\) is

\[ \psi_{s_1\cdots s_N} =\ell A^{s_1}A^{s_2}\cdots A^{s_N}r. \]

If every \(s_i=0\), the product is \(A^0\) and the amplitude is \(1/\sqrt2\). If every \(s_i=1\), the product is \(A^1\) and the amplitude is \(1/\sqrt2\). If a string contains both 0 and 1, then at some point the product includes

\[ A^0A^1=A^1A^0=0, \]

so its amplitude vanishes. Hence the MPS is exactly the GHZ state.

Its norm follows without expanding \(2^N\) amplitudes:

\[ \langle\mathrm{GHZ}_N|\mathrm{GHZ}_N\rangle =\frac12+\frac12=1. \]

For distinct sites \(i\) and \(j\),

\[ \langle Z_i\rangle=0, \qquad \langle Z_iZ_j\rangle=1. \]

The connected correlation is therefore one. Across any cut, the two Schmidt coefficients are \(1/\sqrt2\), so \(S=\ln2\), consistent with \(\chi=2\).

This example also gives a warning. The GHZ state has long-range correlations yet tiny bond dimension.

Conversely, some short-range-looking problems can have difficult entanglement structures. “More correlation” and “larger bond dimension” are not interchangeable slogans.

Boxes that eat and spit

An operator has an input wire and an output wire at each site. Stack another layer of boxes on those pairs:

\[ O=\sum_{\mathbf s,\mathbf s'} W_1^{s_1s'_1}W_2^{s_2s'_2}\cdots W_N^{s_Ns'_N} |s_1\cdots s_N\rangle \langle s'_1\cdots s'_N|, \]

where each \(W_i^{s_is'_i}\) is a matrix on virtual indices. The bold symbol \(\mathbf s\) abbreviates the full sequence \((s_1,\ldots,s_N)\).

That layered product is a matrix product operator, or MPO. It is the MPS idea, now with two physical legs per site.

Expectation values such as \(\langle\psi|O|\psi\rangle\) are obtained by stacking the bra MPS, MPO, and ket MPS, then contracting all physical and virtual indices. A one-dimensional slice of the resulting double-layer network takes the virtual data on one cut to the next.

That slice is a transfer matrix. Its leading eigenvalues govern normalization and, under suitable assumptions, correlation lengths.

MPOs compactly represent sums of local Hamiltonian terms. A compact representation does not make optimization exact; it merely stops the input file from becoming the primary many-body problem.

The same idea on a grid

An MPS follows a chain. Put the same boxes on a higher-dimensional graph and you have a projected entangled pair state, or PEPS [R032]. On a square lattice, a local PEPS tensor can be written

\[ A^s_{lurd}, \]

where \(s\) is the physical index and \(l,u,r,d\) are left, up, right, and down virtual indices. Neighboring virtual indices are contracted. On a general defect graph, use one virtual index per incident edge rather than forcing square-lattice labels.

One construction begins with entangled pairs on graph edges and applies a local map from the virtual spaces meeting at a vertex to its physical space. “Projected entangled pair state” names that construction. Boundary tensors have fewer neighbors or trivial one-dimensional legs.

PEPS naturally match two-dimensional locality, but exact contraction of a generic two-dimensional PEPS is computationally hard; approximation is normally required [R033]. [Theory] This is why Chapter 40 must report both the PEPS bond dimension \(D\) and contraction controls such as an environment dimension \(\chi_{\rm env}\). Increasing only one can conceal the other’s error.

A PEPS is a representation of a state. It may represent an exact fixed-point topological state, a variational approximation to a microscopic ground state, or a completely nontopological state. Running a PEPS algorithm on ordinary hardware is a classical numerical calculation, not physical creation of anyons.

Hidden symmetries on the wires

Topologically ordered PEPS can possess symmetries acting on virtual indices. A virtual symmetry string may pass through local tensors while leaving the physical state unchanged, and noncontractible virtual strings can label distinct ground states. This framework explains ground-state degeneracy, local indistinguishability, topological entropy, and anyonic sectors for important PEPS classes [R034].

The statement needs restraint. A visually loop-like tensor network is not automatically topological.

One must identify the virtual symmetry or algebra, construct the parent Hamiltonian or otherwise establish the phase, and test robustness. Injective PEPS typically describe a unique ground state of an appropriate parent Hamiltonian; topological PEPS require generalized structures such as group or matrix-product-operator symmetries [R034].

Cutting small pieces, sweeping the rest

For an MPS, sweeping QR or singular-value decompositions can move the orthogonality center and produce left- or right-canonical tensors. At a bond, truncating the Schmidt decomposition to the largest \(\chi\) coefficients discards weight

\[ w_{\rm disc}=\sum_{\alpha>\chi}\lambda_\alpha^2. \]

This quantity is local to that truncation. A small discarded weight is useful evidence but not a global theorem that every observable is accurate.

The density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) variationally optimizes an MPS, usually one or two sites at a time [R035]. It is especially effective for one-dimensional and quasi-one-dimensional systems whose entanglement across the chosen ordering is manageable. Mapping a wide two-dimensional lattice to a snake-like chain can make the required bond dimension grow rapidly with width.

PEPS algorithms optimize tensors while approximating their environment. Infinite PEPS works directly with a repeating unit cell; finite PEPS retains boundaries.

The method must match the question. A translation-invariant infinite ansatz is a poor tool for implantation disorder unless disorder is modeled through a larger cell, sampling, or another representation.

Seven steps before you trust a number

For a defect-cluster model, proceed in layers:

  • Declare each physical index. State whether \(s_i\) labels a microscopic spin, a projected cluster pseudospin, or an edge label. Give its dimension \(d_i\).

  • Declare the graph. Every virtual bond should correspond to an intended contraction, not necessarily a physical interaction.

  • Choose an ansatz. Use exact diagonalization for the smallest full clusters; MPS/DMRG for chains and cylinders; PEPS when two-dimensional connectivity and accessible contraction controls justify it.

  • State all numerical controls. Report MPS/PEPS bond dimension, environment dimension, unit-cell size, truncation rule, optimizer tolerance, boundary condition, and initialization strategy.

  • Converge observables separately. Energy can converge before a small gap, correlation length, Wilson loop, or entanglement diagnostic. Plot each claimed observable versus the relevant controls.

  • Use competing initial states. Near first-order transitions or topological-sector barriers, one initialization can remain metastable. Compare energies and diagnostics from multiple sectors.

  • Check the effective-model handoff. Compare a small microscopic calculation with the projected Hamiltonian before applying tensor networks only to the latter.

For Chapter 40’s observables:

  • obtain the gap from excited-state methods or sector-resolved energies, not from ground-state energy convergence alone;

  • calculate entanglement entropy from Schmidt values for MPS, with geometry and logarithm base stated;

  • estimate topological entanglement entropy using a subtraction or scaling protocol whose finite-size errors are tested;

  • represent Wilson loops as MPOs or tensor insertions and examine perimeter/area behavior only over resolved sizes;

  • extract modular data only after constructing and controlling a basis of ground-state sectors.

No single diagnostic proves topological order in a small noisy patch. Agreement among spectrum, degeneracy pattern, loop observables, entanglement structure, and perturbation response is the stronger case.

Ways to get this wrong

  • Leaving indices unlabeled. A reader cannot tell physical from virtual or input from output legs.

  • Calling tensor rank matrix rank. State which meaning is intended.

  • Treating gauge-dependent entries as observables. Insertions of \(GG^{-1}\) change tensors without changing the state.

  • Reporting bond dimension without convergence. \(D=8\) is an input, not an error bar.

  • Ignoring contraction error. A large PEPS \(D\) with a small environment can be less reliable than a smaller, well-converged calculation.

  • Using DMRG outside a sensible geometry. A two-dimensional cylinder may be tractable at one width and misleading at the next.

  • Inferring topology from low variational energy. Competing phases can be close in energy while differing in nonlocal structure.

  • Forgetting the projection error. Accurate solution of an inaccurate effective Hamiltonian is still inaccurate.

  • Inferring topological order from a loop-like drawing. Virtual symmetries and physical diagnostics do the work, not the artwork.

You now have a picture, a few identities, and a checklist. The next time a paper draws boxes and wires, you can read the sums.

Check yourself

What does a joined tensor-network line mean?

Sum over the shared index.

Show that inserting \(G\) and \(G^{-1}\) on a bond leaves the MPS state unchanged.

\(A_i^{s_i}A_{i+1}^{s_{i+1}}=(A_i^{s_i}G)(G^{-1}A_{i+1}^{s_{i+1}})\) for any invertible \(G\), so every amplitude is the same.

Show that \(S\le\ln\chi\) for an MPS cut of bond dimension \(\chi\).

At most \(\chi\) Schmidt coefficients can be nonzero, and \(-\sum p_\alpha\ln p_\alpha\) on a distribution supported on at most \(\chi\) outcomes is at most \(\ln\chi\).

Show that the GHZ MPS is nonzero only for all-zero and all-one strings.

Mixed strings contain the zero products \(A^0A^1\) or \(A^1A^0\).

Does a PEPS diagram prove topological order?

No. Topological structure requires appropriate virtual symmetries and physical diagnostics.

What fails if you report \(D\) without an environment dimension?

A large PEPS bond dimension with a small environment can conceal contraction error. \(D\) is an input, not an error bar.

Global evidence table

A scoreboard. Each row is one claim, with the kind of support it actually has.

A good pair experiment is not a lattice. A circuit that plays anyons is not a crystal that contains them.

Statuses are used as written: experimentally demonstrated, experimentally partial, numerically demonstrated, theoretically established, theoretically proposed, speculative.

Claim | Status | Platform | Evidence | Reference | |

HOST-02 — Diamond is an automatic overall winner | experimentally partial | Diamond color centers | Diamond has the strongest integrated single-node optical-spin evidence in this survey, but demonstrated nanometre-scale uniform interacting arrays are absent; superiority depends on the system metric. | [R074]; [R207] | |

HOST-03 — SiC supplies controllable defect-spin nodes | experimentally demonstrated | 4H-SiC divacancies and silicon vacancies | Individual optical isolation/control and millisecond-scale coherence were demonstrated; later work combined a masked \(8\times8\) pattern with a waveguide electron–nuclear register. | [R096]; [R099] | |

HOST-04 — SiC supplies the required electron-spin interaction graph | experimentally partial | 4H-SiC | Patterned implantation and integrated registers establish several fabrication/control ingredients, but not nanometre-registered electron–electron couplings across the pattern. | [R099]; [R205] | |

HOST-05 — Sapphire matches diamond as an individual-defect platform | experimentally partial | Cr\(^{3+}\):sapphire and sapphire color centers | Ruby experiments demonstrate ensemble ODMR, long low-temperature \(T_1\), and collective cavity coupling; they do not demonstrate the selected single-ion control, \(T_2\), readout, and pair-gate stack required here. | [R088]; [R089] | |

COUP-01 — Nearby defects couple coherently | experimentally demonstrated | Diamond NV\(^-\) pairs | A selected pair about 25 nm apart showed a roughly 5 kHz dipolar interaction and room-temperature entanglement under refocused optimal control. This establishes a pair primitive only. | [R106]; [R080] | |

COUP-02 — Cavity photons mediate defect–defect interaction | experimentally demonstrated | Diamond SiV\(^-\) emitters in one nanocavity | Two spectrally tuned SiV emitters exhibited photon-mediated interaction through a shared cavity mode; uniform low-loss mediation across a lattice was not shown. | [R086] | |

COUP-03 — Nanometre-separated defect pairs can have strong, geometry-sensitive direct exchange | numerically demonstrated | Closely spaced diamond spin centers | Atomistic calculations predict exchange can dominate at very short separation and vary strongly with site and orientation; this pair-level result does not establish an extensive calibrated exchange graph. | [R107] | |

COUP-04 — Ordinary coupled defects imply topological order | theoretically established | Any pair or finite defect register | They do not: a measured two-body coupling supplies a Hamiltonian term, whereas topological order additionally requires an extended gapped phase and nonlocal sectors/observables. | [R080]; [R015] | |

ENC-01 — Encoded defect-associated qubits exist | experimentally demonstrated | NV electron–\(^{13}\)C nuclear-spin registers | Decoherence-protected nuclear-spin subspaces and repeated error correction of a three-spin encoded qubit were demonstrated around NV ancillas. The protection is DFS/active encoding, not emergent topology. | [R116]; [R117] | |

ENC-02 — A fabricated electronic-defect cluster is an isolated pseudospin | theoretically proposed | Three-color-center electronic-spin cluster | Projection onto an isolated doublet is controlled theory, and one triple-NV motif has been observed, but no cited experiment establishes a reproducible static three-center doublet with measured projected operators. | [R025]; [R243] | |

ENC-03 — Encoding a cluster establishes topological protection | theoretically established | Finite spin clusters | It does not: a locally distinguishable cluster code can suppress specified noise or leakage while lacking a thermodynamic phase, deconfined excitations, and nonlocal logical operators. | [R116]; [R015] | |

TOPO-01 — Local two-body spin models can host a non-Abelian phase | theoretically established | Kitaev honeycomb model | The exactly solved bond-dependent model has an emergent Ising-type non-Abelian phase. Its anyons are not Fibonacci anyons. | [R017] | |

TOPO-02 — Engineered analog spin models show topological-phase signatures | experimentally partial | Driven Rydberg-atom arrays | A 219-atom programmable array measured topological-spin-liquid signatures under a driven blockade Hamiltonian; finite size, drive dependence, and preparation prevent an autonomous-memory conclusion. | [R126] | |

TOPO-03 — The Levin–Wen target supports doubled-Fibonacci order | theoretically established | Ideal Fibonacci string-net Hamiltonian | The commuting-projector construction fixes branching and plaquette recoupling data and yields doubled, nonchiral Fibonacci order in the ideal many-body model. It is a target-model theorem, not a defect implementation. | [R018] | |

SIM-01 — Topologically ordered model states can be digitally prepared | experimentally demonstrated | Superconducting processors | Finite gate circuits prepared toric-code-type states and measured stabilizer, entanglement, and string observables. SIM-02 — Digital Fibonacci simulation has been demonstrated | experimentally demonstrated | Superconducting transmon processors | Experiments prepared finite doubled-Fibonacci string-net states and executed fusion/braid operations with ordinary transmons, echo, calibration, and/or error mitigation; neither experiment supplied a native Fibonacci gap. | [R138]; [R165] | |

SIM-03 — A defect processor could digitally simulate Fibonacci anyons | theoretically proposed | Gate-controlled defect-spin processor | Nothing in the algorithm requires the physical qubits themselves to be anyons, but a defect array still needs sufficient gates, connectivity, initialization, readout, and fidelity. GAD-02 — Perturbatively generated plaquette interactions exist | theoretically established | Kitaev honeycomb and code-gadget models | Fourth-order virtual processes generate plaquette operators in the anisotropic honeycomb limit, and two-body code gadgets generate toric-code/quantum-double terms. These are model constructions, not defect devices. | [R017]; [R177] | |

GAD-03 — A defect gadget realizes a Fibonacci plaquette | theoretically proposed | Defect-cluster string-net architecture | No cited mapping derives the full Fibonacci plaquette recoupling operator from available defect tensors while bounding lower-order fields, leakage, and cross-gadget paths. | [R175]; [R018] | |

GAD-04 — The gadget penalty gap is the topological gap | theoretically established | Perturbative Hamiltonian engineering | It is not: the penalty \(\Delta\) suppresses mediator leakage, while the desired coefficient \(K\) and extended model gap are parametrically smaller and must separately beat noise, disorder, and temperature. | [R175]; [R177] | |

GAP-02 — A defect-cluster topological gap has been established | speculative | Proposed defect-cluster arrays | No connected experiment or validated defect-specific many-body calculation supplies \(\Delta_{\rm topo}\); microscopic splittings, pair couplings, and gadget penalties are not substitutes. | [R142]; [R018]; [R080] | |

GAP-03 — Passive feasibility requires a gap budget | theoretically established | Static analog topological memory | The relevant phase gap must dominate thermal energy, projected disorder, decoherence broadening, finite-size splitting, and unwanted local remainders with a task-specific margin. | [R169]; [R142] | |

GAP-04 — A 2D local stabilizer Hamiltonian is automatically a self-correcting memory | theoretically established | Two-dimensional local stabilizer codes | It is not: under the no-go theorem’s assumptions the energy barrier is bounded, so a zero-temperature phase gap alone does not give indefinitely improving finite-temperature storage. | [R168]; [R169] | |

FAB-06 — The required dense usable defect lattice is manufacturable | experimentally partial | Diamond and SiC implantation platforms | Beam registration, stopping/straggle, structural conversion, charge state, optical/spin usability, coherence, bond tolerance, and compound array yield have each been demonstrated only in subsets, not jointly at the required repeated geometry. | [R190]; [R203]; [R207]; [R205] | |

KILL-01 — Cluster-spectrum gate | theoretically proposed | One candidate defect cluster | Stop or redesign if no two-dimensional low-energy manifold remains isolated from leakage across measured hyperfine, strain, and geometric distributions. KILL-04 — Thermal-activation gate | theoretically proposed | Passive analog memory | Use an activation requirement tied to system size and error budget, approximately \(E_{\rm act}/k_BT\gtrsim\ln(N_cg/\epsilon)\) for dilute seeds, then test diffusion kinetics; \(\Delta>k_BT\) alone is not a pass. | [R169]; [R168] | |

KILL-05 — Placement/disorder gate | theoretically proposed | Direct dipolar defect bonds | Because \(J\propto r^{-3}\), small radial spread gives \(\sigma_J/J\approx3\sigma_r/r\) before angular errors. KILL-06 — Preparation-window gate | theoretically proposed | Adiabatic analog preparation | Stop the stated ramp when its adiabatic lower-time bound exceeds the decoherence upper-time bound under the same schedule; making the ramp slower cannot then satisfy both. | [R247] | |

KILL-07 — Compound-yield gate | theoretically proposed | Large fixed defect arrays | Site, species, charge, coherence, addressability, and bond yields must be conditioned and propagated to patch yield; a high single-step yield does not justify monolithic scale-up without repair. | [R258]; [R190]; [R207] | |

KILL-08 — Logical-scaling gate | theoretically proposed | Encoded topological memory | Claim protection only when logical error or lifetime improves with size at fixed physical conditions and frozen analysis/decoder rules; a finite prepared-state signature is not scaling evidence. | [R141]; [R125] | |

KILL-09 — Smallest decisive mechanism test | theoretically proposed | Four encoded clusters; candidate twelve-defect plaquette | After one-cluster and two-cluster validation, four clusters are the smallest scoped device/calculation that can expose a weight-four coefficient and every lower-weight competitor; failure there kills the stated mechanism before Fibonacci scaling. | [R175]; [R243] | |

Glossary

A memory aid, not a prerequisite. If you have not met a word in a chapter yet, skip the entry. “First” means the chapter that taught it here, not the year someone coined it.

Four later distinctions that people mash together:

Ordinary defect qubit. One defect, two levels you can set, flip, and read. Not a crowd, not a particle, not a protected phase. (Chapter 3, then 7.)

Encoded defect cluster. Several defects acting as one quieter bit. Still a local gadget. (Chapter 11.)

Digital anyon simulation. A computer, or a gate machine, playing the part of an anyon model. Good theatre is not a material. (Chapter 20.)

Emergent topological phase. The crystal’s own energy landscape contains the strange particles. A pretty prepared state is not enough. (Chapters 16 and 21.)

A

Abelian anyon. An anyon whose exchange acts on a state by multiplication by a phase.

Successive exchanges therefore commute within the relevant sector. Toric-code \(e\) and \(m\) excitations are standard examples.

(First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids.”)

Active quantum error correction. Protection based on repeated extraction of error information and a recovery action. It differs from passive energetic suppression by a Hamiltonian, although a device may use both. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

Adjoint (\(A^\dagger\)). The conjugate transpose of a matrix or linear operator. An operator satisfying \(A=A^\dagger\) is Hermitian. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Amplitude. A complex number associated with a possible quantum outcome or component of a state. Probabilities come from squared magnitudes and can depend on interference between amplitudes. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Analog Hamiltonian engineering. Arranging physical couplings so that the device itself evolves under a target Hamiltonian, either statically or in a controlled driven regime.

Unlike digital simulation, the target interaction is embodied in the device rather than compiled solely into a gate sequence. Analog engineering does not guarantee that approximations, heating, or unwanted terms are harmless.

(First: Chapter 21, “Analog Hamiltonian engineering.”)

Anyon. A quasiparticle type possible in two spatial dimensions whose exchanges obey braid statistics more general than the boson/fermion alternatives. The term describes exchange and fusion structure; it does not mean “any unusual particle” or “any state on a quantum processor.” (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids.”)

B

Band. A range of allowed electron energies formed when atomic levels spread through a periodic crystal. Band structure depends on the lattice, chemical composition, and electron interactions. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Band gap. An energy interval with no extended bulk electronic states in an idealized band description. A wide gap can help isolate defect levels, but does not by itself produce long coherence or optical addressability. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Bloch sphere. A geometric representation of the pure states of one two-level system as points on a sphere; mixed states lie inside. It is a qubit-state picture, not the same as a Bloch state in a crystal. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems.”)

Bloch state. A spatially extended single-particle state compatible with lattice periodicity, written as a plane-wave factor times a periodic function. Despite the shared name, it has no direct connection to the qubit Bloch sphere. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Born rule. The rule converting a quantum amplitude into an outcome probability. For a normalized state \(|\psi\rangle\) and projector \(P\), the corresponding probability is \(\langle\psi|P|\psi\rangle\). (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Braid. The history of exchanging particle positions in two dimensions while keeping worldlines from crossing. Braids that cannot be continuously deformed into one another can act differently on an anyonic state space. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids.”)

Braid group. The group generated by neighboring exchanges \(\sigma_i\), subject to the braid relations. A non-Abelian anyon model assigns matrices to these generators, giving a braid-group representation. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids.”)

C

Charge state. The net electron-occupation state of a defect relative to a chosen neutral reference, indicated by labels such as NV\(^-\) or NV\(^0\). Different charge states can have entirely different spin and optical properties. (First: Chapter 7, “Diamond color centers.”)

Chirality. A handedness of propagation or topological response. A chiral topological phase is not generally equivalent to the nonchiral doubled theory formed by pairing it with its time reverse. (First: Chapter 19, “Doubled versus chiral Fibonacci.”)

Coherence. Preservation of phase relationships that allow quantum interference. Coherence is quantified by experiment-specific times and is not synonymous with population lifetime, fidelity, or topological protection. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems”; measured in Chapter 4.)

Color center. A localized electronic defect complex in a wide-bandgap crystal that produces characteristic optical absorption or emission. Some color centers also carry useful spins; the optical name alone guarantees neither a qubit nor a scalable array. (First: Chapter 7, “Diamond color centers.”)

Commuting-projector Hamiltonian. A Hamiltonian written as a sum of mutually commuting local projector-like terms. Such models can be exactly solvable and expose topological structure, but their microscopic realization may require interactions not naturally available in hardware. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

Correlation length (\(\xi\)). A length scale over which local connected correlations appreciably decay in a gapped phase. Finite devices must be large compared with relevant correlation lengths before asymptotic topological arguments become reliable. (First: Chapter 21, “Analog Hamiltonian engineering.”)

Crystal field. The electrostatic and covalent environment produced by neighboring atoms, which splits otherwise degenerate electronic orbitals according to local symmetry. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Crystal lattice. The periodic arrangement used to describe an ideal crystal. It provides sites, directions, and symmetries; a real sample also contains boundaries, vibrations, disorder, and defects. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Crosstalk. An unintended response of non-target qubits or couplings during control or readout. In a dense array it can create correlated errors even when each isolated control operation looks accurate. (First: Chapter 35, “Addressing dense arrays.”)

D

Decoherence. Loss of observable phase coherence when a system becomes correlated with uncontrolled degrees of freedom or suffers random evolution. It can turn a pure state into a mixed reduced state without requiring simple energy relaxation. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems.”)

Decoherence-free subspace (DFS). A subspace on which a specified dominant noise interaction acts identically, so relative quantum information is unaffected by that noise. The protection is model-dependent and is not topological order. (First: Chapter 11, “Defect clusters as encoded qubits.”)

Density operator (density matrix, \(\rho\)). A positive, unit-trace operator describing either a pure state or a statistical/marginal mixed state. It is the appropriate state description when classical uncertainty or entanglement with an unobserved environment matters. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems.”)

Defect. A departure from the periodic structure or composition of a crystal.

Point defects include vacancies, substitutions, interstitials, and complexes; extended defects include dislocations and stacking faults. A structural defect is not automatically an optically active spin or a qubit.

(First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states”; taxonomy in Chapter 6.)

Defect cluster. A deliberately selected group of nearby, interacting defects treated as one subsystem. “Cluster” says how microscopic constituents are grouped; only a demonstrated isolated low-energy subspace justifies replacing it by an encoded pseudospin. (First: Chapter 11, “Defect clusters as encoded qubits.”)

Digital quantum simulation. Representation of a target evolution by gates on programmable qubits, usually after discretization and compilation. Correctly reproducing target observables can validate the simulation without turning the hardware into the simulated material phase. (First: Chapter 20, “Digital simulation.”)

Dipolar interaction. Coupling between magnetic dipole moments, scaling as \(1/r^3\) and depending on their orientation relative to the displacement vector. Its long reach is useful, while its anisotropy and unwanted couplings complicate lattice design. (First: Chapter 10, “Defect–defect coupling.”)

Dislocation. An extended line defect characterized by a mismatch in lattice registry. It can generate strain and electronic states over distances much larger than a point defect. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Disorder. Spatial variation of on-site energies, couplings, fields, positions, or other parameters away from an intended model. Disorder can close a gap, localize excitations, broaden transitions, or occasionally stabilize a regime; its effect must be calculated rather than guessed. (First: Chapter 21, “Analog Hamiltonian engineering”; budgeted in Chapter 29.)

Doubled Fibonacci order. A nonchiral topological order that combines Fibonacci topological data with its time-reversed partner, as arises naturally in a corresponding Levin–Wen string-net construction. It is related to, but not synonymous with, a chiral Fibonacci phase. (First: Chapter 18, “Levin–Wen string nets”; distinction developed in Chapter 19.)

E

Effective Hamiltonian. A Hamiltonian for selected low-energy degrees of freedom after higher-energy states have been projected out or treated perturbatively. Its validity depends on scale separation and on the size of omitted corrections. (First: Chapter 11, “Defect clusters as encoded qubits”; derived systematically in Chapter 22.)

Eigenstate and eigenvalue. A state \(|a\rangle\) satisfying \(A|a\rangle=a|a\rangle\). For an observable, \(a\) is a possible measurement outcome; for a Hamiltonian, it is an energy. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Emergence. The appearance of collective low-energy degrees of freedom or laws not identifiable with a single microscopic constituent. In this book, an emergent anyon must be an excitation sector of a many-body phase, not merely a relabelled hardware qubit. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids”; Hamiltonian example in Chapter 17.)

Encoded qubit. A two-dimensional information-bearing subspace embedded in a larger Hilbert space, often across several physical constituents. Encoding may suppress a specified noise or leakage process, but is not automatically error correction or topology. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems”; cluster construction in Chapter 11.)

Entanglement. A property of a composite quantum state that cannot be written as a product state, or as an appropriate classical mixture when mixed-state distinctions matter. Correlation alone is not sufficient evidence of entanglement. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems.”)

Exchange interaction. A short-range spin coupling arising from quantum indistinguishability and overlap of electronic wavefunctions. Unlike magnetic dipolar coupling, its magnitude often changes exponentially with atomic arrangement and is highly sensitive to placement and chemistry. (First: Chapter 10, “Defect–defect coupling.”)

F

\(F\)-move (recoupling move). A unitary change of basis between different orders of fusing the same anyons, such as \((a\times b)\times c\) and \(a\times(b\times c)\). It does not physically exchange anyons. (First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Fidelity. A quantitative overlap or success measure comparing an actual state, gate, or readout with a target. State, process, average-gate, and readout fidelities are different quantities and require their definitions and conditions. (First: Chapter 4, “Stability, coherence, and fidelity.”)

Fibonacci anyon. The nontrivial topological charge \(\tau\) in the Fibonacci theory, obeying \(\tau\times\tau=1+\tau\).

Its fusion spaces grow with Fibonacci counting, and braiding supports a computationally universal gate set under standard encodings and assumptions. A Fibonacci-like circuit signature is not by itself a genuine Fibonacci quasiparticle.

(First: Chapter 15, “Fibonacci theory.”)

Finite-size splitting. A small energy difference between states that become exactly degenerate only in an infinite or ideal topological system, often caused by virtual quasiparticle tunnelling across a finite sample. Small splitting is a scale-dependent protection feature, not exact degeneracy in a device. (First: Chapter 21, “Analog Hamiltonian engineering.”)

Fusion category. Mathematical data describing particle types, allowed fusion channels, associativity changes, and consistency relations. Additional braiding and nondegeneracy data are needed for the full structures used in topological quantum computation. (First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Fusion channel. A possible total topological charge resulting when specified anyons combine. Multiple channels create a fusion space in which quantum information may be encoded. (First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Fusion rule. A rule \(a\times b=\sum_c N_{ab}^{c}c\) listing which total charges \(c\) can result from combining charges \(a\) and \(b\), with multiplicities \(N_{ab}^{c}\). It specifies possibilities, not the complete braid theory. (First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Fusion space. The vector space of consistent fusion histories for a collection of anyons with fixed total charge.

Non-Abelian braids act as matrices on this space. A digitally encoded fusion space remains a simulator state space unless it comes from intrinsic quasiparticles.

(First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids”; formalized in Chapter 14.)

G–H

Gap. An energy separation between designated sectors. This book distinguishes a crystal band gap, a defect-level splitting, a cluster leakage gap, and a many-body topological gap; one cannot substitute for another. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states”; cluster use in Chapter 11 and topological use in Chapter 16.)

Genuine Fibonacci anyon. An intrinsic emergent quasiparticle whose fusion and braiding data realize the stated Fibonacci theory, rather than a hardware qubit programmed to reproduce those data. A claim must also say whether the host phase is chiral Fibonacci, doubled Fibonacci, or another explicitly defined theory; “Fibonacci-like” is not a substitute. (First: Chapter 15, “Fibonacci theory”; phase distinction in Chapter 19.)

Ground-state degeneracy. The existence of more than one lowest-energy state. In topological order, degeneracy and its dependence on spatial topology are nonlocal features; an accidental local doublet is not equivalent. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

Hamiltonian (\(H\)). The operator specifying a closed system’s energies and generating its unitary time evolution. A proposed hardware Hamiltonian must include both intended terms and corrections available in the real platform. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations”; physical defect form in Chapter 26.)

Hermitian operator. An operator equal to its adjoint. Its eigenvalues are real, which makes Hermitian operators suitable for representing observables such as energy. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Hilbert space (\(\mathcal H\)). A complex inner-product vector space of quantum states. Its dimension counts independent state amplitudes, not necessarily particles or physical sites. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Homotopy. Classification by continuous deformation without cutting, crossing a forbidden region, or violating stated boundary conditions. It supplies the language behind winding and braids but is not itself quantum topological order. (First: Chapter 12, “Topology for non-mathematicians.”)

Hyperfine interaction. Coupling between electronic and nuclear magnetic moments. It can provide useful nuclear memories or resolved control, and can also create dephasing and spectral complexity. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

I–L

Initialization. Preparation of a qubit or many-body system in a known state or sector. High-fidelity single-qubit initialization does not imply successful preparation of a topologically ordered ground state. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems.”)

Interaction graph. A graph whose vertices are degrees of freedom and whose edges mark available couplings, often with type, strength, and direction. Geometric proximity does not automatically create the graph required by a target Hamiltonian. (First: Chapter 10, “Defect–defect coupling.”)

Interstitial. An atom occupying a site between the regular lattice sites. It is a point defect and may be mobile or form a complex with other defects. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Ket (\(|\psi\rangle\)). Notation for a vector in Hilbert space. A bra \(\langle\psi|\) is its adjoint, and \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) is an inner product. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Leakage. Evolution out of the subspace chosen to represent a qubit or encoded degree of freedom. A cluster’s energy separation from unwanted states suppresses but does not eliminate leakage under strong, noisy, or resonant control. (First: Chapter 4, “Stability, coherence, and fidelity”; cluster leakage in Chapter 11.)

Locality. The restriction that Hamiltonian terms or operations act on nearby or few-body degrees of freedom. Topological stability statements are normally claims against sufficiently weak local perturbations, not arbitrary global errors. (First: Chapter 12, “Topology for non-mathematicians”; many-body use in Chapter 16.)

Localized state. A state whose spatial weight is concentrated near a defect or region rather than extended across the crystal. Localization can isolate a degree of freedom but may reduce controllable coupling to its neighbors. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Logical qubit. A two-dimensional information-bearing degree of freedom encoded within a larger physical system. It may be an ordinary error-correcting-code qubit, a cluster pseudospin, or a nonlocal topological encoding; the adjective “logical” alone does not specify protection. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems.”)

Low-energy doublet. Two cluster eigenstates selected as an effective qubit and separated from other states by a leakage gap.

Their usefulness also requires controllable projected operators, preparation, and readout. A doublet is not an anyon.

(First: Chapter 11, “Defect clusters as encoded qubits.”)

M–N

Majorana mode. An emergent degree of freedom represented by an operator equal to its own adjoint; in topological settings, spatially separated Majorana zero modes can encode nonlocal information. Majorana/Ising braiding is not computationally universal by braiding alone and is not Fibonacci order. (First: Chapter 17, “Kitaev honeycomb model.”)

Many-body gap. The energy between a many-body ground-state sector and the relevant excitations in a specified size and limit. It controls thermal and perturbative scales but does not alone prove topological order. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code”; feasibility conditions in Chapter 21.)

Measurement (readout). An operation producing a classical outcome with probabilities determined by the quantum state.

Readout fidelity, back-action, locality, and which operator is measured all matter. A local spin signal is not automatically a measurement of topological charge.

(First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations”; qubit implementation in Chapter 3.)

Mixed state. A state described by a density operator with more than one nonzero eigenvalue. It can arise from classical uncertainty or from tracing out part of an entangled state. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems.”)

Non-Abelian anyon. An anyon for which exchanges act by generally noncommuting matrices on a multidimensional fusion space. “Non-Abelian” does not mean Fibonacci specifically; Ising anyons are a different non-Abelian theory. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids.”)

Noise. Uncontrolled fluctuations or couplings that alter states, gates, measurements, or Hamiltonian parameters. The relevant description includes spectrum, spatial correlation, temporal correlation, and coupling operator—not only a single coherence time. (First: Chapter 4, “Stability, coherence, and fidelity”; defect-array model in Chapter 30.)

NV center. A nitrogen-vacancy complex in diamond, commonly discussed in neutral and negatively charged forms. The useful spin, optical, and coherence properties depend on charge state, isotope environment, strain, temperature, and device geometry. (First: Chapter 7, “Diamond color centers.”)

O–P

Operator. A linear map acting on quantum states. Operators can represent observables, transformations, projectors, or parts of a Hamiltonian; their meaning depends on the space on which they act. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Partial trace. The operation that removes an unobserved subsystem from a composite density operator, producing the reduced state of the remaining subsystem. It is how local mixed states arise from globally entangled pure states. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems.”)

Passive protection. Suppression arising from the system’s spectrum, locality, or Hamiltonian without repeated syndrome measurement and recovery. It is conditional on temperature, system size, noise channels, and timescale, and does not suppress every error. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code”; limitations in Chapters 21 and 31.)

Pauli operators. The matrices \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) that generate rotations and describe observables for a two-level system. A physical-spin Pauli and an encoded-pseudospin Pauli act on different Hilbert spaces even if the same symbols are used locally. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems.”)

Perturbative gadget. A construction using auxiliary states and weak couplings so that virtual processes generate a desired effective interaction, often of higher body order. The target term is accompanied by higher-order errors and is usually smaller than the microscopic scales. (First: Chapter 23, “Perturbative gadgets.”)

Phonon. A quantized collective vibration of a crystal lattice. Phonons can relax or dephase defect spins, broaden optical transitions, and sometimes mediate useful interactions. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Physical qubit. A directly controlled hardware two-level subsystem. Several physical qubits may encode one logical qubit; no fixed ratio or protection mechanism follows from the term. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems.”)

Projector (\(P\)). An operator satisfying \(P^2=P\) that selects a subspace. In cluster engineering, \(P\) selects the low-energy encoded sector; projecting an operator gives its action within that approximation. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations”; cluster use in Chapter 11.)

Pseudospin. An effective two-level degree of freedom represented with spin-1/2 mathematics even when its states are collective combinations of several microscopic spins or orbitals. It is a modelling object, not necessarily a literal electron spin. (First: Chapter 11, “Defect clusters as encoded qubits.”)

Q–R

Quantum dimension (\(d_a\)). A measure of the asymptotic growth of the fusion space when many anyons of type \(a\) are added.

It need not be an integer; for Fibonacci \(\tau\), it is the golden ratio. It is not the ordinary dimension of a single local qubit.

(First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Quasiparticle. A collective excitation that behaves as a particle within an effective many-body description. An emergent anyon is a quasiparticle with topological exchange and fusion properties; a bare defect spin is not called an anyon merely because it is localized. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids.”)

Qubit. A controllable quantum degree of freedom with a chosen two-dimensional state space. A usable qubit requires a lifecycle—initialization, coherent operations, and readout—not just two spectral levels. (First: Chapter 3, “Qubits as controllable systems.”)

\(R\)-move. The unitary associated with exchanging two anyons in a specified fusion channel. Together with fusion data and \(F\)-moves, consistent \(R\)-moves determine braid actions. (First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Relaxation time (\(T_1\)). The characteristic time for population to return toward equilibrium, commonly after an excitation. A long \(T_1\) does not imply a long phase-coherence time \(T_2\). (First: Chapter 4, “Stability, coherence, and fidelity.”)

S

Schrieffer–Wolff transformation. A perturbative unitary block-diagonalization used to derive a low-energy Hamiltonian by eliminating virtual transitions between selected and high-energy sectors. It is controlled only when couplings are small relative to appropriate energy denominators. (First: Chapter 22, “Schrieffer–Wolff transformation.”)

Simulated or emulated anyon. A state, defect, code excitation, or gate action intentionally mapped to an anyon model on hardware that may possess no intrinsic anyonic phase. Such a simulation can correctly demonstrate model operations while providing active rather than passive protection. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids”; experimental treatment in Chapter 20.)

Spin. An intrinsic quantum angular momentum. In a solid, the effective spin label may include orbital character and crystal-field effects; it must be tied to specified levels and a Hamiltonian. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations”; defect setting in Chapter 6.)

Spin–orbit coupling. Interaction between spin and orbital motion, strongly shaped by crystal symmetry. It can enable optical selection and large splittings while also opening phonon-mediated relaxation pathways. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Stabilizer. An operator whose specified eigenvalue defines a code or model subspace; a commuting set of stabilizers jointly constrains allowed states. Measuring stabilizers actively is different from realizing the same operators as energetic Hamiltonian terms. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

Stacking fault. An extended planar defect in which the normal sequence of crystal layers is interrupted. It can alter local electronic structure and strain over a broad region. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Strain. Spatial deformation of a crystal. Through strain coupling it shifts or mixes defect levels and can act as noise, inhomogeneity, a tuning control, or a mediated-interaction channel. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

String operator. A product of local operators along a path. In a topologically ordered model, an open string can create excitations at its endpoints and a noncontractible closed string can act logically. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

String-net. A fluctuating network of labelled strings subject to local branching and recoupling rules. In a Levin–Wen Hamiltonian, string-net condensation realizes doubled topological orders; a drawn network alone is not evidence of such a phase. (First: Chapter 18, “Levin–Wen string nets.”)

Substitutional defect. A lattice site occupied by a different atomic species from the ideal host atom. Its electronic behavior depends on chemistry, local symmetry, and charge compensation. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Superexchange. An effective interaction between localized spins mediated virtually through intermediate orbitals or sites. Its sign and magnitude arise from microscopic hopping and energy costs, not simply distance. (First: Chapter 10, “Defect–defect coupling”; perturbative derivation in Chapter 22.)

Superposition. A linear combination of quantum states. It produces new physical predictions because complex amplitudes can interfere; it is not merely ignorance about which classical state is present. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Symmetry-protected subspace. A subspace insulated from selected transitions because a symmetry forbids or suppresses the relevant matrix elements. Breaking the symmetry can remove the protection, and the mechanism is distinct from intrinsic topological order. (First: Chapter 11, “Defect clusters as encoded qubits.”)

T

\(T_2\) and \(T_2^*\). \(T_2\) characterizes homogeneous phase coherence under a specified refocusing convention; \(T_2^*\) commonly describes free-induction decay including quasi-static inhomogeneity. Pulse sequence and fitting model must accompany either number. (First: Chapter 4, “Stability, coherence, and fidelity.”)

Tensor product (\(\otimes\)). The mathematical operation combining quantum state spaces: two qubits have \(\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2\), not a simple choice between the two spaces. Tensor products allow entangled states. (First: Chapter 2, “Composite quantum systems.”)

Topological charge. A label for an anyon sector specifying how an excitation behaves under fusion and braiding. It is conserved according to fusion rules and need not equal electric charge. (First: Chapter 14, “Fusion categories without the fog.”)

Topological error protection. Operational suppression of specified logical errors using nonlocal encoding, a gap, braid structure, active correction, or a combination. It is never a claim of zero error and must name temperature, size, noise, leakage, preparation, and readout assumptions. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code”; limits in Chapter 31.)

Topological invariant. A quantity unchanged under an allowed class of continuous deformations.

A winding number is a classical example. Possessing a classical topological invariant does not imply quantum topological order.

(First: Chapter 12, “Topology for non-mathematicians.”)

Topological order. Intrinsic many-body order characterized by nonlocal structure such as long-range entanglement, topology-dependent ground-state sectors, and anyonic excitations in standard two-dimensional gapped examples. It is not ordinary symmetry breaking, an encoded local cluster, or a digitally prepared wavefunction by itself. (First: Chapter 12, “Topology for non-mathematicians”; concrete model in Chapter 16.)

Topological phase. A phase of matter with specified topological organization of its low-energy states and excitations. In this book the unqualified phrase normally means intrinsic topological order; symmetry-protected topological phases are named explicitly when relevant. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

Topological quantum computation. Storage and processing of information in nonlocal topological degrees of freedom, often using creation, fusion, measurement, and braiding of anyons. Its gate set and protection depend on the anyon theory and physical implementation. (First: Chapter 13, “Anyons and braids”; Fibonacci case in Chapter 15.)

Topology. The study of properties unchanged by continuous deformation under stated rules. In this manuscript it provides intuition and mathematics for global sectors, but the word alone does not imply protection or a quantum phase. (First: Chapter 12, “Topology for non-mathematicians.”)

Toric code. An exactly solvable spin model with commuting star and plaquette terms, topological ground-state degeneracy, and Abelian \(e\) and \(m\) anyons. It is a benchmark for topological order, not a Fibonacci model. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code.”)

U–Z

Unit cell. A repeated building block of a crystal lattice. It contains the basis atoms needed to reconstruct the ideal periodic structure and is distinct from a defect cluster chosen for encoding. (First: Chapter 5, “Crystals, bands, and localized states.”)

Unitary evolution. Reversible quantum evolution \(|\psi(t)\rangle=U(t)|\psi(0)\rangle\) that preserves inner products and total probability for a closed system. An open subsystem generally requires a channel rather than a unitary acting on that subsystem alone. (First: Chapter 1, “Quantum mechanics foundations.”)

Vacancy. A missing atom at a normally occupied lattice site. A vacancy may be mobile, charged, optically dark, or part of a useful complex; the structural label does not determine its qubit properties. (First: Chapter 6, “The defect zoo and its interactions.”)

Virtual excitation. An intermediate high-energy state appearing in perturbation theory without being populated as a long-lived real excitation. Virtual paths can generate superexchange or gadget terms, with strengths suppressed by energy denominators. (First: Chapter 22, “Schrieffer–Wolff transformation.”)

Wilson loop. A closed nonlocal operator used to diagnose or manipulate gauge and topological sectors. A measured local stabilizer is not the same observable as a noncontractible Wilson loop. (First: Chapter 16, “Toric code”; measurement in Chapter 36.)

Winding number. An integer counting how many times a directed loop wraps around a puncture under appropriate conditions. It is robust to allowed deformations but is not by itself a quantum-protected qubit. (First: Chapter 12, “Topology for non-mathematicians.”)

Zero-field splitting. A splitting of spin sublevels present without an applied magnetic field, commonly produced by internal spin–spin and crystal-field-related anisotropy. Its value is a spectral parameter, not a coherence time. (First: Chapter 7, “Diamond color centers.”)

The experiment addresses yield and three-dimensional placement, but optical aberrations, residual damage, and nanometer-scale pair geometry remain separate constraints.

It is among the strongest fabrication results for combining registration and coherence, though the tolerances needed for uniform short-range exchange remain more demanding.

[R243] M. Haruyama et al., “Triple nitrogen-vacancy centre fabrication by C5N4H\(_n\) ion implantation,” Nature Communications 10, 2664 (2019).

The result is especially relevant to cluster-based proposals, but creation of a triple does not guarantee the geometry, charge state, coherence, and coupling uniformity required by a target Hamiltonian.

Experimental topological quantum computing

[R125] K. J.

Satzinger et al., “Realizing topologically ordered states on a quantum processor,” Science 374, 1237–1241 (2021). DOI: 10.1126/science.abi8378; arXiv: 2104.01180.

This superconducting-processor experiment prepared and probed a toric-code-type topologically ordered state. Because the state was digitally assembled and diagnosed on programmable hardware, it demonstrates controllable simulation rather than a naturally gapped topological material.

[R126] G. Semeghini et al., “Probing topological spin liquids on a programmable quantum simulator,” Science 374, 1242–1247 (2021).

DOI: 10.1126/science.abi8794; arXiv: 2104.04119. Semeghini and collaborators probed spin-liquid and topological signatures in a programmable Rydberg-atom array.

The work is a major quantum-simulation milestone, but its driven, measured simulator should not be conflated with passive material protection.

DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-05954-4; arXiv: 2210.10255. This experiment implemented non-Abelian braiding of graph defects on a superconducting processor.

It establishes controlled braiding transformations in a digitally engineered code space, not intrinsic non-Abelian quasiparticles in a defect crystal.

[R138] S. Xu et al., “Non-Abelian braiding of Fibonacci anyons with a superconducting processor,” Nature Physics 20, 1469–1475 (2024).

The experiment is pivotal evidence that the target algebra can be enacted, while explicitly not establishing an autonomous Fibonacci material phase.
